data.method: Counts distinct traditions for indexed motif IDs that map to canonical_motif_groups through raw_motif_group_index, group children/aliases, or normalization aliases.

canonical_motifs.label: Sacred Knowledge and Wisdom
canonical_motifs.description: The acquisition, transmission, protection, or concealment of sacred or transformative knowledge. Includes wisdom teachings, forbidden knowledge, stolen fire/knowledge, divine instruction, and the paradox of knowledge that transforms the knower.

canonical_motifs.label: Initiation and Transformative Ordeal
canonical_motifs.description: The passage from one state of being to another through ordeal, instruction, or encounter. Includes rites of passage, tests, encounters with death as teacher, and the crossing of thresholds that permanently change the initiate.

canonical_motifs.label: Death, Rebirth, and Transformation
canonical_motifs.description: The pattern of death followed by return, renewal, or transformation into a new state. Includes literal resurrection, symbolic rebirth, dying-and-rising figures, and metamorphosis through death.

canonical_motifs.label: The Hero's Journey
canonical_motifs.description: The narrative arc of departure, trial, transformation, and return. Includes the call to adventure, threshold crossing, the abyss, the boon, and the return with knowledge or power.

canonical_motifs.label: Divine Judgment and Moral Reckoning
canonical_motifs.description: The weighing, testing, or evaluation of souls, deeds, or peoples by divine authority. Includes afterlife judgment, earthly punishment for transgression, plagues as retribution, and the moral accounting that follows death.

canonical_motifs.label: World Axis and Sacred Center
canonical_motifs.description: The vertical axis connecting heaven, earth, and underworld. Manifests as world tree, sacred mountain, cosmic pillar, temple, ladder, or any structure that marks the center of the cosmos and enables communication between levels of reality.

canonical_motifs.label: Sacred Exchange and Reciprocity
canonical_motifs.description: The principle of reciprocal giving between humans and the divine, or between sacred parties. Includes gift exchange, hospitality obligations, filial duty, and the idea that sacred relationship requires mutual offering.

canonical_motifs.label: Royal Legitimacy and Sacred Kingship
canonical_motifs.description: The establishment, maintenance, or transfer of legitimate rule through divine sanction, lineage, ordeal, or sacred objects. Includes coronation, succession, regency, and the king as axis mundi figure.

canonical_motifs.label: Duality and Cosmic Opposition
canonical_motifs.description: The fundamental pairing of opposites # light/dark, order/chaos, life/death, yin/yang, good/evil # as structural principle of the cosmos. Includes Zoroastrian dualism, Daoist complementarity, and the tension between opposing forces that generates reality.

canonical_motifs.label: Shapeshifter and Transformation
canonical_motifs.description: The figure who changes form # human to animal, god to mortal, one being to another. Includes voluntary transformation, punishment-transformation, and metamorphosis as escape or transcendence.

canonical_motifs.label: Ascent and Heavenly Journey
canonical_motifs.description: The upward journey toward the divine # climbing the mountain, ascending through heavens, rising to receive revelation or divine knowledge. The complement of descent.

canonical_motifs.label: Descent and Underworld Journey
canonical_motifs.description: The journey downward into the underworld, the land of the dead, or the depths of consciousness. Includes the stripping of identity, trials below, navigation of the afterlife, and the encounter with death or darkness as a transformative passage.

mapped_motifs.label: Descent into the earth at the conclusion of a prophecy

canonical_motifs.label: Cosmic Origin and Creation
canonical_motifs.description: The emergence of the cosmos from void, water, darkness, word, or primordial substance. Includes creation by speech, creation from nothing, and the initial separation of elements.

canonical_motifs.label: Sacrifice and Offering
canonical_motifs.description: The giving up of something precious # life, status, possession, self # to the sacred. Includes burnt offerings, self-sacrifice, the scapegoat, and sacrificial death that creates or renews.

canonical_motifs.label: Flood, Fire, and Cosmic Renewal
canonical_motifs.description: The destruction of the world or the old order by water, fire, or catastrophe, followed by renewal and the establishment of a new world. Includes the flood narrative, the ark/vessel of survival, and the survivor pair who repopulate or restart.

canonical_motifs.label: Miraculous Child and Sacred Birth
canonical_motifs.description: The child born under extraordinary circumstances # virgin birth, divine parentage, threatened infancy, hidden upbringing. Includes the divine child who must be protected, the child who speaks wisdom, and the child whose birth signals a new cosmic era.

canonical_motifs.label: Culture Hero and Founder
canonical_motifs.description: The figure who brings civilization, law, fire, agriculture, or sacred knowledge to humanity. Often overlaps with trickster (Prometheus, Maui) but distinguished by the emphasis on founding or establishing human culture.

canonical_motifs.label: Sacred Twins and Sibling Pairs
canonical_motifs.description: The pair of twins or siblings # often one mortal and one divine, or one light and one dark # whose relationship drives the mythic narrative. Includes hero twins, divine siblings, and fratricidal pairs.

canonical_motifs.label: Covenant and Sacred Bond
canonical_motifs.description: A binding agreement between the human and the divine, or between sacred parties. Includes conditional and unconditional covenants, covenant renewal, and the breaking and restoration of sacred bonds.

canonical_motifs.label: Sacred Time and Ritual Cycle
canonical_motifs.description: The ordering of time through sacred rhythm # sabbath, seasonal ceremonies, jubilee, annual purification. The distinction between sacred time (cyclical, renewable, connected to origins) and profane time (linear, entropic).

canonical_motifs.label: Mystical Quest and Interior Journey
canonical_motifs.description: The spiritual seeker's journey toward union, knowledge, or liberation. Includes the Sufi path of stations, the hero's journey in its contemplative form, and quests where the seeker discovers they are what they sought.

mapped_motifs.label: sacred song as wound and medicine

canonical_motifs.label: Trickster and Boundary Crosser
canonical_motifs.description: The figure who violates boundaries, steals from the gods, deceives authority, and operates at the edges between order and chaos. Often a culture hero who brings gifts through transgression.

canonical_motifs.label: Sacred Love and Longing
canonical_motifs.description: Love as a cosmic or mystical force # the love between divine and human, the love that transcends death, the longing for return to source. Includes the Sufi divine beloved, sacred marriage, and love as the driving force of the quest.

mapped_motifs.label: Love as an affliction cured only by the beloved
Perilous path of love requiring caution

canonical_motifs.label: Serpent and Serpent Guardian
canonical_motifs.description: The serpent as guardian of sacred knowledge, threshold between worlds, or embodiment of danger-and-wisdom. Includes the serpent at the tree, the serpent at the root of the world, and the serpent as both threat and teacher.

canonical_motifs.label: Sacred Waters and Passage Through Water
canonical_motifs.description: Water as boundary, purifier, destroyer, and medium of transformation. Includes baptismal waters, parted seas, rivers of the underworld, and the primordial waters before creation.

canonical_motifs.label: Afterlife Navigation and Passage
canonical_motifs.description: The dead person's journey through the afterlife as a navigable landscape with stages, gates, guardians, and instructions. Includes knowledge of sacred names or words of power as requirements for passage.

canonical_motifs.label: Sacred Feminine and Mother Goddess
canonical_motifs.description: The divine mother, earth goddess, source-feminine, or nurturing-and-terrible goddess figure. Includes the mother who gives birth to the cosmos, the mourning mother, the goddess of fertility and death, and the sacred feminine as cosmic principle.

canonical_motifs.label: Sacred Fire and Divine Light
canonical_motifs.description: Fire as divine presence, purifying force, sacrificial medium, or cosmic principle. Includes the burning bush, Agni, sacred hearth fires, and fire as the element that mediates between human and divine.

canonical_motifs.label: Divine Warrior and Sacred Combat
canonical_motifs.description: The god or hero who fights cosmic battles # against chaos monsters, demons, rival gods, or the forces of darkness. Includes the warrior whose combat establishes or maintains cosmic order.

mapped_motifs.label: Vow of vengeance for a fallen king/hero

canonical_motifs.label: Lament, Mourning, and Tragic Recognition
canonical_motifs.description: The expression of grief, loss, and tragic awareness. Includes mourning songs, laments for fallen heroes, the recognition of what has been lost, and grief as a transformative force.

mapped_motifs.label: Dying hero arranges successor relationship for his bride
Mourning expressed through embracing and kissing the deceased warrior’s horse and equipment
Prolonged mourning without relief leading to physical collapse/death

canonical_motifs.label: Sacred Combat and Ritual Warfare
canonical_motifs.description: Warfare, raiding, or single combat as a sacred or ritually significant activity. Includes cattle raids as cosmic catalysts, single combat at fords, and battles that determine cosmic order.

mapped_motifs.label: violated queen as trigger of vengeance

canonical_motifs.label: Divine Intervention and Guidance
canonical_motifs.description: The direct action of gods or sacred powers in human affairs # sending plagues, parting seas, appearing in dreams, providing animal guides, or redirecting events through supernatural means.

canonical_motifs.label: Sacred Vessel and Container
canonical_motifs.description: The sacred container # cauldron, grail, ark, pot, sealed jar # that holds life, death, wisdom, or transformative power. Includes vessels of resurrection, vessels of preservation, and vessels that must not be opened.

canonical_motifs.label: Sacred Treasures and Power Objects
canonical_motifs.description: Objects of divine origin or power # swords, spears, stones, rings, feathers, sandals # that confer authority, protection, or sacred ability on their bearer.

canonical_motifs.label: Otherworld and Enchanted Realm
canonical_motifs.description: The other world # fairyland, the Country of the Young, the enchanted island, the hidden realm # that exists alongside or beneath ordinary reality. Distinguished from the underworld of the dead by its quality of timelessness, beauty, or enchantment.

canonical_motifs.label: Pride, Hubris, and Downfall
canonical_motifs.description: The pattern of overreaching pride followed by destruction or humbling. Includes failed towers, punished transgressors, kings brought low, and the moral that power without wisdom or humility leads to ruin.

mapped_motifs.label: Endurance of a record contrasted with daily transience
Pride as brief rule followed by downfall/dissolution

canonical_motifs.label: Sacred Law and Social Order
canonical_motifs.description: The divine origin of law, ethical codes, and social obligations. Includes dietary laws, purity codes, social care mandates, and the idea that the moral order reflects the cosmic order.

canonical_motifs.label: Storytelling and Narrative as Sacred Power
canonical_motifs.description: The act of telling stories as a means of survival, transmission of wisdom, or sacred power. Includes frame narratives, stories within stories, and oral transmission as a technology of cultural memory.

canonical_motifs.label: Beauty Paired with Pain and Paradox
canonical_motifs.description: The aesthetic and spiritual insight that beauty and suffering, sweetness and danger, are inseparable. The rose and the thorn. The wisdom that comes through wounding.

mapped_motifs.label: Beauty paired with pain (sweetness with sting)

canonical_motifs.label: Death Attributed to Fate or Destiny
canonical_motifs.description: Death understood as fated, destined, or determined by forces beyond human control. The warrior who cannot escape the death assigned to them. Includes the Norse concept of wyrd, Greek moira, and Islamic qadar.

mapped_motifs.label: Death attributed to non-human agency and to fate/destiny

canonical_motifs.label: Divine Race and Arrival of the Gods
canonical_motifs.description: A race or people of divine or semi-divine origin who arrive, conquer, or settle and bring sacred knowledge, treasures, or civilization. Includes the Tuatha De Danann, the Anunnaki, and the devas.

canonical_motifs.label: Dream, Vision, and Altered Perception
canonical_motifs.description: Dreams, visions, and altered states as sources of sacred knowledge, prophecy, or revelation. Includes prophetic dreams, the dream-reality boundary, opened perception, and the idea that ordinary consciousness conceals a deeper reality.

mapped_motifs.label: Dream imagery of animals foreshadowing or associated with violent consumption

canonical_motifs.label: Primordial Sacrifice and Dismemberment
canonical_motifs.description: The cosmos created through the death, sacrifice, or dismemberment of a primordial being whose body becomes the world.

canonical_motifs.label: Sacred Craft and Divinely Aided Construction
canonical_motifs.description: Building, crafting, or constructing as a sacred act # the bridge built with divine aid, the temple constructed by the gods, the weapon forged with cosmic fire.

canonical_motifs.label: Supreme Ruler and Cosmic Sovereignty
canonical_motifs.description: A supreme ruler figure who descends from above or emerges to rule all lands. Includes the world-emperor, the universal monarch, and the cosmic king.

mapped_motifs.label: Supreme ruler descends/appears from above to rule all lands

canonical_motifs.label: Threshold Guardian
canonical_motifs.description: The figure who guards the boundary between worlds, states, or levels of reality. Must be confronted, appeased, or outwitted before passage is possible.

canonical_motifs.label: Theophany and Divine Manifestation
canonical_motifs.description: The direct manifestation or revelation of the divine to a human witness. Includes cosmic visions, burning bushes, universal forms, and overwhelming encounters with sacred presence.

canonical_motifs.label: Textual and Scholarly Artifacts
canonical_motifs.description: Not a symbolic motif. These are observations about the text itself # its transmission, reconstruction, manuscript tradition, or editorial history. Preserved for provenance but excluded from motif queries.

mapped_motifs.label: Oral transmission producing interpolated and fragmentary poetic tradition
Textual reconstruction through emendation and documentation of variants

data.title: Cultural Timeline Index
notes: Dates are approximate scholarly working ranges for textual composition, redaction, compilation, or earliest recoverable written form.
Negative years represent approximate BCE dates as sortable keys.
Ranges are intentionally broad where oral transmission, layered composition, or later manuscript preservation complicates dating.

entries.title: The Book of the Dead
entries.timeline_label: New Kingdom Egyptian funerary spell tradition
entries.uncertainty: The Book of the Dead is a compilation of funerary spells with older antecedents and later copies; this range marks the New Kingdom period in which the collection became prominent, not a single date of authorship.

entries.title: An Old Babylonian Version of the Gilgamesh Epic
entries.uncertainty: The ingested text represents Old Babylonian Gilgamesh material rather than the later Standard Babylonian epic; dating refers to the approximate period of the Old Babylonian witnesses and tradition.

entries.title: The Upanishads
entries.timeline_label: Vedic and early philosophical Sanskrit tradition
entries.uncertainty: Upanishadic material is layered and internally diverse; this broad range is an orientation for major early/prose and verse Upanishadic strata, not a single date for the translated anthology.

entries.title: The Iliad
entries.uncertainty: The date range is a working orientation for the Homeric epic tradition; the ingested Pope translation is a much later public-domain English rendering.

entries.title: Pentateuch
entries.timeline_label: Ancient Israelite Torah composition and redaction
entries.uncertainty: The Pentateuch is treated here as layered literature with debated composition and redaction histories; the range is broad and should not be read as dating every passage equally.

entries.title: The Analects of Confucius
entries.uncertainty: The Analects preserve sayings and traditions associated with Confucius and disciples through a layered textual history; the range marks a broad Warring States working window for formation.

entries.title: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
entries.uncertainty: The Tao Teh King has a debated compositional history; this range marks a cautious Warring States-era working window for the received textual tradition.

entries.title: Dhammapada, a Collection of Verses
entries.uncertainty: Individual verses may be older than their canonical arrangement; this range is a working estimate for early Buddhist/Pali canonical formation rather than a precise date for every verse.

entries.title: The Song Celestial; Or, Bhagavad-Gita
entries.uncertainty: The Bhagavad-Gita is embedded in the Mahabharata and is usually dated within a broad late BCE to early CE window; this entry does not resolve internal layering or redaction questions.

entries.title: The Koran (Al-Qur'an)
entries.uncertainty: This range follows the traditional period of Muhammad's revelations; the ingested Rodwell text is a public-domain English translation organized in Rodwell's order rather than a critical Arabic edition.

entries.title: Gods and Fighting Men
entries.timeline_label: Medieval Irish mythic and heroic material
entries.uncertainty: Lady Gregory's book is a modern public-domain literary arrangement of older Irish material; use the range as a source-tradition anchor, not the date of the English retelling.

entries.title: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
entries.timeline_label: Archaic Greek poetic and hymnic tradition
entries.uncertainty: The ingested anthology combines Hesiodic poems, Homeric Hymns, and related material with different dates; the range covers the approximate span of these archaic/classical poetic witnesses rather than one work.

entries.title: The Mabinogion
entries.timeline_label: Medieval Welsh narrative and romance tradition
entries.uncertainty: The tales have older oral and literary histories, while surviving manuscripts and translation layers are later; the range is a broad medieval orientation only.

entries.title: The Poetic Edda
entries.timeline_label: Old Norse mythological and heroic poetic tradition
entries.uncertainty: Many Eddic poems likely preserve older oral and poetic material, but the main medieval manuscript witness is much later; this range separates broad traditional formation from exact manuscript dating only imperfectly.

entries.title: The Popol Vuh
entries.timeline_label: Kiche Maya mythic and heroic tradition
entries.uncertainty: The Popol Vuh preserves pre-colonial mythic material through colonial-era textual transmission and later translation; this entry dates the textual witness layer rather than the origin of all narratives.

entries.title: Kalevala: The Epic Poem of Finland
entries.uncertainty: Kalevala is a 19th-century literary compilation from older oral-poetic traditions; motif comparison should distinguish compilation date from traditional age and regional performance contexts.

occurrences.basis: Keeping and doing covenant words is presented as the instructed response to remembered events.

occurrences.source_title: Deuteronomy
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom
occurrences.basis: The passage emphasizes hearing, learning, teaching children, and preserving law and song.

evidence.quote_or_summary: You shall read this law before all Israel in their hearing... this song will testify before them as a witness.

occurrences.passage_locator: Deuteronomy 34:1-12
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom
occurrences.basis: Joshua is explicitly described as full of the spirit of wisdom after Moses lays hands on him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Moses the servant of Yahweh died there in the land of Moab... Joshua the son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom.

occurrences.source_title: Deuteronomy
occurrences.passage_locator: Deuteronomy 4:9-14

You yourself must make an effort. The Tathagatas (Buddhas) are only preachers. The thoughtful who enter the way are freed from the bondage of Mara.

occurrences.basis: The passage names “Sæmund the Wise” and narrates extended scholarly inquiry into authorship, sources, and meaning of “Edda.”

evidence.locator: lines 241-332 (opening paragraphs of 'WHAT IS THE POETIC EDDA?')
evidence.quote_or_summary: States that the poems’ origins are mysterious: unknown composers, dates/places of composition, collectors, and uncertain meaning of the term “Edda.”

evidence.quote_or_summary: Reports Icelandic tradition attributing an Edda to Sæmundr the Wise; says Arngrímur Jónsson argued Snorri was responsible for the prose Edda; suggests Sæmundr might have compiled a verse Edda used as a source by Snorri.

evidence.locator: lines 241-332 (closing paragraphs on the meaning of 'Edda')
evidence.quote_or_summary: Reviews proposed meanings of “Edda,” including a link to “Poetics” and Jacob Grimm’s identification with a word in Rigsthula conjecturally meaning “great-grandmother,” while criticizing the fit of such meanings to the prose/verse works.

occurrences.source_title: The Poetic Edda
occurrences.passage_locator: THIS VOLUME IS ENDOWED IN PART BY CHARLES S. PETERSON OF CHICAGO / ACKNOWLEDGEMENT / GENERAL INTRODUCTION / WHAT IS THE POETIC EDDA?; lines 334-363
occurrences.motif_label: Renowned learning / 'the Wise' as a marker of expertise
occurrences.basis: Sæmundr is explicitly labeled “the Wise” and is described as famed for learning and as a diligent student of tradition and history.

evidence.quote_or_summary: States Eirikr Magnusson’s proposed solution that “Edda” is the genitive of “Oddi”; describes Oddi as a settlement in southwest Iceland, home of Snorri for many years and traditionally home of Sæmundr the Wise; argues that naming a work “The Book of Oddi” would be reasonable and that such naming was common.

Says it is an open question whether Sæmundr had anything to do with compiling the Poetic Edda and that the 17th-century attribution to him is negligible; describes him as learned and a student of tradition/history, notes no surviving works, education in Paris, and probable use of Latin rather than the vernacular.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation

occurrences.motif_label: Lowly safety preferred to valuable vulnerability
occurrences.basis: The bramble argues that the fir-tree's usefulness exposes it to cutting, and the explicit moral prefers poverty without care to wealth with obligations.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The bramble replies that men may come with axes and saws to cut the fir-tree down, making it wish it were a bramble.
"Better poverty without a care than wealth with its many obligations."

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation

occurrences.motif_label: Boast answered by practical reversal
occurrences.basis: The fir-tree boasts over the bramble, but the bramble reverses the valuation by showing that the fir-tree's apparent advantage brings danger.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The fir-tree boasts to the bramble, calls it useless, and says the fir is useful for many things, especially when men build houses.
The bramble replies that men may come with axes and saws to cut the fir-tree down, making it wish it were a bramble.

occurrences.basis: The Cock avoids the Fox's lure by directing him to the Dog hidden in the tree trunk, resulting in the Fox's death.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At daybreak the Cock crows; a Fox hears him and wants to make a breakfast of him.
The Fox says he would like "to make the acquaintance of one who has such a beautiful voice."
The Cock replies, "Would you just wake my porter who sleeps at the foot of the tree? He'll open the door and let you in."
The Fox raps on the trunk; the Dog rushes out and tears him in pieces.

occurrences.basis: The gnat imagines its presence and departure may concern the bull, but the bull says he did not notice either; the moral states that people may overrate their own consequence.

evidence.locator: lines 1513-1515, THE GNAT AND THE BULL
evidence.quote_or_summary: The gnat says to the bull, “Do you mind if I go now?”

evidence.locator: lines 1515-1517, THE GNAT AND THE BULL

evidence.locator: lines 1518-1519, THE GNAT AND THE BULL moral
evidence.quote_or_summary: “We may often be of more consequence in our own eyes than in the eyes of our neighbours.”

evidence.locator: lines 1522-1524, THE BEAR AND THE TRAVELLERS
evidence.quote_or_summary: Before the bear observes them, one traveller climbs into the branches of a roadside tree and hides.

evidence.locator: lines 1530-1536, THE BEAR AND THE TRAVELLERS
evidence.quote_or_summary: The survivor says the bear told him “never again to travel with a friend who deserts you at the first sign of danger.”

evidence.locator: lines 1537-1540, THE BEAR AND THE TRAVELLERS moral
evidence.quote_or_summary: “Misfortune tests the sincerity of friendship.”

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation

occurrences.motif_label: moral judgment against pity for the wicked
occurrences.basis: The man states that bad things must be destroyed despite slight harm, and the closing moral warns not to waste pity on a scamp.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "whatever is bad has got to be destroyed, no matter how slight the harm it does."
"Do not waste your pity on a scamp."

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE BEAR AND THE TRAVELLERS / THE SLAVE AND THE LION / THE FLEA AND THE MAN / THE BEE AND JUPITER; lines 1593-1606
occurrences.motif_label: harmful wish rebounds on the wisher
occurrences.basis: The Queen Bee asks for a lethal weapon against honey-robbers, but the granted sting kills the bee who uses it; the moral explicitly generalizes this as evil wishes returning.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Queen Bee asks for bees to receive stings so they can kill people who rob their honey.
Jupiter grants stings such that when a bee stings a man, the sting stays in the wound and the bee dies.
“Evil wishes, like fowls, come home to roost.”

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation

occurrences.motif_label: survival through yielding rather than resistance
occurrences.basis: The reeds explicitly contrast the oak's stubborn resistance with their own practice of bowing and yielding, which allows them to survive the gale.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The reeds reply that the oak was stubborn and fought the stronger storm, but they bow and yield to every breeze, so the gale passed harmlessly over them.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE BEE AND JUPITER / THE OAK AND THE REEDS / THE BLIND MAN AND THE CUB / THE BOY AND THE SNAILS; lines 1622-1644
occurrences.motif_label: early revelation of harmful nature
occurrences.basis: The blind man judges the cub unsafe for a sheepfold, and the explicit moral says evil tendencies are shown early.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A wolf cub is placed in his hands; he says he is not sure whether it is a wolf's cub or a fox's, but it would not do to trust it in a sheepfold.
“Evil tendencies are early shown.”

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE BEE AND JUPITER / THE OAK AND THE REEDS / THE BLIND MAN AND THE CUB / THE BOY AND THE SNAILS; lines 1622-1644
occurrences.motif_label: discernment without sight
occurrences.basis: The blind man lacks sight but can identify animals by touch and reaches a practical judgment about the cub.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The blind man has a fine sense of touch and can identify animals placed in his hands by feeling them.
A wolf cub is placed in his hands; he says he is not sure whether it is a wolf's cub or a fox's, but it would not do to trust it in a sheepfold.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation

occurrences.motif_label: flattery rewarded by a vain ruler
occurrences.basis: The king rewards the traveller who falsely praises him and his subjects.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The lying traveller calls the king “a most noble and mighty monarch” and says the subjects are worthy of their royal master.
The Ape is delighted by the flattering answer and gives the lying traveller a handsome present.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE OAK AND THE REEDS / THE BLIND MAN AND THE CUB / THE BOY AND THE SNAILS / THE APES AND THE TWO TRAVELLERS; lines 1647-1668
occurrences.motif_label: truth punished when spoken before power
occurrences.basis: The traveller who tells the truth to the king receives a death sentence instead of the reward he expected.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The truthful traveller reasons that, if a lie was rewarded, truth should receive an even greater reward.
The truthful traveller says, “I think you are a very fine Ape, and all your subjects are fine Apes too.”
The King of the Apes is enraged and orders the truthful traveller taken away and clawed to death.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE BLIND MAN AND THE CUB / THE BOY AND THE SNAILS / THE APES AND THE TWO TRAVELLERS / THE ASS AND HIS BURDENS; lines 1671-1689
occurrences.motif_label: lesson through reversal of outcome
occurrences.basis: The narrative teaches the moral that a useful tactic can be overused, using the reversal from lighter to heavier burden as the lesson.

evidence.quote_or_summary: When the ass lies down in the stream again, the sponges absorb water, and the ass rises with a larger burden than before.
“You may play a good card once too often.”

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE BOY AND THE SNAILS / THE APES AND THE TWO TRAVELLERS / THE ASS AND HIS BURDENS / THE SHEPHERD'S BOY AND THE WOLF; lines 1692-1706
occurrences.motif_label: false alarm causing loss of credibility
occurrences.basis: The boy repeatedly lies about danger, so the villagers do not believe him when the danger is real.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The boy repeats the hoax more than once; each time the villagers find there is no wolf.
A wolf really comes, and the boy cries "Wolf! wolf!" as loudly as he can.
The villagers, used to his calls, take no notice of his cries for help.
You cannot believe a liar even when he tells the truth.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE BOY AND THE SNAILS / THE APES AND THE TWO TRAVELLERS / THE ASS AND HIS BURDENS / THE SHEPHERD'S BOY AND THE WOLF; lines 1692-1706
occurrences.motif_label: deceiver harmed by consequences of deception
occurrences.basis: The boy's hoaxes cause the villagers to disregard his later true appeal, resulting in loss among the sheep under his care.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The boy pretends a wolf is attacking and shouts, "Wolf! wolf!"
The boy repeats the hoax more than once; each time the villagers find there is no wolf.
The villagers, used to his calls, take no notice of his cries for help.
The wolf has its own way and kills sheep after sheep.
You cannot believe a liar even when he tells the truth.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE APES AND THE TWO TRAVELLERS / THE ASS AND HIS BURDENS / THE SHEPHERD'S BOY AND THE WOLF / THE FOX AND THE GOAT; lines 1709-1730
occurrences.motif_label: failure to consider exit before entering
occurrences.basis: The Goat enters the well to drink without securing a way out; the Fox’s final rebuke and the moral state that one should look before leaping.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Goat thinks only of quenching his thirst, jumps into the well, drinks, and then cannot find a way out.
“you wouldn't have got into the well without making certain that you could get out again.” Moral: “Look before your leap.”

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE SHEPHERD'S BOY AND THE WOLF / THE FOX AND THE GOAT / THE FISHERMAN AND THE SPRAT / THE BOASTING TRAVELLER; lines 1733-1757
occurrences.motif_label: certain small gain preferred over uncertain future gain
occurrences.basis: The fisherman refuses to release a small fish on the promise that it may be larger and useful later, because future recapture is uncertain.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The sprat begs to be put back into the water, saying it is small now but will grow big one day and could be caught again later.
The fisherman says he will keep the sprat now because if he puts it back he is unlikely ever to see it again.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE SHEPHERD'S BOY AND THE WOLF / THE FOX AND THE GOAT / THE FISHERMAN AND THE SPRAT / THE BOASTING TRAVELLER; lines 1733-1757
occurrences.motif_label: boast tested by immediate performance
occurrences.basis: The listener rejects reliance on distant verification and requires the traveller to prove his claim by action in the present place.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A man returns from foreign travel, tells wonderful stories, and claims he made an unbeatable jump at Rhodes with witnesses who could confirm it.
A listener says there is no need to go to Rhodes; they can imagine the place is Rhodes and the traveller should jump now.
Deeds, not words.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: BY G. K. CHESTERTON / AND ILLUSTRATIONS / BY ARTHUR RACKHAM / INTRODUCTION; lines 175-222
occurrences.motif_label: animals as bearers of wisdom
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly says animal fables hand down truisms, philosophical certainties, and simple truths.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Fable is justified as a way to teach plain truths simply through non-speaking animals; replacing wolf or fox with human types such as baron or diplomatist would force attention back to human complexity.

Animals used austerely like heraldic shields or ancient hieroglyphics hand down truisms; the lion and ibis are fixed signs, and creatures become a kind of animal alphabet for philosophical certainties.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE FISHERMAN AND THE SPRAT / THE BOASTING TRAVELLER / THE CRAB AND HIS MOTHER / THE ASS AND HIS SHADOW; lines 1760-1783
occurrences.motif_label: example stronger than instruction
occurrences.basis: The fable explicitly concludes that example is better than precept after the Old Crab cannot model the behavior she demands of her son.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In THE CRAB AND HIS MOTHER, the Old Crab criticizes her son’s sideways walking; the Young Crab asks her to demonstrate straight walking; she fails and realizes her fault-finding was foolish.
“Example is better than precept.”

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE FISHERMAN AND THE SPRAT / THE BOASTING TRAVELLER / THE CRAB AND HIS MOTHER / THE ASS AND HIS SHADOW; lines 1760-1783
occurrences.motif_label: quarrel over a trivial claim causing greater loss
occurrences.basis: The traveller and owner fight over use of the Ass’s shadow, and the Ass escapes while they are fighting.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The owner claims the hiring covered the Ass but not its shadow, while the traveller claims control of the Ass for the hired period.
The dispute escalates from words to blows, and the Ass runs away while the men are fighting.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE BOASTING TRAVELLER / THE CRAB AND HIS MOTHER / THE ASS AND HIS SHADOW / THE FARMER AND HIS SONS; lines 1786-1797
occurrences.motif_label: deathbed secret that induces productive labor
occurrences.basis: A dying father gives his sons a secret about hidden treasure; their search fails literally but their labor improves the vineyard and yields an exceptional crop.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A farmer near death calls his sons and says that a hidden treasure lies in his vineyard, instructing them to dig for it.
After the father dies, the sons take spade and fork and repeatedly turn up the vineyard soil while searching for the treasure, but find none.
After the thorough digging, the vines produce a crop such as had never before been seen.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE CRAB AND HIS MOTHER / THE ASS AND HIS SHADOW / THE FARMER AND HIS SONS / THE DOG AND THE COOK; lines 1800-1820
occurrences.motif_label: favor at another’s expense brings danger
occurrences.basis: The plot shows a dog accepting access to a feast through another servant’s invitation and suffering expulsion; the closing moral explicitly warns against such favors.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A rich man invites friends and acquaintances to a banquet; his dog invites another dog to dine with him at the feast.
The cook sees a strange dog in the kitchen, becomes annoyed, catches him by the hind legs, and throws him out of the window.
The dog has a nasty fall, limps away howling, and is later asked by other dogs what sort of dinner he got.
“Be shy of favours bestowed at the expense of others.”

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE ASS AND HIS SHADOW / THE FARMER AND HIS SONS / THE DOG AND THE COOK / THE MONKEY AS KING; lines 1823-1836
occurrences.motif_label: unworthy or unwise king
occurrences.basis: The Monkey is made King because he delights the animals, but his immediate capture in a simple trap leads the Fox to challenge his fitness as King of the Beasts.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At a gathering of all the animals, the Monkey dances, delights them, and is made King.
The Monkey goes toward the meat, is caught in the trap, and reproaches the Fox for leading him into danger.
“O Monkey, you call yourself King of the Beasts and haven't more sense than to be taken in like that!”

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE FARMER AND HIS SONS / THE DOG AND THE COOK / THE MONKEY AS KING / THE THIEVES AND THE COCK; lines 1839-1849
occurrences.motif_label: plea for life rejected because virtue harms wrongdoers
occurrences.basis: The cock's claim to be useful to honest workers becomes the thief's reason for killing him, since that usefulness obstructs thieves.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "Pray do not kill me: you will find me a most useful bird, for I rouse honest men to their work in the morning by my crowing."
"Yes, I know you do, making it still harder for us to get a livelihood. Into the pot you go!"

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE FARMER AND HIS SONS / THE DOG AND THE COOK / THE MONKEY AS KING / THE THIEVES AND THE COCK; lines 1839-1849
occurrences.motif_label: animal captive argues for usefulness
occurrences.basis: The captured cock speaks to save himself by citing his practical usefulness in waking honest men.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "Pray do not kill me: you will find me a most useful bird, for I rouse honest men to their work in the morning by my crowing."

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE DOG AND THE COOK / THE MONKEY AS KING / THE THIEVES AND THE COCK / THE FARMER AND FORTUNE; lines 1852-1865
occurrences.motif_label: misdirected gratitude for a divine or personified gift
occurrences.basis: The farmer thanks the Goddess of the Earth, while Fortune claims she bestowed the gift and the moral instructs gratitude where it is due.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The farmer is overjoyed and from then on makes a daily offering at the shrine of the Goddess of the Earth.
Fortune is displeased and tells the farmer that she bestowed the gift, that he did not thank her for his good luck, and that she would be blamed if he lost what he gained.
“Show gratitude where gratitude is due.”

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE THIEVES AND THE COCK / THE FARMER AND FORTUNE / JUPITER AND THE MONKEY / FATHER AND SONS; lines 1881-1895
occurrences.motif_label: Unity taught by the unbreakable bundle
occurrences.basis: The passage uses a practical demonstration with bundled and separated sticks to teach the moral that union gives strength.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The father has the sons fetch a bundle of sticks and invites each to break it across his knee; all try and fail.
The father undoes the bundle and hands the sticks to the sons one by one; they break them without difficulty.
“united you will be more than a match for your enemies: but if you quarrel and separate, your weakness will put you at the mercy of those who attack you.”
“Union is strength.”

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE THIEVES AND THE COCK / THE FARMER AND FORTUNE / JUPITER AND THE MONKEY / FATHER AND SONS; lines 1881-1895
occurrences.motif_label: Division brings vulnerability to enemies
occurrences.basis: The father warns that if the sons quarrel and separate, their weakness will put them at the mercy of attackers.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “united you will be more than a match for your enemies: but if you quarrel and separate, your weakness will put you at the mercy of those who attack you.”

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: JUPITER AND THE MONKEY / FATHER AND SONS / THE LAMP / THE OWL AND THE BIRDS; lines 1898-1928
occurrences.motif_label: ignored wise warning later proven true
occurrences.basis: The owl gives repeated practical warnings that are rejected and mocked; later events confirm her words and the birds recognize her wisdom.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The owl calls the birds together at the first oak sprout and advises them to destroy it, warning that mistletoe and birdlime from it will threaten them.
At the first sowing of flax, the owl tells the birds to eat the seed because men will later make nets from flax to catch them.
On seeing the first archer, the owl warns the birds that he will use their feathers on arrows and shoot them.
The birds ignore and laugh at the owl, later respect her when her warnings come true, and thereafter attend upon her, though she no longer advises them.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE LAMP / THE OWL AND THE BIRDS / THE ASS IN THE LION'S SKIN / THE SHE-GOATS AND THEIR BEARDS; lines 1931-1952
occurrences.motif_label: outward sign does not equal underlying power
occurrences.basis: Jupiter's reply distinguishes the visible beard from actual strength, advising the he-goats not to object.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Jupiter tells the he-goats not to object, says a tuft of hair is insignificant, and says the she-goats can never match them in strength.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE OWL AND THE BIRDS / THE ASS IN THE LION'S SKIN / THE SHE-GOATS AND THEIR BEARDS / THE OLD LION; lines 1955-1968
occurrences.motif_label: Wise avoidance through reading signs
occurrences.basis: The fox infers danger from the one-way footprints and refuses to enter the cave.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A fox comes to the cave, suspects the truth, and speaks to the lion from outside instead of going in.
"all the footprints point towards the cave and none the other way"

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE SHE-GOATS AND THEIR BEARDS / THE OLD LION / THE BOY BATHING / THE QUACK FROG; lines 1971-1994
occurrences.motif_label: practical help preferred over advice in danger
occurrences.basis: The fable contrasts a crisis requiring rescue with a bystander's scolding, and its moral explicitly prioritizes assistance over advice.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A boy bathing in a river gets out of his depth and is in great danger of drowning.
A man hears the boy's cries, goes to the riverside, scolds him for carelessness, and makes no attempt to help.
"please help me first and scold me afterwards."
"Give assistance, not advice, in a crisis."

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE SHE-GOATS AND THEIR BEARDS / THE OLD LION / THE BOY BATHING / THE QUACK FROG; lines 1971-1994
occurrences.motif_label: healer unable to heal himself
occurrences.basis: The frog claims to cure all diseases, but the fox challenges him because he has not cured his own ailments; the moral states, "Physician, heal thyself."

evidence.quote_or_summary: A frog leaves the marshes and proclaims to the world that he is a learned physician skilled in drugs and able to cure all diseases.
A fox in the crowd asks how the frog can heal others when he cannot cure his own lame legs and blotched, wrinkled skin.
"Physician, heal thyself."

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE OLD LION / THE BOY BATHING / THE QUACK FROG / THE SWOLLEN FOX; lines 1997-2009
occurrences.motif_label: advice to wait until bodily change reverses
occurrences.basis: The passing fox advises the trapped fox that he can get out once he shrinks to his former size.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Another fox learns the situation and says the trapped fox must stay there until he shrinks to his former size, after which he can get out.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE SWOLLEN FOX / THE MOUSE, THE FROG, AND THE HAWK / THE BOY AND THE NETTLES / THE PEASANT AND THE APPLE-TREE; lines 2029-2056
occurrences.motif_label: practical wisdom learned through painful contact
occurrences.basis: The boy's painful encounter with the nettle leads to a direct practical lesson from his mother.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A boy gathering berries from a hedge is stung by a nettle and tells his mother he only touched it lightly.
"if you had grasped it firmly, it wouldn't have hurt you in the least."

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE SWOLLEN FOX / THE MOUSE, THE FROG, AND THE HAWK / THE BOY AND THE NETTLES / THE PEASANT AND THE APPLE-TREE; lines 2029-2056
occurrences.motif_label: hidden utility revealed in a seemingly barren tree
occurrences.basis: The tree appears useless because it bears no fruit, but hidden bees and honey reveal another form of value, prompting the peasant to spare it.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A peasant has a fruitless apple-tree in his garden that shelters sparrows and grasshoppers; disappointed, he fetches an axe to cut it down.
The peasant cuts into the hollow trunk, finds bees and honey, throws down his axe, and says the old tree is worth keeping.
"Utility is most men's test of worth."

occurrences.motif_label: Moral blindness to one's own faults
occurrences.basis: The fable explains that people see others' faults while failing to see their own.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Every person carries two bags full of faults; the front one holds neighbours' faults and the rear one holds the person's own faults.
"men do not see their own faults, but never fail to see those of others."

occurrences.motif_label: Externalized faults carried before and behind
occurrences.basis: Faults are represented as objects in two bags, with neighbours' faults visible in front and one's own faults behind.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Every person carries two bags full of faults; the front one holds neighbours' faults and the rear one holds the person's own faults.
"men do not see their own faults, but never fail to see those of others."

occurrences.passage_locator: THE DOG IN THE MANGER / THE TWO BAGS / THE OXEN AND THE AXLETREES / THE BOY AND THE FILBERTS; lines 2108-2132
occurrences.motif_label: Those least burdened complain most
occurrences.basis: The Oxen bear the load while the Axletrees make the noise; the explicit moral states that those who suffer least complain most.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A pair of Oxen draw a heavily loaded wagon along the highway; as they strain at the yoke, the Axletrees creak and groan.
"Why do you make such a noise when we do all the work?"

occurrences.basis: The passage describes Jupiter as despising the folly of the Frogs’ request; their dissatisfaction leads from an inert king to a predatory one.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Frogs are discontented because they have no ruler and send a deputation to Jupiter asking him to give them a king.
Jupiter regards the request as foolish, casts a log into the pool where the Frogs live, and says it will be their king.
The Frogs judge the sluggish king an insult to their dignity and ask Jupiter to remove it and give them a better one.
The Stork begins catching and eating the Frogs as quickly as it can.

"There are two sides to every question."

evidence.quote_or_summary: A blacksmith has a little dog that sleeps when the master works and wakes when it is time for meals.
"When I am hammering away at my anvil, you just curl up and go to sleep... you wake up and wag your tail to be fed."
"Those who will not work deserve to starve."

occurrences.motif_label: misvalued usefulness and fatal vanity
occurrences.basis: The stag values his impressive antlers over his legs, but the legs help him escape while the antlers cause his death; the explicit moral states that what is worth most is often valued least.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A thirsty stag goes to a pool, sees his reflection in the water, admires his spreading antlers, and despises the weakness and slenderness of his legs.
A lion attacks the stag; the stag outruns him on open ground, but in a wood his antlers catch in branches and he is killed by the lion’s teeth and claws.
“I despised my legs, which might have saved my life: but I gloried in my horns, and they have proved my ruin.”
“What is worth most is often valued least.”

occurrences.basis: The oxen intend violent revenge, but an old ox counsels against it by reasoning that their condition would become worse under inexperienced replacements.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The oxen decide to revenge themselves on the butchers for the havoc among their ranks and plot to kill them on a given day.
An old ox rises and says the oxen have reason to hate the butchers, but the butchers understand their trade and avoid unnecessary pain.
The old ox says that if the butchers are killed, inexperienced people will be set to slaughter the oxen and will inflict great suffering by bungling it.
The old ox concludes that even if all the butchers die, mankind will never go without beef.

occurrences.basis: The old ox argues that the butchers are harmful but skilled, while their replacements would still slaughter the oxen and cause more pain.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An old ox rises and says the oxen have reason to hate the butchers, but the butchers understand their trade and avoid unnecessary pain.

The old ox concludes that even if all the butchers die, mankind will never go without beef.

occurrences.motif_label: refusal of credit to untrustworthy partners
occurrences.basis: The sheep refuses to lend wheat because the proposed surety is known to take without paying and because both the borrower and surety could evade collection.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A stag asks a sheep to lend him a measure of wheat and says the wolf will be his surety.
The sheep fears cheating and refuses, saying the wolf takes without paying and both the wolf and stag can outrun her when the debt is due.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE SOLDIER AND HIS HORSE / THE OXEN AND THE BUTCHERS / THE WOLF AND THE LION / THE SHEEP, THE WOLF, AND THE STAG; lines 2770-2793
occurrences.motif_label: two wrongs do not make a right
occurrences.basis: The closing moral states that two wrongs do not make a right, and the first fable shows a thief complaining when robbed by another predator.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A wolf steals a lamb from the flock to devour later, then meets a lion who takes the prey and walks off with it.
The wolf does not resist but later says the lion has unjustly taken what is his; the lion laughs and questions whether the prey was justly the wolf's.
Two blacks do not make a white.

occurrences.motif_label: friends' quarrels aid foes
occurrences.basis: The closing moral explicitly states that quarrels of friends are opportunities for foes.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The quarrels of friends are the opportunities of foes.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE HORSE AND HIS RIDER / THE GOAT AND THE VINE / THE TWO POTS / THE OLD HOUND; lines 2835-2859
occurrences.motif_label: Unequal companions make unsafe friends
occurrences.basis: The fable contrasts a fragile earthenware pot with a stronger brass pot and explicitly concludes that equals make the best friends.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Two pots, one earthenware and one brass, are carried away down a river in flood.
The brass pot urges the other to stay close for protection; the earthenware pot asks him not to come near because a touch would break him.
"Equals make the best friends."

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE HORSE AND HIS RIDER / THE GOAT AND THE VINE / THE TWO POTS / THE OLD HOUND; lines 2835-2859
occurrences.motif_label: Past service deserves honor despite present weakness
occurrences.basis: The hound explains that age has weakened his body though not his will, and asks the master to honor his former service rather than abuse his present condition.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A hound who had served his master well for years begins to lose strength and speed because of age.
The master starts a powerful wild boar and sets the hound on it; the hound seizes the boar by the ear but cannot hold it because his teeth are gone, so the boar escapes and the master scolds him.
"My will is as strong as ever, master, but my body is old and feeble. You ought to honour me for what I have been instead of abusing me for what I am."

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE HORSE AND HIS RIDER / THE GOAT AND THE VINE / THE TWO POTS / THE OLD HOUND; lines 2835-2859
occurrences.motif_label: Age weakens the body but not intention
occurrences.basis: The hound explicitly contrasts his still-strong will with his old and feeble body.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "My will is as strong as ever, master, but my body is old and feeble. You ought to honour me for what I have been instead of abusing me for what I am."

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE GOAT AND THE VINE / THE TWO POTS / THE OLD HOUND / THE CLOWN AND THE COUNTRYMAN; lines 2862-2889
occurrences.motif_label: Faulty judgment favors imitation over reality
occurrences.basis: The spectators praise the clown's imitation as more true to life than the squeal of an actual hidden pig, and the countryman exposes their poor judgment.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The countryman hides a young pig under his smock, pinches its ear so it squeals, but the spectators say the clown's imitation is more true to life.
"There, that shows what sort of judges you are!"

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE TWO POTS / THE OLD HOUND / THE CLOWN AND THE COUNTRYMAN / THE LARK AND THE FARMER; lines 2892-2910
occurrences.motif_label: self-help as effective action
occurrences.basis: The mother lark treats the farmer's decision to act himself as the sign of imminent danger, and the explicit moral states that self-help is best.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The mother lark tells her children they must leave because the farmer no longer speaks of friends and will take things in hand himself.
Self-help is the best help.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE TWO POTS / THE OLD HOUND / THE CLOWN AND THE COUNTRYMAN / THE LARK AND THE FARMER; lines 2892-2910
occurrences.motif_label: delay caused by reliance on others
occurrences.basis: The mother lark says a man who looks to friends for help will take his time, and she does not move the brood until the farmer plans direct action.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The mother says there is no hurry, because a man who looks to friends for help will take his time.
The mother lark tells her children they must leave because the farmer no longer speaks of friends and will take things in hand himself.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE TWO POTS / THE OLD HOUND / THE CLOWN AND THE COUNTRYMAN / THE LARK AND THE FARMER; lines 2892-2910
occurrences.motif_label: animal wisdom from overheard human speech
occurrences.basis: The larks hear the farmer's plans, and the mother lark draws practical conclusions about when the family must flee.

evidence.quote_or_summary: One young lark overhears the farmer, becomes frightened, and asks the mother if they should move house at once.
The mother says there is no hurry, because a man who looks to friends for help will take his time.
The farmer says he will put it off no longer and will hire men that day to begin work at once.
The mother lark tells her children they must leave because the farmer no longer speaks of friends and will take things in hand himself.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE OLD HOUND / THE CLOWN AND THE COUNTRYMAN / THE LARK AND THE FARMER / THE LION AND THE ASS; lines 2913-2924
occurrences.motif_label: boast answered by ironic correction
occurrences.basis: After the ass boasts that he scared the goats well, the lion responds with an ironic remark that depends on knowing the noise came from an ass.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “Well, I scared them pretty well, didn't I?”
The lion says that, had he not known the speaker was an ass, he would have turned and run himself.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE CLOWN AND THE COUNTRYMAN / THE LARK AND THE FARMER / THE LION AND THE ASS / THE PROPHET; lines 2927-2938
occurrences.motif_label: seer unable to foresee personal misfortune
occurrences.basis: The fable turns on the contrast between the prophet's claimed knowledge of others' futures and his failure to anticipate the theft at his own house.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A prophet sits in the marketplace and tells fortunes for anyone who hires him.
A person runs up and reports that the prophet's house has been broken into by thieves who carried off whatever they could take.
“Our friend professes to know what is going to happen to others, but it seems he's not clever enough to perceive what's in store for himself.”

occurrences.passage_locator: THE HOUND AND THE HARE / THE LION, THE MOUSE, AND THE FOX / THE TRUMPETER TAKEN PRISONER / THE WOLF AND THE CRANE; lines 2966-2988
occurrences.motif_label: indirect incitement treated as culpability
occurrences.basis: The captors reject the Trumpeter's claim that he killed no one because his music encourages others to fight.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In THE TRUMPETER TAKEN PRISONER, a trumpeter encourages soldiers with warlike tunes, is captured, pleads that he has killed no one and has only a trumpet, and is told by his captors that inciting others to fight is reason for death.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE HOUND AND THE HARE / THE LION, THE MOUSE, AND THE FOX / THE TRUMPETER TAKEN PRISONER / THE WOLF AND THE CRANE; lines 2966-2988
occurrences.motif_label: dangerous helper denied promised reward
occurrences.basis: The Crane performs a risky service for the Wolf after a promised reward, but the Wolf refuses payment and reframes her survival as compensation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In THE WOLF AND THE CRANE, a wolf with a bone stuck in his throat asks a crane to remove it with her long bill and promises to make it worth her while; the crane removes the bone easily.
After the crane asks for her fee, the wolf bares his teeth and says she can boast that she put her head into a wolf's mouth and was not bitten.

occurrences.motif_label: ingratitude after rescue
occurrences.basis: The Wolf is relieved of the bone by the Crane but answers her request for payment with threat and refusal.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In THE WOLF AND THE CRANE, a wolf with a bone stuck in his throat asks a crane to remove it with her long bill and promises to make it worth her while; the crane removes the bone easily.
After the crane asks for her fee, the wolf bares his teeth and says she can boast that she put her head into a wolf's mouth and was not bitten.

occurrences.motif_label: Prudent refusal of a predator's request
occurrences.basis: The sheep recognizes that giving water to the wolf would likely enable the wolf to eat him, and refuses.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A wolf, badly bitten by dogs and hungry after reviving, asks a passing sheep to bring water from a nearby stream and says he can manage meat if he gets drink.
"if I brought you the water, you would have no difficulty about the meat. Good-morning."

occurrences.motif_label: self-interested counsel
occurrences.basis: The tradesmen’s recommendations align with their own trades, and the explicit moral states that each person acts for himself.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A carpenter recommends wood, describing it as readily procurable and easily worked.
A stone-mason objects that wood is inflammable and recommends stones instead.
“In my opinion there's nothing like leather.”
“Every man for himself.”

occurrences.passage_locator: THE WOLF AND THE SHEEP / THE TUNNY-FISH AND THE DOLPHIN / THE THREE TRADESMEN / THE MOUSE AND THE BULL; lines 3055-3069
occurrences.motif_label: small creature overcomes stronger adversary
occurrences.basis: The mouse survives and prevails over the bull through speed, refuge, and timing, and the moral states that strength does not always win.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The mouse is too quick for the bull and slips into a hole in a wall.
When quiet returns, the mouse darts out, bites the bull again, and returns to the hole.
"You big fellows don't always have it your own way, you see: sometimes we little ones come off best."
"The battle is not always to the strong."

occurrences.basis: The contrast between the big bull and little mouse is resolved by the small animal's success, summarized in the final moral.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "You big fellows don't always have it your own way, you see: sometimes we little ones come off best."
"The battle is not always to the strong."

occurrences.motif_label: greater motive in flight from mortal danger
occurrences.basis: The hound contrasts his own pursuit of dinner with the hare's flight for life, explaining the outcome through unequal stakes.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A hound starts a hare from her form, pursues her, but gives up after she gains during the chase.
The rustic taunts the hound; the hound replies, "it's one thing to be running for your dinner, but quite another to be running for your life."

occurrences.motif_label: simple safety preferred to dangerous luxury
occurrences.basis: The country mouse rejects rich food in town because danger accompanies it and chooses simple food in peace.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In town, the country mouse is shown a larder containing flour, oatmeal, figs, honey, and dates.
When people enter the larder, the two mice repeatedly flee and hide in a narrow, uncomfortable hole.
The country mouse says town luxury is "surrounded by dangers" and prefers his simple dinner of roots and corn "in peace."

occurrences.motif_label: Trap avoided by recognizing visible signs
occurrences.basis: The bull sees the preparations and no sheep, infers the danger, and leaves before becoming the victim; the moral explicitly says an openly visible net is spread in vain.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The bull accepted, arrived at the lion's den, and saw saucepans and spits but no sheep.
The bull turned on his heel and walked quietly away.
The bull says the preparations showed that the victim was to be a bull and not a sheep.
“The net is spread in vain in sight of the bird.”

occurrences.passage_locator: THE TOWN MOUSE AND THE COUNTRY MOUSE / THE LION AND THE BULL / THE WOLF, THE FOX, AND THE APE / THE EAGLE AND THE COCKS; lines 3127-3150
occurrences.motif_label: Dishonest reputation undermines trust
occurrences.basis: The moral explicitly states that dishonest people receive no credit even if they act honestly, and the Ape's judgment treats both Wolf and Fox as untrustworthy.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In 'The Wolf, the Fox, and the Ape,' a Wolf charges a Fox with theft; an Ape hears both sides and says the Wolf likely never lost the claimed item, while the Fox is still guilty despite denials.
The dishonest get no credit, even if they act honestly.

occurrences.motif_label: Ambiguous animal judgment
occurrences.basis: The Ape judges a dispute by denying the Wolf's claim while also condemning the Fox, producing a judgment based on character and reputation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In 'The Wolf, the Fox, and the Ape,' a Wolf charges a Fox with theft; an Ape hears both sides and says the Wolf likely never lost the claimed item, while the Fox is still guilty despite denials.

occurrences.motif_label: Boastful victor is destroyed
occurrences.basis: The Cock who wins and crows from the roof is seen by an Eagle and carried off; the moral states that pride comes before a fall.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In 'The Eagle and the Cocks,' two Cocks fight in the same farmyard for mastery; the beaten one hides in a dark corner, while the victor flies to the stable roof and crows.
An Eagle sees the victorious Cock from high in the sky, swoops down, carries him off, and the other Cock comes out to rule the roost without a rival.
Pride comes before a fall.

occurrences.motif_label: misfortune from an unexpected quarter
occurrences.basis: The narrative and explicit moral state that the stag’s ruin comes from the direction he did not fear.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “I bethought me of the dangers of the land, whence none assailed me: but I feared no peril from the sea, yet thence has come my ruin.”
“Misfortune often assails us from an unexpected quarter.”

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation

occurrences.motif_label: misplaced vigilance
occurrences.basis: The stag watches the land against expected hounds but does not guard against danger from the sea.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A one-eyed stag grazes close to the sea-shore, turns his sound eye toward land to watch for hounds, and turns his blind eye toward the sea because he expects no danger there.
“I bethought me of the dangers of the land, whence none assailed me: but I feared no peril from the sea, yet thence has come my ruin.”

occurrences.motif_label: practical need valued over wealth
occurrences.basis: The Cock, while seeking food, judges a grain of corn more desirable than jewels.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Cock scratching for food turned up a Jewel that had by chance been dropped there.
The Cock says the Jewel would delight its owner, but he would prefer one grain of corn to all jewels.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation

occurrences.motif_label: misplaced trust in a natural enemy
occurrences.basis: The story presents a shepherd who comes to trust a wolf with his sheep and then recognizes his mistake after the wolf kills many of them.

evidence.quote_or_summary: As time passed and the wolf did not meddle with the flock, the shepherd began to regard him more as a protector than as an enemy.
When an errand took the shepherd to the city, he was not uneasy about leaving the wolf with the sheep.
As soon as the shepherd’s back was turned, the wolf attacked the sheep and killed the greater number.
"It serves me right for trusting my flock to a Wolf."

occurrences.motif_label: Judgment by bad company
occurrences.basis: The stork is punished because he is found among cranes who damage the crops, and the moral states that choosing bad companions makes one appear bad.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The farmer says it is nothing to him what the stork is: he found him among cranes who ruin his crops, and “like them, you shall suffer.”
“If you choose bad companions no one will believe that you are anything but bad yourself.”

occurrences.motif_label: acceptance of changing fortune
occurrences.basis: The miller states that regret is useless and that fortune has ups and downs to be taken as they come.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "Fortune has many ups and downs: you must just take them as they come."

occurrences.passage_locator: THE FARMER AND THE STORK / THE CHARGER AND THE MILLER / THE GRASSHOPPER AND THE OWL / THE GRASSHOPPER AND THE ANTS; lines 3315-3328
occurrences.motif_label: industrious provision contrasted with improvident leisure
occurrences.basis: The Ants work and store corn, while the Grasshopper explains that she spent summer singing and is left without food in winter.

evidence.quote_or_summary: On a fine winter day after a long rainy spell, Ants dry their damp store of corn.
The Ants briefly stop work and ask what she did all summer and why she did not collect winter food.
“I was so busy singing that I hadn't the time.”
The Ants say that if she spent summer singing, she should spend winter dancing; they chuckle and resume work.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE GRASSHOPPER AND THE OWL / THE GRASSHOPPER AND THE ANTS / THE FARMER AND THE VIPER / THE TWO FROGS; lines 3331-3356
occurrences.motif_label: ignored warning to leave an unsafe place
occurrences.basis: The marsh frog warns the lane frog to move to a safer place, but the lane frog refuses because of habit and dies under wagon wheels.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Two neighbouring frogs live in different places: one in a marsh with plenty of water, the other in a lane with only rainwater in ruts; the marsh frog urges the other to move to the safer marsh.
The lane frog refuses to move from his accustomed place; a few days later a heavy wagon comes down the lane and crushes him under its wheels.

occurrences.basis: The lane frog cannot bring himself to move from his accustomed place, and that place becomes the site of his death.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The lane frog refuses to move from his accustomed place; a few days later a heavy wagon comes down the lane and crushes him under its wheels.

occurrences.basis: The king's final speech emphasizes the folly of entrusting lives to someone not trusted even with his own trade.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "Here is this Cobbler to whom no one will send his boots to be mended, and yet you have not hesitated to entrust him with your lives!"

occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom learned too late from failed revolt
occurrences.basis: The members recognize only after the collapse that their action was foolish.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The members see too late that they had been foolish.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE COBBLER TURNED DOCTOR / THE ASS, THE COCK, AND THE LION / THE BELLY AND THE MEMBERS / THE BALD MAN AND THE FLY; lines 3412-3423
occurrences.motif_label: intent distinguishes blame for harm
occurrences.basis: The bald man distinguishes between his own unintended self-harm and the fly's intentional harmful biting, presenting a practical moral distinction about intention.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The man replies that he bears no grudge for the blow because he never intended himself harm.

occurrences.basis: The Wolf says he was taught to kill and should have kept to that trade instead of attempting to cure.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "my father taught me to kill, and I ought to have stuck to that trade instead of attempting to cure."

evidence.quote_or_summary: On the third visit, the patient says he feels feverish; the doctor calls it a very good sign and says the patient is doing nicely.
"My dear friend, I'm dying of good signs."

occurrences.passage_locator: THE FLEA AND THE OX / THE BIRDS, THE BEASTS, AND THE BAT / THE MAN AND HIS TWO SWEETHEARTS / THE EAGLE, THE JACKDAW, AND THE SHEPHERD; lines 3531-3549

The jackdaw flies up, descends onto a big ram, gets its claws caught in the wool, and flaps while stuck, making matters worse.

occurrences.motif_label: Trying to please everyone leads to pleasing no one
occurrences.basis: The narrative repeatedly shows the miller obeying each new criticism and ends with the explicit conclusion that he pleased none by trying to please all.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The miller and his young son drive their ass to market to sell him; girls on the road mock them for walking, so the son mounts the ass.
Old acquaintances say the son will be spoiled if he rides while the miller walks, so the miller rides and the son walks behind.
Women and children call the miller selfish for riding while the boy walks, so the miller has his son get up behind him.
Travellers ask about the ass and warn that with such a load he will be exhausted before market; they say the miller would do better to carry him.
The miller and son tie the ass’s legs, sling him on a pole, and carry him into town; crowds come out to laugh and mock them.
“in trying to please all he had pleased none, and had lost his Ass into the bargain.”

evidence.quote_or_summary: The miller and his young son drive their ass to market to sell him; girls on the road mock them for walking, so the son mounts the ass.

“in trying to please all he had pleased none, and had lost his Ass into the bargain.”

evidence.quote_or_summary: The fable introduces a man with two children, a boy and a girl; the boy is good-looking, while the girl is plain.
While playing together in their mother's chamber, the children find a mirror and see their own features for the first time.
The boy boasts about his handsomeness; the girl is upset by her plainness and interprets his remarks as an insult.
The father tells them to make good use of the glass: the boy should be as good as he is handsome, and the girl should offset plain features with sweetness of disposition.

The lion's spirits rise because, if the huge elephant fears a gnat, the lion need not be ashamed of fearing a cock, which is much bigger than a gnat.

occurrences.basis: The cottager avoids openly offending the Lion, devises an expedient, and overcomes him after removing his dangerous features.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The father is unwilling to give his daughter to so fearsome a husband but does not want to offend the Lion, so he devises an expedient.
The cottager tells the Lion that he cannot consent unless allowed to draw the Lion's teeth and pare his nails, because the daughter is afraid of them.
Once the Lion is disarmed, the cottager no longer fears him and drives him away with a club.

occurrences.motif_label: retaliation against the wrong target
occurrences.basis: The bees respond to the damage by stinging the bee-keeper, while the thief who stole the honey escapes; the stated moral generalizes this into advice about identifying the correct target before striking back.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The bees return from gathering honey, find the hives overturned and the keeper standing by, and attack him with their stings.
The bee-keeper angrily says that the bees let the thief escape and then stung the one who had always cared for them.
When you hit back make sure you have got the right man.

occurrences.basis: The narrative and moral both focus on a claimed gift that costs the giver nothing because the item is unusable to him.

"For your sake I have left it untouched"; the wolf says he will enjoy hearing the horse munch the ripe grain.
"If wolves could eat oats... you would hardly have indulged your ears at the cost of your belly."
"There is no virtue in giving to others what is useless to oneself."

occurrences.basis: The explicit moral generalizes the narrative into a statement about human concern for recovering what has been lost.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “All men are more concerned to recover what they lose than to acquire what they lack.”

occurrences.motif_label: lesson learned after danger
occurrences.basis: The closing moral states that prior harm or danger leads to later caution, and the dog avoids repeating his vulnerable position.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The dog answers that if the wolf ever catches him lying by the gate again, he should not wait for a feast.
Once bitten, twice shy.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The lark says she was a fool and that such a city will take a long time to fill with enough fools.

occurrences.basis: Demades' audience ignores his public speech but listens intently when he offers to tell an Aesop fable.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Demades speaks in the Assembly at Athens; when the people are inattentive, he offers to tell one of Aesop's fables, and everyone listens intently.

occurrences.basis: Demades stops the river-crossing story and uses the audience's curiosity to criticize them for preferring fables to public business.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Demades begins a fable in which Demeter, a swallow, and an eel travel together to a bridgeless river; the swallow flies over and the eel swims across.
When listeners ask what happened to Demeter, Demades says she is angry at them for listening to fables when they should mind public business.

occurrences.motif_label: False identity exposed by a test of local knowledge
occurrences.basis: The Monkey claims to be Athenian and of distinguished family, but his claim to know the Piræus as a personal friend reveals his ignorance to the Dolphin.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Near the Piræus, the port of Athens, the Dolphin asks the Monkey whether he is an Athenian.
The Monkey replies that he is Athenian and says he comes from a very distinguished family.
"Then, of course, you know the Piræus," continued the Dolphin.
The Monkey thought he was referring to some high official or other, and replied, "Oh, yes, he's a very old friend of mine."
Detecting the Monkey's hypocrisy, the Dolphin dives below the surface, and the Monkey is quickly drowned.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "I am going to give up a certain prize on the chance of a better" is rejected by the hawk, who says he sees no sign of the better prize.
