evidence.quote_or_summary: The Wolves send a deputation proposing lasting peace with the Sheep if the Sheep give up the sheep-dogs to instant death; the Sheep agree.
An old Ram, whose years have brought him wisdom, intervenes and asks how they can expect peace, since even with the dogs protecting them they are not secure from the Wolves' attacks.

occurrences.basis: Mercury punishes and questions the man after the man condemns divine injustice but himself destroys many unoffending ants for the act of one.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “They care nothing for a man's character,” said he, “but let the good and the bad go to their deaths together.”
The man angrily stamps on the ant-heap and crushes hundreds of unoffending ants.
Mercury appeared, belaboured him with his staff, and said, “You villain, where's your nice sense of justice now?”

The lion asks why the bull wears ugly horns and says he would do better without them.
The bull is foolishly persuaded by the lion's flattery to have his horns cut off.
After losing his only means of defense, the bull falls easy prey to the lion.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The ass divides everything into three equal parts; the lion becomes furious, attacks the ass, and tears him to pieces.
The lion orders the fox to make a new division; the fox gives almost all to the lion and keeps only the smallest morsel.
The fox replies that he "took a lesson from the Ass."
"Happy is he who learns from the misfortunes of others."

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Fox and a Leopard argue over their looks; the Leopard cites his smart coat, and the Fox replies that his wits are smarter.

The Horse finds “that in the man he had got a master for good.”

occurrences.basis: The man reasons that gods unable to catch thieves in their own temples are unlikely to identify the thief of his spade.

One wild goat replies that the goatherd's very good treatment put them on guard, since favoring newcomers over his own flock suggested they could later be neglected for still newer arrivals.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Aesop's fame is said to rest on common-sense fables that belong to humanity and anonymous universal tradition, though a central collector gains fame for creating them.
The tradition called Fables is said to have existed before Aesop and remained after him; Aesop's Fables are not simply Aesop's own fables.

occurrences.basis: The passage describes fable animals as impersonal types whose fixed traits speak for themselves and convey fable meaning.

evidence.quote_or_summary: For fable, all persons are said to be impersonal, like algebraic abstractions or chess pieces; the lion is stronger than the wolf, the fox moves crookedly, and the sheep marches on.
Fables are said to assume each creature remains itself: the wolf is wolfish and the fox foxy; animal forces drive like inanimate forces such as rivers or growing trees.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The man and wife begin to think they are not getting rich fast enough.
They imagine the bird is made of gold inside and decide to kill it to secure the whole store of precious metal at once.
They neither become rich at once nor continue receiving the daily addition to their wealth.
“Much wants more and loses all.”

evidence.quote_or_summary: The tale explains that good-hearted men could grow rich, while bad-hearted men angered the gods, causing even a gold puppy to excrete dung; listeners are told not to be bad-hearted.
Branches break and crash down; he wakes as a man again, worships the tree, returns home, and thereafter does not misbehave.

occurrences.basis: The axe, tray, and pestle know causes and tell the boy hidden information, enabling him to diagnose and treat sickness.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The axe appears as a handsome man; the axe, tray, and pestle become the boy's siblings, and the axe is described as a god who knows causes and events.
Because the divine implements tell him hidden causes and treatments, the boy is regarded as a great soothsayer and wizard who could turn death into life.

occurrences.basis: The man leaps from a mountain peak onto clouds, travels over the world of men and gods, and returns with a map; the mountain god says the journey made him wiser.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In 'The Wicked Wizard punished,' a wizard says a man can leap from a mountain peak onto clouds and ride them; the man does so, sees the world, and returns with a map of the worlds of men and gods.
The mountain god appears in a dream and says the wizard received deserved punishment, while the good man was protected and shown the world to become wiser.

occurrences.basis: Panaumbe chooses the narrow path after the crow's statement and survives, while Penaumbe takes the broad path after the crow calls him a fool and dies.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At a divided path, an old crow on a tree calls Panaumbe clever; he chooses the narrow left path, the sea-lion gets stuck, and Panaumbe kills it, takes its flesh and skin, and becomes rich.

At the divided path, the old crow calls Penaumbe a fool; he takes the broad right road, the sea-lion catches and eats him, and the narrator says he might have become rich if he had listened to advice.

occurrences.basis: The narrator explicitly states that Penaumbe might have become rich if he had listened to Panaumbe’s advice, but became poor because he did not listen.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The narrator says Penaumbe could have had food and wealth if he had listened to Panaumbe’s advice, but he became poor because he did not listen.

occurrences.basis: The Chief of the Upper Current of the River accepts the command to drink the sea dry, then makes fulfillment depend on the challenger first closing all river mouths, causing the challenger to concede.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In “Drinking the Sea dry,” the vainglorious Chief of the Mouth of the River challenges the Chief of the Upper Current of the River to drink the sea dry or forfeit his possessions.

At the beach the challenged chief drinks a few drops from a cup, says the sea is harmless but polluted by rivers, and requires all river mouths in Aino-land and Japan to be closed first; the challenger is ashamed and gives him treasures.

occurrences.motif_label: Dream instruction by local deity
occurrences.basis: Both the salmon chief and pine-tree goddess convey crucial knowledge and ritual instructions through dreams.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "I am no human being. I am the chief of the salmon, the divine fish." He says he saved the Aino from the waves and that one night was actually a whole year.
The divine old man asks the Aino to offer rice-beer, set up divine symbols, and worship him with a libation formula; he warns that failure will make the Aino poor.
The pine-tree goddess says: "Why did you eat of the poisonous fruits of Hades?" and instructs him to climb the pine-tree and fling himself down to recover his shape.
In a second dream, the pine-tree goddess says he cannot stay long after eating Hades' fruit; a goddess in Hades wished to marry him and had assumed bear form to lure him underground.

occurrences.motif_label: dream warning restores family
occurrences.basis: The former husband is warned in a dream to take back the younger wife and child, after which they live happily.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The former husband is warned in a dream to take back his younger wife and child; the three live happily, and the tale says most men thereafter abandon polygyny.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Okikurumi knew everything by means of two charms or treasures, a piece of writing and an abacus, which told him many things.

occurrences.motif_label: Instruction in animal cunning enables escape from a hunter
occurrences.basis: The young stag obeys instruction, applies learned survival tricks by feigning death, and escapes after the hunter loosens the bonds.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The stag’s sister asks him to instruct her son in deer devices; the nephew comes at the appointed time and receives instruction.
The Bodisat assures his sister that the nephew has learned the devices of deer and recites that the nephew has six tricks with which he will outdo the foe.

The young stag lies still, arranges his limbs, throws up earth and grass, hangs out his tongue, wets his body, swells his belly, breathes through one nostril, stiffens his frame, and appears like a corpse while flies and crows gather.
The hunter strikes the stag’s stomach, thinks the animal was caught early and is already putrid, loosens the bands, and begins collecting leaves and branches to dress the flesh.
The young stag rises, stands, shakes himself, stretches out his neck, and swiftly returns to his mother.

occurrences.basis: The Bodisat hermit explains that cold occurs whenever wind blows, whether in the dark or light half, and thereby pacifies the lion and tiger.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The tiger says cold comes in the dark half of the month, the lion says it comes in the light half, and they ask the Bodisat to solve the difficulty.
The Bodisat states that cold occurs whenever the wind blows, in either half of the month, because cold is caused by wind; he pacifies the two friends.

occurrences.basis: The goat speaks, recalls former births, and explains the moral consequence of taking life to the Brāhman.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After being prepared, the goat laughs loudly, then weeps loudly, and tells the young Brāhman to ask about it in the teacher's presence.

The goat, remembering former births, says he had once been a Brāhman who killed a goat for the Feast of the Dead; because of this he has had his head cut off in five hundred births, less one, and this is the last.
The Brāhman says he will not kill the goat and will protect it, while the goat replies that he cannot escape death that day and that his past evil is powerful.

occurrences.motif_label: tree spirit appears in the sky as moral teacher
occurrences.basis: The Bodisat is born as the Genius of a tree, appears cross-legged in the sky, and teaches the multitude to abstain from taking life.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At that time the Bodisat had been born as the Genius of a tree growing at that spot.
The tree Genius seats himself cross-legged in the sky and teaches: “The living would not slay the living; / For he who taketh life shall surely grieve!”
The Great Being preaches the Truth, frightens the people with fear of hell, and after hearing him they give up taking life, give gifts, and do other good deeds.
The Teacher summarizes the Jātaka: “I at that time was the Genius of the tree.”

occurrences.motif_label: Tree spirit as moral instructor
occurrences.basis: A deity associated with a banyan-tree speaks from the tree to rebuke the landholder's attempt to fulfill a vow by killing animals, and the community changes its conduct afterward.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In Kāsi, a village landed proprietor promises an offering to the Genius of a Banyan-tree by the village gate and, after returning safely, slays animals and goes to the tree to free himself from the vow.
The tree-god, standing in a fork of the tree, says: “Not by such deeds as these are the wise made free.”
From that time people refrain from life-destroying deeds and live righteously.
The Teacher sums up the Jātaka: “I at that time was the Genius of the Tree.”

The recalled stanza says: “I saw the marks of feet that had gone down, / I saw no marks of feet that had returned,” followed by the plan to drink water through a reed without becoming the demon's prey.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The demon admits he haunts the spot and has power over those who go down into the pool, even birds, and threatens to devour all the monkeys.
The Bodisat says the monkeys will drink through Naḷa-canes from the pond without entering it, so the demon will have no power to eat them.

occurrences.basis: The monkey king devises a safe way for the troop to drink, and the antelope uses careful observation and inference to avoid the hunter’s trap.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Bodisat appeals to the Ten Great Perfections, blows into Naḷa-canes so they become hollow, and commands all canes around the pond to be perforated throughout.
The Bodisat and eighty thousand monkeys drink water through canes while seated safely on the bank; the water-demon fails to gain power over them and returns sorrowfully.

When Brahma-datta reigns in Benares, the Bodisat is a Kurunga antelope eating fruit; a deerstalker tracks deer, builds a platform in the fruit tree, waits with a javelin, and the antelope pauses to reconnoitre for danger.
The hunter throws fruit down in front of the antelope; the antelope infers that a hunter is above, discerns him, addresses the tree about its abnormal fruit-falling, and says he will go elsewhere.
The hunter hurls his javelin and says he has lost the antelope; the Bodisat replies that the hunter has not escaped the hells and torments resulting from his conduct, then escapes.

occurrences.motif_label: wise animal incarnation corrects a king
occurrences.basis: The Bodisat as a dog exposes the king’s unjust judgment, proves the truth, and teaches righteousness.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Bodisat comes to life as a dog and lives in a great cemetery attended by several hundred dogs.
The Bodisat questions the justice of killing all dogs without knowing the culprits and argues that exempting royal dogs while killing poor dogs is partiality and slaughter of the weak.
The Bodisat names the king’s own thoroughbred dogs as culprits and proves it by having them drink crushed Dabba grass in buttermilk, after which they vomit bits of leather.
The king, delighted, gives his sceptre to the Bodisat; the Bodisat teaches righteousness and the Five Commandments, exhorts the king to continue in well doing, and returns the sceptre.

The king remains firm in the Bodisat’s teaching, does charity and good deeds for life, and after death is reborn in the world of the gods.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At Jetavana, the Teacher addresses a monk who had lost heart and says that formerly the wise exerted themselves unremittingly and did not give up after receiving a check.

evidence.locator: lines 10751-10871, wounded horse’s speech and stanza
evidence.quote_or_summary: The wounded horse says no other horse can break the remaining line or take the last king and asks to be helped up and armored again: “Though fallen on his side, / And wounded sore with darts, / The Bhoja’s better than a hack!”
The knight helps the Bodisat up, binds his wound, harnesses him, rides him through the seventh line, captures the seventh king alive, and delivers him to the guard.

The Teacher says the wise formerly did not give in after receiving a check; the discouraged monk is established in Arahatship; the Teacher identifies the king as Ānanda, the knight as Sāriputta, and the Bhoja thoroughbred as himself.

occurrences.motif_label: cross-cultural transmission of moral tales
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly describes Buddhist tales moving through Greek, Persian, Arabic, Hebrew, Latin, and European languages and becoming moral lesson literature.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After Alexander's time, tales also found in the Buddhist collection became current in Greece and were preserved in poetic versions by Babrius and Phaedrus; they are called probably Buddhist in origin.

Around the first Crusade, an Arabic translation of a Persian work containing tales found in the Buddhist book was translated by Jews into Greek, Hebrew, and Latin, followed by translations into major European languages.

In the eleventh or twelfth century, a Latin translation of Barlaam and Josaphat was made from a Greek romance attributed to St. John of Damascus and based on the Buddhist Jataka book; European translations and adaptations followed.
The introduced fables and stories became popular in the Middle Ages and were used in sermons, story-books, romances, poems, and edifying dramas, with influence on European literary revival.

A collection of these and similar stories, ascribed to Aesop, became common European household literature and a moral lesson-book for children in the West, though described as first invented in the distant East.

occurrences.basis: The note links Nirvāna with extinction of fires and troubles and describes worldly existence as houses on fire.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Nirvāna is explained as a lasting state of happiness and peace reached by extinction of the passage’s fires and troubles.
“The three Bhavas seemed like houses on fire.”

occurrences.motif_label: Moral struggle toward liberation
occurrences.basis: The Great Struggle is described as overcoming delusion and sin through disciplined effort and attaining Nirvāna.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Great Struggle is moral training: mastery over passions, suppression of sinful thoughts, meditation on seven kinds of Wisdom, and fixed attention, leading to overcoming delusion and sin and attaining Nirvāna.

occurrences.motif_label: Council schism over discipline and sacred authority
occurrences.basis: The passage describes a council dividing the monastic order over rules, followed by rival claims about orthodox teaching and textual preservation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Order divided at the Council into a party advocating relaxation of ten rules and a stricter party; the laxer side was the majority and later held its own Great Council.

The Dīpavaŋsa says the monks of the Great Council turned the religion upside down, broke up original scriptures, made a new recension, distorted the Five Nikāyas, and put aside texts including a portion of the Jātaka.

occurrences.motif_label: Contested recension of sacred texts
occurrences.basis: The Dīpavaŋsa accuses the Great Council monks of breaking up original scriptures, rearranging discourses, changing meanings, and making substitute texts.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Dīpavaŋsa says the monks of the Great Council turned the religion upside down, broke up original scriptures, made a new recension, distorted the Five Nikāyas, and put aside texts including a portion of the Jātaka.

occurrences.motif_label: Liberating wisdom destroys delusion and craving
occurrences.basis: The cited Ādi Granth passage depicts divine knowledge as a storm that blows away delusion and breaks down the house-like supports of blindness and craving.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says the house figure is also found in Manu, the Lalita Vistara, and the Ādi Granth; the quoted Ādi Granth passage presents divine knowledge as a storm that removes delusion and breaks the supports and roof of craving.

occurrences.motif_label: self-cultivated wisdom leading to liberation
occurrences.basis: The passage describes meditation, realization of impermanence, self-produced inward change, and the disciple working out enlightenment.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The note says Buddhists had no prayer in this context; salvation consists in self-produced inward change. Kammaṭṭhāna meditation can lead to conviction of impermanence; a disciple may ask a teacher which way to adopt but must work out his own enlightenment.
Successful Kammaṭṭhāna leads to brotherhood, humility, holy calm, Nirvāna, and escape from transmigration.

occurrences.motif_label: beneficent supernatural or enlightened perception
occurrences.basis: The Buddha is represented as bringing the world before his mind’s eye and perceiving whom he could benefit during the day.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Buddha is frequently represented in later books as bringing the world before his mind’s eye in the morning and perceiving whom he could benefit during the day.

occurrences.motif_label: external ascetic signs do not purify inner doubt
occurrences.basis: The verse explicitly denies purifying power to nakedness, matted or plaited hair, dirt, fasting, ground-lying, ashes, and vigils when doubt remains.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “Not nakedness, not plaited hair, not dirt, / Not fasting oft, nor lying on the ground; / Not dust and ashes, nor vigils hard and stern, / Can purify that man who still is tossed / Upon the waves of doubt!”

occurrences.motif_label: body contemplated as impure beneath deceptive appearance
occurrences.basis: The body-verses enumerate internal parts and impurities, contrast appearance with reality, and call the admirer of bodily beauty a fool.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The verses describe the body as bound with bones and sinews, covered by flesh and skin, and filled with organs, mucus, sweat, fat, blood, bile, marrow, and other matter.
The verses say impurity flows from nine orifices, that a fool thinks the body beautiful, and that the body resembles an upas-tree and a filthy corpse.

occurrences.basis: The notes identify Happiness with Arahatship or Nirvāna and describe Nirvāna as the chief Fruit or highest result.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The notes explain that “Happiness” is also a name of Arahatship or Nirvāna, and that the chief Fruit refers to Nirvāna itself.
The note says it is striking that women among early Buddhists are several times declared to have reached the highest result of intellectual activity and earnest zeal, namely Nirvāna.

occurrences.basis: The note says real superiority and true Brāmanship come from self-culture and self-control rather than birth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Samaṇas are glossed as self-conquering renunciants; true Brāmanship is said to arise from self-culture and self-control, not birth.

occurrences.basis: The Buddha teaches deluded angels and, in a later legend, descends into hell for a similar purpose.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A December festival marks the close of the rainy season; the Buddha spent the period among angels to teach them, and a later legend says he descended into hell for a similar purpose.

occurrences.motif_label: Animal fable of apparent privilege hiding mortal danger
occurrences.basis: The cock and calf examples both contrast an animal’s apparent advantage with danger of being eaten or sacrificed, while the serving or laboring animal survives or benefits.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An analogous tale has a falcon praise his service to humans while a cock explains that he avoids capture because cocks are brought to table or fried in pans.
An Aesop-type fable has a calf laugh at a draught ox; later the ox has a holiday while the calf is led off to sacrifice.

occurrences.basis: The editor states that Sakka conquers the Titans not by might but through kindness to animals.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The editor says Sakka is made to conquer the Titans not by might but through kindness to animals.

occurrences.motif_label: didactic animal fable teaching moral conduct
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly describes animal fables used to teach good character and warn against talkativeness.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A lion-and-jackal fable is described as teaching the advantage of good character and as allowing titles based on the lion, jackal, or good character.
A tortoise fable is described as teaching the bad consequences of talkativeness and as being known under both 'Chatterbox' and 'Tortoise' titles.

occurrences.motif_label: Buddhist source claimed for a popular fable collection
occurrences.basis: Benfey is quoted as concluding that the Pancha Tantra was originally a Buddhist book, in part because many fables and tales in it can be traced in Buddhist writings.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage quotes Benfey’s conclusion that the Pancha Tantra was originally a Buddhist book, supported by the number of its fables and tales traceable in Buddhist writings and by the relation between their forms.

occurrences.motif_label: Instruction in worldly wisdom and royal conduct
occurrences.basis: The passage says the older collection was designed to teach princes right government and conduct, and that Bidpai composed the work to instruct Dabschelim in worldly wisdom.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Benfey is reported as arguing that the Pancha Tantra originally contained eleven to thirteen books and was designed to teach princes right government and conduct.
Arabic authors assign the translated work to Bidpai, who is said to have composed it to instruct Dabschelim, Alexander's successor in Indian possessions, in worldly wisdom.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE BARLAAM AND JOSAPHAT LITERATURE. / SUMMARY. / PART II. / ON THE HISTORY OF THE BIRTH STORIES IN INDIA.; lines 1933-2022
occurrences.motif_label: Transmission and adaptation of Buddhist story material
occurrences.basis: The passage proposes that Jātaka or Buddhist story material was taken to Bagdad, adapted into Barlaam and Josaphat and Kalilag and Damnag traditions, and altered to remove overt Buddhist markers.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says Barlaam and Josaphat and Kalilag and Damnag began at the same time and place, were based on Buddhist originals taken to Bagdad in the sixth century, and could have drawn from Birth Stories.
The passage suggests the work ascribed to Bidpai may have selected Jātaka stories focused on conduct of life and been preceded by a sketch of the Buddha's life in his last birth.

The passage asks why copies of Kalilah and Dimnah differ from each other and from Syriac Kalilag and Damnag, and why translations from a Buddhist book lack references to the Buddha or Buddhist expressions.
The passage proposes that later writers may have taken subject matter from Buddhist works while composing new works and discarding expressions that conflicted with their own religious beliefs.

occurrences.basis: The passage cites a principle attributed to early Buddhism that only teachings of the Buddha not contrary to sound reason are true.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “only that teaching of the Buddha’s is true which contraveneth not sound reason”

evidence.quote_or_summary: Headings include the last Bodisat’s descent from heaven, birth, song of angels, prophecies by Kāḷa Devala and Brāhman priests, ploughing festival, skill and wisdom, four visions, and the birth of the Bodisat’s son.

occurrences.basis: The passage notes multiple stories told to a love-sick monk as warnings and describes verses added by way of moral.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Some Introductory Stories repeat the principal idea of the story they introduce; different Birth Stories may be assigned the same time, place, and question, including ten stories told to a love-sick monk as warnings.
Some conclusions include moral verses called Abhisambuddha-gāthā, spoken by the Buddha after Buddhahood, distinguished from verses in the Birth Story spoken by the Bodisat.

occurrences.motif_label: successive accumulation of perfection toward Buddhahood
occurrences.basis: The Bodisat’s insight, goodness, and moral and intellectual perfection are described as the accumulated result of many generations of successive Bodisats.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Bodisat is described not as a soul transferred between bodies, but as the inheritor of character acquired by previous Bodisats; Buddhahood is the accumulated result of many generations of successive Bodisats.

occurrences.basis: The passage describes stories where the Bodisat functions as a chorus or moralizer only, not as an actor in the plot.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “the Bodisat appears as a sort of chorus, a moralizer only, and not an actor in the play” and in many stories is a “rukkha-devatā--the fairy or genius of a tree.”

occurrences.basis: The passage notes many stories in which the Bodisat is a rukkha-devatā, glossed as the fairy or genius of a tree.

occurrences.motif_label: Moral teaching through parable and fable
occurrences.basis: The passage says the Buddha taught by parables and may have invented fables or previous-birth tales to explain conduct and draw morals.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Buddha is described as teaching by parables and possibly inventing ‘some fable or some tale of a previous birth’ to address conduct among monks or draw a moral from events.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE BARLAAM AND JOSAPHAT LITERATURE. / SUMMARY. / PART II. / ON THE HISTORY OF THE BIRTH STORIES IN INDIA.; lines 2286-2335
occurrences.motif_label: preserved wisdom and ancestral custom
occurrences.basis: The passage presents the Jātakas as a valuable record for understanding earlier beliefs, habits, customs, and social life.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says the stories are valuable not only as evidence of intercommunication between East and West but also as assistance to folklore study, defined as study of beliefs and habits in earlier stages of development.
"in the Jātakas we have a nearly complete picture ... of the social life and customs and popular beliefs"
"the ancient Book of the Buddhist Jātaka Tales as a priceless record of the childhood of our race"

occurrences.motif_label: wisdom and fable literature transmission
occurrences.basis: The passage concerns the Kalilag and Damnag/Bidpai fable tradition and includes titles such as a book of the wise, the Seven Wise Masters, and moral or didactic later versions.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Kalilah wā Dimnah is listed as an Arabic version of the Syriac text by Abd-allah, son of Almokaffa, dated about 750 A.D., with recensions and editions noted.

The table lists English, German, Greek, Latin, Persian, French, Italian, and Hebrew versions; John of Capua's Latin Directorium Humanæ Vitæ is said to be among the best evidence for the lost earlier books.

The table continues with German, Ulm dialect, Latin, Spanish, Italian, and English versions or adaptations, including works connected to Baldo, Don Juan Manuel, Bonaventure des Periers, Firenzuola, Doni, and North.

occurrences.motif_label: Instruction through tales and fables
occurrences.basis: The passage states that one version includes tales told by Barlaam and that an English prose romance contains a fable of the Nightingale and the Fowler.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Provençal prose tale is described as containing the story of Josafat and the tales told by Barlaam, without the moralizations.

The English section lists versions of the legend and an English prose romance titled The History of the Five Wise Philosophers, or the Wonderful Relation of the Life of Jehoshaphat the Hermit, Son of Avenerian, King of Barma in India; it is described as an abridged translation of an Italian version and as containing one fable, the Nightingale and the Fowler.

occurrences.basis: Titles such as “Holding to the Truth,” “On True Divinity,” “The Wise Bird and the Fools,” and other moralizing headings indicate ethical or didactic themes in the listed stories.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ethical or religiously framed titles include “Holding to the Truth,” “On True Divinity,” “On Offering Food to the Dead,” “On Offerings given under a Vow,” “On Mercy to Animals,” and “The Wise Bird and the Fools.”

occurrences.passage_locator: PLACES AT WHICH THE TALES WERE TOLD. / TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII.; lines 3004-3127
occurrences.motif_label: many births as progressive fulfillment of Buddhahood
occurrences.basis: The passage says the Teacher and Leader fulfilled the conditions of Buddhahood through many former births and later attained omniscience.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The opening of the Nidānakathā describes the former births recounted by the Great Sage, the Teacher and Leader who desired the salvation of mankind and fulfilled the conditions of Buddhahood; it mentions collecting these births into the canon as the Jātaka and invokes the Great Sage, the Law, the Clergy, and the Three Gems.

The commentary is to be expounded through three Epochs: the Distant Epoch from the Bodhisatta’s resolution at Dīpankara’s feet to rebirth in Tusita after Vessantara; the Intermediate Epoch from leaving Tusita to omniscience on the throne of Knowledge; and the Proximate Epoch in the places of his earthly ministry.

occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 3130-3233
occurrences.motif_label: quest for deathless release
occurrences.basis: Sumedha deliberately seeks Nirvāṇa, the road to release from existence, through secluded contemplation and doctrinal reasoning.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “I am subject to birth, to decay, to disease, to death” and “There is, there must be a road ... that I may obtain release from existence.”
Sumedha reasons that as pain has pleasure, heat has cold, and evil has good, so existence and birth must have cessation; the fires of lust and passion have an extinction in Nirvāṇa.

occurrences.source_title: Buddhist birth stories; or, Jataka tales, Volume 1
occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 3235-3348
occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom through corrective similes
occurrences.basis: Sumedha reasons and ponders through repeated similes distinguishing the availability of Nirvana, the road, and the teacher from a person's failure to seek them.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sumedha reasons with three prose similes: a man in filth should seek a lotus pond; a man surrounded by robbers should use a way of escape; a sick man should seek a physician. These are applied to Nirvana, the road to Nirvana, and the spiritual guide.
Verses 24-29 restate the similes of the lake of Nirvana, the way of bliss, and the teacher or healer, emphasizing that failure to seek them is not their fault.

After pondering nine similes, Sumedha gives away treasure, renounces pleasures, departs from Amara to Himavanta, builds a hermitage near Dhammaka, embraces Rishi ascetic life, wears bark garments, lives at a tree foot on wild fruits, and practices strenuously.

occurrences.source_title: Buddhist birth stories; or, Jataka tales, Volume 1
occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 3350-3445
occurrences.motif_label: ascetic renunciation and attainment of supernatural faculties
occurrences.basis: Sumedha leaves ordinary shelter for tree-foot asceticism, rejects cultivated food, practices strenuously, and attains supernatural faculties.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sumedha says he built a cloister, put on bark raiment, left the hut, and went to the tree-foot.
Sumedha rejects sown and planted grain, eats fruits of the earth, strives while sitting, standing, and walking, and attains the might of the Faculties within seven days.

occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 3447-3547
occurrences.motif_label: Bodhisattva vow to save beings before personal liberation
occurrences.basis: Sumedha says he could end his passions and attain Nirvāṇa, but instead resolves to attain omniscience and become a Buddha to save men and angels.

evidence.locator: lines 3447-3547; prose after verse 63 and verses 64-65
evidence.quote_or_summary: While lying in the mire, Sumedha thinks he could destroy human passions and enter Nirvāṇa, but asks why he should do so in disguise and resolves to attain omniscience and become a Buddha.

evidence.locator: lines 3447-3547; prose after verse 63 and verses 66-68
evidence.quote_or_summary: “Embarking in the ship of the Truth, I will carry across with me men and angels.”

occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 3549-3662
occurrences.motif_label: Prophecy of a future Buddha
occurrences.basis: A Buddha uses prescient vision to foretell Sumedha’s eventual Buddhahood as Gotama after vast ages and gives details of the future life.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Dīpankara stands by Sumedha’s head, sees him lying in the mire, uses prescient gaze, and declares that after four asankheyyas and a hundred thousand cycles he will become Buddha Gotama.
The prophecy names Kapilavatthu, Māyā, Suddhodana, Upatissa, Kolita, Ānanda, Khemā, and Uppalavaṇṇā as figures in Gotama’s future life and community.

The prophecy describes Gotama’s departure, austerities, rice-milk or rice-pottage meal, Neranjarā riverbank, approach to the Bodhi-tree, salutation of the Bodhi throne, and Buddhahood beneath an Indian fig tree called Assattha.

occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 3549-3662
occurrences.motif_label: Omens confirming future Buddhahood
occurrences.basis: Angels say that the auguries appearing for former Bodhisattas have appeared for Sumedha and that one to whom these omens appear will surely become Buddha.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Bodhisatta sits cross-legged on a heap of flowers to investigate the Perfections; angels from ten thousand worlds assemble, applaud, say the auguries of former Bodhisattas have appeared, and urge him to exert himself.

occurrences.motif_label: Remembered former lives used as moral exempla
occurrences.basis: The orthodox account says the Buddha remembers many previous births and uses that experience to explain events, point morals, and tell tales.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The orthodox Buddhist account says the Buddha told stories of his own previous births to explain events; disciples learned and repeated them; 550 were collected, transmitted in Pāli, carried to Ceylon by Mahinda, translated into Siŋhalese, and later re-translated into Pāli.

occurrences.motif_label: Sacred stories preserved through disciples and missionary transmission
occurrences.basis: The passage describes disciples learning and repeating the stories, a collection of 550 Jātakas, and later transmission to Ceylon by Mahinda.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The orthodox Buddhist account says the Buddha told stories of his own previous births to explain events; disciples learned and repeated them; 550 were collected, transmitted in Pāli, carried to Ceylon by Mahinda, translated into Siŋhalese, and later re-translated into Pāli.

occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 3664-3798
occurrences.motif_label: Prophecy of future Buddhahood
occurrences.basis: The Bodhisatta is repeatedly told by cosmic witnesses that he will become a Buddha, and he accepts the prophecy as certain because Buddha-speech is unfailing.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Dwellers of ten thousand worlds behold him and proclaim, “Surely thou shalt be a Buddha”; the omens are said to match those seen in former ages when Bodhisatta sat cross-legged.
An exhortation urges strenuous effort; the Bodhisatta is glad and reflects that Buddhas or Conquerors do not speak doubtful, vain, or false words, so he will become a Buddha.
After hearing the words of Dīpankara Buddha and the angels of ten thousand worlds, the Bodhisatta is filled with immeasurable resolution and concludes that the word of Buddhas cannot fail.

occurrences.motif_label: Unfailing sacred speech verified by natural certainties
occurrences.basis: The Bodhisatta states that Buddhas do not speak false or doubtful words and compares their word to certain events such as falling objects, death, sunrise, lion-roaring, and childbirth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An exhortation urges strenuous effort; the Bodhisatta is glad and reflects that Buddhas or Conquerors do not speak doubtful, vain, or false words, so he will become a Buddha.
The Buddhas’ word is compared in certainty to a clod falling to the ground, mortal death, sunrise after night, a lion’s roar after leaving its den, and childbirth.

occurrences.source_title: Buddhist birth stories; or, Jataka tales, Volume 1
occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 3800-3919
occurrences.motif_label: Quest for Buddha-making conditions
occurrences.basis: Sumedha deliberately searches through all directions for the conditions that mature Buddhaship and identifies perfections to undertake.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sumedha resolves, “I shall surely become Buddha,” and searches “above and below, in all the ten directions” for Buddha-making conditions.
He beholds the first Gift-perfection or Almsgiving, described as the high road followed by former sages, and undertakes it for Buddhaship.
Sumedha identifies the second perfection, Morality or Moral Practice, practiced by former sages, and resolves to undertake it for Buddhahood.
Sumedha identifies the third perfection, Abnegation, and is told to look upon all births as prison-houses and set his face toward self-abnegation for release from existence.
Sumedha identifies the fourth perfection, Wisdom, and is instructed to avoid no subject of knowledge and to question wise men constantly.

occurrences.source_title: Buddhist birth stories; or, Jataka tales, Volume 1
occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 3800-3919
occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom gained by questioning all wise persons
occurrences.basis: The fourth perfection instructs Sumedha to avoid no subject of knowledge and to approach all wise men with questions.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sumedha identifies the fourth perfection, Wisdom, and is instructed to avoid no subject of knowledge and to question wise men constantly.
Wisdom is compared to a monk who avoids no small, great, or middling families on begging rounds and obtains subsistence.

occurrences.source_title: Buddhist birth stories; or, Jataka tales, Volume 1
occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 3921-4041
occurrences.motif_label: progressive search for Buddha-making conditions
occurrences.basis: Sumedha repeatedly reasons that more conditions remain, seeks or investigates them, and beholds successive perfections leading toward Buddhahood.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sumedha beholds the fifth Perfection of Exertion, said to have been practised by former sages, resolves to attain it, and is instructed to exert himself like a lion, king of beasts, in order to attain Buddhahood.

Sumedha beholds the sixth Perfection of Longsuffering, said to have been practised by former Buddhas, and is instructed to endure praise and reproach as the earth endures pure and impure things thrown upon it.

Sumedha beholds the seventh Perfection of Truth, said to have been practised by former Buddhas, and is instructed not to utter a conscious lie even if a thunderbolt descends, but to keep to truth as Venus keeps its path.

Sumedha beholds the eighth Perfection of Resolution, said to have been practised by former Buddhas, resolves to attain it, and is instructed to remain immovable like a rocky mountain unshaken by winds.
Sumedha beholds the ninth Perfection of Good-will and is instructed to have one mind toward friends and foes, like water that refreshes good men and bad alike.

occurrences.source_title: Buddhist birth stories; or, Jataka tales, Volume 1
occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 4043-4161
occurrences.motif_label: Ten Perfections as the necessary conditions for Buddhahood
occurrences.basis: The passage states that the ten Perfections are all the conditions that bring Buddhaship to perfection and that Sumedha investigates and masters them.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sumedha concludes that the ten Perfections alone are the conditions for Buddhahood, finds them in his heart, masters them in repeated orders, calls them sacrifices of limbs, property, and life, and is compared to one churning the Cakkavāla ocean with Mount Meru.

The Teacher tells them not to fear; he says wise Sumedha, predicted that day to become the Buddha Gotama, is mastering the Perfections, and that his piety causes the ten thousand worlds to quake and thunder.

Verses recap that the attending multitude swooned, jars were crushed, the frightened crowd approached the Buddha, and Dīpankara explained that the predicted future Buddha was investigating the time-honoured Conditions followed by Buddhas, causing the earth of ten thousand worlds to shake.

occurrences.source_title: Buddhist birth stories; or, Jataka tales, Volume 1
occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 4163-4291
occurrences.motif_label: Bodhisatta’s great vow and undertaking of perfections
occurrences.basis: Sumedha takes on the Perfections, makes a firm resolve before Dīpankara, and declares his future attainment of Buddhahood after a vast span.

evidence.quote_or_summary: People of Ramma hear the Buddha’s words, bring offerings to the Bodhisatta, bow to him, and return; the Bodhisatta takes on the Perfections, resolves, bows to Dīpankara, and rises from his seat.
The Bodhisatta resolves that after fulfilling the ten Perfections for four asankheyyas and a hundred thousand cycles he will become a Buddha; he rises into the air and returns to Himavanta.

Verses describe angels and men sprinkling flowers, blessing the Bodhisatta, urging fulfillment of the ten Perfections, and using similes of trees, moon, sun, rivers, and ocean; he takes the ten Conditions and enters the forest.

occurrences.source_title: Buddhist birth stories; or, Jataka tales, Volume 1
occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 4163-4291
occurrences.motif_label: Buddha as universal teacher and converter
occurrences.basis: Dīpankara preaches the Law, establishes followers in refuges and practices, converts multitudes, awakens distant persons, and teaches in the angel world.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The people of Ramma support the priesthood; Dīpankara preaches the Law, establishes followers in refuges and faith, completes the duties of a Buddha, and attains Nirvāṇa in an element where no trace remains.

Verses state that Dīpankara establishes people in refuges, precepts, priesthood, Fruitions, Knowledges, Acquisitions, Wisdoms, and supernatural Faculties; he saves many, awakens distant persons, and converts vast numbers including in the angel world.

occurrences.source_title: Buddhist birth stories; or, Jataka tales, Volume 1
occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 4293-4363
occurrences.motif_label: Prophecy of future Buddhahood followed by renunciation
occurrences.basis: The Bodhisatta receives the prediction that he will become a Buddha, hears the preaching, gives up his kingdom, becomes a monk, masters the three Treasuries, gains faculties, and practices meditation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Bodhisatta is born as the universal monarch Vijitāvin, gives offerings to the priesthood, receives the prediction “He will become a Buddha,” hears the Law, gives up his kingdom, becomes a monk, gains faculties, practices meditation, and is reborn in the Brahma heavens.

occurrences.source_title: Buddhist birth stories; or, Jataka tales, Volume 1
occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 4522-4607
occurrences.motif_label: Truth as light dispelling darkness
occurrences.basis: A verse states that Mangala dispelled darkness in the world and held aloft the torch of truth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “Dispelling darkness in the world, held aloft the torch of truth.”

occurrences.source_title: Buddhist birth stories; or, Jataka tales, Volume 1
occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 4609-4690
occurrences.motif_label: Acquisition of wisdom by the vowed sage
occurrences.basis: The Bodisat as a sage is said to have acquired five kinds of Wisdom and eight sublime Acquisitions.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Nārada has three assemblies; the Bodisat as a vowed sage has five kinds of Wisdom and eight sublime Acquisitions, donates to the Order headed by the Buddha, offers red sandal wood, and receives a prophecy of future Buddhahood. Nārada's attributes and Bo-tree are listed.

occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 4692-4781
occurrences.motif_label: Prior-life offering followed by prophecy of future Buddhahood
occurrences.basis: Across multiple episodes, the Bodisat performs a devotional act before a Buddha or the Order and receives a prophecy of future Buddhahood.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sujāta has three assemblies; the Bodisat as universal monarch hears the Law, gives his kingdom with seven treasures to the Order, takes vows, and receives prophecy. Sujāta's city, family, disciples, Bambu Bo-tree, body height, and lifespan are listed.

Piyadassin appears after eighteen hundred world-cycles; the Bodisat as Kassapa hears the Law, builds a monastery, keeps the Refuges and Precepts, and receives a prophecy after eighteen hundred kalpas. Piyadassin's Priyaŋgu Bo-tree and other attributes are listed.

Atthadassin has three assemblies; the Bodisat as the ascetic Susima brings from heaven a sunshade of Mandārava flowers and offers it to the Teacher, who prophesies to him. Atthadassin's Champaka Bo-tree and bodily glory are listed.

Dhammadassin has three assemblies; the Bodisat as Sakka king of the gods offers sweet-smelling heavenly flowers and heavenly music, and the Teacher prophesies to him. Dhammadassin's red Kuravaka Bo-tree is listed.

Siddhattha appears ninety-four world-cycles ago; the Bodisat as the ascetic Mangala brings a great jambu fruit to the Tathāgata. After eating it, the Teacher prophesies Buddhahood ninety-four kalpas later. Siddhattha's Kanikāra Bo-tree is listed.

occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 4692-4781
occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom or enlightenment as dispelling darkness
occurrences.basis: Verses describe Atthadassin and Dhammadassin as dispelling thick darkness and Siddhattha as rising like the sun and ending darkness.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Verse descriptions say Atthadassin dispelled thick darkness and attained enlightenment, Dhammadassin dispelled thick darkness and illumined earth and heaven, and Siddhattha rose like the sun, ending darkness.

occurrences.passage_locator: SUPPLEMENTARY TABLES. / THE BIRTH STORIES. / INDEX                                              339 / INTRODUCTION.; lines 476-594
occurrences.motif_label: Bodisat as moral interpreter
occurrences.basis: The future Buddha pronounces a moral stanza in the ass story and serves as adviser seeking to cure the king's talkativeness in the tortoise story.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The frightened ass cries out like an ass, and the future Buddha speaks a stanza saying this is not a lion, tiger, or panther, but an ass dressed in a lion's skin.
The narrator notes that the tale's moral is contained in stanzas, one spoken by the Bodisat or future Buddha, and that the Bodisat identification is the essentially Buddhistic element.

The passage introduces a fable proper, 'The Talkative Tortoise'; Brahma-datta reigns in Benāres, the future Buddha becomes his adviser, and the king is so talkative that the future Buddha seeks a cure.

occurrences.motif_label: Talkativeness corrected by exemplary tale
occurrences.basis: The future Buddha seeks a cure for the talkative king, and the narrative immediately presents the fallen tortoise caused by failure to keep silent.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage introduces a fable proper, 'The Talkative Tortoise'; Brahma-datta reigns in Benāres, the future Buddha becomes his adviser, and the king is so talkative that the future Buddha seeks a cure.
Villagers call out that two wild ducks are carrying a tortoise on a stick; the tortoise tries to reply, lets go over the king's palace in Benāres, falls into the open courtyard, and splits in two.
A general cry arises about the fallen tortoise; the king goes with the future Buddha and courtiers to the place and asks the Bodisat how the tortoise came to fall there.

occurrences.motif_label: Instruction, doctrine, and moral perfection
occurrences.basis: In the Phussa episode the Bodisat learns the three Piṭakas, preaches the Law to the people, and fulfills the Perfection of Morality; in the Vessabhū episode he becomes righteous and meditates on the Buddha.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Phussa appears in the same Maṇḍakalpa. The Bodisat is born as warrior-chief Vijitavī, lays aside his kingdom, takes vows under the Teacher, learns the three Piṭakas, preaches the Law, fulfills the Perfection of Morality, and receives a prophecy. Phussa’s city, family, disciples, Āmalaka Bo-tree, height, and lifespan are listed.

Vessabhū appears after Sikhin. The Bodisat is born as king Sudassana, gives robes and other things to the Order with the Buddha at their head, takes vows, becomes righteous in conduct, meditates on the Buddha, and receives a prophecy. Vessabhū’s city, family, disciples, Sal Bo-tree, height, and lifespan are listed.

occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 4875-4993
occurrences.motif_label: Successive Buddhas prophesy the future Buddha
occurrences.basis: The Bodisat receives prophecy from Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, Kassapa, and, in summary, from each of the twenty-four Buddhas beginning with Dīpaŋkara.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Kakusandha has one assembly of forty thousand monks. The Bodisat as King Kshema gives robes, bowls, collyriums, and drugs to the Order, hears the Law, takes vows, and receives prophecy; Kakusandha’s city, family, disciples, Sirīsa Bo-tree, height, and age are listed.

Koṇāgamana has one assembly of thirty thousand monks. The Bodisat as King Pabbata goes with ministers to the Teacher, hears the Law, gives silk and fine gold-woven cloths, takes vows, and receives prophecy; Koṇāgamana’s city, family, disciples, Udumbara Bo-tree, height, and age are listed.

Kassapa has one assembly of twenty thousand monks. The Bodisat as the Brahman youth Jotipāla, friend of Ghaṭīkāra, goes to the Teacher, hears the Law, takes vows, learns the three Piṭakas, serves the religion of the Buddhas, and receives prophecy; Kassapa’s birthplace, family, disciples, Nigrodha Bo-tree, height, and age are listed.

The Bodisat is said to have come down through four asaŋkheyyas plus one hundred thousand kalpas, making resolve in the presence of twenty-four Buddhas beginning with Dīpaŋkara; after Kassapa there is no other Buddha besides the present supreme Buddha, and the Bodisat received prophecy from each of the twenty-four Buddhas.

occurrences.motif_label: Long quest through many births to Buddhahood
occurrences.basis: The Bodisat comes through vast kalpas and many births, searches for Buddha-making conditions, fulfills Perfections, and proceeds up to Vessantara.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Bodisat is said to have come down through four asaŋkheyyas plus one hundred thousand kalpas, making resolve in the presence of twenty-four Buddhas beginning with Dīpaŋkara; after Kassapa there is no other Buddha besides the present supreme Buddha, and the Bodisat received prophecy from each of the twenty-four Buddhas.

The Bodisat exerts himself according to his resolve at Dīpaŋkara’s feet, searches for Buddha-making conditions, beholds the Perfection of Almsgiving, and comes down through many births fulfilling the Perfections up to Vessantara.

Verses praise rewards of Bodisats destined for Buddhahood: they traverse a long road through vast ages and are not born in hell, between worlds, as hungry ghosts, as small animals, or with certain impairments when born among humans.

occurrences.motif_label: Buddhas as lights dispelling darkness
occurrences.basis: The catalogue says the perfect Buddhas appeared like suns, dispelled thick darkness, and blazed like flames of fire before going out.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A verse catalogue names many perfect Buddhas from Taṇhaŋkara and Dīpaŋkara through Kassapa and says the perfect Buddhas were sinless and well-controlled, appearing like suns, dispelling darkness, blazing like flames of fire, and going out.

occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom reveals a hidden serpent
occurrences.basis: As Senaka, the Bodisat uses wisdom to identify a snake hidden in bellows and free a brahman from pain.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In the Sattubhatta Birth as Senaka, the Bodisat uses wisdom to free a brahman from pain by pointing out a snake that had entered the bellows.

occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 5145-5241
occurrences.motif_label: salvific quest for omniscience
occurrences.basis: The deities state that the Bodisat fulfilled the Ten Perfections with the hope of reaching Omniscience for the salvation of mankind.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “Now has the moment come, O Blessed One, for thy Buddhahood; now has the time, O Blessed One, arrived!”

occurrences.motif_label: Dual destiny of sacred ruler or renunciant sage
occurrences.basis: The interpreters predict that the child will become a Universal Monarch if he remains a householder, or a Buddha if he adopts religious life.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Brāhmans tell the king not to be anxious: the queen has conceived a male child, a son who will become a Universal Monarch if he lives as a householder, but a Buddha who removes ignorance and sin if he leaves home for religious life.

occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 5434-5543
occurrences.motif_label: Salvific teaching and perfected wisdom
occurrences.basis: After the Tathāgata's enlightenment, Nālaka hears the way of salvation, returns to the Himālayas, and reaches Arahatship.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After the Tathāgata attains complete Enlightenment, Nālaka hears the way of salvation, returns to the Himālayas, reaches Arahatship, and dies near a Golden Hill after seven more months.

occurrences.motif_label: twofold royal or spiritual destiny
occurrences.basis: The marked child is predicted either to become a Universal Monarch if he remains a householder or a Buddha if he takes vows; Kondanya resolves the alternative toward Buddhahood.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “If a man having such marks should remain a householder, he becomes a Universal Monarch; but if he takes the vows, he becomes a Buddha.”
Kondanya sees the perfection of the auspicious marks, raises one finger, and says the Bodisat will become a Buddha and remove veils of sin and ignorance from the world.

occurrences.motif_label: prophecy by reading bodily signs
occurrences.basis: Specialists in signs interpret the Bodisat's marks and make predictions about his future destiny.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Eight Brahmans are called recognizers of signs and are said to have interpreted the dream on the night of conception.
“If a man having such marks should remain a householder, he becomes a Universal Monarch; but if he takes the vows, he becomes a Buddha.”
Kondanya sees the perfection of the auspicious marks, raises one finger, and says the Bodisat will become a Buddha and remove veils of sin and ignorance from the world.

occurrences.motif_label: miraculous contemplative child under a tree
occurrences.basis: As a child, the Bodisat enters the first Jhāna beneath a Jambu-tree, and the tree's shadow remains fixed and circular.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The king takes his son to the festival site and has the child's couch placed under a dense Jambu-tree shade, with a star-inlaid golden canopy and curtain.
When the nurses leave, the future Buddha looks around, sees no one, sits cross-legged, holds his breath, and enters the first Jhāna.
The shadows of other trees turn, but the Jambu-tree's shadow remains steady and circular; the nurses return, see the Bodisat sitting cross-legged and report the shadow miracle to the king.

occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 5655-5757
occurrences.motif_label: Four Omens prompting world-renunciation
occurrences.basis: Divine beings show the Bodisat old age, sickness, death, and a mendicant; these sights agitate him and lead him to cherish renunciation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Angels decide Siddhattha’s Enlightenment is near and show Omens by making a son of the gods represent an aged man visible only to the Bodisat and charioteer.
The Bodisat asks about the aged man, laments the decay of living beings, returns agitated, and the king orders entertainments and guards to prevent renunciation.
On later outings the Bodisat sees a sick man and then a dead man represented by the gods; each time he returns agitated, and the king repeats and increases guarding measures.
The Bodisat sees one who has abandoned the world; the charioteer, inspired by the gods, calls him a mendicant friar and describes renunciation, which the Bodisat begins to cherish.

occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 5759-5862
occurrences.motif_label: awakening reflection prompted by a song
occurrences.basis: Kisā Gotamī's praise prompts the Bodisat to reflect on lasting peace and the extinction of passions.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Kisā Gotamī sees the Bodisat's beauty and majesty from a palace roof and sings that his mother, father, and wife are blessed.

The Bodisat reflects that peace is gained when the fires of lust, hatred, delusion, pride, credulity, and other sins cease; he resolves that day to break from household cares, renounce the world, and follow Nirvāna.

occurrences.source_title: Buddhist birth stories; or, Jataka tales, Volume 1
occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 5759-5862
occurrences.motif_label: sensual beauty revealed as decay or corpse-like repulsion
occurrences.basis: The entertainers' sleeping bodies transform the Bodisat's perception from pleasure to disgust, and the splendid room seems like a charnel-house.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Beautifully arrayed women skilled in dance and song perform with instruments, but the Bodisat takes no pleasure and falls asleep.
The women stop performing and sleep; the Bodisat wakes and sees them with stage properties laid aside, foaming, grinding teeth, yawning, muttering, gaping, and disordered in dress.

The Bodisat becomes more disgusted with lusts; the splendid apartment seems like a charnel-house, and life in various worlds seems like staying in a house taken by devouring flames. He resolves on the Great Renunciation.

occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 5759-5862
occurrences.motif_label: worldly life as burning house
occurrences.basis: Life in multiple worlds appears to the Bodisat as residence in a house overcome by devouring flames.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Bodisat becomes more disgusted with lusts; the splendid apartment seems like a charnel-house, and life in various worlds seems like staying in a house taken by devouring flames. He resolves on the Great Renunciation.

occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 5958-6057
occurrences.motif_label: Extraordinary mendicant mistaken for a superhuman being
occurrences.basis: The Bodisat begs in Rājagaha, and the guards and king are unsure whether he is a god, man, Nāga, Supaṇṇa, or other being.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Bodisat spends seven days in the mango grove Anūpiya, then walks to Rājagaha and begs food from door to door; the city is stirred by his beauty.
The guards tell the king they cannot tell whether the beggar is a god, man, Nāga, Supaṇṇa, or something else; the king orders them to observe how he leaves or eats.

occurrences.passage_locator: SUPPLEMENTARY TABLES. / THE BIRTH STORIES. / INDEX                                              339 / INTRODUCTION.; lines 596-738
occurrences.motif_label: Excessive speech brings ruin
occurrences.basis: The tortoise dies by speaking while holding the stick, and the incident is used as a direct admonition against talking beyond measure.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The future Buddha reasons that the tortoise made friends with wild ducks, bit a stick while they carried him through the air, tried to speak, let go, fell from the sky, and died.
“Verily the tortoise killed himself / Whilst uttering his voice”; the verses tell the king to speak wise words and not out of season.
The king asks whether the Teacher speaks of him; the Bodisat answers that whoever talks beyond measure meets mishap, and the king thereafter becomes a man of few words.

occurrences.passage_locator: SUPPLEMENTARY TABLES. / THE BIRTH STORIES. / INDEX                                              339 / INTRODUCTION.; lines 596-738
occurrences.motif_label: Supernatural witness exposes flatterers
occurrences.basis: The tree-god observes the crow and jackal, condemns their lying praise, and frightens them away.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The tree-god sees the crow and jackal flattering one another and eating Jambus, calls them chatterers of lies, makes himself visible in awful shape, and frightens them away.

occurrences.source_title: Buddhist birth stories; or, Jataka tales, Volume 1
occurrences.passage_locator: SUPPLEMENTARY TABLES. / THE BIRTH STORIES. / INDEX                                              339 / INTRODUCTION.; lines 596-738
occurrences.motif_label: Wise judge reveals true mother through compassion
occurrences.basis: The future Buddha devises a pulling test over a line, and the mother releases the child because his suffering moves her to grief.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The disputing mother and Yakshiṇī pass the future Buddha’s Judgment Hall; he hears them, summons them, asks if they will accept his decision, draws a line, and tells them to pull the child across it.
When the two pull the child, the mother sees his suffering, grieves as if her heart would break, lets him go, and stands weeping.

occurrences.motif_label: quest for Wisdom beyond inadequate paths
occurrences.basis: The Bodisat rejects trance attainments and later penance as not the way to wisdom, while aiming at complete enlightenment.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A king comes after hearing his men, offers the Bodisat his kingdom; the Bodisat refuses wealth and pleasures in hope of complete enlightenment; the king predicts Buddhahood and asks for a future visit.
The Bodisat grants the king's request, studies the ecstatic trance systems of Āḷāra Kāḷāma and Uddaka, rejects them as not the way to wisdom, and goes to Uruvela for the Great Struggle.
The six years' penance becomes widely known; the Bodisat perceives penance is not the way to Wisdom, resumes ordinary food, and regains the Thirty-two signs and gold-like color.

occurrences.motif_label: radiant holy figure beneath a sacred tree
occurrences.basis: The Bodisat sits at the foot of the tree, lights the eastern region, and later spends seven times seven days at the foot of the Tree of Wisdom.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sujātā tells Puṇṇā to watch the holy place. The Bodisat, after five dreams, concludes that he will become a Buddha that day and sits at the foot of the tree, lighting it with his glory.

Puṇṇā sees the Bodisat at the tree, the eastern region lit up, and the tree gold-colored by rays from his body; she thinks the god has descended from the tree to receive the offering and reports to Sujātā.

evidence.locator: lines 6257 and following passage text supplied
evidence.quote_or_summary: After dressing in the garb of Arahats, he sits facing east, divides the rice into forty-nine balls, eats it without water, and for forty-nine days at the Tree of Wisdom has no other food, bathing, tooth-washing, or natural cravings, living on meditative joys.

occurrences.motif_label: miraculous nourishment sustaining sacred transformation
occurrences.basis: The milk-rice is miraculously produced and divinely infused, then becomes the Bodisat’s only food for forty-nine days during the period after becoming a Buddha.

evidence.quote_or_summary: On the same morning she milks the eight cows; calves stay away, milk streams into vessels, and the boiling rice-milk shows wonders: right-turning bubbles, no lost drops, and no smoke.
Four guardian angels keep watch; Brahma holds a canopy, Sakka lights the fire, and gods gather and infuse Sap of life into the vessel of milk-rice for the day of Buddhahood.

occurrences.motif_label: recurrent Buddha-pattern on enlightenment day
occurrences.basis: The passage states that receiving a golden vessel is proper on the day of Buddhahood, that many Bodisats bathed at the same ferry on the day of complete Enlightenment, and that the garb had been worn by many Buddhas.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage generalizes several details: gods infuse food in special ways on the day of Buddhahood and Death; a golden vessel is proper on the day of attaining Buddhahood; many Bodisats have gone down into the same bathing place on their day of complete Enlightenment; and the garb was worn by many Buddhas.

occurrences.motif_label: omen confirming destined awakening
occurrences.basis: The golden vessel is explicitly cast as a test of whether the Bodisat will become a Buddha that day, and its upstream motion is followed by recognition from the snake king.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After eating milk-rice, the Bodisat casts a golden vessel into the river as an omen; it moves upstream, reaches Kāḷa Nāgarāja’s palace, strikes bowls of three previous Buddhas, and the snake king praises the new Buddha.

occurrences.motif_label: sacred tree as awakening place
occurrences.basis: The Bodisat proceeds to the Tree of Wisdom and sits at the Bo-tree at the place where all Buddhas sit for attaining Buddhahood.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Bodisat spends the day in a sāla grove and proceeds toward the Tree of Wisdom along a divinely adorned path, while superhuman beings offer flowers and heavenly songs.
The eastern place is identified as where all Buddhas sit cross-legged and as unshaken; the grass forms a fourteen-cubit seat, and the Bodisat vows not to leave until complete insight is attained.

occurrences.basis: The Bodisat vows that his body may dry up but that he will not leave the seat until attaining complete insight.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The eastern place is identified as where all Buddhas sit cross-legged and as unshaken; the grass forms a fourteen-cubit seat, and the Bodisat vows not to leave until complete insight is attained.

occurrences.motif_label: Demonic assault overcome by perfected virtue
occurrences.basis: Māra attacks Siddhattha with hosts, elements, weapons, and darkness, but Siddhattha remains seated and relies on perfected virtues.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Māra tells his host to attack Siddhattha from behind; Siddhattha sees the gods have fled, notes he has no relatives to help him, and resolves to use the ten cardinal virtues as shield and sword while meditating on the Ten Perfections.
Māra sends a destructive whirlwind and then a mighty rain and flood, but through the Great Being's goodness the wind cannot shake his robe and the flood cannot wet even a dew-drop-sized place on it.

Māra sends storms of rocks, weapons, charcoal, ashes, sand, and mud; these come with smoke, flame, or heat but become heavenly flowers, sandalwood dust, or heavenly perfume at the future Buddha's feet.

Māra brings fourfold darkness to terrify Siddhattha, but it vanishes before the future Buddha; the passage lists nine failed assaults: wind, rain, rocks, weapons, charcoal, ashes, sand, mud, and darkness.

occurrences.motif_label: Contest for a sacred seat or throne
occurrences.basis: Māra claims the seat is meant for him; Siddhattha says it belongs to the one who has perfected virtues and is at the throne of Buddhas-to-be on the day of Enlightenment.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Māra commands his host to seize, slay, or drive away the prince, mounts the Mountain-girded, approaches the future Buddha, and tells Siddhattha to get up from the seat because it is meant for Māra.

The Great Being tells Māra that Māra has not perfected the cardinal, lesser, or higher virtues, nor sacrificed himself in the five great acts of self-renunciation, nor sought knowledge, the salvation of the world, and wisdom; therefore the seat belongs to Siddhattha.
"I have reached the throne on which sit the Buddhas-to-be when they are perfect in all goodness, on that day when they shall reach Enlightenment."

occurrences.motif_label: Past self-renunciation and almsgiving validate present spiritual attainment
occurrences.basis: Siddhattha grounds his claim to the seat in perfected virtues, great acts of self-renunciation, seeking knowledge and salvation, and alms in the Wessantara birth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Great Being tells Māra that Māra has not perfected the cardinal, lesser, or higher virtues, nor sacrificed himself in the five great acts of self-renunciation, nor sought knowledge, the salvation of the world, and wisdom; therefore the seat belongs to Siddhattha.

Siddhattha declares he has reached the throne of Buddhas-to-be on the day of Enlightenment. Māra calls his followers as witnesses to his almsgiving, and they shout agreement. Siddhattha says he has no living witness and calls the great solid earth to witness the seven hundredfold great alms he gave as Wessantara.

occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 6477-6591
occurrences.motif_label: Enlightenment as supreme wisdom
occurrences.basis: The passage centers on the acquisition of special knowledges, realization of causation, Omniscience, and complete Enlightenment.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Before sunset the Great Being routs the Evil One's army; while the Bo-tree seems to pay homage, he gains knowledge of past, present, and the causal chain in the three watches of the night.

On realizing the twelvefold chain of causation and attaining complete Enlightenment at dawn, ten thousand world-systems quake and become glorious, with banners, flowers, light, sweet waters, halted rivers, restored faculties, and loosened bonds.
After attaining Omniscience, he sings the Hymn of Triumph, described as sung by all Buddhas, about many births, the cause of individuality, broken house-beams, Nirvāna, and the end of craving.

occurrences.motif_label: contemplative wisdom after awakening
occurrences.basis: The Master reflects on the place of omniscience, thinks out the Abhidhamma Pitaka, meditates on Truth, and is described as sinless and wise in the cited verses.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Master stands northeast of the throne, thinks that he attained omniscience there, gazes at the spot for seven days, and the place becomes the Dāgaba of the Steadfast Gaze.

For the fourth week angels create a house of gems northwest of the Bo-tree; the Master sits there cross-legged and thinks out the Abhidhamma Pitaka. Abhidhammikas give two explanations of the House of Gems.
After four weeks near the Bo-tree, the Master goes in the fifth week to the Shepherd’s Nigrodha-tree, sits meditating on Truth, and enjoys the sweetness of Nirvāna.

The Blessed One says, “Depart ye! Why strive ye thus?” and declares, “I have put away lust, have put away ill-will, have put away folly,” followed by verses asking how the Sinless, Wise One could be allured to a fall.

occurrences.motif_label: heavenly request for wisdom teaching
occurrences.basis: The Blessed One doubts whether he can explain the deep Truth; the ruler of the Brahma heavens asks him to proclaim it, and he grants the request.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Perfectly Enlightened One returns to the Shepherd’s Nigrodha-tree and, considering the depth of the Truth gained, doubts whether he can explain it to others.
The great Ruler of the Brahma heavens, with rulers and archangels from many world-systems, asks the Blessed Lord to proclaim the Truth.

occurrences.motif_label: journey to inaugurate first teaching
occurrences.basis: The Master chooses the five mendicants at the Deer-forest and determines to go there to inaugurate the Kingdom of Righteousness, then travels toward Benares.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Master grants the request, considers Aḷāra and Uddaka but perceives them dead, then chooses the five mendicants at the Deer-forest in Benares and resolves to inaugurate the Kingdom of Righteousness there.
At dawn he takes robe and bowl, travels halfway, meets the Hindu mendicant Upaka, announces how he became a Buddha, and arrives near Benares that evening.

occurrences.motif_label: Teaching that initiates stages of awakening
occurrences.basis: Multiple named discourses and proclamations cause hearers to attain the First Path, Nirvana, Arahatship, or lay discipleship.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Surrounded by myriads of angels, the Buddha teaches The Foundation of the Kingdom of Righteousness; Kondanya and then the other elders attain the First Path, and all five attain Nirvana after the discourse On the Non-existence of the Soul.
Yasa leaves home, hears “Follow me, Yasa!”, attains the First Path and Arahatship, and his fifty-four companions are received into the order and attain Arahatship.

At Uruvela the Buddha overcomes three ascetic brothers and their thousand disciples by 3,500 miracles, receives them into the Order, establishes them in Arahatship through a discourse on fire, and goes to the Palm-grove near Rajagaha.

The multitude praises the power of the Buddhas; the Buddha says he overcame Kassapa in former ages, utters the Maha Narada Kassapa Jataka, proclaims the Four Truths, and the king with nearly all his retinue attains the First Path.

occurrences.motif_label: Miraculous conversion of rival ascetics
occurrences.basis: The Buddha overcomes the ascetic brothers by miracles, receives them into the Order, and Uruvela Kassapa publicly declares discipleship and rejects fire sacrifice.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At Uruvela the Buddha overcomes three ascetic brothers and their thousand disciples by 3,500 miracles, receives them into the Order, establishes them in Arahatship through a discourse on fire, and goes to the Palm-grove near Rajagaha.

The assembly wonders about the relation between the Great Mendicant and Uruvela Kassapa; the Buddha questions Kassapa, Kassapa rejects reliance on sacrifice and offerings, declares the Buddha his master, and rises into the air to heights of one through seven palm-trees.

The multitude praises the power of the Buddhas; the Buddha says he overcame Kassapa in former ages, utters the Maha Narada Kassapa Jataka, proclaims the Four Truths, and the king with nearly all his retinue attains the First Path.

occurrences.motif_label: Sending forth enlightened disciples to teach
occurrences.basis: After many become arahats, the Master sends sixty mendicants in different directions to preach and teach.

evidence.quote_or_summary: When sixty-one persons are arahats, the Master sends sixty mendicants in different directions with the words, “Go forth ... preaching and teaching.”

occurrences.motif_label: wisdom-endowed sacred teacher draws praise and devotion
occurrences.basis: The Buddha is described as beautiful, endowed with the tenfold power of Wisdom, praised by Sakka, and sought by a vast crowd.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Eighteen koṭis from Rājagaha go to the Grove of Reeds to see the Buddha; the road and grove are crowded, and the place is associated with praise of a Buddha's characteristics and beauty.
Sakka's throne becomes hot as a warning; he understands that the Buddha may lack nourishment, takes the form of a young Brāhman, descends, makes way, and praises the Buddha, Truth, and Order.
Sakka's verses praise the Blessed One as glorious, freed from sin, one who has crossed the flood, and attended by a retinue; when questioned, the young Brāhman says he is the Buddha's servant.
