occurrences.motif_label: conversion through transmitted wisdom saying
occurrences.basis: Sāriputta is converted after hearing Assaji's causal verse, and Moggallāna is converted after Sāriputta repeats it.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sāriputta and Moggallāna, ascetics seeking salvation, are converted through a verse associated with Assaji, leave Sanjaya, take orders under the Master, attain Arahatship, and are appointed Chief Disciples.

occurrences.motif_label: worldly mission abandoned after enlightenment
occurrences.basis: Messengers sent on the king’s business attain Arahatship and then neglect or do not deliver the worldly message.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A messenger with a thousand followers listens to the Sage, attains Arahatship with his retinue, asks to enter the Order, and appears with miraculously created robes and bowls.
Arahats are said to become indifferent to worldly things; the first messenger does not deliver the message, and later courtiers with retinues also attain Arahatship and stay away in silence.
Kāḷa Udāyin receives the king’s message, goes to Rājagaha, hears the Master’s instruction, attains Arahatship with his followers, and is received into the Order.

occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom expressed as self-restraint
occurrences.basis: The king’s daughter is praised for adopting disciplined practices, and the Blessed One says that formerly she watched over herself even without a protector.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The mother of Rāhula says the Blessed One will come to her if she has value in his eyes; he visits with two chief disciples, she bows at his feet, and the king recounts her adoption of yellow dress, one meal, floor sleeping, and renunciation of garlands and unguents. The Blessed One says she formerly watched over herself while wandering among mountains and tells the Moonsprite birth story.

occurrences.motif_label: Conversion through hearing the Truth
occurrences.basis: Anātha Piṇḍika hears the Truth from the Teacher and becomes converted.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Anātha Piṇḍika, with merchandise in five hundred carts, hears at a trader friend's house that a Buddha has arisen; he goes to the Teacher through a door opened by angelic power, hears the Truth, becomes converted, gives a great donation, and receives the Teacher's promise to come to Sāvatthi.

occurrences.motif_label: true mother revealed by compassionate relinquishment
occurrences.basis: The future Buddha infers maternity from the claimant who lets go of the child rather than harm him, while the false claimant is exposed.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The future Buddha asks which hearts are tender to babes and whether the mother is the woman holding the child or the woman who let go; the bystanders answer that the one who let go is the mother.
“Verily this is a Yakshiṇī, who took the child to eat it.”
The future Buddha explains that he knew because the claimant’s eyes did not wink, were red, and because she had no fear or pity.

occurrences.motif_label: moral conversion or restraint of a dangerous being by vows
occurrences.basis: After exposing the Yakshiṇī, the future Buddha rebukes her, imposes the Five Commandments, and releases her.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The future Buddha rebukes the Yakshiṇī, says her birth as a Yakshiṇī resulted from former sins, lays a vow on her to keep the Five Commandments, and lets her go.

occurrences.basis: The Blessed One is said to have attained omniscience under the Bo-tree before living at the spot until death.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Blessed One lived at that spot from attaining omniscience under the Bo-tree until his death.

occurrences.motif_label: Taking refuge after hearing sacred teaching
occurrences.basis: The five hundred hear the Teacher’s discourse, give up wrong belief as their refuge, and take refuge in the Buddha.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The followers salute the Blessed One; they see his full-moon-like countenance, marks, surrounding brightness, and paired rays; he preaches in a powerful, sweet, and pleasant voice.

After hearing the Teacher’s discourse, the men are pleased, bow to the One Mighty by Wisdom, give up wrong belief as refuge, take refuge in the Buddha, and thereafter attend the Wihāra with offerings and observances.

occurrences.motif_label: Meditation on sacred objects of refuge leads to enlightenment
occurrences.basis: The Teacher says meditation on the Buddha, Truth, and Order gives the entrance and fruit of the first four Paths, and a cited passage says meditation on the Buddhas leads to higher knowledge, complete enlightenment, and Nirvāna.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Teacher says meditation on the Buddha, the Truth, and the Order gives the Entrance and Fruit of the First, Second, Third, and Fourth Paths, and says they did wrong to reject such salvation.

A cited passage says one practice, meditation on the Buddhas, leads to weariness of worldly vanities, the end of longings, destruction of excitement, peace of mind, higher knowledge, complete enlightenment, and Nirvāna.

occurrences.motif_label: wise adherence to true refuge versus fatal reliance on false refuge
occurrences.basis: The frame explicitly contrasts those who mistake a non-refuge for refuge and perish with those who hold right belief and are saved; the Bodisat is also positioned as the prudent figure in the embedded tale.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Blessed One says that formerly men trusting their own reason mistook a non-refuge for refuge, became prey to demons in a wilderness, and ended disastrously, while those adhering to right belief found good fortune there.
Anātha Piṇḍika rises, bows, praises the Blessed One, and asks him to explain the destruction of the self-sufficient reasoners and the rescue of those who held to truth.
The Bodisat sees advantages in going second: the first caravan will smooth rough ground, consume old grass, dig water sources, and establish prices.

occurrences.motif_label: Wise leader detects supernatural deception through practical signs
occurrences.basis: The Bodisat stores water, recognizes the demon's physical signs, refuses to discard supplies, and tests claims about rain through observable evidence.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Bodisat later departs, reaches the desert mouth, fills vessels, stores plentiful water, orders that no cupful be used without asking him, and warns against eating unfamiliar parts of poisonous trees.
In the middle of the desert the demon appears as before; the Bodisat knows him, reflecting that the arid desert has no water and that the figure is red-eyed, bold, and shadowless.
"We are travelling merchants, and don’t throw away the water we’ve got till we see some more"

The followers report the apparent water signs and suggest discarding water; the Bodisat asks whether they know of lakes in the desert and whether any rain-wind, cloud, lightning, or thunder has been perceived; they answer no.

The Bodisat says the figures are demons who want the caravan to throw away its water and be destroyed in weakness; he predicts the earlier merchant's fate and orders his men not to discard even a half-pint.

occurrences.motif_label: Fatal credulity contrasted with resourceful foresight
occurrences.basis: The first merchant believes the demon and loses his caravan, while the Bodisat preserves water and reasons carefully with his followers.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The demon asks about the carts, identifies the heavy last cart as carrying water, tells the merchants to break the pots and pour the water away, and the foolish merchant does so without saving even a cupful.
At night's end demons come from their city, kill all the men and oxen, eat their flesh, leave bones behind, and the five hundred loaded carts remain.

occurrences.motif_label: truth-guided escape from demonic danger
occurrences.basis: The Teacher states that those who held to truth escaped the hands of demons, reached their destination, and returned home.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Teacher says those relying on their own reason were destroyed, while those holding to truth escaped demons, went where they wished, and returned home.

occurrences.motif_label: wise leader preserves caravan through vigilance
occurrences.basis: The wise merchant forms a defensive encampment, keeps armed watch, reorganizes resources, and leads the company to successful trade and return.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The merchant finds five hundred loaded carts and scattered bones, arranges wagons in a circle as a strong encampment, feeds men and oxen, and keeps armed watch through the three watches of the night.

At dawn he sees to necessary tasks, leaves weak carts, chooses strong ones, replaces lower-value goods with higher-value goods, reaches the mart, sells profitably, and returns with his company to his city.

occurrences.motif_label: false reasoning leads to destruction while truth leads to liberation
occurrences.basis: The Teacher contrasts reliance on one’s own reason and the Untrue with holding to Truth, happy rebirths, Arahatship, and conversion.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Teacher says those relying on their own reason were destroyed, while those holding to truth escaped demons, went where they wished, and returned home.
A verse says some speak what cannot be questioned, mere logicians do not, and the wise person recognizes and takes as true what is truth.

The Blessed One teaches that life according to Truth leads to happy states and Arahatship, while life according to the Untrue leads to hells and low rebirths; after the discourse all five hundred disciples attain the Fruit of Conversion.

occurrences.motif_label: Discouraged practitioner restored by exemplary past-life perseverance
occurrences.basis: The Buddha uses the mendicant’s former determination in a desert crisis to strengthen his present resolve after he has abandoned meditative effort.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A young man at Jetavana hears the Teacher, enters the Order, practices meditation, spends three months in the forest without attaining insight, concludes he is incapable, and returns to Jetavana.
The mendicant’s companions rebuke him for returning from solitude and bring him to the Buddha; the Buddha asks whether he has given up trying, and he says that it is true.

The Buddha says the mendicant was formerly full of determination and that by his energy alone the men and bullocks of five hundred waggons obtained water in the sandy desert and were saved; the mendicants ask to hear how this happened.

occurrences.motif_label: Persevering leader detects hidden water from a natural sign
occurrences.basis: When the caravan despairs, the Bodisat refuses to lose heart, sees Kusa-grass, and reasons that water must lie beneath it.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Bodisat thinks that if he loses heart all will perish, walks while the morning is cool, sees Kusa-grass, and reasons that water must be beneath it.

occurrences.motif_label: perseverance through obstacle reveals life-sustaining resource
occurrences.basis: The narrative contrasts despair with the Bodisat's inference and the page's continued effort, leading to water and survival; the verse explicitly generalizes this as firm resolve and continued effort.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The group brings a hoe, digs sixty cubits, strikes a rock with the spade, and gives up in despair.

The Bodisat reasons that water must be under the rock, enters the well, listens to the stone, hears water gurgling beneath, and tells his page not to lose heart but to strike the rock with an iron hammer.
The page obeys, goes down determinedly, strikes the stone, the rock splits and falls below, the stream is unblocked, and water rises to the height of a palm-tree in the well.
"The men of firm resolve dug on into the sand... And so the wise, strong by continuing effort, / Finds--if he weary not--Rest for his heart!"

occurrences.motif_label: teaching brings listener to liberation
occurrences.basis: After the Buddha's discourse and declaration of the Four Truths, the despairing priest is established in Arahatship.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "The men of firm resolve dug on into the sand... And so the wise, strong by continuing effort, / Finds--if he weary not--Rest for his heart!"
After the discourse, the Buddha declares the Four Truths, and the despairing priest is established in the highest Fruit, Arahatship, identified as Nirvāna.

occurrences.motif_label: truthful valuation versus greedy deception
occurrences.basis: The avaricious hawker lies about the dish's value, while the Bodisat correctly declares that it is gold and worth a hundred thousand.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The avaricious hawker is offered the dish, scratches it with a needle, recognizes it as gold, but says it is not worth a halfpenny and throws it down, hoping to obtain it for nothing.
“Mother! this dish is worth a hundred thousand. All the goods in my possession are not equal to it in value!”

occurrences.motif_label: teaching leading to liberation
occurrences.basis: The Teacher’s discourse on the Four Truths leads to a monk’s establishment in Nirvāna, and later Great Roadling’s repeated hearing of the Truth leads toward renunciation and attainment.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Teacher discourses toward Arahatship, dwells on the Four Truths, and the despondent monk is established in Nirvāna.
Great Roadling grows up in his grandfather’s house, goes with him to hear the Buddha preach, turns toward renunciation, asks to enter the Order, and receives his grandfather’s support.
The Teacher has a monk ordain Great Roadling, the monk teaches meditation on the body’s perishability, and Great Roadling later learns scripture, becomes a full member, and attains Arahatship.

occurrences.motif_label: spiritual insight through a soiled white cloth
occurrences.basis: Little Roadling's observation of a white cloth becoming soiled leads him to perceive changeability, and the vision converts the stain into a teaching about lust, anger, and delusion.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Teacher seats Little Roadling before his apartment, gives him a very white cloth, and tells him to face east and rub it while repeating, 'The removal of impurity.'
As Little Roadling rubs the cloth it becomes soiled; he reflects that it has lost its former condition and that all component things are changeable.
A glorious vision of the Teacher appears and teaches that the real stains are lust, anger, and delusion, not dust, and that monks must remove these stains.
When the stanzas are finished, Little Roadling attains Arahatship and the intellectual gifts of an Arahat, by which he understands all the Scriptures.

occurrences.motif_label: repeated prior-life insight from a soiled white garment
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly connects Little Roadling's conversion by impurity transfer to an earlier life where a white robe became soiled and prompted insight into impermanence.

evidence.quote_or_summary: As Little Roadling rubs the cloth it becomes soiled; he reflects that it has lost its former condition and that all component things are changeable.

In a former life as a king, he wiped sweat from his forehead with a pure white robe; seeing it become dirty, he realized impermanency, which explains the later conversion through transfer of impurity.

occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom turns a worthless object into the beginning of wealth
occurrences.basis: Chullaka reads the circumstances around a dead mouse and says a discerning young man could start trade with it; a poor young man follows the advice and earns a farthing.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Long ago, when Brahma-datta reigned in Benares in Kāsi, the Bodisat was born in a treasurer’s family, became treasurer, was called Chullaka, and was wise, skilful, and knowledgeable in omens.
Chullaka sees a dead mouse on the road, considers the state of the stars, and says a young fellow with eyes in his head could pick it up, start a trade, and support a wife.
A poor young man of good birth hears Chullaka, judges that he must have a reason, takes the mouse, gives it at a shop for the cat, and receives a farthing.

occurrences.motif_label: small beginnings raised to greatness through practical wisdom
occurrences.basis: The plot repeatedly shows the young man turning tiny resources into wealth, and the Buddha’s verse explicitly states that an able and far-seeing man can raise himself to wealth with the smallest capital.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The young man buys molasses, carries water, gives molasses and water to garland-makers, receives flowers and flowering shrubs, and gains eight pennies.
The young man gives molasses to children, who collect the leaves and sticks into a heap; the king’s potter buys the heap as firewood and the young man gains sixteen pennies and five vessels.

A land-trader tells him a horse-dealer is coming with five hundred horses; the young man asks the grass-cutters for bundles and asks them not to sell first; the horse-dealer buys his grass for a thousand pence.

About a hundred merchants from Benares come to buy the goods, are told a great merchant has paid a deposit, and then pay the young man to become shareholders and again for him to relinquish his remaining share.
“As one might nurse a tiny flame, / The able and far-seeing man, / E’en with the smallest capital, / Can raise himself to wealth!”

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Buddha explains that Little Roadling has now become great in religion through him and formerly became great in riches through him, then identifies Chullaka’s pupil as Little Roadling and Chullaka the high treasurer as himself.

occurrences.motif_label: Wise adviser exposes foolish judgment through public test
occurrences.basis: The Bodisat advises the horse-dealer to ask the foolish valuer in the king’s presence to value the measure of rice, leading to an absurd declaration that exposes him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Bodisat tells the horse-dealer to bribe the valuer and ask him publicly what a measure of rice is worth; the valuer accepts and agrees.

In the royal audience, the horse-dealer asks the king to have the valuer value the measure of rice; the valuer repeats that five hundred horses are worth a measure of rice and says the measure is worth all Benares within and without the walls.
The passage explains the valuer first undervalued the horses to please the king and then, after taking the dealer’s bribe, valued the measure of rice at the whole city and suburbs.

occurrences.motif_label: just king seeks criticism of his own faults
occurrences.basis: The future Buddha rules justly, then deliberately seeks someone who will identify faults in him so he can practice virtue.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In the Rājovāda Jātaka, the future Buddha is born from the chief queen as Prince Brahma-datta, studies at Takkasilā, ascends the throne, and rules with impartial justice.
Because justice is administered fairly, lawsuits cease; the future Buddha decides to examine his own faults and seeks someone who will tell him of any fault, but hears only praise.

After finding no fault-finder in palace, city, suburbs, or gates, the king gives the kingdom to his ministers, mounts his chariot, takes only his charioteer, and leaves the city in disguise to search the country.

occurrences.motif_label: wise judgment exposes foolish judgment
occurrences.basis: The foolish valuation is publicly mocked, the Bodisat articulates its absurdity, and the king replaces the foolish valuer with the wise one.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The ministers clap, laugh, and scorn the valuer, saying the great royal city is worth only a measure of rice by his account.
The Bodisat recites a stanza asking what a measure of rice is worth, answering with Benares and its environs, and asking what five hundred horses are worth, answering with the same measure of rice.
The king is ashamed, drives out the fool, and appoints the Bodisat to the office of Valuer.
The Teacher finishes the discourse, makes the connection, and identifies the foolish peasant valuer as Udāyin the Simpleton and the wise valuer as himself.

occurrences.basis: The pond is controlled by a water-sprite who seizes entrants and asks whether they know true divinity, eating those who do not know.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Vessavana gives the pond to a water-sprite, granting him as prey those who go down into the water except those who know what true divinity is.
The water-sprite asks those entering the water about the characteristic signs of divine beings and eats alive those who do not know.
The Sun Prince steps into the pond without hesitation; the demon seizes him and asks if he knows what is divine, and he replies that the Sun and Moon are called gods.

occurrences.motif_label: wisdom answer releases captives
occurrences.basis: The water-sprite preys on those who cannot identify divine beings, but the Bodisat's correct moral teaching moves him and leads to the brothers' release.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The demon says he has been granted those who go into the pond, except those who know what beings are divine; the Bodisat offers to tell him.
"The pure in heart who fear to sin, / The good, kindly in word and deed-- / These are the beings in the world, / Whose nature should be called divine."
The moved water-sprite offers one brother; the Bodisat asks for the younger and explains that the younger's political danger caused the forest exile, so his loss would bring blame and disbelief.
The water-sprite says the Bodisat both knows and acts according to divine nature, then brings out both brothers and gives them back.

occurrences.motif_label: Grey hair as sign prompting renunciation
occurrences.basis: A single grey hair causes Makhā Deva to reflect on age, mortality, and passions, and he resolves to leave the world for religious life.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The barber finds one grey hair, removes it with golden pincers, puts it in the king's hand, and the king becomes deeply agitated, reflecting on his failure to overcome passions.
Makhā Deva resolves to leave the world that day, grants the barber a valuable village, tells his eldest son to assume sovereignty, and says he will enter religious life in Makhā Deva's Mango-park.
Makhā Deva says the grey hairs are 'angel messengers' and that it is time to devote himself to holy thought.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Makhā Deva resolves to leave the world that day, grants the barber a valuable village, tells his eldest son to assume sovereignty, and says he will enter religious life in Makhā Deva's Mango-park.

Makhā Deva gives up sovereignty, becomes a hermit in the Mango-grove, practices goodwill and meditation for eighty-four thousand years, is born in Brahma heaven, later becomes King Nimi in Mithilā, reunites his family, becomes a hermit again, and returns to Brahma heaven.

occurrences.motif_label: Instruction of a king by an ascetic teacher
occurrences.basis: The Bodisat addresses the king’s displeasure with a discourse and a verse intended to instruct him in righteousness.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Bodisat explains that the ascetic was once a king and is reflecting that royal splendour with armed guards did not give him the joy he now finds in meditation and religious life.
The Bodisat recites a verse teaching that one who needs no defenders and has no one to defend lives at ease, untroubled by yearnings or lusts.
After the discourse the king is satisfied and returns to the palace; the disciple returns to the Himālaya region; the Bodisat remains in meditation until death and is reborn in the Brahma heaven.

occurrences.basis: Beauty’s careful timing and avoidance of danger preserve all five hundred deer, and Sāriputta likewise returns with a retinue.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sāriputta returns with the mendicants; the mendicants praise him as returning with five hundred disciples, while Devadatta is without followers.
Beauty is described as learned, clever, and resourceful; he avoids village gates, does not travel by day, dawn, or twilight, travels at midnight, and reaches the forest without losing any animal.
After four months and after the crops are cut, Brownie loses the rest of his herd and arrives alone, while Beauty comes to his parent with all five hundred deer.
The Master says Brownie was Devadatta, Brownie’s attendants were Devadatta’s attendants, Beauty was Sāriputta, Beauty’s attendants were the Buddha’s followers, and the father was the Master himself.

After four months and after the crops are cut, Brownie loses the rest of his herd and arrives alone, while Beauty comes to his parent with all five hundred deer.

occurrences.basis: The woman rejects bodily adornment and gives an extended reflection on the body's decay, disease, death, and charnel-ground destiny.

evidence.quote_or_summary: During a city feast, she does not anoint or dress herself for the celebration; her husband asks why she does not adorn herself.
She describes the body as made of constituent parts, born in corruption, subject to impermanence, disease, death, and the charnel-house, and compares adornment to painting a sepulchre.

occurrences.motif_label: compassionate intercession expanding from one life to all creatures
occurrences.basis: After securing the roe's safety, the Bodisat repeatedly asks the king to extend protection to more categories of beings.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The king praises the golden-coloured King of the Deer for forbearance, kindness, and compassion, grants life to him and the roe, and then grants life to the rest of the deer.
Through the Bodisat's successive questions, the king grants security to deer outside the park, four-footed creatures, birds, and fish.

In Benares, King Brahma-datta has a gardener named Sanjaya. A swift antelope frequents the garden; Sanjaya says he could bring it into the palace with honey.

Sanjaya smears honey on grass where the antelope comes; after eating it, the deer is bound with the lust of taste and comes only to the garden. It gradually gains confidence and eats grass from Sanjaya’s hand.
Sanjaya prepares a branch-strewn path, carries honey and grass, sprinkles honey-smeared grass before the antelope, and leads it within the palace.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “Formerly also, by your surliness and your refusing to accept the admonition of the wise, you were caught in a snare and came to destruction.”
The nephew does not go at the appointed time; after disregarding seven admonitions over seven days and not learning the devices of deer, he is caught in a snare.

The Master concludes by connecting the former story to the present: the nephew deer was the abusive monk, the sister was Uppala-vaṇṇā, and the admonishing deer was the Master himself.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The gardener asks, “Will you water my garden while I am away?” and the monkeys cry, “Oh yes, yes, yes!”

Each monkey takes a watering-pot; they pull up plants, measure roots, water more for long roots and less for short roots, then put the plants back.
The gardener returns after a day or two and finds many plants drooping, dead, or dying while monkeys are still pulling up the rest.

Streaky must fly back by himself, returns tired and hungry, spends the rest of his days on the dust-heap eating carrion, and the King Goose never visits again.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The boar loses his conceit, and an old wise boar advises him to roll in mud because lions are clean beasts and dislike dirt.
The boar rolls in dirty places until he is "like a big cake of dirt."

evidence.quote_or_summary: Godfrey wonders whether he is as good as people say and asks people in palace and city to tell him his faults, but receives only praise.
Godfrey disguises himself as a traveller, takes a carriage and pair, and asks people throughout the country what they think of the king; they speak well of him behind his back too.

occurrences.motif_label: narrow-road precedence contest resolved by virtue
occurrences.basis: Two royal carriages are blocked in a narrow lane; worldly measures of precedence are equal, so the drivers compare moral qualities and the morally superior king is allowed to pass.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In a narrow lane sunk between steep banks, Godfrey’s carriage meets another carriage carrying the king of the next country, who is also travelling in disguise to learn public opinion; neither carriage gives way at first.
The coachmen compare the two kings by age, wealth, kingdom size, population, and ancestral glory, but the kings are alike in all those respects.
The other driver’s verse says his king is “Rough to the rough,” mild to the mild, masters the good by goodness, and pays the bad with badness.
Godfrey’s driver says: “He conquers wrath by mildness, the bad with goodness sways, / By gifts the miser vanquishes and lies with truth repays.”

The other driver admits Godfrey’s master is better; the other king gets out, the horses are loosened, and the carriage is pulled up the slope. Godfrey gives advice, both kings say goodbye, return home, and rule well until death.

evidence.quote_or_summary: During the crossing, the crocodile sinks and tells the monkey that his wife wants the monkey’s heart to eat.
The monkey replies that monkeys do not carry hearts inside them and points to round things in a tree, claiming they are monkey hearts; the crocodile believes him and takes him across.
The monkey leaps off, climbs the fig-tree, eats figs, mocks the crocodile for thinking a creature keeps its heart in a tree, and the crocodile returns to his wife feeling foolish.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The man tests whether the diamond caused the miracle by wishing himself down and then back up into the tree, confirming that it is magical.
The pig wakes after the man drops a nut on its nose; it is explained that the pig is really a wicked great magician in pig shape, and that all his power lies in the diamond.
The pig rages below the tree; the man drops more nuts; the pig charges and sticks its tusks in the trunk, after which the man descends and kills it with a stone.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The young man tells the giant about the wishing-bowl that gives any desired food, and the giant trades his drum for the bowl.
The giant wishes aloud for a bowlful of blood and begins drinking; the young man commands the axe with 'Heads,' and the axe splits the giant's head in two.

The city king is described as cruel, robbing and murdering subjects and showing no mercy to strangers; he sends soldiers, then a regiment, then all his army to capture the young man, while the drum makes the first forces flee.
The young man tips over the wishing-bowl, releasing a roaring torrent of water that floods the plain and drowns every soldier in the army except the king, who escapes to the city wall.
The young man commands the axe to take the king's head; it flies like a boomerang, slices off the king's head, returns, and the people inside the city cheer.

occurrences.motif_label: small animal survives predator through clever stratagem
occurrences.basis: After the cat coerces the mouse, the farmer uses a glass inkstand to protect the mouse; the cat swallows the hidden object and dies, allowing the mouse to escape.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The farmer's black cat Grimalkin catches the fat mouse. The mouse offers to bring meat daily if released, and the cat agrees but threatens death if a day is missed. The cat is described as lazy and fond of sitting by the fire.

The farmer puts the mouse inside a beautiful piece of glass with a hole in the middle, possibly an inkstand, turns it upside down before the mouse's hole, and tells him to refuse Grimalkin's next demand.
Grimalkin demands meat; the mouse refuses. In rage, Grimalkin pounces and swallows the mouse, inkstand and all, not realizing the transparent glass is there.

The cat cannot digest the glass inkstand and dies from worsening pain. The mouse exits through Grimalkin's throat, returns to his hole, and lives happily, continuing to bring the farmer a sovereign each day for a meat dinner.

occurrences.motif_label: Garland or wreath divination by water
occurrences.basis: In the Russian custom, girls throw garlands into water and read their own fate from how the garlands float.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In the Russian Nerechta custom, girls go to a birch wood, bind a birch and twist its branches into a wreath, kiss through it, enact a sleeper awakened and kissed, make garlands, and throw them into water to read their fate; Frazer suggests the sleeper was probably once a lad.

occurrences.motif_label: Plant growth used as omen of fortune, love, sickness, or death
occurrences.basis: The passage describes grain, St. John’s plants, and St. John’s wort blooming, fading, or sprouting well or badly as omens for marriage, love, luck, sickness, and death.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says gardens of Adonis, like May-trees or May-boughs, may be supposed to bring good luck; after this belief fades, omens may still be drawn from them for family or individual fortune.
An anonymous Italian sixteenth-century writer records sowing barley and wheat before St. John’s and St. Vitus’s festivals; good sprouting signified fortune and a good spouse, poor sprouting ill luck.
In Italy and Sicily, plants are placed in water or earth on St. John’s Eve, and blooming or fading on St. John’s Day supplies omens, especially about fortune in love.
In Prussia, servants gathered St. John’s wort at midsummer; plants were assigned to persons and placed in wall or beams, and failure to bloom indicated that the person would soon fall sick or die.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Osiris is introduced as son of the earth-god Qeb/Seb; as king on earth he reclaims Egyptians from savagery, gives laws, and teaches worship of the gods.
Isis, sister and wife of Osiris, discovers wild wheat and barley; Osiris introduces cultivation of these grains, and the people abandon cannibalism for a corn diet.
Osiris travels spreading civilization; on return Set/Typhon and seventy-two others plot against him, seal him in a decorated coffer with molten lead, cast it into the Nile, and it floats to the sea.

occurrences.motif_label: gifted maiden-poetess calms dangerous waters through verse-prayer
occurrences.basis: Hase-Hime is known as a gifted young poetess and is asked to write a poem-prayer; when she reads it at the river and raises it heavenward, the roaring water becomes quiet and the Emperor recovers.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At thirteen, Hase-Hime is already mentioned as a poetess of some merit, an accomplishment valued among women of old Japan.

Court circles identify Princess Hase as a gifted poetess and recall Ono-no-Komachi, a maiden-poetess said to have moved Heaven by verse and brought rain during drought, suggesting Hase’s poem-prayer might stop the river noise.

Hase-Hime is told she must save the Emperor by the merit of her verse; she writes a poem on gold-flecked paper, goes to the torrent’s bank, raises her heart to Heaven, reads the poem aloud, and lifts it heavenward in both hands.
“The waters ceased their roaring, and the river was quiet in direct answer to her prayer. After this the Emperor soon recovered his health.”

occurrences.motif_label: devout heroine remembered for wisdom and sacred craft
occurrences.basis: Hase-Hime is found reading Buddhist scriptures with devotion, is later remembered as wise and devout, and is credited with a Buddha tapestry preserved in a temple.

evidence.quote_or_summary: He approaches a tiny house after hearing a clear voice and finds a beautiful girl “reading the Buddhist scriptures with great devotion,” then sees that she is Hase-Hime.
Prince Toyonari adopts a noble’s younger son as heir and Hase-Hime’s husband; Hase-Hime lives to old age, is praised as wise, devout, and beautiful, and presents her son to her father.
A Buddhist temple in Kioto preserves a Buddha tapestry embroidered with threads from the lotus stem, said to be the work of Princess Hase’s hands.

occurrences.motif_label: quest for perpetual life redirected toward ordinary moral life
occurrences.basis: The passage names the land of Perpetual Life and the Elixir of Life, but the messenger teaches Sentaro to abandon escape from death and follow precepts for a good life.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The messenger says Jofuku sent him, allowed Sentaro to see the land of Perpetual Life in a dream, and tested him by letting him drop into the sea and sending a shark to swallow him.

The messenger says it is vain for Sentaro to seek hermitage or the Elixir of Life, and instructs him to return home, live industriously, honor ancestors, provide for children, and give up escaping death.
The messenger gives Sentaro a book of precepts intended to guide him in the advised way of life.
The angel disappears; Sentaro returns home with the book, gives up vain wishes, follows its lessons, and his household prospers.

occurrences.motif_label: filial virtue sustained by memory of the dead mother
occurrences.basis: The mother's instruction and the daughter's daily mirror practice lead the girl to become gentle, kind, and dutiful.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The mother tells her daughter that nothing can save her, asks her to care for her father, and explains that her death is ordained by a previous state of existence.
Every morning and evening the girl gazes at the mirror for strength and consolation, believes the reflection to be her mother's soul, and grows gentle, kind, and dutiful.
After a year of mourning, the father remarries; the daughter is under a stepmother's authority and resolves to be filial and dutiful to her father's wife.

occurrences.motif_label: Threatened animal avoids slaughter through a stratagem
occurrences.basis: The monkey learns he is to be killed and, with the boar's plan, uses a staged rescue to make the owners spare him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The monkey overhears the conversation, realizes he is to be killed, laments his master's cruelty, and thinks of seeking the wild boar's counsel.
The monkey goes to the forest, finds the boar, praises his wisdom, and asks what to do about being sold to the butcher.
The boar, pleased by flattery, proposes to seize the master's infant child so that the monkey can rescue it and win the parents' pity.
The parents admire the monkey's conduct and are grateful when it brings the child safely back.
The wife argues that the monkey saved their child; the husband agrees to send the butcher away and feed the monkey too.
The butcher is sent away with an order for boar meat, and the monkey is petted, lives peacefully, and is never struck again.

occurrences.motif_label: mysterious helper provides guidance and transport
occurrences.basis: A suddenly appearing old man identifies the problem, advises the Happy Hunter to seek the Dragon King, and makes a basket for sea travel.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “an old man suddenly appeared carrying a stick in his hand” while the Happy Hunter stood on the beach.
The old man names himself Shiwozuchino Okina, says he lives nearby, and explains that the hook is not on the shore but may be at the bottom of the sea or inside a fish.
The old man advises the Happy Hunter to go to Ryn Gu and ask Ryn Jin, the Dragon King of the Sea, to find the hook; the Happy Hunter notes that this realm is said to be at the bottom of the sea.
The old man says he can make something for sea travel, makes a basket, and gives it to the Happy Hunter, who mounts it at the water.

occurrences.motif_label: compassionate judgment and pardon
occurrences.basis: The Happy Hunter argues against punishment of the Tai and is described as a wise and compassionate judge.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ryn Jin wishes to punish the Tai, but the Happy Hunter pleads for forgiveness, saying the Tai has already suffered and acted heedlessly; Ryn Jin forgives it, and the fish praise the Happy Hunter.

occurrences.motif_label: clever animal threatened with death plans escape
occurrences.basis: After learning that his liver is wanted, the monkey hides his fear and starts thinking of a way to escape.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Half-way across, the jelly fish asks whether the monkey has his liver, then explains that the Dragon Queen is ill and that a doctor said only a live monkey's liver would cure her.
The monkey is horrified and angry at the trick, trembles with fear, but conceals it and begins thinking of an escape before speaking cheerfully to the jelly fish.

occurrences.motif_label: compassionate supernatural healer restores an animal
occurrences.basis: Okuni-nushi-no-Mikoto pities the injured hare and gives effective instructions using pond water and flowers, after which the hare recovers.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A kind man carrying a great bag stops; the hare tells how it tricked crocodiles into making a bridge, mocked them, was revenged upon, and was later deceived by men like the present helper.
The man prescribes washing in a pond and rolling on kaba flowers; the hare does so, its white fur grows back, pain ceases, and it recovers.
The helper says he is Okuni-nushi-no-Mikoto, not a King's son; his brothers have gone to seek Princess Yakami of Inaba, while he follows as an attendant carrying a large bag.
The closing note says Okuni-nushi-no-Mikoto is worshiped as a god in some parts of Japan, the hare is famous as the White Hare of Inaba, and the crocodiles' fate is unknown.

occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom defeats destructive magic
occurrences.basis: Shikuyu knows Kokai's secret, uses ashes to neutralize the flood, detects Kokai's deceptive retreat, and knows the counter-charm to the Water Devil.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Shikuyu returns with Eiko, is asked to become Generalissimo, assures Jokwa he will kill Kokai, leads thirty thousand soldiers, and orders them to burn a certain shrub and bag the ashes.
Kokai boasts that he can extinguish the Fire King, raises floods as high as mountains by incantation, and Shikuyu has the soldiers scatter ashes that turn the water into stiff mud.
Eiko fights Kokai, Hako replaces him, Kokai pretends to retreat in order to surprise Hako, and Shikuyu identifies the deception and urges Hako to attack.
Shikuyu orders Jokwa's soldiers to charge and rout Kokai's forces; Kokai calls on the Water Devil, but Shikuyu knows the counter-charm; Kokai dashes his head against Mount Shu and dies.

occurrences.motif_label: Prudent leadership averts danger
occurrences.basis: The thrifty merchant takes practical protective measures against demons, is not attacked, and safely completes the journey.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The thrifty merchant has his wagons drawn up in a circle and places the oxen and some men in the middle.
The merchant and head men stand guard with swords, waiting for demons, but the demons do not bother them.
Early the next day, the merchant takes the best wagons left by the foolish merchant and goes safely to the city across the desert.

occurrences.basis: The wise man finds no bodily ailment, infers that Girly-face has been affected by bad talk, and prescribes good talk as the remedy.

The wise man tells the king to send good men to talk where Girly-face can hear; the men say it is wrong to hurt or kill and that everyone should be gentle and good.

occurrences.motif_label: merciful ruler transforms a violent ruler
occurrences.basis: The Banyan Deer king’s compassionate action causes the human king to praise his kindness and stop hunting deer.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The human king asks why he is lying there after being granted life; the Banyan Deer king explains that a mother with a young baby came to him and he could not ask anyone else to take her place.
The human king says he has never seen such kindness and mercy, grants life to the Banyan Deer king and the mother, and says he will no longer hunt deer in park or forest.

occurrences.motif_label: supernatural guardian poses a life-or-death question at water
occurrences.basis: A water-sprite controls a pond and captures those who enter or approach without giving the correct answer to a question.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Fairy King has given the pond to a water-sprite, granting him power over all who go down into the water except those who correctly answer the question, 'What are the Good Fairies like?'
Sun Prince enters the pond, answers that the Good Fairies are like the Sun and Moon, and the water-sprite says he does not know and carries him into the cave.
Moon Prince goes to find his brother, answers that the Good Fairies are like the sky above, and the water-sprite drags him into the cave where Sun Prince sits.
The eldest brother answers that the Good Fairies are like: "The pure in heart who fear to sin, / The good, kindly in word and deed."

The water-sprite says the Wise Prince knows what the good should do and is kind, and he brings back both brothers.

occurrences.motif_label: intended victim outwits predator
occurrences.basis: The crab requires a hold on the crane's neck before traveling and kills the crane when the crane reveals his intent to eat him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The crab says he cannot ride on the crane's back and asks to hold the crane's neck with his claws. The crane knows crabs have a tight grip and dislikes the idea, but agrees because he is hungry.

At the place where the crane had eaten the fishes, the crane tells the crab to let go and walk. The crab sees no pond, only a pile of fish bones. The crane admits that the crab's shell will be all that remains if he lets go.
The crab pinches the crane's neck so that the crane's head falls off, then says the crane's bones, not the crab's shell, will dry with the fishes' bones.

occurrences.basis: The old Crow argues against the Owl's kingship by judging the Owl's expression and warning how he might look when angry.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An old Crow says he does not want the Owl as king, pointing to the Owl's sour look and asking how he would look when angry.

occurrences.motif_label: Clever prey escapes predator through deceptive speech
occurrences.basis: The monkey avoids being killed by inventing the claim that his heart is in the tree, leading the crocodile to return him to safety.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The crocodile says he will kill the monkey by keeping him underwater because his mother wants monkey-heart.
The monkey says that if the crocodile had told him, he could have brought his heart; he then claims he left it in the tree and asks to return for it.
The crocodile refuses to go first to the fruit island and instead takes the monkey straight back to the tree to get his heart.
The monkey jumps to the riverbank, runs up the tree, and calls down: "My heart is way up here! If you want it, come for it, come for it!"

occurrences.motif_label: Practical knowledge defeats danger
occurrences.basis: The monkey survives because he recognizes the changed rock, tests it with speech, and uses knowledge of crocodile behavior to escape.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At night the monkey stops, notices the rock seems too high, infers the crocodile is on it, and calls repeatedly to the rock.
The crocodile thinks the rock answers the monkey at night and answers in place of the rock.
The monkey knows crocodiles shut their eyes when they open their mouths wide; the crocodile lies with mouth open and eyes shut.
The monkey does not jump into the crocodile's mouth; he lands on the crocodile's head, springs to the bank, and goes up into his tree.
The crocodile says the monkey has great cunning and no fear and will be left alone; the monkey thanks him but says he will remain watchful.

occurrences.motif_label: escape through deceptive protest
occurrences.basis: The turtle saves itself by pretending that the one proposed action that will save it is especially cruel, causing the king to order that action.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The turtle asks what it has done to deserve such a dreadful thing and says, “to throw me into the lake! Don’t speak of such a cruel thing!”
After hearing the turtle, the king tells his men to take it at once and throw it into the lake.
The turtle laughs as it slides down the river to its old home and says, “those people do not know how safe I am in the water!”

occurrences.motif_label: Greed defeated by its own deceit
occurrences.basis: The greedy merchant lies about the bowl’s value to obtain it cheaply, but his delay allows an honest merchant to acquire it, leaving him angry over a lost fortune.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The greedy merchant is shown the bowl, scratches it with a needle, discovers it is gold, says it is worth not even a halfpenny, throws it down, and leaves.
The greedy merchant returns asking for the bowl, learns another merchant paid a great price for it, becomes angry over losing a small fortune, and calls for the boatman to stop.

occurrences.passage_locator: PART II / HOW THE TURTLE SAVED HIS OWN LIFE / THE MERCHANT OF SERI / THE TURTLE WHO COULDN'T STOP TALKING; lines 495-538
occurrences.motif_label: Fatal failure to keep silence
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly makes silence the condition of safe travel, and the turtle dies when he tries to speak in response to ridicule.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The geese say they will take the turtle if he keeps his mouth shut and says nothing; the turtle agrees to do as they wish.
The geese bring a stick, hold its ends, and tell the turtle to take the middle in his mouth and not speak until they reach home.
The turtle looks down, starts to answer the children, lets go, falls, and dies at their feet.
As the geese fly on, people who see the turtle say he could not keep his mouth shut, had to talk, and so lost his life.

occurrences.source_title: Jataka tales
occurrences.passage_locator: PART II / HOW THE TURTLE SAVED HIS OWN LIFE / THE MERCHANT OF SERI / THE TURTLE WHO COULDN'T STOP TALKING; lines 495-538
occurrences.motif_label: Mockery provokes self-destructive response
occurrences.basis: The village children mock the turtle, prompting him to begin answering; this action makes him fall and die.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Village children see the geese carrying the turtle by a stick and ridicule the sight.
The turtle looks down, starts to answer the children, lets go, falls, and dies at their feet.
As the geese fly on, people who see the turtle say he could not keep his mouth shut, had to talk, and so lost his life.

occurrences.passage_locator: HOW THE TURTLE SAVED HIS OWN LIFE / THE MERCHANT OF SERI / THE TURTLE WHO COULDN'T STOP TALKING / THE OX WHO WON THE FORFEIT; lines 540-606
occurrences.motif_label: Kind speech and respectful treatment enable cooperation
occurrences.basis: The ox refuses to work when beaten and insulted, explains the cause, and later succeeds after apology, feeding, garlanding, praise, and gentle handling.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The owner says, “Get up, you wretch! Get along, you rascal!”; the ox stands still, and neither blows nor hard names make him move.
At feeding time, the ox asks why he was whipped and called “wretch” and “rascal,” saying this had never happened before.
The man says he will never treat the ox badly again, apologizes for the whipping and name-calling, and asks forgiveness.
The next morning the owner feeds the ox well and hangs a garland of flowers about his neck before returning to the village.
The village men mock the owner; he raises the forfeit to two thousand pieces of silver, then praises the ox and pats and strokes him.
The ox pulls with all his strength, moving the carts until the last cart stands where the first had been.

occurrences.passage_locator: HOW THE TURTLE SAVED HIS OWN LIFE / THE MERCHANT OF SERI / THE TURTLE WHO COULDN'T STOP TALKING / THE OX WHO WON THE FORFEIT; lines 540-606
occurrences.motif_label: Speaking animal corrects human conduct
occurrences.basis: The ox speaks to the owner, identifies the owner’s harsh treatment as the problem, and agrees to help after the owner repents.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At feeding time, the ox asks why he was whipped and called “wretch” and “rascal,” saying this had never happened before.
The man says he will never treat the ox badly again, apologizes for the whipping and name-calling, and asks forgiveness.
The ox accepts and says that the next day he will draw the one hundred carts, noting that the man had always been a kind master until that day.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE MERCHANT OF SERI / THE TURTLE WHO COULDN'T STOP TALKING / THE OX WHO WON THE FORFEIT / THE SANDY ROAD; lines 608-698
occurrences.motif_label: Resourceful leader saves caravan by refusing despair
occurrences.basis: The merchant explicitly rejects giving up, reasons that water must be found, and leads actions that save the people and oxen.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The merchant says to himself that this is no time to sleep; he must find water for the oxen, the men, and cooking, because if he gives up all will be lost.
“There must be water somewhere below, or that grass would not be there.”
The merchant calls for the spade and hammer; the men dig where the grass grows, strike rock, and the merchant listens at the rock and says he hears water running underneath.
The merchant tells a serving-lad that if he gives up they are lost; the boy strikes the rock hard with the hammer, breaks it, and the well fills with cool water.
The men drink, water the oxen, bathe, split spare yokes and axles for firewood, cook rice, rest, and set a flag on the well for travelers to see.

occurrences.motif_label: Hidden water discovered in a wasteland through a natural sign
occurrences.basis: A tuft of grass in the desert is treated as evidence of water below, leading to digging, breaking rock, and the filling of the well.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “There must be water somewhere below, or that grass would not be there.”
The merchant calls for the spade and hammer; the men dig where the grass grows, strike rock, and the merchant listens at the rock and says he hears water running underneath.
The merchant tells a serving-lad that if he gives up they are lost; the boy strikes the rock hard with the hammer, breaks it, and the well fills with cool water.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE TURTLE WHO COULDN'T STOP TALKING / THE OX WHO WON THE FORFEIT / THE SANDY ROAD / THE QUARREL OF THE QUAILS; lines 700-761
occurrences.motif_label: wise leader devises communal survival strategy
occurrences.basis: The wisest quail recognizes the fowler's method and instructs the group in a successful escape plan.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Many quails live together in a forest, and the wisest quail is their leader.

The wise leader tells the birds that the fowler is carrying many away and instructs them to put their heads through the holes of the net, fly together to a thorn-bush, leave the net there, and be free.
The fowler throws the net over the quails; they lift it, fly to a thorn-bush, leave it there, and return to tell their leader the plan worked.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE TURTLE WHO COULDN'T STOP TALKING / THE OX WHO WON THE FORFEIT / THE SANDY ROAD / THE QUARREL OF THE QUAILS; lines 700-761
occurrences.motif_label: discord causes collective downfall
occurrences.basis: After the quails quarrel and divide into sides, they fail to cooperate and are caught by the fowler.

evidence.quote_or_summary: One quail accidentally steps on another's head; the second asks angrily who did it, the first apologizes, and the second remains angry and says mean things.
All the quails take sides in the quarrel.
When the fowler nets them, one side says, "Now, you lift the net," and the other replies, "Lift it yourself"; neither side begins.
While the quails quarrel, the fowler catches them all in his net, takes them to town, and sells them for a good price.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE OX WHO WON THE FORFEIT / THE SANDY ROAD / THE QUARREL OF THE QUAILS / THE MEASURE OF RICE; lines 763-845
occurrences.motif_label: wise counsel exposes foolish judgment
occurrences.basis: The honest former Valuer devises a public test that reveals the absurdity of the foolish Valuer's pricing.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The former Valuer advises the horse-dealer to give the Valuer a fine present and ask him to state before the king what a measure of rice is worth.
The horse-dealer and Valuer go before the king and ministers; the horse-dealer asks the king to ask the Valuer the value of the measure of rice.
The Valuer says five hundred horses are worth a measure of rice and then says the measure of rice is worth the king's whole city.
The ministers clap their hands, laugh, call the Valuer foolish, and say the city had been thought beyond price but he equates it with a measure of rice.

occurrences.source_title: Jataka tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE SANDY ROAD / THE QUARREL OF THE QUAILS / THE MEASURE OF RICE / THE FOOLISH, TIMID RABBIT; lines 847-946
occurrences.motif_label: wise ruler investigates fear and corrects error
occurrences.basis: The lion, called the King of Beasts and described as wise, suspects a mistake, investigates the origin of the report, and explains the real cause.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The lion sees the animals running, hears their cry, thinks there must be a mistake, and roars three times at the foot of a hill to stop them.
The lion asks who saw it; the elephant points to the fox, the fox to the rabbits, and the rabbits say another rabbit told them, until the first rabbit is reached.
The first rabbit tells the lion he heard the sound while under the palm-tree. The lion says they will go back and see what is the matter, then carries the rabbit there.
The lion sees the coconut near where the rabbit slept and says, "It must have been the sound of the cocoanut falling to the ground that you heard."
The lion tells the other animals what happened; the passage says that without the wise King of Beasts they might still be running.

occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom teaching through layered moral tales
occurrences.basis: The passage emphasizes lessons suitable for children and deeper meanings to be understood later.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker says they were captivated by the Jataka Tales and saw excellent use for them in teaching children.
The passage says many obvious lessons suit little people, with deeper meanings beneath that may be fathomed later.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE QUARREL OF THE QUAILS / THE MEASURE OF RICE / THE FOOLISH, TIMID RABBIT / THE WISE AND THE FOOLISH MERCHANT; lines 948-1073
occurrences.motif_label: wise and foolish travelers face the same test
occurrences.basis: The two merchants encounter the same desert danger and demonic deception, but the foolish merchant discards the water while the wise merchant preserves it after testing the evidence.

evidence.locator: lines 1000-1022, false report of water ahead
evidence.quote_or_summary: The disguised demon claims that the dark streak ahead is a forest with ponds and frequent rain, asks about the carts, and advises the merchant to empty the water-jars because they are no longer needed.

evidence.locator: lines 1024-1033, consequence for the foolish caravan
evidence.quote_or_summary: The foolish merchant empties every jar. The dark line proves to be clouds, no water is found, men and oxen become hungry and thirsty, and demons carry off every man at night while leaving the loaded carts.
The wise man knew the man was a demon because he cast no shadow; he says they do not throw away water until they see more.

evidence.locator: lines 1043-1067, wise merchant questions his men
evidence.quote_or_summary: The men propose discarding the water, but the wise merchant asks whether anyone knows of a pond or lake, feels damp wind, or sees a rain cloud. After negative answers, he says the strangers were demons and orders that not even a half-pint of water be thrown away.

occurrences.motif_label: life-preserving resource must not be discarded on false assurance
occurrences.basis: The water-jars determine survival in the desert; the foolish merchant empties them on hearsay, while the wise merchant keeps them until actual water is seen.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The foolish merchant leaves the city, reaches a desert, fills great water-jars, loads them into a large wagon, and begins crossing.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE OTTERS AND THE WOLF / HOW THE MONKEY SAVED HIS TROOP / THE HAWKS AND THEIR FRIENDS / THE BRAVE LITTLE BOWMAN; lines 1000-1096
occurrences.motif_label: underestimated small hero proves superior skill
occurrences.basis: The little bowman is physically small and expects rejection, but his skill kills dangerous animals and wins a battle.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage introduces a little crooked-backed man called the wise little bowman because he uses bow and arrow very well and thinks the king would dismiss him because of his size.
The little bowman finds a big strong ditch-digger and proposes that the big man seek army service while the bowman secretly does the assigned work and they divide the pay.
A tiger in the forest has carried off many people; the king orders the big man to kill it, but the little bowman shoots it, and the big man receives gifts and praise.
The king orders the big man to kill a buffalo running on a road; the little man shoots it, and the king gives the big man a bag of money.
The little bowman says 'And now to win,' drives the war-elephant into battle, breaks into the enemy camp, drives the foreign king back, and leads the army into the city.
The king and people call the victor the brave little bowman, and the king makes him chief of the army and gives him rich gifts.

occurrences.passage_locator: HOW THE MONKEY SAVED HIS TROOP / THE HAWKS AND THEIR FRIENDS / THE BRAVE LITTLE BOWMAN / THE FOOLHARDY WOLF; lines 1098-1170
occurrences.motif_label: Foolish pride after prosperity leads to destruction
occurrences.basis: The wolf grows large and strong from the lion's shared food, becomes proud, disregards the lion's warning, attempts a feat beyond him, and is killed.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The wolf grows bigger and stronger from fine meat, becomes proud, and says he will kill an elephant for himself rather than live on another's food.
The wolf asks to lie in the den while the lion scouts and summons him to an elephant; the lion warns that only lions can kill elephants, but the wolf refuses to yield and the lion allows him to try.

The lion sees an elephant, calls the wolf from the cave mouth, and the wolf runs out, howls three times, springs at the elephant, misses, falls at its feet, and is killed by the elephant's right foot.
“You will no more come forth in your might, you foolhardy Wolf.”

occurrences.passage_locator: HOW THE MONKEY SAVED HIS TROOP / THE HAWKS AND THEIR FRIENDS / THE BRAVE LITTLE BOWMAN / THE FOOLHARDY WOLF; lines 1098-1170
occurrences.motif_label: Dependent imitates superior's dangerous feat and fails
occurrences.basis: The wolf tries to exchange roles with the lion and kill an elephant after seeing the lion kill large animals, but the lion explicitly says only lions can kill elephants and the wolf dies in the attempt.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Day after day the wolf scouts prey, returns to the den, speaks the summons, and the lion kills the animal and shares meat with the wolf.
The wolf asks to lie in the den while the lion scouts and summons him to an elephant; the lion warns that only lions can kill elephants, but the wolf refuses to yield and the lion allows him to try.

The lion sees an elephant, calls the wolf from the cave mouth, and the wolf runs out, howls three times, springs at the elephant, misses, falls at its feet, and is killed by the elephant's right foot.

occurrences.motif_label: Rejected warning before fatal action
occurrences.basis: The lion warns the wolf to abandon his plan; the wolf refuses and proceeds to the fatal attack.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The wolf asks to lie in the den while the lion scouts and summons him to an elephant; the lion warns that only lions can kill elephants, but the wolf refuses to yield and the lion allows him to try.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE HAWKS AND THEIR FRIENDS / THE BRAVE LITTLE BOWMAN / THE FOOLHARDY WOLF / THE STOLEN PLOW; lines 1172-1239
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom through analogy in judgment
occurrences.basis: The decisive argument is an analogy: if birds cannot carry off boys, then mice cannot eat plows; the judge acts on this reasoning.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In court, the village trader asks, “If birds cannot carry off boys, can mice eat plows?” and explains that if mice can eat plows, then birds can carry off boys.
The judge tells the town trader to give back the plow and says the village trader will give the son back; by night-time each has recovered what was missing.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE BRAVE LITTLE BOWMAN / THE FOOLHARDY WOLF / THE STOLEN PLOW / THE LION IN BAD COMPANY; lines 1241-1305
occurrences.motif_label: Ignoring wise parental counsel leads to destruction
occurrences.basis: The young Lion is warned by his parents and later by his father, but he disregards the warnings and dies after continuing the dangerous behavior.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The young Lion had been told by his father and mother not to make friends with wolves, but accepts this Wolf after the Wolf calls him "Great Lion."
The Lion's father dislikes having the Wolf there, but the young Lion thinks he knows better, so the Wolf remains in the den.
The father warns that the ponies belong to the king, who has many skilled archers, and tells his son not to take another pony.
The young Lion likes horse-meat and catches and kills pony after pony.
The Lion falls down dead.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE STOLEN PLOW / THE LION IN BAD COMPANY / XVIII / THE WISE GOAT AND THE WOLF; lines 1308-1379
occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom preserves the vulnerable from predators
occurrences.basis: The goat survives by caution, inference, and a verbal countermeasure against stronger predators.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Many wild goats live in a cave in a hill; a wolf and his mate live nearby, eat goats, and fail to catch the one goat wiser than the others.
The male wolf raises his head; the goat sees him and runs back to her cave; the mate asks why he raised his head while pretending to be dead.
The goat recognizes another trick and says she will come with friends: two hounds, Old Gray and Young Tan, the large dog Four-Eyes, and each dog's mate.
The wolf runs back to her mate after hearing this, and the goat never sees either wolf again.

occurrences.source_title: More Jataka Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: XVIII / THE WISE GOAT AND THE WOLF / PRINCE WICKED AND THE GRATEFUL ANIMALS / BEAUTY AND BROWNIE; lines 1582-1626
occurrences.motif_label: wise obedience to elder counsel preserves the group
occurrences.basis: The narrative contrasts Beauty, who follows his father’s counsel and saves his herd, with Brownie, who forgets the counsel and loses most of his herd.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The father says he, the mother, and older deer will stay in the forest, while Beauty and Brownie must lead their herds to the high hills until the crops are cut.
The father tells them to travel by night so hunters will not see them, and not to take the herd near villages where hunters live.
Beauty travels at night, avoids villages, brings his herd safely to the high hills, and loses no deer.
Brownie forgets the father’s words, travels in the daytime, leads his herd past villages, and hunters kill many deer from his herd.
When crops are cut, the deer return; Beauty brings all his herd back, while Brownie again travels by day past villages and reaches the forest with only a few deer left.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE WISE GOAT AND THE WOLF / PRINCE WICKED AND THE GRATEFUL ANIMALS / BEAUTY AND BROWNIE / THE ELEPHANT AND THE DOG; lines 1628-1695
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom in diagnosing emotional suffering
occurrences.basis: The chief servant observes that the elephant has no bodily ailment and correctly identifies the loss of the dog as the cause of sadness.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The king sends his chief servant to investigate; the servant finds nothing wrong with the elephant's body, asks if he has lost a playmate, and later reports that the elephant is lonely without the dog.

occurrences.source_title: More Jataka Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: XIX PRINCE WICKED AND THE GRATEFUL ANIMALS / XX BEAUTY AND BROWNIE / XXI THE ELEPHANT AND THE DOG / THE GIRL MONKEY AND THE STRING OF PEARLS; lines 166-262
occurrences.motif_label: clever investigator solves theft by inference
occurrences.basis: The chief guard reasons that no outsider entered the guarded garden, suspects a monkey, and devises a successful test.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The chief guard reasons that the pearls were lost in the garden, the gates were strongly guarded, and many monkeys were present, so perhaps a Girl Monkey took them.
The chief guard buys bright-colored glass beads and has the guards hang them on low bushes in the garden after dark.
The king asks how the chief guard found the thief; the guard explains his inference and bead trick, and the king praises and thanks him.

occurrences.passage_locator: XX BEAUTY AND BROWNIE / XXI THE ELEPHANT AND THE DOG / THE GIRL MONKEY AND THE STRING OF PEARLS / THE THREE FISHES; lines 264-305
occurrences.motif_label: prudent warning against danger
occurrences.basis: Very-Thoughtful recognizes danger from fishermen and urges a return to safer waters before the danger occurs.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Very-Thoughtful says there is danger because fishermen come to catch fish with nets and lines, and urges the others to go back to the wild country.

occurrences.source_title: More Jataka Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: XX BEAUTY AND BROWNIE / XXI THE ELEPHANT AND THE DOG / THE GIRL MONKEY AND THE STRING OF PEARLS / THE THREE FISHES; lines 264-305
occurrences.motif_label: clever rescue of trapped companions
occurrences.basis: Very-Thoughtful devises an action that deceives the fisherman and frees the two fishes from the net.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “I must save them,” said Very-Thoughtful.
Very-Thoughtful swims around the net and splashes first in front and then behind it, imitating fish that have broken through and gone upriver and downriver.
The fisherman thinks the fish have broken through the net, one going upriver and one downriver, so he pulls in the net by one corner and lets the two fishes out.
The rescued fishes say that Very-Thoughtful saved their lives and that they are now willing to go back to the wild country.

occurrences.passage_locator: XXI THE ELEPHANT AND THE DOG / THE GIRL MONKEY AND THE STRING OF PEARLS / THE THREE FISHES / THE TRICKY WOLF AND THE RATS; lines 307-358
occurrences.motif_label: wise leader exposes hidden danger
occurrences.basis: The Chief Rat notices the pattern of disappearing rats, tests the wolf by going last, escapes the attack, and defeats him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The rats notice fewer rats each night and ask the Chief Rat what is wrong; he is not sure but suspects the wolf.
The Chief Rat tells the others to go first while he goes last; the wolf springs at him, but the Chief Rat escapes.
The Chief Rat exposes the wolf's trick, bites the wolf's throat so that he dies, and afterward the rats live happily in peace and quiet.

occurrences.source_title: More Jataka Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE GIRL MONKEY AND THE STRING OF PEARLS / THE THREE FISHES / THE TRICKY WOLF AND THE RATS / THE WOODPECKER, TURTLE, AND DEER; lines 360-453
occurrences.motif_label: cooperative rescue through complementary abilities
occurrences.basis: The Woodpecker uses flight and harassment to delay the hunter, the Turtle uses teeth to gnaw the trap, and the Deer uses speed and horns to rescue the Turtle.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Woodpecker and Turtle come to help; the Woodpecker tells the Turtle to gnaw the leather trap while she keeps the hunter away.
The hunter comes out with a knife; the Woodpecker flies at his face at the front door and then again at the back door, making him turn back twice.
The Woodpecker warns that the hunter is coming; the Turtle has gnawed all but one piece of the trap, injuring his mouth, and the Deer breaks the last piece and runs into the woods.
The Deer sees the Turtle has been taken, decides to save him, lets the hunter see him, and leads the hunter into the forest while staying just out of reach.
The Deer slips away, returns by another route, hears the Turtle call from a bag hanging on a tree, lifts the bag with his horns, throws it down, tears it open, and frees him.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE THREE FISHES / THE TRICKY WOLF AND THE RATS / THE WOODPECKER, TURTLE, AND DEER / THE GOLDEN GOOSE; lines 455-503
occurrences.motif_label: greed destroys continuing gift
occurrences.basis: The mother's attempt to seize all the feathers at once causes the feathers to lose their value and ends the goose's visits.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The mother suggests taking all the feathers next time because the goose may stop coming; the daughters refuse, saying it will hurt the goose.
The mother, described as greedy, grabs the goose and pulls out every feather; feathers plucked against the goose's wish turn white and lose their value.
The goose's feathers grow again, and he flies home and never returns.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE TRICKY WOLF AND THE RATS / THE WOODPECKER, TURTLE, AND DEER / THE GOLDEN GOOSE / THE STUPID MONKEYS; lines 505-550
occurrences.motif_label: Foolish helpers destroy what they are asked to preserve
occurrences.basis: The monkeys accept a caretaking task but use a destructive method, uprooting the young trees they are supposed to water.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "Oh, yes!" said the Chief of the Monkeys. "We shall be glad to do that."
When the monkeys ask how to know each tree has enough water, the chief says to pull up each young tree, look at root length, and water long-rooted trees more than short-rooted ones.
The monkeys pull up all the young trees to see which roots are long and which are short.
"When the gardener came back the next day, the poor young trees were all dead."

occurrences.source_title: More Jataka Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE TRICKY WOLF AND THE RATS / THE WOODPECKER, TURTLE, AND DEER / THE GOLDEN GOOSE / THE STUPID MONKEYS; lines 505-550
occurrences.motif_label: Misguided literal test leads to ruin
occurrences.basis: The chief proposes judging water needs by physically pulling up the trees to inspect root length, and this procedure kills the trees.

evidence.quote_or_summary: When the monkeys ask how to know each tree has enough water, the chief says to pull up each young tree, look at root length, and water long-rooted trees more than short-rooted ones.
The monkeys pull up all the young trees to see which roots are long and which are short.
"When the gardener came back the next day, the poor young trees were all dead."

occurrences.source_title: More Jataka Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE WOODPECKER, TURTLE, AND DEER / THE GOLDEN GOOSE / THE STUPID MONKEYS / THE CUNNING WOLF; lines 552-594
occurrences.motif_label: deception exposed by a cautious animal
occurrences.basis: The King of the Wolves suspects a trick, tests the supposed corpse by pulling the club, and correctly explains the deception.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "That man is playing a trick on us, I believe," said the King of the Wolves; he tells the others to stay while he tests whether the man is dead or pretending.
The King of the Wolves creeps up and pulls at the man's club; the man immediately pulls back on the club.
The wolf says the man would not have pulled back if dead and says, "You pretend you are dead so that you may kill one of us for your supper."

occurrences.source_title: More Jataka Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE WOODPECKER, TURTLE, AND DEER / THE GOLDEN GOOSE / THE STUPID MONKEYS / THE CUNNING WOLF; lines 552-594
occurrences.motif_label: counter-trick defeats the original trick
occurrences.basis: The man admits that he tried to trick the animals but that the cunning Wolf played a better trick on him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The man tells his friends that he tried to get meat by tricking the animals, "but the cunning Wolf played a better trick on me."

occurrences.source_title: More Jataka Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE GOLDEN GOOSE / THE STUPID MONKEYS / THE CUNNING WOLF / THE PENNY-WISE MONKEY; lines 596-622
occurrences.motif_label: losing much to gain little
occurrences.basis: The monkey drops all the peas he has in order to search for one pea, and the king explicitly interprets this as losing much to gain a little.

evidence.quote_or_summary: When one pea falls to the ground, the monkey drops all the peas in his hands to search for the lost one and cannot find it.
"To get more, I threw away what I had," he said to himself.
The king watches the monkey and decides not to be like the foolish monkey who lost much to gain a little.

occurrences.source_title: More Jataka Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE GOLDEN GOOSE / THE STUPID MONKEYS / THE CUNNING WOLF / THE PENNY-WISE MONKEY; lines 596-622
occurrences.motif_label: animal behavior as moral lesson for ruler
occurrences.basis: The king observes the monkey's foolish action and changes his political-military decision as a result.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The king watches the monkey and decides not to be like the foolish monkey who lost much to gain a little.
The king and his men march back home.

occurrences.source_title: More Jataka Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE GOLDEN GOOSE / THE STUPID MONKEYS / THE CUNNING WOLF / THE PENNY-WISE MONKEY; lines 596-622
occurrences.motif_label: renunciation of conquest after cautionary example
occurrences.basis: The king is marching to take another country but returns home after reflecting on the monkey's loss.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A king of a large and rich country gathers an army to take a faraway little country, marches all morning, and camps in the forest.
The king watches the monkey and decides not to be like the foolish monkey who lost much to gain a little.
The king and his men march back home.

occurrences.source_title: More Jataka Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE STUPID MONKEYS / THE CUNNING WOLF / THE PENNY-WISE MONKEY / THE RED-BUD TREE; lines 624-671
occurrences.motif_label: partial perspectives on one reality
occurrences.basis: Each prince reports a different appearance of the same tree from a single visit, and the king explains the difference as a matter of timing.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The princes report conflicting descriptions of the tree: dead-looking and bare, red-budded, green-leaved, or covered in bean-pods.
"My sons, you have all four seen the same tree, but each of you saw it at a different time of the year."

occurrences.source_title: More Jataka Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE STUPID MONKEYS / THE CUNNING WOLF / THE PENNY-WISE MONKEY / THE RED-BUD TREE; lines 624-671
occurrences.motif_label: instructive resolution by a king
occurrences.basis: The king listens to the princes' conflicting claims and resolves them with an explanation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The princes report conflicting descriptions of the tree: dead-looking and bare, red-budded, green-leaved, or covered in bean-pods.
"My sons, you have all four seen the same tree, but each of you saw it at a different time of the year."

occurrences.source_title: More Jataka Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE CUNNING WOLF / THE PENNY-WISE MONKEY / THE RED-BUD TREE / THE WOODPECKER AND THE LION; lines 673-720
occurrences.motif_label: Cautious helper rescues a dangerous animal
