occurrences.basis: The Woodpecker helps the Lion but takes a practical precaution before entering the predator’s mouth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Woodpecker lands on a nearby tree branch, asks what ails the Lion, and says she fears entering his mouth because he might eat her.
The Lion tells the Woodpecker not to be afraid, promises not to eat her, and asks her to save his life if she can.
The Woodpecker asks the Lion to open his mouth, decides to be careful, and places a stick between the Lion’s upper and lower jaws so he cannot shut his mouth.
The Woodpecker enters the Lion’s mouth, strikes the bone with her beak until it falls out, then exits and knocks out the stick so the Lion can shut his mouth.

occurrences.source_title: More Jataka Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE CUNNING WOLF / THE PENNY-WISE MONKEY / THE RED-BUD TREE / THE WOODPECKER AND THE LION; lines 673-720
occurrences.motif_label: Avoidance of an untrustworthy beneficiary
occurrences.basis: After the Lion reframes sparing the Woodpecker as a favor and refuses her request, the Woodpecker keeps away from him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Later in the summer the Woodpecker asks the Lion to do something for her; the Lion refuses and says that letting her go when she was in his mouth is all she can expect.
The Woodpecker says no more and keeps away from the Lion from that day on.

occurrences.source_title: More Jataka Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE RED-BUD TREE / THE WOODPECKER AND THE LION / THE OTTERS AND THE WOLF / HOW THE MONKEY SAVED HIS TROOP; lines 773-865
occurrences.motif_label: wise leader devises escape from mortal danger
occurrences.basis: The Chief assesses the danger of drowning and creates a practical solution that saves the troop.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Chief says, “Do not fear; I will save you,” and the monkeys are comforted because he has helped them before.
The Chief runs onto a branch over the river, sees that the opposite branches do not meet, and reasons that some monkeys would fall into the water and drown if they tried to jump.
The Chief decides, “I shall make a bridge of my back,” reaches the longest branch across the river, and calls the monkeys to step on his back.
The monkeys follow the Chief's command, cross by stepping on his back to the other branch, descend, and go home.

occurrences.source_title: More Jataka Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE WOODPECKER AND THE LION / THE OTTERS AND THE WOLF / HOW THE MONKEY SAVED HIS TROOP / THE HAWKS AND THEIR FRIENDS; lines 867-998
occurrences.motif_label: danger averted through practical foresight
occurrences.basis: The Mother Hawk’s earlier advice to make friends provides the means of rescue when the hunters threaten the nest.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Mother Hawk asks about nearby friends and tells the Father Hawk to make friends with the Kingfisher, Lion, and Turtle so they can receive help in danger or trouble.
The Mother Hawk says the men plan to eat their young and sends the Father Hawk to the Kingfisher, who promises to help.
“You have saved us. Friends in need are friends indeed.”

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE. / THE SIEGE OF TROY. / RETURN OF THE GREEKS FROM TROY.; lines 10201-10297
occurrences.motif_label: hero consults the dead for knowledge of the future
occurrences.basis: Odysseus travels to the lower-world entrance, performs sacrifice, and receives prophetic instruction from Tiresias among the dead.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odysseus stays with Circe for a year; at his companions' urging he leaves. Circe, unable to detain him after vowing not to use spells, warns him of dangers, commands him to consult Tiresias in Hades, provisions the ship, and bids farewell.
Odysseus follows Circe's directions to the Cimmerian land at the far end of the world beyond Oceanus, landing where Acheron and Cocytus mingle at the entrance to the lower world.

Odysseus digs a trench, sacrifices a black ram and ewe, and shades rise from a gulf eager to drink the blood, which can temporarily restore their mental vigour; he keeps them back with his sword until Tiresias appears.
Tiresias comes with a golden staff, drinks the sacrifice, reveals Odysseus' future fate, and warns him how to avoid dangers on the voyage and after returning to Ithaca.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: RHEA (OPS). / DIVISION OF THE WORLD. / THEORIES AS TO THE ORIGIN OF MAN. / THIRD DYNASTY--OLYMPIAN DIVINITIES.; lines 1081-1171
occurrences.motif_label: Allegorical sacred marriages of a high god
occurrences.basis: Zeus's immortal marriages are explicitly said to convey allegorical meanings, including power allied to wisdom, justice, law, grace, beauty, memory, and genius.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Zeus's unions with Metis, Themis, Eurynome, and Mnemosyne are said to allegorically represent power joined with wisdom, justice, grace, beauty, memory, and genius.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: RETURN OF THE GREEKS FROM TROY. / PRONOUNCING INDEX. / A COMPLETE COURSE IN THE STUDY OF ENGLISH. / NOTES; lines 11775-11823
occurrences.motif_label: exceptional wisdom or awareness among the dead
occurrences.basis: Tiresias alone among the shades is described as retaining full mental vigor.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Tiresias alone among the shades is said to be in full possession of mental vigor.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THIRD DYNASTY--OLYMPIAN DIVINITIES. / JUPITER. / HERA (JUNO). / JUNO.; lines 1413-1428
occurrences.motif_label: warning goddess and civic shrine
occurrences.basis: Juno is worshipped on the Arx as Juno Moneta, the warning goddess, with the public mint adjacent to the shrine.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Juno had a temple on the Arx where she was worshipped as Juno Moneta, the warning goddess.
The public mint was adjacent to the shrine of Juno Moneta.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: JUPITER. / HERA (JUNO). / JUNO. / PALLAS-ATHENE (MINERVA).; lines 1430-1518
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom deity as counsellor and deputy of supreme god
occurrences.basis: Athene is goddess of Wisdom, Zeus's faithful counsellor, and his empowered deputy.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Athene is introduced as goddess of Wisdom and Armed Resistance; she issues from Zeus's head fully armed, and Olympus, earth, sea, and Helios respond to her advent.

Athene enters the assembly of the gods, becomes Zeus's counsellor, is described as his favourite child and counterpart, and receives prerogatives including thunderbolts, life extension, prophecy, and deputy authority.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: JUPITER. / HERA (JUNO). / JUNO. / PALLAS-ATHENE (MINERVA).; lines 1430-1518
occurrences.motif_label: culture-bringing inventor and teacher
occurrences.basis: Athene teaches or presides over agriculture, numbers, navigation, chariots, the wooden horse, weaving, and the flute.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Athene protects the state, law, and right; supports the Greeks in the Trojan war; institutes the Areopagus; and presides over learning, agriculture, numbers, trumpets, chariots, the Argo, and the wooden horse.

Athene presides over spinning and weaving, makes garments for herself, Hera, and Jason, accepts Arachne's challenge, is defeated, strikes Arachne with a shuttle, and changes her into a spider after Arachne hangs herself.
Athene invents the flute, is laughed at by gods and goddesses for her facial contortions while playing, looks at herself in a fountain, throws the flute away, and never plays it again.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: JUPITER. / HERA (JUNO). / JUNO. / PALLAS-ATHENE (MINERVA).; lines 1521-1553
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom-bearing goddess
occurrences.basis: Athene is described as thoughtful and replete with wisdom, and her appearance embodies strength, grandeur, and majesty.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Athene is represented fully draped with a serious, thoughtful, wise aspect, strength, grandeur, majesty, and a slightly masculine appearance.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: HERA (JUNO). / JUNO. / PALLAS-ATHENE (MINERVA). / MINERVA.; lines 1556-1567
occurrences.motif_label: Divine patronage of wisdom, learning, and useful arts
occurrences.basis: Minerva is explicitly said to preside over learning and useful arts, with schools under her especial care.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva, like Pallas-Athene, presides over learning and useful arts and is patroness of sewing, spinning, weaving, and similar accomplishments.
Schools are under Minerva's care; schoolboys have holidays during her Greater Quinquatria festivals and bring their master a gift called the Minerval.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: JUNO. / PALLAS-ATHENE (MINERVA). / MINERVA. / THEMIS.; lines 1569-1632
occurrences.motif_label: Divine wisdom and prophetic counsel guiding a chief god
occurrences.basis: Themis is said to have great wisdom; Zeus seeks her counsel and follows her advice, and she is also a prophetic divinity with an oracle.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Themis is daughter of Cronus and Rhea, wife of Zeus, personification of justice and order, presider over assemblies and hospitality laws, convoker of the gods' assembly, mistress of ritual and ceremony, counselor of Zeus, and prophetic divinity with an oracle near the Cephissus in Boeotia.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: JUNO. / PALLAS-ATHENE (MINERVA). / MINERVA. / THEMIS.; lines 1569-1632
occurrences.motif_label: Inherited prophetic power through merging of older and younger deity
occurrences.basis: The elder Themis inherits prophecy from Gaea and transmits it to the younger Themis when the two are merged.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says Themis takes the place of a more ancient deity of the same name, a daughter of Uranus and Gaea, who inherited prophecy from Gaea and transmitted it to her younger representative when merged with her.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VENUS. / HELIOS (SOL). / EOS (AURORA). / PHOEBUS-APOLLO.; lines 2279-2363
occurrences.motif_label: prophetic all-seeing deity
occurrences.basis: Apollo's prophetic power is tied to his all-seeing sun-god nature and his power to reveal hidden future secrets.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Apollo's prophetic power is emphasized above his other attributes; as sun-god, his all-seeing eye penetrates hidden recesses and future secrets.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: HELIOS (SOL). / EOS (AURORA). / PHOEBUS-APOLLO. / ROMAN APOLLO.; lines 2666-2715
occurrences.motif_label: Prophetic books preserved for the state
occurrences.basis: Sibylline oracles and books are described as containing predictions important to the Romans and being preserved in temples.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Augustus built a Palatine temple to Apollo; at the foot of Apollo's statue were two gilt chests containing Sibylline oracles, collected to replace books destroyed in the burned temple of Jupiter.

The Cumaean Sibyl offers nine books to Tarquinius Superbus, burns three after each refusal, and Tarquin buys the remaining three after the Augurs advise him to do so; the books contain important predictions for the Romans.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: HELIOS (SOL). / EOS (AURORA). / PHOEBUS-APOLLO. / ROMAN APOLLO.; lines 2666-2715
occurrences.motif_label: Rejected sacred knowledge becomes diminished but more urgently valued
occurrences.basis: Tarquin refuses the Sibyl's books twice; she burns portions while keeping the same price, and the Augurs then urge him to buy the remaining books.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Cumaean Sibyl offers nine books to Tarquinius Superbus, burns three after each refusal, and Tarquin buys the remaining three after the Augurs advise him to do so; the books contain important predictions for the Romans.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: NEPTUNE. / SEA DIVINITIES. / OCEANUS. / NEREUS.; lines 3427-3436
occurrences.motif_label: Prophetic sea elder
occurrences.basis: Nereus is portrayed as an old sea-deity with the gift of prophecy.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “Nereus appears to have been the personification of the sea in its calm and placid moods” and is described as the most important sea-deity after Poseidon.
Nereus is represented as a kind, benevolent old man with prophecy who presides over the Aegean Sea as its protecting spirit.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: SEA DIVINITIES. / OCEANUS. / NEREUS. / PROTEUS.; lines 3438-3467
occurrences.motif_label: reluctant shapeshifting seer compelled to reveal knowledge
occurrences.basis: Proteus possesses prophetic power, resists consultation, changes into many forms when seized, and gives information only after being held long enough to resume his true form.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Proteus, known as the Old Man of the Sea, is a son of Poseidon, has prophetic power, and resists being consulted as a seer.
The favorable moment is to seize Proteus; he changes into many forms to avoid demands, but if held long enough he tires, resumes his true form, and gives the desired information.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: MARS. / NIKE (VICTORIA). / VICTORIA. / HERMES (MERCURY).; lines 3819-3892
occurrences.motif_label: serpents associated with wisdom
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly says that the serpents on the Caduceus typify wisdom.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Apollo brings Hermes to Olympus, obtains an oath by the Styx, gives him the Caduceus, and Hermes uses it to reconcile two fighting snakes; the wand, serpents, and wings are interpreted as power, wisdom, and despatch.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VICTORIA. / HERMES (MERCURY). / MERCURY. / DIONYSUS (BACCHUS).; lines 4043-4125
occurrences.motif_label: Dangerous literal wish becomes a curse
occurrences.basis: Midas asks that everything he touches turn to gold, but food, wine, and his couch become gold, making the gift a source of suffering.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Silenus wanders intoxicated into Midas's rose-gardens, is brought to Midas, receives hospitality for ten days, and is returned to Dionysus, who offers Midas a favor; Midas asks for the golden touch.

evidence.locator: lines 4043-4125, paragraph 3, effects of golden touch
evidence.quote_or_summary: Midas discovers that food, wine, and his couch turn to gold at his touch, causing hunger, thirst, weariness, and regret.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VICTORIA. / HERMES (MERCURY). / MERCURY. / DIONYSUS (BACCHUS).; lines 4127-4148
occurrences.motif_label: prophetic deity with mountain oracle
occurrences.basis: Dionysus is described as a prophetic divinity with a principal oracle on Mount Rhodope.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Dionysus is described as a prophetic divinity with oracles, chiefly the oracle on Mount Rhodope in Thrace.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: MORPHEUS. / THE GORGONS. / GRAEAE. / SPHINX.; lines 4682-4726
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom embodied as composite divine creature
occurrences.basis: The Egyptian Sphinx is explicitly said to personify wisdom and fertility and is represented in composite lion-woman form.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Sphinx was an ancient Egyptian divinity who personified wisdom and the fertility of nature.
The Egyptian Sphinx is represented as a reclining lion with a woman's head and bust and a distinctive hood around the head and face.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: MORPHEUS. / THE GORGONS. / GRAEAE. / SPHINX.; lines 4682-4726
occurrences.motif_label: lethal riddle challenge at a threshold
occurrences.basis: The Greek Sphinx occupies a pass, asks riddles of those who come by, and kills those who cannot solve them; Oedipus survives by giving the correct answer.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Sphinx sits on a rocky eminence near Thebes, controls a pass used by the Thebans, asks riddles, and tears apart those who cannot solve them.
Oedipus receives the riddle about a creature moving on four legs in the morning, two at noon, and three in the evening, and answers that it is man in infancy, adulthood, and old age with a staff.
After hearing Oedipus's correct solution, the Sphinx flings herself over the precipice and dies in the abyss below.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: HEBE (JUVENTAS). / JUVENTAS. / GANYMEDES. / THE MUSES.; lines 5052-5157
occurrences.motif_label: Divine patrons bestow wisdom and artistic inspiration
occurrences.basis: The Muses grant knowledge, wisdom, understanding, eloquence, poetic thought, and musical harmony to chosen favourites.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Muses are honoured by mortals and immortals, led by Apollo in Olympus, invoked with libations and supplications, and said to grant knowledge, wisdom, eloquence, poetic thought, and musical harmony.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: OCEANIDES, NEREIDES, AND NAIADES. / OCEANIDES. / THE NEREIDES. / THE NAIADES.; lines 5367-5384
occurrences.motif_label: prophetic water under divine oversight
occurrences.basis: Waters presided over by the Naiades are believed to inspire drinkers with the ability to foretell future events.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Like all nymphs, the Naiades possess prophecy; many springs and fountains they preside over are believed to give drinkers power to foretell future events.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: NYMPHS OF THE VALLEYS AND MOUNTAINS. / NAPAEAE AND OREADES. / THE WINDS. / PAN (FAUNUS).; lines 5499-5583
occurrences.motif_label: prophetic power transmitted between gods
occurrences.basis: Pan is said to possess prophecy and to impart it to Apollo.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Pan has prophetic power, is said to impart it to Apollo, and has an ancient oracle in Arcadia.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: FAUNUS. / THE SATYRS. / PRIAPUS. / ASCLEPIAS (AESCULAPIUS).; lines 5661-5710
occurrences.motif_label: divine healing wisdom transmitted by a teacher
occurrences.basis: Chiron teaches Asclepias knowledge, especially herbs, and Asclepias discovers hidden powers of plants.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Asclepias is named as god of healing, son of Apollo and Coronis, and pupil of Chiron, who especially taught him the properties of herbs.
Asclepias discovers cures, perfects healing so that he wards off death and restores the dead to life, and is popularly believed to be aided by Medusa's blood given by Pallas-Athene.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: FAUNUS. / THE SATYRS. / PRIAPUS. / ASCLEPIAS (AESCULAPIUS).; lines 5661-5710
occurrences.motif_label: serpent as healing and wisdom emblem
occurrences.basis: The serpent is identified as Asclepias' distinguishing symbol and is linked with cures, prudence, and wisdom.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Epidaurus statue shows Asclepias as an old bearded man leaning on a staff around which a serpent climbs; the serpent is his distinguishing symbol, connected with cures, prudence, and wisdom.
The usual attributes of Asclepias are listed as staff, bowl, herbs, pineapple, dog, and serpent.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: FAUNUS. / THE SATYRS. / PRIAPUS. / ASCLEPIAS (AESCULAPIUS).; lines 5661-5710
occurrences.motif_label: dream revelation at a healing shrine
occurrences.basis: Sufferers sleep in Asclepias' temple and receive dream appearances revealing cures.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Asclepias' shrines are placed in healthy sites or by healing wells; sufferers sleep in the temple, receive dream instructions from the god, and record cures on tablets.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: ASCLEPIAS (AESCULAPIUS). / AESCULAPIUS. / ROMAN DIVINITIES. / JANUS.; lines 5712-5790
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom through knowledge of past and future
occurrences.basis: Cronus/Saturn gives Janus knowledge of past and future events, enabling wise measures for his subjects' welfare.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Janus is said to have been an ancient Italian king deified after wise rule; Saturn, identified with Greek Cronus, gave him knowledge of past and future events, explaining his two opposite-facing faces.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: LIBITINA. / LAVERNA. / COMUS. / THE CAMENAE.; lines 5955-5976
occurrences.motif_label: Prophetic female nymphs as revered wisdom figures
occurrences.basis: The Camenae are explicitly described as prophetic nymphs held in high veneration.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Camenae were prophetic nymphs venerated by ancient Italians; they were four in number, with Carmenta and Egeria the best known.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: LIBITINA. / LAVERNA. / COMUS. / THE CAMENAE.; lines 5955-5976
occurrences.motif_label: Religious initiation by a female divine or nymphic instructor
occurrences.basis: Egeria is said to have initiated Numa Pompilius in forms of religious worship that he then introduced among his people.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Egeria is said to have initiated Numa Pompilius in forms of religious worship that he introduced among his people.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: ALTARS. / PRIESTS. / SACRIFICES. / ORACLES.; lines 6289-6325
occurrences.motif_label: seeking divine prophetic knowledge
occurrences.basis: The passage centers on people seeking knowledge of the future through oracles and priestly interpretation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage states that humans desire to know the future to avert danger, and that Greeks sought prophetic knowledge from oracles whose predictions were interpreted by appointed priests.
Apollo's oracle at Delphi is called the most famous oracle and is described as widely consulted by people from far and near.
The Pythia became ecstatic and uttered extraordinary phrases regarded as Apollo's utterance; priests interpreted these for the people, often ambiguously.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: ALTARS. / PRIESTS. / SACRIFICES. / ORACLES.; lines 6289-6325
occurrences.motif_label: ecstatic oracle as divine mouthpiece
occurrences.basis: The Pythia enters an ecstatic state and utters phrases regarded as Apollo's own utterance, which priests interpret.

evidence.quote_or_summary: She sat on a tripod placed over the mouth of a cave from which sulphurous vapours issued.
The Pythia became ecstatic and uttered extraordinary phrases regarded as Apollo's utterance; priests interpreted these for the people, often ambiguously.
Clouds of incense filled the temple, hid the priestess from the uninitiated, and she was later returned fainting to her cell.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: ALTARS. / PRIESTS. / SACRIFICES. / ORACLES.; lines 6289-6325
occurrences.motif_label: ambiguous prophecy fulfilled by reversal
occurrences.basis: Croesus interprets the oracle's prediction in his favour, but the prediction is fulfilled through the destruction of his own empire.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Croesus consulted an oracle before war with Cyrus; the oracle said crossing a river would destroy a great empire, and after Croesus crossed it he was defeated and his own empire was destroyed.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: AUGURS. / FESTIVALS. / GREEK FESTIVALS. / ELEUSINIAN MYSTERIES.; lines 6361-6392
occurrences.motif_label: teaching of soul immortality in mystery rites
occurrences.basis: The priests teach initiates, and the principal belief inculcated is stated to be the immortality of the soul, along with moral lessons.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Priests taught initiates secret moral meanings drawn from Demeter and Persephone myths, with immortality of the soul named as the most important belief taught.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VESTALIA. / PART II.--LEGENDS. / CADMUS. / PERSEUS.; lines 6633-6734
occurrences.motif_label: forced exchange for hidden knowledge
occurrences.basis: Perseus deprives the Graeae of their eye and tooth and restores them only after receiving directions to the Nymphs.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Perseus needs winged sandals, a magic wallet, and Aides' helmet from the Nymphs; guided by Hermes and Pallas-Athene, he takes the Graeae's single eye and tooth until they give directions.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CADMUS. / PERSEUS. / THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE.; lines 6955-7048
occurrences.motif_label: Prophetic timber embedded in a vessel
occurrences.basis: The Argo contains a board from the speaking oak of Zeus at Dodona that retains prophetic powers.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Jason invited young heroes to join him. Argos, guided by Pallas-Athene, built the Argo, a fifty-oared galley with a prophetic board from the speaking oak of Dodona; the ship was strong, light, and ornamented.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE. / PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES).; lines 7986-8074
occurrences.motif_label: shapeshifting informant compelled to reveal hidden route
occurrences.basis: Nereus alone knows the way and is forced to give information after Heracles restrains him through various metamorphoses.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Heracles kills Cycnus, Ares comes to avenge him, Zeus intervenes with a thunderbolt, and Heracles later receives route guidance from the Nymphs and compels shapeshifting Nereus to reveal the way.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: HERACLES (HERCULES). / BELLEROPHON. / THESEUS. / OEDIPUS.; lines 8727-8823
occurrences.motif_label: monster's riddle solved to free a city and win kingship
occurrences.basis: The Sphinx kills those who fail her riddles; Oedipus solves one, causing her death and gaining the throne and Jocaste.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hera sends the Sphinx as punishment to Thebes; from a rocky height the Sphinx asks riddles and devours those who fail.
After Laius's death, Creon rules and proclaims that kingship and Jocaste's hand will go to whoever solves a Sphinx riddle.
Oedipus enters Thebes, requests a riddle, solves it, and the Sphinx kills herself; Oedipus becomes king and husband of Jocaste.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: BELLEROPHON. / THESEUS. / OEDIPUS. / THE SEVEN AGAINST THEBES.; lines 8825-8917
occurrences.motif_label: prophetic warning of a doomed expedition
occurrences.basis: Amphiaraus foresees that the expedition will end disastrously and that only Adrastus will survive.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Adrastus gathers chiefs for the expedition; Amphiaraus foresees disaster, warns against the plan, refuses to join, and hides.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THESEUS. / OEDIPUS. / THE SEVEN AGAINST THEBES. / THE EPIGONI.; lines 8979-9016
occurrences.motif_label: prophetic guidance determines collective action
occurrences.basis: The Delphic oracle determines the expedition's commander, and Tiresias' counsel determines the Thebans' evacuation for survival.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Delphic oracle advises that Alcmaeon command; he hesitates because of his father's injunction; Thersander bribes Eriphyle with Harmonia's veil to induce Alcmaeon and Amphilochus to join the war.

After losing their leader and many warriors, the Thebans retreat behind the walls and consult the blind old seer Tiresias, who says they can save their lives only by abandoning the city with wives and families.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE EPIGONI. / ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE. / THE SIEGE OF TROY.; lines 9323-9415
occurrences.motif_label: Heroic wound and healing establish enduring friendship
occurrences.basis: Achilles heals Patroclus' wound using knowledge associated with Chiron, and the passage states that their celebrated friendship dates from this incident.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Patroclus is wounded while fighting beside Achilles; Achilles binds and heals the wound, and their celebrated friendship begins from this incident.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE EPIGONI. / ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE. / THE SIEGE OF TROY.; lines 9687-9774
occurrences.motif_label: coerced prophet reveals prerequisites for conquest
occurrences.basis: Helenus is captured and compelled to use prophecy against Troy by revealing three necessary conditions for its conquest.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odysseus captures Helenus, a prophet like Cassandra, and coerces him into revealing three conditions for Troy's conquest: Achilles' son, Heracles' arrows, and the Palladium.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: RHEA (OPS). / DIVISION OF THE WORLD. / THEORIES AS TO THE ORIGIN OF MAN. / THIRD DYNASTY--OLYMPIAN DIVINITIES.; lines 986-1079
occurrences.motif_label: oracular revelation through sacred tree
occurrences.basis: The passage describes Zeus's will and mortal destiny being heard in the rustling leaves of a giant oak and interpreted by priests.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Zeus is first worshipped at Dodona near Mount Tomarus and Lake Joanina; his voice is heard in a giant oak's leaves and interpreted by priests called Selli.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: RHEA (OPS). / DIVISION OF THE WORLD. / THEORIES AS TO THE ORIGIN OF MAN. / THIRD DYNASTY--OLYMPIAN DIVINITIES.; lines 986-1079
occurrences.motif_label: prophecy-averting swallowing of mother
occurrences.basis: Metis, personification of wisdom and prophecy, foretells a child who will surpass Zeus; Zeus swallows her to avert the prediction.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Metis is an Oceanid, personification of prudence and wisdom, administers the potion that makes Cronus yield his children, prophesies a child will surpass Zeus, and is swallowed by Zeus.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS / INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN; lines 1440-1580
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom gained through bodily sacrifice
occurrences.basis: Odin receives a wisdom-giving draught only after giving one of his eyes to Mimir.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odin visits Mimir's spring, the source of wit, wisdom, and memory, and Mimir requires one of Odin's eyes in exchange for a draught.
Odin plucks out an eye; Mimir sinks it into the fountain, leaving Odin with one eye, which the passage associates with solar imagery and, in verse, contrasts with the moon-like pledged eye.
Odin drinks from Mimir's fountain, gains knowledge, breaks a branch from the sacred tree Yggdrasil, and fashions the spear Gungnir from it.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS / INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN; lines 1440-1580
occurrences.motif_label: sacred well of knowledge and future vision
occurrences.basis: Mimir's spring is called the fountain of wit and wisdom and is said to mirror the future in its depths.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odin visits Mimir's spring, the source of wit, wisdom, and memory, and Mimir requires one of Odin's eyes in exchange for a draught.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS / INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN; lines 1440-1580
occurrences.motif_label: life-staked contest of wisdom
occurrences.basis: Odin and Vafthrudnir compete in questions and answers, with the loser's head as the stake.

evidence.quote_or_summary: To test his wisdom, Odin visits Vafthrudnir, the most learned giant, for a contest of wit in which the loser's head is at stake.

Odin disguises himself as a Wanderer named Gangrad; he and Vafthrudnir exchange questions about cosmic and divine matters, and Vafthrudnir recognizes Odin when asked what Allfather whispered to Balder on the funeral pyre.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS / INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN; lines 1440-1580
occurrences.motif_label: disguised god tests a giant's knowledge
occurrences.basis: Odin, advised by Frigga, disguises himself as a Wanderer named Gangrad and competes with Vafthrudnir in wisdom.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odin disguises himself as a Wanderer named Gangrad; he and Vafthrudnir exchange questions about cosmic and divine matters, and Vafthrudnir recognizes Odin when asked what Allfather whispered to Balder on the funeral pyre.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS / INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN; lines 1440-1580
occurrences.motif_label: divine knowledge of cosmic doom
occurrences.basis: Odin's acquired wisdom includes awareness that all things are transitory and that the gods are doomed to pass away.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odin's insight into the future reveals transience and the doomed fate of the gods, leaving him melancholy and contemplative.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS / INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN; lines 1582-1707
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom won through self-sacrifice
occurrences.basis: Odin gains knowledge and runes only after hanging nine nights on Yggdrasil while wounded with his own spear.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odin is identified as god of wisdom and inventor of runes; runes are described as mysterious characters first used for divination and later for inscriptions and records.
Odin relates that he hung nine nights on the wind-rocked sacred tree, wounded with a spear and offered to himself, while seeking knowledge and looking into Nifl-heim.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS / INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN; lines 1582-1707
occurrences.motif_label: magical signs granting power
occurrences.basis: Runes are described as mysterious characters first used for divination, and Odin's gained rune-knowledge gives him power over all things.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odin is identified as god of wisdom and inventor of runes; runes are described as mysterious characters first used for divination and later for inscriptions and records.

After mastering rune-knowledge, Odin cuts magic runes on Gungnir, Sleipnir's teeth, bear claws, and many other things; because of his hanging over the abyss, he becomes patron of those hanged or killed by the noose.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS / INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN; lines 1709-1827
occurrences.motif_label: daily drinking with goddess of history beneath a river
occurrences.basis: Odin visits Saga at Sokvabek to drink from golden cups and hear songs about old times and vanished races.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odin marries Saga or Laga and daily visits her crystal hall of Sokvabek beneath an ever-flowing river to drink and listen to songs about old times and vanished races.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS / INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN; lines 1709-1827
occurrences.motif_label: mythological instruction through visionary encounter
occurrences.basis: Gylfi questions figures in Odin's palace, receives a long explanation of Northern mythology, and the palace vanishes after the instruction ends.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Gylfi journeys south to test reports about the Æsir, reaches Odin's palace, sees Har, Iafn-har, and Thridi enthroned, receives answers from Gangler, and then the palace vanishes; this is said to be recorded in the Younger Edda.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS / INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN; lines 1830-1874
occurrences.motif_label: divine wisdom teaching
occurrences.basis: Odin is said to give a law code and teach moral qualities, practical conduct, and burial instructions in the Hávamál.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odin is supposed to have given his people a code of laws in the Hávamál, teaching virtues and giving instructions for burial of the dead.
"At home let a man be cheerful, / And toward a guest liberal" and the passage continues with advice on wise conduct, memory, speech, and knowledge.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA; lines 1877-1990
occurrences.motif_label: goddess as keeper of unrevealed future knowledge
occurrences.basis: Frigga knows what is to come but refuses to disclose it.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Frigga is goddess of atmosphere or clouds, queen of the gods, permitted to sit beside Odin on Hlidskialf, able to view the world, and possessed of unrevealed future knowledge.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA; lines 1992-2120
occurrences.motif_label: trickery at a divine threshold
occurrences.basis: Frigga anticipates Odin's plan, alters his sleeping orientation, and uses disguise and naming custom to secure victory for her supplicants.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odin avoids choosing immediately and says he will give victory to those whom his eyes first rest upon in the morning.
Odin expects to face the Vandals when he wakes, but Frigga turns his couch while he sleeps and sends instructions to the Winilers about the dawn arrangement.
"Take thou thy women-folk, / Maidens and wives... / Over your lips / Plait long tresses with cunning"
Odin wakes, sees the armed host, asks what Longbeards they are, and Frigga says he has given them a new name and must give a baptismal gift.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA; lines 2123-2236
occurrences.motif_label: divine knowledge and foreknowledge
occurrences.basis: Vör knows all that will occur, and Snotra has mastered all knowledge.

evidence.locator: lines 2123-2236, Vara, Vör and Snotra section
evidence.quote_or_summary: Vara hears oaths, punishes perjurers, and rewards oath-keepers; Vör knows what will occur throughout the world; Snotra is goddess of virtue and has mastered all knowledge.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA; lines 2238-2359
occurrences.motif_label: Divine teaching of flax and linen crafts
occurrences.basis: Holda teaches the peasant and his wife how to harvest flax and spin, weave, and bleach linen.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A misty form blesses the field; the flax blooms with blue flowers; Holda teaches harvesting, spinning, weaving, and bleaching linen, bringing prosperity.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR; lines 2611-2730
occurrences.motif_label: Knowledge test used to defeat a dangerous suitor
occurrences.basis: Thor makes Alvis prove his knowledge and deliberately prolongs the questioning until sunrise overtakes him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Alvis sues for Thrud; Thor tests his knowledge, prolongs the examination until sunrise, and daylight petrifies Alvis.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR; lines 2942-3047
occurrences.motif_label: deceptive trials against personified and cosmic forces
occurrences.basis: Utgard-Loki reveals that the contests were magical deceptions against wild fire, thought, the ocean, the Midgard snake, and old age.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Utgard-Loki tells the gods he used magic, identifies himself as Skrymir, and says a mountain protected his head from Thor's blows, with clefts in it showing Thor's strength.
Utgard-Loki explains the hidden identities of the contests: Logi as wild fire, Hugi as thought, the drinking horn as connected to the ocean, the cat as the Midgard snake, and Elli as old age.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas / CONTENTS / LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS / INTRODUCTION; lines 296-325
occurrences.motif_label: preservation and recovery of ancestral lore
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly frames old lore, old Faith, pagan poetry, and knowledge of ancestral religion as preserved, collected, and recovered for the present.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says old lore was preserved because Icelandic remained nearly unchanged; Iceland was colonised by Norsemen fleeing Harold Fairhair after Hafrsfirth, and their poetic genius took root there.
The Christian priest Sæmund is said to have collected pagan poetry into the Elder Edda, described as a chief foundation for knowledge of Norse ancestral religion.
"To know the old Faith" is quoted as bringing people into closer relation with the Past, which is called a possession of the Present.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR / CHAPTER V: TYR; lines 3369-3493
occurrences.motif_label: victory runes inscribed on weapons
occurrences.basis: The passage states that warriors engraved Tyr's rune on sword blades and quotes instruction to know victory-runes, carve them on the sword, and name Tyr.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says priests called Druids or Godi made human sacrifices to Tyr on stone altars called dolmens, and that Tyr's rune was engraved on sword blades to obtain victory.
“Sig-runes thou must know, / If victory (sigr) thou wilt have, / And on thy sword's hilt rist them ... And twice name the name of Tyr.”

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR / CHAPTER V: TYR; lines 3614-3719
occurrences.motif_label: Unbreakable magical object made from impossible materials
occurrences.basis: Gleipnir is made by magical arts from impalpable materials and cannot be broken, becoming stronger under strain.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The dark elves make a slender silken rope from impalpable materials and say no strength can break it; the verse names it Gleipnir and says Skirnir brings it to Odin.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR / CHAPTER V: TYR / CHAPTER VI: BRAGI; lines 3722-3817
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom being made from a peace-making exchange
occurrences.basis: Kvasir is created from the saliva of reconciled divine groups and is described as wise, good, and beneficial to mankind.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After the Æsir and Vanas agree to peace, both parties spit into a vase; from this saliva the gods create Kvasir, a wise and good being who answers questions and benefits mankind.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR / CHAPTER V: TYR / CHAPTER VI: BRAGI; lines 3722-3817
occurrences.motif_label: slain wise being transformed into inspiration drink
occurrences.basis: Kvasir's blood is collected and mixed with honey to create a drink that gives poetic and enchanting song ability.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Fialar and Galar kill sleeping Kvasir, drain his blood into Od-hroerir, Son, and Boden, and mix the blood with honey to make a beverage that turns its drinker into a poet and charming singer.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR / CHAPTER V: TYR / CHAPTER VI: BRAGI; lines 3722-3817
occurrences.motif_label: guarded magical drink in mountain cave
occurrences.basis: The powerful mead is hidden and then guarded by Gunlod in a hollow mountain where gods and mortals are forbidden to taste it.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Suttung avenges Gilling by seizing the dwarfs and placing them on a sea shoal; they save themselves by promising the mead. Suttung gives it to Gunlod, who guards the three vessels in a hollow mountain, while Hugin and Munin discover the hiding place.

Odin, already wise from runic lore and Mimir's fountain, learns of the draught's power, becomes anxious to obtain it, dons hat and cloak, and travels to Jötun-heim, where he sees nine thralls making hay.
When winter comes, Baugi hesitates to ask Suttung openly and says he will try guile; Bolwerk and Baugi go to the mountain, and Odin produces the auger Rati so Baugi can bore a hole into the cave.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR / CHAPTER V: TYR / CHAPTER VI: BRAGI; lines 3819-3966
occurrences.motif_label: Sacred theft of the mead of inspiration
occurrences.basis: Odin drains the guarded vessels, flees with the stolen mead, and brings the draught of inspiration to gods and selected mortals.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Inside the mountain cave, Odin appears before Gunlod, woos her, spends three days with her, receives permission to sip from each vessel, and drains all three vessels of mead.
Odin uses eagle plumes and flies toward Asgard; Suttung assumes eagle form and pursues him; the Æsir light fuel, singeing Suttung’s wings and causing him to fall into the fire and die.

Odin disgorges the stolen mead into vessels for the gods; scattered drops fall to earth and become the portion of lesser poets, while the gods reserve the main draught and sometimes grant it to favored mortals.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR / CHAPTER V: TYR / CHAPTER VI: BRAGI; lines 3968-3988
occurrences.motif_label: divine patron of poetry and song
occurrences.basis: Bragi is explicitly named as god of poetry, eloquence, and song, and his name is attached to poets and poetry.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Bragi is called god of poetry, eloquence, and song; poetry and scalds are named after him; his health is drunk at solemn and festive occasions, especially funeral feasts and Yuletide.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS / INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN; lines 880-1012
occurrences.motif_label: All-seeing high god on world-surveying throne
occurrences.basis: Odin is the chief god and god of universal wisdom; from Hlidskialf he can oversee the whole world and learn what happens among many classes of beings.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odin is introduced as the highest god, Allfather, god of universal wisdom and victory; he sits in Asgard on Hlidskialf, from which he can overlook the whole world.
Hugin and Munin, Odin's ravens, sit on his shoulders, fly through the world daily, and return at night to tell him what they have seen and heard.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS / INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN; lines 880-1012
occurrences.motif_label: Animal messengers gathering divine knowledge
occurrences.basis: Hugin and Munin fly over the earth each day and report news to Odin, keeping him informed about events on earth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hugin and Munin, Odin's ravens, sit on his shoulders, fly through the world daily, and return at night to tell him what they have seen and heard.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XX / BOOK XXI / BOOK XXII / BOOK XXIII; lines 10119-10211
occurrences.motif_label: wise concealment through false celebration
occurrences.basis: Telemachus calls Ulysses the wisest counsellor, and Ulysses uses dance, song, and a supposed wedding to conceal the deaths of the suitors from outsiders.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus tells Ulysses to decide what to do, calling him the wisest counsellor and promising support.
Ulysses orders washing and dressing, tells Phemius to play a dance tune, and explains that outsiders should think a wedding is taking place until the household can withdraw to his land.
The house echoes with dancing, and people outside say that the queen must have finally married, not knowing what has happened.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XXI / BOOK XXII / BOOK XXIII / BOOK XXIV; lines 10724-10815
occurrences.motif_label: prophetic warning ignored by a faction
occurrences.basis: Halitherses, who knows past and future, warns the Ithacans not to go against Ulysses; some disregard him and arm under Eupeithes.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Halitherses, who knows both past and future, tells the men of Ithaca their troubles are their own fault and warns them not to go out against Ulysses.
More than half leave the assembly; the rest side with Eupeithes, arm themselves, and follow him as he seeks vengeance for his son, though the narration says he will not return.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: The Odyssey / PREFACE TO FIRST EDITION; lines 113-185
occurrences.motif_label: divine invocation for epic knowledge
occurrences.basis: The speaker asks the Muse or goddess, daughter of Zeus, to declare the story of the wandering man.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “Tell me, Muse, of that man ... who wandered far and wide” after Troy and suffered on the deep while seeking life and return.

The quoted opening says the company were not saved: they perished after devouring the oxen of Helios Hyperion, and the god took away their day of returning; the goddess, daughter of Zeus, is asked to declare these things.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I / BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS.; lines 1136-1230
occurrences.motif_label: divine guide gives courage and instruction
occurrences.basis: Minerva leads Telemachus, instructs him to question Nestor, and gives him courage to speak.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva leads the way and Telemachus follows her.
Minerva tells Telemachus not to be shy, because he has taken the voyage to learn where his father is buried and how he came to his end, and tells him to ask Nestor for the truth.
Minerva answers that instinct and heaven will prompt Telemachus, and that the gods have been with him since birth.
Telemachus answers boldly because Minerva has given him courage to ask about his father and gain a good name.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I / BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS.; lines 1136-1230
occurrences.motif_label: supplication for truthful testimony about the missing dead or lost
occurrences.basis: Telemachus asks Nestor to tell the truth plainly about Ulysses, whether from sight or report.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva tells Telemachus not to be shy, because he has taken the voyage to learn where his father is buried and how he came to his end, and tells him to ask Nestor for the truth.
Telemachus says no one can certify where Ulysses perished, whether on land or at sea, and asks Nestor as a suppliant to tell plainly what he saw or heard.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I / BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS.; lines 1232-1327
occurrences.motif_label: heavenly sign guiding travel
occurrences.basis: Nestor's group asks heaven for a sign and changes course according to the sign toward the safer sea route.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At Lesbos, Nestor's group debates the route, asks heaven for a sign, and is shown that crossing the open sea to Euboea will get them soonest out of danger.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I / BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS.; lines 1329-1422
occurrences.motif_label: quest for truthful news from an elder or returned witness
occurrences.basis: Telemachus seeks true knowledge from Nestor, who is described as exceptionally knowing, and Nestor directs him to Menelaus as another truthful source.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus asks Nestor, reputed very knowledgeable, to tell the truth about Agamemnon's death, Menelaus' absence, and Aegisthus' action.
Nestor warns Telemachus not to stay away too long or leave property among dangerous people, and advises him to visit Menelaus, who will speak truthfully.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS. / BOOK IV; lines 1663-1760
occurrences.motif_label: guest seeking counsel because the father is absent
occurrences.basis: Pisistratus says Telemachus has come for counsel or suggestion because Odysseus is absent and he lacks supporters.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Pisistratus identifies the young man as Telemachus, says Nestor sent him as escort, and explains that Telemachus seeks counsel because his father is absent and he lacks supporters.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS. / BOOK IV; lines 1663-1760
occurrences.motif_label: youth displaying inherited prudence
occurrences.basis: Menelaus says Pisistratus’ discretion is beyond his years and that one can see he is son of a man blessed by heaven.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Menelaus praises Pisistratus’ discretion as beyond his years, connects it to Nestor’s blessed household, and says they will end the weeping and speak fully in the morning.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS. / BOOK IV; lines 1849-1948
occurrences.motif_label: Divine helper teaches a stratagem to gain hidden knowledge
occurrences.basis: Idothea instructs the speaker how to capture Proteus, who can reveal routes, events at home, and the cause of divine obstruction.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker asks which immortal is hindering him and how to reach home; Idothea says Proteus lives under the sea, serves Neptune, knows the sea bottom, and can reveal the voyage and home news.
Idothea explains that at noon Proteus comes up from the waves, sleeps in a great sea cave, and is surrounded by seals from the grey sea.

Idothea instructs the speaker to seize Proteus after he counts the seals and sleeps, hold him through transformations into creatures, fire, and water, and question him when he returns to his original form.
The next morning Idothea brings four fresh seal skins, digs four pits, covers the speaker and three men, and places fragrant ambrosia under their nostrils to counter the seal stench.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS. / BOOK IV; lines 2135-2239
occurrences.motif_label: secret departure on a quest for news of the father
occurrences.basis: Telemachus has sailed to Pylos and Lacedaemon to learn whether his father is dead or alive, and Euryclea says his departure was concealed from Penelope under oath.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “They are going to try and murder Telemachus as he is coming home from Pylos and Lacedaemon” after seeking news of his father.
Euryclea says she knew of Telemachus' departure, supplied bread and wine, and swore not to tell Penelope for ten or twelve days unless asked or unless Penelope heard of it.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VI / THE MEETING BETWEEN NAUSICAA AND ULYSSES. / BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS.; lines 2992-3088
occurrences.motif_label: goddess-taught domestic arts
occurrences.basis: Phaeacian women excel in weaving because Minerva has taught them useful arts and intelligence is attributed to them.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Fifty maidservants grind grain, weave, and spin; Phaeacian women excel in weaving because Minerva taught them useful arts.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: THE MEETING BETWEEN NAUSICAA AND ULYSSES. / BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS. / BOOK VIII; lines 3295-3396
occurrences.motif_label: inspired blind singer with divine gift and loss
occurrences.basis: Demodocus is loved by the Muse, endowed with divine song, deprived of eyesight, and inspired to sing heroic matters at the feast.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The servant leads in Demodocus, a famous bard loved by the Muse, who gave him the divine gift of song and robbed him of eyesight.

After the company eats and drinks, the Muse inspires Demodocus to sing heroic feats, especially the quarrel between Ulysses and Achilles at a banquet and the beginning of evils for Danaans and Trojans by Jove's will.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: THE MEETING BETWEEN NAUSICAA AND ULYSSES. / BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS. / BOOK VIII; lines 3398-3494
occurrences.motif_label: Speech distinguishes wisdom from mere appearance
occurrences.basis: Ulysses says the gods distribute speech, person, and understanding unevenly, contrasting handsome appearance with lack of discretion.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses rebukes Euryalus, says the gods do not grace all men equally in speech, person, and understanding, and says he had been among the foremost athletes before hardship weakened him.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: THE MEETING BETWEEN NAUSICAA AND ULYSSES. / BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS. / BOOK VIII; lines 3698-3785
occurrences.motif_label: divinely inspired bardic knowledge
occurrences.basis: The passage says bards are taught by the Muse, Ulysses attributes Demodocus's accuracy to the Muse and Apollo, and the bard is called inspired of heaven.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses sends Demodocus a fatty piece of roast pork and says he will salute him despite the pain his songs may cause, because bards are honored and taught by the Muse.
Ulysses praises Demodocus's accuracy about the Achaeans' return and asks him to sing of the wooden horse made by Epeus with Minerva's help and filled with the men who sacked Troy.
The bard begins with Argives setting fire to their tents and sailing away while others wait hidden with Ulysses inside the horse in the Trojan assembly place.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS. / BOOK VIII / BOOK IX; lines 4170-4268
occurrences.motif_label: Prophecy fulfilled in unexpected form
occurrences.basis: Polyphemus recalls that Telemus foretold he would lose his sight by Ulysses, though he expected a more imposing attacker.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Polyphemus groans that an old prophecy is coming true: Telemus son of Eurymus, an excellent seer, said he would lose his sight by the hand of Ulysses.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VIII / BOOK IX / BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE.; lines 4492-4586
occurrences.motif_label: divine helper gives foreknowledge before a dangerous encounter
occurrences.basis: Mercury warns Odysseus of Circe's intended actions and gives detailed instructions for how to survive them.

evidence.quote_or_summary: On the way through the charmed grove toward Circe's house, Odysseus meets Mercury with a golden wand, disguised as a young man; Mercury tells him his men are in pigstyes and offers a protective herb.
Mercury explains that Circe will drug a drink but the herb will block her spells; he tells Odysseus to draw his sword when she strikes with her wand and to make her swear not to plot further harm.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VIII / BOOK IX / BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE.; lines 4680-4781
occurrences.motif_label: consulting the dead prophet for knowledge of the way home
occurrences.basis: Teiresias retains understanding in death and is expected to tell Ulysses the stages of his voyage and how to reach home.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Circe says they need not stay, but must first go to the house of Hades and Proserpine to consult the ghost of Teiresias, who retains understanding in death.
Circe instructs sacrifice of a ram and black ewe, prayers to Hades and Proserpine, and guarding the blood with a drawn sword until Teiresias comes and tells Ulysses how to reach home.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE. / BOOK XI / THE VISIT TO THE DEAD.88; lines 4783-4874
occurrences.motif_label: necromantic blood rite for prophetic consultation
occurrences.basis: Ulysses offers libations, sacrifices sheep, controls the blood, and allows Teiresias to drink so that he can answer questions truly.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Perimedes and Eurylochus hold the victims while Ulysses digs a cubit-square trench and makes drink-offerings to the dead with honey and milk, wine, water, and barley meal.
Ulysses cuts the throats of two sheep so blood runs into the trench, and many ghosts from Erebus gather with screaming around it.
Ulysses orders the men to flay and burn the sheep and pray to Hades and Proserpine, while he sits with sword drawn to keep the ghosts from the blood until Teiresias answers.
The ghost of Theban Teiresias appears with a golden sceptre, recognizes Ulysses, asks him to withdraw sword and let him drink blood, then begins prophecy after drinking.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE. / BOOK XI / THE VISIT TO THE DEAD.88; lines 4876-4967
occurrences.motif_label: prophetic conditions for return home
occurrences.basis: Teiresias gives Odysseus conditional instructions and forecasts the hardships, losses, revenge, and later rites connected to his return.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Teiresias says heaven will make Odysseus' return hard and that Neptune still bears a bitter grudge because Odysseus blinded his son.
At Thrinacia Odysseus will find the Sun's sheep and cattle; if the flocks are left unharmed, he may reach Ithaca after hardship, but if they are harmed his ship and men will be destroyed.
Odysseus may return after losing his men and will find his house overrun by people devouring his substance while courting his wife; he will take revenge on the suitors by force or fraud.

Odysseus must carry a well-made oar to a country where people do not know the sea, ships, or oars; when a wayfarer calls it a winnowing shovel, he must plant it and sacrifice a ram, bull, and boar to Neptune.
After the inland sacrifice, Odysseus must return home, offer hecatombs to all the gods, and will eventually die gently from the sea in old age and peace.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE. / BOOK XI / THE VISIT TO THE DEAD.88; lines 5070-5169
occurrences.motif_label: secret return after warning of betrayal
occurrences.basis: Agamemnon advises Ulysses to conceal knowledge even from his wife and to bring his ship to Ithaca secretly.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Agamemnon advises Ulysses not to tell even his wife everything, but says Penelope is admirable and unlikely to murder him; he expects Ulysses and his grown son to have a joyful meeting.
Agamemnon advises Ulysses to bring his ship to Ithaca secretly and asks whether Ulysses has news of his son Orestes.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XI / THE VISIT TO THE DEAD.88 / BOOK XII / THE SIRENS, SCYLLA AND CHARYBDIS, THE CATTLE OF THE SUN.; lines 5320-5420
occurrences.motif_label: Wise guide gives route instructions after an underworld return
occurrences.basis: Circe explains dangers and precautions to Ulysses after knowing he has returned from Hades.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Circe, knowing they returned from Hades, arrives with servants bringing bread, meat, and wine; she calls their living descent to Hades bold, says they will have died twice, and promises to explain the route.
After a day of feasting, the men sleep by the ship; Circe takes Ulysses aside by the hand, reclines by him, and asks about his adventures before giving advice.

Circe warns that the Sirens enchant nearby sailors to death; bones lie around them. She tells Ulysses to plug the crew's ears with wax and, if he listens, to be bound to the mast and bound tighter if he begs release.
Circe presents two courses and describes the Wandering Rocks, where birds and ships are destroyed; only the Argo escaped, because Juno piloted it for Jason.

Circe describes the high rock and west-facing cavern of Scylla, a dreadful monster with twelve feet, six necks, six heads, and rows of teeth, who catches sea creatures and men from every passing ship.

Circe describes the lower rock with a leafy fig tree and Charybdis beneath it, whose waters are expelled and sucked down three times daily; she advises steering near Scylla because losing six men is better than losing the whole crew.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XI / THE VISIT TO THE DEAD.88 / BOOK XII / THE SIRENS, SCYLLA AND CHARYBDIS, THE CATTLE OF THE SUN.; lines 5422-5511
occurrences.motif_label: Forbidden or dangerous knowledge offered by enchanting singers
occurrences.basis: The Sirens' song promises charm and knowledge of Troy and the whole world, but safe passage requires the crew not to hear it and Ulysses to be restrained while hearing it.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses tells the men Circe's prophecies, including the warning to avoid the Sirens who sing in a field of flowers; he says he alone may hear them and orders himself bound upright to the mast, tighter if he asks release.
The Sirens call Ulysses to listen, saying that whoever hears them goes on 'not only charmed, but wiser,' and that they know the ills at Troy and events over the whole world.
Ulysses longs to hear more and signals for release; the crew rows faster, and Eurylochus and Perimedes bind him more strongly until the Sirens are out of hearing, then remove the wax and unbind him.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XI / THE VISIT TO THE DEAD.88 / BOOK XII / THE SIRENS, SCYLLA AND CHARYBDIS, THE CATTLE OF THE SUN.; lines 5422-5511
occurrences.motif_label: Heroic counsel preserves companions in danger
occurrences.basis: Ulysses explains prophecy to the crew, sets precautions against the Sirens, and later rallies the frightened men with commands and recollection of an earlier escape.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses tells the men Circe's prophecies, including the warning to avoid the Sirens who sing in a field of flowers; he says he alone may hear them and orders himself bound upright to the mast, tighter if he asks release.
At the Sirens' island the wind falls calm; the crew rows, Ulysses softens wax in the sun and stops the men's ears, and the men bind him hands and feet to the mast while rowing onward.
Ulysses longs to hear more and signals for release; the crew rows faster, and Eurylochus and Perimedes bind him more strongly until the Sirens are out of hearing, then remove the wax and unbind him.
Ulysses exhorts the crew, recalling their escape from the Cyclops's cave, tells them to trust Jove and row hard, and orders the coxswain to steer away from steaming rapids and hug the rock.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: PREFACE TO SECOND EDITION / HENRY FESTING JONES. / THE ODYSSEY / BOOK I; lines 589-680
occurrences.motif_label: divine counsel initiates a quest for news
occurrences.basis: Minerva, later recognized as divine, instructs Telemachus to take a ship and seek information about Ulysses at Pylos and Sparta.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva says heaven will determine Ulysses' return, then advises Telemachus to call an assembly, order the suitors away, send Penelope to her father if she wants remarriage, sail with twenty men to Pylos and Sparta for news, perform rites and build a barrow if Ulysses is dead, and consider killing the suitors; she cites Orestes' fame for killing Aegisthus.
Minerva flies away like a bird into the air, gives Telemachus courage, intensifies his thoughts of his father, and Telemachus recognizes that the stranger had been a god.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XII / THE SIRENS, SCYLLA AND CHARYBDIS, THE CATTLE OF THE SUN. / BOOK XIII / ULYSSES LEAVES SCHERIA AND RETURNS TO ITHACA.; lines 6001-6093
occurrences.motif_label: Divine guide reveals hidden or obscured land
occurrences.basis: Minerva identifies the landscape and disperses mist so Ulysses can see and understand where he is.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva describes Ulysses' shrewdness, says he returned safely but lost his men, notes Neptune's anger, and identifies the haven of Phorcys, the olive tree, the Naiad cave, the cavern of offerings, and mountain Neritum.
Minerva disperses the mist; Ulysses sees his land, rejoices, kisses the soil, lifts his hands, and prays to the Naiad nymphs with a promise of offerings.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XIII / ULYSSES LEAVES SCHERIA AND RETURNS TO ITHACA. / BOOK XIV / ULYSSES IN THE HUT WITH EUMAEUS.; lines 6290-6372
occurrences.motif_label: oracular consultation at sacred tree
occurrences.basis: Ulysses is said to go to Dodona to learn Jove’s mind from the god’s high oak tree about how to return to Ithaca.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Pheidon says he hosted Ulysses, shows Ulysses’ treasure, reports that Ulysses went to Dodona to learn Jove’s mind from the high oak about whether to return to Ithaca openly or secretly, swears a ship and crew were ready, and sends the speaker toward Dulichium.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: ULYSSES LEAVES SCHERIA AND RETURNS TO ITHACA. / BOOK XIV / ULYSSES IN THE HUT WITH EUMAEUS. / BOOK XV; lines 6733-6832
occurrences.motif_label: prophetic lineage and divine bestowal of seercraft
occurrences.basis: Theoclymenus is a seer descended from Melampus, and Apollo makes Polypheides the greatest seer after Amphiaraus dies.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The newcomer is a seer fleeing Argos after killing a man; his ancestor Melampus was exiled, imprisoned, escaped, drove cattle to Pylos, avenged a wrong, and later went to Argos.

The genealogy continues: Amphiaraus was beloved by Jove and Apollo but died at Thebes; Aurora carried off Cleitus for his beauty; Apollo made Polypheides the greatest seer, and he prophesied in Hyperesia.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: PREFACE TO SECOND EDITION / HENRY FESTING JONES. / THE ODYSSEY / BOOK I; lines 682-759
occurrences.motif_label: divine counsel in human disguise
occurrences.basis: Telemachus identifies the stranger as Mentes to others, but the narration says he knows it had been the goddess; he later thinks of Minerva’s counsel.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Eurymachus says heaven decides who will be chief, acknowledges Telemachus’s mastery over his own house and possessions, asks about the stranger, and Telemachus identifies him as Mentes while knowing inwardly that he had been the goddess.

After singing and dancing until evening, the suitors go home. Telemachus goes to his high tower room, led by Euryclea with blazing torches. Euryclea is described as his nurse and attendant. Telemachus lies under a woollen fleece thinking all night about his intended voyage and Minerva’s counsel.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XV / BOOK XVI / ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII; lines 7528-7613
occurrences.motif_label: Omen and prophetic announcement of hidden presence
occurrences.basis: Theoclymenus claims divinatory certainty, cites an omen from the ship, and states that Ulysses is already in Ithaca.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Theoclymenus tells Penelope he can divine surely, invokes Zeus, hospitality, and Ulysses' hearth, and says Ulysses is in Ithaca investigating evil deeds and preparing a day of reckoning; he cites an omen seen on the ship.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: HENRY FESTING JONES. / THE ODYSSEY / BOOK I / BOOK II; lines 762-849
occurrences.motif_label: cunning weaving delays unwanted remarriage
occurrences.basis: Antinous describes Telemachus’s mother as artful and says she used a large piece of needlework for Laertes’ pall as a reason to delay marriage.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Antinous calls Telemachus insolent, denies the suitors are to blame, and says Telemachus’s mother is artful and has deceived the suitors for nearly four years.
Antinous says Telemachus’s mother set up a great tambour frame in her room and began a very large piece of fine needlework.
Antinous reports that she asked the suitors not to press her to marry until she had completed a pall for Laertes against the time of his death.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XVI / ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII / BOOK XVIII; lines 8177-8277
occurrences.motif_label: cunning speech used to obtain gifts
occurrences.basis: The narrator says Ulysses is glad because Penelope is extracting presents from the suitors by flattering them with words she does not mean.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The narrator says Ulysses was glad to hear Penelope trying to get presents from the suitors and flattering them with fair words that he knew she did not mean.

Antinous allows Penelope to accept presents but says the suitors will not leave until she marries the best man among them; the suitors bring a decorated dress, gold brooches, a gold and amber chain, earrings, a necklace, and other presents.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII / BOOK XVIII / BOOK XIX; lines 8452-8531
occurrences.motif_label: weaving stratagem to delay unwanted marriage
occurrences.basis: Penelope invents a delaying device by publicly weaving a pall and secretly undoing the work at night until the deception is exposed.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Penelope describes setting up a large frame, claiming she must finish a pall for Laertes before remarriage, working by day, and undoing the stitches by torchlight at night for three years.
Penelope says maids betrayed her, suitors caught her and forced her to finish, and now she faces pressure from parents while her son resents the wasting of his estate.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: HENRY FESTING JONES. / THE ODYSSEY / BOOK I / BOOK II; lines 851-936
occurrences.motif_label: weaving deception used to delay remarriage
occurrences.basis: Penelope's daily weaving and nightly unweaving deceives the suitors for three years and delays the demanded marriage choice.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Penelope was seen "working on her great web all day long," and at night she would "unpick the stitches again by torchlight."
The ruse lasted three years; in the fourth year a maid disclosed it, and the suitors caught Penelope undoing her work, forcing her to finish.
The suitors' answer is: "Send your mother away, and bid her marry" according to her and her father's choice.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII / BOOK XVIII / BOOK XIX; lines 8533-8618
occurrences.motif_label: oracle consultation at sacred tree
occurrences.basis: Ulysses is said to go to Dodona to learn Jove’s mind from a high oak tree about the manner of his return.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “Ulysses had gone to Dodona that he might learn Jove’s mind from the high oak tree” and learn whether to return openly or secretly.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XVII / BOOK XVIII / BOOK XIX / BOOK XX; lines 9148-9215
occurrences.motif_label: rejected prophet warns the doomed
occurrences.basis: Theoclymenus announces the threatening vision and the suitors laugh at him as senseless before he leaves and repeats that they will not escape.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Theoclymenus says darkness covers the men, tears wet their cheeks, wailing fills the air, walls and roof-beams drip blood, ghosts crowd the gate and court toward hell, the sun is blotted out, and gloom covers the land.
The suitors laugh at Theoclymenus; Eurymachus says the stranger has lost his senses and tells servants to turn him into the streets.
