Theoclymenus says he has his own eyes, ears, feet, and understanding mind; he sees mischief overhanging those insulting and plotting ill in Ulysses' house, says none will escape, and goes back to Piraeus, who welcomes him.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: HENRY FESTING JONES. / THE ODYSSEY / BOOK I / BOOK II; lines 938-1036
occurrences.motif_label: prayer at water before divine response
occurrences.basis: Telemachus washes his hands in the waves, prays to Minerva, and receives counsel and practical instructions from the goddess.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus goes “all alone by the sea side,” washes his hands “in the grey waves,” and prays to Minerva about obeying her instruction to sail in search of his father.
“Minerva came close up to him in the likeness and with the voice of Mentor.”

Minerva says she will find a ship and come with Telemachus; he is to prepare provisions, including wine in jars and barley meal in leathern bags, while she gathers volunteers and chooses the best ship.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 1039-1112
occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom as inward inscription and growth
occurrences.basis: The passage describes true writing as written in the soul and true teaching as growing from within, using seed and tree imagery.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates’ point is summarized as: what is truly written is written in the soul, and what is truly taught grows in the soul from within.
“When planted in a congenial soil the little seed becomes a tree, and ‘the birds of the air build their nests in the branches.’”

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 1039-1112
occurrences.motif_label: Living word over dead writing
occurrences.basis: The passage contrasts living speech with writing and treats living, embodied truth as higher than written preservation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage contrasts living speech with writing and describes speech as transitory and adaptable, writing as permanent and addressed to all the world.

The passage says that living is higher than writing, using images of being the book or epistle, truth embodied in a person, and the Word made flesh; it also names Socrates and Christ as examples of speaking and acting rather than writing.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 1114-1188
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom through self-knowledge rather than hidden allegory
occurrences.basis: The passage says hidden interpretations of Homer and mythology draw a person away from knowledge of himself, while Plato seeks another use of myth and poetry.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says Plato is free from Euhemerism, rejects hidden-meaning interpretations of Homer and mythology, treats them as drawing people away from self-knowledge, and still uses poetry and mythology as vehicles of thought and feeling.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 1190-1207
occurrences.motif_label: mystical quest for divine knowledge
occurrences.basis: The soul waits in wonder and works reverently to learn what God may reveal, in connection with the infinity of knowledge and love of the good, true, and one.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Mysticism is defined as reason concentrated in feeling, enthusiastic love of the good, true, and one, and a sense of infinite knowledge and human faculties.
The soul waits in wonder and works reverently to find out what God may reveal in this or another life.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE.; lines 1210-1298
occurrences.motif_label: False speech opposed to truth and wisdom
occurrences.basis: Rhetoric is characterized as a sham detached from fact and truth, and as lacking the knowledge of human nature necessary for true composition.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Plato's Phaedrus is said to satirize rhetoric and its professors; rhetoric is described as popular but a sham without relation to fact or truth, and lacking knowledge of human nature.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE.; lines 1300-1387
occurrences.motif_label: ascent toward knowledge
occurrences.basis: The passage contrasts a backward-looking age with the unattempted movement to go forward and scale the heights of knowledge.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The age "did not attempt to pierce the mists" or "scale the heights of knowledge," but was lost in doubt and rested on tradition and authority.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE.; lines 1300-1387
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom through education and cultivation
occurrences.basis: The passage presents wider education, training in the best literatures, and intergenerational learning as ways to enlarge minds and produce future intelligence.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The progress of education and wider access to knowledge may lead to new combinations of thought and language; youth trained in the best literatures may grow intellectually and think for themselves.
Natural capacity is likened to a "seed" that dies without cultivation, and human intelligence to a "reservoir or treasure-house" from which "new waters may flow and cover the earth."
The passage says future generations may begin at a higher point, keep the results of the past, benefit from cooperation, and inherit favorable educational conditions from educated parents.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE.; lines 1389-1409
occurrences.motif_label: Transmission of wisdom across generations
occurrences.basis: Earlier writers remain as materials of education for coming generations, and world literatures become available for reading.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Great writers of ancient and modern times will remain to furnish educational materials for coming generations.
“The religions and literatures of the world will be open books” to those who will read them.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE.; lines 1389-1409
occurrences.motif_label: Search for truth
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly describes better understanding of the whereabouts of truth and greater success in the search for it.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Greater freedom from prejudice and party may allow better understanding of truth and more success in the search for it.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 1412-1536
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom-bearing written discourse
occurrences.basis: The passage centers on the carrying, reading, and discussion of a composed discourse attributed to Lysias.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Phaedrus says Lysias wrote about a fair youth being tempted, not by a lover, and argued that the non-lover should be accepted rather than the lover.
Socrates says Phaedrus must show what he has in his left hand under his cloak, suspecting that the roll is the actual discourse.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 1538-1589
occurrences.motif_label: Self-knowledge before mythic speculation
occurrences.basis: Socrates rejects extended inquiry into allegories and says he must first know himself according to the Delphian inscription.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says such allegories require much labour and would require rehabilitating 'Hippocentaurs and chimeras dire,' Gorgons, winged steeds, and many other portentous natures.
Socrates says, 'I must first know myself, as the Delphian inscription says,' and asks whether he is more monstrous than 'the serpent Typho' or a gentler creature.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 1538-1589
occurrences.motif_label: Text or book as enchantment drawing the knowledge-seeker onward
occurrences.basis: Socrates says Phaedrus has found a spell to draw him out of the city and that holding up a book could lead him through Attica and the wide world.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates replies that he is a lover of knowledge, that city-dwellers are his teachers rather than trees or countryside, and that a book can lure him through Attica and the world; he then lies down and asks Phaedrus to read.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 154-206
occurrences.motif_label: Divine madness as blessing
occurrences.basis: Socrates glorifies madness, divides it into sacred forms, and states that madness may be one of heaven’s blessings and better than sense.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates begins by glorifying madness and divides it into divination or prophecy, purification by mysteries, poetry inspired by the Muses, and love; the passage compares parts of this discussion to Cratylus, Io, and Ion.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 1591-1673
occurrences.motif_label: Rational non-lover preferred over passionate lover
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly argues that the non-lover is more prudent, self-controlled, socially beneficial, and likely to form lasting friendship than the lover.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage contrasts lovers, who later repent of kindnesses when passion ceases, with non-lovers, who act freely and without compulsion.
The speaker says there are more non-lovers than lovers, so the addressee has a larger and better chance of finding a worthy friend among non-lovers.
Non-lovers are described as not jealous of the beloved's companions and as thinking friendship with others can benefit the beloved.
The speaker says that, if listened to, he will seek future advantage, remain self-mastered, forgive unintentional offences, try to prevent intentional ones, and offer marks of lasting friendship.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 1591-1673
occurrences.motif_label: Enduring friendship through self-mastery
occurrences.basis: The speaker presents self-control, forgiveness, concern for future advantage, and prevention of intentional offences as marks of a lasting friendship.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker says that, if listened to, he will seek future advantage, remain self-mastered, forgive unintentional offences, try to prevent intentional ones, and offer marks of lasting friendship.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 1675-1779
occurrences.motif_label: inspired speech from earlier wisdom
occurrences.basis: Socrates claims he can speak because he has been filled through the ears from another source, possibly ancient sages such as Sappho or Anacreon.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says ancient sages, men and women, would judge against him if he agreed with Phaedrus, and names Sappho and Anacreon as possible sources.
Socrates says he has been "filled through the ears, like a pitcher, from the waters of another."

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 1781-1894
occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom through definition before judgment
occurrences.basis: The embedded speech says good counsel requires knowing what is being advised about and agreeing first on the nature and power of love before judging its advantage or disadvantage.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The embedded speech says good counsel begins with knowing what one is advising about, and proposes defining the nature and power of love before deciding whether love brings advantage or disadvantage.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 1896-1985
occurrences.motif_label: withholding of wisdom
occurrences.basis: The lover is said to bar the beloved from society that would give wisdom and to banish divine philosophy from him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The lover is said to reduce the beloved to inferiority, delight in or implant defects, act jealously, bar useful society, prevent wisdom, banish divine philosophy, and keep the beloved ignorant and dependent.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 1987-2094
occurrences.motif_label: purgation of mythological error by recantation
occurrences.basis: Socrates invokes an ancient purgation in which Stesichorus corrected his error about Helen through recantation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says he needs a purgation and recalls Stesichorus, who lost his eyes as penalty for reviling Helen and then purged himself with a recantation denying that Helen went to Troy.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 208-288
occurrences.motif_label: Recollection of heavenly knowledge through beauty
occurrences.basis: The philosopher remembers divine realities when beholding earthly beauty, recalling knowledge gained among the gods.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The philosopher recollects knowledge gained among the gods when seeing earthly beauty; the soul once beheld mysteries in pure light before being entombed in the body and is compared to a bird eager to leave its cage.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2096-2186
occurrences.motif_label: divine madness as superior wisdom
occurrences.basis: Socrates argues that inspired madness is divine in origin, grants major blessings, and can surpass sane-minded human activity.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “there is also a madness which is a divine gift, and the source of the chiefest blessings granted to men”

Socrates appeals to ancient names, linking prophecy (mantike) with madness (manike), contrasting it with rational investigation of futurity by birds or other signs, and ranking divine madness above sane mind.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2096-2186
occurrences.motif_label: prophecy through inspired possession
occurrences.basis: The prophetess at Delphi, priestesses at Dodona, the Sibyl, and inspired persons are described as giving beneficial or saving foreknowledge when out of their senses.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Prophecy is called a madness; the prophetess at Delphi and priestesses at Dodona benefit Hellas when out of their senses, and the Sibyl and other inspired persons give saving intimations of the future.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2096-2186
occurrences.motif_label: poetic inspiration by divine possession
occurrences.basis: Possession by the Muses is said to inspire poetic frenzy that produces lyric and other measures and instructs posterity through heroic actions.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The third kind of madness is possession by the Muses, which inspires frenzy in a delicate and virgin soul, awakens lyric and other measures, and adorns ancient heroic actions for posterity.
The person without the Muses' madness who seeks entry to the poetic temple by art alone is not admitted, and the sane poet disappears in rivalry with the mad poet.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2188-2244
occurrences.motif_label: immortal self-moving soul
occurrences.basis: The passage presents a doctrinal proof that the self-moving soul is immortal, unbegotten, and indestructible.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage argues that what is ever self-moving is immortal, unbegotten, indestructible, and the beginning of motion; the soul is identified with this self-moving nature.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2246-2321
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom and truth as nourishment of the soul
occurrences.basis: Beauty, wisdom, goodness, pure knowledge, truth, and the plain of truth nourish or replenish the soul and its wing.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The wing is described as akin to the divine, tending to soar upward; it is nourished by beauty, wisdom, and goodness, but wastes when fed by evil and foulness.
Beyond heaven abides true being: a colorless, formless, intangible essence visible only to mind; divine intelligence rejoices in beholding reality and truth.
Souls eagerly seek the plain of truth because pasture suited to the highest part of the soul is found there, and it nourishes the wing on which the soul soars.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2323-2387
occurrences.motif_label: mystery initiation through recollection
occurrences.basis: The one who rightly uses memories of divine realities is initiated into perfect mysteries and becomes truly perfect.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The philosopher recollects the things the soul saw while following God; the philosopher's mind has wings and is initiated into perfect mysteries through these memories.
Philosophers once followed Zeus and others followed other gods; they saw beauty shining, a blessed mystery, and calm apparitions in pure light before later evils.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2323-2387
occurrences.motif_label: recollection of a lost divine vision
occurrences.basis: Souls once beheld true being and pure-light visions with the gods, and only some retain and respond to images of that other world.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Every human soul has beheld true being, but many fail to recall the other world; few retain remembrance and are amazed by earthly images of it.
Philosophers once followed Zeus and others followed other gods; they saw beauty shining, a blessed mystery, and calm apparitions in pure light before later evils.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2459-2497
occurrences.motif_label: divine imitation as acquisition of wisdom and character
occurrences.basis: Followers gaze on and recollect their god, receive character and disposition from him, and cultivate corresponding qualities in the beloved.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Followers of Zeus desire a beloved with a Zeus-like soul, seek someone philosophical and imperial, and try to confirm that nature in him.
Their recollection clings to the god; they receive character from him as far as humans can participate in God, and, like Bacchic Nymphs, “pour out their own fountain” on the beloved.

Followers of Here seek royal love; followers of Apollo and every other god seek a beloved made like the god served, imitate the god, persuade the beloved to imitate, and educate him into the god’s manner and nature without envy or jealousy.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2499-2549
occurrences.motif_label: beloved as catalyst for recollection of higher beauty
occurrences.basis: The beloved's visible beauty causes the charioteer to remember true beauty, associated with Modesty and holy imagery.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At the beloved's flashing beauty, the charioteer remembers true beauty with Modesty, falls back in adoration, and pulls the reins so both horses retreat.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2551-2634
occurrences.motif_label: Philosophical wisdom as salvation of the soul
occurrences.basis: Philosophy and the better elements of the mind lead to order, harmony, self-mastery, and the highest blessing described in the passage.

evidence.quote_or_summary: If self-control, order, and philosophy prevail, the pair live in happiness and harmony, master themselves, enslave vicious elements, emancipate virtuous elements, and become light and winged for flight.

The speaker addresses Eros, asks forgiveness and preservation of sight and the art of love, blames Lysias for the earlier speech, names Polemarchus as a philosophical example, and asks that Phaedrus dedicate himself to love and philosophical discourses.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2636-2763
occurrences.motif_label: resisting lulling voices by disciplined discourse
occurrences.basis: Socrates urges the interlocutors not to be lulled into midday sleep by the grasshoppers but to keep conversing, comparing this to Odysseus passing the Sirens.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates notes grasshoppers chirruping overhead in the midday heat; he says they might laugh if the men slept instead of conversed and compares disciplined discourse to Odysseus sailing past Siren voices.
Socrates says they should talk and not sleep at midday; Phaedrus agrees, and they return to the proposed discussion of rules for writing and speech.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2636-2763
occurrences.motif_label: philosophical honor under heavenly Muses
occurrences.basis: Calliope and Urania are said to be chiefly concerned with heaven and thought, divine as well as human, and the grasshoppers report philosophers to them.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The grasshoppers' reports win the love of Terpsichore for dancers, Erato for lovers, and Calliope and Urania for philosophers; Calliope and Urania are associated with heaven and thought.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2765-2908
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom as knowledge of truth before persuasive speech
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly contrasts persuasion from opinion with speaking grounded in truth, and concludes that ignorance of a subject prevents accurate judgment of likeness.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates asks whether the speaker must know the truth; Phaedrus reports that oratory is said to rely on what the many approve and on opinion rather than truth.
Rhetoric is personified as saying it does not force anyone to speak without truth and would advise arriving at truth first, while still claiming truth alone does not provide persuasion.
"there never is nor ever will be a real art of speaking which is divorced from the truth"
Socrates argues that deception is easier where differences are small, and that one who would deceive others and not be deceived must know the real likenesses and differences of things.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2765-2908
occurrences.motif_label: knowledge of likeness and difference as protection against deception
occurrences.basis: Socrates states that one who would deceive and not be deceived must know real likenesses and differences.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates argues that deception is easier where differences are small, and that one who would deceive others and not be deceived must know the real likenesses and differences of things.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 290-374
occurrences.motif_label: Truthful wisdom versus enchanting speech
occurrences.basis: Good speaking is grounded in truth, while rhetoric is described as enchantment and dialectic as ordered synthesis and analysis.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Good speaking requires knowing and speaking truth; rhetoric is called an art of enchantment that can make things appear good or evil, like or unlike, as the speaker chooses.
Socrates identifies synthesis and analysis as principles of division and generalization dear to the dialectician and contrasts them with rhetorical technicalities.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2910-3059
occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom as prerequisite for persuasive art
occurrences.basis: The passage states that true rhetorical art requires knowledge of reality, classification of disputed and undisputed matters, and keen observation of particulars.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says error enters through resemblances when notions are at variance with realities, and that the rhetorical master must know the real nature of everything.

Phaedrus reads Lysias' opening; Socrates distinguishes agreed matters such as iron and silver from disputed matters such as justice and goodness, and identifies rhetoric's power in uncertain subjects.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 3061-3191
occurrences.motif_label: divine madness as release from ordinary custom
occurrences.basis: The passage contrasts madness from human infirmity with divine release of the soul from custom and convention, then names prophetic, initiatory, poetic, and erotic forms.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates states that there are two kinds of madness: one from human infirmity and one a divine release of the soul from custom and convention.
Divine madness is divided into prophetic, initiatory, poetic, and erotic forms, associated respectively with Apollo, Dionysus, the Muses, and Aphrodite with Eros.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 3061-3191
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom through seeing unity and plurality
occurrences.basis: Socrates praises the person who can see 'a One and Many' in nature and associates this art with dialecticians.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says he loves division and generalization and follows anyone who can see 'a One and Many' in nature as if he were a god; he calls such people dialecticians.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 3193-3311
occurrences.motif_label: preliminaries mistaken for complete art
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly contrasts isolated techniques in rhetoric, medicine, tragedy, and music with full understanding of the relevant art.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Phaedrus says that if the claimant lacks such knowledge, he would be called a madman or pedant with prescriptions but no real understanding of medicine.
Phaedrus says Sophocles and Euripides would laugh at someone who did not know tragedy requires arranging elements suitably to one another and to the whole.
Socrates imagines a musician gently telling a would-be harmonist that knowing how to pitch highest and lowest notes is preliminary, not harmony itself.
Socrates says Sophocles would call the display only the preliminaries of tragedy, and Acumenus would say the same about medicine.
Socrates imagines Adrastus or Pericles saying that people lacking dialectical skill mistake preliminary conditions for the whole art of rhetoric and leave effective use and composition to disciples.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 3193-3311
occurrences.motif_label: true skill requires knowledge of measure, timing, and recipient
occurrences.basis: The medicine analogy states that knowing drugs is insufficient without knowing to whom, when, and how much they should be given; this supports Socrates' broader critique of rhetoric.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates imagines a person claiming to be a physician because he knows how to apply heating, cooling, vomiting, and purging drugs.
Phaedrus says they would ask whether he knew "to whom" he would give medicines, and "when," and "how much."
Socrates says the finished orator needs natural power aided by art, knowledge, and practice, and that rhetoric's art does not lie in the direction of Lysias or Thrasymachus.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 3193-3311
occurrences.motif_label: inquiry into the true art of persuasion
occurrences.basis: Phaedrus asks where and how true rhetoric and persuasion are acquired, and Socrates answers in terms of nature, knowledge, and practice.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Phaedrus agrees with Socrates' description of existing rhetoric teaching and asks where and how true rhetoric and persuasion are to be acquired.
Socrates says the finished orator needs natural power aided by art, knowledge, and practice, and that rhetoric's art does not lie in the direction of Lysias or Thrasymachus.
"I conceive Pericles to have been the most accomplished of rhetoricians."

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 3313-3435
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom through knowledge of nature and the whole
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly ties true art and rhetoric to knowledge of nature, the whole, the soul, and reasoned analysis rather than empirical procedure.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says great arts require discussion and speculation about truths of nature; he presents Pericles as having gained higher philosophy from Anaxagoras and applying it to speaking.
Socrates compares rhetoric to medicine: medicine defines the body to impart health, while rhetoric defines the soul to implant conviction or virtue by words and training.
Socrates asks if one can know the soul without knowing the whole; Phaedrus cites Hippocrates that the body too can only be understood as a whole.
Socrates says inquiry should determine whether the thing is simple or multiform, number its forms if multiform, and examine its power of acting or being acted upon.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 3313-3435
occurrences.motif_label: instructional mastery through analysis and correct timing
occurrences.basis: Socrates presents mastery as requiring classification, practical recognition, and knowledge of when to speak or refrain.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says a serious teacher of rhetoric will describe the soul, explain how it acts and is acted upon, classify men and speeches, and explain why one soul is persuaded by one argument and another is not; he criticizes current writers for concealing the nature of the soul.
"Oratory is the art of enchanting the soul"; Socrates says the orator must learn the differences of human souls and divide speeches into classes.
Socrates says the pupil must gain experience in life, recognize which person or character requires which argument, and know when to speak, refrain, or use particular rhetorical modes.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 3437-3548
occurrences.motif_label: true wisdom distinguished from persuasive appearance
occurrences.basis: The passage contrasts rhetoric based on probability and conviction with an art requiring knowledge of truth, likenesses of truth, classification, and proper orientation of action.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates describes the rhetorical claim that in courts of law people care not about truth but about conviction and probability; Phaedrus says rhetoric teachers treat this as all-important.

Socrates argues that probability is engendered by likeness to truth, that the one who knows truth best finds such resemblances, that the rhetorician must classify hearers and things under single ideas, and that the good person should speak and act acceptably to God even if the road is long.
Socrates and Phaedrus agree that enough has been said about true and false art of speaking, and Phaedrus affirms the point.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 3437-3548
occurrences.motif_label: speech and action judged by divine acceptability
occurrences.basis: Socrates says the good person should speak what is acceptable to God and act acceptably to Him rather than chiefly pleasing fellow-servants.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates argues that probability is engendered by likeness to truth, that the one who knows truth best finds such resemblances, that the rhetorician must classify hearers and things under single ideas, and that the good person should speak and act acceptably to God even if the road is long.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 3437-3548
occurrences.motif_label: appeal to ancient tradition for teaching
occurrences.basis: Socrates introduces a teaching by saying he has heard a tradition of the ancients, while qualifying that only they know its truth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates introduces propriety and impropriety of writing, asks how one can speak or act about rhetoric acceptably to God, and says he has heard a tradition of the ancients whose truth only they know.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 3550-3661
occurrences.motif_label: False wisdom through external signs
occurrences.basis: Thamus says letters produce forgetfulness, reliance on external characters, semblance of truth, and the appearance rather than reality of wisdom.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Theuth claims letters will improve wisdom and memory; Thamus replies that the father of letters overvalues them, because writing will create forgetfulness, reliance on external characters, reminiscence rather than memory, and the show of wisdom without reality.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 3550-3661
occurrences.motif_label: Prophetic speech from tree or stone
occurrences.basis: Socrates mentions a Dodona tradition in which oaks first gave prophetic utterances and says truth could be heard from oak or rock.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates cites a Dodona temple tradition that oaks first gave prophetic utterances, and says earlier people accepted truth even from oak or rock.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 3550-3661
occurrences.motif_label: Living knowledge planted in the soul
occurrences.basis: Socrates contrasts written words with an intelligent word graven in the learner’s soul and develops seed-sowing imagery for serious instruction.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates describes a better speech as an intelligent word graven in the learner’s soul, able to defend itself and to know when to speak or be silent; Phaedrus calls it the living word of knowledge, with the written word as its image.

Socrates asks whether a sensible husbandman would seriously plant valued seeds in a Garden of Adonis for quick beauty, instead of sowing in fitting soil and waiting months for perfection; Phaedrus agrees the former is play and the latter earnest.
Socrates says one who knows justice, goodness, and honor would not seriously write thoughts in water with pen and ink, sowing words unable to speak for themselves or adequately teach truth.
Socrates says the garden of letters may be planted for recreation, amusement, and memorials against the forgetfulness of old age, giving the writer pleasure in their tender growth.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 3550-3661
occurrences.motif_label: Speech unable to defend itself
occurrences.basis: Written speeches are personified as unable to answer, choose audiences, or defend themselves without a parent.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says writing is like painting: painted creations look alive but remain silent; written speeches seem intelligent but give one answer, circulate indiscriminately, and cannot protect or defend themselves.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 3663-3779
occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom reserved for the divine and pursued by humans
occurrences.basis: Socrates says the name wise belongs to God alone and that the modest title for suitable humans is lovers of wisdom or philosophers.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says, “Wise, I may not call them; for that is a great name which belongs to God alone,” and calls them lovers of wisdom or philosophers.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 3663-3779
occurrences.motif_label: Teaching as planting seed in the soul
occurrences.basis: The dialectician is described as sowing and planting words in a congenial soul; these words bear seed and are raised in other soils.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says the dialectician, finding a congenial soul, “sows and plants therein words” that contain seed and become fruitful in other soils.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 3663-3779
occurrences.motif_label: Living knowledge versus written reminder
occurrences.basis: Socrates contrasts writings as reminiscences with orally communicated principles graven in the soul as the true way of writing.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says the best writings are reminders, while principles of justice, goodness, and nobility taught orally and graven in the soul are the true way of writing and legitimate offspring.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 3663-3779
occurrences.motif_label: Sacred place as source of instruction
occurrences.basis: Socrates says he and Phaedrus went down to the fountain and school of the Nymphs and were bidden by them to convey a message.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says, “to the fountain and school of the Nymphs we went down,” and that the Nymphs bade them convey a message to speech composers, poets, and law-writers.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 376-455
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom through knowledge of truth rather than persuasion
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly contrasts probability, school rhetoric, and flattery with knowledge of truth, philosophy, and principles of justice and truth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: True rhetoric is likened to medicine: the rhetorician must know the natures of souls and adapt speech to persons, times, and seasons.
Some professors prefer probability to truth, but the passage says probability depends on truth; the good man should please the gods.
The conclusion says one must know truth and adapt it to others; living word is better than written word, and spoken justice and truth are legitimate offspring.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 376-455
occurrences.motif_label: cultivation of the soul
occurrences.basis: The husbandman metaphor describes sowing in the natural soil of the human soul and bringing forth fruit in minds.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The husbandman metaphor contrasts sowing in a hot-bed or garden of Adonis with sowing in the deep natural soil of the human soul.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 3781-3808
occurrences.motif_label: Divine inspiration leading a human to higher pursuits
occurrences.basis: Socrates says Isocrates has divine inspiration that will lead him to higher things and an element of philosophy in his nature.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says Isocrates has genius above Lysias' orations, will improve with age, will surpass former rhetoricians, will not be satisfied with rhetoric, has divine inspiration leading him higher, and has philosophy in his nature.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 3781-3808
occurrences.motif_label: Inner and outer harmony sought through prayer
occurrences.basis: Socrates prays for beauty in the inward soul and for the outward and inward man to be at one.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “Beloved Pan, and all ye other gods who haunt this place, give me beauty in the inward soul; and may the outward and inward man be at one.”

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 3781-3808
occurrences.motif_label: Temperance over material wealth
occurrences.basis: Socrates prays to reckon the wise wealthy and to have only as much gold as a temperate man can bear and carry.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “May I reckon the wise to be the wealthy, and may I have such a quantity of gold as a temperate man and he only can bear and carry.”

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 457-547
occurrences.motif_label: inspired love as path toward knowledge
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly links love, inspiration, beauty, knowledge, dialectic, and ideas, presenting true knowledge as based on enthusiasm or love of ideas.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage lists the main subjects of the Phaedrus: false or conventional rhetoric, love or inspiration of beauty and knowledge as madness, dialectic, true rhetoric based on dialectic, and the superiority of spoken over written word.

Higher rhetoric is based on dialectic; dialectic is inspiration akin to love; true knowledge of heaven and earth rests on enthusiasm or love of ideas present in this world and another. Love is divided into interested love, disinterested or mad love fixed on sense objects, and disinterested love directed toward the unseen.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 457-547
occurrences.motif_label: ascent from sense-bound love to unseen objects
occurrences.basis: The three degrees of love move from interested love to sense-directed mad love and then to disinterested love directed toward the unseen and dialectic.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Higher rhetoric is based on dialectic; dialectic is inspiration akin to love; true knowledge of heaven and earth rests on enthusiasm or love of ideas present in this world and another. Love is divided into interested love, disinterested or mad love fixed on sense objects, and disinterested love directed toward the unseen.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 457-547
occurrences.motif_label: true speech founded on knowledge of truth and character
occurrences.basis: True rhetoric is defined as persuasion founded on knowledge of truth and knowledge of character, and Socrates' second speech is praised for order and definition.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage lists the main subjects of the Phaedrus: false or conventional rhetoric, love or inspiration of beauty and knowledge as madness, dialectic, true rhetoric based on dialectic, and the superiority of spoken over written word.

Socrates is described in the second speech as beating the rhetoricians at their own weapons while professing the speech is not his own. Its superiority is said to lie chiefly in better arrangement, a definition of love, general maxims, and liveliness.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 457-547
occurrences.motif_label: living spoken word privileged over writing
occurrences.basis: The passage identifies the superiority of the spoken over the written word as one of the subjects of the Phaedrus.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage lists the main subjects of the Phaedrus: false or conventional rhetoric, love or inspiration of beauty and knowledge as madness, dialectic, true rhetoric based on dialectic, and the superiority of spoken over written word.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 549-637
occurrences.motif_label: movement from deficient love to higher view
occurrences.basis: The passage describes passionate and interested forms of love yielding to a higher view of love.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Plato is said to have a higher purpose than showing Socrates as a rival of Athenian rhetoricians; Lysias’ speech contains a germ of truth, Socrates develops it, and successive views of love yield to a higher view.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 63-152
occurrences.motif_label: love and philosophy joined as a path toward an ideal
occurrences.basis: The introduction says love and philosophy join hands and that the spiritual and emotional part is elevated into the ideal.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The introduction connects Phaedrus with Symposium, says the two contain Plato's philosophy of love, joins love with philosophy, and describes an ideal sought as recovery from a former state of existence.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 63-152
occurrences.motif_label: self-knowledge preferred over monstrous mythic inquiry
occurrences.basis: Socrates says he does not yet know himself and contrasts self-study with concern for unearthly monsters such as the serpent Typho.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Phaedrus asks about the local tradition of Boreas and Oreithyia; Socrates rejects rationalizing mythology, says he does not yet know himself, and compares self-study with inquiry into the serpent Typho.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 63-152
occurrences.motif_label: inspired speech after invocation
occurrences.basis: Socrates invokes the Muses before beginning his speech on the nature and power of love.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates veils his face, invokes the Muses, ironically assumes the person of the non-lover, and begins to inquire into the nature and power of love.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 639-716
occurrences.motif_label: vision of absolute truth after purification
occurrences.basis: The reunited souls see justice, holiness, and truth as absolute and trace the works of creation to their author.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In that other state they see justice, holiness, and truth not as imperfect worldly copies but as absolutes.
They converse with blessed souls, serve God, fulfill their own nature, see wonders of earth and heaven, and trace creation to its author.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 718-802
occurrences.motif_label: soul's preexistent vision and recovery of truth
occurrences.basis: The soul has a previous existence, partly beholds absolute truth, and spends later existence attempting to regain it.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The triple soul is said to have had a previous existence, to have followed in the train of a god, and to have partially and imperfectly seen absolute truth.
The soul's after-existence passes through many forms of humans and animals and is spent regaining the vision, while animal desires of the inferior steed hinder it.
The passage describes Plato's concern with abstract knowledge, an inner unseen world, and the attempt to regain saving knowledge of the ideas.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 718-802
occurrences.motif_label: ascent or journey by chariot toward truth and light
occurrences.basis: In the comparison to Parmenides, a chariot approaches regions of light and the house of the goddess of truth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The charioteer-and-steeds image is compared with Parmenides, but the passage says Parmenides' horses are not allegorical and that the poet approaches in a chariot to regions of light and the house of the goddess of truth.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 804-884
occurrences.motif_label: Former existence as source of knowledge
occurrences.basis: Recognition of universals known in a former state distinguishes humans from animals, and reason is described as not being lost.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Men are distinguished from animals by recognition of the universal known in a former state, and reason cannot be obliterated or lost.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 804-884
occurrences.motif_label: Philosophical madness or inspired lover
occurrences.basis: The philosopher or philosopher-lover is described as a sort of madman, while philosophy is represented as inspired by love.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The philosopher, or philosopher and lover together, is described as a sort of madman and compared with the Republic and Theaetetus; the myth is said to describe figuratively things beyond human faculties or inaccessible to the age.
Philosophy is represented as the inspiration of love, a conception connected with the Symposium and with the Greek passion of friendship.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 886-959
occurrences.motif_label: ascent from animal desire to contemplation of forms
occurrences.basis: Higher love is described as rising above animal wants and contemplating forms of justice, temperance, and holiness.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage distinguishes lower and higher love, describes higher love as contemplating forms with religious awe, compares the opposition to flesh and spirit in St. Paul, and mentions the rational soul mastering both steeds in spiritual combat.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 886-959
occurrences.motif_label: visible image as shadow of higher truth
occurrences.basis: The passage states that visible or described images do not provide the substance but only the shadow of truth in heaven.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage describes a yearning for justice, temperance, and wisdom to appear as visible beauty, compares this to the Madonna in Christian art, and says images are only the shadow of heavenly truth.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 886-959
occurrences.motif_label: dialectic as higher knowledge than rhetoric
occurrences.basis: Dialectic is distinguished from rhetoric and linked with higher philosophy and psychological analysis.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage turns to criticism of rhetoric as persuasion without knowledge of truth and contrasts rhetoric with dialectic, higher philosophy, and psychological analysis.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 961-1037
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom as truth over appearance and popular opinion
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly opposes truth, reality, proof, and understanding of wholes to appearances, rhetoric, popular approval, and unverified opinion.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says dialectic and rhetoric are neglected, describes Socrates as piercing differences of times and countries, and frames his question about preferring appearances to reality.
Politics is described as following the will of the many rather than truth; some politicians know only what the many approve, while others lack persuasion and insight into characters.
Medical science is described as routine use of drugs from a book rather than lifelong study, and Hippocrates is cited for seeing that the body's nature must be understood as a whole.
Socrates is imagined addressing newspapers and theology, while the passage says people search for belief, deplore unbelief, and prefer popular contradictory opinions to proven unpopular truths.

Preachers are said to praise God without regard to truth or falsehood, and the Church is similarly praised without regard to history or experience; the passage asks whether people care more for truth or for speaker and country.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS. / THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I.; lines 10055-10189
occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom and justice identified
occurrences.basis: Justice is explicitly identified with wisdom and virtue, while injustice is identified with ignorance and vice.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates elicits that the just is like the wise and good and the unjust like the evil and ignorant; Thrasymachus admits this reluctantly, perspiring and blushing.
Socrates resumes the question whether injustice has strength, using the example of an unjust state enslaving other states and asking whether such power can exist with or without justice.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS. / THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I.; lines 10191-10359
occurrences.motif_label: justice as soul-excellence leading to happy life
occurrences.basis: The passage presents a reasoned inquiry linking the soul’s proper function, justice as excellence, and the conclusion that the just person lives well and happily.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “has not the soul an end which nothing else can fulfil? for example, to superintend and command and deliberate and the like.”
The soul is said to have an excellence; an evil soul rules badly and a good soul rules well; justice is admitted as the soul’s excellence and injustice as its defect.
The speakers agree that the just soul and just man live well, that living well is blessed and happy, and that the unjust man is miserable; injustice is not more profitable than justice.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS. / THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I.; lines 10191-10359
occurrences.motif_label: inquiry ending in acknowledged ignorance
occurrences.basis: After deriving conclusions about justice and happiness, Socrates says he still does not know what justice is and therefore cannot securely know its attributes or consequences.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says he was not well entertained and compares himself to an epicure tasting each dish in succession before enjoying the previous one, because he moved from one topic to another.
Socrates states that he knows nothing because he does not know what justice is, and therefore cannot determine whether it is virtue or whether the just person is happy or unhappy.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 10362-10458
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom sought through adversarial dialogue
occurrences.basis: Glaucon challenges Socrates, classifies goods, asks for justice to be praised in itself, and requests inquiry into how justice and injustice work in the soul.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Glaucon is dissatisfied after Thrasymachus' retirement and asks Socrates whether he wants really to persuade them that justice is always better than injustice.
Glaucon asks Socrates to classify goods into three kinds: those welcomed for their own sake, those desirable in themselves and for results, and disagreeable goods pursued for reward or result.
Glaucon says the nature of justice and injustice has not been made clear and asks to know what they are in themselves and how they work in the soul, apart from rewards and results.

Glaucon proposes to revive Thrasymachus' argument: first to describe the common view of justice's nature and origin, then to show people practice it unwillingly, and third to argue the unjust life is better if that view is true.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 10724-10811
occurrences.motif_label: quest for wisdom about justice's intrinsic nature
occurrences.basis: The passage centers on a demand for knowledge of the true nature of justice and injustice in the soul, rather than reliance on reputation, honor, or external rewards.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker says people are generally not just willingly, except perhaps someone inspired by the divinity within or someone who has attained knowledge of truth.
The speaker claims that panegyrists from ancient heroes to the present praise justice for honors and benefits, not for its essential nature in the soul.
The speaker asks Socrates to exclude reputation and show what justice and injustice do to their possessors, whether seen or unseen by gods and humans.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 10813-10978
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom inquiry by analogy from greater to lesser
occurrences.basis: The passage presents an investigation of justice using a methodological image: read the larger case first, then compare it with the smaller case.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker says the inquiry is serious and illustrates a method by comparing it to reading larger letters before smaller ones.
Justice is discussed as a virtue of both individual and State; the speaker proposes examining it first in the larger State, then in the individual.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1100-1178
occurrences.motif_label: justice tested apart from reputation
occurrences.basis: The argument asks Socrates to prove justice superior while the just person is thought unjust and deprived of ordinary conditions of happiness.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A speaker asks Socrates to show the power of justice and injustice in the soul, unseen by human or divine eye, and to prove justice superior while the just is thought unjust and the unjust just.
The two brothers ask Socrates to prove that the just person is happy after removing what happiness is ordinarily supposed to consist in; the passage says the ideal is a paradox beside ordinary life.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 11115-11284
occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom through dialectical selection
occurrences.basis: Socrates proceeds by questioning, identifying perplexity, and refining the criteria by which a guardian nature can be recognized.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The guardian’s duties require time, skill, art, application, and natural aptitude; suitable natures must be selected to guard the city.
Socrates asks how to find a gentle nature with great spirit; the combination appears contradictory, and without both qualities the good guardian seems impossible.
Socrates, in perplexity, says they have lost sight of the image before them and asserts that natures gifted with the opposite qualities do exist.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 11286-11457
occurrences.motif_label: animal model of wise discrimination
occurrences.basis: The dog is used as an animal example of distinguishing friend from enemy by knowledge and ignorance, and is explicitly called a philosopher or lover of learning.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Well-bred dogs are described as gentle to familiars and acquaintances and the reverse to strangers; this is offered as an example for the guardian's qualities.
A dog is angry at a stranger and welcomes an acquaintance; the speaker says it distinguishes friend and enemy by knowing and not knowing and is therefore a lover of learning, or philosopher.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 11286-11457
occurrences.motif_label: education as formation of the heroic guardian
occurrences.basis: The passage frames the education of guardians as the education of heroes, beginning with music, literature, and early formative stories.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The dialogue asks how the guardians are to be reared and educated, calls the coming account the education of heroes, and divides traditional education into gymnastic for the body and music for the soul.
Music includes literature; literature may be true or false; children first receive stories that are mainly fictitious before they are old enough for gymnastics.
"the beginning is the most important part of any work... for that is the time at which the character is being formed"

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 11286-11457
occurrences.motif_label: authorized tales shaping the young soul
occurrences.basis: The passage proposes controlling stories told to children because early tales shape character and mind.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "the beginning is the most important part of any work... for that is the time at which the character is being formed"
The speaker proposes censorship of fiction: censors are to accept good tales and reject bad ones, and mothers and nurses are to tell children only authorized tales, fashioning the mind with them.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 11459-11608
occurrences.motif_label: Regulation of sacred stories for the education of the young
occurrences.basis: The passage centers on rules for which tales about gods and heroes may be told to future guardians, with concern for moral formation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speakers say future guardians should not be told of wars in heaven, divine plots and fights, battles of giants, or quarrels of gods and heroes with friends and relatives.
A young person cannot judge allegorical from literal meaning, and what is received into the mind at that age is likely to become indelible and unalterable.
Socrates says they are founders of a State, not poets; founders should know the forms and limits poets must observe, though they need not make the tales.
“God is not the author of all things, but of good only.”

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 11459-11608
occurrences.motif_label: Good deity not author of evil
occurrences.basis: The speakers distinguish good from evil causation and state that God is cause of good only, with evil causes to be sought elsewhere.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The argument states that God must be represented as truly good; what is good does not hurt or cause evil; therefore God is cause of good only, not of most human evils.
“God is not the author of all things, but of good only.”

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 11610-11780
occurrences.motif_label: mythic falsehood as useful approximation
occurrences.basis: The passage says that because people do not know the truth about ancient times, falsehood in mythological tales may be made as much like truth as possible and turned to account.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker says spoken falsehood can be useful against enemies, as a preventive for friends in madness or illusion, and in mythological tales about ancient times when truth is unknown.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1180-1263
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom through inquiry into justice and order
occurrences.basis: The passage centers on philosophical inquiry into the nature of justice, its internal principle, and its relation to universal order or well-being.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Adeimantus argues that people value justice for rewards and reputation; the passage also notes arguments of Thrasymachus and Glaucon and raises whether morality is determined by consequences.
Socrates is said to enlarge justice into universal order or well-being in State and individual, and to treat one virtue as the ordering principle of three others.

Socrates' indirect answer restores man to natural condition, uses the image of large letters, seeks justice in society before the individual, and says justice and happiness coincide in the perfect State; the rack is mentioned in a rejected Stoical paradox.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1180-1263
occurrences.motif_label: inner virtue over external reward
occurrences.basis: The passage discusses justice as an internal principle and says duty should be done first, with happiness as an attendant result.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates is said to enlarge justice into universal order or well-being in State and individual, and to treat one virtue as the ordering principle of three others.

The passage mentions the philosopher who retires under a wall and concludes with the maxim that duty comes first, followed by happiness, illustrated by a quotation about seeking God's kingdom and righteousness.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III.; lines 11800-11967
occurrences.motif_label: Wise dead seer singled out among shades
occurrences.basis: Tiresias is described as the one to whom Persephone granted mind after death, while other souls are flitting shades.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Tiresias is cited as one to whom Persephone granted mind after death; other souls are described as flitting shades, and a soul is said to go to Hades lamenting its fate.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III.; lines 11800-11967
occurrences.motif_label: Civic education through selection and removal of sacred poetry
occurrences.basis: The speaker proposes telling some tales, withholding others, striking out underworld passages, and composing a nobler strain for guardians.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speakers state that principles of theology determine which tales should be told to youths so that they honor gods and parents and value friendship.
The speaker proposes controlling narrators of such tales and asking them to commend rather than revile the world below, because their descriptions are untrue and harmful to future warriors.
Quoted poetic imagery describes a soul passing like smoke beneath the earth and compares shrilling souls to bats in a hollow mystic cavern clinging together.
After saying a nobler strain must be composed, the speakers agree to remove weepings and wailings of famous men.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III.; lines 12131-12273
occurrences.motif_label: Denial that gods are authors of evil
occurrences.basis: The speaker explicitly says citizens should not be persuaded that gods are authors of evil and presents this as a rule for poetic education.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "We will not have them trying to persuade our youth that the gods are the authors of evil, and that heroes are no better than men"

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III.; lines 12275-12403
occurrences.motif_label: imitation forming character
occurrences.basis: The speaker argues that imitations beginning in youth become habits and second nature affecting body, voice, and mind, and therefore guardians must imitate only suitable virtues.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Guardians are to dedicate themselves to maintaining freedom in the State; if they imitate, they should imitate only courageous, temperate, holy, free, and similar characters, because repeated imitation becomes habit and second nature affecting body, voice, and mind.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III.; lines 12275-12403
occurrences.motif_label: specialized guardians restricted to proper roles
occurrences.basis: The guardians are assigned one craft, the maintenance of freedom in the State, and are instructed not to practise or imitate unrelated or base roles.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker asks whether poets should be allowed to imitate in whole or part, whether tragedy and comedy should enter the State, and whether guardians should be imitators under the rule that one person can only do one thing well.

Guardians are to dedicate themselves to maintaining freedom in the State; if they imitate, they should imitate only courageous, temperate, holy, free, and similar characters, because repeated imitation becomes habit and second nature affecting body, voice, and mind.

The speaker says guardians should not imitate women in specified conditions such as quarrelling, affliction, sickness, love, or labour, and should not represent male or female slaves performing slave duties.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III.; lines 12405-12538
occurrences.motif_label: education through selective imitation of virtue
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly treats poetic and narrative imitation as a means of education and restricts imitation to virtuous models for the health of souls.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A just and good narrator may personate another good man, especially acting firmly and wisely, but avoids studying or sustaining the likeness of an unworthy person.
Adeimantus would admit only the pure imitator of virtue; the State is described as one in which 'one man plays one part only.'

The pantomimic poet who can imitate anything is to be worshipped as sweet, holy, and wonderful, anointed with myrrh, crowned with wool, and sent away; the State will use a rougher poet who imitates virtue for souls' health and soldier education.
The discussion of music or literary education concerning story or myth is declared finished, with both matter and manner discussed.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III.; lines 12540-12667
occurrences.motif_label: ethical regulation of music for civic character
occurrences.basis: The passage treats musical words, harmonies, instruments, and rhythms as objects of rational selection according to courage, temperance, military fitness, and civic education.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Words set to music and words not set to music are said to follow the same laws, and melody and rhythm are said to depend upon the words.
Drunkenness, softness, and indolence are called utterly unbecoming to the character of the guardians.
The speaker asks to keep one harmony for a brave man facing danger, wounds, death, or misfortune with endurance, and another for peaceful, prayerful, persuasive, moderate, and wise conduct.

The speaker says rhythms should follow the same rules as harmonies, avoiding complexity and seeking rhythms that express a courageous and harmonious life, with foot and melody adapted to words of like spirit.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1265-1334
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom as condition of proper guardianship
occurrences.basis: The human watchdogs must be philosophers or lovers of learning, and education is required to make them gentle.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Guardians need both gentleness to friends and fierceness to enemies; dogs are gentle to friends and fierce to strangers, and human watchdogs must be philosophers or lovers of learning, requiring education.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III.; lines 12669-12786
occurrences.motif_label: formation of the soul through ordered sound and beauty
occurrences.basis: The passage presents musical training, rhythm, harmony, and beauty as means by which the soul becomes graceful, noble, and ready to recognize reason.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speakers connect words, style, the temper of the soul, and the beauty of style, harmony, grace, and good rhythm with a rightly and nobly ordered mind and character.
Youth should dwell among “fair sights and sounds”; beauty should flow into the eye and ear “like a health-giving breeze from a purer region.”

Socrates tells Glaucon that musical training is especially powerful because rhythm and harmony enter the inward places of the soul, impart grace, and prepare the educated person to recognize reason as familiar.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III.; lines 12669-12786
occurrences.motif_label: recognition through copies and reflections
occurrences.basis: The passage uses the analogy of recognizing letters and their reflections in water or mirrors to describe learned recognition across different appearances.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates compares training perception to learning alphabet letters in all combinations and recognizing their reflections in water or in a mirror.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III.; lines 12788-12962
occurrences.motif_label: education in discernment of virtue and vice
occurrences.basis: The guardians must learn to recognize essential forms of virtues, contrary forms, and their images wherever found.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Guardians must be educated in music until they know and recognize forms of virtues, their opposites, and their images in small and great things.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III.; lines 12964-13082
occurrences.motif_label: Simplicity as the source of health and temperance
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly contrasts simplicity with complexity and connects simplicity to temperance of soul and bodily health.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Complexity is said to engender licence and disease; simplicity in music produces temperance in the soul, and simplicity in gymnastic produces bodily health.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III.; lines 12964-13082
occurrences.motif_label: Ancestral healer contrasted with overrefined medicine
occurrences.basis: Asclepius and the older Asclepiad practice are presented as wiser than later medicine that prolongs invalidism, with Herodicus as the negative counterexample.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker cites Homer: wounded Eurypylus drinks Pramnian wine mixed with barley-meal and grated cheese; the sons of Asclepius at Troy do not blame the damsel who gives it or Patroclus, who treats him.

Before Herodicus, the guild of Asclepius is said not to practise disease-educating medicine; Herodicus combines training and doctoring, tends his mortal disease, and struggles on to old age in torment.
Asclepius is said not to teach valetudinarian arts because in well-ordered states every person has an occupation and no leisure to spend continually being ill.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III.; lines 12964-13082
occurrences.motif_label: Occupation as protection against perpetual illness
occurrences.basis: The artisan's need to return to work limits medical dependence, while the rich man's lack of appointed work is contrasted with Phocylides' saying about livelihood and virtue.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A carpenter asks for rough remedies such as emetic, purge, cautery, or knife; he refuses prolonged dietetics, resumes ordinary habits, and either recovers and works or dies without further trouble.
The rich man is said to lack a specially appointed work, and Phocylides is cited as saying that once a man has a livelihood he should practise virtue.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III.; lines 13084-13196
occurrences.motif_label: selective healing for the health of the state
occurrences.basis: The passage presents a normative account of medical practice in which treatment is limited by usefulness to the person and the state.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Asclepius is described as healing generally healthy people with definite ailments, but not attempting to prolong lives of bodies thoroughly penetrated by disease.
The sons of Asclepius are said to refuse unhealthy and intemperate subjects, even if they were as rich as Midas.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III.; lines 13084-13196
occurrences.motif_label: knowledge through observation rather than corruption
occurrences.basis: The ideal judge should know evil from late and long observation, with knowledge as guide rather than personal experience.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A judge governs mind by mind and should learn evil from long observation of others rather than from personal contamination or experience of crime.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
