occurrences.passage_locator: PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III.; lines 13198-13348
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom through virtuous formation
occurrences.basis: The passage states that the virtuous, not the vicious, person has wisdom because a virtuous nature educated by time can know both virtue and vice.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker says the sought judge is not the vicious man, since vice cannot know virtue; the virtuous nature educated by time can know virtue and vice, and the virtuous person has wisdom.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III.; lines 13350-13505
occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom as qualification for rule
occurrences.basis: The best guardians are described as wise and efficient, educated through harmony of music and gymnastic, and selected for steadfast understanding of the State's interest.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A person who best mingles music with gymnastic and tempers them to the soul is called a true musician and harmonist; such a presiding genius is required if the State is to last.
The dialogue turns to who should rule and who should be subject: elders over younger people, the best over others, and the best guardians as wise, efficient, and specially careful of the State.

Guardians must be selected from those who eagerly do what benefits their country and avoid what harms it; they are to be watched at every age so they do not forget or cast off duty under force or enchantment.

Candidates are watched from youth and made to perform actions likely to cause forgetfulness or deception; those who remember and are not deceived are selected, failures rejected, with further proof through toils, pains, and conflicts.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1336-1415
occurrences.motif_label: Regulated sacred narrative for moral formation
occurrences.basis: The passage proposes selecting and suppressing stories for children because early narrative instruction shapes future character.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Education is discussed as music and gymnastic; music includes literature; children hear stories early, and impressionable children should not learn what they must later unlearn, so nursery tales are to be censored.

Homer and Hesiod are criticized for improper divine stories about Uranus and Saturn, Zeus, Hephaestus, divine strife, and family violence; such stories may have mystical interpretation but youth cannot understand allegory.

The speakers say they are legislators who set principles for books. The first principle is that God must be represented as author of good only, not as cause of evil, sin, treaty-breaking, suffering, or war.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV.; lines 13653-13780
occurrences.motif_label: ordered whole over privileged part
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly frames the just and happy State as a whole whose parts must receive due proportion rather than maximum private benefit.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says the founding aim is not the disproportionate happiness of one class but the greatest happiness of the whole State, in which justice is more likely to be found.
Socrates compares the State to a statue: one should not over-beautify the eyes so that they cease to be eyes, but should give each feature its due proportion to make the whole beautiful.

Socrates says guardians, auxiliaries, and all others must be compelled or induced to do their own work in the best way, so the whole State grows in noble order and each class receives its assigned proportion of happiness.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV.; lines 13782-13921
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom through education and nurture
occurrences.basis: The passage presents education and nurture as the sufficient central care by which citizens become sensible and the state improves.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker says the one sufficient care is education and nurture, by which citizens become sensible and civic arrangements follow the principle that friends have all things in common.
“the State, if once started well, moves with accumulating force like a wheel”

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV.; lines 13923-14069
occurrences.motif_label: Formation of character through ordered initiation into practice
occurrences.basis: Youth are to be trained from the first through ordered play and music so that their future actions and civic character are shaped by order.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Youth should be trained from the first in a stricter system, because lawless amusements make lawless youths who cannot become well-conducted and virtuous citizens.

evidence.locator: lines 13923-14069, good beginning in play and music
evidence.quote_or_summary: A good beginning in play, aided by music, produces a habit of order that accompanies all actions and can raise fallen places in the State.

evidence.locator: lines 13923-14069, manners not legislated in detail
evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage lists respect before elders, honour to parents, dress, hair, deportment, and manners, and says precise written enactments about such matters are unlikely to last.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV.; lines 13923-14069
occurrences.motif_label: False remedies without moral reform
occurrences.basis: Invalids who refuse to abandon harmful habits seek drugs, cautery, spells, and amulets, but truthful counsel says these remedies will not avail.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates compares such lawmaking people to invalids who have no self-restraint and will not abandon habits of intemperance.
The invalids keep doctoring themselves and seek cures, but neither drug, cautery, spell, amulet, nor other remedy will help unless they stop eating, drinking, wenching, and idling.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV.; lines 14071-14242
occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom as ruling knowledge
occurrences.basis: The city is called wise because a small presiding guardian class possesses knowledge concerning the good of the whole State.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Wisdom is identified with good counsel, a form of knowledge that advises about the whole State and its dealings with itself and other States.
This knowledge is said to be found among the guardians, the smallest class, whose knowledge makes the whole State wise.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1417-1481
occurrences.motif_label: education by morally directed fiction
occurrences.basis: The passage states that children may first be trained through falsehood or imagination before truth, and that Plato values fictions when they have a good moral effect.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Plato is said to affirm that a child must be trained in falsehood first and truth afterward; the passage interprets this as education through imagination as well as reason and gradual development of the mind.

The passage contrasts modern limits on accommodation with Plato's view that fictions are acceptable if morally beneficial, while falsehood as a dangerous weapon should be used only by rulers for great objects.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1417-1481
occurrences.motif_label: moral truth placed before historical truth in religion
occurrences.basis: The passage says religious morality is considered before the truth of documents or events and later states that Plato and the modern reader may agree in placing moral truth before historical truth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says religious narratives were suspected as fictions when seen as immoral, and generalizes that in religions morality is considered before document truth or the truth of narrated natural or supernatural events.

The passage says facts of ancient or religious history are important but often uncertain, and that readers may agree with Plato in placing the moral before the historical truth of religion while tolerating early religious misstatements.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV.; lines 14244-14387
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom-guided restraint of desire
occurrences.basis: The passage says the meaner desires of the many are held down by the virtuous desires and wisdom of the few.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage places manifold pleasures and desires among children, women, servants, and the lowest numerous class, while simple moderate desires guided by reason and true opinion belong to the few best born and best educated; the desires of the many are held down by the wisdom of the few.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV.; lines 14389-14543
occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom as governing watchfulness
occurrences.basis: Wisdom and watchfulness are located in the rulers, and wisdom is one of the virtues that makes the state excellent.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Justice is described as the remaining virtue when temperance, courage, and wisdom are abstracted, and as the cause, condition, and preservative of the other virtues; wisdom and watchfulness are associated with rulers.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV.; lines 14545-14687
occurrences.motif_label: quest for wisdom through analogical inquiry
occurrences.basis: The passage stages a philosophical search for justice by moving from the larger case of the State to the individual soul and by testing principles through reasoned examples.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says the account should be tested in the individual after being found in the State, using the State as the larger example.
"The friction of the two when rubbed together may possibly strike a light in which justice will shine forth"
The State was just when its three classes did their own work; the individual is assumed to have the same three principles in the soul.
Socrates states the rule that the same thing cannot act or be acted upon in contrary ways in the same part, relation, and time.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV.; lines 14545-14687
occurrences.motif_label: illumination of hidden truth
occurrences.basis: The passage uses the image of friction striking light so that justice may shine forth and be fixed in the soul.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "The friction of the two when rubbed together may possibly strike a light in which justice will shine forth"

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV.; lines 14689-14843
occurrences.motif_label: instruction through bodily analogy
occurrences.basis: The speaker uses the archer's two hands pushing and pulling a bow to clarify a distinction about contrary actions and parts.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker compares the point to an archer: one should not say that the archer's hands push and pull the bow at the same time, but that one hand pushes and the other pulls.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1483-1541
occurrences.motif_label: philosophical reinterpretation of inherited mythology
occurrences.basis: The passage describes allegorical interpretation, explaining away unaltered myths, and transforming Zeus and Heracles into philosophical or moral figures.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Allegorical interpretation of mythology, said to begin with Theagenes of Rhegium, was established in Plato's age and rejected by him here.
Zeus is reinterpreted as Plato's 'royal mind'; Heracles becomes a knight-errant and benefactor of mankind through later philosophical transformations.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1483-1541
occurrences.motif_label: inner falsehood opposed to outward or poetic deception
occurrences.basis: The 'lie in the soul' is contrasted with the 'lie in words,' distinguishing corruptive ignorance from verbal or literary accommodation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The lie in the soul is described as a true lie: corruption of highest truth and deception of the highest part of the soul, with examples involving false claims about God and knowledge.
The lie in words is contrasted as deception in play, poem, allegory, figure of speech, or accommodation, useless to gods but sometimes useful to humans.
Socrates answers the question about deceiving a madman and contrasts God and man; God is Truth, while mankind may appear partial or false.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV.; lines 14845-14992
occurrences.motif_label: Reason as inner ruler and source of wisdom
occurrences.basis: The rational principle forbids appetite, reasons about better and worse, and corresponds to the quality by which State and individual are wise.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker distinguishes a soul-principle that bids a man to drink from a stronger forbidding principle, then names the reasoning element rational and the loving, hungering, thirsting element irrational or appetitive.

The passage argues that passion or spirit is a third element, distinct from desire and reason, naturally auxiliary to reason; children, brute animals, and a Homeric line about smiting the breast and rebuking the soul are cited.

The argument concludes that the same three principles exist in State and individual; wisdom, courage, and justice are treated analogously, and justice consists in each class or quality doing its own work.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV.; lines 14994-15155
occurrences.motif_label: rightful rule of wisdom within the soul
occurrences.basis: The rational part is wise, rules the soul, knows the interest of all parts and the whole, and presides over just action as wisdom.

evidence.locator: 14994-15155; opening exchange on rational and spirited principles
evidence.quote_or_summary: Reason is described as wise and caring for the whole soul, while the spirited principle is to be its subject and ally.
Wisdom belongs to the small ruling part that knows what is in the interest of each of the three parts and of the whole.

The just person orders the inner life, is master and law to himself, is at peace, and binds the three principles like higher, lower, and middle notes of a scale into one temperate and adjusted nature.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV.; lines 15157-15248
occurrences.motif_label: ascent to a vantage point for seeing truth
occurrences.basis: Socrates says they are near a place where truth may be seen clearly, invites the interlocutor to come up, and compares the argument’s position to a height or tower of speculation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “we are near the spot at which we may see the truth in the clearest manner with our own eyes”
“Come up hither... and behold the various forms of vice”
The argument is said to have reached a height, like a tower of speculation, from which one may see that virtue is one and vice has innumerable forms, with four special ones worth noting.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V.; lines 15251-15379
occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom inquiry under risk of error
occurrences.basis: The passage emphasizes discourse, inquiry, truth, and the danger of misleading others about beauty, goodness, justice, and laws.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Glaucon and Thrasymachus agree that Socrates must answer; Thrasymachus contrasts seeking gold with hearing discourse, and Glaucon says the whole of life is the limit for wise men hearing such discourse.

Socrates says the answer is difficult, may be doubted in practicality and value, may be only a dream, and is dangerous because he may miss the truth and deceive friends about beauty, goodness, justice, and laws; he prays Nemesis not to visit him for his words.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V.; lines 15381-15526
occurrences.motif_label: reason overcoming ridicule of new custom
occurrences.basis: Socrates contrasts ridicule directed at unusual customs with experience, reason, and judgment by the good rather than outward appearance.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates expects the proposals to seem ridiculous, especially women naked in the palaestra exercising with men, including older women.
The passage anticipates jokes about women’s music, gymnastic training, wearing armour, and riding on horseback.
Socrates recalls that Hellenes once thought male nakedness ridiculous and improper, while Cretans and Lacedaemonians introduced the custom.
Experience showed uncovering to be better than covering, and reason asserted that the beautiful should be judged by the good, not mere outward appearance.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V.; lines 15381-15526
occurrences.motif_label: true reasoning versus verbal contention
occurrences.basis: The passage distinguishes defining and dividing in fair discussion from merely verbal opposition and contentious disputing.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says many people merely dispute because they cannot define and divide the subject, pursuing verbal opposition rather than fair discussion.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1543-1614
occurrences.motif_label: purification of myth for civic courage
occurrences.basis: The passage frames the removal of certain religious and poetic tales as a means to banish fear and educate youth toward courage, temperance, and obedience.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Religion is to be purified to banish fear of death; poets are asked not to abuse hell and to remove untrue and discouraging tales about the world below.

Examples to be removed include Achilles's words about serving rather than ruling the dead, squalid mansions, shadows, souls beneath the earth like smoke or bats, Cocytus, Styx, ghosts, sapless shades, and Tartarean terms; such tales are not proper food for soldiers.

Youth must be temperate; temperance is self-control and obedience to authority. Homer sometimes teaches silent awe of leaders but elsewhere uses abusive drunken language that will not teach self-control.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1543-1614
occurrences.motif_label: divine and heroic exemplars as models for imitation
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly says portrayals of gods and heroes may be imitated by young men and therefore must be admitted or rejected according to moral effect.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Divine weakness is rejected, including goddesses lamenting and the king of heaven mourning inability to save Hector or grieving Sarpedon's doom, because young men may imitate such portrayals.

Youth must be temperate; temperance is self-control and obedience to authority. Homer sometimes teaches silent awe of leaders but elsewhere uses abusive drunken language that will not teach self-control.

The amatory exploits of Peirithous and Theseus are called unworthy; the passage says either such sons of gods were not sons of gods or were not as poets imagined, and that gods are not authors of evil.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1543-1614
occurrences.motif_label: state-controlled salutary falsehood
occurrences.basis: Falsehood is compared to medicine and reserved for state use, while common lying to rulers is prohibited.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Truth is highly valued; falsehood is useless to gods and useful to men only as medicine, with its use reserved to the state rather than common people lying to rulers.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V.; lines 15528-15704
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom through dialectical classification
occurrences.basis: The speaker uses questioning and examples to clarify the meaning of same and different natures before assigning pursuits.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker warns of a verbal opposition and says the argument had not considered what sameness or difference of nature means when assigning pursuits.
The speaker gives the jesting example of bald and hairy men as cobblers, then distinguishes relevant differences by comparing a physician with a carpenter.
The speaker proposes inviting an opponent into the argument and examining whether women have anything peculiar in constitution that affects administration of the State.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V.; lines 15706-15845
occurrences.motif_label: wise legislation through usefulness
occurrences.basis: The passage links nobility with usefulness and frames the proposed laws as beneficial, orderly, and consistent with rational argument.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker says wives of guardians should strip, with virtue as their robe, share war and defense, receive lighter labours because they are weaker natures, and otherwise have the same duties; he adds that the useful is noble and the hurtful base.

The speaker asks to feast his mind with a day dream, pass over the question of possibility, assume the proposal possible, and examine how rulers would carry it out and how it would benefit the state and guardians.

Glaucon names a necessity known to lovers; the speaker says the matter must proceed orderly, licentiousness is unholy and forbidden, and matrimony must be made sacred in the highest degree, with what is most beneficial deemed sacred.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1616-1687
occurrences.motif_label: civic purification of art
occurrences.basis: The passage describes banishing certain poetic, musical, instrumental, and metrical forms to preserve simplicity, temperance, and harmony of the soul.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A polyphonous pantomimic performer is treated with respect but refused a place in the State; the rough, honest poet and original models are preferred, with a parenthetical reference to Laws.
Lamenting and convivial harmonies are banished; Dorian and Phrygian remain, one for war and courage and the other for peace, obedience, instruction, or religious feeling.
Various instruments are rejected, especially the complex flute; lyre and harp are permitted in town and Pan’s-pipe in the fields.
The passage describes a purgation of music and metres, cites Damon on measures and rhythms, and states that style should conform to subject and metre to style.
The simplicity and harmony of the soul should be reflected in poetic and musical form and learned from youth through arts and natural forms.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V.; lines 16290-16451
occurrences.motif_label: Moderation expressed through the saying that half is more than the whole
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly cites Hesiod's saying as a lesson for a guardian tempted to seize the whole state for private happiness.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A guardian tempted to appropriate the whole state must learn Hesiod's saying, 'half is more than the whole.'

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 165-251
occurrences.motif_label: search for justice and wisdom through philosophical inquiry
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly frames the argument as the search after Justice and later notes philosophy, the unity of knowledge, and contemplation of the idea of good.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage states that Plato influenced Renaissance and later thought, calls the Republic the first treatise upon education, compares Plato to Dante or Bunyan for a revelation of another life and to Bacon for unity of knowledge, and calls him father of idealism.

The argument of the Republic is summarized as the search after Justice, moving through Cephalus, Socrates, Polemarchus, Thrasymachus, Glaucon, and Adeimantus, until justice reappears in the ideal State constructed by Socrates.

The passage outlines five natural divisions of the Republic, including the construction of states and education, philosopher-rule and contemplation of the idea of good, review of perverted states and individuals, and a conclusion crowned by the vision of another life.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V.; lines 16613-16748
occurrences.motif_label: ideal model guiding imperfect realization
occurrences.basis: Socrates treats justice and the perfect State as ideals by which actual persons and cities may be judged or approximated.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates recalls that the discussion began in search of justice and injustice and used the perfectly just and unjust as standards.
Socrates compares the theory to a painter's ideal of a perfectly beautiful man and says the theory of the perfect State is not worse if exact realization cannot be proven.
Socrates argues that actual things fall short of the truth expressed in language and that it is enough to show how a city might be governed nearly as proposed.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V.; lines 16750-16884
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom joined to political rule
occurrences.basis: The passage states that cities will not rest from evils until philosophers are kings or kings and princes acquire philosophical power, so political greatness and wisdom meet in one.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “Until philosophers are kings... and political greatness and wisdom meet in one... cities will never have rest from their evils.”

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V.; lines 16750-16884
occurrences.motif_label: true lover of wisdom seeks the whole
occurrences.basis: Socrates defines the philosopher as one who loves the whole of wisdom, has a taste for every sort of knowledge, and is never satisfied with learning.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says the philosopher is “a lover, not of a part of wisdom only, but of the whole.”
One with “a taste for every sort of knowledge,” curious to learn and never satisfied, may be termed a philosopher.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V.; lines 16750-16884
occurrences.motif_label: vision of truth distinguishes true philosopher from imitation
occurrences.basis: The passage distinguishes lovers of sights and musical amateurs from true philosophers, whom Socrates calls lovers of the vision of truth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Glaucon notes that lovers of sights and musical amateurs delight in learning and attend Dionysiac festivals, but Socrates replies that they are only an imitation of philosophers.
Socrates identifies true philosophers as “lovers of the vision of truth.”

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V.; lines 16886-17066
occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom as discernment of reality from appearance
occurrences.basis: The passage contrasts those who mistake copies or beautiful objects for the real with those who know absolute beauty and distinguish idea from participants.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker distinguishes lovers of sounds and sights from philosophers; the former love tones, colours, forms, and artificial products but cannot see or love absolute beauty.

The passage contrasts the dreamer, who puts a copy in place of the real object, with one who recognizes absolute beauty and distinguishes the idea from participating objects; the latter is called wide awake.
The speaker says the mind of one who knows has knowledge and the mind of one who opines has opinion, then prepares to question the holder of opinion.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1689-1772
occurrences.motif_label: Disciplined education of the soul toward wisdom and virtue
occurrences.basis: Music, art, and the analogy of learning letters are used to describe gradual formation of judgment, recognition of beauty and deformity, and attainment of the essential forms of virtues.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Artists and poets are warned against unseemliness; sculpture, painting, and music must conform to simplicity; guardians should grow among health and beauty, and music enters the innermost soul to shape the sense of beauty and deformity.

The passage compares moral education to learning letters and their combinations, speaks of essential forms of the virtues, a music of the soul answering to world harmony, and true love as the daughter of temperance.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V.; lines 17068-17208
occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom as love of truth beyond appearances
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly reserves the name lovers of wisdom for those who love truth in each thing and know the absolute, eternal, and immutable rather than merely apprehending appearances.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Those who see many beautiful and just things but not absolute beauty or justice are said to have opinion, while those who see the absolute, eternal, and immutable are said to know.

The passage contrasts those who love subjects of knowledge with those who love subjects of opinion, including people drawn to sweet sounds and fair colours; it concludes that those who love truth in each thing are lovers of wisdom, not lovers of opinion.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 17211-17397
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom as qualification for rulership
occurrences.basis: The passage argues that rulers or guardians should be those who know the truth of each thing and can guard the laws and institutions of the State.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “philosophers only are able to grasp the eternal and unchangeable,” while others “wander in the region of the many and variable”; the speaker asks which class should rule the State.
“Whichever of the two are best able to guard the laws and institutions of our State—let them be our guardians.”

The speaker says a guardian should have eyes, then describes those without knowledge of true being or a clear pattern in the soul as lacking the painter-like vision needed to order laws about beauty, goodness, and justice, and says they are much like blind persons.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 17211-17397
occurrences.motif_label: vision and blindness as knowledge and ignorance
occurrences.basis: The passage contrasts guardians with eyes and perfect vision of truth against persons lacking knowledge of true being, who are described as blind.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker says a guardian should have eyes, then describes those without knowledge of true being or a clear pattern in the soul as lacking the painter-like vision needed to order laws about beauty, goodness, and justice, and says they are much like blind persons.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 17211-17397
occurrences.motif_label: philosopher as lover and seeker of eternal truth
occurrences.basis: Philosophical minds are described as loving knowledge of the eternal and unchangeable and as desiring all truth from youth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “philosophical minds always love knowledge of a sort which shows them the eternal nature not varying from generation and corruption.”
The philosophical mind is said to love all true being, to possess truthfulness, to detest falsehood, and to desire all truth from earliest youth.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 17211-17397
occurrences.motif_label: turning desire from bodily pleasures toward the soul
occurrences.basis: The speaker contrasts pleasures of the soul with bodily pleasure and uses the image of a stream drawn into another channel.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker says strong desires in one direction are weaker in others, like a stream drawn into another channel; the true philosopher’s desires are drawn toward knowledge and pleasures of the soul rather than bodily pleasure.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 17399-17515
occurrences.motif_label: wise navigator dismissed as useless
occurrences.basis: The true pilot possesses the relevant navigational knowledge but is called a prater, star-gazer, and good-for-nothing by the mutinous sailors; Socrates links this to the true philosopher in the State.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The true pilot must attend to the year, seasons, sky, stars, winds, and the art of command, but in a mutinous vessel he is called a prater, star-gazer, and good-for-nothing.
Socrates says the figure describes the true philosopher in relation to the State, and Adeimantus agrees that he understands.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 17399-17515
occurrences.motif_label: rightful expertise versus popular acclaim
occurrences.basis: Those who help the sailors take the ship are praised as pilots and able seamen, while the actually qualified pilot is abused as useless.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The sailors beg for the helm, kill or throw rivals overboard, drug or intoxicate the captain, mutiny, seize the ship, consume stores, and praise accomplices as pilots or able seamen.
The true pilot must attend to the year, seasons, sky, stars, winds, and the art of command, but in a mutinous vessel he is called a prater, star-gazer, and good-for-nothing.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 17517-17660
occurrences.motif_label: unrecognized wise guide
occurrences.basis: The true helmsman or philosopher is competent to guide but is dismissed as useless by those who should be governed or guided.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker says the best philosophers are useless only because others do not use them; those who need governance should go to one able to govern, as the sick go to physicians.
"the present governors of mankind ... may be justly compared to the mutinous sailors, and the true helmsmen to those who are called by them good-for-nothings and star-gazers."

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 17517-17660
occurrences.motif_label: quest for truth and being
occurrences.basis: The lover of knowledge follows truth, strives after being, approaches and mingles with being, and reaches knowledge after travail.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "Truth, as you will remember, was his leader, whom he followed always and in all things"
The true lover of knowledge strives after being and does not rest in the multiplicity of individual appearances.
The lover of knowledge attains the true nature of essence, draws near to and mingles with being, begets mind and truth, and then ceases from travail.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 17662-17790
occurrences.motif_label: Wise seeker preserved against hostile society
occurrences.basis: The philosopher has gifts but is threatened by public opinion, social censure, and bad education, and may be preserved only by divine power.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The philosopher is "like a plant" that with proper nurture grows into virtue, but in alien soil becomes a noxious weed unless preserved by divine power.
Socrates says philosophers must fall under the censure of the world and of individuals who consort with the mob and seek to please them.
Socrates asks how the philosopher can be preserved in his calling, recalling the philosopher’s gifts of quickness, memory, courage, and magnificence.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 17662-17790
occurrences.motif_label: False wisdom as management of a powerful beast
occurrences.basis: The sophist’s knowledge of popular opinion is compared to a handler’s knowledge of a beast’s moods, wrongly named wisdom.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says mercenary sophists teach nothing but the opinion of the many, specifically the opinions of assemblies, and call this wisdom.
Socrates compares such a teacher to a man who studies a mighty beast’s temper, desires, handling, dangerous times, cries, and reactions, then teaches this as an art.
The beast-handler calls honorable, dishonorable, good, evil, just, and unjust whatever accords with the beast’s tastes, without knowing their true nature or differences.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 17662-17790
occurrences.motif_label: Multitude unable to perceive the absolute
occurrences.basis: The world is said to recognize many beautiful things but not absolute beauty or absolute kinds, and therefore cannot be philosophical.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates asks whether the world can believe in absolute beauty rather than many beautiful things, or absolutes rather than many instances; Adeimantus says it cannot, and Socrates concludes the world cannot be a philosopher.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1774-1852
occurrences.motif_label: wise judge uncorrupted by evil
occurrences.basis: The ideal judge gains insight into evil by observation while retaining an uncorrupted mind.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates distinguishes the physician, who cures with mind and may know disease bodily, from the judge, whose mind should not be corrupted by crime.
The judge should be of a certain age, innocent in youth, and learn evil through observing others rather than practicing it.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 17792-17900
occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom sought or corrupted by unworthy seekers
occurrences.basis: The passage contrasts true understanding and wisdom with the failure of gifted natures and the production of sophisms by unworthy entrants into philosophy.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Someone gently tells the proud youth that he is foolish and must gain understanding through effort, but the speaker says he is unlikely to listen under adverse circumstances.
The speaker concludes that traits fitting a person for philosophy may divert him from philosophy when badly educated, as can wealth and other goods of life.
Such marriages are said to have vile and bastard issue; unworthy alliances with philosophy generate sophisms pleasing to the ear but lacking genuine kinship with true wisdom.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 17902-18011
occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom preserved by a small remnant
occurrences.basis: The passage describes only a small class as true disciples of philosophy who remain devoted while the wider multitude and political life are corrupting.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker describes a small remnant of genuine disciples of philosophy, names examples of people kept from corruption or politics, and mentions a rare internal sign or monitor.
The small class has tasted philosophy and seen the madness of the multitude; the just person is compared to someone among wild beasts and to one sheltering behind a wall in a storm.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 17902-18011
occurrences.motif_label: Solitary just person withdrawing from corrupt society
occurrences.basis: The just philosopher avoids joining wrongdoing, cannot oppose the multitude alone, shelters himself, and aims to live free from unrighteousness.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The small class has tasted philosophy and seen the madness of the multitude; the just person is compared to someone among wild beasts and to one sheltering behind a wall in a storm.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 17902-18011
occurrences.motif_label: True nature requiring proper soil or polity
occurrences.basis: The philosophic nature is compared to an exotic seed distorted by foreign soil, while a suitable state would allow larger growth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Adeimantus says the private just philosopher has done a great work; the speaker says the greatest work requires a suitable state, where he can save country and self.
No existing government is adapted to philosophic nature; philosophy is compared to exotic seed in foreign soil, and would be seen as divine if matched with a suitable state.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 17902-18011
occurrences.motif_label: Lifelong initiation into wisdom
occurrences.basis: The speaker prescribes age-appropriate philosophical education, bodily preparation, increasing exercise of the soul, and later freedom oriented toward happiness in this life and another.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker proposes age-suited education: early philosophy, bodily training, later gymnastics of the soul, and freedom after civic and military duties, ending in happiness here and another life.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 18013-18130
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom rule and philosophical governance
occurrences.basis: The passage centers on true philosophy, truth-seeking, the philosopher’s knowledge of divine order, and the claim that the State is perfected by philosophical rule.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says the many have never seen philosophy realized in a human being and city shaped according to virtue, and contrasts truth-seeking with controversy aimed at opinion and strife.

Socrates states that cities, states, and individuals will not be perfected until philosophers are compelled to care for the State and the State obeys them, or until royal figures are divinely inspired with true love of true philosophy.
Socrates says the true philosopher’s mind is fixed on true being, sees immutable things ordered by reason, imitates them, and becomes orderly and divine as far as human nature allows.

Socrates says the philosopher can fashion human nature, states, and individuals into justice, temperance, and civic virtue, and that no State is happy unless designed by artists who imitate the heavenly pattern.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 18013-18130
occurrences.motif_label: royal legitimacy through philosophical or divine inspiration
occurrences.basis: Socrates allows that kings, princes, or royal sons may become fit for rule if divinely inspired with true love of true philosophy.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates states that cities, states, and individuals will not be perfected until philosophers are compelled to care for the State and the State obeys them, or until royal figures are divinely inspired with true love of true philosophy.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 18013-18130
occurrences.motif_label: imitation of a heavenly pattern
occurrences.basis: The philosopher imitates divine order, and the happy State is said to be designed by artists who imitate a heavenly pattern.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says the true philosopher’s mind is fixed on true being, sees immutable things ordered by reason, imitates them, and becomes orderly and divine as far as human nature allows.

Socrates says the philosopher can fashion human nature, states, and individuals into justice, temperance, and civic virtue, and that no State is happy unless designed by artists who imitate the heavenly pattern.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 18132-18283
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom rule as cure for civic evil
occurrences.basis: The passage says philosophers are lovers of truth and being and that states and individuals will not rest from evil until philosophers rule.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage defends the philosopher as a lover of truth and being, akin to the highest good, and says that until philosophers rule, states and individuals will have no rest from evil.
The speaker says, “the perfect guardian must be a philosopher.”

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 18132-18283
occurrences.motif_label: royal or princely philosopher as possible founder
occurrences.basis: The passage considers whether sons of kings or princes may be philosophers by nature and says one such man with an obedient city could establish the ideal polity.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speakers say that one man with a city obedient to his will would be enough to bring the ideal polity into existence, and that citizens may obey the laws and institutions he imposes.
The speakers ask whether anyone will deny that there may be sons of kings or princes who are philosophers by nature, and whether one such person might escape destruction.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 18285-18436
occurrences.motif_label: quest for highest wisdom
occurrences.basis: The passage centers on the idea of good as the highest knowledge and on the guardian's need to pursue it through a longer course of learning.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “The guardian then... must be required to take the longer circuit, and toil at learning as well as at gymnastics.”
The speaker identifies the idea of good as the highest knowledge and says other knowledge or possessions profit nothing without knowledge of beauty and goodness.
The speaker says one ignorant of the good will not truly know the beautiful and the just, and that a guardian with this knowledge would perfectly order the State.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 18438-18615
occurrences.motif_label: illumination as knowledge
occurrences.basis: Light and sunlight enable sight in the visible world, and the good is analogized as enabling mind and understanding in the intelligible world; the soul understands when turned toward truth and being.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates asks about the senses and argues that sight and color require a third nature before the eye can see or colors can be visible; this third nature is named as light.
“Noble, then, is the bond which links together sight and visibility ... for light is their bond.”

Socrates calls the sun the child of the good, begotten in the good's likeness, and says it stands in the visible world to sight and things of sight as the good stands in the intellectual world to mind and things of mind.

The soul is like the eye: when it rests on what truth and being shine upon, it understands and is radiant with intelligence; when turned toward becoming and perishing, it blinks about with shifting opinion.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 18438-18615
occurrences.motif_label: turning of the soul toward truth
occurrences.basis: The soul is said to perceive and understand when resting on what truth and being illuminate, while it has unstable opinion when turned toward becoming and perishing.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The soul is like the eye: when it rests on what truth and being shine upon, it understands and is radiant with intelligence; when turned toward becoming and perishing, it blinks about with shifting opinion.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1854-1938
occurrences.motif_label: inherited poetic authority reinterpreted for higher truth
occurrences.basis: Plato’s use of Homer is described as drawing higher truth from inherited poetic language, even through fanciful or rhetorically powerful interpretation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Plato is described as appealing to Homer as authority, using Homeric words as vehicles of higher truth, satirizing Homeric interpretation, and resembling modern Scripture citation and Socratic adaptation.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 18617-18744
occurrences.motif_label: supreme good as source of knowledge and being
occurrences.basis: The passage describes the good as imparting truth and knowledge and as the author of knowledge, being, and essence.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The good imparts truth to the known and knowing power to the knower; it is the cause of science and truth and is more beautiful than either, as light and sight are like the sun but are not the sun.
The sun is said to cause visibility, generation, nourishment, and growth; likewise the good is said to cause knowledge, being, and essence while exceeding essence in dignity and power.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 18617-18744
occurrences.motif_label: ascent from hypotheses to a higher principle
occurrences.basis: The higher intellectual subdivision is described as the soul going up beyond hypotheses to a principle above hypotheses.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The lower intellectual subdivision uses figures as images and proceeds hypothetically downward; the higher passes out of hypotheses and goes up to a principle above hypotheses, through ideas themselves.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 18746-18778
occurrences.motif_label: Ascent to a first principle and return through ordered levels
occurrences.basis: Dialectic is described as using hypotheses as steps, soaring beyond them to the first principle of the whole, and descending again through ideas.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Reason, by dialectic, uses hypotheses as steps and points of departure into a world above hypotheses, soars to the first principle of the whole, and descends again through ideas without sensible objects.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 18746-18778
occurrences.motif_label: Fourfold hierarchy of cognition
occurrences.basis: The passage names four faculties in the soul and places them on a scale according to clearness and the truth of their objects.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker assigns four faculties in the soul: reason, understanding, faith or conviction, and perception of shadows, arranged on a scale by clearness and truth.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 18781-18911
occurrences.motif_label: Painful initiation into clearer vision
occurrences.basis: The liberated prisoner undergoes compulsion, pain, disorientation, gradual acclimation, and eventual understanding of the sun's role.

evidence.quote_or_summary: When a prisoner is liberated and compelled to stand, turn, walk, and look toward the light, he suffers pain, is distressed by glare, and is perplexed when shown the objects.
The prisoner grows accustomed to the upper world, first seeing shadows, then reflections in water, then objects, then moon, stars, and the night sky.
Last of all, the prisoner can see the sun itself, not merely its reflection in water, and contemplate it in its own place.
The prisoner reasons that the sun gives seasons and years, guards the visible world, and is in a certain way the cause of what he and his fellows had seen.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 18781-18911
occurrences.motif_label: Shadow-world contrasted with real objects
occurrences.basis: The den presents a contrast between shadows taken as truth and later-seen objects and sunlight treated as clearer vision.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The prisoners see only their own shadows, one another's shadows, and the shadows of the carried objects.
If the prison had an echo, prisoners would think a passer-by's spoken voice came from the passing shadow; the truth for them would be only shadows of images.
When a prisoner is liberated and compelled to stand, turn, walk, and look toward the light, he suffers pain, is distressed by glare, and is perplexed when shown the objects.
Last of all, the prisoner can see the sun itself, not merely its reflection in water, and contemplate it in its own place.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 18781-18911
occurrences.motif_label: Solar source of visible order
occurrences.basis: The sun is described as giving seasons and years and as a cause of the visible things the prisoners had beheld.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The prisoner reasons that the sun gives seasons and years, guards the visible world, and is in a certain way the cause of what he and his fellows had seen.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 18913-19020
occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom as vision of the good
occurrences.basis: The good is described as difficult to see, as the source of reason and truth, and as the object toward which the soul must be turned.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The idea of good appears last and with effort; when seen it is inferred to be author of all beautiful and right things, parent of light and source of reason and truth.
The capacity of learning exists in the soul already; the whole soul must turn from becoming toward being and learn to endure the sight of the good.
Wisdom is said to contain a divine element that remains, becoming useful and profitable by conversion or harmful and useless otherwise.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 18913-19020
occurrences.motif_label: Initiatory turning or conversion of the whole soul
occurrences.basis: Learning is described as a gradual turning of the whole soul toward being and the good, not as the external insertion of knowledge.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker says certain educators are wrong when they claim to put knowledge into the soul as if putting sight into blind eyes.
The capacity of learning exists in the soul already; the whole soul must turn from becoming toward being and learn to endure the sight of the good.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19022-19142
occurrences.motif_label: ascent from darkness below to light and knowledge
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly describes ascent to the good, being brought from darkness to light, and the soul's ascent from below to the true day of being.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The founders must compel the best minds to ascend until they arrive at the good; after they have ascended and seen enough, they must descend again among the prisoners in the den and share their labours and honours.
"brought from darkness to light,—as some are said to have ascended from the world below to the gods"
The process is not the turning over of an oyster-shell but the turning around of a soul from a day little better than night to the true day of being, called the ascent from below and true philosophy.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19022-19142
occurrences.motif_label: return of the enlightened ruler to the dark abode
occurrences.basis: Those who have ascended and seen the good must descend again among the prisoners and learn to see in the dark for the benefit of the State.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The founders must compel the best minds to ascend until they arrive at the good; after they have ascended and seen enough, they must descend again among the prisoners in the den and share their labours and honours.

The philosophers have been educated to be rulers; each must go down to the general underground abode, gain the habit of seeing in the dark, and then understand the images because they have seen the beautiful, just, and good in truth.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19022-19142
occurrences.motif_label: initiation through turning of the soul
occurrences.basis: The process of producing guardians is described as a transformation from near-night to the true day of being, effected by the turning around of the soul.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "brought from darkness to light,—as some are said to have ascended from the world below to the gods"
The process is not the turning over of an oyster-shell but the turning around of a soul from a day little better than night to the true day of being, called the ascent from below and true philosophy.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19022-19142
occurrences.motif_label: reluctant righteous rulership
occurrences.basis: The best-governed State is said to be ruled by those most reluctant to govern, who value philosophy, virtue, and wisdom above political ambition.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The pupils may spend most of their time in heavenly light, but will take office as a stern necessity rather than in the manner of present rulers.
The passage contrasts rulers rich in virtue and wisdom with those poor and hungry for private advantage; lovers of rule become rivals and fight.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19144-19306
occurrences.motif_label: ascent of the soul through knowledge
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly frames the desired study as one that draws the soul from becoming toward being, with arithmetic proposed as a means of turning the soul to reflection.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speakers ask what knowledge would “draw the soul from becoming to being” and add that it should have usefulness in war for young warrior athletes.
Arithmetic is described as a study that leads to reflection and whose true use is “to draw the soul towards being.”

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19144-19306
occurrences.motif_label: perplexing opposites prompting higher inquiry
occurrences.basis: Opposed qualities such as great/small, hard/soft, and light/heavy are presented as sensory intimations that perplex the soul and require explanation by thought.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker distinguishes sense-objects that do not invite thought from those that do, saying that some sensations are adequate while others are untrustworthy and demand inquiry.

The speaker asks whether sight and touch adequately perceive great and small, thick and thin, hard and soft, light and heavy; the soul is said to be perplexed by the same thing being indicated through opposed qualities.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19144-19306
occurrences.motif_label: number as civil and military ordering knowledge
occurrences.basis: Number and calculation are said to be universal elements of education and necessary for war, and the Palamedes example links number to counting ships and arranging army ranks.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker proposes a universal element of education: “number and calculation,” used by all arts and sciences and also by the art of war.
Palamedes is said to declare in tragedy that he invented number, numbered the ships, and arranged the army ranks at Troy; this makes Agamemnon seem unfit as a general if ignorant of number.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19308-19466
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom through disciplined number
occurrences.basis: Arithmetic and calculation lead the mind toward truth, compel use of pure intelligence, and are prescribed for the best natures.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Arithmetic and calculation deal with number and lead the mind toward truth; the man of war needs number to array troops, and the philosopher must rise out of the sea of change and grasp true being; the guardian is both warrior and philosopher.

Legislation should prescribe arithmetic for the principal men of the State, who must study numbers with the mind only, not for trade; arithmetic elevates the soul, reasons about abstract number, preserves indivisible unity, and requires pure intelligence for pure truth.
Natural calculators are said to be quick at other knowledge, and arithmetic training makes even dull learners quicker; arithmetic is difficult and should be taught to the best natures.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1940-1994
occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom as moral discernment
occurrences.basis: The passage emphasizes reason, truth, beauty, virtue, and knowledge of character, including the claim that virtue may give insight into vice.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says Plato’s true art is not fanciful and imitative, but simple, ideal, and expressive of the highest moral energy.
Living among noble plastic art or listening to noble strains is described as the best influence for youth, forming taste and a feeling for truth and beauty.
Although poets are to be expelled, art is recognized as another aspect of reason, compared with love in the Symposium, and acts through habit in preliminary education.
The passage questions the reasoning and suggests that intuition or directness in virtue may be consistent with abhorring evil and may give insight into vice.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19468-19613
occurrences.motif_label: turning of the soul toward truth
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly describes mathematical study as turning the soul’s gaze toward the good, eternal being, and truth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Geometry is tested by whether it aids the “vision of the idea of good” and turns the soul’s gaze toward “the full perfection of being.”
Socrates says geometricians speak of practical operations, but knowledge is the object of geometry, and that knowledge concerns the eternal rather than the transient.
Geometry will “draw the soul towards truth,” create philosophy, and “raise up” what has fallen down.
Astronomy is proposed; Socrates says there is an “eye of the soul” that can be “purified and re-illumined” and by which truth is seen.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19468-19613
occurrences.motif_label: inner vision restored by discipline
occurrences.basis: Socrates describes an eye of the soul that is lost and dimmed by other pursuits but purified and re-illumined by these studies.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Astronomy is proposed; Socrates says there is an “eye of the soul” that can be “purified and re-illumined” and by which truth is seen.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19468-19613
occurrences.motif_label: ordered initiation through sciences
occurrences.basis: The dialogue lays out a sequence of studies—geometry, solid geometry, and astronomy—through which learners are guided toward higher knowledge.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says the city’s inhabitants should learn geometry, which also brings military advantages and quickness of apprehension.
Socrates corrects the order of studies: plane geometry should be followed by solid geometry before astronomy; he says neglected studies need state support, directors, and earnest search.
The interlocutor says astronomy “compels the soul to look upwards” and leads from “this world to another.”

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19615-19736
occurrences.motif_label: ascent from sensory appearance to intelligible knowledge
occurrences.basis: The passage contrasts looking down toward sensory particulars with the soul looking upward toward being, the unseen, reason, intelligence, true number, and the beautiful and good.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Knowledge of being and the unseen makes the soul look upward; sensory particulars, whether found in the heavens, ground, water, or land, are not science.
The visible starry heaven is beautiful but inferior to true motions, true number, and true figure, which are apprehended by reason and intelligence, not sight.
In astronomy, as in geometry, one should employ problems and leave the visible heavens alone in order to make reason useful.
The inquiry is useful if sought with a view to the beautiful and good, but useless if pursued otherwise.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19615-19736
occurrences.motif_label: visible cosmos as pattern for higher order
occurrences.basis: The starry heavens are described as beautiful visible patterns that should prompt higher reasoning rather than be treated as final truth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The visible starry heaven is beautiful but inferior to true motions, true number, and true figure, which are apprehended by reason and intelligence, not sight.

The spangled heavens should be used as a pattern for higher knowledge, like finely wrought figures or pictures by Daedalus or another great artist, not as the place to find true mathematical proportions.
In astronomy, as in geometry, one should employ problems and leave the visible heavens alone in order to make reason useful.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19615-19736
occurrences.motif_label: harmony of number beyond heard sound
occurrences.basis: The passage criticizes sensory study of musical sounds and directs inquiry toward natural harmonies of number and the beautiful and good.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Teachers of harmony compare sounds and consonances that are only heard, and their labor is said to be vain, like that of astronomers who fall short of the higher object.
Some people put their ears beside strings, dispute about intermediate notes and intervals, and set their ears before their understanding.
The Pythagoreans investigate numbers of heard harmonies but do not reach problems or natural harmonies of number, nor why some numbers are harmonious and others not.
The inquiry is useful if sought with a view to the beautiful and good, but useless if pursued otherwise.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19615-19736
occurrences.motif_label: duality of sight and hearing as parallel disciplines
occurrences.basis: Astronomy and harmony are compared as sister sciences, one related to eyes and stars, the other to ears and harmonious motions.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The second science is related to ears as the first is to eyes; eyes look at stars, ears hear harmonious motions, and these are called sister sciences by the Pythagoreans.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19738-19854
occurrences.motif_label: Quest for wisdom through disciplined knowledge
occurrences.basis: Dialectic is presented as the culmination of prior studies and as the method that reaches the first principle and the absolute good.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Prior studies are valuable when connected with one another; Socrates says they are only a prelude to the actual strain to be learned.
Dialectic begins by reason alone and, without sense, perseveres until reaching perception of the absolute good, at the end of the intellectual world as sight reaches the end of the visible.
Glaucon asks about the nature, divisions, and paths of dialectic; Socrates says dialectic alone can reveal the truth in question, and only to a disciple of the previous sciences.
Mathematical sciences are said to dream about being while hypotheses remain unexamined; dialectic goes to the first principle, removes hypotheses, and lifts the eye of the soul upward from a slough.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19738-19854
occurrences.motif_label: Inner faculty lifted from mire to vision
occurrences.basis: The eye of the soul is described as buried in a slough and lifted upward by dialectic.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Mathematical sciences are said to dream about being while hypotheses remain unexamined; dialectic goes to the first principle, removes hypotheses, and lifts the eye of the soul upward from a slough.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19856-19996
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom through dialectical knowledge of the good
occurrences.basis: The passage centers on dialectic, knowledge of essences, rational definition of the good, and truth rather than opinion as the highest form of understanding.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The dialectician is described as one who 'attains a conception of the essence of each thing.'

Knowledge of the good requires rational definition and answering objections by truth; without it one apprehends only a shadow by opinion, dreams and slumbers in life, and then arrives at the world below.
Dialectic is called 'the coping-stone of the sciences' and no other science can be placed higher.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1996-2074
occurrences.motif_label: myth as veiled instruction
occurrences.basis: The passage says mythology supplies a figure by which a lesson may be taught and lets Plato introduce new principles indirectly.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Mythology supplies a figure for teaching the lesson and lets Plato touch lightly on new principles without details.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1996-2074
occurrences.motif_label: sacred numerical harmony linking sense and ideas
occurrences.basis: The passage says intervals of sound and number are sacred, rise above sense, and connect with the world of ideas.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Plato is said to have a Pythagorean reverence for numbers and numerical proportion.
Intervals of sound and number are called sacred things with their own law; they rise above sense and connect with the world of ideas.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19998-20152
occurrences.motif_label: Quest for wisdom through dialectic
occurrences.basis: Preparatory sciences lead toward dialectic, which tests whether candidates can attain absolute being with truth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Calculation, geometry, and other instruction preparatory to dialectic should be presented in childhood without forcing the education system.
After necessary gymnastics, selected twenty-year-olds are promoted and their sciences are brought together so they can see their relation to each other and to true being.
At thirty, the most comprehensive and steadfast candidates are selected and tested by dialectic to learn who can give up sight and the other senses and attain absolute being with truth.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19998-20152
occurrences.motif_label: Dangerous knowledge that unsettles inherited order
occurrences.basis: Dialectic is described as requiring great caution because refutation can dissolve inherited beliefs about justice and honour before truth is found, producing lawlessness.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker says "great caution is required" because students of dialectic are "filled with lawlessness."
When questioning asks what is fair or honourable, a person answers as the legislator taught, but many arguments refute his words and unsettle valued notions.
When a person no longer regards inherited notions as honourable and does not discover the true, he is expected to pursue the life that flatters his desires.
"from being a keeper of the law he is converted into a breaker of it"
Because the condition is natural and pitiable, every care must be taken in introducing thirty-year-old citizens to dialectic.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 20154-20256
occurrences.motif_label: ascent of vision toward illuminating truth
occurrences.basis: The qualified rulers raise the eye of the soul to the universal light and behold the absolute good as the governing pattern.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At fifty, those who survive and distinguish themselves must 'raise the eye of the soul' to the universal light and behold the absolute good.
The absolute good is the pattern for ordering the State, individual lives, and the rulers’ remaining lives.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 20154-20256
occurrences.motif_label: return from contemplation to rule for the community
occurrences.basis: Those who behold the good must still toil at politics and rule for the public good as a duty.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The absolute good is the pattern for ordering the State, individual lives, and the rulers’ remaining lives.
The rulers make philosophy their chief pursuit but also engage in politics and rule for the public good as duty.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 20154-20256
occurrences.motif_label: philosopher-ruler establishes just order
occurrences.basis: True philosopher kings make the constitution possible, despise worldly honors, esteem right, serve justice, and set the city in order.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The State is possible when true philosopher kings arise, despise worldly honors, esteem right, regard justice as necessary, and set their city in order.
The rulers send inhabitants older than ten into the country, take the children, and train them in the rulers’ habits and laws so the State may attain happiness.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII.; lines 20259-20385
occurrences.motif_label: wise rulers over the ideal community
occurrences.basis: The perfect State is said to have the best philosophers and bravest warriors as kings.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates asks Glaucon to affirm that in the perfect State wives, children, education, war and peace pursuits are common, and the best philosophers and bravest warriors are kings.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII.; lines 20387-20491
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom failing before hidden generative law
occurrences.basis: The rulers' wisdom and education do not discover the laws regulating human fecundity and sterility.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Fertility and sterility of soul and body occur according to completed circular periods, but the rulers' wisdom and education will not attain knowledge of human fecundity and sterility.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII.; lines 20387-20491
occurrences.motif_label: turn from philosopher-rule to warrior-rule
occurrences.basis: The later state fears admitting philosophers to power and turns toward passionate characters fitted for war, stratagems, and everlasting wars.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The later state fears admitting philosophers to power, turns to passionate characters fitted for war rather than peace, values military stratagems, and wages everlasting wars.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII.; lines 20493-20627
occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom as guardian of virtue
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly identifies philosophy tempered with music as the best guardian and only saviour of virtue throughout life.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “Philosophy... tempered with music... is the only saviour of his virtue throughout life.”

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 2076-2139
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom as self-command and harmonizing reason with desire
occurrences.basis: The passage treats the rightful superiority of the restraining principle, the coordination of reason and desire, and care over time as a form of responsible self-rule.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage asks how far mind can control body, whether they are antagonistic or harmonious, describes higher and lower principles that may take up arms or reconcile, and says the body may become the mind’s ally or instrument.
One tendency says, ‘Drink’; another says, ‘Do not drink; it is not good for you,’ followed by remarks on rightful superiority, responsibility for health, and limited human freedom.
