occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR / CHAPTER V: TYR; lines 3369-3493
occurrences.motif_label: human sacrifice to a war deity
occurrences.basis: The passage says priests offered human sacrifices on Tyr's altars, using prisoners of war as victims.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says priests called Druids or Godi made human sacrifices to Tyr on stone altars called dolmens, and that Tyr's rune was engraved on sword blades to obtain victory.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR / CHAPTER V: TYR; lines 3614-3719
occurrences.motif_label: Bodily pledge enabling containment
occurrences.basis: Fenris requires a god’s hand in his mouth as a pledge before accepting the bond; Tyr gives the pledge and loses the hand once Fenris is captive.

evidence.quote_or_summary: With Gleipnir, the gods go with Fenris to Lyngvi in Lake Amsvartnir; Fenris mistrusts the slight bond and requires an Æsir to put a hand in his mouth as a good-faith pledge.
All the gods draw back except Tyr, who places his hand in Fenris’s jaws; the gods bind Fenris with Gleipnir, and when he cannot escape, he bites off Tyr’s hand at the wrist.
Quoted Eddic exchange: Loki says Fenris took Tyr’s right hand; Tyr replies, “I of a hand am wanting,” and says the wolf must remain in bonds until the gods’ destruction.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XX / BOOK XXI / BOOK XXII / BOOK XXIII; lines 10213-10296
occurrences.motif_label: prophetic post-return journey to appease the sea god
occurrences.basis: Teiresias directs Ulysses, after return, to carry an oar inland, plant it, sacrifice to Neptune, return home, and honor the gods.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses tells Penelope that their troubles are not over and that Teiresias prophesied a long, difficult task when Ulysses went down into Hades to ask about his return.

Ulysses reports that Teiresias ordered him to travel with an oar to a country whose people have never heard of the sea, ships, salt, or oars, and where a wayfarer will ask if the oar is a winnowing shovel.

The prophecy instructs Ulysses to fix the oar in the ground, sacrifice a ram, bull, and boar to Neptune, return home, offer hecatombs to all the gods, and later die gently from the sea in old age while blessed by his people.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XXI / BOOK XXII / BOOK XXIII / BOOK XXIV; lines 10351-10444
occurrences.motif_label: Heroic funeral with cremation, sacrifice, and lament
occurrences.basis: Achilles’ funeral includes extended mourning, divine lamenters, cremation, animal slaughter, offerings, bone collection, and burial.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The daughters of the old man of the sea and the nine Muses lament Achilles; mortals and immortals mourn him for seventeen days and nights.
On the eighteenth day Achilles is cremated; sheep and oxen are slain, he is burned with divine raiment, resins, and honey, and warriors clash armour around the pyre.
After the flames, Achilles’ bones are gathered with ointments and wine; Thetis brings a golden vase, gift of Bacchus and work of Vulcan, in which Achilles’ bones are mingled with Patroclus’.

The Argives build a noble tomb over the Hellespont; Thetis offers divine prizes for contests, and Agamemnon says Achilles’ fame and name endure, while his own return ended in destruction by Aegisthus and his wife.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XXII / BOOK XXIII / BOOK XXIV / FOOTNOTES:; lines 10818-10944
occurrences.motif_label: sacrificial meal preparation sequence
occurrences.basis: The note describes the sequence of eating inner organs first while other meat cooked and discusses thigh bones used in cooking.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The note says inner parts were eaten first while bone meat cooked and suggests thigh bones may have functioned like a gridiron.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XXII / BOOK XXIII / BOOK XXIV / FOOTNOTES:; lines 10946-11057
occurrences.motif_label: heifer slaughter in epic household context
occurrences.basis: The note emphasizes the slaughter of a heifer and the inclusion of Nestor's wife and daughter in enjoying it.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The note says the writer interrupts an Iliadic passage to dwell on the slaughter of a heifer and to let Nestor's wife and daughter enjoy it.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I / BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS.; lines 1136-1230
occurrences.motif_label: ritual sacrifice and feast before inquiry
occurrences.basis: The Pylians sacrifice bulls to Neptune, share meat and wine, pray, and only after the meal does Nestor ask the strangers' identity.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Pylians gather on the seashore to sacrifice black bulls to Neptune; nine guilds of five hundred men each have nine bulls per guild, eating inward meats and burning thigh bones on embers.
Pisistratus gives the strangers inward meats, pours wine into a golden cup, and hands it first to Minerva.
Pisistratus asks Minerva to pray to Neptune and make a drink offering, then pass the cup to her companion; he says precedence is given to her as the older guest.
Minerva prays to Neptune to grant the prayers, bless Nestor and his sons, reward the Pylians for the hecatomb, and grant success to Telemachus and herself.
Minerva passes the cup to Telemachus, who prays likewise; the roasted meat is served and all eat and drink.
After dinner Nestor asks the strangers who they are, from what port they sailed, and whether they are traders or sea rovers.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I / BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS.; lines 1232-1327
occurrences.motif_label: sacrifice to appease or thank a deity
occurrences.basis: Agamemnon proposes hecatombs to appease Minerva, and Nestor's group offers sacrifices to Neptune after receiving help on the voyage.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At a sunset meeting, Menelaus wanted to sail home, while Agamemnon wanted to wait and offer hecatombs to appease Minerva; the Achaeans split in opinion.
A fair wind gives quick passage to Geraestus, where many sacrifices are offered to Neptune; Diomed reaches Argos, while Nestor continues to Pylos with favorable wind.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I / BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS.; lines 1329-1422
occurrences.motif_label: ritual offering to gods after successful or festival action
occurrences.basis: Aegisthus offers many burnt sacrifices after his success, and Minerva later calls for victims' tongues and wine for drink-offerings to Neptune and the immortals.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After the bard's removal, Clytemnestra went willingly to Aegisthus' house; Aegisthus made burnt sacrifices and decorated temples with tapestries and gilding.
At sunset Minerva orders the victims' tongues cut and wine mixed for drink-offerings to Neptune and the other immortals before bed.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I / BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS.; lines 1424-1514
occurrences.motif_label: Sacrifice to a deity
occurrences.basis: Nestor vows and begins preparing a heifer sacrifice for Minerva, including gilding the horns and ritual handling of water, barley, and fire.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva flies away as an eagle; Nestor marvels, recognizes Jove's daughter, prays for favor upon himself and household, and vows an unyoked heifer with gilded horns.
Nestor orders preparations to propitiate Minerva: bring a heifer, invite the crew, fetch Laerceus the goldsmith, prepare dinner, seats, logs for a burnt offering, and clear spring water.

The heifer, crew, and goldsmith arrive; the smith gilds the horns; sons assist with water, barley, axe, and bucket; Nestor washes, sprinkles barley, prays, and puts a lock from the heifer's head on the fire.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I / BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS.; lines 1516-1558
occurrences.motif_label: ritual animal sacrifice before communal meal
occurrences.basis: The passage presents prayer, barley sprinkling, killing of a heifer, preparation of thigh bones with fat, burning on a wood fire, wine poured over the offering, and subsequent eating.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After prayer and barley sprinkling, Thrasymedes strikes the heifer and cuts through tendons at the base of her neck.
The heifer's head is lifted, Pisistratus cuts its throat, and after it bleeds and dies, it is cut up.
The thigh bones are wrapped in fat with raw meat on top; Nestor places them on the wood fire and pours wine over them while young men stand by with five-pronged spits.
After the thighs are burned and inward meats tasted, the remaining meat is cut, placed on spits, and toasted over the fire.
The meat is served, the company eats dinner, and henchmen pour wine in golden cups.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS. / BOOK IV; lines 1849-1948
occurrences.motif_label: Ritual dues and divine obstruction
occurrences.basis: The speaker says the gods detained him because his hecatombs had not given them full satisfaction and the gods are strict about their dues.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker says the gods detained him in Egypt because his hecatombs had not given them full satisfaction and the gods are strict about their dues.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: The Odyssey / PREFACE TO FIRST EDITION; lines 187-272
occurrences.motif_label: sacrifice and divine favor questioned
occurrences.basis: Poseidon receives a hecatomb, and Athene reminds Zeus of Odysseus' sacrifices in Trojan land while questioning Zeus' anger.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Poseidon has gone to the distant Ethiopians to receive a hecatomb of bulls and rams and feast, while the other gods gather in Zeus' halls.
Athene asks whether Odysseus made free offerings of sacrifice to Zeus by the Argive ships in Trojan land and asks why Zeus was angry with him.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS. / BOOK IV; lines 1950-2039
occurrences.motif_label: sacrifice required before successful return
occurrences.basis: Menelaus cannot finish his voyage until he returns to Egypt and offers holy hecatombs to the gods.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Proteus says Menelaus must sacrifice to Jove and the gods, return to Egypt, and offer holy hecatombs before the gods will let him finish his voyage.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS. / BOOK IV; lines 2041-2133
occurrences.motif_label: sacrifice to appease divine anger
occurrences.basis: Menelaus offers hecatombs after returning to Egypt, explicitly to appease heaven's anger before receiving a fair wind home.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker offers sufficient hecatombs to appease heaven's anger, raises a barrow for Agamemnon's memory, and then receives a fair wind from the gods for a quick passage home.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS. / BOOK IV; lines 2135-2239
occurrences.motif_label: prayer invoking prior sacrifice for divine aid
occurrences.basis: Penelope prays to Minerva to remember Ulysses' past burned offerings and save Telemachus; the goddess hears the prayer.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Penelope stops crying, washes, changes clothes, goes upstairs with the maids, places bruised barley in a basket, and begins praying to Minerva.
Penelope asks Minerva to remember if Ulysses “burned you fat thigh bones of sheep or heifer” and to save her son from the suitors.
Penelope cries aloud and the goddess hears her prayer.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS. / BOOK VIII / BOOK IX; lines 3996-4072
occurrences.motif_label: Ritual offering before danger
occurrences.basis: The Achaeans offer some of the Cyclops' cheeses in sacrifice before the Cyclops returns.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Achaeans light a fire, sacrifice some cheeses, eat others, and wait in the cave for the Cyclops.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS. / BOOK VIII / BOOK IX; lines 4270-4293
occurrences.motif_label: sacrifice not accepted by deity
occurrences.basis: Ulysses burns the ram's thigh bones to Jove, but Jove does not heed the sacrifice and thinks of destroying the ships and comrades.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses receives the ram as an extra share, sacrifices it on the sea shore, burns its thigh bones to Jove, but Jove does not heed the sacrifice and thinks of destroying the ships and comrades.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VIII / BOOK IX / BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE.; lines 4680-4781
occurrences.motif_label: offerings and blood sacrifice to summon or manage the dead
occurrences.basis: Circe prescribes libations, prayers, promised sacrifices, animal sacrifice, and guarding the blood until Teiresias answers.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Circe instructs Ulysses to dig a cubit-sized trench, pour libations of honey-milk, wine, and water with barley, pray to the ghosts, and promise sacrifices including a black sheep for Teiresias.
Circe instructs sacrifice of a ram and black ewe, prayers to Hades and Proserpine, and guarding the blood with a drawn sword until Teiresias comes and tells Ulysses how to reach home.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE. / BOOK XI / THE VISIT TO THE DEAD.88; lines 4783-4874
occurrences.motif_label: necromantic blood rite for prophetic consultation
occurrences.basis: Ulysses offers libations, sacrifices sheep, controls the blood, and allows Teiresias to drink so that he can answer questions truly.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Perimedes and Eurylochus hold the victims while Ulysses digs a cubit-square trench and makes drink-offerings to the dead with honey and milk, wine, water, and barley meal.
Ulysses cuts the throats of two sheep so blood runs into the trench, and many ghosts from Erebus gather with screaming around it.
Ulysses orders the men to flay and burn the sheep and pray to Hades and Proserpine, while he sits with sword drawn to keep the ghosts from the blood until Teiresias answers.
The ghost of Theban Teiresias appears with a golden sceptre, recognizes Ulysses, asks him to withdraw sword and let him drink blood, then begins prophecy after drinking.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE. / BOOK XI / THE VISIT TO THE DEAD.88; lines 4783-4874
occurrences.motif_label: unburied dead demanding funeral rites
occurrences.basis: Elpenor explains that his body is unburied and asks Ulysses to burn him with his armour, build a sea-shore barrow, and plant his oar over the grave.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Elpenor's ghost appears first; he says he was left unburied and died after drunkenly falling from the roof of Circe's house and breaking his neck.
Elpenor asks Ulysses not to leave him unburied, but to burn him with his armour, build a sea-shore barrow, and plant his rowing oar over the grave; Ulysses agrees.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XI / THE VISIT TO THE DEAD.88 / BOOK XII / THE SIRENS, SCYLLA AND CHARYBDIS, THE CATTLE OF THE SUN.; lines 5610-5710
occurrences.motif_label: Improper or desperate sacrifice under hunger
occurrences.basis: The crew kills the cattle and performs sacrificial actions with substitute materials because they lack barley and wine.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Eurylochus tells the starving comrades that famine is worst, proposes driving in the best cows and sacrificing them, and suggests later building a temple to the sun-god if they reach Ithaca.
The men approve, drive in the best cattle, pray, substitute young oak-shoots for barley, kill the cows, prepare thigh bones and meat, and pour water because they lack wine.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XII / THE SIRENS, SCYLLA AND CHARYBDIS, THE CATTLE OF THE SUN. / BOOK XIII / ULYSSES LEAVES SCHERIA AND RETURNS TO ITHACA.; lines 5712-5817
occurrences.motif_label: Sacrifice before departure
occurrences.basis: Alcinous sacrifices a bull to Jove before the departure sequence and feast.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At dawn the Phaeacians bring cauldrons to the ship, Alcinous checks the stowage, and he sacrifices a bull in honor of Jove.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XII / THE SIRENS, SCYLLA AND CHARYBDIS, THE CATTLE OF THE SUN. / BOOK XIII / ULYSSES LEAVES SCHERIA AND RETURNS TO ITHACA.; lines 5819-5919
occurrences.motif_label: sacrifice to avert divine wrath
occurrences.basis: Alcinous orders twelve picked bulls sacrificed to Neptune so that he may show mercy and not bury the city under the mountain.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Phaeacians wonder who rooted the ship in the sea; Alcinous recalls his father's prophecy of Neptune's anger, a wrecked escort ship, and a city buried under a mountain, then orders an end to escorts and sacrifice of twelve bulls; the people fear and pray at Neptune's altar.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XIII / ULYSSES LEAVES SCHERIA AND RETURNS TO ITHACA. / BOOK XIV / ULYSSES IN THE HUT WITH EUMAEUS.; lines 6096-6194
occurrences.motif_label: sacrificial meal for a guest
occurrences.basis: Eumaeus selects two young pigs, sacrifices, cooks, and serves them, while wine and barley meal accompany the meal.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Eumaeus sacrifices two young pigs, prepares and cooks them, serves them to Ulysses, who sprinkles barley meal, and mixes wine in an ivy-wood bowl.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XIII / ULYSSES LEAVES SCHERIA AND RETURNS TO ITHACA. / BOOK XIV / ULYSSES IN THE HUT WITH EUMAEUS.; lines 6290-6372
occurrences.motif_label: sacrifice before voyage
occurrences.basis: Before sailing from Crete, the speaker provides victims for sacrifice to the gods and for the men’s feasting.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker says he rose among the Cretans, led ships to Troy with Idomeneus, fought nine years, sacked Priam’s city, returned home briefly, then fitted out nine ships, sacrificed, feasted, and sailed from Crete toward Egypt.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XIII / ULYSSES LEAVES SCHERIA AND RETURNS TO ITHACA. / BOOK XIV / ULYSSES IN THE HUT WITH EUMAEUS.; lines 6374-6464
occurrences.motif_label: animal sacrifice preceding communal meal
occurrences.basis: Eumaeus orders a pig sacrificed for the stranger, offers bristles and portions to divine recipients, prays, and distributes roasted meat.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The swineherds bring in pigs for the night; Eumaeus orders the best pig sacrificed for the stranger, cuts firewood, has a five-year-old boar brought to the altar, throws facial bristles into the fire, and prays for Ulysses' return.

The pig is stunned, slaughtered, singed, cut up, prepared with fat and barley meal, roasted, divided into seven portions, with one set apart for Mercury and the nymphs, and Ulysses receives an honored loin portion.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XIII / ULYSSES LEAVES SCHERIA AND RETURNS TO ITHACA. / BOOK XIV / ULYSSES IN THE HUT WITH EUMAEUS.; lines 6466-6544
occurrences.motif_label: Ritual offering before communal meal
occurrences.basis: The passage describes a burnt sacrifice and drink-offering to the immortal gods before eating and drinking.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A first piece is offered as burnt sacrifice to the immortal gods; a drink-offering follows; Mesaulius brings bread, the group eats and drinks, and the remainder is removed before bed.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: ULYSSES LEAVES SCHERIA AND RETURNS TO ITHACA. / BOOK XIV / ULYSSES IN THE HUT WITH EUMAEUS. / BOOK XV; lines 6650-6731
occurrences.motif_label: drink-offering before departure
occurrences.basis: Menelaus brings a golden goblet of wine so that a drink-offering may be made before Telemachus and Pisistratus set out.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus and Pisistratus yoke the horses; Menelaus follows with a golden goblet of wine for a drink-offering and asks them to tell Nestor of his treatment of them.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XV / BOOK XVI / ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII; lines 7528-7613
occurrences.motif_label: Sacrifice before meal and wayfarers' altar
occurrences.basis: The suitors sacrifice animals before dinner, and the fountain has an altar to the nymphs where wayfarers used to sacrifice.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Inside the house, the suitors lay down their cloaks and sacrifice fat sheep, goats, pigs, and a heifer to prepare for their meal.

Near the city, they reach the citizens' fountain made by Ithacus, Neritus, and Polyctor, circled by water-loving poplars, fed by clear cold water from a high rock, with an altar to the nymphs above it.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XV / BOOK XVI / ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII; lines 7925-7968
occurrences.motif_label: preparation for sacrifice
occurrences.basis: Telemachus instructs Eumaeus to return in the morning with victims to be sacrificed for the day.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus tells Eumaeus to go home after dinner and return in the morning with victims to sacrifice for the day, leaving the rest to heaven and himself.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XVII / BOOK XVIII / BOOK XIX / BOOK XX; lines 9045-9146
occurrences.motif_label: Sacrifice and communal feast before escalating conflict
occurrences.basis: The suitors sacrifice animals, distribute portions, mix wine, and feast before further insolent action occurs.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The suitors enter, sacrifice sheep, goats, pigs, and a heifer, cook the meats, mix wine, and distribute bread and cups.
After Antinous responds to Telemachus, Minerva keeps the suitors insolent so that Ulysses will become more bitter; Ctesippus is introduced as a wealthy suitor courting Ulysses’ wife.
Ctesippus calls his action a present for the stranger, throws a heifer’s foot at Ulysses, and misses when Ulysses turns aside; the object hits the wall.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XVII / BOOK XVIII / BOOK XIX / BOOK XX; lines 9148-9215
occurrences.motif_label: fatal feast before destruction
occurrences.basis: The suitors' meal is linked with blood and foreboding, and the coming supper is called gruesome, to be laid before them by a goddess and brave man because they brought doom on themselves.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “Minerva now made the suitors fall to laughing immoderately, and set their wits wandering”; their laughter is forced, their meat is smeared with blood, their eyes fill with tears, and their hearts are heavy with forebodings.

The dinner had been abundant after many sacrifices, but the coming supper is described as gruesome, to be laid before the suitors by a goddess and a brave man because they had brought doom on themselves.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XVIII / BOOK XIX / BOOK XX / BOOK XXI; lines 9416-9503
occurrences.motif_label: offering before dangerous or decisive action
occurrences.basis: The suitors make drink-offerings and Antinous proposes sacrificing goat thigh bones to Apollo before resuming the bow trial.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Antinous says it is Apollo's feast, advises putting aside the bow, calls for drink-offerings, and proposes goat thigh bones for Apollo before trying the bow again.
Servants wash guests' hands, pages mix wine and water, drink-offerings are made, and Ulysses craftily begins to speak.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 10635-10722
occurrences.motif_label: Propitiating gods through sacrifice and prayer
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly reports claims that sacrifices, prayers, libations, odours of fat, and offerings can avert divine wrath, turn gods, or allow unjust people to avoid punishment.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Mendicant prophets visit rich men's doors, claim divine power to atone for sins by sacrifices or charms, and promise to harm enemies through magic arts and incantations that bind heaven.
Poets are invoked: Hesiod is cited for the easy path of vice and toil before virtue, and Homer for gods being turned by prayers, sacrifices, entreaties, libations, and the odour of fat.

The argument considers whether gods can be deceived or compelled, then says poetic tradition claims gods may be influenced by sacrifices, soothing entreaties, and offerings; unjust people could pray and sacrifice to avoid punishment.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 11286-11457
occurrences.motif_label: restricted sacred knowledge in mystery setting
occurrences.basis: Objectionable stories of gods are to be buried in silence or, if necessary, heard only by a chosen few in a mystery accompanied by an extraordinary sacrificial victim.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage names Hesiod's stories of Uranus, Cronus, and the suffering Cronus's son inflicted on him, and says such stories should be silenced or restricted to a chosen few in a mystery with an extraordinary victim rather than a common Eleusinian pig.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III.; lines 12131-12273
occurrences.motif_label: Funerary violence and offering at a hero's pyre
occurrences.basis: The rejected Achilles tale includes an offering of hair to dead Patroclus and slaughter of captives at the pyre.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker rejects allegations that Achilles challenged a river-god, offered dedicated hair to dead Patroclus, dragged Hector around Patroclus' tomb, and slaughtered captives at the pyre; Achilles is described as Cheiron's pupil, son of a goddess and Peleus, and descended from Zeus.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1336-1415
occurrences.motif_label: Restricted tale disclosed only through mystery and sacrifice
occurrences.basis: Improper divine tales are said, if spoken at all, to belong in a mystery after sacrifice rather than in ordinary instruction of the young.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Homer and Hesiod are criticized for improper divine stories about Uranus and Saturn, Zeus, Hephaestus, divine strife, and family violence; such stories may have mystical interpretation but youth cannot understand allegory.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV.; lines 14071-14242
occurrences.motif_label: Sacrificial and temple institution
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly names the institution of temples and sacrifices and the service of gods, demigods, and heroes as sacred matters to be ordered.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage assigns to Apollo the institution of temples and sacrifices, service of gods, demigods, and heroes, repositories of the dead, and rites for propitiating inhabitants of the world below.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1417-1481
occurrences.motif_label: sacrifice before mysteries
occurrences.basis: The passage mentions offering an almost unprocurable victim when impure mysteries are to be celebrated.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage lists humorous but serious examples: Glaucon's disappointment at the 'city of pigs,' the guardian illustrated by the dog, an almost unprocurable victim for impure mysteries, and the behavior of Zeus to his father and Hephaestus to his mother.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1483-1541
occurrences.motif_label: offering to a healing deity
occurrences.basis: The philosopher is described as not refusing to offer a cock to Aesculapius.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The philosopher's religion is described as dwelling in ideas while still offering a cock to Aesculapius and praying at sunrise.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1543-1614
occurrences.motif_label: funeral cruelty at the pyre
occurrences.basis: Achilles is said to drag Hector's body and slay captives at the pyre, a combination characterized as cruelty.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Achilles's curse of Apollo, insolence to Scamander, dedication of hair to Patroclus despite prior dedication to Spercheius, dragging Hector's body, and slaying captives at the pyre are condemned as meanness and cruelty.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1854-1938
occurrences.motif_label: sacrifice before guarded settlement
occurrences.basis: The guardians are directed to sacrifice and set up tents in a defensible high place.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The earthborn men go out under rulers, pitch camp in a high safe place, sacrifice, set up tents, and are to be soldiers, watchdogs, and guardians rather than shopkeepers; luxury and avarice would make them wolves and tyrants.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII.; lines 21563-21745
occurrences.motif_label: human consumption leading to wolf transformation
occurrences.basis: The cited Arcadian tale states that tasting human entrails mixed with sacrificial entrails makes the eater destined to become a wolf.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A tale of the Arcadian temple of Lycaean Zeus says that one who tastes a human victim's entrails mixed with other victims' entrails is destined to become a wolf.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 4013-4089
occurrences.motif_label: blessed posthumous destination and cultic honors
occurrences.basis: The ruler departs in peace to the islands of the blest and receives sacrifices and oracle-approved worship.

evidence.quote_or_summary: When his time comes, he departs in peace to the islands of the blest, is honored with sacrifices, and receives worship approved by the Pythian oracle.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 415-470
occurrences.motif_label: sacrifice by an elder householder
occurrences.basis: Cephalus, the patriarch of the house, is described as engaged in offering a sacrifice.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Cephalus is called the patriarch of the house, engaged in offering sacrifice, almost done with life, at peace, and drawing nearer to the world below.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 4623-4685
occurrences.motif_label: Human-to-wolf transformation through eating human flesh
occurrences.basis: The cited fable of Zeus Lycaeus says that tasting human flesh mixed with victims’ flesh turns a person into a wolf.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The people nurse a protector into greatness; from this root the tree of tyranny springs. The Lycaean fable says tasting human flesh among victims turns one into a wolf, and the protector who tastes human blood becomes a wolf, that is, a tyrant.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 668-755
occurrences.motif_label: sacrifice as ritual frame for philosophical discussion
occurrences.basis: Cephalus is explicitly crowned for sacrifice and later leaves the argument to attend to sacrifices, making sacrificial activity part of the narrative frame.

evidence.quote_or_summary: They return to the house of Cephalus, who is in extreme old age, seated on a cushion, crowned for sacrifice, and asks Socrates to visit more often because he is too old to go out.
Polemarchus invokes Simonides for the definition; Cephalus retires to attend sacrifices, and Socrates jokes that the argument has passed to Polemarchus as heir.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS. / THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I.; lines 8772-8893
occurrences.motif_label: sacrifice as ritual duty
occurrences.basis: Cephalus leaves the conversation because he must look after sacrifices.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Cephalus says he must go look after the sacrifices, hands the argument to Polemarchus and the company, and goes away laughing.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 1320-1353
occurrences.motif_label: death willingly accepted for the beloved
occurrences.basis: The passage states that Love makes people dare to die for the beloved, with Alcestis and Achilles as examples.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “Love will make men dare to die for their beloved--love alone; and women as well as men.”
Alcestis, daughter of Pelias, is willing to lay down her life on behalf of her husband when no one else will.
Achilles gives his life to avenge his friend Patroclus after Patroclus is dead.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 1610-1659
occurrences.motif_label: Ritual communion between gods and humans
occurrences.basis: Sacrifice and divination are explicitly described as communion between gods and men and as means to preserve good love and heal evil love.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sacrifices and divination are described as the art of communion between gods and men; divination is called “the peacemaker of gods and men.”

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 2102-2198
occurrences.motif_label: sacrifice before plague and delayed disease
occurrences.basis: The Athenians are said to have offered sacrifice before the plague, and Diotima is credited with delaying the disease ten years.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says he heard a tale of love from Diotima of Mantineia, a woman wise in many kinds of knowledge, who delayed the disease ten years when the Athenians offered sacrifice, and who instructed him in the art of love.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 2318-2392
occurrences.motif_label: offspring protected through self-sacrifice
occurrences.basis: Animals are said to fight stronger creatures, die, suffer hunger, or endure anything to maintain their young.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Diotima describes animals, birds, and beasts as agonized by procreative desire, seeking union, caring for offspring, and enduring danger, hunger, or death for their young; Socrates asks to be taught the cause and mysteries of love.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 64-148
occurrences.motif_label: Self-sacrificial death for spouse followed by return from the dead
occurrences.basis: Alcestis dies for her husband and is allowed to come again from the dead as recompense for virtue.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Alcestis is presented as a true love who dared to die for her husband and was allowed to return from the dead as recompense for virtue.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 64-148
occurrences.motif_label: Foreknown death accepted to avenge beloved
occurrences.basis: Achilles is willing to avenge Patroclus even though he knows his own death will immediately follow.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Achilles' love is called courageous and true because he avenges Patroclus despite knowing his own death will follow; the gods reward him by sending him to the islands of the blest.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 999-1123
occurrences.motif_label: Victory sacrifice followed by feast
occurrences.basis: Agathon’s victory with his first tragedy is associated with a sacrifice of victory and the later feast or banquet at his house.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Apollodorus says the meeting was long ago, when Agathon won a prize with his first tragedy, on the day after Agathon and his chorus offered the sacrifice of victory.

Aristodemus meets Socrates fresh from the bath and wearing unusual sandals; Socrates says he is going to Agathon’s banquet, has dressed finely for Agathon, and asks Aristodemus to come with him unasked.

occurrences.source_title: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
occurrences.passage_locator: Theogony ll. 507-616
occurrences.motif_label: trickster at sacrificial boundary
occurrences.basis: Prometheus uses deceptive food portions in a divine-human dispute that explains altar practice.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "For when the gods and mortal men had a dispute at Mecone... Prometheus was forward to cut up a great ox and set portions before them, trying to befool the mind of Zeus."
"Zeus... saw and failed not to perceive the trick... and because of this the tribes of men upon earth burn white bones to the deathless gods upon fragrant altars."

occurrences.source_title: Maha-bharata
occurrences.passage_locator: Fall of Bhishma
occurrences.motif_label: oath-bounded defeat
occurrences.basis: Bhishma himself declares the condition under which he will not fight, and that vow becomes the means of his own fall.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Bhishma says he will not betray Duryodhana and lists the sorts of foes he will not fight, including one born female.
Krishna tells Arjuna there is hope because Sikhandin, once born female, can stand in front and cause Bhishma to leave the fight.
In battle Arjuna places Sikhandin in front, Bhishma remembers his vow, drops his arms, and falls as the day declines.

occurrences.source_title: Maha-bharata
occurrences.passage_locator: Fall of Bhishma
occurrences.motif_label: filial reluctance before necessary violence
occurrences.basis: Arjuna resists the strategy because Bhishma has been like a father, yet the battle requires him to accept the elder's death.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Arjuna calls the plan shameful because Bhishma has been like a father, and Krishna answers that Bhishma himself has shown the way.
Both sides gather in grief, Arjuna's arrows form Bhishma's dying bed, and Bhishma begins his final counsel to Duryodhana.

occurrences.source_title: Maha-bharata
occurrences.passage_locator: Fall of Bhishma
occurrences.motif_label: dying elder on arrow bed
occurrences.basis: Bhishma's fall onto a bed of arrows immediately converts the slain warrior into a dying counselor whose final voice still carries authority.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In battle Arjuna places Sikhandin in front, Bhishma remembers his vow, drops his arms, and falls as the day declines.
Both sides gather in grief, Arjuna's arrows form Bhishma's dying bed, and Bhishma begins his final counsel to Duryodhana.

occurrences.source_title: The Ramayan of Valmiki
occurrences.passage_locator: Book II, Cantos CXII-CXIV: The Sandals; Bharat's Return; Bharat's Departure
occurrences.motif_label: regency by self-abnegation
occurrences.basis: Bharat refuses ordinary royal enjoyment, adopts hermit signs, and binds his own life to Ráma's timely return.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Bharat vows to live in hermit's dress outside the kingdom, delegate rule to the sandals, and enter fire if Ráma does not return at the close of fourteen years.
Bharat reverently circles Ráma, places the bright sandals above his brows, and has them bound upon the royal elephant before departing.

occurrences.source_title: Mystics and Saints of Islam
occurrences.passage_locator: Mystics and Saints of Islam, Rabia, the Woman Sufi
occurrences.motif_label: divine beloved excludes worldly possession
occurrences.basis: Rabia rejects the whole world because divine love is treated as incompatible with worldly attachment.

evidence.locator: Mystics and Saints of Islam, Rabia, lines 1037-1047
evidence.quote_or_summary: A voice tells Rabia she cannot keep both the world and divine love; Rabia turns from earthly love and prays for absorption in God's love.

motifs.label: Sacred Exchange

occurrences.source_title: Deuteronomy
occurrences.passage_locator: Deuteronomy 30:15-20
occurrences.motif_label: sacred_exchange
occurrences.basis: The passage links human obedience and attachment to Yahweh with life and blessing.

evidence.quote_or_summary: I have set before you today life and prosperity, and death and evil... choose life, that you may live.

occurrences.source_title: Deuteronomy
occurrences.passage_locator: Deuteronomy 29:1-15
occurrences.motif_label: sacred_exchange
occurrences.basis: The passage describes reciprocal covenant identity: Israel as Yahweh's people and Yahweh as their God.

evidence.quote_or_summary: These are the words of the covenant... All of you stand today in the presence of Yahweh your God.

occurrences.source_title: Deuteronomy
occurrences.motif_label: sacred_exchange
occurrences.basis: Law and song function as obligations and witnesses in the divine-human covenant relationship.

evidence.quote_or_summary: You shall read this law before all Israel in their hearing... this song will testify before them as a witness.

occurrences.source_title: Genesis
occurrences.motif_label: sacred_exchange
occurrences.basis: Candidate motif from literal passage evidence.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Noah built an altar to Yahweh... I establish my covenant with you, and with your offspring after you.

occurrences.source_title: The Sayings of Confucius
occurrences.passage_locator: Individual Virtue
occurrences.motif_label: reverent filial duty
occurrences.basis: Filial piety is defined through reverent service, burial, sacrifice, and sustained concern for parents.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Filial piety means serving parents in the proper spirit, burying them with proper rites, and worshipping them with proper sacrifices.
Parents should be spared anxiety about their children except in sickness.
Without the feeling of reverence, what is there to distinguish filial support from feeding dogs and horses?
A son may remonstrate gently, remain deferential when ignored, and keep the age and condition of parents continually in mind.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE BEAR AND THE TRAVELLERS / THE SLAVE AND THE LION / THE FLEA AND THE MAN / THE BEE AND JUPITER; lines 1593-1606
occurrences.motif_label: gift to deity followed by promised reward
occurrences.basis: The Queen Bee gives honey to Jupiter, and Jupiter promises to grant whatever she asks.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Queen Bee from Hymettus flies to Olympus with fresh honey from the hive as a present to Jupiter.
Jupiter is pleased with the gift and promises to give the Queen Bee anything she asks.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE DOG AND THE COOK / THE MONKEY AS KING / THE THIEVES AND THE COCK / THE FARMER AND FORTUNE; lines 1852-1865
occurrences.motif_label: offering made after good fortune
occurrences.basis: After finding the coins, the farmer makes daily offerings at a goddess's shrine.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The farmer is overjoyed and from then on makes a daily offering at the shrine of the Goddess of the Earth.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: MERCURY AND THE SCULPTOR / THE FAWN AND HIS MOTHER / THE FOX AND THE LION / THE EAGLE AND HIS CAPTOR; lines 2342-2354
occurrences.motif_label: gifts directed toward a dangerous enemy for self-protection
occurrences.basis: The fox advises the eagle that gifts should go to the original captor so that he may not capture and clip the eagle again.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A fox advises the eagle to give gifts to the first captor, reasoning that this may prevent a second capture and clipping of his wings.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE BEAR AND THE FOX / THE ASS AND THE OLD PEASANT / THE OX AND THE FROG / THE MAN AND THE IMAGE; lines 2498-2508
occurrences.motif_label: ineffective piety contrasted with profitable irreverence
occurrences.basis: Daily prayer and honor bring no riches, while insult and violence are followed by the discovery of gold.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A poor man has a wooden image of a god and prays to it daily for riches for a long time, yet remains poor.
In disgust the man hurls the image against the wall; the blow splits its head and gold coins fall to the floor.
“When I honoured you, you did me no good whatever: but no sooner do I treat you to insults and violence than you make a rich man of me!”

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE TWO SOLDIERS AND THE ROBBER / THE LION AND THE WILD ASS / THE MAN AND THE SATYR / THE IMAGE-SELLER; lines 2611-2622
occurrences.motif_label: divine image commodified for promised gain
occurrences.basis: The passage centers on a wooden image of Mercury being sold as a god that will bring luck and gain.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A man made a wooden image of Mercury and exposed it for sale in the market.
“A god for sale! a god for sale! One who'll bring you luck and keep you lucky!”
“he brings gain, it is true, but he takes his time about it; whereas I want money at once.”

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE KID AND THE WOLF / THE DEBTOR AND HIS SOW / THE BALD HUNTSMAN / THE HERDSMAN AND THE LOST BULL; lines 3907-3930
occurrences.motif_label: Conditional vow of sacrifice to a deity
occurrences.basis: The herdsman promises Jupiter a calf if the thief is found, then promises a full-grown bull if he escapes the lion.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A herdsman misses a fine young bull, searches without success, and vows to sacrifice a calf to Jupiter if he discovers the thief.
Terrified, the herdsman raises his hands to heaven, calls on Jupiter, and promises a full-grown bull if he escapes unharmed.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE DOGS AND THE FOX / THE NIGHTINGALE AND THE HAWK / THE ROSE AND THE AMARANTH / THE MAN, THE HORSE, THE OX, AND THE DOG; lines 4550-4579
occurrences.motif_label: hospitality repaid by animal gifts
occurrences.basis: The Man gives shelter, fire, and food to animal guests, who then repay him by endowing parts of human life with their qualities.

evidence.quote_or_summary: On a winter day during a severe storm, a Horse, Ox, and Dog beg a Man for shelter; he admits them, lights a fire, gives oats to the Horse, hay to the Ox, and dinner remains to the Dog.
When the storm abates and the animals are about to leave, they decide to show gratitude by dividing the life of Man among themselves and endowing each part with their own qualities.

The Horse takes youth, explaining high spirit and impatience; the Ox takes middle age, explaining steadiness and hard work; the Dog takes old age, explaining peevishness, attachment to comfort-givers, and snapping at unfamiliar or disliked people.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE WILY LION / THE PARROT AND THE CAT / THE STAG AND THE LION / THE IMPOSTOR; lines 4698-4726
occurrences.motif_label: false fulfillment of a sacred vow punished
occurrences.basis: The man vows a sacrifice to the gods, substitutes tallow oxen, and is punished through a divine dream that results in his sale for one hundred crowns.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A very sick man vows to sacrifice one hundred oxen to the gods if they grant him restored health.
The gods cause the man to recover quickly in order to see how he keeps the vow.
Having no ox, the man makes one hundred small oxen from tallow and offers them on an altar.
"Ye gods, I call you to witness that I have discharged my vow."
The gods send the man a dream telling him to go to the seashore to fetch one hundred crowns he will find there.
At the shore the man meets robbers, who seize him, carry him off, and sell him as a slave for one hundred crowns.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE PARTRIDGE AND THE FOWLER / THE RUNAWAY SLAVE / THE HUNTER AND THE WOODMAN / THE SERPENT AND THE EAGLE; lines 5178-5192
occurrences.motif_label: reciprocal rescue after aid given
occurrences.basis: The countryman saves the eagle, and the eagle later saves the countryman from drinking poison; the moral explicitly frames this as reciprocal benefit.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A countryman witnesses the encounter, assists the eagle, frees him from the serpent, and enables him to escape.
The eagle knocks the horn from the man's hand and spills its contents on the ground.
One good turn deserves another.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: HONORARY SECRETARIES. / INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA.; lines 1011-1094
occurrences.motif_label: rewarded animal helpers explain food-sharing
occurrences.basis: Crows and foxes help prevent the sun's swallowing and in return share in human food.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At sunrise in the east, a devil tries to swallow the sun; someone puts crows or foxes into the devil's mouth so the sun rises, and these animals share human food in return.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA. / II.--MORAL TALES.; lines 1097-1202
occurrences.motif_label: kind gift to animal repaid by divine reward
occurrences.basis: The fisherman gives a cleaned fish to a hungry raven, who is a divine daughter; her father rewards him with wealth-producing puppies.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A man lays a net across the river, catches many fish, sees a hungry raven beside him, washes one fish, and throws it to the raven.
"Though it was a raven, it spoke thus, just like a human being" and invited the man to visit its old father.
The raven flies and the man follows on foot to a large house; inside, the raven appears human in form as a divine girl, with a divine old man and divine old woman present.
The divine old man says he is grateful because the man fed his daughter good fish and has brought him to be rewarded.
A gold puppy and a silver puppy are given; the divine old man explains that one excretes gold and the other silver, enriching the man if he sells the excrement.
The man returns home, feeds the puppies a little at a time, and becomes rich by selling the gold and silver they excrete.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA. / II.--MORAL TALES. / IV.--MISCELLANEOUS TALES.; lines 1719-1809
occurrences.motif_label: Divine aquatic rescuer establishes worship obligation
occurrences.basis: The chief of the salmon says he saved the Aino from the waves and requires rice-beer, divine symbols, and libation worship, warning of poverty if ignored.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "I am no human being. I am the chief of the salmon, the divine fish." He says he saved the Aino from the waves and that one night was actually a whole year.
The divine old man asks the Aino to offer rice-beer, set up divine symbols, and worship him with a libation formula; he warns that failure will make the Aino poor.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA. / II.--MORAL TALES. / IV.--MISCELLANEOUS TALES.; lines 1811-1905
occurrences.motif_label: Dream as purchasable valuable object
occurrences.basis: The senior chief tells subordinate chiefs that he will buy a good dream if one is reported.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A populous village has six chiefs, the oldest ruling the others; he holds a rice-beer feast and tells the five chiefs to report their overnight dreams so he can buy a good one.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA. / II.--MORAL TALES. / IV.--MISCELLANEOUS TALES.; lines 1907-2004
occurrences.motif_label: Divine reward for care of a deity-associated place
occurrences.basis: The God of the Privy says he rescued and protected the junior chief because the privy was kept clean.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The senior chief is called bad and the junior chief good; the God of the Privy rescues the junior chief from a hole, restores memory of a dream, and says he protected him because the privy was kept clean.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA. / II.--MORAL TALES. / IV.--MISCELLANEOUS TALES.; lines 2006-2100
occurrences.motif_label: exorcism by substitute likeness offered to possessing being
occurrences.basis: The father carves an exact likeness of his daughter and offers it to the fox with respectful worship to exorcise it.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The girl returns home; her father exorcises the fox by carving an exact likeness of his daughter and offering it to the fox with respectful worship; she later marries, has children, and is happy.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA. / II.--MORAL TALES. / IV.--MISCELLANEOUS TALES. / V.--SCRAPS OF FOLK-LORE.; lines 2201-2329
occurrences.motif_label: marked animal helper bringing game and wealth
occurrences.basis: The ancestor ties divine symbols to a kept deer's horns, and the deer brings other deer from the mountains, enriching him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An earliest ancestor kept a deer with divine symbols tied to its horns; it went to the mountains and brought back other deer, which the ancestor killed, becoming enriched.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA. / II.--MORAL TALES. / IV.--MISCELLANEOUS TALES. / V.--SCRAPS OF FOLK-LORE.; lines 2331-2395
occurrences.motif_label: auspicious sacred exchange with a mountain god before hunting
occurrences.basis: A hunter’s dream of meeting a god in the mountains, giving presents, and making obeisance is said to ensure killing a bear.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Before hunting, dreaming of meeting a god in the mountains, giving presents, and making obeisance is very lucky and guarantees killing a bear.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: LOCAL SECRETARIES. / HONORARY SECRETARIES. / INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE.; lines 266-349
occurrences.motif_label: ritual libation to gods using borrowed named drink
occurrences.basis: The passage says Ainos offer Japanese rice-beer, under the Japanese name sake, in libations to their gods.

evidence.quote_or_summary: He cites Japanese influence in language, customs, and religion, including sake libations to gods, an apparently archaic Japanese word for prayer, and reverence for the Japanese hero Yoshitsune.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: HONORARY SECRETARIES. / INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA.; lines 610-713
occurrences.motif_label: Origin of ritual worship through negotiated exchange
occurrences.basis: The man avoids death by promising rice-beer, divine symbols, worship, and fish offerings to the foxes, which the foxes accept; the tale explains fox worship as the result.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The man apologizes, promises to brew rice-beer, set up divine symbols, worship the foxes forever, and offer fish; the foxes accept, and the tale says Japanese and Ainu people worship the fox for this reason.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: HONORARY SECRETARIES. / INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA.; lines 715-800
occurrences.motif_label: Treasure exchange for food or spouse
occurrences.basis: The boy offers treasures for food, the dragon-god proposes an exchange of treasures, and the boy asks for the wife instead of the treasures.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The boy brings in the cloth bag given by his sister, offers its precious treasures as payment for food, and the divine-looking man takes them away, saying he will bring his own treasures in exchange.
The woman tells the lad she is the bear-goddess, her husband is the jealous dragon-god, and the boy should ask to buy the woman rather than exchange treasures.

The dragon-god returns with two sets of treasures; the boy asks for the wife, thunder sounds, the house disappears, the dragon-husband leaves in rage, the boy and goddess live together, and the narrator explains the bear's half-human likeness.

occurrences.passage_locator: END OF THE STORY OF THE DART OF LOVE. / END OF THE STORY OF THE SWIFT ANTELOPE. / END OF THE STORY OF THE DEER WHO WOULD NOT LEARN. / END OF THE STORY ON FOOD OFFERED TO THE DEAD.; lines 10302-10448
occurrences.motif_label: Vowed offering criticized as bondage rather than liberation
occurrences.basis: The passage presents vows and animal offerings to gods or a tree spirit, then has the tree-god condemn such deeds as not freeing the wise and leading fools into bondage.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At Jetavana, the Teacher tells of men who, before trading journeys, kill animals, offer them to gods, and vow to make further offerings if they return safely.
After safe and successful return, the men think this happened through the god's power, kill animals, and make offerings to release themselves from the vow.

In Kāsi, a village landed proprietor promises an offering to the Genius of a Banyan-tree by the village gate and, after returning safely, slays animals and goes to the tree to free himself from the vow.
The tree-god, standing in a fork of the tree, says: “Not by such deeds as these are the wise made free.”

occurrences.motif_label: Gift mirrored by heavenly counterpart
occurrences.basis: Piety's pinnacle, Thoughtful's pleasure-ground, and Pleasing's pond are followed by corresponding heavenly structures or places connected with their names.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Thoughtful makes a pleasure ground, Pleasing makes a pond, Well-born does nothing, and the Bodisat fulfills seven religious duties.
Piety, Thoughtful, and Pleasing are reborn as Sakka's attendants; a Hall of Piety, Thoughtful's Creeper Grove, and the Pond of Pleasing arise in connection with their gifts.

occurrences.basis: The old-woman form of Sakka refuses money and gives golden cucumbers only to one who lives righteously.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Well-born is reborn in a potter’s household in Benares; Sakka appears as an old woman with a cart of golden cucumbers, offers them only to the righteous, and leaves them and the cart for Well-born.

occurrences.motif_label: religious giving as valued treasure
occurrences.basis: Anātha Piṇḍika spends great wealth on the Buddhist Faith, brings offerings to services, and regards the Three Treasures as his true treasure.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The next Jātaka begins. Anātha Piṇḍika is said to have spent immense wealth on the Buddhist Faith and to value only the Three Treasures: the Buddha, the Truth, and the Order.
Anātha Piṇḍika attends services daily and brings offerings: porridge in the morning, ghee, butter, honey, and molasses after breakfast, and perfumes, garlands, and robes in the evening.
His house keeps rice ready for five hundred members of the Order; it is compared to a public pool at a four-road meeting place, and the Buddha, Eighty Chief Elders, and many other monks come and go.

occurrences.motif_label: right-hearted offering outweighs material value
occurrences.basis: The Buddha teaches that even stale gruel is not a trifling gift if the heart is believing and the recipients are Buddhas or disciples.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Buddha tells the merchant not to be troubled by unpleasant or poor gifts, because a gift given with a right or believing heart to Buddhas, Pacceka Buddhas, or disciples is not trifling.

occurrences.motif_label: worthy recipient determines value of gift
occurrences.basis: The Velāma teaching contrasts immense gifts to unfit recipients with poorer gifts to noble religious recipients.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Buddha tells the merchant not to be troubled by unpleasant or poor gifts, because a gift given with a right or believing heart to Buddhas, Pacceka Buddhas, or disciples is not trifling.

The Buddha says that when he was Velāma he gave away the Seven Treasures in an immense donation likened to the five great rivers made one mass of water, yet did not attain refuge or precepts because the recipients were unfit.

occurrences.passage_locator: END OF THE STORY OF THE FORD. / END OF THE STORY ON CONSTANCY. / END OF THE STORY OF THE BULL WHO WON THE BET. / END OF THE STORY OF THE WISE BIRD AND THE FOOLS.; lines 13359-13469
occurrences.motif_label: Wrongdoing repaired through restitution before pardon
occurrences.basis: The Fairy is told to refill the Merchant’s treasury as punishment before asking pardon, and she reports completing this restitution before receiving forgiveness.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sakka instructs the Fairy to assume the Merchant’s manager’s form, use young ogres and demon power to recover debts, retrieve wealth washed from the Aciravatī riverbank to the sea, gather ownerless treasure, and refill the treasury with fifty-four thousands of thousands.

The Fairy follows Sakka’s instructions, appears visibly in the Merchant’s bed-chamber at midnight, confesses her ignorance, reports restoring three sums of eighteen thousands of thousands, and asks Anātha Piṇḍika for pardon.

At the close of the verses the Fairy is established in the Fruit of Conversion, falls at the Teacher’s wheel-marked feet, asks pardon for wicked words spoken in ignorance, and receives pardon from both the Teacher and the Merchant.

occurrences.passage_locator: END OF THE STORY OF THE FORD. / END OF THE STORY ON CONSTANCY. / END OF THE STORY OF THE BULL WHO WON THE BET. / END OF THE STORY OF THE WISE BIRD AND THE FOOLS.; lines 13471-13594
occurrences.motif_label: Steadfast almsgiving despite supernatural obstruction
occurrences.basis: The Bodisat insists on giving alms to the Pacceka Buddha even when Māra creates a fiery pit to prevent the gift.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Māra is agitated and says the Pacceka Buddha has gone seven days without food; if he gets none today he will perish, so Māra must destroy the donor and stop the gift.
Māra creates in the house an eighty-fathom-deep pit of Acacia-wood charcoal, burning and flaming like Avīci, and remains in the sky.
The Bodisat thinks Vasavatti Māra is obstructing his almsgiving and states that he cannot be shaken by hundreds or thousands of Māras; he will test whose power is greater.

The Bodisat takes the rice dish, stands at the edge of the fire pit, questions Māra, and hears Māra admit he made it to stop the almsgiving and destroy the Pacceka Buddha; the Bodisat refuses to allow either.
“Far rather will I fall into this hell ... than do a deed that is unworthy!” The Bodisat holds the rice firmly and walks into the fiery furnace.

A large lotus-flower rises from the bottom of the fiery pit, receives the Bodisat’s feet, scatters pollen like golden dust over him, and he pours the food into the Pacceka Buddha’s bowl while standing on the lotus.

occurrences.motif_label: gift of alms to a holy recipient
occurrences.basis: The former alms-giver gives alms to the Pacceka Buddha.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "he who gave alms to the Pacceka Buddha, standing on the lotus after defeating the Tempter, was I myself."

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Pacceka Buddha is defined as one who can gain salvation for himself but not give others knowledge of it; the Birth Story is about a gift to a Pacceka Buddha.

occurrences.motif_label: devotional offering and preparation for a sacred visitor
occurrences.basis: The townspeople bring offerings, worship Dīpankara, invite him, prepare almsgiving, and decorate and repair the road for his arrival.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The dwellers of Ramma hear of Dīpankara’s arrival, bring requisites and offerings, worship him, hear his preaching, invite him for the next day, and depart.

The next day the townspeople prepare almsgiving, decorate the town, repair and level the road, scatter silver-like sand, sprinkle fragrant roots and flowers, raise flags and banners, and set up banana arches and rows of brimming jars.

occurrences.motif_label: Sacred meal before awakening
occurrences.basis: The future Gotama is said to receive a meal of rice milk or rice pottage at a tree and by the Neranjarā before going to the Bodhi-tree.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The prophecy describes Gotama’s departure, austerities, rice-milk or rice-pottage meal, Neranjarā riverbank, approach to the Bodhi-tree, salutation of the Bodhi throne, and Buddhahood beneath an Indian fig tree called Assattha.

occurrences.motif_label: Total giving as self-emptying
occurrences.basis: The first perfection requires giving all to those who ask, with the simile of a water-jar emptied until nothing remains.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Almsgiving is compared to a water-jar that “Discharges entirely all the water, and retains none within.”
If Sumedha gives away wealth, fame, family, and goods to all who ask until nothing remains, he will sit at the foot of the tree of Bodhi and become a Buddha.

occurrences.motif_label: Homage, offerings, and blessing around a holy figure
occurrences.basis: People and angels offer flowers, perfumes, and other gifts, while blessings are pronounced for Sumedha’s attainment.

evidence.quote_or_summary: People of Ramma hear the Buddha’s words, bring offerings to the Bodhisatta, bow to him, and return; the Bodhisatta takes on the Perfections, resolves, bows to Dīpankara, and rises from his seat.

Angels from the ten thousand worlds assemble, offer garlands and perfumes, praise Sumedha’s resolve at Dīpankara’s feet, bless him against sickness and hindrance, and compare his attainment to trees flowering in season.

Verses describe angels and men sprinkling flowers, blessing the Bodhisatta, urging fulfillment of the ten Perfections, and using similes of trees, moon, sun, rivers, and ocean; he takes the ten Conditions and enters the forest.

occurrences.motif_label: Meritorious former-life deed producing later Buddha attribute
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly states that Mangala Buddha’s later radiance results from a former-life prayer and deed.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage states that other Buddhas possess comparable power at will, but Mangala Buddha’s permanent vast radiance results from a prayer made in a former existence.

In a former Bodhisatta existence like the Vessantara existence, he lives with wife and children on a mountain; the demon Kharadāthika comes disguised as a brahmin, asks for the two children, receives them, devours them, and the Bodhisatta rejoices and prays for future rays of light.

occurrences.motif_label: divine helper responds to merit
occurrences.basis: Suruci’s meritorious intention warms Indra’s throne; Indra descends to help and says he should obtain a share of Suruci’s merit.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Suruci worries about room for the monks, and his thought causes Indra’s marble throne, very far away, to become warm.
Indra sees Suruci with the divine eye, decides to go and share his merit, assumes the form of a carpenter with an axe, and offers to build a hall for hire.

occurrences.motif_label: vast almsgiving to a sacred assembly
occurrences.basis: Suruci feeds a million million monks for a week and gives them medicinal substances and robes; the act precedes a prediction of future Buddhahood.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Suruci gives gavapāna alms for seven days to a million million priests; angels and men wait upon them, and the monks seat themselves by supernatural power when the space is insufficient.
On the last day Suruci has the bowls washed, fills them with clarified and unclarified butter, honey, and molasses for medicinal use, and gives robes and cloaks.
The Teacher returns thanks, perceives Suruci’s future, and predicts that after two asankheyyas and four thousand cycles he will become a Buddha named Gotama.

occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 4522-4607
occurrences.motif_label: Sacred giving to Buddha and monastic order
occurrences.basis: The Bodhisatta repeatedly gives offerings, garments, an upper robe, or donations to a Buddha and monastic order before receiving confirmation of future Buddhahood.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sumana appears after Mangala and has three assemblies. The Bodhisatta is the Nāga king Atula, leaves the Nāga world with kinsmen, offers celestial music, gives garments of fine cloth, is established in the Three Refuges, and is foretold to become a Buddha. Sumana’s details include the Golden Mountain assembly and Nāga Bodhi-tree.

Revata appears after Sumana and has three assemblies. The Bodhisatta is born as the brahmin Atideva, hears the Teacher’s preaching, is established in the Three Refuges, raises clasped hands, praises the Teacher, presents a monk’s upper robe, and receives the prediction that he will become a Buddha. Revata’s details include a Nāga-tree as Bo-tree.

Sobhita appears after Revata and has three assemblies. The Bodhisatta is born as the brahman Ajita, hears the Teacher’s preaching, is established in the Three Refuges, gives a great donation to the order with the Buddha at its head, and receives a prophecy of future Buddhahood. Sobhita’s details include a Nāga-tree as Bo-tree.

After an asaŋkheyya, Anomadassin, Paduma, and Nārada are born in one kalpa. Anomadassin has three assemblies. The Bodhisatta is a mighty Yakkha chief, lord of many yakkhas, who comes after hearing that a Buddha has appeared, gives a great donation to the order with the Buddha at its head, and receives the prophecy that he will be a Buddha. Anomadassin’s details include an Arjuna-tree as Bo-tree.

occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 4609-4690
occurrences.motif_label: Devotional act or offering followed by prophecy of future Buddhahood
occurrences.basis: Across the episodes, the Bodisat venerates or gives offerings to a Buddha and the Order, and the Buddha prophesies his future Buddhahood.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Paduma has three assemblies and dwells in a forest grove; the Bodisat as a lion venerates him in trance, attends seven days without seeking prey, puts faith in the Order, and receives a prophecy of future Buddhahood. Paduma's city, kin, disciples, Bo-tree, height, and age are listed.

Nārada has three assemblies; the Bodisat as a vowed sage has five kinds of Wisdom and eight sublime Acquisitions, donates to the Order headed by the Buddha, offers red sandal wood, and receives a prophecy of future Buddhahood. Nārada's attributes and Bo-tree are listed.

Padumuttara appears in a distant kalpa and has assemblies, including one on Vebhāra Mountain; the Bodisat as Jaṭila offers robes to the Order headed by the Buddha and receives a prophecy. The passage says all men and angels took refuge in the Buddha, and lists Padumuttara's attributes and Bo-tree.

Sumedha appears after Padumuttara; the Bodisat as the brahman youth Uttara gives eight hundred millions of money to the Order headed by the Buddha, listens to the Law, accepts the Refuges, abandons home, takes vows, and receives a prophecy. Sumedha's attributes and Bo-tree are listed.

occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 4692-4781
occurrences.motif_label: Prior-life offering followed by prophecy of future Buddhahood
occurrences.basis: Across multiple episodes, the Bodisat performs a devotional act before a Buddha or the Order and receives a prophecy of future Buddhahood.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sujāta has three assemblies; the Bodisat as universal monarch hears the Law, gives his kingdom with seven treasures to the Order, takes vows, and receives prophecy. Sujāta's city, family, disciples, Bambu Bo-tree, body height, and lifespan are listed.

Piyadassin appears after eighteen hundred world-cycles; the Bodisat as Kassapa hears the Law, builds a monastery, keeps the Refuges and Precepts, and receives a prophecy after eighteen hundred kalpas. Piyadassin's Priyaŋgu Bo-tree and other attributes are listed.

Atthadassin has three assemblies; the Bodisat as the ascetic Susima brings from heaven a sunshade of Mandārava flowers and offers it to the Teacher, who prophesies to him. Atthadassin's Champaka Bo-tree and bodily glory are listed.

Dhammadassin has three assemblies; the Bodisat as Sakka king of the gods offers sweet-smelling heavenly flowers and heavenly music, and the Teacher prophesies to him. Dhammadassin's red Kuravaka Bo-tree is listed.

Siddhattha appears ninety-four world-cycles ago; the Bodisat as the ascetic Mangala brings a great jambu fruit to the Tathāgata. After eating it, the Teacher prophesies Buddhahood ninety-four kalpas later. Siddhattha's Kanikāra Bo-tree is listed.

occurrences.motif_label: Sacred gift before a Buddha
occurrences.basis: The Bodisat offers heavenly flowers, a jeweled chair, robes, a jeweled elephant, or other gifts to a Buddha or to the Order with the Buddha at their head, followed by prophetic recognition.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Tissa appears ninety-two world-cycles ago. The Bodisat is born as warrior-chief Sujāta, takes vows, gains rishi powers, offers a heaven-grown lotus and Pāricchattaka flowers to Tissa, spreads a flower awning in the sky, and receives a prophecy that he will become a Buddha. Tissa’s city, family, disciples, Asana Bo-tree, height, and lifespan are listed.

Vipassin appears ninety world-cycles ago. The Bodisat is born as the mighty snake king Atula and gives Vipassin a golden chair inlaid with seven kinds of gems; Vipassin prophesies that he will become a Buddha. Vipassin’s city, family, disciples, Pāṭali Bo-tree, height, bodily radiance, and lifespan are listed.

Sikhin appears thirty-one world-cycles ago. The Bodisat is born as king Arindama, gives robes and other things to the Order with the Buddha at their head, offers a superb elephant decked with seven gems, and receives a prophecy. Sikhin’s city, family, disciples, Puṇḍarīka Bo-tree, height, bodily radiance, and lifespan are listed.

Vessabhū appears after Sikhin. The Bodisat is born as king Sudassana, gives robes and other things to the Order with the Buddha at their head, takes vows, becomes righteous in conduct, meditates on the Buddha, and receives a prophecy. Vessabhū’s city, family, disciples, Sal Bo-tree, height, and lifespan are listed.

occurrences.motif_label: Sacred giving followed by vows and prophecy
occurrences.basis: In the Kakusandha and Koṇāgamana episodes, the Bodisat gives substantial donations to the Order, takes vows, and receives prophecy; Kassapa’s episode includes hearing the Law, vows, and prophecy.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Kakusandha has one assembly of forty thousand monks. The Bodisat as King Kshema gives robes, bowls, collyriums, and drugs to the Order, hears the Law, takes vows, and receives prophecy; Kakusandha’s city, family, disciples, Sirīsa Bo-tree, height, and age are listed.

Koṇāgamana has one assembly of thirty thousand monks. The Bodisat as King Pabbata goes with ministers to the Teacher, hears the Law, gives silk and fine gold-woven cloths, takes vows, and receives prophecy; Koṇāgamana’s city, family, disciples, Udumbara Bo-tree, height, and age are listed.

Kassapa has one assembly of twenty thousand monks. The Bodisat as the Brahman youth Jotipāla, friend of Ghaṭīkāra, goes to the Teacher, hears the Law, takes vows, learns the three Piṭakas, serves the religion of the Buddhas, and receives prophecy; Kassapa’s birthplace, family, disciples, Nigrodha Bo-tree, height, and age are listed.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Among many almsgiving births, the Wise Hare sees one coming for food and offers his own self, giving up his life to acquire the Supreme Perfection of Almsgiving.

occurrences.basis: In the Vessantara birth, the newborn asks whether there is anything in the house so that he may give a gift, and his mother places wealth in his hand.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In the Vessantara birth, the newborn stretches out his right hand asking whether there is anything in the house so he may give a gift; his mother places a bag containing a thousand in his hand.

occurrences.motif_label: gift as teacher's fee misunderstood as love token
occurrences.basis: The Bodisat sends pearls to Kisā Gotamī as a teacher's fee, while she thinks he has fallen in love with her.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Bodisat sends a valuable pearl necklace to Kisā Gotamī as a teacher's fee, but she thinks it is a love gift; he enters the palace and reclines on a couch of state.

occurrences.motif_label: votive exchange with a sacred tree
occurrences.basis: Sujātā prays to a Nigrodha-tree and promises an annual offering if marriage and childbirth wishes are granted; the prayer is said to take effect.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sujātā of Senāni's household prays to a Nigrodha-tree for marriage into an equal-rank family and a firstborn son, promising a yearly offering; the prayer takes effect.
