occurrences.motif_label: foundation of local sacred rites after divine revelation
occurrences.basis: After revealing herself, Demeter orders temple and altar construction and promises to teach rites and ceremonies in her honour.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Demeter orders a temple and altar to be built on a neighbouring hill at Eleusis and promises to direct sacred rites and ceremonies in her honour before departing.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THEMIS. / VESTA. / CERES. / APHRODITE (VENUS).; lines 1878-1983
occurrences.motif_label: Magic love-bestowing garment
occurrences.basis: Aphrodite's cestus can be lent out and gives its wearer the power to inspire affection and appear beautiful and fascinating.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Aphrodite's magic girdle, the cestus, can inspire affection for the wearer and confer grace, beauty, and fascination.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VENUS. / HELIOS (SOL). / EOS (AURORA). / PHOEBUS-APOLLO.; lines 2365-2439
occurrences.motif_label: Conditional sacred gift followed by broken promise and curse-like limitation
occurrences.basis: Cassandra receives prophecy from Apollo on condition of marriage, refuses the condition, and Apollo makes the gift ineffective by ensuring disbelief.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Cassandra, daughter of Priam, promises marriage in exchange for Apollo's gift of prophecy, then refuses; Apollo cannot recall the gift and makes her predictions fail to gain belief.
Cassandra warns Paris, the Trojans, and Agamemnon about disasters, including the wooden horse, but her prophecies are never believed.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VENUS. / HELIOS (SOL). / EOS (AURORA). / PHOEBUS-APOLLO.; lines 2441-2527
occurrences.motif_label: life exchanged through substitute death
occurrences.basis: Admetus may avoid death if a family member dies in his place; Alcestis chooses to die for him after his parents refuse.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Apollo obtains from the Fates a conditional reprieve for Admetus: someone in his family may die in his stead; his parents refuse, but Alcestis secretly devotes herself to death and dies while Admetus recovers.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: HELIOS (SOL). / EOS (AURORA). / PHOEBUS-APOLLO. / ROMAN APOLLO.; lines 2666-2715
occurrences.motif_label: Divine aid repaid by temple dedication
occurrences.basis: Augustus calls on Apollo before battle, credits victory to the god, and erects and enriches a temple with spoil.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Augustus invoked Apollo before Actium, credited his victory to Apollo's influence, and erected a temple enriched with part of the spoil.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: HELIOS (SOL). / EOS (AURORA). / PHOEBUS-APOLLO. / ROMAN APOLLO.; lines 2666-2715
occurrences.motif_label: Rejected sacred knowledge becomes diminished but more urgently valued
occurrences.basis: Tarquin refuses the Sibyl's books twice; she burns portions while keeping the same price, and the Augurs then urge him to buy the remaining books.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Cumaean Sibyl offers nine books to Tarquinius Superbus, burns three after each refusal, and Tarquin buys the remaining three after the Augurs advise him to do so; the books contain important predictions for the Romans.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: HECATE. / SELENE (LUNA). / ARTEMIS (DIANA). / ARCADIAN ARTEMIS.; lines 2881-2924
occurrences.motif_label: victory by distracting objects
occurrences.basis: Hippomenes receives golden apples through Aphrodite's help and uses them to distract Atalanta during the race.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hippomenes enters the race, obtains three golden apples from the Hesperides with Aphrodite's help, drops them during the course, and wins when Atalanta stops to gather the fruit.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: BRAURONIAN ARTEMIS. / SELENE-ARTEMIS. / DIANA. / HEPHAESTUS (VULCAN).; lines 3109-3194
occurrences.motif_label: Sacred exchange of divine weapon and marriage
occurrences.basis: Hephaestus forges Zeus's thunderbolts, and Zeus responds by giving Aphrodite to him in marriage.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hephaestus builds a golden palace on Olympus, makes dwellings for the gods, is attended by two moving golden female statues, forges Zeus's thunderbolts with the Cyclops, and receives Aphrodite in marriage; Aphrodite does not love him and mocks him.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: DIANA. / HEPHAESTUS (VULCAN). / VULCAN. / POSEIDON (NEPTUNE).; lines 3209-3294
occurrences.motif_label: Maritime propitiation through libation and sacrifice
occurrences.basis: Before voyages Poseidon is invoked and propitiated by libation, and after safe voyages he receives sacrifices and thanksgivings.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Poseidon is invoked and propitiated by libation before a voyage, and receives sacrifices and thanksgivings after safe sea journeys.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: DIANA. / HEPHAESTUS (VULCAN). / VULCAN. / POSEIDON (NEPTUNE).; lines 3296-3398
occurrences.motif_label: Contest of divine gifts deciding city patronage
occurrences.basis: Poseidon and Athene compete by offering gifts to mankind; the gods judge Athene's olive-tree superior to Poseidon's horse and grant her naming rights over Athens.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Poseidon and Athene contest naming Cecropia; Poseidon strikes the ground with his trident and the horse appears, while Athene produces the olive-tree; the gods award victory to Athene and the city is called Athens.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: MARS. / NIKE (VICTORIA). / VICTORIA. / HERMES (MERCURY).; lines 3819-3892
occurrences.motif_label: sacred exchange resolving conflict
occurrences.basis: The conflict over the stolen herd is resolved when Apollo accepts Hermes' lyre in exchange for the oxen and grants Hermes dominion over animals.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hermes plays the lyre; Apollo desires it and exchanges the oxen and animal dominion for it, leading to reconciliation between the brothers.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: NIKE (VICTORIA). / VICTORIA. / HERMES (MERCURY). / MERCURY.; lines 3938-3952
occurrences.motif_label: ritual use of holy water to secure prosperity
occurrences.basis: Merchants perform a ritual sprinkling of themselves and their merchandise with holy water in order to secure large profits.

evidence.quote_or_summary: On Mercury's festival on May 25, merchants sprinkled themselves and their merchandise with holy water to ensure large profits.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VICTORIA. / HERMES (MERCURY). / MERCURY. / DIONYSUS (BACCHUS).; lines 4043-4125
occurrences.motif_label: Hospitality rewarded by a divine favor
occurrences.basis: Midas hospitably entertains Silenus and returns him to Dionysus; Dionysus offers to grant him any favor.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Silenus wanders intoxicated into Midas's rose-gardens, is brought to Midas, receives hospitality for ten days, and is returned to Dionysus, who offers Midas a favor; Midas asks for the golden touch.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: MERCURY. / DIONYSUS (BACCHUS). / BACCHUS OR LIBER. / AIDES (PLUTO).; lines 4150-4244
occurrences.motif_label: sacred exchange with the dead or underworld personnel
occurrences.basis: Sacrificial blood temporarily restores the shades' mental vigor, and an obolus is required as Charon's toll for passage.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In the Homeric-age belief summarized here, shades live in shadowy form and semi-consciousness, revived temporarily by drinking sacrificial blood offered by living friends.
Charon ferries shades over Styx only if they received funerary rites and carry an obolus toll, often placed under the tongue; otherwise they wander the banks for a hundred years.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: BACCHUS OR LIBER. / AIDES (PLUTO). / PLUTO. / PLUTUS.; lines 4365-4377
occurrences.motif_label: wealth distributed blindly and indiscriminately
occurrences.basis: Plutus, as god of wealth, is said to be blind and foolish because he gives gifts without discrimination, often to unworthy recipients.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Plutus is described as son of Demeter and the mortal Iasion, and as god of wealth.
Plutus is considered blind and foolish because he gives gifts without discrimination, frequently to unworthy recipients.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: ANANKE (NECESSITAS). / MOMUS. / EROS (CUPID, AMOR) AND PSYCHE. / HYMEN.; lines 4964-4987
occurrences.motif_label: rescue exchanged for marriage consent
occurrences.basis: Hymen promises to restore the abducted maidens if their parents will give him the maiden he loves in marriage.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In Athens, Hymen finds the maidens' parents distressed and promises restoration of their children if they will give him the maiden he loves in marriage.
After the parents agree, Hymen returns to the island, brings the maidens safely back to Athens, marries his beloved, and their happy union makes his name synonymous with conjugal felicity.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: HEBE (JUVENTAS). / JUVENTAS. / GANYMEDES. / THE MUSES.; lines 5052-5157
occurrences.motif_label: Offering and supplication to gain divine aid
occurrences.basis: Libations are poured to the Muses and their assistance is supplicated before intellectual tasks; specific libation substances are listed.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Muses are honoured by mortals and immortals, led by Apollo in Olympus, invoked with libations and supplications, and said to grant knowledge, wisdom, eloquence, poetic thought, and musical harmony.
"The libations to these divinities consisted of water, milk, and honey, but never of wine."

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: GANYMEDES. / THE MUSES. / PEGASUS. / THE HESPERIDES.; lines 5189-5203
occurrences.motif_label: sacred marriage gift
occurrences.basis: The golden-apple tree is presented by Gaea to Hera on the occasion of Hera’s marriage with Zeus.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hera appoints the Hesperides as guardians of a tree bearing golden apples, which Gaea had presented to Hera at Hera’s marriage with Zeus.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE MUSES. / PEGASUS. / THE HESPERIDES. / CHARITES (GRATIAE) GRACES.; lines 5205-5246
occurrences.motif_label: Divine favor sought through offerings and banquet libation
occurrences.basis: The passage describes people entreating the Graces' favour through temples, altars, incense, invocation, and libation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Temples and altars honour the Graces; people seek their favour; incense is burnt daily, and banquet invocations and libations are made to them, partly because they moderate wine's effects.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: NYMPHS OF THE VALLEYS AND MOUNTAINS. / NAPAEAE AND OREADES. / THE WINDS. / PAN (FAUNUS).; lines 5499-5583
occurrences.motif_label: offerings and sacrifices to rural deity
occurrences.basis: The passage lists milk, honey, and animal sacrifices made to Pan.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Offerings to Pan are milk and honey in shepherds’ bowls; cows, lambs, and rams are sacrificed to him.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: PAN (FAUNUS). / FAUNUS. / THE SATYRS. / PRIAPUS.; lines 5635-5659
occurrences.motif_label: Ritual sacrifice and first-fruits offering to a fertility god
occurrences.basis: Asses are sacrificed to Priapus, and he receives first-fruits and a libation of milk and honey.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Priapus is chiefly worshipped at Lampsacus; asses are sacrificed to him, and first-fruits with a milk-and-honey libation are offered.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: FAUNUS. / THE SATYRS. / PRIAPUS. / ASCLEPIAS (AESCULAPIUS).; lines 5661-5710
occurrences.motif_label: sacred exchange of a potent healing substance
occurrences.basis: Pallas-Athene gives Asclepias Medusa's blood, which is believed to assist his cures.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Asclepias discovers cures, perfects healing so that he wards off death and restores the dead to life, and is popularly believed to be aided by Medusa's blood given by Pallas-Athene.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: ASCLEPIAS (AESCULAPIUS). / AESCULAPIUS. / ROMAN DIVINITIES. / JANUS.; lines 5712-5790
occurrences.motif_label: cult transfer during crisis and grateful temple foundation
occurrences.basis: The worship and statue of AEsculapius are brought from Epidaurus during a plague, and the Romans respond to deliverance by erecting a temple.

evidence.quote_or_summary: AEsculapius worship was brought to Rome from Epidaurus during a great pestilence; after deliverance, Romans built a temple to him on an island near the Tiber mouth.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE CAMENAE. / GENII. / MANES. / LEMURES (LARVAE) AND LARES.; lines 6006-6046
occurrences.motif_label: propitiation of feared spirits by festival
occurrences.basis: The Lemuralia is said to be celebrated in order to propitiate the feared Lemures.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Lemures are described as evil spirits haunting former earthly homes at night in frightening forms, causing alarm, and receiving propitiation through the Lemuralia.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE CAMENAE. / GENII. / MANES. / LEMURES (LARVAE) AND LARES.; lines 6006-6046
occurrences.motif_label: domestic offerings to a household guardian
occurrences.basis: The household Lar receives meal portions, greetings, thanksgiving, and garlands in connection with protection of hearth and home.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The household Lar's statue stands in the place of honor beside the hearth, is associated with the family founder, is venerated by the family, and receives a portion of each meal.
Before travel the master salutes the Lar's statue; on return he offers thanksgiving for protection, and the statue is crowned with flower garlands on family rejoicing occasions.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE CAMENAE. / GENII. / MANES. / LEMURES (LARVAE) AND LARES.; lines 6006-6046
occurrences.motif_label: civic guardian spirits receiving public sacrifice
occurrences.basis: Public Lares guard communal domains and receive sacrifices for the welfare of the state or city.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Public Lares guard the state, highroads, country, and sea; their temples are open, and sacrifices are offered on their altars for civic welfare.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: LEMURES (LARVAE) AND LARES. / PENATES. / PUBLIC WORSHIP OF THE ANCIENT GREEKS AND ROMANS. / TEMPLES.; lines 6070-6142
occurrences.motif_label: Costly offerings contrasted with sincere devotion
occurrences.basis: Lycurgus says magnificent edifices and costly sacrifices are less pleasing to the gods than true piety and unfeigned devotion.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Lacedaemonians had no stately temples because Lycurgus required minimal outlay in worship and valued piety and devotion above costly buildings and sacrifices.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: TEMPLES. / STATUES. / ALTARS. / PRIESTS.; lines 6182-6199
occurrences.motif_label: sacrifice and offerings to the gods
occurrences.basis: Priests offer sacrifices and instruct the people about vows, gifts, and offerings acceptable to the gods.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Priests are described as chosen mediators between gods and men who offer prayers and sacrifices for the people and instruct them on acceptable vows, gifts, and offerings.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: STATUES. / ALTARS. / PRIESTS. / SACRIFICES.; lines 6201-6287
occurrences.motif_label: sacrifice as sacred exchange with divine recipients
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly presents offerings, libations, animal victims, prayers, and vows as acts directed to gods in response to benefits, to appease anger, to gain success, or to fulfill obligations.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sacrifice is said to arise from gratitude to gods for protecting care and abundance lavished on mankind.
Free-will offerings are grateful acknowledgments for benefits received and usually consist of first-fruits or the finest unblemished animals.
Propitiatory offerings are brought to appease the anger of the gods.
Sacrifices may be made to obtain success in an enterprise, fulfill a vow, or follow an oracle's command.
Every sacrifice includes salt and a libation, usually wine in a full cup; sacrifices to infernal gods use blood in the libation cup.

After the service the priest tastes the libation, has the congregation taste it, pours the remainder between the victim's horns, strews frankincense on the altar, pours meal and water on the animal, and kills it.
Sacrifices to aerial divinities add music, altar dances, and sacred hymns praising divine deeds and gifts; the gods are invoked for continued favor and the service ends with a feast.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: STATUES. / ALTARS. / PRIESTS. / SACRIFICES.; lines 6201-6287
occurrences.motif_label: communal feast after sacrifice
occurrences.basis: The passage states that, after hymns and invocation at sacrifices to aerial divinities, the service ends with a feast.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sacrifices to aerial divinities add music, altar dances, and sacred hymns praising divine deeds and gifts; the gods are invoked for continued favor and the service ends with a feast.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: ORACLES. / SOOTHSAYERS (AUGURS). / AUGURS. / FESTIVALS.; lines 6341-6359
occurrences.motif_label: first-fruits offered to gods after harvest
occurrences.basis: The passage describes harvest or vintage festivals in which first-fruits were offered to the gods with prayers and thanksgiving.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The most ancient festivals followed the harvest or vintage and included many days of rejoicing, first-fruit offerings to the gods, prayers, and thanksgiving.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: ELEUSINIAN MYSTERIES. / THESMOPHORIA. / DIONYSIA. / PANATHENAEA.; lines 6448-6480
occurrences.motif_label: Processional offering to a guardian deity
occurrences.basis: The passage describes a public procession carrying a specially woven garment to the temple and depositing it on the statue of Athene-Polias, guardian of the state.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Panathenaea is described as an Athenian festival in honor of Athene-Polias, guardian of the state; the Lesser is annual and the Greater is every fourth year over several days.

For the Greater Panathenaea, Athenian maidens weave a gold-embroidered Peplus representing Athene’s victory over the Giants; it is suspended from a ship’s mast and moved in the procession by invisible machinery.
The population carries olive branches in the procession, which goes with music and rejoicing to the temple of Athene-Polias, where the Peplus is deposited on the goddess’s statue.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: PANATHENAEA. / DAPHNEPHORIA. / ROMAN FESTIVALS. / SATURNALIA.; lines 6496-6519
occurrences.motif_label: festival gift exchange
occurrences.basis: Friends sent presents to each other during the festival.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The festival brought rejoicing, cessation from labour, school holidays, gift-giving among friends, closed law-courts, and no business transactions.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VESTALIA. / PART II.--LEGENDS. / CADMUS. / PERSEUS.; lines 6633-6734
occurrences.motif_label: forced exchange for hidden knowledge
occurrences.basis: Perseus deprives the Graeae of their eye and tooth and restores them only after receiving directions to the Nymphs.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Perseus needs winged sandals, a magic wallet, and Aides' helmet from the Nymphs; guided by Hermes and Pallas-Athene, he takes the Graeae's single eye and tooth until they give directions.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: PART II.--LEGENDS. / CADMUS. / PERSEUS. / THE ARGONAUTS.; lines 6904-6953
occurrences.motif_label: divine helper tests or is aided in disguised form
occurrences.basis: Jason helps an old woman across a dangerous river; she reveals herself as Hera and promises future guidance and protection.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Jason reaches a broad, foaming river, sees an old woman asking for help, and carries her across despite the fierce torrent.
The old woman transforms into Hera, promises to guide and protect Jason, disappears, and Jason notices he has lost one sandal.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CADMUS. / PERSEUS. / THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE.; lines 7145-7238
occurrences.motif_label: Ritual offering at arrival in foreign sacred territory
occurrences.basis: After reaching Colchis and seeing the Fleece, Jason offers wine from a golden cup to mother-earth, local gods, and deceased heroes.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Argonauts anchor in the river Phases, see Ceuta and the grove of Ares, where the Golden Fleece hangs glittering from a magnificent oak-tree, and Jason offers a wine libation from a golden cup.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE. / PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES).; lines 7687-7783
occurrences.motif_label: divine gifts equip the hero
occurrences.basis: After Heracles' victory, named gods give him a sword, arrows, a golden quiver, and a leather coat.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Creon rewards Heracles with Megara in marriage, and Hermes, Phoebus-Apollo, Hephaestus, and Athene give him a sword, arrows, a golden quiver, and a leather coat.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE. / PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES).; lines 7785-7884
occurrences.motif_label: hospitality breached by opening restricted communal substance
occurrences.basis: Pholus hosts Heracles, but the shared wine is opened outside the normal communal rule, drawing Centaurs and leading to violence.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Pholus gives Heracles food and shelter; Heracles persuades him to open wine that belongs to all Centaurs, and the odor attracts many Centaurs armed with rocks and fir-trees.

Heracles drives back the Centaurs with fire-brands and arrows; they take refuge in Chiron’s cave, where a poisoned dart wounds Chiron, whose immortal suffering is ended by death from the gods at Heracles’ intercession.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE. / PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES).; lines 7785-7884
occurrences.motif_label: broken reward agreement after impossible task
occurrences.basis: Augeas promises a tenth of the herds for cleansing the stables, but refuses payment after the task is performed and banishes Heracles and Phyleus.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Eurystheus commands Heracles to cleanse Augeas’s stables in one day; Augeas, rich in cattle, agrees before Phyleus to give Heracles a tenth of the herds if he succeeds.
Augeas refuses the promised reward after learning the cleansing was one of Eurystheus’s labours; Heracles appeals to court and calls Phyleus as witness, but Augeas banishes both before the verdict.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE. / PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES).; lines 7886-7984
occurrences.motif_label: exchange of persons or gifts for heroic reward
occurrences.basis: Melanippe is restored to Hippolyte in exchange for the girdle, and Laomedon promises horses to Heracles as reward for saving Hesione and killing the monster.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hippolyte agrees to give Heracles the girdle, but Hera disguises herself as an Amazon and spreads a rumor; the Amazons attack, Melanippe is wounded, and Heracles restores her to Hippolyte in exchange for the girdle.
Laomedon asks Heracles to save Hesione and rid the country of the monster, promising as reward the horses Zeus had given Tros in compensation for Ganymede.
Heracles accepts, attacks and kills the monster with a sword, but Laomedon breaks faith; Heracles vows future vengeance and presents the girdle to Eurystheus.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE. / PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES).; lines 8076-8168
occurrences.motif_label: binding food of the underworld
occurrences.basis: Persephone's swallowing of pomegranate seeds offered by her husband binds her to Aides forever.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Heracles recognizes Ascalaphus, who revealed Persephone's swallowing of pomegranate seeds; Ascalaphus groans beneath Demeter's rock until Heracles removes it.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE. / PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES).; lines 8170-8264
occurrences.motif_label: hero's temporary servitude as expiation
occurrences.basis: Heracles submits to being sold as a slave for three years, and the purchase price is assigned as compensation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Pythia commands Heracles to expiate the crime by being sold by Hermes for three years as a slave, with the price given to Eurytus as compensation.
Heracles submits, is conducted by Hermes to Omphale of Lydia, is bought for three talents, and later performs strong and courageous services for Omphale, including clearing robbers.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE. / PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES).; lines 8170-8264
occurrences.motif_label: ransom naming of a royal survivor
occurrences.basis: Podarces is ransomed with Hesione's golden diadem and thereafter bears the name Priam, explained as the ransomed one.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Heracles gives Hesione to Telamon; Hesione chooses to release Podarces and ransoms him with her golden diadem, after which he is called Priam, the ransomed one.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: OEDIPUS. / THE SEVEN AGAINST THEBES. / THE EPIGONI. / ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE.; lines 9018-9107
occurrences.motif_label: Cursed precious objects passing through bribery, marriage, deception, murder, and dedication
occurrences.basis: Harmonia's necklace and veil are obtained through bribes, given as bridal gifts, recovered by deception, cause ruin among possessors, and end as sacred offerings at Delphi.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Alcmaeon returns from the Theban expedition, resolves to avenge Amphiaraus on Eriphyle for bribery and betrayal, kills her, and leaves with Harmonia's necklace and veil.
The gods punish Alcmaeon with madness and a pursuing Fury; at Psophis, Phegeus purifies him, gives him Arsinoe, and Alcmaeon gives her the necklace and veil.
Alcmaeon and Calirrhoe have two sons; Calirrhoe hears of Harmonia's necklace and veil and strongly desires them.

Alcmaeon conceals his former marriage, falsely says the objects are hidden in a cave, then tells Arsinoe and Phegeus an oracle requires him to deposit them at Delphi; Arsinoe returns the bridal gifts.
The necklace and veil are said to bring ruin to possessors; a servant reveals Alcmaeon's union with Calirrhoe, and Phegeus's sons ambush and kill Alcmaeon.

Calirrhoe's sons kill the sons of Phegeus at Tegea, then kill Phegeus and his wife at Psophis, return to Calirrhoe with the necklace and veil, and deposit them in Apollo's temple at Delphi by Achelous's command.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE EPIGONI. / ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE. / THE SIEGE OF TROY.; lines 9323-9415
occurrences.motif_label: Failed embassy before war
occurrences.basis: The Greeks attempt a peaceful solution by embassy and demand Helen's surrender, but Priam rejects the demand.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After ten years of preparations, a Greek embassy including Menelaus and Odysseus demands Helen's surrender from Priam; the demand is rejected and the fleet is ordered to Aulis.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE EPIGONI. / ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE. / THE SIEGE OF TROY.; lines 9514-9591
occurrences.motif_label: Embassy offers restitution to restore the absent hero
occurrences.basis: Agamemnon offers Briseis, marriage, and towns to persuade Achilles to help the Greeks, but Achilles refuses.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Agamemnon sends distinguished chiefs to ask Achilles for aid, offering Briseis, marriage to his daughter, and seven towns, but Achilles refuses.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS / INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN; lines 1014-1160
occurrences.motif_label: sacred exchange between warrior and god
occurrences.basis: Warriors dedicate themselves to Odin and seek armed death; Odin rewards favorites with gifts and invincibility until their appointed end.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Fighting men dedicate themselves to Odin, vow to die armed, and may wound themselves with spears to avoid death from old age or sickness.
Odin rewards favored warriors with a magic sword, spear, or horse and invincibility until their final hour, when he appears and Valkyrs bear the heroes to Valhalla.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS / INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN; lines 1163-1296
occurrences.motif_label: reward and punishment for joining a supernatural cry
occurrences.basis: Mocking participants are taken away, while faithful participants receive a horse's leg that becomes gold.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Mocking the wild halloo results in being snatched up and whirled away; joining in good faith brings a horse's leg from above that becomes gold by morning if kept.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS / INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN; lines 1440-1580
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom gained through bodily sacrifice
occurrences.basis: Odin receives a wisdom-giving draught only after giving one of his eyes to Mimir.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odin visits Mimir's spring, the source of wit, wisdom, and memory, and Mimir requires one of Odin's eyes in exchange for a draught.
Odin plucks out an eye; Mimir sinks it into the fountain, leaving Odin with one eye, which the passage associates with solar imagery and, in verse, contrasts with the moon-like pledged eye.
Odin drinks from Mimir's fountain, gains knowledge, breaks a branch from the sacred tree Yggdrasil, and fashions the spear Gungnir from it.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS / INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN; lines 1582-1707
occurrences.motif_label: compassionate offering to a suffering captive
occurrences.basis: Agnar gives Odin a horn of ale during the captivity, and this act is singled out as relieving Odin's severe thirst.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odin appears as Grimnir, refuses to explain himself, and Geirrod has him bound between two fires for eight days and nights without food. Agnar, secretly a menial in the palace, gives the captive a horn of ale.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS / INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN; lines 1709-1827
occurrences.motif_label: humane helper rewarded with kingship and prosperity
occurrences.basis: Agnar's humane act and ale-giving are repaid by Odin with the throne and future prosperity.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Geirrod draws his sword to kill the singer, is dismayed by a transformation, falls on the blade, and dies as Odin foretold; Odin then rewards Agnar with the throne and prosperity for his humanity and ale.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS / INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN; lines 1830-1874
occurrences.motif_label: sacred performance and gift reward
occurrences.basis: At Odin's shrine on festive occasions, scalds perform songs and receive golden bracelets or armlets as rewards.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The first festival toast was drunk in Odin's honour; the first of May and Woden's day were sacred to him; people assembled at his shrine to hear scalds, who received golden bracelets or armlets called Odin's serpents.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA; lines 1877-1990
occurrences.motif_label: bargain for concealment of wrongdoing
occurrences.basis: A dwarf prevents the statue from denouncing Frigga after she grants him a gracious smile.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Frigga steals gold from Odin's statue for a necklace made by dwarfs; Odin seeks to make the statue speak through runes; Fulla brings a dwarf who puts guards to sleep and breaks the statue.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA; lines 1992-2120
occurrences.motif_label: name confers obligation and gift
occurrences.basis: Frigga argues that because Odin has given the people a new name, custom requires him also to give a baptismal gift, identified as victory.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odin wakes, sees the armed host, asks what Longbeards they are, and Frigga says he has given them a new name and must give a baptismal gift.
Frigga urges Odin to give them victory; Odin, outwitted, does so, and the Winilers keep the name and receive his later care and blessings.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA; lines 2238-2359
occurrences.motif_label: Goddess in mountain cave grants a conditional gift
occurrences.basis: Holda offers the shepherd a choice, gives him blue flowers linked to his lifespan, and gives seed to sow.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The shepherd enters a jewelled stalactite cave, sees a silvery central woman with maidens, chooses blue flowers, and Holda gives them with a lifespan condition plus seed to sow.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA; lines 2238-2359
occurrences.motif_label: Meagre divine payment becomes gold
occurrences.basis: The wheelwright repairs Holda's chariot, keeps a few chips as payment, and finds them changed into gold.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A wheelwright repairs Holda's damaged chariot; told to keep chips as pay, he keeps a few and finds them changed to gold the next day.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA; lines 2362-2458
occurrences.motif_label: life-beginning egg gift
occurrences.basis: Coloured eggs are exchanged as presents and are explained as signs of the beginning of life and later of Resurrection.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Eástre/Ostara is described as a spring goddess identified with Frigga; her feast preserves customs of coloured eggs, flower-crowned Easter-stones, dancing, and bonfires.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA; lines 2362-2458
occurrences.motif_label: sacred procession that suspends warfare
occurrences.basis: Nerthus's yearly cow-drawn procession blesses the land; during her passage people cease warfare, lay aside weapons, and observe festal peace.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage connects Vrou-elde, the Milky Way name, Nerthus/Mother Earth, a guarded sacred car, a veiled yearly journey to bless the land, suspension of warfare, and ritual bathing in a secret lake that swallows assisting slaves.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR; lines 2611-2730
occurrences.motif_label: Wagered contest of craftsmanship with trickster interference
occurrences.basis: Loki wagers his head against Brock's claim about Sindri's superior skill, then interferes by becoming a gadfly and stinging Brock during the forging.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Brock says Sindri can make three superior objects; Loki wagers his head against Brock's on the result.
Sindri throws gold in the fire; Brock blows the bellows while Loki as a gadfly stings him; Sindri produces Gullin-bursti with luminous golden bristles and swift aerial travel.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR; lines 2733-2850
occurrences.motif_label: magical artifacts forged from fire and assigned to gods
occurrences.basis: The dwarfs produce divine objects from fire and the artifacts are presented to Odin, Frey, and Thor in the context of a wager.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sindri puts more gold on the fire and leaves Brock to blow the bellows; Loki, disguised as a gadfly, stings Brock, but Brock continues until Sindri draws out the ring Draupnir, which produces eight rings every ninth night and is called an emblem of fertility.

A lump of iron is cast in the flames; Loki again appears as a gadfly and stings Brock above the eye until blood blocks his sight. Brock briefly raises his hand, and the resulting hammer is short in the handle.

Brock presents Draupnir to Odin, Gullin-bursti to Frey, and Miölnir to Thor. Loki presents Gungnir to Odin, Skidbladnir to Frey, and golden hair to Thor; the hair grows on Sif's head. The gods judge Brock winner because Miölnir will be invaluable against frost giants on the last day.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR; lines 2942-3047
occurrences.motif_label: sacred hospitality restrains vengeance against an enemy guest
occurrences.basis: The Æsir host Hrungnir despite enmity and prevent Thor from shedding blood by invoking the sacred rights of hospitality.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Æsir host Hrungnir in their halls; after drinking heavenly mead he boasts that he will destroy Asgard and the gods while sparing Freya and Sif.
Thor returns, hears Hrungnir's threat concerning Sif, brandishes his hammer, is restrained by the gods because Hrungnir is a guest, and arranges a holmgang at Griottunagard three days later.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR; lines 3050-3168
occurrences.motif_label: theft of divine weapon with bride-ransom demand
occurrences.basis: Thrym steals and buries Thor's hammer and demands Freya as bride before returning it.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Thor wakes to find his hammer gone and warns Loki that giants might attack Asgard if they learn it is missing.
Loki borrows Freya's falcon plumes, flies to Jötun-heim, and learns that Thrym has buried the hammer and demands Freya as bride.
Freya rejects the proposal to marry Thrym; in her anger her necklace bursts.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR / CHAPTER V: TYR; lines 3614-3719
occurrences.motif_label: Bodily pledge enabling containment
occurrences.basis: Fenris requires a god’s hand in his mouth as a pledge before accepting the bond; Tyr gives the pledge and loses the hand once Fenris is captive.

evidence.quote_or_summary: With Gleipnir, the gods go with Fenris to Lyngvi in Lake Amsvartnir; Fenris mistrusts the slight bond and requires an Æsir to put a hand in his mouth as a good-faith pledge.
All the gods draw back except Tyr, who places his hand in Fenris’s jaws; the gods bind Fenris with Gleipnir, and when he cannot escape, he bites off Tyr’s hand at the wrist.
Quoted Eddic exchange: Loki says Fenris took Tyr’s right hand; Tyr replies, “I of a hand am wanting,” and says the wolf must remain in bonds until the gods’ destruction.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR / CHAPTER V: TYR / CHAPTER VI: BRAGI; lines 3722-3817
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom being made from a peace-making exchange
occurrences.basis: Kvasir is created from the saliva of reconciled divine groups and is described as wise, good, and beneficial to mankind.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After the Æsir and Vanas agree to peace, both parties spit into a vase; from this saliva the gods create Kvasir, a wise and good being who answers questions and benefits mankind.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR / CHAPTER V: TYR / CHAPTER VI: BRAGI; lines 3722-3817
occurrences.motif_label: ransom exchange for life after vengeance
occurrences.basis: Suttung threatens the dwarfs with death on a sea shoal, and they redeem their lives by promising the mead.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Suttung avenges Gilling by seizing the dwarfs and placing them on a sea shoal; they save themselves by promising the mead. Suttung gives it to Gunlod, who guards the three vessels in a hollow mountain, while Hugin and Munin discover the hiding place.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR / CHAPTER V: TYR / CHAPTER VI: BRAGI; lines 3968-3988
occurrences.motif_label: ritual toast with sacred sign and binding vow
occurrences.basis: The Bragaful involves a sacred hammer sign over a toast and a public pledge to perform a deed of valor within the year.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Bragaful toast is served in ship-shaped cups, and the sacred sign of the hammer is made over it.
The new ruler or family head vows to perform a deed of valor within the year; guests then make similar vows, and the source connects the custom with the verb "to brag."

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER IV: THOR / CHAPTER V: TYR / CHAPTER VI: BRAGI / CHAPTER VII: IDUN; lines 3991-4133
occurrences.motif_label: coerced ransom oath leading to betrayal
occurrences.basis: Loki promises any ransom for release and swears to lure Idun out of Asgard as the price of freedom.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An eagle in a tree prevents the fire from cooking the meat, bargains for food, then takes too much; Loki strikes it with a stake, but the stake adheres to both, and Loki is dragged until he promises ransom.
The seeming eagle is the storm giant Thiassi, who frees Loki only after Loki swears to lure Idun out of Asgard so Thiassi can obtain her and her fruit.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER IV: THOR / CHAPTER V: TYR / CHAPTER VI: BRAGI / CHAPTER VII: IDUN; lines 4277-4407
occurrences.motif_label: Divine hostage exchange after war
occurrences.basis: The passage says the Æsir and Vanir exchanged hostages after war, sending Hoenir to Vana-heim and Niörd with his children to Asgard.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Æsir and Vanir exchange hostages after war; Hoenir goes to Vana-heim, while Niörd, Frey, and Freya take up abode in Asgard.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CONTENTS / LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS / INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING; lines 865-877
occurrences.motif_label: treaty ratified by exchange of hostages
occurrences.basis: The treaty between the Æsir and Vanas is explicitly ratified by exchanging hostages, including named divine figures relocating between realms.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The two sides conclude that unity brings strength, compose their differences, make peace, and ratify the treaty by exchanging hostages.
Niörd comes to Asgard with his children Frey and Freya, while Hoenir, Odin's brother, takes up residence in Vana-heim.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XX / BOOK XXI / BOOK XXII / BOOK XXIII; lines 10298-10348
occurrences.motif_label: hospitable conveyance home with gifts
occurrences.basis: The Phaeacians treat Ulysses as though divine, send him home by ship, and give him gold, bronze, and clothing.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Phaeacians treat Ulysses as though he were a god, send him to his country by ship with gifts, and then deep sleep overtakes him and eases his sorrows.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: HENRY FESTING JONES. / THE ODYSSEY / BOOK I / BOOK II; lines 1038-1133
occurrences.motif_label: ritual offering before or during voyage
occurrences.basis: After the ship is underway, the men fill mixing bowls and make drink offerings to the immortal gods, especially Minerva.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The crew secures the ship, fills mixing bowls, makes drink offerings to the immortal gods, especially the grey-eyed daughter of Jove, and sails through the night until dawn.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XXII / BOOK XXIII / BOOK XXIV / FOOTNOTES:; lines 11174-11276
occurrences.motif_label: sacred offering to deity
occurrences.basis: The note discusses a drink-offering to Jove, Neptune, or Mercury and mentions Echeneus proposing an offering to Jove.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The note says the final drink-offering should have gone to Jove or Neptune; it also says Echeneus proposes a drink-offering to Jove and characterizes Mercury as the god of thievishness and rascality likely to be useful to the Phaeacians.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XXII / BOOK XXIII / BOOK XXIV / FOOTNOTES:; lines 11174-11276
occurrences.motif_label: gift promise and withheld gift
occurrences.basis: The note contrasts a goblet that Alcinous says he will give with actual gifts of a chest, cloak, and shirt.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The note says Alcinous never actually gives the goblet, though he gives a chest, cloak, and shirt and probably supplies corn and wine.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I / BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS.; lines 1136-1230
occurrences.motif_label: ritual sacrifice and feast before inquiry
occurrences.basis: The Pylians sacrifice bulls to Neptune, share meat and wine, pray, and only after the meal does Nestor ask the strangers' identity.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Pylians gather on the seashore to sacrifice black bulls to Neptune; nine guilds of five hundred men each have nine bulls per guild, eating inward meats and burning thigh bones on embers.
Pisistratus gives the strangers inward meats, pours wine into a golden cup, and hands it first to Minerva.
Pisistratus asks Minerva to pray to Neptune and make a drink offering, then pass the cup to her companion; he says precedence is given to her as the older guest.
Minerva prays to Neptune to grant the prayers, bless Nestor and his sons, reward the Pylians for the hecatomb, and grant success to Telemachus and herself.
Minerva passes the cup to Telemachus, who prays likewise; the roasted meat is served and all eat and drink.
After dinner Nestor asks the strangers who they are, from what port they sailed, and whether they are traders or sea rovers.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I / BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS.; lines 1136-1230
occurrences.motif_label: hospitality to unknown strangers
occurrences.basis: The strangers are welcomed, seated, fed, and included in prayer before being questioned about their identity.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The strangers are welcomed, taken by the hand, and seated by Pisistratus on soft sheepskins near Nestor and Thrasymedes.
Pisistratus gives the strangers inward meats, pours wine into a golden cup, and hands it first to Minerva.
Pisistratus asks Minerva to pray to Neptune and make a drink offering, then pass the cup to her companion; he says precedence is given to her as the older guest.
After dinner Nestor asks the strangers who they are, from what port they sailed, and whether they are traders or sea rovers.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I / BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS.; lines 1424-1514
occurrences.motif_label: Sacred exchange of divine favor and vowed offering
occurrences.basis: Nestor asks Minerva to send grace upon himself and his household and promises a valuable heifer in return.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva flies away as an eagle; Nestor marvels, recognizes Jove's daughter, prays for favor upon himself and household, and vows an unyoked heifer with gilded horns.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS. / BOOK IV; lines 1561-1661
occurrences.motif_label: hospitality to unknown strangers before inquiry
occurrences.basis: Menelaus orders that the strangers' horses be tended and that they be brought in for supper; he welcomes them to eat before asking their identity.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Menelaus orders: "Take their horses out, of course, and show the strangers in that they may have supper."
Menelaus welcomes them to eat, says he will ask who they are afterward, and says they must descend from sceptre-bearing kings; he gives them a prime piece of roast loin.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS. / BOOK IV; lines 1762-1847
occurrences.motif_label: Guest hospitality after heroic narration
occurrences.basis: After the exchange of stories, Helen orders beds, coverings, cloaks, and servants for the guests.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus comments sadly on Ulysses and asks for sleep; Helen orders beds made with rugs, coverlets, and cloaks; servants carry a torch, make the beds, and the guests sleep in the forecourt.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: The Odyssey / PREFACE TO FIRST EDITION; lines 187-272
occurrences.motif_label: sacrifice and divine favor questioned
occurrences.basis: Poseidon receives a hecatomb, and Athene reminds Zeus of Odysseus' sacrifices in Trojan land while questioning Zeus' anger.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Poseidon has gone to the distant Ethiopians to receive a hecatomb of bulls and rams and feast, while the other gods gather in Zeus' halls.
Athene asks whether Odysseus made free offerings of sacrifice to Zeus by the Argive ships in Trojan land and asks why Zeus was angry with him.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS. / BOOK IV; lines 2041-2133
occurrences.motif_label: hospitality exchange of prestige gifts
occurrences.basis: Menelaus offers Telemachus gifts, modifies the gift to suit the guest, and gives a precious vessel with divine craftsmanship and royal provenance.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Menelaus asks Telemachus to stay ten or twelve days more and offers a chariot, three horses, and a beautiful chalice for remembering him during drink-offerings to the immortal gods.
Telemachus says he would enjoy staying but must return to his crew at Pylos; he asks for plate rather than horses because Ithaca lacks open fields and racecourses and is better suited for goats.
Menelaus takes Telemachus' hand, praises his good family, and promises a pure silver mixing bowl with gold-inlaid rim, made by Vulcan and given by Phaedimus, king of the Sidonians.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS. / BOOK IV; lines 2135-2239
occurrences.motif_label: prayer invoking prior sacrifice for divine aid
occurrences.basis: Penelope prays to Minerva to remember Ulysses' past burned offerings and save Telemachus; the goddess hears the prayer.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Penelope stops crying, washes, changes clothes, goes upstairs with the maids, places bruised barley in a basket, and begins praying to Minerva.
Penelope asks Minerva to remember if Ulysses “burned you fat thigh bones of sheep or heifer” and to save her son from the suitors.
Penelope cries aloud and the goddess hears her prayer.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS. / BOOK IV / BOOK V; lines 2289-2384
occurrences.motif_label: divine hospitality with ambrosia and nectar
occurrences.basis: Calypso welcomes Mercury, seats him, and serves ambrosia and nectar before he states his mission.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Calypso recognizes Mercury, welcomes him, offers to do what he asks if possible, and sets ambrosia and red nectar before him.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS. / BOOK IV / BOOK V; lines 2386-2472
occurrences.motif_label: solemn divine oath as guarantee of safe counsel
occurrences.basis: Ulysses demands an oath before accepting Calypso's plan, and Calypso swears by heaven, earth, and Styx that she means no harm.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses shudders, suspects a hidden motive, says a raft is dreadful for such a distant voyage, and requires Calypso to swear she means no mischief.
Calypso smiles, caresses Ulysses, and swears by heaven, earth, and the waters of Styx that she means him no harm and is advising him honestly.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS. / BOOK IV / BOOK V; lines 2561-2653
occurrences.motif_label: divine helper gives protective object for a dangerous crossing
occurrences.basis: Ino gives Ulysses an enchanted veil that prevents harm while he swims, with instructions for its return to the sea after landfall.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ino says Neptune is angrily troubling Ulysses but will not kill him; she tells him to abandon the raft, swim to the Phaeacian coast, wear her enchanted veil, and throw it back into the sea after reaching land.
Ino takes off her veil, gives it to Ulysses, dives like a sea-gull, and vanishes beneath the dark blue waters.

Neptune sends a great wave that breaks the raft; Ulysses rides a plank, removes Calypso's clothes, binds Ino's veil under his arms, plunges into the sea to swim, and Neptune taunts him before driving to Aegae.

occurrences.motif_label: return of a divine token after rescue
occurrences.basis: Ulysses returns the scarf that Ino had given him by casting it into the salt stream, and Ino receives it from the wave.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After recovering breath, Ulysses removes Ino's scarf and throws it back into the salt stream; Ino receives it from the wave.

occurrences.motif_label: Protected hospitality for distressed foreigners
occurrences.basis: Nausicaa promises clothing and aid and says distressed strangers and foreigners are under Jove’s protection before ordering food, drink, and washing.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Nausicaa calls Ulysses sensible, says Jove distributes prosperity, promises clothes and other reasonable aid, identifies the Phaeacians, and names herself daughter of Alcinous.

Nausicaa tells her maids not to fear Ulysses, says the Phaeacians are dear to the gods and live apart by the sea, identifies him as a poor lost man, states that distressed strangers are under Jove’s protection, and orders food, drink, and washing in a sheltered stream.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV / BOOK V / BOOK VI / THE MEETING BETWEEN NAUSICAA AND ULYSSES.; lines 2882-2972
occurrences.motif_label: Hospitality to an unknown stranger
occurrences.basis: The stranger receives shelter, clothing, oil, food, and instructions leading toward further aid.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The maids stop fleeing, seat Ulysses in shelter, bring a shirt, cloak, and golden cruse of oil, and tell him to wash in the stream.
Food and drink are set before Ulysses, who eats and drinks ravenously because he has long been without food.
Nausicaa describes the route to town, its wall, harbors, narrow entrance, ships, marketplace, temple of Neptune, ship gear, oar-making, and Phaeacian seafaring identity.

evidence.locator: lines 2970-2972 and following passage text in supplied range
evidence.quote_or_summary: Nausicaa instructs Ulysses to ask for Alcinous's house, pass through gates and courts, approach her mother by the fire as she spins purple wool, clasp her knees, and gain hope of returning home.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey

occurrences.motif_label: prayer for aid before entering a host community
occurrences.basis: Ulysses prays to Minerva for pity and asks to find friends and be hospitably received by the Phaeacians.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses asks Minerva to hear him, recalls that she did not heed him when Neptune was wrecking him, and asks to “find friends and be hospitably received by the Phaeacians.”

occurrences.motif_label: supplication at knees of royal woman
occurrences.basis: Ulysses places his hands on Arete's knees and asks for help returning home; this act initiates the host's obligations toward him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses reaches Arete and Alcinous, lays hands upon the queen's knees, the miraculous darkness falls away, and those present are surprised to see him.
Ulysses addresses Queen Arete, her husband, and the guests, praying for help to return to his own country after long trouble away from friends.

Echeneus, an elder and excellent speaker, tells Alcinous it is improper for a stranger to sit among hearth ashes and urges him to seat the stranger, mix wine and water, make offering to Jove, and provide supper.
Alcinous raises Ulysses from the hearth, seats him in Laodamas's place, and servants bring washing water in gold and silver vessels, a table, bread, and food; Ulysses eats and drinks.

occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VI / THE MEETING BETWEEN NAUSICAA AND ULYSSES. / BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS.; lines 3090-3174

occurrences.basis: Ulysses sits among the hearth ashes; Echeneus insists this is improper, and Alcinous raises him, seats him, feeds him, and makes offerings for the suppliant.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After speaking, Ulysses sits on the hearth among the ashes; the assembly remains silent until Echeneus speaks.

Echeneus, an elder and excellent speaker, tells Alcinous it is improper for a stranger to sit among hearth ashes and urges him to seat the stranger, mix wine and water, make offering to Jove, and provide supper.
Alcinous raises Ulysses from the hearth, seats him in Laodamas's place, and servants bring washing water in gold and silver vessels, a table, bread, and food; Ulysses eats and drinks.
Alcinous orders Pontonous to mix wine and water and circulate it for drink offerings to Jove, protector of well-disposed suppliants; the offerings are made and the company drinks.

occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VI / THE MEETING BETWEEN NAUSICAA AND ULYSSES. / BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS.; lines 3176-3259
occurrences.motif_label: guest aid through food, clothing, and escort
occurrences.basis: Ulysses receives or requests food, clothing, washing, and escort from hosts and helpers after shipwreck.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses asks to sup despite sorrow and asks that at daybreak they help him get home.
Everyone approves arranging an escort; drink offerings are made, and the others go home.
Arete recognizes the shirt, cloak, and clothes as work of herself and her maids and questions Ulysses.
The daughter gives Ulysses bread, wine, washing in the river, and the clothes he is wearing.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VI / THE MEETING BETWEEN NAUSICAA AND ULYSSES. / BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS.; lines 3261-3292
occurrences.motif_label: hospitality exchange between royal host and stranger
occurrences.basis: Alcinous offers Ulysses lodging, possible marriage alliance, property, and safe transport; Arete arranges bedding for him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Alcinous wishes Ulysses would stay, marry his daughter, become his son-in-law, and receive a house and estate.
Alcinous says no one shall keep Ulysses there against his will and promises to address the matter of his escort the next day.
Alcinous says Ulysses can sleep during the voyage while men sail him over smooth waters to his own home or wherever he wishes.
Arete orders her maids to set a bed in the gatehouse room with red rugs, coverlets, and woollen cloaks for Ulysses.
The maids go out with torches, make the bed, and tell Ulysses to come because his bed is ready; he is glad to rest.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE MEETING BETWEEN NAUSICAA AND ULYSSES. / BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS. / BOOK VIII; lines 3295-3396
occurrences.motif_label: guest-host exchange through hospitality and conveyance
occurrences.basis: Alcinous receives the stranger, organizes a feast, and orders a ship and crew for his onward journey, saying such escort has been given to others before.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Alcinous tells the Phaeacian leaders that the stranger wants an escort, orders a new ship and fifty-two young sailors prepared, and invites the leaders to help entertain the guest with Demodocus singing.
Crowds fill the outer buildings, yards, and precincts, and Alcinous slaughters twelve sheep, eight grown pigs, and two oxen for a magnificent banquet.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: THE MEETING BETWEEN NAUSICAA AND ULYSSES. / BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS. / BOOK VIII; lines 3599-3696
occurrences.motif_label: hospitality gift exchange for a departing guest
occurrences.basis: Alcinous commands clothing, gold, and a goblet for Ulysses; Euryalus adds a sword with apology; Arete packs the gifts for travel.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Alcinous says the guest has singular judgment and orders thirteen leaders to give clothing and gold; he says Euryalus must apologize and give a present.
Euryalus promises satisfaction, gives Ulysses a bronze sword with silver hilt and ivory scabbard, apologizes, and wishes him a safe return.
Alcinous tells Arete to fetch the best chest, pack clothing and gifts, heat water for a bath, and says he will give Ulysses a golden goblet for future drink offerings.
Arete’s maids place a tripod full of bath water on a clear fire; Arete brings a chest and packs gold, raiment, cloak, and shirt inside it.
“for fear any one should rob you by the way when you are asleep in your ship”

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: THE MEETING BETWEEN NAUSICAA AND ULYSSES. / BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS. / BOOK VIII; lines 3698-3785
occurrences.motif_label: guest and suppliant honored through feast, gifts, and escort
occurrences.basis: Alcinous describes the festivities, presents, and escort as being in the guest's honor and states that a guest and suppliant should be treated like a brother.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Alcinous tells the Phaeacian leaders to stop Demodocus's song because the guest has been groaning and lamenting, and the festivities, escort, and presents are in his honor.
"he ought to treat a guest and a suppliant as though he were his own brother"
Alcinous asks the guest to end concealment, state the name given by his parents, and identify his country, nation, and city so Phaeacian ships can take him there.

occurrences.motif_label: sacrificial exchange with gods
occurrences.basis: Neptune accepts a hecatomb among the Ethiopians, and Minerva reminds Jove that Ulysses offered many burnt sacrifices before Troy.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Neptune has gone to the Ethiopians at the world's end to accept a hecatomb, while the other gods meet at the house of Olympian Jove.

Minerva says her heart bleeds for Ulysses on a lonely sea-girt forest island, where Atlas' daughter keeps him with blandishments so that he longs for home; she also recalls his burnt sacrifices to Jove.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS. / BOOK VIII / BOOK IX; lines 3900-3994
occurrences.motif_label: Hospitality test and expected guest-gift
occurrences.basis: Odysseus frames the visit as an inquiry into whether the people are hospitable and later waits for the cave owner because he hopes for a present.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odysseus says he will go with his ship to see whether the people are “uncivilised savages, or a hospitable and humane race.”
The men ask to steal cheeses and livestock and return to the ship, but Odysseus refuses because he wants to see the owner and hopes for a present.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey

occurrences.motif_label: Violated hospitality toward suppliants
occurrences.basis: Ulysses asks for hospitality and visitor gifts under Jove's protection, while the Cyclops refuses and attacks the guests.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses says they are Achaeans returning from Troy, driven off course, and asks the Cyclops for hospitality and visitor gifts under Jove's protection.
The Cyclops calls Ulysses foolish, denies fearing the gods or Jove, claims Cyclopes are stronger, and asks where the ship is fastened.
The Cyclops seizes two men, kills and eats them, drinks milk, sleeps among the sheep, and Ulysses refrains from stabbing him because the stone would trap them.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS. / BOOK VIII / BOOK IX; lines 4170-4268
occurrences.motif_label: Hospitality violation punished by gods
occurrences.basis: Ulysses accuses Polyphemus of eating visitors in his house and says Jove and the other gods have punished him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses taunts the Cyclops for eating visitors in his cave and says, “Jove and the other gods have punished you.”

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS. / BOOK VIII / BOOK IX; lines 4270-4293
occurrences.motif_label: division of captured livestock
occurrences.basis: The Cyclops' sheep are landed and divided equitably, with the ram assigned to Ulysses as an extra share.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At the island where the rest of the ships were left, the returning men find comrades lamenting and waiting, beach the vessel, land the Cyclops' sheep, and divide them equitably.
Ulysses receives the ram as an extra share, sacrifices it on the sea shore, burns its thigh bones to Jove, but Jove does not heed the sacrifice and thinks of destroying the ships and comrades.

occurrences.motif_label: harm-preventing oath before union
occurrences.basis: Ulysses requires a solemn oath of non-harm before agreeing to go to bed with Circe.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses says he will not go to bed with Circe unless she swears not to harm him; she swears, and he then goes to bed with her.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VIII / BOOK IX / BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE.; lines 4680-4781
occurrences.motif_label: offerings and blood sacrifice to summon or manage the dead
occurrences.basis: Circe prescribes libations, prayers, promised sacrifices, animal sacrifice, and guarding the blood until Teiresias answers.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Circe instructs Ulysses to dig a cubit-sized trench, pour libations of honey-milk, wine, and water with barley, pray to the ghosts, and promise sacrifices including a black sheep for Teiresias.
Circe instructs sacrifice of a ram and black ewe, prayers to Hades and Proserpine, and guarding the blood with a drawn sword until Teiresias comes and tells Ulysses how to reach home.

occurrences.motif_label: blood offering enabling speech with the dead
occurrences.basis: Teiresias explains that ghosts who taste the blood may speak, and Odysseus' mother recognizes him after tasting it.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “Any ghost that you let taste of the blood will talk with you like a reasonable being” while those denied blood will go away.
Teiresias returns to the house of Hades after speaking his prophecies; Odysseus remains until his mother tastes the blood, recognizes him, and speaks fondly.

occurrences.motif_label: food and information exchange with a guest
occurrences.basis: Telemachus offers food before requesting the visitor’s identity, origin, ship, and relation to his father’s house.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus sees Minerva while brooding among the suitors, goes to the gate, takes her hand and spear, welcomes her, and offers food before questions.
Servants bring washing water in a golden ewer and silver basin, a clean table, bread, meats, cups of gold, and wine.

Telemachus says the suitors’ entertainment is paid for from his absent father’s goods, imagines their fear if Ulysses returned, says he does not expect to see him again, and asks the visitor’s identity, origin, ship, people, and prior connection to the house.

occurrences.motif_label: blood enabling ordered communication with the dead
occurrences.basis: The ghosts gather around blood, and the narrator prevents them from drinking all at once so each can be questioned.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Proserpine sends up ghosts of famous wives and daughters; they gather around blood, and the narrator draws his blade to prevent them all from drinking at once while he questions them one by one about lineage.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE. / BOOK XI / THE VISIT TO THE DEAD.88; lines 4969-5068
occurrences.motif_label: bride won through cattle raid condition
occurrences.basis: Neleus will give Pero only to whoever raids Iphicles' cattle, and the seer who attempts it is captured and later released.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Chloris marries Neleus after priceless presents and bears several children including Pero; Neleus sets a cattle raid as the condition for marrying Pero, and an unnamed seer is captured, imprisoned for a year, and later released after expounding oracles.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE. / BOOK XI / THE VISIT TO THE DEAD.88; lines 5070-5169
occurrences.motif_label: generous host gift and escort for a returning guest
occurrences.basis: The Phaeacian hosts discuss gifts, delay, and escort for Ulysses' homeward return.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The queen asks the Phaeacians whether Ulysses is tall, good-looking, and clever, and urges them not to send him away hastily or be stingy with gifts.
Alcinous says Ulysses should stay until tomorrow while gifts are gathered and that escorting him concerns all the Phaeacians, especially himself.
Ulysses says he would gladly stay even twelve months if then sent home with noble gifts, returning to Ithaca fuller-handed and more respected.

occurrences.motif_label: Departure with escort and gifts
occurrences.basis: Ulysses is sent off with gifts, provisions, an escort, prayers, and drink-offerings.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Alcinous notes the guest's packed gifts of clothing, gold, and valuables and proposes additional tripods and cauldrons from the Phaeacians.
Ulysses bids farewell, asks for drink-offerings, thanks the Phaeacians for escort and gifts, and wishes peace and good fortune to their households and people.
Alcinous orders Pontonous to mix wine for prayer to father Jove; the people make drink-offerings, and Ulysses places the double cup in Arete's hands and bids her farewell.
Ulysses crosses the threshold; Alcinous sends a guide, Arete sends maidservants with clothing, a strong box, corn, and wine, and the crew puts these and other provisions aboard.

occurrences.passage_locator: PREFACE TO SECOND EDITION / HENRY FESTING JONES. / THE ODYSSEY / BOOK I; lines 589-680
occurrences.motif_label: deferred reciprocal gift between host and divine guest
occurrences.basis: Telemachus offers a keepsake gift; Minerva tells him to keep it until she returns and promises an equivalent gift in return.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus thanks the visitor as one speaking to him like a son and offers bath, refreshment, and a valuable keepsake. Minerva refuses delay and tells him to keep the gift until her return, when she will reciprocate with one of equal value.

occurrences.motif_label: Offering promised to local divinities after safe return
occurrences.basis: Ulysses promises offerings to the Naiad nymphs if Minerva grants him life and brings his son to manhood.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva disperses the mist; Ulysses sees his land, rejoices, kisses the soil, lifts his hands, and prays to the Naiad nymphs with a promise of offerings.

occurrences.motif_label: hospitality to the stranger under divine sanction
occurrences.basis: Eumaeus welcomes the stranger with shelter, bread, wine, bedding, and meat, and explicitly says strangers and beggars are from Jove.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Eumaeus tells the old man the dogs nearly attacked him, laments his lost master, and invites him inside for bread and wine before telling his story.
Eumaeus leads Ulysses into the hut, lays down rushes and a chamois skin, and Ulysses asks Jove and the gods to reward the welcome.

Eumaeus says it is wrong to insult even a poorer stranger because all strangers and beggars are from Jove; he laments his absent master and connects his absence to Helen, Ilius, the Trojans, and Agamemnon.
Eumaeus sacrifices two young pigs, prepares and cooks them, serves them to Ulysses, who sprinkles barley meal, and mixes wine in an ivy-wood bowl.

occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XIII / ULYSSES LEAVES SCHERIA AND RETURNS TO ITHACA. / BOOK XIV / ULYSSES IN THE HUT WITH EUMAEUS.; lines 6196-6288
occurrences.motif_label: hospitality exchange with news, oath, and delayed reward
occurrences.basis: The stranger is fed and given wine, discusses news of the absent master, invokes hospitality in an oath, and refuses a shirt and cloak until his report proves true.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses eats and drinks ravenously without speaking while brooding revenge; the swineherd fills his usual bowl with wine and gives it to him.

Ulysses swears by king Jove, the rites of hospitality, and Ulysses' hearth that Ulysses will return within the year and take vengeance on those mistreating his wife and son; he refuses reward until this occurs.

occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XIII / ULYSSES LEAVES SCHERIA AND RETURNS TO ITHACA. / BOOK XIV / ULYSSES IN THE HUT WITH EUMAEUS.; lines 6374-6464
occurrences.motif_label: guest protected by sacred hospitality
occurrences.basis: Eumaeus treats the stranger kindly out of respect for Jove as god of hospitality and refuses to kill a received guest.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Eumaeus says he will treat the stranger kindly only "out of respect for Jove the god of hospitality" and from fear and pity.
Eumaeus says he would be disgraced if he killed the stranger after receiving him into his hut and showing him hospitality.

occurrences.motif_label: oath or wager before the gods
occurrences.basis: Ulysses proposes a bargain about the master's return and calls all the gods in heaven to witness it.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses proposes that all the gods witness a bargain: if the master comes home, he receives clothing and passage; if not, Eumaeus' men may throw him from a precipice as a warning to lying tramps.

occurrences.motif_label: Ritual offering before communal meal
occurrences.basis: The passage describes a burnt sacrifice and drink-offering to the immortal gods before eating and drinking.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A first piece is offered as burnt sacrifice to the immortal gods; a drink-offering follows; Mesaulius brings bread, the group eats and drinks, and the remainder is removed before bed.
