occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XIII / ULYSSES LEAVES SCHERIA AND RETURNS TO ITHACA. / BOOK XIV / ULYSSES IN THE HUT WITH EUMAEUS.; lines 6466-6544
occurrences.motif_label: Hospitality to a stranger in distress
occurrences.basis: Eumaeus states that the stranger will not lack clothing or other reasonable needs and then gives him bedding and a cloak.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Eumaeus praises the story and says the old man will lack neither clothing nor other reasonable needs for the present, though the next morning he must wear his old rags again until Ulysses’ son can provide cloak and shirt.
Eumaeus makes a bed for Ulysses from goatskins and sheepskins before the fire and covers him with a heavy cloak kept for unusually bad weather.

occurrences.motif_label: guest-host farewell gift exchange
occurrences.basis: Pisistratus and Menelaus both emphasize proper guest-host farewell practice, and Menelaus gives valuable parting gifts to Telemachus.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva returns to Olympus; Telemachus wakes Pisistratus and calls for the horses and chariot, while Pisistratus says they should wait until morning for Menelaus’s gifts and farewell.
At daybreak Menelaus meets Telemachus, agrees not to detain him, explains proper treatment of a guest, and offers gifts, dinner, and even a tour through Hellas or the Peloponnese.

Menelaus wishes Telemachus safe return, presents a silver mixing bowl with a gold-inlaid rim said to be Vulcan’s work and received from Phaedimus, gives the double cup, and Helen stands by with the robe.

occurrences.passage_locator: ULYSSES LEAVES SCHERIA AND RETURNS TO ITHACA. / BOOK XIV / ULYSSES IN THE HUT WITH EUMAEUS. / BOOK XV; lines 6650-6731
occurrences.motif_label: hospitality gifts and guest-friendship exchange
occurrences.basis: The passage includes Helen's keepsake, Menelaus's beautiful presents, a formal meal, and hospitable lodging at Pherae.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Helen gives Telemachus a robe as a keepsake for his future bride and says his mother should keep it until the wedding day.
Pisistratus puts the presents into the chariot and admires them.
Menelaus brings the guests inside for a meal; servants provide handwashing water, bread, meat, and wine, and the guests eat and drink.
The travelers drive through town and open country, reach Pherae, spend the night with Diocles, are treated hospitably, and continue toward Pylos at dawn.
Pisistratus decides to turn toward the ship, places Menelaus's gifts of gold and raiment in the stern, and urges Telemachus to board before Nestor can come fetch him.

occurrences.passage_locator: ULYSSES LEAVES SCHERIA AND RETURNS TO ITHACA. / BOOK XIV / ULYSSES IN THE HUT WITH EUMAEUS. / BOOK XV; lines 6834-6930
occurrences.motif_label: Hospitality as setting for reciprocal sorrow-telling
occurrences.basis: The hut scene joins food, wine, shelter, and narration of remembered misfortunes between host and guest.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Eumaeus tells the stranger to sit, drink wine, and listen during the long night, saying that those who have suffered take pleasure in recalling old sorrows.

occurrences.motif_label: revenge vow with promised offerings
occurrences.basis: Telemachus instructs Penelope to promise hecatombs to the gods if Jove grants revenge, and Penelope makes the vow.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus tells Penelope not to scold him after his narrow escape, but to wash, change dress, go upstairs with her maids, and promise hecatombs to all the gods if Jove grants revenge upon the suitors.
Penelope obeys, washes, changes dress, and vows full hecatombs to the gods if they grant revenge upon the suitors.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XV / BOOK XVI / ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII; lines 7434-7526
occurrences.motif_label: formal guest hospitality
occurrences.basis: Theoclymenus is brought home and receives bathing, anointing, clothing, hand-washing, and a meal.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus takes Theoclymenus home; they lay down cloaks, bathe, are washed and anointed by maids, receive cloaks and shirts, wash hands from a golden ewer into a silver basin, and eat bread and other food.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XV / BOOK XVI / ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII; lines 7528-7613
occurrences.motif_label: Hospitality and reciprocal gift promise
occurrences.basis: Nestor's hospitable reception of Telemachus and Penelope's promise of gifts to Theoclymenus both frame social exchange around guest-host relations.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus tells Penelope that Nestor hosted him like a son, knew nothing of Ulysses' fate, and sent him with horses and chariot to Menelaus; he also says he saw Helen at Lacedaemon.
Penelope says that if Theoclymenus' words come true, he will receive gifts and good will from her.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XV / BOOK XVI / ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII; lines 7717-7818
occurrences.motif_label: Hospitality and refusal of giving
occurrences.basis: Food is sent to the stranger; several suitors give bread and meat, while Antinous resists giving and is criticized for preferring to eat rather than give.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus takes bread and meat and tells Eumaeus to take it to the stranger and tell him to beg from the suitors.
Telemachus tells Antinous to give something to the stranger, but says he knows Antinous is more fond of eating than giving.
Antinous replies harshly, draws the stool from under his feet as if to throw it at Ulysses, while the other suitors give food and fill Ulysses's wallet.
Ulysses asks Antinous for a gift, says Antinous seems a chief and should be a better giver, and recalls that he was once wealthy and gave to tramps.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XV / BOOK XVI / ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII; lines 7820-7923
occurrences.motif_label: Truth-tested stranger rewarded with clothing
occurrences.basis: Penelope promises the stranger a shirt and cloak if she is satisfied that he is speaking the truth about Ulysses.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus sneezes loudly as Penelope speaks; Penelope laughs and interprets it as meaning that all the suitors will be killed, then promises the stranger clothing if she believes him truthful.
Eumaeus relays Penelope's summons and tells the stranger she will give him a shirt and cloak if satisfied that he speaks the truth.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XVI / ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII / BOOK XVIII; lines 8074-8175
occurrences.motif_label: ritual libation before ominous departure
occurrences.basis: Ulysses makes a drink-offering, drinks, returns the cup, and Amphinomus departs with foreboding of evil.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses makes a drink-offering, drinks, returns the gold cup, and Amphinomus walks away serious with foreboding; the narration says Minerva doomed him to fall by Telemachus.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XVI / ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII / BOOK XVIII; lines 8177-8277
occurrences.motif_label: courtship exchange violated and restored through gifts
occurrences.basis: Penelope contrasts proper wooing, which includes feast animals and gifts, with the suitors' consumption of the household; the suitors then provide costly presents.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Penelope replies that heaven took her beauty when Ulysses sailed to Troy; she recalls his instruction to care for the household and remarry when their son grew a beard; she criticizes the suitors for consuming property instead of following courtship custom with feasts and presents.

Antinous allows Penelope to accept presents but says the suitors will not leave until she marries the best man among them; the suitors bring a decorated dress, gold brooches, a gold and amber chain, earrings, a necklace, and other presents.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XVI / ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII / BOOK XVIII; lines 8279-8350
occurrences.motif_label: Sacral closure of a disorderly feast through libation
occurrences.basis: After disorder and counsel against violence, wine and water are distributed and drink-offerings are made to the gods before the suitors depart.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Amphinomus advises the suitors not to take offense and not to do violence to the stranger or to any of Ulysses’ servants, leaving the stranger to Telemachus.
Mulius mixes wine and water, it is handed around, drink-offerings are made to the gods, and the suitors go to their own homes.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII / BOOK XVIII / BOOK XIX; lines 8620-8703
occurrences.motif_label: sacrificial exchange with gods and uncertain favor
occurrences.basis: Euryclea says Ulysses offered sacrifices to Jove but was still prevented from returning, while Autolycus’ offerings to Mercury are linked to Mercury’s favor.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Euryclea covers her face, weeps, laments Ulysses, says Jove hates him despite sacrifices and prayers, and says Jove has prevented him from reaching home.
Autolycus is described as the most accomplished thief and perjurer; Mercury endowed him with this gift and enjoyed his companionship because of offerings of thigh bones of goats and kids.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII / BOOK XVIII / BOOK XIX; lines 8705-8786
occurrences.motif_label: hospitality feast before hunt
occurrences.basis: Autolycus’ household welcomes Ulysses, prepares a bull, feasts, and later gives him splendid presents.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses goes to Parnassus to receive gifts from Autolycus; he is welcomed by Autolycus, his sons, and Amphithea, and the household prepares a bull and feasts until sunset.

The sons of Autolycus tend the boar carcass, bind Ulysses’ wound, say a spell to stop bleeding, and later Autolycus and his sons heal Ulysses, give him presents, send him to Ithaca, where he tells his parents how he got the scar.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XVII / BOOK XVIII / BOOK XIX / BOOK XX; lines 9045-9146
occurrences.motif_label: Violation and defense of guest treatment
occurrences.basis: Telemachus protects the stranger as a guest, while Ctesippus throws a heifer’s foot at him and Telemachus condemns insults to guests.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus seats Ulysses at a small table with food and wine in a gold cup, warns the suitors not to use gibes or blows, and says the house belongs to Ulysses and has passed to him.
Ctesippus calls his action a present for the stranger, throws a heifer’s foot at Ulysses, and misses when Ulysses turns aside; the object hits the wall.

Telemachus tells Ctesippus he would have speared him if he had hit the stranger, says he is now grown enough to understand good and evil, and denounces the suitors for consuming livestock, grain, and wine, insulting guests, and abusing women servants.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XVIII / BOOK XIX / BOOK XX / BOOK XXI; lines 9218-9315
occurrences.motif_label: Friendship sealed by reciprocal gift of weapons
occurrences.basis: Iphitus gives Ulysses the bow, Ulysses gives a sword and spear in return, and the passage says this begins a fast friendship.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The bow's history is recounted: Iphitus and Ulysses meet while pursuing lost livestock; Iphitus gives Ulysses the bow, Ulysses gives a sword and spear in return, and Hercules later kills Iphitus as his guest and keeps the mares.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XVIII / BOOK XIX / BOOK XX / BOOK XXI; lines 9416-9503
occurrences.motif_label: offering before dangerous or decisive action
occurrences.basis: The suitors make drink-offerings and Antinous proposes sacrificing goat thigh bones to Apollo before resuming the bow trial.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Antinous says it is Apollo's feast, advises putting aside the bow, calls for drink-offerings, and proposes goat thigh bones for Apollo before trying the bow again.
Servants wash guests' hands, pages mix wine and water, drink-offerings are made, and Ulysses craftily begins to speak.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 1675-1779
occurrences.motif_label: votive reward for inspired or superior speech
occurrences.basis: Phaedrus promises to set up golden images at Delphi if Socrates produces a new and better oration.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Phaedrus asks Socrates to make a new and better oration and promises, like the nine Archons, to set up golden images at Delphi of both of them.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2551-2634
occurrences.motif_label: Sacred pledges between lovers
occurrences.basis: The pair are said to have given and taken the most sacred pledges, which they must not break into enmity.

evidence.quote_or_summary: If they leave philosophy for ambition, wine, or carelessness, the wanton animals bring the souls together in bodily desire; afterward the pair consider that they have exchanged sacred pledges and must not break them into enmity.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2636-2763
occurrences.motif_label: divine messenger reports human honor to heavenly patrons
occurrences.basis: After death, the grasshoppers go to the Muses in heaven and inform them which people honor the Muses on earth; the Muses' favor is associated with different human activities.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The former humans live again as grasshoppers, do not hunger or thirst, sing from birth without eating or drinking, and after death go to the Muses in heaven to report who honors them.
The grasshoppers' reports win the love of Terpsichore for dancers, Erato for lovers, and Calliope and Urania for philosophers; Calliope and Urania are associated with heaven and thought.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 3781-3808
occurrences.motif_label: Sharing a blessing among friends
occurrences.basis: Phaedrus asks for the same prayer for himself, stating that friends should have all things in common.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “Ask the same for me, for friends should have all things in common.”

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1014-1098
occurrences.motif_label: Ritual payment or offering as atonement for sin
occurrences.basis: Mendicant prophets promise atonement through sacrifices, games, charms, and invocations; the imagined argument says one may sin and pay for indulgences from the proceeds of sin.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Mendicant prophets promise rich men atonement for their own or ancestral sins through sacrifices, games, charms, and invocations; they appeal to books attributed to Musaeus and Orpheus and promise to get souls out of purgatory.

The imagined argument says that gods are known from poets and may be appeased by sacrifices; one may sin and pay for indulgences, and atoning powers in the world below are confirmed by poets and the State.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 10635-10722
occurrences.motif_label: Propitiating gods through sacrifice and prayer
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly reports claims that sacrifices, prayers, libations, odours of fat, and offerings can avert divine wrath, turn gods, or allow unjust people to avoid punishment.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Mendicant prophets visit rich men's doors, claim divine power to atone for sins by sacrifices or charms, and promise to harm enemies through magic arts and incantations that bind heaven.
Poets are invoked: Hesiod is cited for the easy path of vice and toil before virtue, and Homer for gods being turned by prayers, sacrifices, entreaties, libations, and the odour of fat.

The argument considers whether gods can be deceived or compelled, then says poetic tradition claims gods may be influenced by sacrifices, soothing entreaties, and offerings; unjust people could pray and sacrifice to avoid punishment.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III.; lines 11969-12129
occurrences.motif_label: gifts persuading gods and kings
occurrences.basis: The passage cites and rejects songs about gifts persuading gods and kings, along with stories of Achilles acting for gifts or payment.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker rejects love of money, songs about gifts persuading gods and kings, Phoenix’s advice to Achilles about Greek gifts, and stories of Achilles acting for gifts or payment.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1483-1541
occurrences.motif_label: offering to a healing deity
occurrences.basis: The philosopher is described as not refusing to offer a cock to Aesculapius.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The philosopher's religion is described as dwelling in ideas while still offering a cock to Aesculapius and praying at sunrise.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1543-1614
occurrences.motif_label: corrupting sacred exchange and bribery
occurrences.basis: The passage rejects lines claiming gifts persuade gods and kings, and condemns gift-taking, payment-seeking, and ransom behavior associated with Achilles and Phoenix.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Citizens must not receive bribes or endorse sayings that gifts persuade gods and kings; Phoenix's advice to Achilles to seek money and Achilles's receipt of gifts or ransom are rejected.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VI. / BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII. / BOOK IX.; lines 22998-23129
occurrences.motif_label: destructive exchange for wealth
occurrences.basis: The passage rejects gold, silver, or a necklace gained at the cost of enslaving or destroying what is most noble or beloved.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage asks whether gold and silver would profit someone who enslaves the noblest part to the worst, compares this with selling children into slavery, and cites Eriphyle taking a necklace as the price of her husband’s life.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS. / THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I.; lines 8632-8770
occurrences.motif_label: Ritual visit to a goddess and communal festival
occurrences.basis: Socrates goes to pray to Bendis; the passage also describes processions, a festival, and a sacrifice by Cephalus.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “I went down yesterday to the Piraeus with Glaucon... that I might offer up my prayers to the goddess (Bendis, the Thracian Artemis.)” and to see the new festival and processions.
Adeimantus mentions “the torch-race on horseback in honour of the goddess”; Polemarchus says a night festival will be celebrated and urges Socrates to stay.

The group goes to Polemarchus’ house and finds Lysias, Euthydemus, Thrasymachus, Charmantides, Cleitophon, and Cephalus, who is aged, seated on a cushioned chair, garlanded, and recently sacrificing; chairs are arranged in a semicircle.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS. / THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I.; lines 8772-8893
occurrences.motif_label: sacred obligations before death
occurrences.basis: Cephalus links peace of mind before departure below to fulfilling offerings due to gods and debts owed to men.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Cephalus says wealth helps a good person avoid deception and fraud, depart to the world below without fear about offerings due to gods or debts owed to men, and gain peace of mind.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 1320-1353
occurrences.motif_label: divine reward for self-sacrificial love
occurrences.basis: Alcestis receives return to earth, and Achilles receives the Islands of the Blest because the gods honor their devotion.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Gods and humans admire Alcestis' noble action, and the gods grant her the privilege of returning alive to earth.
The gods honor Achilles above Alcestis and send him to the Islands of the Blest.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 1493-1543
occurrences.motif_label: love as mutual pursuit of wisdom and virtue
occurrences.basis: The lover provides wisdom and virtue while the beloved seeks education and improvement; the exchange is honorable when directed toward virtue rather than gain.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Voluntary service to another for improvement in wisdom or virtue is not dishonorable or flattery.
The lover serves the beloved; the beloved shows kindness to one making him wise and good; one communicates wisdom and virtue while the other seeks them for education and wisdom.
Accepting a lover believed to be good, in hope of moral improvement, is described as virtuous even if the lover proves villainous; the error is called noble.
Acceptance for the sake of virtue is noble; this love is called heavenly, of the heavenly goddess, and valuable to individuals and cities; other loves are offspring of the common goddess.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 1610-1659
occurrences.motif_label: Ritual communion between gods and humans
occurrences.basis: Sacrifice and divination are explicitly described as communion between gods and men and as means to preserve good love and heal evil love.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sacrifices and divination are described as the art of communion between gods and men; divination is called “the peacemaker of gods and men.”

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 1833-1883
occurrences.motif_label: praise offered as tribute to a deity
occurrences.basis: Phaedrus describes the encomium on Love as something owed from each speaker and as a tribute to the god.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Phaedrus interrupts, saying Socrates may become absorbed in conversation with a good-looking partner, and reminds the group that each owes an encomium on Love as a tribute to the god.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 2200-2261
occurrences.motif_label: intermediary spirit mediating divine-human exchange
occurrences.basis: Love is explicitly described as an intermediate daimon who conveys prayers and sacrifices upward and commands and replies downward, binding together gods and humans.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Diotima says Love is neither mortal nor immortal, but a great daimon between divine and mortal; he conveys prayers and sacrifices to gods and divine commands and replies to humans, spanning the chasm between them.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 233-318
occurrences.motif_label: Love as cosmic and social harmonizer
occurrences.basis: Agathon attributes to Love the power to create animals, invent arts, rule gods, and make people of one mind at a banquet.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Agathon attributes voluntary obedience, justice, temperance, courage, wisdom, poetic power, creation of animals, invention of arts, authority over gods, and banquet harmony to Love.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 233-318
occurrences.motif_label: Mediating spirit between gods and humans
occurrences.basis: Diotima's teaching describes Love as an intermediate power conveying prayers from humans to gods and commands from gods to humans.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates reports that Diotima, a wise woman of Mantinea, taught that Love is between fair and foul, good and evil, and is a demon or intermediate power conveying prayers to gods and commands to humans.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 2571-2651
occurrences.motif_label: crowning the praised figure
occurrences.basis: Alcibiades requests ribands from Agathon and crowns Socrates before praising him, creating a ceremonial exchange of honor within the feast.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Alcibiades asks Agathon for ribands to crown Socrates' head, calls Socrates a universal despot and conqueror of all mankind in conversation, then crowns Socrates and reclines.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 2763-2834
occurrences.motif_label: sacred or unequal exchange
occurrences.basis: The proposed transaction is described as an exchange of beauty for beauty, with Socrates warning that Alcibiades would gain true beauty for mere appearance, like gold for brass.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates replies ironically that if Alcibiades sees in him a higher beauty, the proposed sharing would let Alcibiades gain true beauty for appearance, like Diomede receiving gold for brass, and warns him to look again.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 2836-2933
occurrences.motif_label: courageous rescuer who yields honor to another
occurrences.basis: Socrates rescues Alcibiades and his arms, is said to deserve the prize of valour, but is eager for Alcibiades to receive it.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Alcibiades says Socrates saved his life when he was wounded, rescued him and his arms, and deserved the prize of valour but wanted Alcibiades to receive it.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 504-591
occurrences.motif_label: returned love favoured by gods
occurrences.basis: Phaedrus is summarized as saying that gods favour returned love from the beloved more than the original sentiment, because the lover is nobler and more divine.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Phaedrus' discourse is described as half-mythical and half-ethical; it treats honour and dishonour, love's antiquity, the blessing of having a lover, love as an incentive to daring deeds, examples of Alcestis and Achilles, and the claim that gods favour returned love from the beloved because the lover is nobler and more divine.

occurrences.source_title: Maha-bharata
occurrences.passage_locator: Draupadi in the Council Hall; Draupadi's Plaint; Insult and Vow of Revenge
occurrences.motif_label: corrupt sacred exchange
occurrences.basis: The dice game acts like a binding transfer of persons and status, but Draupadi rejects it as invalid once the gambler has lost himself.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Yudhishthira loses wealth, kin, himself, and then Draupadi in the dice game and the Pandavas are reduced to exile.
Draupadi asks whether a man who has already become a bondsman can still stake his queen and declares the wager void.

occurrences.source_title: The Upanishads
occurrences.passage_locator: Katha-Upanishad, Part First VII-Part Second IV
occurrences.motif_label: sacred guest exchange
occurrences.basis: Yama grants three boons because the Brahmana guest has remained three nights without food.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Nachiketas went to Death's abode and waited without food or drink for three days.
Yama says Nachiketas remained three nights without food and may choose three boons.

occurrences.source_title: Persian Literature, Volume 1
occurrences.passage_locator: Birth of Rustem; Simurgh aid, prodigious growth, and the white elephant feat
occurrences.motif_label: sacred_birth_aided_by_guardian
occurrences.basis: A dangerous birth is resolved through the summoned Simurgh, which foretells the child and enables a successful delivery.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "A child will be born of mighty power, who will become the wonder of the world."
The Simurgh's advice saves Rudabeh, and Rustem is born so prodigious that he looks a year old on his first day.

occurrences.source_title: Persian Literature, Volume 1
occurrences.passage_locator: Zal, the son of Sam; exposure on Alberz, Simurgh fosterage, and return
occurrences.motif_label: rescue_feather_token
occurrences.basis: The Simurgh leaves a feather that materializes an ongoing bond and can call down aid at moments of danger.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Simurgh tells Zal it has nursed him, named him Dustn, taught him language and understanding, and now must return him to Sam.
The Simurgh gives Zal a feather to burn whenever danger comes, then presents him to Sam as worthy of throne and diadem.

motifs.label: Return

occurrences.source_title: Gods and Fighting Men
occurrences.passage_locator: Book Eleven, Chapter I: Oisin's Story; journey to and return from the Country of the Young
occurrences.motif_label: return_from_otherworld_with_time_shift
occurrences.basis: Oisin returns from the Country of the Young to a changed Ireland and immediately ages when he violates the return condition.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Oisin returns long after Niamh took him away; the time seemed short to him, but he is later found old and fallen from the white horse.
Niamh allows Oisin to return but warns that touching the ground will prevent return and make him old, blind, and withered.
Oisin forgets the warning, dismounts by the stone trough, the years come upon him, and the horse leaves him.

occurrences.source_title: The Mabinogion
occurrences.passage_locator: Pwyll Prince of Dyved; encounter with Arawn and year in Annwvyn
occurrences.motif_label: return_with_new_status
occurrences.basis: Pwyll returns from Annwvyn after ruling and gains the title Chief of Annwvyn.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Arawn restores Pwyll's form, Pwyll returns to Dyved, friendship is strengthened, and Pwyll is called Chief of Annwvyn.

occurrences.source_title: Persian Literature, Volume 1
occurrences.passage_locator: KAI-KS / THE SEVEN LABORS OF RUSTEM / INVASION OF IRN BY AFRSIYB / THE RETURN OF KAI-KS; lines 5019-5036
occurrences.motif_label: Hero returns home after victory and reports to rulers
occurrences.basis: Rustem reports victory by letter to Kai-ks and the party returns home to pay respects to the Persian king.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Rustem and companions fall back to the sporting-grounds; from there Rustem informs Kai-ks by letter of the victory gained.
The party returns home to pay their respects to the Persian king.

occurrences.source_title: The Poetic Edda
occurrences.passage_locator: HELGAKVITHA HJORVARTHSSONAR / THE LAY OF HELGI THE SON OF HJORVARTH / INTRODUCTORY NOTE / OF HJORVARTH AND SIGRLIN; lines 11252-11299
occurrences.motif_label: Hero's death and being 'born again' (rebirth of hero and beloved)
occurrences.basis: The passage reports Helgi's fatal wounding/fall and then explicitly states that Helgi and Svava were born again.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sigar reports Helgi fell in the morning at Frekastein; calls him the noblest king beneath the sun; says Alf has the joy of victory.
Helgi greets Svava, says this is their last meeting in life, and describes his bleeding wounds and a sword near his heart.
The text states that Helgi and Svava were born again.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA. / II.--MORAL TALES. / IV.--MISCELLANEOUS TALES.; lines 1629-1717
occurrences.motif_label: Return from an unfamiliar land by instructed route
occurrences.basis: The chief and sons return to Iwanai by sailing with a fair wind; the old chief gives the fisherman instructions for returning with his people by boat.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The chief and sons sail away with a fair wind, reach Iwanai, find their wives wearing widows' caps, recount woman-land, and show the marked scabbard.
The old chief says some of his people will go to the fisherman's country for trade and warns him to lie down, hide his head, and not look while being taken by them in the boat.

evidence.quote_or_summary: When the man hears the proclamation he releases the dog; the dog hastens back, and the elephant lifts him with his trunk, places him on his forehead, weeps, sets him down, watches him eat, and then eats.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Stories Planudes borrowed indirectly from India are said to have been restored to India through translations, including translations by an Englishman into Indian languages and a Sanskrit translation by Narayan Balkrishna Godpole.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Headings include Kisā Gotamī’s song, the Great Renunciation, struggle against sin, victory over Satan, bliss of Nirvāna, hesitation to publish the good news, and foundation of the Kingdom of Righteousness.
Headings include Uruvela Kassapa’s conversion, a triumphal entrance into Rājagaha, foundation of the order, return home, and presentation of the first monastery to the Buddha.

occurrences.motif_label: Deferred salvation under a future teacher
occurrences.basis: The multitudes say that if they fail to attain paths and fruition under Dīpankara, they may do so in the future presence of Sumedha when he becomes Buddha.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The multitudes compare their hope to men who cross a river at a lower ford if they miss the opposite ford; if they fail under Dīpankara, they hope to attain paths and fruition before Sumedha as a future Buddha.

occurrences.motif_label: Sending forth enlightened disciples to teach
occurrences.basis: After many become arahats, the Master sends sixty mendicants in different directions to preach and teach.

evidence.quote_or_summary: When sixty-one persons are arahats, the Master sends sixty mendicants in different directions with the words, “Go forth ... preaching and teaching.”

occurrences.motif_label: return to family or native town
occurrences.basis: Kāḷa Udāyin asks the Buddha to show favour to his relations, and the Buddha starts toward Kapilavatthu to see the king.

evidence.quote_or_summary: On the March full moon Udāyin notes that spring has come, crops and journeys begin, the earth is green, woods are flowering, and roads are fit; his verses compare red blossoms to glowing fires and say the season is neither too hot nor too cold.
The Master asks why Udāyin sings of travel; Udāyin replies that the Master’s father wants to see him, and the Master agrees to favor his relations and tells the Order to journey.
The Blessed One, attended by twenty thousand sin-free mendicants, starts from Rājagaha and travels a league a day toward Kapilavatthu, sixty leagues away, intending to arrive in two months.
Udāyin rises into the air, appears in the king’s house, is welcomed and offered food, and tells the king that the Master has set out with twenty thousand mendicants to see him.

occurrences.motif_label: truth-guided escape from demonic danger
occurrences.basis: The Teacher states that those who held to truth escaped the hands of demons, reached their destination, and returned home.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Teacher says those relying on their own reason were destroyed, while those holding to truth escaped demons, went where they wished, and returned home.

occurrences.motif_label: return to kin and transfer of children
occurrences.basis: The parents return to Rājagaha so the children can know their relatives; the grandparents refuse the parents but accept the children.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The child asks his mother about relatives after hearing other children speak of uncles and grandparents; she says they have a rich grandfather and many relations at Rājagaha.
The parents take the children to Rājagaha and stay at a public resting-place; the grandparents send money for the parents to leave but allow the children to be sent to them.

occurrences.motif_label: return from forest exile to righteous kingship
occurrences.basis: The brothers' forest exile is explained; after the father's death, the Bodisat returns to Benares, assumes the kingdom, appoints his brothers, and rules righteously.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The moved water-sprite offers one brother; the Bodisat asks for the younger and explains that the younger's political danger caused the forest exile, so his loss would bring blame and disbelief.

The converted ogre protects the Bodisat; the Bodisat reads his father's death in the stars, returns to Benares, becomes king, appoints Moon Prince and Sun Prince, provides for the water-sprite, and rules righteously.

occurrences.motif_label: dangerous journey to refuge and return
occurrences.basis: The deer leaders are instructed to take their herds to the mountainous forest during crop season and return after the crops are cut; one journey succeeds and one fails.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The old Bodisat tells his sons to lead their herds to the mountainous part of the forest during the growing crops and return when the crops are cut.

Brownie does not know proper travel times and leads his herd early and late, at dawn and evening twilight, past village gates; men kill many deer, and he returns to the forest with diminished numbers.
Beauty is described as learned, clever, and resourceful; he avoids village gates, does not travel by day, dawn, or twilight, travels at midnight, and reaches the forest without losing any animal.
After four months and after the crops are cut, Brownie loses the rest of his herd and arrives alone, while Beauty comes to his parent with all five hundred deer.

occurrences.motif_label: supernatural animal rescue and return home
occurrences.basis: A fairy’s winged horse speaks to the men, receives them on its back, and carries those who want to leave safely home.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A kind fairy who hates the goblins sends a flying horse; the captain sees a beautiful horse with white and gold wings, and the horse asks in a human voice who wants to go home.
The sailors who want to leave climb on the horse; although it appears ordinary-sized, there is room for all, and it flies them safely home.

occurrences.motif_label: Revival when the absent soul returns
occurrences.basis: The Santal man revives when the lizard returns to his body, and the Transylvanian woman wakes when the fly enters her mouth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Santal story says a sleeping man's soul, in lizard form, enters a water pitcher, is trapped when the pitcher is covered, and the man dies; when the lizard is released and returns, the body revives.
A Transylvanian witch-trial account describes a motionless woman with open mouth; a captured fly is later released, flies into her mouth, and she wakes, leading the men to regard her as a witch.

occurrences.motif_label: Ritual recall and guidance of an absent soul
occurrences.basis: The Mongol practice calls the patient's name, makes the body attractive, uses a cord to show the way home, and performs actions when the soul is said to return.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The soul may leave during waking hours as well as sleep, and sickness or death may result if the absence is prolonged; Mongol explanations of sickness include the soul's absence or inability to find its way back.

The Mongol procedure places valued things near the patient, washes and incenses him, has friends circle the hut and call his name, stretches a colored cord from head to door, has a priest recite dangers, and then throws seed over the patient; the cord is worn seven days.

occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER I. THE KING OF THE WOOD. / MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE.; lines 3265-3343
occurrences.motif_label: ritual return or restoration of a lost soul
occurrences.basis: Multiple rites aim to call, lure, catch, carry, or command the soul back into or onto the patient or vulnerable person.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Karen funeral practices include tying children during a passing funeral, using split bamboo and sticks at the grave to show souls how to climb out, avoiding burying souls with bamboos, carrying the bamboos away, and using three branch-hooks while calling the spirit to prevent it from remaining with the dead.

Burmese belief says a baby's 'butterfly' or soul may follow its dead mother; a wise woman uses a mirror, cotton down, cloth, and entreaties to recover it. Similar rites may be used for a dead playmate's surviving companion or for a bereaved spouse.

In Bolang Mongondo sickness is ascribed to ancestral spirits carrying off the patient's soul. Priestesses acting as physicians use a cloth doll on a spear, dance and charms, colored cloths, head-wrapping, pursuit around the house, and restoration of the recaptured soul to a sick boy.
"Much in the same way an Australian medicine-man will sometimes bring the lost soul of a sick man into a puppet and restore it to the patient by pressing the puppet to his breast."

In Uea, the dead are credited with stealing souls of the living; a soul-doctor and a troop go to the graveyard, use flutes and whistling to lure the soul home, lead it back with open palms, and command it to enter the patient's body.

In Madagascar, friends of a sick man go to the family tomb, make a hole, ask the patient's father's soul to give a soul for his son, fold the soul into a bonnet, bring it to the patient, and the patient puts the bonnet on his head.

occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER I. THE KING OF THE WOOD. / MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE.; lines 3892-3959
occurrences.motif_label: Purification after return from journey
occurrences.basis: Multiple examples describe returnees from journeys or long absences undergoing cleansing, washing, marking, fat-giving, water-sprinkling, or other precautions before reintegration.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A returning traveler may be thought to have contracted magical evil from strangers and must undergo purification before rejoining tribe and friends.
Bechuanas purify themselves after journeys, including by shaving their heads, to avoid witchcraft or sorcery contracted from strangers.
In parts of Western Africa, a returning man washes with a particular fluid and receives a forehead mark from a sorcerer before visiting his wife, to counteract a possible spell from a stranger woman.
Damaras returning home after a long absence receive a small portion of fat from particular animals believed to possess virtues.
In some Moluccas communities, a young girl greets a returning brother or young blood-relation at the door with water in a caladi leaf, throws it over his face, and welcomes him.

occurrences.motif_label: descent and return through lower and upper worlds
occurrences.basis: Adonis is said to spend part of each year in the lower world and the rest in the upper world, which the passage connects to buried and reappearing vegetation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says Adonis spends half or a third of the year in the lower world and the rest in the upper world, and Frazer interprets this as vegetation or corn buried in earth and reappearing above ground.

occurrences.motif_label: descent to the dead to retrieve a mother
occurrences.basis: A variant myth has Dionysus descending into Hades to bring Semele up from the dead.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A different form of the myth says Dionysus descended into Hades to bring his mother Semele up from the dead.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 1 of 2)

occurrences.motif_label: return from the underworld through water with offering
occurrences.basis: The Argive rite summons Dionysus from the Alcyonian lake and includes a lamb offering to the warder of the dead.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Argive tradition says Dionysus descended through the Alcyonian lake; the Argives annually celebrated his return by summoning him from the water with trumpet blasts and throwing a lamb into the lake for the warder of the dead.

occurrences.passage_locator: MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE. / CHAPTER III. KILLING THE GOD.; lines 8746-8810
occurrences.motif_label: ritual lament for slain or absent corn-spirit and desired return
occurrences.basis: The reapers' song for Bormus is interpreted as lamentation over the corn-spirit's death and a prayer for return in renewed vigor next year.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Frazer says the Bithynian Bormus resembles Lityerses: Bormus, a king's son or son of a wealthy distinguished man, was annually mourned by reapers after his death or disappearance; he disappeared while fetching water and in one version was carried off by water nymphs.

The passage interprets Bormus's disappearance as a reminiscence of binding a farmer in a corn-sheaf and throwing him into water; the reapers' mournful song is interpreted as lament over the corn-spirit's death and a prayer for return in fresh vigor next year.

occurrences.motif_label: ritual journey to a sacred place and return with living animals
occurrences.basis: The Zuni procession departs to the city of the Ka-ka and returns four days later bearing living turtles.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An eyewitness sees a procession of fifty men go westward, led by a painted, shell-bedecked priest and followed by the torch-bearing Shu-lu-wit-si, or God of Fire.
“They are going,” said he, “to the city of the Ka-ka and the home of our others.”

Four days later the men return at sunset, costumed and masked, each bearing a basket of living turtles; the turtles are carried tenderly, some wrapped in blankets and likened to little children on pilgrims’ backs.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS; lines 2371-2451
occurrences.motif_label: Dead return as visitors and are sent away again
occurrences.basis: The passage states that spirits of the dead are commonly believed to return to old homes, be welcomed and feasted, and then be sent away; Frazer applies this pattern to the Zuni turtle ceremony.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Frazer asks why a turtle believed to contain a kinsman’s soul would be killed; he proposes communication with the other world, returning spirits welcomed and sent away, and the Zuni dead fetched back as turtles and sent to spirit-land by killing, while noting the meaning is obscure.

occurrences.motif_label: departure from community and return after transformation
occurrences.basis: Belli-Paaro youths are taken to the forest and later returned to parents; Huskanaw youths are confined in the woods and later brought back into towns under supervision.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At the king’s order a forest place is appointed; youths are brought there weeping, told they must suffer death, dispose of property, and are instructed by initiated persons in a dance called killing and songs praising Belli.

After instruction, novices are shut in huts, interact with women bringing food, pretend ignorance of people and customs, wear bird feathers and bark caps, dance the dance of Belli publicly, and are taken to their parents’ houses.

Huskanaw among the Indians of Virginia is described as an initiatory ceremony in which youths are confined alone in the woods for months and receive only an intoxicating root infusion, leading to a period of madness.

The Huskanaw account says the youths drink enough Wysoccan, likened to water of Lethe, to forget parents, possessions, and language; doctors gradually restore them, keepers guard them, and they must relearn speech and recognition, thereby commencing men by forgetting they had been boys.

occurrences.passage_locator: JAPANESE FAIRY TALES / MY LORD BAG OF RICE / THE TONGUE-CUT SPARROW / THE STORY OF URASHIMA TARO, THE FISHER LAD; lines 1101-1205
occurrences.motif_label: return from otherworld to an altered home
occurrences.basis: Urashima returns from the Sea King’s realm to his home shore but finds unfamiliar people, a changed house, and evidence that three hundred years have passed.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The tortoise brings Urashima into the familiar bay and to the shore from which he left, then returns to the Sea King’s realm.
Urashima sees the same shore and hills but unfamiliar people; he goes to the place of his old home, calls for his father, and meets a strange man.
“It is true that once upon a time a man called Urashima Taro did live in this village, but that is a story three hundred years old.”
Urashima realizes that the few days in the Sea King’s palace were hundreds of years at home; his parents and former acquaintances have died, and he resolves to return to his wife beyond the sea.

occurrences.motif_label: restoration after vengeance
occurrences.basis: After the badger’s death is reported, the old farmer says he can sleep and eat as before, and the rabbit joins his household.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The rabbit tells the old farmer that the badger has been killed; the farmer thanks him, says he can again sleep and eat, and invites the rabbit to share his home as a friend.

occurrences.motif_label: lost child rediscovered during a hunt
occurrences.basis: Prince Toyonari searches unsuccessfully, later hunts in the mountains, hears a voice at a cottage, and finds his lost daughter, leading to her return home.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Prince Toyonari returns, hears the stepmother’s claim that Hase-Hime did wrong and ran away, becomes anxious, keeps the matter quiet, and searches without success.
Prince Toyonari orders a hunt in the mountains, rides to the Hibari Mountains, gets far ahead, and finds himself in a narrow valley.
He approaches a tiny house after hearing a clear voice and finds a beautiful girl “reading the Buddhist scriptures with great devotion,” then sees that she is Hase-Hime.
Prince Toyonari is astonished and indignant, gives up the hunt, hurries home with Hase-Hime, and the stepmother flees in disgrace when her wickedness is discovered.

occurrences.motif_label: return by the same magical conveyance
occurrences.basis: After praying to Jofuku, the paper crane reappears and carries Sentaro back toward Japan.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sentaro prays to Jofuku; the paper crane emerges undamaged, grows large, and carries him across the sea toward Japan while he looks back with regret and cannot stop it.

occurrences.motif_label: return from visionary journey with instruction
occurrences.basis: After waking from the dream and hearing the messenger's instruction, Sentaro receives a book, returns home, and prospers by following its lessons.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The messenger gives Sentaro a book of precepts intended to guide him in the advised way of life.
The angel disappears; Sentaro returns home with the book, gives up vain wishes, follows its lessons, and his household prospers.

occurrences.motif_label: Hero returns home with supernatural gifts
occurrences.basis: Hidesato insists on returning home and is accompanied by the Dragon King's retainers bearing gifts, which are later found to have magic power.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A more sumptuous feast is prepared; Hidesato insists on returning home, and the Dragon King asks him to accept gifts in gratitude for deliverance from the centipede.

The Dragon King accompanies Hidesato to the bridge; gift-bearing servants go with him home, vanish after putting down the presents, and the gifts are found to be magical except for one ordinary bell given to a nearby temple.

occurrences.motif_label: celestial woman returns to her otherworldly home
occurrences.basis: Princess Moonlight is loved on earth but says she belongs to the moon and is taken back by moon envoys in a flying chariot.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Emperor leaves sadly, regards Princess Moonlight as uniquely beautiful, sends love poems, and receives verses saying she can never marry anyone on earth.
Princess Moonlight says she came from the moon, will be fetched on the fifteenth day of August, has parents there, and has forgotten them and the moon-world during her earthly life.
The cloud obscures the sky and hovers near the ground; in it is a flying chariot with luminous beings, including a kinglike chief who calls to the old man.
The messenger leads Princess Moonlight to the chariot; she comforts the old man and tells him to think of her when looking at the moon.

occurrences.motif_label: returning traveler brings meaningful gifts
occurrences.basis: After returning from the capital, the father gives the child gifts and gives his wife a mirror that is explicitly described as precious and symbolically significant.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The husband returns after about a month of travel, sunburned by weather; wife and child recognize and greet him eagerly.
The father opens a bamboo basket and gives the little girl a doll and a lacquer box full of cakes as a prize for caring for mother and house.

The husband gives the wife a square wooden box tied with red and white string; inside is a handled metal disk, bright on one side and decorated with pine-trees and storks on the other; she sees somebody looking at her in it.

The husband explains that the disk is a mirror showing the viewer’s own form, says mirrors are necessary for women in the capital, quotes a proverb comparing a woman’s mirror to a samurai’s sword, says it indexes the heart, and says it is among the Emperor’s insignia.
The wife is pleased by the precious gift, says she will treasure it if it represents her soul, raises it to her forehead, shuts it in its box, and puts it away.

occurrences.motif_label: return from an enchanted otherworld after elapsed time
occurrences.basis: The Happy Hunter spends three happy years in the Sea Realm but becomes homesick and asks to return to Japan and his brother.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Happy Hunter wants to return to his kingdom and reconcile with the Skillful Fisher, but Ryn Jin and his daughters persuade him to stay in Ryn Gu; after three years he becomes homesick and asks permission to return because he governs Japan and must return the hook to his brother.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE BAMBOO-CUTTER AND THE MOON-CHILD / THE GOBLIN OF ADACHIGAHARA / THE SAGACIOUS MONKEY AND THE BOAR / THE HAPPY HUNTER AND THE SKILLFUL FISHER; lines 4436-4526
occurrences.motif_label: Return from a sea realm with supernatural gifts
occurrences.basis: The Happy Hunter leaves the realm of Ryn Gu with two tide jewels given by Ryn Jin and returns to Japan by crocodile.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ryn Jin teaches the Happy Hunter how to use the two talismans, gives him the Jewel of the Flood Tide and Jewel of the Ebbing Tide, and the Sea King, Tayotama, Tamayori, and palace inhabitants say goodbye as he leaves.
At the beach a huge crocodile, eight fathoms long and ordered by the Sea King, waits and carries the Happy Hunter back to Japan faster than any steamboat.
The Happy Hunter rules without family strife, Japan has peace for a long time, and he prizes the Jewels of the Flow and Ebb of the Tide given by Ryn Jin, the Dragon King of the Sea.
