occurrences.basis: The Homeric example includes a prayer that the Achaeans take Troy and have a safe return.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Homeric example describes a priest praying to Apollo that the Achaeans take Troy and return safely if Agamemnon gives back his daughter; the Greeks assent and Agamemnon becomes angry.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 18781-18911
occurrences.motif_label: Return of the enlightened figure to former darkness
occurrences.basis: The prisoner who has seen the sun is imagined returning suddenly to the old situation and being unable to see in the darkness.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A person coming suddenly from the sun back to the old situation would have eyes full of darkness.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 18913-19020
occurrences.motif_label: Return of the enlightened figure to darkness
occurrences.basis: The passage describes one who returns from above or from divine contemplations into the den or human affairs and is mocked or disoriented.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A returned ascender would compete in measuring shadows with prisoners who had never left the den, while his sight was still weak; others would say he went up and came back without his eyes.
Those attaining the beatific vision are unwilling to descend to human affairs because their souls hasten toward and desire the upper world.

One who passes from divine contemplations to human affairs may appear ridiculous while blinking in darkness and arguing about images or shadows of justice with those who have not seen absolute justice.
The passage distinguishes bewilderment caused by coming from light into darkness from bewilderment caused by going from darkness into light, applying this to both bodily and mental vision.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19022-19142
occurrences.motif_label: return of the enlightened ruler to the dark abode
occurrences.basis: Those who have ascended and seen the good must descend again among the prisoners and learn to see in the dark for the benefit of the State.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The founders must compel the best minds to ascend until they arrive at the good; after they have ascended and seen enough, they must descend again among the prisoners in the den and share their labours and honours.

The philosophers have been educated to be rulers; each must go down to the general underground abode, gain the habit of seeing in the dark, and then understand the images because they have seen the beautiful, just, and good in truth.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 20154-20256
occurrences.motif_label: return from contemplation to rule for the community
occurrences.basis: Those who behold the good must still toil at politics and rule for the public good as a duty.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The absolute good is the pattern for ordering the State, individual lives, and the rulers’ remaining lives.
The rulers make philosophy their chief pursuit but also engage in politics and rule for the public good as duty.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII.; lines 21107-21266
occurrences.motif_label: banishment and return of desires
occurrences.basis: Some desires die or are banished during a period of restored order, but fresh kindred desires later spring up and multiply.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sometimes the democratic principle yields to the oligarchical; some desires die, others are banished, reverence enters the soul, and order is restored.
After old desires are driven out, fresh kindred desires spring up and become fierce and numerous because their father does not know how to educate them.
The desires draw the young man to old associates, hold secret intercourse with them, and breed and multiply in him.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII.; lines 21268-21405
occurrences.motif_label: exile and return of personified qualities
occurrences.basis: Virtues are expelled, while personified vices are brought back to the house; later some exiled virtues may be re-admitted.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A battle is won; modesty and temperance are cast out, while moderation and orderly expenditure are driven beyond the border by evil appetites.

The soul is emptied and swept clean while being initiated in great mysteries; garlanded vices return and are praised with favorable names; the young man moves into libertinism of unnecessary pleasures.
After time passes, if he is fortunate, he re-admits some exiled virtues and balances pleasures by letting each govern him in turn.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII. / BOOK IX. / BOOK X.; lines 23923-24065
occurrences.motif_label: banished figure conditionally allowed to return
occurrences.basis: Poetry is personified as an exiled figure sent from the State who may return only after making a successful defense.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker defends sending imitative poetry out of the State, says there is an ancient quarrel between philosophy and poetry, cites hostile sayings, and acknowledges poetry's charm, especially in Homer.
The speaker proposes that poetry may return from exile only if she defends herself, and that prose defenders may argue that poetry is useful as well as pleasant.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII. / BOOK IX. / BOOK X.; lines 24305-24376
occurrences.motif_label: revival after death as witness to the other world
occurrences.basis: Er is slain, remains undecayed, returns to life, and reports what he saw in the other world.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Er son of Armenius, a Pamphylian, is introduced as a hero who was slain in battle.
After ten days Er's body is found undecayed; on the twelfth day, while lying on the funeral pile, he returns to life.
Er is told that he is to be the messenger carrying the report of the other world to men, and is instructed to hear and see everything there.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII. / BOOK IX. / BOOK X.; lines 24483-24572
occurrences.motif_label: afterlife journey with return to life
occurrences.basis: The report maps a post-mortem passage through choice, destiny, forgetfulness, rebirth, and the messenger’s return to his body.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After all souls choose, Lachesis sends each chosen genius as guardian and fulfiller; the genius leads the soul to Clotho and Atropos, where destiny is ratified and made irreversible, and the souls pass beneath Necessity’s throne.
The souls march in scorching heat to the barren plain of Forgetfulness, without trees or verdure, and camp by the river of Unmindfulness, whose water no vessel can hold.
All souls must drink a certain quantity from the river; those not saved by wisdom drink too much, and each forgets all things as he drinks.
After rest, at midnight a thunderstorm and earthquake occur, and the souls are driven upward in many ways to their birth, like shooting stars.
The reporting messenger is hindered from drinking the water and cannot tell how he returned to the body; in the morning he wakes suddenly lying on the pyre.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII. / BOOK IX. / BOOK X.; lines 24483-24572
occurrences.motif_label: revival on the funeral pyre
occurrences.basis: The messenger, who has not drunk the water, returns to his body and wakes on a pyre.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The reporting messenger is hindered from drinking the water and cannot tell how he returned to the body; in the morning he wakes suddenly lying on the pyre.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 3196-3254
occurrences.motif_label: return to discussion in another life
occurrences.basis: Socrates refers to a future time in another life when similar discussions may be taken up again.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates is addressed as earnest; Thrasymachus is mentioned; Socrates says he will try to convince Thrasymachus and mankind, or prepare for a future time when in another life similar discussions may be resumed.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 3736-3821
occurrences.motif_label: return of the enlightened figure to the dark place
occurrences.basis: The person who has seen the sun descends again into the den, and philosopher-rulers are required to return among the captives.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The ascender descends into the old dwelling, sees poorly at first, is mocked as having lost his eyes, and any would-be liberator could be killed by the den inhabitants.

Pleasure and desire are described as leaden weights binding the soul to earth; rulers must be chosen from natures able to ascend to light and knowledge, but must be forced down again among the captives.
The philosopher is told he has been trained to be ruler and king of the hive, must descend into the den, learn to use his eyes in the dark, and rule from waking knowledge for the State's salvation.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 4013-4089
occurrences.motif_label: descent into den followed by return
occurrences.basis: The student is instructed to go down into the den for practical experience and later return to the end of all things.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The second gymnastic training of the soul lasts about five or six years from thirty; afterward the student goes down into the den, commands armies, and gains life experience for fifteen years.
At fifty the student returns to the end of all things, lifts his eyes to the idea of good, and orders life after that pattern.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 4241-4307
occurrences.motif_label: ascent from darkness to light and return
occurrences.basis: The passage describes ascent to an upper world, contact with light or eternal ideas, and return or descent to the lower world, with changed perception.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says the allegory has political and philosophical meaning; the den or cave represents the narrow sphere of politics or law, and the light of eternal ideas affects those who return to the lower world.
Those who return are first unable to compete with den inhabitants in measuring shadows and are derided and persecuted, but later see things below in truer proportions than those who never ascended.
The passage symbolizes two kinds of disordered eyesight: the captive transferred from darkness to day and the heavenly messenger who voluntarily descends into the den for the good of fellow-men.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 4241-4307
occurrences.motif_label: enlightened benefactor descends to aid others
occurrences.basis: The heavenly messenger voluntarily descends into the den for the good of fellow-men.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage symbolizes two kinds of disordered eyesight: the captive transferred from darkness to day and the heavenly messenger who voluntarily descends into the den for the good of fellow-men.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 4571-4620
occurrences.motif_label: banishment and return of personified qualities
occurrences.basis: Modesty and temperance are expelled, while vices are brought back, crowned, and renamed; later some exiles may be restored.

evidence.quote_or_summary: False spirits shut the castle gates, win the battle, ally with desires, banish modesty and temperance, and bring back vices crowned with garlands under new names.

The person later alternates between necessary and unnecessary pleasures, sometimes restores some exiles, denies distinctions among pleasures, and shifts among drinking, abstinence, exercise, idleness, philosophy, politics, war, and business.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 4623-4685
occurrences.motif_label: Exiled protector returns to power
occurrences.basis: The protector may be driven out, soon return from exile, obtain a bodyguard, and become tyrant.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The protector may return from exile, face assassination plots, request and receive a bodyguard, and after crushing rivals stand in the chariot of State as a full-blown tyrant.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 5706-5773
occurrences.motif_label: return as messenger from the world below
occurrences.basis: Er’s soul goes to the world below and he is instructed to observe as a messenger to humans before returning to life.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The story of Er is introduced: Er, son of Armenius, is thought killed in battle, remains uncorrupted, is placed on a funeral pyre on the twelfth day, revives, and reports what he saw below.
Er is told to look and listen because he is to be a messenger to humans from the world below.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic

occurrences.motif_label: exceptional return from deathlike state
occurrences.basis: Er is prevented from drinking, remembers enough to report, and awakens on a pyre after the souls go to birth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The souls travel in scorching heat to the plain of Forgetfulness, rest by the river Unmindful, and drink water that causes total forgetfulness if drunk beyond the required amount; Er is prevented from drinking.
At midnight thunderstorms and earthquakes occur; souls are driven in different directions like stars to birth; Er awakens in the morning lying on the pyre.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 6284-6350
occurrences.motif_label: afterlife journey with return to the body
occurrences.basis: The passage describes a thousand-year pilgrimage, a meadow, a column of light, waters of Forgetfulness, souls going to birth, and Er returning to the body after apparent death.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The narrative includes a thousand-year pilgrimage, Ardiaeus, Er coming to life on the twelfth day, seven days in a meadow, four days to a column of light, a twentieth lot, souls blaming others, waters of Forgetfulness, Er not drinking, Odysseus desiring rest, Er's return to the body, and other souls shooting like stars to birth.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic

evidence.quote_or_summary: The practical statesman sees these reflections as visionary; the philosopher sees them as possible and can imagine common property becoming as fixed as private property, asking whether the end may revert to the beginning.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage reports dreams of a Golden Age that once existed, might exist in an unknown land, or might return in the remote future, contrasting this with the absence of an idea of regular progressive state growth.

occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 1320-1353

occurrences.basis: Alcestis is granted the privilege of returning alive to earth after laying down her life.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Alcestis, daughter of Pelias, is willing to lay down her life on behalf of her husband when no one else will.
Gods and humans admire Alcestis' noble action, and the gods grant her the privilege of returning alive to earth.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 1746-1831
occurrences.motif_label: Separated halves seeking reunion
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly describes people as halves of an original whole who seek their own true loves and a return to their primeval nature.

evidence.quote_or_summary: When one meets the other half of himself, the pair are absorbed in love, friendship, and intimacy, remain together, and feel an intense yearning of the soul beyond ordinary intercourse.

The speaker says the wish to become one expresses an ancient need: humans were once one and whole; God dispersed them because of wickedness; further disobedience could cause further splitting, like profile figures or tallies.

The speaker exhorts piety, calls Love lord, minister, and greatest benefactor, says Love leads people back to their own nature, and promises restoration, healing, happiness, and blessedness if humans are pious.

occurrences.basis: The speaker says Love leads people back to their own nature and promises that, if they are pious, he will restore them to their original state and heal them.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker exhorts piety, calls Love lord, minister, and greatest benefactor, says Love leads people back to their own nature, and promises restoration, healing, happiness, and blessedness if humans are pious.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE BOYS AND THE FROGS / THE NORTH WIND AND THE SUN / THE MISTRESS AND HER SERVANTS / THE GOODS AND THE ILLS; lines 1301-1320
occurrences.motif_label: divine decree explaining present human condition
occurrences.basis: Jupiter responds to the Goods’ petition by issuing a decree that explains why Goods are rare among humans and Ills are common.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Goods went to heaven, complained to Jupiter, and asked him for protection from Ills and advice about how to deal with humans.
Jupiter granted protection and decreed that Goods should no longer go among humans openly together, but singly, unobserved, and at rare unexpected intervals.
The fable concludes that earth is full of Ills, which come and go freely, while Goods come one by one from heaven and are seldom seen.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE BEAR AND THE TRAVELLERS / THE SLAVE AND THE LION / THE FLEA AND THE MAN / THE BEE AND JUPITER; lines 1593-1606
occurrences.motif_label: divine grant limited by concern for mankind
occurrences.basis: Jupiter is displeased because he loves mankind, yet fulfills his promise in a way that prevents bees from killing without cost to themselves.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Jupiter is displeased because he loves mankind, but he has given his word.
Jupiter grants stings such that when a bee stings a man, the sting stays in the wound and the bee dies.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE MONKEY AS KING / THE THIEVES AND THE COCK / THE FARMER AND FORTUNE / JUPITER AND THE MONKEY; lines 1868-1878
occurrences.motif_label: divine judgment contest
occurrences.basis: A divine figure, Jupiter, establishes a contest and reserves judgment over which offspring is most beautiful.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Jupiter proclaims to all beasts that he will award a prize to the one who, in his judgment, produces the most beautiful offspring.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE BOY AND THE NETTLES / THE PEASANT AND THE APPLE-TREE / THE JACKDAW AND THE PIGEONS / JUPITER AND THE TORTOISE; lines 2075-2086
occurrences.motif_label: divine punishment explaining an animal trait
occurrences.basis: A divine figure responds to the Tortoise's absence and explanation by decreeing the permanent condition that he carry his house on his back.

evidence.quote_or_summary: All the animals come except the Tortoise, whose absence surprises Jupiter.
Jupiter asks why the Tortoise missed the banquet; the Tortoise replies, "there's no place like home."
Annoyed by the reply, Jupiter decrees that the Tortoise must carry his house on his back and never be able to get away from home.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE TWO BAGS / THE OXEN AND THE AXLETREES / THE BOY AND THE FILBERTS / THE FROGS ASKING FOR A KING; lines 2135-2152
occurrences.motif_label: Divine punitive response to repeated petition
occurrences.basis: Jupiter is annoyed at being pestered and sends a Stork whose rule results in the Frogs being eaten.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Jupiter, annoyed at being pestered, sends a Stork to rule over the Frogs.
The Stork begins catching and eating the Frogs as quickly as it can.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE EAGLE AND THE COCKS / THE ESCAPED JACKDAW / THE FARMER AND THE FOX / VENUS AND THE CAT; lines 3181-3193
occurrences.motif_label: divine reversal after failed test
occurrences.basis: After the transformed woman chases the mouse, Venus is disgusted and changes her back into a cat.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The young woman immediately pursues the mouse; Venus is disgusted and changes her back into a cat.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE PACK-ASS AND THE WILD ASS / THE ASS AND HIS MASTERS / THE PACK-ASS, THE WILD ASS, AND THE LION / THE ANT; lines 4060-4073
occurrences.motif_label: divine punishment for theft or covetousness
occurrences.basis: Jupiter is angered by the former men's covetousness and changes them into ants.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The former men were dissatisfied with their own work, desired the crops and fruits of their neighbours, stole them when possible, and added them to their own store.
Jupiter became angry at their covetousness and changed them into ants.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE SNAKE AND JUPITER / THE WOLF AND HIS SHADOW / THE PLOUGHMAN AND THE WOLF / MERCURY AND THE MAN BITTEN BY AN ANT; lines 4649-4660
occurrences.motif_label: divine rebuke of human hypocrisy
occurrences.basis: Mercury punishes and questions the man after the man condemns divine injustice but himself destroys many unoffending ants for the act of one.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “They care nothing for a man's character,” said he, “but let the good and the bad go to their deaths together.”
The man angrily stamps on the ant-heap and crushes hundreds of unoffending ants.
Mercury appeared, belaboured him with his staff, and said, “You villain, where's your nice sense of justice now?”

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE WILY LION / THE PARROT AND THE CAT / THE STAG AND THE LION / THE IMPOSTOR; lines 4698-4726
occurrences.motif_label: false fulfillment of a sacred vow punished
occurrences.basis: The man vows a sacrifice to the gods, substitutes tallow oxen, and is punished through a divine dream that results in his sale for one hundred crowns.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A very sick man vows to sacrifice one hundred oxen to the gods if they grant him restored health.
The gods cause the man to recover quickly in order to see how he keeps the vow.
Having no ox, the man makes one hundred small oxen from tallow and offers them on an altar.
"Ye gods, I call you to witness that I have discharged my vow."
The gods send the man a dream telling him to go to the seashore to fetch one hundred crowns he will find there.
At the shore the man meets robbers, who seize him, carry him off, and sell him as a slave for one hundred crowns.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE WILY LION / THE PARROT AND THE CAT / THE STAG AND THE LION / THE IMPOSTOR; lines 4698-4726
occurrences.motif_label: deceptive bargain with the gods returned against the deceiver
occurrences.basis: The man attempts to satisfy a vow with symbolic substitutes while claiming full discharge, and the gods respond with an apparent opportunity that leads to his enslavement.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Having no ox, the man makes one hundred small oxen from tallow and offers them on an altar.
"Ye gods, I call you to witness that I have discharged my vow."
The gods send the man a dream telling him to go to the seashore to fetch one hundred crowns he will find there.
At the shore the man meets robbers, who seize him, carry him off, and sell him as a slave for one hundred crowns.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE WILY LION / THE PARROT AND THE CAT / THE STAG AND THE LION / THE IMPOSTOR; lines 4698-4726
occurrences.motif_label: dream as divine instruction leading to judgment
occurrences.basis: The gods send a dream instructing the man to go to the seashore, which leads to the punitive sale for one hundred crowns.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The gods send the man a dream telling him to go to the seashore to fetch one hundred crowns he will find there.
At the shore the man meets robbers, who seize him, carry him off, and sell him as a slave for one hundred crowns.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE FOWLER, THE PARTRIDGE, AND THE COCK / THE GNAT AND THE LION / THE FARMER AND HIS DOGS / THE EAGLE AND THE FOX; lines 4806-4828
occurrences.motif_label: betrayed pact of friendship punished
occurrences.basis: The eagle violates friendship by taking the fox's cubs; the eagle's own young then die through the burning nest, and the moral explicitly says false faith cannot escape divine punishment.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The eagle and fox become friends, choose to live near each other, the eagle nests in a high tree, and the fox lives in a thicket below and has cubs.
While the fox is away foraging, the eagle takes the fox's cubs up into the tree as a meal for herself and her family.
Villagers sacrifice a goat on a neighboring altar; the eagle carries burning flesh to her nest, wind ignites the nest, and the fledglings fall half-roasted to the ground.
False faith may escape human punishment, but cannot escape the divine.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE GNAT AND THE LION / THE FARMER AND HIS DOGS / THE EAGLE AND THE FOX / THE BUTCHER AND HIS CUSTOMERS; lines 4831-4844
occurrences.motif_label: divine witnesses cannot be deceived by human lies
occurrences.basis: The butcher explicitly warns that the men may cheat him with lying but cannot cheat the gods, who will not let them off lightly.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "You may cheat me with your lying, but you can't cheat the gods"

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE FOX AND THE BRAMBLE / THE FOX AND THE SNAKE / THE LION, THE FOX, AND THE STAG / THE MAN WHO LOST HIS SPADE; lines 5125-5141
occurrences.motif_label: Theft investigated through a temple oath
occurrences.basis: The man attempts to use a sworn oath in a temple as a way to expose guilt, relying on divine detection.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The labourers deny knowledge; the man insists they go to town and swear in a temple, because he distrusts country deities and expects the town gods to be shrewder about theft.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE ROGUE AND THE ORACLE / THE HORSE AND THE ASS / THE DOG CHASING A WOLF / GRIEF AND HIS DUE; lines 5224-5249
occurrences.motif_label: Divine allocation of domains or privileges
occurrences.basis: Jupiter distributes privileges among the gods and decides what portion remains for Grief.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Jupiter assigns the various gods their privileges.
Grief is not present with the rest; after all have received their share, he enters and claims his due.
With nothing else left, Jupiter decides that tears shed for the dead should belong to Grief.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA. / II.--MORAL TALES.; lines 1097-1202
occurrences.motif_label: grudging imitation punished by failed magical reward
occurrences.basis: The second man imitates the gift but gives a mud-smeared fish; the divine old man is angry, and the puppies produce only dung when improperly treated.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Another man imitates the act, catches fish, smears a fish with mud, gives it to the raven, follows it, and reaches the large house.
The divine old man angrily says the man has a bad heart for giving his daughter a mud-smeared fish, but gives him gold and silver puppies with a warning that proper treatment will benefit him.
The second man feeds the puppies plentifully, even on dirty things; they excrete no metal, only dirty dung, filling his house.
The tale explains that good-hearted men could grow rich, while bad-hearted men angered the gods, causing even a gold puppy to excrete dung; listeners are told not to be bad-hearted.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA. / II.--MORAL TALES.; lines 1097-1202
occurrences.motif_label: divine punishment for immoral conduct
occurrences.basis: The tale says gods become angry at bad-hearted men's misdeeds, and the divine woman says the liar became a bad god or devil as divine punishment.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The tale explains that good-hearted men could grow rich, while bad-hearted men angered the gods, causing even a gold puppy to excrete dung; listeners are told not to be bad-hearted.
In a dream, a divine woman calls him bad and says he became a bad god or devil as divine punishment for his misdeeds.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA. / II.--MORAL TALES.; lines 1204-1297
occurrences.motif_label: Divine judgment through pollution and punishment
occurrences.basis: The divine dream speaker says the rat's presence polluted the village, and the second tale says gods punish discarding ancestral belongings.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In a dream a divine-appearing person says the wicked rat took the shape of a little boy, polluted the village, and that the couple shall have a child; the tale says they did get one.
The second tale concludes that one should never throw away ancestral belongings, because the gods will punish it.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA. / II.--MORAL TALES.; lines 1204-1297
occurrences.motif_label: Neglected ancestral object causes illness until restored
occurrences.basis: The boy's illness is attributed to the axe's anger after being thrown away and left rusting; restoration and honor cure him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: When the boy is near death, the divine girl says she is a tray, the divine boy is a pestle, both made with the grandfather's axe; the discarded rusting axe is angry and caused the illness.
The father finds the axe under the floor, polishes it, gives it a new handle, sets up divine symbols, and the son is immediately healed.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA. / II.--MORAL TALES.; lines 1299-1389
occurrences.motif_label: Malicious false advice becomes safe for the innocent but fatal for the deceiver
occurrences.basis: The wizard's intended death-trap becomes a divinely supported journey for the good man, while the wizard dies by trying the same act.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In 'The Wicked Wizard punished,' a wizard says a man can leap from a mountain peak onto clouds and ride them; the man does so, sees the world, and returns with a map of the worlds of men and gods.
The wizard is astonished because his advice was intended as a fatal lie; he tries the cloud leap himself and is dashed to pieces in the valley.
The mountain god appears in a dream and says the wizard received deserved punishment, while the good man was protected and shown the world to become wiser.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA. / II.--MORAL TALES.; lines 1391-1474
occurrences.motif_label: animal antagonist punished and used as warning
occurrences.basis: The shark dies in a degraded way after opposing Okikurumi, and a warning is addressed to present-day sharks.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The shark dies and washes ashore at Saru; the harpoon tip remains in its flesh, and materials connected with the spear and rope are described in relation to its body; scavenging animals refuse to eat it and it rots to earth.
The narrator warns present-day sharks not to die as this shark died; the tale is attributed to Ishanashte and dated 24 November 1886.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA. / II.--MORAL TALES. / IV.--MISCELLANEOUS TALES.; lines 1719-1809
occurrences.motif_label: Divine aquatic rescuer establishes worship obligation
occurrences.basis: The chief of the salmon says he saved the Aino from the waves and requires rice-beer, divine symbols, and libation worship, warning of poverty if ignored.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "I am no human being. I am the chief of the salmon, the divine fish." He says he saved the Aino from the waves and that one night was actually a whole year.
The divine old man asks the Aino to offer rice-beer, set up divine symbols, and worship him with a libation formula; he warns that failure will make the Aino poor.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA. / II.--MORAL TALES. / IV.--MISCELLANEOUS TALES.; lines 1907-2004
occurrences.motif_label: Good man aided by divine beings against a wicked rival
occurrences.basis: A good junior chief receives divine aid, while the wicked senior chief dies after imitating the burial arrangement.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The senior chief is called bad and the junior chief good; the God of the Privy rescues the junior chief from a hole, restores memory of a dream, and says he protected him because the privy was kept clean.

The junior chief is led up a stream through woods to the badger-goddess's skin-carpeted house; she comforts and feeds him and instructs him to tell the senior chief a deceptive explanation involving the god of door-posts and beautiful clothes.
The senior chief imitates the burial and dies; the badger-goddess comes to the village, marries the good man, and he becomes senior of all the chiefs.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA. / II.--MORAL TALES. / IV.--MISCELLANEOUS TALES.; lines 1907-2004
occurrences.motif_label: Divine punishment of a wicked mother
occurrences.basis: After the husband kills the mother, the narrative explicitly says this was how the gods chose to punish her.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The wife, thinking she is telling an old fairy-tale, recounts the actual events; the husband kills her, and the narrative states that this was how the gods chose to punish her.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: HONORARY SECRETARIES. / INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA.; lines 485-608
occurrences.motif_label: Divine punishment for disobedient messenger
occurrences.basis: The cock disobeys the order to return immediately, flies back toward the sky, and is beaten down by God.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After creating the world and returning to the sky, the Creator sends the cock to inspect the world and return, but the cock lingers because the world is beautiful.
God angrily beats the cock down to earth while it is flying back to the sky; this explains why the cock cannot fly high.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: HONORARY SECRETARIES. / INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA.; lines 610-713
occurrences.motif_label: Etiological divine decree explaining human behavior
occurrences.basis: God's angry reply to the ancestor of men is presented as the cause of humans copulating at all times.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The ancestor of men asks when he shall copulate; God, still angry, replies, 'Whenever you like,' and the tale says humans therefore copulate at all times.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: HONORARY SECRETARIES. / INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA.; lines 902-1009
occurrences.motif_label: Divine provider withdraws after human transgression
occurrences.basis: Okikurumi feeds the people in a dangerous world, but after the taboo violation he becomes angry, stops feeding them, and departs.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In ancient days, the new world is unsettled and burning beneath a thin crust, so people stay in huts; Okikurumi fishes for them and sends Turesh with food, while commanding them not to ask questions or look at her face.

An Aino disobeys by seizing Turesh's hand and pulling her into the hut; she becomes a wriggling dragon, thunder and lightning destroy the hut, and Okikurumi angrily stops feeding the people and departs.

occurrences.motif_label: moral consequence announced as hell punishment
occurrences.basis: The antelope warns the hunter that hells, bondage, and torment are the result of his conduct.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The hunter hurls his javelin and says he has lost the antelope; the Bodisat replies that the hunter has not escaped the hells and torments resulting from his conduct, then escapes.

occurrences.passage_locator: END OF THE STORY OF THE THOROUGHBRED. / END OF THE STORY OF THE FORD. / END OF THE STORY ON CONSTANCY. / END OF THE STORY OF THE BULL WHO WON THE BET.; lines 11905-12036
occurrences.motif_label: Meritorious conduct rewarded by heavenly rebirth
occurrences.basis: The Bodisat's religious duties are followed by rebirth as Sakka in heaven, and the women who made gifts are reborn as attendants with corresponding heavenly places.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Thoughtful makes a pleasure ground, Pleasing makes a pond, Well-born does nothing, and the Bodisat fulfills seven religious duties.
A stanza praises support of parents, honor to seniors, gentle speech, truth, and self-control; the Bodisat is reborn as Sakka in the heaven of the Great Thirty Three.
Piety, Thoughtful, and Pleasing are reborn as Sakka's attendants; a Hall of Piety, Thoughtful's Creeper Grove, and the Pond of Pleasing arise in connection with their gifts.

occurrences.passage_locator: END OF THE STORY OF THE FORD. / END OF THE STORY ON CONSTANCY. / END OF THE STORY OF THE BULL WHO WON THE BET. / END OF THE STORY OF THE WISE BIRD AND THE FOOLS.; lines 13359-13469
occurrences.motif_label: Divine refusal to aid one who has attacked religion
occurrences.basis: The Fairy is refused by multiple higher beings, including Sakka, because her speech is described as a blow against the religion of the Conqueror.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After being refused by an initial helper and by the four Archangels, the Fairy appeals to Sakka; Sakka says she has done wrong by aiming a blow at the religion of the Conqueror and cannot intercede directly.

occurrences.source_title: The Giant Crab, and Other Tales from Old India
occurrences.passage_locator: THE GRATEFUL BEASTS AND THE UNGRATEFUL PRINCE / THE GOBLIN IN THE POOL / THE FOOLISH FARMER AND THE KING / THE PIOUS WOLF; lines 1489-1529
occurrences.motif_label: Supernatural punishment for hypocrisy
occurrences.basis: The fairy denounces the wolf’s pretense and imposes a week-long fast as punishment.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The fairy calls the wolf a humbug, says he fasts because he cannot help it rather than from goodness, and punishes him to stay on the rock and fast for a week.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 1 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: PREFACE. / J. G. FRAZER. / CHAPTER I. THE KING OF THE WOOD. / MACAULAY.; lines 1319-1362
occurrences.motif_label: Punishment or deposition of ruler after communal calamity
occurrences.basis: Rulers or a high priest are bound, insulted, beaten, or deposed when rain, crops, health, or fishing fail.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In parts of West Africa, if prayers and offerings to the king fail to bring rain, subjects bind him and take him to his forefathers’ grave to obtain rain.
The Scythians are said to have put their king in bonds when food was scarce.
The Banjars credit their king with rain or fine weather, reward him in fine weather, and insult and beat him during long drought or rain until the weather changes.
The people of Loango accuse their king of a “bad heart” and depose him when harvest fails or heavy surf prevents fishing.
On the Pepper Coast, the Bodio is responsible for health, fertility, and fish abundance and is deposed if the country suffers in these respects.
The Burgundians of old deposed their king if crops failed.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 1 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: PREFACE. / J. G. FRAZER. / CHAPTER I. THE KING OF THE WOOD. / MACAULAY.; lines 1685-1753
occurrences.motif_label: Punishment for injuring sacred trees or groves
occurrences.basis: Spirits are said to resent injury, make hands or feet crooked, and cause sickness or death when sacred groves or trees are harmed.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Battas refused to cut certain trees because mighty spirits dwelled there; Curka Coles believed spirits in treetops would be disturbed and take vengeance; Samogitians believed injury to certain groves or their animals would cause crooked hands or feet.

Frazer says sacred inviolable groves are generally assumed to be inhabited or animated by sylvan deities; in Livonia a tree-feller or branch-breaker in a sacred grove would die within the year, and a Russian who hewed a Wotjak sacred-grove tree fell sick and died next day.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS; lines 2803-2868
occurrences.motif_label: Animal souls avenge mistreatment or warn their species
occurrences.basis: Dead animal or fish souls are said to observe bodily treatment, avenge wrongs, warn others, or prevent capture.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Elan, deer, and elk bones and fat are not to be given to dogs or fire because dead animals' souls see the treatment of their bodies and tell other beasts, affecting whether the species will be taken.
A medicine-man tells a sick man that a deer or turtle soul entered his body to avenge discarded flesh; the Sioux avoid sticking an awl or needle into a turtle to avoid future punishment.
Otawa and Huron fishers do not burn fish bones because fish souls may be displeased, pass into other fish bodies, or warn other fish not to be caught.
Heligoland fishermen attribute the disappearance of herring in 1530 to two lads whipping a freshly caught herring and flinging it back into the sea.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS / NOTE. OFFERINGS OF FIRST-FRUITS.; lines 8514-8594
occurrences.motif_label: ritual acknowledgment required before consuming new produce
occurrences.basis: The Tahitian example links failure to offer first produce with death inflicted on the landholder, and the Roman example says people may not eat new corn or drink new wine before priestly offerings.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Tahitians offered first fish, sacred fish, garden and orchard first-fruits, and livestock to an altar; in Huahine first-fruits were brought to Tani at the temple, with amounts varying by rank.

The passage says old Prussian first-fruits offerings to Curcho have been affirmed but are doubtful; Romans sacrificed first corn to Ceres and first new wine to Liber before people could eat or drink the new produce.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE TONGUE-CUT SPARROW / THE STORY OF URASHIMA TARO, THE FISHER LAD / THE FARMER AND THE BADGER / THE ADVENTURES OF KINTARO, THE GOLDEN BOY; lines 2053-2152
occurrences.motif_label: poison intended for innocent victim returns upon plotter’s own child
occurrences.basis: Terute prepares poisoned wine for Hase-Hime, but her nervous mistake causes her own child to drink it and die; the narrator explicitly calls this the wicked woman’s punishment.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Terute secretly poisons sweet wine in one bottle, keeps good wine in another similar bottle, and brings the two bottles with cakes while Hase-Hime and her stepbrother play during the Boys’ Festival.
Terute mistakenly gives the poisoned cup to her own child; the boy screams, falls in pain, and dies within the hour, while the death is attributed to convulsions caused by wine disagreeing with him.
The narrator states that the wicked woman was punished by losing her own child when she tried to kill Hase-Hime, yet she hates Hase-Hime more afterward.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE STORY OF URASHIMA TARO, THE FISHER LAD / THE FARMER AND THE BADGER / THE ADVENTURES OF KINTARO, THE GOLDEN BOY / THE STORY OF THE MAN WHO DID NOT WISH TO DIE; lines 2251-2371
occurrences.motif_label: Supernatural guide evaluates the seeker
occurrences.basis: Jofuku appears in a luminous cloud, judges Sentaro's desire selfish, and explains why he is unfit for hermit discipline.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sentaro prays at Jofuku's shrine for seven days; at midnight on the seventh day the inner shrine opens and Jofuku appears in a luminous cloud.
Jofuku calls Sentaro's wish selfish and describes hermit life as austere, world-renouncing, desire-free, and eventually able to ride a crane or carp and walk on water.
Jofuku says Sentaro is idle and unsuited to hermit life, but will be helped by being sent to the country of Perpetual Life, where people live forever.

occurrences.motif_label: human efforts fail against celestial summons
occurrences.basis: The Emperor's warriors and the foster-parents' precautions are described as powerless against the moon people's purpose.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Emperor sends two thousand warriors to guard the house, half on the roof and half around the entrances, and the foster-parents hide Princess Moonlight in an inner room.
The old man orders everyone to keep watch; Princess Moonlight says the measures will be useless when her people come and expresses sorrow at leaving her foster-parents.
The bamboo-cutter denies that his foster-daughter could be the one sought; the messenger summons Princess Moonlight, and her room screens open of their own accord, revealing her shining radiance.
The messenger leads Princess Moonlight to the chariot; she comforts the old man and tells him to think of her when looking at the moon.

occurrences.motif_label: hero threatened by divine anger after boastful speech
occurrences.basis: Yamato Take mocks the sea, and the storm is explicitly attributed to the Sea Dragon King’s anger at the jeer.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “This is not the sea! This is only a brook! ... I could jump this if I would.”
After they embark, the sky clouds, a storm arises, waves rise high, and the boat carrying Yamato Take, Ototachibana, and the men is violently tossed.
Kin Jin, the Dragon King of the Sea, is said to have heard Yamato Take’s jeer and raised the storm in anger.

occurrences.motif_label: voyage home threatened by monsters and divine prohibitions
occurrences.basis: Tiresias and Circe warn Odysseus of dangers during his homeward voyage; Scylla kills six men, and Helios' sacred herds are forbidden to the crew.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Tiresias comes with a golden staff, drinks the sacrifice, reveals Odysseus' future fate, and warns him how to avoid dangers on the voyage and after returning to Ithaca.
As Odysseus steers beneath the great rock near Scylla and Charybdis, Scylla swoops down and seizes six crewmen from the deck.

The ship reaches Trinacria, where Helios pastures sacred flocks and herds; Odysseus remembers Tiresias' warning to avoid the island, but the mutinous crew insists on landing, and he makes them swear not to touch the herds.

occurrences.motif_label: Sacred animals violated and divine punishment follows
occurrences.basis: The crew kill sacred cattle belonging to Helios; Helios demands punishment, and Zeus destroys the ship, drowning the offenders.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Bad weather keeps the party at Trinacria; their provisions are exhausted, and Eurylochus persuades the hungry men to break vows and kill sacred oxen while Odysseus sleeps.
Helios is angered; the slaughtered hides creep, the joints bellow, and Helios threatens to withdraw his heavenly light unless Zeus punishes the crew.

Zeus promises vengeance; after seven days of feasting, the crew sail, a storm and lightning destroy the ship, all the crew drown except Odysseus, who floats on a mast for nine days and reaches Ogygia after escaping Charybdis.

occurrences.basis: Europa's sons include Minos, Aeacus, and Rhadamanthus; Minos is made a judge of the lower world with his brothers.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Europa is mother of Minos, Aeacus, and Rhadamanthus; Minos becomes king of Crete and later a judge of the lower world with his brothers.

occurrences.basis: Zeus and Hermes visit in human form seeking hospitality; the wicked place is destroyed while the hospitable couple is rewarded.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says Greeks believed Zeus sometimes took human form and came down to visit mankind, usually to punish the guilty or reward the deserving.
Zeus and Hermes travel through Phrygia seeking hospitality; only Philemon and Baucis welcome them, and the miraculous refilling of the wine bowl reveals their guests' divine nature.

The gods announce the wicked village's doom, lead the couple to a hill, show them a watery plain where the village stood, and transform their cottage into a temple; the couple asks to serve there and die together.

occurrences.motif_label: afterlife allotment for morally neutral shades
occurrences.basis: The shades of mortals neither virtuous nor vicious are said to be condemned to a joyless existence in the Asphodel meadows of Hades.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Shades of mortals neither virtuous nor vicious are condemned to a monotonous, joyless existence in the Asphodel meadows of Hades.

occurrences.motif_label: divine investigation and judgment of human wickedness
occurrences.basis: Zeus investigates reports of wickedness and then punishes Lycaon and his sons after the human-flesh test.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Zeus journeys through Arcadia to verify reports of mankind's wickedness; the Arcadians recognize him as king of heaven and receive him with respect and veneration.
Before murdering Zeus, Lycaon decides to test him by killing a boy and placing before Zeus a dish containing human flesh.
Zeus is not deceived; he reacts with horror and loathing, overturns the table, turns Lycaon into a wolf, and destroys all fifty sons by lightning except Nyctimus, saved by Gaea's intervention.

occurrences.basis: Hera, Athene, and Aphrodite appeal to Paris to decide who should receive the golden apple.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hera, Athene, and Aphrodite appeal to Paris on Mount Ida; Hermes conducts them; Hera offers dominions, Athene martial fame and glory, Aphrodite the loveliest woman, and Paris awards the apple to Aphrodite.

occurrences.basis: Hera's anger at Paris extends to Priam's family, and Trojan sufferings are attributed to her influence.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hera is indignant that Paris did not prefer her; she never forgives him, persecutes him and Priam's family, and her hostility is linked to Trojan suffering and quarrels with Zeus, who supports the Trojans.

occurrences.motif_label: divine patron of civic justice and lawful order
occurrences.basis: Athene institutes the Areopagus, casts the deciding vote for the accused, defends right, and protects civic order.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Athene protects the state, law, and right; supports the Greeks in the Trojan war; institutes the Areopagus; and presides over learning, agriculture, numbers, trumpets, chariots, the Argo, and the wooden horse.
Cities depend on Athene's care, her temples are generally built on citadels, and she watches over walls, fortifications, harbours, and state prosperity as Athene-Polias.

occurrences.motif_label: Impartial divine justice with sword, scales, and covered eyes
occurrences.basis: Themis personifies justice and order and is represented with a sword of justice, scales for careful weighing of each cause, and bandaged eyes so the individual's identity does not affect the verdict.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Themis is daughter of Cronus and Rhea, wife of Zeus, personification of justice and order, presider over assemblies and hospitality laws, convoker of the gods' assembly, mistress of ritual and ceremony, counselor of Zeus, and prophetic divinity with an oracle near the Cephissus in Boeotia.
Themis is represented as a mature, fair, majestic woman in a flowing garment, holding the sword of justice and scales, with bandaged eyes so personality carries no weight in the verdict.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Stellio ridicules Demeter while she eats porridge during her search; she throws the remaining food in his face and changes him into a spotted lizard.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Helios is invoked for solemn oaths because of his all-seeing eye; he informs Demeter of her daughter's fate and is said to possess flocks and herds that may represent days, nights, or stars.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The scorched earth calls on Zeus; Zeus hurls a thunderbolt at Phaethon, stops the steeds, and Phaethon's body falls into the Eridanus, where stream nymphs bury him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Apollo is said to accept repentance as atonement, pardon the contrite sinner, and protect those, like Orestes, whose crimes require long expiation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Apollo seeks Marpessa; Idas carries her off in a Poseidon-given winged chariot; Apollo pursues and seizes her; Zeus rules she must choose, and she chooses mortal Idas.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Apollo marries Coronis; a crow reports her affection for a youth of Haemonia; Apollo kills her, cannot restore her to life, and punishes the crow by changing its plumage from white to black and banning it from other birds.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Asclepius, Coronis' son and later god of medicine, can cure sickness and restore the dead; Aides complains to Zeus that fewer shades arrive, and Zeus kills Asclepius with a thunderbolt.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Apollo destroys the Cyclops who forged the fatal thunderbolts; Zeus, after Leto's intercession, mitigates punishment to loss of power and dignity and nine years' servitude as Admetus' shepherd.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Marsyas, a satyr, finds the flute discarded by Athene; because it touched a goddess' lips it plays by itself, and Marsyas joyfully challenges Apollo to a musical contest.
The Muses judge the contest, with flaying alive as the penalty for defeat; Apollo wins by adding his voice to the lyre, and Marsyas undergoes the penalty.

occurrences.motif_label: divine punishment for bad judgment or insult
occurrences.basis: Apollo punishes Midas for rejecting the judgment in the musical contest; Apollo and Artemis punish Niobe’s insult to Leto by killing her children.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Pan challenges Apollo in music; Apollo is judged victor, Midas alone dissents, and Apollo gives Midas ass’s ears.
Niobe, daughter of Tantalus and wife of Amphion, boasts of seven sons and seven daughters, ridicules Leto’s worship, and asks Thebans to honor her instead.
Apollo and Artemis avenge the insult to Leto with invisible arrows; Apollo kills the sons and Artemis kills the daughters, including the youngest after Niobe begs for one child to be spared.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At Aulis, Agamemnon kills a stag in Artemis's sacred grove; Artemis sends continuous calms, and Calchas says Iphigenia must be sacrificed to appease her.

occurrences.basis: The gods are said to punish evil-doers and bring calamities upon mortals who neglect worship or despise rites.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The gods have higher mental qualities but human passions, punish evil-doers and impious mortals, visit mankind, unite with mortals, produce heroes or demi-gods, and remain immortal though not invulnerable.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A temple on Mount Etna honours Hephaestus and admits only the pure and virtuous; guarding dogs discern the righteous from the unrighteous, caressing the good and driving away evil-doers.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ares kills Halirrhothios after he insults Alcippe; Poseidon summons Ares before an Olympian tribunal on a hill in Athens; Ares is acquitted, and the episode is linked with the name Areopagus.

occurrences.motif_label: divine judgment on opponents of worship
occurrences.basis: Lycurgus is punished with madness after opposing Dionysus, and Pentheus is destroyed after prohibiting and spying on Dionysian rites.

evidence.quote_or_summary: On return to Greece, Dionysus encounters Lycurgus, who drives the nymphs from Nysa; Dionysus leaps into the sea and is received by Thetis; Lycurgus is punished with madness and kills Dryas, mistaking him for a vine.
Pentheus forbids Bacchanalian rites; Dionysus appears as a youth and warns him; Pentheus imprisons him and prepares execution, but prison doors open and his chains burst so he escapes.
Agave and her sisters join women-only Bacchanalian rites on Mount Cithaeron; Pentheus hides behind a tree to watch, is discovered by Bacchantes, and is torn apart by Agave and her sisters.

occurrences.basis: The pirates seize Dionysus as a youth; divine signs follow, he assumes lion form, and the crew is punished while the pious pilot is spared.

evidence.locator: lines 4043-4125, paragraph 1, opening of pirate episode
evidence.quote_or_summary: Tyrrhenian pirates see Dionysus as a beautiful youth in radiant garments, seize and bind him, and take him aboard to sell in Asia.

evidence.locator: lines 4043-4125, paragraph 1, fetters and pilot warning
evidence.quote_or_summary: The fetters fall from Dionysus's limbs; the pilot perceives the miracle and warns the crew that he is a god and should be returned to shore.
After the crew refuses, the ship stands still; vines and ivy cover masts and sails, fragrant wine floods the vessel, and heavenly music is heard.
Dionysus assumes lion form; a bear attacks the captain; the sailors leap overboard and become dolphins; only the pious steersman is spared.

occurrences.basis: All shades appear before Minos, confess earthly actions, and receive a sentence of happiness or misery according to deeds.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Across the Styx is Minos's tribunal, where shades confess earthly actions and receive sentence; Cerberus, a three-headed dog with snake-bristling necks, guards it and prevents return.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Guilty souls go from Minos to Hades' judgment-hall, surrounded by fiery Phlegethon; Rhadamanthus declares torments and Furies scourge and drag sinners into Tartarus.

occurrences.motif_label: Offence against divine order punished by descent to Tartarus
occurrences.basis: Multiple named figures commit offences against gods, kin, or cosmic hierarchy and are consigned to Tartarus or the lower world for punishment.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Tartarus is a vast gloomy place far below Hades; Titans, Otus and Ephialtes, and the principal sufferers Tityus, Tantalus, Sisyphus, Ixion, and the Danaides are named there.
Tityus, an earth-born giant, insults Hera and is punished in Tartarus by two vultures perpetually gnawing his liver.
Tantalus is favoured by the gods but offends Zeus, steals nectar and ambrosia, kills Pelops and serves him to the gods, and is punished with receding water and unreachable fruit.
Sisyphus is described as a tyrant who murdered travellers in some accounts and is punished by endlessly rolling a huge stone up a steep hill that rolls back.
Ixion, after being admitted to divine banquets, aspires to Hera's favour; Zeus strikes him and commands Hermes to throw him into Tartarus and bind him to an ever-revolving wheel.

The Danaides, daughters of Danaus, marry the sons of AEgyptus and kill their husbands by their father's command, Hypermnestra excepted; their lower-world punishment is filling a vessel full of holes with water.

occurrences.passage_locator: PLUTO. / PLUTUS. / MINOR DIVINITIES. / THE HARPIES.; lines 4379-4402
occurrences.motif_label: divine agents punish the guilty
occurrences.basis: The Harpies are explicitly described as instruments used by the gods for punishing the guilty.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Harpies, like the Furies, are employed by the gods as instruments for punishing the guilty; they are three female divinities, daughters of Thaumas and Electra, named Aello, Ocypete, and Celaeno.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: PLUTUS. / MINOR DIVINITIES. / THE HARPIES. / ERINYES, EUMENIDES (FURIAE, DIRAE).; lines 4404-4453
occurrences.motif_label: Divine punishment of moral wrongdoing
occurrences.basis: The Erinyes punish criminal shades in the lower world and pursue murderers, perjurers, and other offenders on earth; later they are said to uphold morality and social order by punishing sin.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Their abode is the lower world, where Aides and Persephone employ them to chastise and torment shades who committed crimes and were not reconciled to the gods.
On earth they act as avenging deities, punishing murderers, perjurers, failures in duty to parents or strangers, and disrespect toward old age; no place lies beyond their reach.
Later the Furies are regarded as salutary agencies punishing sin and upholding morality and social order; in Athens they appear as earnest maidens with a snake-shaped wand.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: MINOR DIVINITIES. / THE HARPIES. / ERINYES, EUMENIDES (FURIAE, DIRAE). / MOIRAE OR FATES (PARCAE).; lines 4455-4503
occurrences.motif_label: divine specification of punishment for the wicked
occurrences.basis: The Moirae indicate to the Furies the precise torture that the wicked should undergo for crimes.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “It was considered the function of the Moirae to indicate to the Furies the precise torture which the wicked should undergo for their crimes.”

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE HARPIES. / ERINYES, EUMENIDES (FURIAE, DIRAE). / MOIRAE OR FATES (PARCAE). / NEMESIS.; lines 4505-4546
occurrences.motif_label: divine judgment according to human actions
occurrences.basis: Nemesis assigns fate according to actions, rewards merit, punishes crime and wrongdoing, and humbles the proud.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Nemesis, daughter of Nyx, adjusts the balance of human affairs by awarding deserved fate, rewarding merit, punishing crime, removing undeserved fortune, humiliating the proud, and visiting evil on wrongdoers.
Although originally a distributor of both rewards and punishments, Nemesis is said to have become regarded finally as an avenging goddess only.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE HARPIES. / ERINYES, EUMENIDES (FURIAE, DIRAE). / MOIRAE OR FATES (PARCAE). / NEMESIS.; lines 4505-4546
occurrences.motif_label: divine vengeance against pride
occurrences.basis: The Niobe example is used to illustrate Nemesis punishing the proud and arrogant, with Apollo and Artemis acting as instruments.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The punishment of Niobe is cited as an example: Apollo and Artemis are instruments for avenging an insult to their mother, but Nemesis prompts the deed and presides over its execution.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: NYX (NOX). / THANATOS (MORS) AND HYPNUS (SOMNUS). / MORPHEUS. / THE GORGONS.; lines 4616-4661
occurrences.motif_label: Divine punishment by bodily transformation
occurrences.basis: Athene punishes Medusa for her offence by transforming her hair, eyes, and skin into monstrous forms and leaving her under a curse.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Medusa loves Poseidon and is united to him in marriage; Athene punishes her by turning her hair into venomous snakes, changing her eyes, and altering her skin.
Under Athene’s curse, Medusa turns to stone whoever she gazes upon until death at the hands of Perseus comes as deliverance.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: MORPHEUS. / THE GORGONS. / GRAEAE. / SPHINX.; lines 4682-4726
occurrences.motif_label: divine punishment through a monster
occurrences.basis: Hera sends the Sphinx to Thebes as punishment for the Thebans' offences.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hera, displeased with the Thebans, sends the Sphinx as punishment for their offences.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: TYCHE (FORTUNA) AND ANANKE (NECESSITAS). / TYCHE (FORTUNA). / FORTUNA. / ANANKE (NECESSITAS).; lines 4767-4807
occurrences.motif_label: weighing of personal fate for life or death
occurrences.basis: The Ker appointed to each person is weighed in a balance when fate is decided, and life or death is awarded according to worth or worthlessness.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Each human has a Ker appointed at birth; it develops for good or evil, is weighed in a balance when fate is decided, and life or death is awarded according to its worth or worthlessness.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: HEBE (JUVENTAS). / JUVENTAS. / GANYMEDES. / THE MUSES.; lines 5052-5157
occurrences.motif_label: Divine punishment of presumptuous challengers
occurrences.basis: Mortal or rival singers challenge the Muses and are punished after defeat through blindness, loss of song, transformation, or humiliation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Thamyris, a Thracian bard, challenges the Muses to a musical trial; after defeating him, they blind him and remove his power of song.
The daughters of King Pierus challenge the Muses on Mount Helicon; the mortal song darkens the sky, the Muses' song makes nature rejoice, and the defeated Pierides are transformed into singing birds.
The Sirens enter a similar contest; their deceptive songs are contrasted with the Muses' loyal and true songs, and after defeat they are deprived of their feathers.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE NAIADES. / DRYADES, OR TREE NYMPHS. / NYMPHS OF THE VALLEYS AND MOUNTAINS. / NAPAEAE AND OREADES.; lines 5415-5467
occurrences.motif_label: Divine punishment through self-love
occurrences.basis: Aphrodite punishes Narcissus by making him fall in love with his own image in a fountain.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Aphrodite punishes Narcissus by making him love his own image in a fountain; he wastes away from unrequited love and becomes the flower named after him.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: STATUES. / ALTARS. / PRIESTS. / SACRIFICES.; lines 6201-6287
occurrences.motif_label: divinatory omen from sacrificial victim
occurrences.basis: The victim's restlessness, escape, or peaceful death is interpreted as evil or auspicious omen.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A victim escaping the stroke or becoming restless is treated as an evil omen, while a victim expiring without a struggle is auspicious.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CEREALIA. / VESTALIA. / PART II.--LEGENDS. / CADMUS.; lines 6563-6631
occurrences.motif_label: divine punishment commuted to servitude
occurrences.basis: Ares seeks to kill Cadmus for slaying the dragon, but Zeus mediates and the punishment becomes eight years of servitude.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ares is enraged that Cadmus killed his dragon; Zeus intervenes and the punishment is mitigated to eight years of servitude.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VESTALIA. / PART II.--LEGENDS. / CADMUS. / PERSEUS.; lines 6633-6734
occurrences.motif_label: divine punishment by flood and monster
occurrences.basis: After Cassiopea's boast, the Nereides appeal to Poseidon, who devastates Ethiopia with inundation and a devouring monster.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Perseus arrives in Ethiopia, sees flood devastation and Andromeda chained to a rock; Cassiopea's boast against the Nereides led them to ask Poseidon for vengeance, and he sent inundation and a devouring monster.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VESTALIA. / PART II.--LEGENDS. / CADMUS. / PERSEUS.; lines 6736-6832
occurrences.motif_label: Poisoned drink exposed through ritual libation and animal death
occurrences.basis: Ion pours wine as a libation before drinking; a dove drinks it and dies, revealing the poison.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At Ion's adoption banquet, Creusa's old servant poisons the wine; Ion pours a libation before drinking, a dove drinks the wine, quivers, and dies.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CADMUS. / PERSEUS. / THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE.; lines 7050-7143
occurrences.motif_label: Divine punishment of a prophet
occurrences.basis: Phineus is punished by the gods with premature old age and blindness for abusing prophecy.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In Bithynia, the aged blind prophet-king Phineus has been punished by the gods for abusing prophecy and is tormented by Harpies who spoil his food; Zetes and Calais recognize him as kin by marriage and promise aid.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CADMUS. / PERSEUS. / THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE.; lines 7334-7430
occurrences.motif_label: Blood-guilt, divine wrath, and ritual purification
occurrences.basis: The Erinyes witness the murder, Zeus' wrath is announced, and Circe purifies Jason and Medea through rites involving fire, sacrifice, and offerings.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The prophetic board from the Dodonean oak declares that the Erinyes witnessed the murder and that Zeus' wrath will remain until Circe purifies the offenders; Castor and Pollux pray for aid.

Jason and Medea reach Circe, supplicate her, confess the crime, and receive purification involving Naiads, altar fire, a sacrificed dog, and burned sacred cakes; Circe rebukes them, and Medea leaves veiled and weeping.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: SATURN. / RHEA (OPS). / DIVISION OF THE WORLD. / THEORIES AS TO THE ORIGIN OF MAN.; lines 746-830
occurrences.motif_label: Flood destroys degenerate humanity
occurrences.basis: The gods decide to destroy mankind by flood because of degeneration, and Zeus later drowns the evil Iron Age race.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Because humanity became degenerate, the gods resolved to destroy mankind by flood; Deucalion, son of Prometheus, and Pyrrha alone are saved because of piety.

evidence.locator: lines 746-830; Iron Age and Zeus’s flood
evidence.quote_or_summary: In the Iron Age the earth yields only after toil, wickedness worsens, and Zeus releases waters from above to drown every individual of the evil race except Deucalion and Pyrrha.
