occurrences.passage_locator: THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE. / PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES).; lines 7886-7984
occurrences.motif_label: divine punishment for failed obligation
occurrences.basis: Poseidon punishes Minos for substituting a sacrifice, and Apollo and Poseidon punish Laomedon after he refuses their reward.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minos vows to sacrifice the first sea-born animal to Poseidon, keeps the magnificent bull, substitutes one of his own, and Poseidon makes the bull mad and destructive.
Apollo and Poseidon, temporarily serving on earth, build Troy's walls for Laomedon; when he refuses their reward, Apollo sends pestilence and Poseidon sends a flood with a marine monster.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE. / PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES).; lines 8170-8264
occurrences.motif_label: pollution, purification, and expiation after killing
occurrences.basis: Heracles seeks purification after killing Iphitus and receives an oracular expiation requiring three years of slavery and compensation money.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Heracles wanders seeking purification for Iphitus's murder and reaches Admetus's palace, where he restores Alcestis after a struggle with Death.
The Pythia commands Heracles to expiate the crime by being sold by Hermes for three years as a slave, with the price given to Eurytus as compensation.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE. / PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES).; lines 8170-8264
occurrences.motif_label: divine combat stopped by higher divine arbitration
occurrences.basis: Apollo and Heracles fight over the sanctuary, and Zeus ends the combat with lightning.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At Delphi the priestess refuses Heracles an oracle because of Iphitus's murder; Heracles seizes the tripod, Apollo defends the sanctuary, and Zeus stops the struggle with lightning.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE. / PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES).; lines 8170-8264
occurrences.motif_label: vengeance against oath-breakers or treacherous rulers
occurrences.basis: Heracles attacks and kills Laomedon and Augeas as retribution for their treacherous or perfidious conduct.

evidence.quote_or_summary: When the term of bondage expires, Heracles leaves Omphale's palace and resolves to take revenge against Laomedon and Augeas.
Heracles gathers companions, collects a fleet, sails to Troy, takes the city, and kills Laomedon.
Heracles attacks Augeas, storms Elis, kills Augeas and his sons, spares Phyleus, and gives Phyleus the throne.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE. / PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES).; lines 8170-8264
occurrences.motif_label: accidental killing followed by voluntary exile
occurrences.basis: Heracles accidentally kills a youth at a banquet, is absolved by the father, but chooses to banish himself according to local law.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At Oeneus's banquet Heracles accidentally kills a noble serving youth; although the father absolves him, Heracles chooses legal exile and leaves for Trachin with Deianeira and Hyllus.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: SATURN. / RHEA (OPS). / DIVISION OF THE WORLD. / THEORIES AS TO THE ORIGIN OF MAN.; lines 832-898
occurrences.motif_label: divine punishment of humans through a crafted woman
occurrences.basis: Zeus orders Hephaestus to create Pandora from clay so that trouble and misery will come into the world through her.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Zeus determines to punish mankind and commands Hephaestus to mold a beautiful woman from clay through whom trouble and misery will enter the world.
The gods endow Pandora with gifts; Hermes gives speech and brings her to Epimetheus, who ignores Prometheus’s warning and marries her.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: SATURN. / RHEA (OPS). / DIVISION OF THE WORLD. / THEORIES AS TO THE ORIGIN OF MAN.; lines 832-898
occurrences.motif_label: regenerative torment followed by heroic release
occurrences.basis: Prometheus is chained and his liver is eaten daily and restored nightly until Heracles kills the eagle and releases him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Zeus chains Prometheus to a rock on Mount Caucasus and sends an eagle to eat his liver daily; the liver regrows nightly until Heracles kills the eagle and releases him.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE. / PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES). / BELLEROPHON.; lines 8325-8402
occurrences.motif_label: prideful ascent to heaven punished by a god
occurrences.basis: Bellerophon attempts to mount to heaven on Pegasus; Zeus punishes him by sending a gadfly, causing his fall and later desolation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Iobates gives Bellerophon rule and his daughter in marriage. Later Bellerophon becomes proud, tries to mount to heaven on Pegasus, and is punished by Zeus, who sends a gadfly; Pegasus throws him, and he wanders in remorse and melancholy.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES). / BELLEROPHON. / THESEUS.; lines 8592-8681
occurrences.motif_label: false accusation followed by fatal curse through divine agency
occurrences.basis: Phaedra's letter accuses Hippolytus; Theseus curses him and asks Poseidon to destroy him; Poseidon's monster causes the fatal catastrophe before Theseus learns the truth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Theseus marries Phaedra; Phaedra loves Hippolytus, is rejected, dies, and leaves a letter accusing him.
Theseus calls on Poseidon to destroy Hippolytus; a monster rises from the deep, terrifies the horses, wrecks the chariot, and drags Hippolytus.
Theseus learns the truth from Phaedra's old servant, reaches Hippolytus too late, and affirms his son's honor and innocence.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES). / BELLEROPHON. / THESEUS.; lines 8683-8725
occurrences.motif_label: Divine or underworld punishment for overreaching ambition
occurrences.basis: Hades captures the intruders, and Pirithoeus is left forever to punishment for his daring ambition under an injunction of the gods.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hades is forewarned and orders the two friends seized, chained, and secured to an enchanted rock at the entrance of Hades.
Heracles passes by while searching for Cerberus, releases Theseus, and leaves Pirithoeus to perpetual punishment under divine injunction.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: HERACLES (HERCULES). / BELLEROPHON. / THESEUS. / OEDIPUS.; lines 8727-8823
occurrences.motif_label: communal plague caused by unpunished blood-guilt
occurrences.basis: The gods afflict Thebes with pestilence, and the oracle says it will continue until Laius's blood is purified and the murderer punished.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A grievous pestilence afflicts Thebes; an oracle says the land must be purified of Laius's blood because his murderer remains unpunished in Thebes.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: BELLEROPHON. / THESEUS. / OEDIPUS. / THE SEVEN AGAINST THEBES.; lines 8919-8977
occurrences.motif_label: retributive ruin of a ruler's household
occurrences.basis: After Creon's harsh decree and punishment of Antigone, the passage states that retribution is at hand and narrates the deaths of Haemon and Eurydice, leaving Creon widowed and childless.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Creon condemns Antigone to be entombed alive in a subterranean vault; Haemon enters, finds Antigone hanged by her veil, invokes curses on his father, and kills himself with his sword beside her.
A messenger reports that Eurydice has killed herself after hearing of Haemon's death, leaving Creon widowed and childless.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: RHEA (OPS). / DIVISION OF THE WORLD. / THEORIES AS TO THE ORIGIN OF MAN. / THIRD DYNASTY--OLYMPIAN DIVINITIES.; lines 900-984
occurrences.motif_label: Divine judgment of moral conduct
occurrences.basis: Zeus rewards truth, charity, and uprightness and punishes perjury, cruelty, and inhospitality.

evidence.quote_or_summary: As father of men, Zeus watches over mortals, rewards virtues, punishes perjury, cruelty, and inhospitality, and advocates for distressed wanderers.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: OEDIPUS. / THE SEVEN AGAINST THEBES. / THE EPIGONI. / ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE.; lines 9018-9107
occurrences.motif_label: Divine punishment for kin-slaying
occurrences.basis: The gods punish Alcmaeon's killing of his mother with madness, a pursuing Fury, drought, and a curse on lands that shelter him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The gods punish Alcmaeon with madness and a pursuing Fury; at Psophis, Phegeus purifies him, gives him Arsinoe, and Alcmaeon gives her the necklace and veil.

A drought affects Alcmaeon's adopted land; Delphi's oracle says any land sheltering him will be cursed until he reaches a country not existing when he murdered his mother, so he leaves his wife and son.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE SEVEN AGAINST THEBES. / THE EPIGONI. / ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE.; lines 9109-9206
occurrences.motif_label: Divine punishment through weather, famine, and pestilence after religious offense
occurrences.basis: After Hippolytes kills a soothsayer, the gods send tempests that destroy the fleet, while famine and pestilence decimate the army.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Temenus builds ships and gathers an army; Aristodemus is struck by lightning, Hippolytes kills a soothsayer mistaken for a spy, and the gods send tempests that destroy the fleet while famine and pestilence decimate the army.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE SEVEN AGAINST THEBES. / THE EPIGONI. / ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE.; lines 9109-9206
occurrences.motif_label: Pestilence as obstacle to occupation
occurrences.basis: A pestilence spreads over the Peloponnesus and forces the Heraclidae to evacuate after twelve months.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After twelve months in the Peloponnesus, a pestilence spreads across the peninsula and forces the Heraclidae to return to Attica.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE SEVEN AGAINST THEBES. / THE EPIGONI. / ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE.; lines 9208-9222
occurrences.motif_label: oracular command determines punishment and leadership
occurrences.basis: A consulted oracle identifies the offender's penalty and sets a condition for legitimate military command.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The oracle advises that Hippolytes, as offender, be banished for ten years and that troop command be delegated to a man with three eyes.
In obedience to the oracle, Hippolytes is banished, an army and fleet are equipped again, and Oxylus is elected commander-in-chief.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE EPIGONI. / ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE. / THE SIEGE OF TROY.; lines 9224-9321
occurrences.motif_label: Unheeded prophetic warning before disaster
occurrences.basis: Cassandra warns Paris that bringing home a wife from Greece will ruin Troy and Priam's house, but the narrative proceeds toward Helen's abduction.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Before Paris leaves, Cassandra warns him not to bring home a wife from Greece and predicts ruin for Troy and Priam's house if he ignores the warning.
After Menelaus leaves for a hunting expedition, Paris resolves to rob his host of Helen, storms the royal castle with followers, seizes treasures, and carries her off.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE EPIGONI. / ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE. / THE SIEGE OF TROY.; lines 9417-9512
occurrences.motif_label: Divine obstruction of voyage after sacrilege
occurrences.basis: Artemis sends continuous calms after Agamemnon kills her sacred hind, preventing the fleet from sailing.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Agamemnon kills Artemis' sacred hind; Artemis sends calms; Calchas says Iphigenia's sacrifice is required, and the passage notes Artemis saves her.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE EPIGONI. / ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE. / THE SIEGE OF TROY.; lines 9417-9512
occurrences.motif_label: Divine plague after insult to priest
occurrences.basis: Apollo sends pestilence because Agamemnon insulted Chryses, Apollo's priest, and refused to surrender Chryseis.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Chryses comes to ransom his daughter; Agamemnon refuses and insults him; Chryses prays to Apollo, who sends a pestilence on the Greek camp.
Achilles consults Calchas, who says Apollo sent the plague because his priest was insulted and that surrendering Chryseis will appease Apollo.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE EPIGONI. / ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE. / THE SIEGE OF TROY.; lines 9417-9512
occurrences.motif_label: Ransom refused for captive child leading to divine vengeance
occurrences.basis: Chryses seeks to ransom his daughter Chryseis; Agamemnon refuses, Chryses prays, and Apollo sends plague.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Chryses comes to ransom his daughter; Agamemnon refuses and insults him; Chryses prays to Apollo, who sends a pestilence on the Greek camp.
Achilles consults Calchas, who says Apollo sent the plague because his priest was insulted and that surrendering Chryseis will appease Apollo.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE EPIGONI. / ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE. / THE SIEGE OF TROY.; lines 9687-9774
occurrences.motif_label: divine weighing of mortal fates before combat
occurrences.basis: Zeus weighs the fates of Achilles and Memnon and the result foretells Memnon's death.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Thetis and Eos hasten to Olympus to intercede for their sons; Zeus refuses to oppose the Moirae, weighs the heroes' fates in golden scales, and Memnon's fate sinks, portending death.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE EPIGONI. / ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE. / THE SIEGE OF TROY.; lines 9776-9867
occurrences.motif_label: Serpent punishment interpreted as divine judgment
occurrences.basis: The Trojans interpret the serpent-killing of Laocoon and his sons as punishment sent by Zeus for sacrilege against the horse.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Two enormous serpents rise from the sea and kill Laocoon and his sons at the altar; the Trojans interpret this as Zeus's punishment for sacrilege against the horse.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE. / THE SIEGE OF TROY. / RETURN OF THE GREEKS FROM TROY.; lines 9913-10010
occurrences.motif_label: dangerous return after sacrilege
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly links the Greeks' troubled homeward voyages to divine wrath after desecration and cruelty at Troy.

evidence.locator: lines 9913-10010; RETURN OF THE GREEKS FROM TROY, opening paragraph
evidence.quote_or_summary: During the sack of Troy the Greeks commit desecration and cruelty; the gods' wrath makes their homeward voyage full of dangers and deaths.

The rats attack from all directions and “were sent to do judgment on him.”

occurrences.motif_label: disguised god tests hospitality
occurrences.basis: Odin assumes the guise of a Wanderer to test Geirrod's generosity after Frigga accuses Geirrod of inhospitable conduct.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odin and Frigga sit on Hlidskialf and discuss the brothers. Odin praises Geirrod's power; Frigga says poverty is better than hardheartedness and accuses Geirrod of violating hospitality by mistreating guests.

Odin declares he will test Geirrod by going as a Wanderer, dressed in cloud-hued raiment with slouch hat and pilgrim staff. Frigga sends a messenger warning Geirrod about a man in wide mantle and broad-brimmed hat.

Odin appears as Grimnir, refuses to explain himself, and Geirrod has him bound between two fires for eight days and nights without food. Agnar, secretly a menial in the palace, gives the captive a horn of ale.

occurrences.basis: Odin prophesies that Geirrod will soon perish by his own sword, after which Odin's divine identity is revealed.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odin sings a prophecy that Geirrod will perish by his own sword and that the Dísir are angry with him; then the chains fall, the fires go out, and Odin appears in divine form.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "Ragnarok was to undo their gods because they had stumbled from their higher standards."

occurrences.motif_label: divine decision of battle outcome
occurrences.basis: The battle's outcome is decided through the favor of Odin, whose first morning glance determines which people receive victory.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odin and Frigga sit on Hlidskialf watching the Winilers and Vandals prepare for battle; the Vandals pray to Odin and the Winilers seek Frigga's aid.
Odin avoids choosing immediately and says he will give victory to those whom his eyes first rest upon in the morning.
Odin wakes, sees the armed host, asks what Longbeards they are, and Frigga says he has given them a new name and must give a baptismal gift.
Frigga urges Odin to give them victory; Odin, outwitted, does so, and the Winilers keep the name and receive his later care and blessings.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Syn guards Frigga’s palace door, refuses unauthorized entry, and presides over tribunals and trials; a veto may be phrased as Syn being against it.

occurrences.basis: Vara hears all oaths, punishes perjurers, and rewards faithful oath-keepers.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Vara hears oaths, punishes perjurers, and rewards oath-keepers; Vör knows what will occur throughout the world; Snotra is goddess of virtue and has mastered all knowledge.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Bertha is a patron of spinning who visits households during the twelve nights, rewarding careful maidens and damaging the work or punishing careless ones.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Brock presents Draupnir to Odin, Gullin-bursti to Frey, and Miölnir to Thor. Loki presents Gungnir to Odin, Skidbladnir to Frey, and golden hair to Thor; the hair grows on Sif's head. The gods judge Brock winner because Miölnir will be invaluable against frost giants on the last day.

occurrences.motif_label: divine anger resolved by offering children as lifelong servants
occurrences.basis: Thor becomes wrathful after Thialfi's disobedience, and the peasant offers Thialfi and Roskva to serve Thor forever as compensation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Thialfi, encouraged by Loki, breaks a bone and sucks out the marrow. In the morning Thor strikes the goat skins with Miölnir, and the goats return alive, one lame. Thialfi admits fault, and the peasant offers Thialfi and Roskva to serve Thor forever.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At Geirrod’s house, Thor sits in a chair that rises; he braces Grid’s staff against the ceiling, forces the chair down, and crushes Geirrod’s daughters Gialp and Greip, who had hidden beneath it to kill him.

occurrences.motif_label: doomed possessor dies by his own sacred weapon
occurrences.basis: The prophetess reports that the sword's wielder will conquer the world and die by it; Vitellius later loses the sword and is beheaded with it.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Cheru's sword was made by the sons of Ivald, kept sacred in a temple, believed to give victory to its possessors, then disappeared; a prophetess revealed that the Norns decreed its wielder would conquer the world and die by it.
Vitellius discovered the theft, did not fight, hid in his palace, was dragged to the Capitoline Hill, and was beheaded by the German soldier with the sacred sword, fulfilling the prophecy.

occurrences.basis: Penelope proposes that a god angry with the suitors' wickedness has ended them because of their iniquity.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Penelope warns Euryclea not to exult, doubts that Ulysses has returned, and says perhaps a god ended the wicked suitors.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey

occurrences.motif_label: divine punishment after violation of sacred cattle
occurrences.basis: After Ulysses' men eat the cattle of the sun-god, Jove strikes the ship with thunderbolts and all the men except Ulysses perish.

evidence.quote_or_summary: His men eat the cattle of the sun-god; Jove strikes the ship with thunderbolts, all the men perish, and Ulysses alone survives.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XXI / BOOK XXII / BOOK XXIII / BOOK XXIV; lines 10446-10532
occurrences.motif_label: divinely aided vengeance in the household
occurrences.basis: Amphimedon says Jove's will inspired Ulysses and that one of the gods was plainly helping during the slaughter of the suitors.

evidence.quote_or_summary: When the will of Aegis-bearing Jove inspires him, Ulysses and Telemachus take the armour and hide it in an inner chamber, bolting the doors.

Ulysses pours out his arrows, first kills Antinous, and then the suitors fall thickly; Amphimedon says it was plain that a god was helping as the attackers struck throughout the cloisters and the ground filled with blood.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XXI / BOOK XXII / BOOK XXIII / BOOK XXIV; lines 10624-10722
occurrences.motif_label: Divine sanction of vengeance
occurrences.basis: Laertes interprets the suitors’ punishment as evidence that the gods remain in Olympus, and Medon states Ulysses did not act against heaven’s will because a god aided him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Laertes is overcome by the proofs, embraces Ulysses, says the gods are still in Olympus if the suitors have been punished, and fears retaliation by Ithaca and the Cephallenians.
Medon and Phemius come from Ulysses’ house; Medon tells the Ithacans that Ulysses acted with heaven’s will and that he saw an immortal god in Mentor’s form aiding him against the suitors.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XXI / BOOK XXII / BOOK XXIII / BOOK XXIV; lines 10724-10815
occurrences.motif_label: divine intervention stopping human bloodshed
occurrences.basis: Minerva commands the Ithacans to cease war, Jove sends a thunderbolt, and Minerva warns Ulysses to stop or incur Jove’s anger.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva raises her voice and tells the men of Ithaca to cease the dreadful war and settle without more bloodshed.
Ulysses cries out and swoops down like a soaring eagle; Jove sends a fiery thunderbolt that falls in front of Minerva.
Minerva tells Ulysses to stop the war or Jove will be angry; Ulysses gladly obeys.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: The Odyssey / PREFACE TO FIRST EDITION; lines 113-185
occurrences.motif_label: divine punishment for consuming a god's cattle
occurrences.basis: The company devour the oxen of Helios Hyperion and perish; a god removes their day of returning.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The quoted opening says the company were not saved: they perished after devouring the oxen of Helios Hyperion, and the god took away their day of returning; the goddess, daughter of Zeus, is asked to declare these things.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XXII / BOOK XXIII / BOOK XXIV / FOOTNOTES:; lines 11490-11612
occurrences.motif_label: Holy figure destroys attackers at a harbour rock
occurrences.basis: The local legend has the Madonna di Trapani crushing a pirate ship under a rock as the pirates enter port intending to attack Trapani.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A rock at the end of the Northern harbour of Trapani is called Malconsiglio, 'the rock of evil counsel'; a legend says a Turkish pirate ship intending to attack Trapani was crushed under the rock by the Madonna di Trapani, and exactly three drops of oil on the nearby water reveal the ship at the bottom.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I / BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS.; lines 1232-1327
occurrences.motif_label: divine displeasure obstructing human return
occurrences.basis: Jove vexes the Argives, Minerva's displeasure causes quarrel, and Nestor attributes bad outcomes to divine anger or decision.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After Priam's city was sacked, Jove vexed the Argives on their voyage home, and Minerva's displeasure brought about a quarrel between the sons of Atreus.
At a sunset meeting, Menelaus wanted to sail home, while Agamemnon wanted to wait and offer hecatombs to appease Minerva; the Achaeans split in opinion.
Jove is said to hatch mischief; some Achaeans launch ships, others remain with Agamemnon, and later some turn back under Ulysses while Nestor presses onward.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I / BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS.; lines 1329-1422
occurrences.motif_label: divine control of death and travel peril
occurrences.basis: Minerva says gods cannot save a man once his death-hour comes; Apollo kills Phrontis, and Jove sends destructive winds and waves against Menelaus.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva says heaven can save a man, that safe homecoming is worth suffering for, and that not even the gods can save a man when his hour of death comes.
At Sunium Apollo kills Phrontis, the steersman of Menelaus' ship, and Menelaus waits to bury him and perform funeral rites.
Near the Malean heads Jove sends hard winds and high waves; Menelaus' fleet is divided, some ships are wrecked near Crete, and five ships are carried to Egypt.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Odyssey / PREFACE TO FIRST EDITION; lines 187-272
occurrences.motif_label: warning ignored and vengeance fulfilled
occurrences.basis: Aegisthus ignores Hermes' warning, kills the returning husband, and is later slain by Orestes as vengeance.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Zeus says mortals blame gods for self-caused sorrows; he recalls Aegisthus taking the son of Atreus' wife and killing him despite Hermes' warning, after which Orestes avenges him.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS. / BOOK IV; lines 1950-2039
occurrences.motif_label: divine obstruction and release of homecoming
occurrences.basis: Menelaus asks which immortal hinders him, and Proteus says the gods will permit the voyage after sacrifice.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Menelaus asks the old man which immortal is hindering him and how he may sail the sea to reach home.
Proteus says Menelaus must sacrifice to Jove and the gods, return to Egypt, and offer holy hecatombs before the gods will let him finish his voyage.

occurrences.motif_label: boast against gods followed by punitive drowning
occurrences.basis: Ajax claims the gods cannot drown him; Neptune responds by splitting the rock and Ajax drowns in the sea.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Proteus recounts Ajax's wreck at Gyrae, his boast that the gods could not drown him, Neptune's splitting of the rock with a trident, and Ajax's drowning in salt water.

occurrences.motif_label: divine punishment of divine-mortal unions
occurrences.basis: Calypso's examples describe Orion killed after Dawn's love and Iasion killed by Jove's thunderbolts after union with Ceres.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Calypso cites Dawn's love for Orion, followed by Diana killing him, and Ceres' union with Iasion, followed by Jove killing Iasion with thunderbolts.

occurrences.motif_label: ambiguous divine visitor at a feast
occurrences.basis: Alcinous says the stranger may be an immortal from heaven, while explaining that gods commonly appear openly to the Phaeacians at feasts and to solitary wayfarers.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Alcinous says the stranger might be an immortal from heaven, though Phaeacian gods usually appear openly at hecatombs, feasts, and encounters with solitary wayfarers because of kinship with gods, Cyclopes, and giants.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: THE MEETING BETWEEN NAUSICAA AND ULYSSES. / BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS. / BOOK VIII; lines 3698-3785
occurrences.motif_label: divine punishment threatened against helpers of travelers
occurrences.basis: Alcinous recalls that Neptune is angry at the Phaeacians for escorting people and may wreck a returning ship and bury their city beneath a high mountain.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Alcinous remembers his father saying Neptune was angry at Phaeacian escorts and might wreck a returning ship and bury their city under a high mountain, though the god's decision is uncertain.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: PREFACE TO SECOND EDITION / HENRY FESTING JONES. / THE ODYSSEY / BOOK I; lines 390-492
occurrences.motif_label: divine council determines mortal fate
occurrences.basis: The gods meet in council, discuss Aegisthus' fate and Ulysses' suffering, and decide on actions affecting Ulysses and Telemachus.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Neptune has gone to the Ethiopians at the world's end to accept a hecatomb, while the other gods meet at the house of Olympian Jove.
Jove says mortals blame gods for their own folly and cites Aegisthus, who ignored Mercury's warning, took Agamemnon's wife, killed Agamemnon, and was avenged by Orestes.
Jove praises Ulysses but explains that Neptune is angry because Ulysses blinded Polyphemus, son of Neptune and Thoosa; Neptune prevents the return, but the gods can plan together to help Ulysses.

Minerva proposes sending Mercury to Ogygia to announce the decision to Calypso, while she goes to Ithaca to strengthen Telemachus, confront the suitors, and send him to Sparta and Pylos for news of Ulysses.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: PREFACE TO SECOND EDITION / HENRY FESTING JONES. / THE ODYSSEY / BOOK I; lines 390-492
occurrences.motif_label: punishment after ignored divine warning
occurrences.basis: Jove states that Mercury warned Aegisthus not to commit adultery and murder, but Aegisthus ignored the warning and paid in full through Orestes' revenge.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Jove says mortals blame gods for their own folly and cites Aegisthus, who ignored Mercury's warning, took Agamemnon's wife, killed Agamemnon, and was avenged by Orestes.

occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS. / BOOK VIII / BOOK IX; lines 4170-4268
occurrences.motif_label: Hospitality violation punished by gods
occurrences.basis: Ulysses accuses Polyphemus of eating visitors in his house and says Jove and the other gods have punished him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses taunts the Cyclops for eating visitors in his cave and says, “Jove and the other gods have punished you.”

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS. / BOOK VIII / BOOK IX; lines 4270-4293
occurrences.motif_label: sacrifice not accepted by deity
occurrences.basis: Ulysses burns the ram's thigh bones to Jove, but Jove does not heed the sacrifice and thinks of destroying the ships and comrades.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses receives the ram as an extra share, sacrifices it on the sea shore, burns its thigh bones to Jove, but Jove does not heed the sacrifice and thinks of destroying the ships and comrades.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VIII / BOOK IX / BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE.; lines 4296-4397
occurrences.motif_label: failed supplication after divine-disfavor interpretation
occurrences.basis: Ulysses asks Aeolus to repair the mischief, but Aeolus refuses because he interprets Ulysses as abhorred of heaven.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses goes with a herald and one man to Aeolus's house, sits as a suppliant at the threshold, and says his men and cruel sleep have ruined him.
Aeolus answers that he will not help one 'abhorred of heaven' and sends Ulysses sorrowing from his door.

occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE. / BOOK XI / THE VISIT TO THE DEAD.88; lines 4969-5068
occurrences.motif_label: divine punishment or divine exposure of transgression
occurrences.basis: The gods reveal the story of Epicaste and Oedipodes; Apollo kills Otus and Ephialtes; Diana kills Ariadne because of Bacchus's words.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Epicaste, mother of Oedipodes, unknowingly marries her son after he has killed his father; the gods reveal the story, she hangs herself, and avenging spirits haunt him.

Iphimedeia, wife of Aloeus, boasts of Neptune's embrace and bears Otus and Ephialtes; the giant youths threaten Olympus and try to pile Ossa on Olympus and Pelion on Ossa to scale heaven, but Apollo kills them before maturity.
The narrator sees Phaedra, Procris, and Ariadne, daughter of Minos; Theseus carries Ariadne from Crete toward Athens, but Diana kills her on Dia because of what Bacchus said against her.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE. / BOOK XI / THE VISIT TO THE DEAD.88; lines 4969-5068
occurrences.motif_label: carried-off beloved prevented from union by divine killing
occurrences.basis: Theseus carries Ariadne away from Crete toward Athens, but Diana kills her before he enjoys her.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The narrator sees Phaedra, Procris, and Ariadne, daughter of Minos; Theseus carries Ariadne from Crete toward Athens, but Diana kills her on Dia because of what Bacchus said against her.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE. / BOOK XI / THE VISIT TO THE DEAD.88; lines 5171-5269
occurrences.motif_label: judgment of the dead
occurrences.basis: Minos sits in Hades with a golden sceptre, judging the dead while ghosts gather to hear his sentences.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses sees Minos son of Jove holding a golden sceptre and sitting in judgement on the dead, with ghosts gathered around to learn his sentences.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE. / BOOK XI / THE VISIT TO THE DEAD.88; lines 5171-5269
occurrences.motif_label: eternal bodily punishment for transgression against a divine beloved
occurrences.basis: Tityus is tormented by vultures because he violated Leto, described as Jove’s mistress.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses sees Tityus son of Gaia stretched over nine acres while two vultures tear at his liver; the passage explains that he had violated Leto on her journey through Panopeus toward Pytho.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE. / BOOK XI / THE VISIT TO THE DEAD.88; lines 5271-5317
occurrences.motif_label: punitive afterlife ordeals
occurrences.basis: Tantalus and Sisyphus are shown undergoing continuing punishments among the dead; Tantalus' deprivation is attributed to the spite of heaven.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Tantalus stands in a lake up to his chin, but whenever he stoops to drink, the water dries up and vanishes.
Fruit trees over Tantalus bear pears, pomegranates, apples, figs, and olives, but the branches are tossed back when he reaches for them.
Sisyphus tries with hands and feet to roll a prodigious stone uphill; near the top the stone thunders back down, and he starts again.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XI / THE VISIT TO THE DEAD.88 / BOOK XII / THE SIRENS, SCYLLA AND CHARYBDIS, THE CATTLE OF THE SUN.; lines 5422-5511
occurrences.motif_label: Sacred animals under divine taboo
occurrences.basis: The sun-god's herds and flocks are marked as divine property, tended by goddesses, and harming them is said to cause destruction of ship and comrades.

evidence.quote_or_summary: On Thrinacia are seven herds of cattle and seven flocks of sheep belonging to the sun-god, each with fifty animals, neither breeding nor diminishing; Phaethusa and Lampetie, daughters of Hyperion by Neaera, tend them.

The goddess warns that if the flocks are left unharmed Ulysses may reach Ithaca after hardship, but if harmed, the ship and comrades will be destroyed and Ulysses will return late and in bad condition if he survives.

Ulysses asks whether Minerva and Jove are sufficient allies, and Telemachus answers that they are powerful allies who dwell among the clouds and have power over gods and men.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Amphinomus, described as a leading suitor from Dulichium and of good disposition, says he does not favor killing Telemachus, calls killing one of noble blood heinous, and advises first consulting the oracles of Jove.
Penelope learns from Medon of the plot, comes down with her maidens, stands beside a bearing-post holding a veil before her face, and begins to rebuke Antinous.

Penelope accuses Antinous of plotting against Telemachus despite Jove's witness over suppliants, recalls that Ulysses saved Antinous' father from an enraged crowd, and condemns the suitors for consuming Ulysses' property and trying to kill his son.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After the suitors applaud the bard, Minerva prompts Ulysses to beg from each suitor so he may distinguish good from bad, while she will not save any of them.
Ulysses goes around from left to right, stretching out his hands as though a real beggar; some suitors pity him and ask who he is and where he came from.
Antinous replies harshly, draws the stool from under his feet as if to throw it at Ulysses, while the other suitors give food and fill Ulysses's wallet.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses asks Antinous for a gift, says Antinous seems a chief and should be a better giver, and recalls that he was once wealthy and gave to tramps.
Ulysses says Jove took his wealth away and sent him with roving robbers to Egypt, where he stationed ships in the river Aegyptus and ordered his men to keep guard.
In the tale, the men disobey, ravage Egyptian land, kill men, take wives and children captive, and are defeated after Jove spreads panic among them.
Ulysses says the Egyptians killed many, took the rest alive for forced labour, and gave him to Dmetor son of Iasus to take to Cyprus, from which he came in misery.

Telemachus sneezes loudly as Penelope speaks; Penelope laughs and interprets it as meaning that all the suitors will be killed, then promises the stranger clothing if she believes him truthful.

“give me the bow that I may prove the power of my hands among you all”

evidence.quote_or_summary: The suitors throw their spears, but Minerva makes them ineffective; the spears strike a door post, the door, and the wall.
The suitors aim a second time, but Minerva again makes most weapons ineffective; only Telemachus and Eumaeus receive slight wounds.
Minerva holds up her deadly aegis from the rafter; the suitors become afraid and flee like cattle driven by a gadfly.
Ulysses and his men are compared to vultures attacking smaller birds; they strike the suitors on every side, and the ground seethes with blood.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Euryclea finds Ulysses among the corpses, bloodied like a lion after devouring an ox; she begins to cry out for joy, but Ulysses restrains her and says it is unholy to vaunt over dead men, whose destruction came through Heaven’s doom and their evil deeds.
Euryclea says there are fifty women in the house and that twelve have misbehaved and lacked respect toward her and Penelope; she says some god has sent Penelope to sleep.

The women are confined in a narrow space; Telemachus says he will not let them die a clean death, fastens a ship’s cable, and they put their heads in nooses, compared to thrushes or doves caught in a net.
Melanthius is taken through the cloister into the inner court, where his nose, ears, hands, and feet are cut off and his raw vitals are given to dogs.

occurrences.motif_label: divine sign forbids departure until atonement
occurrences.basis: Socrates’ sign forbids him to cross the stream, and a voice says he has committed impiety and must atone before leaving.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says that as he was about to cross the stream his usual sign forbade him, and he heard a voice say he had committed impiety and must atone before going away.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 208-288
occurrences.motif_label: Afterlife judgment and postmortem destinations
occurrences.basis: Souls are judged after death, with bad souls sent under the earth and good souls to joyful heavenly places.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “After death comes the judgment”; bad souls go under the earth, good souls to heavenly joy, and after a thousand years souls choose another life; some eventually regain wings, and souls may pass into beasts and return to human form.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2323-2387
occurrences.motif_label: afterlife judgment and allotted destinations
occurrences.basis: Souls are judged after life and sent to under-earth punishment or heavenly reward, then later return to choose new lives.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The philosopher is not subject to judgment; others are judged after a first life and go either to under-earth correction and punishment or to a heavenly place borne by justice.
After a thousand years good and evil souls draw lots and choose a second life; a human soul may enter a beast's life or return from beast to human form.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 3550-3661
occurrences.motif_label: Divine judgment of a cultural invention
occurrences.basis: The god-king Thamus evaluates Theuth’s arts and specifically judges letters by their effects on memory and wisdom.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says Theuth of Naucratis is an old god with the ibis sacred to him, inventor of arts including letters; Theuth presents inventions to Thamus, god-king of Egypt at Thebes/Ammon, who praises or censures them.

Theuth claims letters will improve wisdom and memory; Thamus replies that the father of letters overvalues them, because writing will create forgetfulness, reliance on external characters, reminiscence rather than memory, and the show of wisdom without reality.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1014-1098
occurrences.motif_label: Righteous sufferer punished despite true justice
occurrences.basis: The ideal just man is truly just but unrewarded, misjudged, tortured, blinded, and impaled, while the unjust man prospers through appearances.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The unjust man is imagined as expert, wealthy, eloquent, strong, villainous but highly reputed; the just man is noble and simple, being rather than seeming, clothed only in justice.
The just man is said to be scourged, racked, bound, blinded, and at last crucified or impaled; the unjust man clings to appearance, becomes a ruler, gains wealth, and worships the gods better.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1014-1098
occurrences.motif_label: Blessed afterlife feast for the virtuous
occurrences.basis: Orphic poets are said to depict virtuous heroes on couches at a festival with garlands, enjoying immortal drunkenness as the reward of virtue.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Orphic poets add another-life picture: heroes of Musaeus and Eumolpus recline on festival couches with garlands and enjoy immortal drunkenness as the reward of virtue.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1014-1098
occurrences.motif_label: Futile postmortem punishment of the wicked
occurrences.basis: The wicked are said to be buried in a slough and made to carry water in a sieve.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The wicked are buried in a slough and made to carry water in a sieve; in this life infamy is attributed to them.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 10549-10633
occurrences.motif_label: Rewards and punishments for justice and wickedness
occurrences.basis: The passage reports divine or heavenly benefits for the just and pious, afterlife reward for the just, and Hades punishments for the wicked.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Adeimantus says parents and tutors urge justice for the sake of character and reputation, offices, marriages, and the good opinion of gods, who are said to rain benefits on the pious.
Hesiod is cited for oaks bearing acorns and bees and sheep heavy with fleeces; Homer is cited for a blameless king whose just rule is accompanied by wheat, barley, fruit, sheep, and fish.
Musaeus and his son are said to take the just into the world below, where saints lie on couches at a feast, drunk and crowned with garlands.

Some say the posterity of the faithful and just survives to the third and fourth generation; the wicked are buried in a slough in Hades, made to carry water in a sieve, and given infamy and punishments while alive.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 10635-10722
occurrences.motif_label: Divine judgment complicated by moral inversion
occurrences.basis: The speaker reports that gods are said to give misery to many good people and happiness to wicked people, while also raising the possibility of heavenly vengeance or punishment for unjust deeds.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker says common opinion calls justice honourable but toilsome, vice easy, dishonesty profitable, wicked influential men happy, and gods as giving misery to good people and happiness to wicked people.

The argument considers whether gods can be deceived or compelled, then says poetic tradition claims gods may be influenced by sacrifices, soothing entreaties, and offerings; unjust people could pray and sacrifice to avoid punishment.

A fear is raised that there is a world below where people or descendants suffer for unjust deeds; the reply invokes mysteries and powerful atoning deities, supported by cities and poets or prophets called children of the gods.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 10724-10811
occurrences.motif_label: divine and postmortem evaluation of moral appearance
occurrences.basis: The speaker discusses how justice or injustice may fare with gods and humans in life and after death, and asks about what is seen or unseen by gods and humans.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker asks why justice should be chosen if injustice, combined with deceptive appearances, can secure desired outcomes with gods and humans in life and after death.
The speaker asks Socrates to exclude reputation and show what justice and injustice do to their possessors, whether seen or unseen by gods and humans.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 11459-11608
occurrences.motif_label: Divine punishment as just and beneficial correction
occurrences.basis: The passage allows poets to say that God punishes justly and that the wicked are benefited by receiving punishment, while denying that God authors evil.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Poets may say God punishes justly and benefits the wicked by punishment, but must deny that God, being good, is author of evil, misery, or impious fiction.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III.; lines 12275-12403
occurrences.motif_label: divine punishment invoked by wronged supplicant
occurrences.basis: After rejection, the priest prays to Apollo that the Achaeans repay his tears through the god’s arrows.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker rewrites a Homeric passage as simple narration: the priest comes with ransom for his daughter, supplicates the Greeks, Agamemnon angrily refuses, the priest leaves in fear and silence, and he prays to Apollo for recompense through the god’s arrows.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III.; lines 13084-13196
occurrences.motif_label: punishment by lightning for illicit healing
occurrences.basis: Tragedians and Pindar are reported as saying Asclepius was bribed to heal a rich dying man and was struck by lightning for it.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Tragedians and Pindar are reported as saying Asclepius was son of Apollo, accepted a bribe to heal a rich dying man, and was struck by lightning; Socrates rejects believing both divine sonship and avarice.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1336-1415
occurrences.motif_label: Divine judgment and corrective punishment
occurrences.basis: The passage allows that if gods performed punitive actions, God was just and humans were better for being punished, while rejecting God as author of evil.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speakers say they are legislators who set principles for books. The first principle is that God must be represented as author of good only, not as cause of evil, sin, treaty-breaking, suffering, or war.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III.; lines 13507-13621
occurrences.motif_label: oracle validating civic hierarchy
occurrences.basis: The tale includes an oracle that the State will be destroyed if a brass or iron man becomes guardian.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The tale cites an oracle saying the State will be destroyed when a man of brass or iron guards it.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V.; lines 15251-15379
occurrences.motif_label: Divine punishment feared for wrongful speech
occurrences.basis: Socrates prays to Nemesis not to visit punishment upon him for words he may utter while discussing high matters.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says the answer is difficult, may be doubted in practicality and value, may be only a dream, and is dangerous because he may miss the truth and deceive friends about beauty, goodness, justice, and laws; he prays Nemesis not to visit him for his words.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1689-1772
occurrences.motif_label: Restoration to life followed by thunderbolt punishment
occurrences.basis: The Pindaric story reports that Asclepius restored a rich man to life and was killed by a thunderbolt.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A story attributed to Pindar says Asclepius was slain by a thunderbolt for restoring a rich man to life; the passage calls this a lie and says either he did not take bribes or was not the son of a god.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VI. / BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII. / BOOK IX.; lines 22998-23129
occurrences.motif_label: punishment as moral restoration
occurrences.basis: The detected and punished unjust person is said to have the brutal part silenced and humanized, the gentler part liberated, and the soul ennobled by justice, temperance, and wisdom.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Undetected injustice worsens a person, while detection and punishment silence and humanize the brutal part, liberate the gentler element, and ennoble the soul through justice, temperance, and wisdom.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII. / BOOK IX. / BOOK X.; lines 24190-24303
occurrences.motif_label: divine knowledge and moral judgment of just and unjust
occurrences.basis: The passage states that the gods truly know the just and unjust, count one as friend and the other as enemy, and give rewards to the just.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker demands that justice's estimation by gods and men be restored; he states that the nature of just and unjust is truly known to the gods, and that one is friend and the other enemy of the gods.

The friend of the gods is said to receive all things at their best except necessary consequences of former sins; even poverty, sickness, or seeming misfortune will work for good to the just person in life and death because the gods care for one pursuing virtue and likeness to God.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII. / BOOK IX. / BOOK X.; lines 24190-24303
occurrences.motif_label: virtue rewarded in life and after death
occurrences.basis: Justice and other virtues are said to procure rewards from gods and men in life and after death, and further recompenses after death are explicitly anticipated.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker addresses Glaucon and proposes to enumerate the rewards justice and other virtues procure from gods and men in life and after death, after recalling an argumentative assumption about the just appearing unjust and the unjust appearing just.
The speaker says present rewards from gods and men are small compared with recompenses awaiting both just and unjust after death, and Glaucon asks to hear them.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII. / BOOK IX. / BOOK X.; lines 24305-24376
occurrences.motif_label: postmortem judgment with rewards and punishments
occurrences.basis: Judges assign the just and unjust to different routes, and the passage specifies tenfold punishments and proportionate rewards.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The judges send the just upward to the right and the unjust downward to the left; the souls bear symbols or sentences of their deeds.
For each wrong, souls suffer tenfold over a thousand years; rewards for beneficence, justice, and holiness are proportionate, with further retributions for impiety and murder.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII. / BOOK IX. / BOOK X.; lines 24305-24376
occurrences.motif_label: incurable sinners blocked at threshold and returned to punishment
occurrences.basis: The cavern mouth roars and refuses certain grave offenders; fiery figures seize and punish them further.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At the cavern mouth, Ardiaeus and other grave offenders attempt to ascend, but the mouth roars instead of admitting them.
Wild men of fiery aspect seize the offenders, bind them, scourge and drag them on thorns, declare their crimes, and take them away to be cast into hell.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII. / BOOK IX. / BOOK X.; lines 24483-24572
occurrences.motif_label: cosmic ratification of destiny by divine figures
occurrences.basis: The souls’ chosen destinies are ratified by Clotho, made irreversible by Atropos, and sealed under Necessity after Lachesis assigns the guardian genius.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After all souls choose, Lachesis sends each chosen genius as guardian and fulfiller; the genius leads the soul to Clotho and Atropos, where destiny is ratified and made irreversible, and the souls pass beneath Necessity’s throne.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 253-329
occurrences.motif_label: afterlife rewards and punishments
occurrences.basis: Justice is said to reappear finally as the principle of rewards and punishments in another life.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After the State is completed, justice reappears as the inner law of the individual soul and finally as the principle of rewards and punishments in another life.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 5706-5773
occurrences.motif_label: divine or postmortem judgment
occurrences.basis: Judges assign souls to different afterlife routes according to justice or injustice, with seals of judgment and proportional rewards or punishments.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Judges sit between the chasms, directing the just upward on the right with a seal set before them and the unjust downward on the left with a seal behind them.
Er is told to look and listen because he is to be a messenger to humans from the world below.
For every evil deed there is tenfold punishment, the journey lasts a thousand years, and rewards of virtue are in the same proportion; infants and severe murderers are briefly mentioned.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 5775-5855
occurrences.motif_label: responsibility before divine order
occurrences.basis: The interpreter declares that the responsibility for choosing lies with the soul and that God is blameless; the first chooser later wrongly blames chance and the gods.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “A new period of mortal life has begun”; souls may choose, and “the responsibility of choosing is with you—God is blameless.”
The first soul chooses tyranny, fails to see that it entails devouring his children, and later laments while blaming chance, gods, and others rather than himself.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 6209-6282
occurrences.motif_label: postmortem retribution of good and evil
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly mentions retribution of the good and evil after death.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says there are traces of Homer in the description of the meadow and in the retribution of the good and evil after death.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 757-835
occurrences.motif_label: moral questioning of divine punishment
occurrences.basis: The quoted saying asks whether the Divine being differs from the speaker if evil is punished by evil.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Aphoristic morality is called inadequate; poetic authority is set aside through the 'winding mazes of dialectic'; a Persian mystic poet’s words to the Divine being are compared with Plato in relation to punishment by evil and forgiveness of injuries.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 8152-8239
occurrences.motif_label: Divine judgment before the true city appears
occurrences.basis: Christian and Pagan are said to be brought before the judgment-seat before the true City of God appears.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Augustine is characterized as polemical, lacking a vision of the ecclesiastical kingdom from Rome’s ruins, and looking forward to Christian and Pagan being brought before the judgment-seat when the true City of God appears.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 8401-8479
occurrences.motif_label: collective confession and absolution by civic rulers
occurrences.basis: Citizens confess secretly to magistrates, magistrates confess to their chief, and collective absolution is granted without naming individuals.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The City of the Sun preserves Christian or Catholic elements: admiration of apostolic common goods, use of the prayer taught by Jesus, secret confession to magistrates and chief, collective absolution, perpetual prayer by hourly priests, worship of God as Wisdom, Love, and Power, the sun as divine reflection, and rejection of graven images.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS. / THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I.; lines 8772-8893
occurrences.motif_label: judgment or punishment after death
occurrences.basis: Cephalus describes fears that tales of the world below and punishment for deeds done here may be true when a person nears death.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Cephalus says that near death a person fears tales of the world below and punishment for deeds done here, reflects on wrongs, and may wake in fear with dark forebodings.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 1661-1745
occurrences.motif_label: divine punishment for assault on heaven
occurrences.basis: Primeval humans attack the gods, and Zeus imposes a bodily transformation to humble them.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The primeval humans are powerful, have great thoughts, and attack the gods; the tale of Otys and Ephialtes is cited as a similar daring attempt to scale heaven and seize the gods.
The gods debate whether to destroy humans with thunderbolts as they had the giants, but hesitate because this would end sacrifices and worship.
Zeus proposes to humble humans by cutting them in two, decreasing their strength, increasing their numbers, and threatening further division if they remain insolent.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 1746-1831
occurrences.motif_label: Divine punishment by dispersal or splitting
occurrences.basis: God is said to have dispersed humans because of wickedness, and disobedience to the gods is said to risk further splitting.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker says the wish to become one expresses an ancient need: humans were once one and whole; God dispersed them because of wickedness; further disobedience could cause further splitting, like profile figures or tallies.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 233-318
occurrences.motif_label: Rebellion against heaven and divine punishment
occurrences.basis: Original humans attempt to scale heaven and attack the gods; Zeus responds by halving them to reduce their strength.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The original beings are described as strong and swift, attempting to scale heaven and attack the gods; the gods deliberate over human pride and the fear of losing sacrifices.
Zeus proposes cutting the beings in two so that their strength is halved and sacrifices are doubled.
Zeus splits them, and Apollo is told to turn their faces, rearrange their bodies, remove wrinkles, and tie the skin at the navel.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 233-318
occurrences.motif_label: Piety averts further division
occurrences.basis: The passage exhorts humans to piety so that they may be reconciled to God and avoid being divided again.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says God has halved humans and may divide them again if they do not behave; humans are exhorted to piety, reconciliation with God, and finding true loves.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 64-148
occurrences.motif_label: Divine punishment and reward according to courage in love
occurrences.basis: The gods punish Orpheus for cowardliness and reward Achilles for courageous love by sending him to the islands of the blest.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Orpheus, called a miserable harper, goes alive to Hades to bring back his wife, receives only an apparition, and is later punished by the gods for cowardliness.
Achilles' love is called courageous and true because he avenges Patroclus despite knowing his own death will follow; the gods reward him by sending him to the islands of the blest.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 64-148
occurrences.motif_label: Blessed afterlife destination as reward
occurrences.basis: The gods reward Achilles by sending him to the islands of the blest.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Achilles' love is called courageous and true because he avenges Patroclus despite knowing his own death will follow; the gods reward him by sending him to the islands of the blest.

occurrences.source_title: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
occurrences.passage_locator: Theogony ll. 507-616
occurrences.motif_label: divine retaliation for transgression
occurrences.basis: Zeus responds to Prometheus's trick and theft by withholding fire, creating a price for fire, and binding Prometheus.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage names Prometheus as clever and full of wiles, then describes Zeus binding him with chains and an eagle eating his immortal liver until Heracles later releases him.

"From that time he was always mindful of the trick, and would not give the power of unwearying fire... But the noble son of Iapetus outwitted him and stole the far-seen gleam of unwearying fire in a hollow fennel stalk."
"Forthwith he made an evil thing for men as the price of fire; for the very famous Limping God formed of earth the likeness of a shy maiden as the son of Cronos willed."
"So it is not possible to deceive or go beyond the will of Zeus; for not even the son of Iapetus, kindly Prometheus, escaped his heavy anger..."

occurrences.source_title: The Iliad
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I, The Contention of Achilles and Agamemnon
occurrences.motif_label: divine_judgment
occurrences.basis: Apollo's destructive response is linked to Agamemnon's offence against his priest.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Agamemnon rejects Chryses, and the poem says that for the king's offence the people died.
God of the silver bow! thy shafts employ, Avenge thy servant, and the Greeks destroy.
Apollo descends from Olympus, his arrows strike animals and then men, and the funeral pyres burn for nine nights.

occurrences.source_title: The Iliad
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I, The Contention of Achilles and Agamemnon
occurrences.motif_label: plague_as_sacred_retribution
occurrences.basis: The plague is explained as Apollo's rage and may be removed through ritual diagnosis and appeasement.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Apollo descends from Olympus, his arrows strike animals and then men, and the funeral pyres burn for nine nights.
Achilles asks for a prophet or sacred sage to explore Apollo's rage and learn how the vengeance may be removed.

occurrences.source_title: The Song Celestial; Or, Bhagavad-Gita
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER XI
occurrences.motif_label: divine_time_and_battlefield_doom
occurrences.basis: Krishna identifies himself as Time who kills and states that hostile chiefs will not leave the battlefield alive.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Thou seest Me as Time who kills, Time who brings all to doom, The Slayer Time, Ancient of Days, come hither to consume;
By Me they fall--not thee! the stroke of death is dealt them now, Even as they show thus gallantly; My instrument art thou!

occurrences.source_title: The Ramayan of Valmiki
occurrences.passage_locator: Book VI, Cantos XXI-XXII: Ocean Threatened
occurrences.motif_label: natural power compelled into negotiation
occurrences.basis: Rama's threatened violence against the sea culminates in the appearance of Ocean, who only then offers terms for passage.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Angered by Ocean's silence, Rama says gentleness toward the base wins only contempt and resolves to dry the sea so the vanaras may cross its bed on foot.
Rama prepares the unfailing Brahma weapon, and darkness, thunder, meteors, lightning, violent wind, and shaking mountains register cosmic alarm.
Ocean rises in majestic jeweled form with Ganga, Sindhu, and other waters attending him, says he must remain unfordable by nature, and promises support for a road across the tide.

occurrences.source_title: The Ramayan of Valmiki
occurrences.passage_locator: Book VI, Cantos XXI-XXII: Ocean Threatened
occurrences.motif_label: redirected world-wounding weapon becomes landscape marker
occurrences.basis: The unfailing arrow is diverted from the sea to the north, where it wounds the earth, creates a named well, and transforms the region.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ocean tells Rama to spend the weapon northward against hostile peoples; the arrow wounds the earth, creates the well of Vrana, dries the region's waters, and is followed by a fertility boon.

occurrences.source_title: The Koran (Al-Qur'an)
occurrences.passage_locator: 2. Entitled, The Cow; Adam taught the names, homage, and descent
occurrences.motif_label: garden_fall_with_guidance
occurrences.basis: Adam and his wife are expelled from the garden after Satan's action, yet God follows the descent with prayer, reconciliation, and promised direction.

evidence.quote_or_summary: God places Adam and his wife in the garden, permits them to eat freely, and forbids approach to one tree.
Satan causes the pair to forfeit paradise, they are sent down to earth in enmity, and Adam learns words of prayer that bring divine reconciliation.
God promises direction after the descent and says followers of that direction need not fear, while unbelievers remain with hell fire.

occurrences.source_title: The Koran (Al-Qur'an)
occurrences.passage_locator: SURA XCIX, The Earthquake
occurrences.motif_label: divine_judgment
occurrences.basis: The passage stages universal accountability in which deeds are revealed under divine authority.

evidence.quote_or_summary: On that day shall she tell out her tidings, Because thy Lord shall have inspired her.
On that day shall men come forward in throngs to behold their works.
Whosoever shall have wrought an atom's weight of good shall behold it.

occurrences.source_title: The Koran (Al-Qur'an)
occurrences.passage_locator: SURA XCIX, The Earthquake
occurrences.motif_label: deeds_weighed_or_measured
occurrences.basis: Good and evil are made visible even at an atom's weight.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Whosoever shall have wrought an atom's weight of good shall behold it.

occurrences.source_title: The Popol Vuh
occurrences.passage_locator: The First Book, wooden mannikins
occurrences.motif_label: failed_creation
occurrences.basis: The wooden mannikins are created as a human substitute but are destroyed after displeasing the gods.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The divine beings create wooden mannikins to supply the absence of humans, but resolve to destroy them after their lack of reverence.
The waters were swollen, and a great flood came upon the mannikins of wood.

occurrences.source_title: The Popol Vuh
occurrences.passage_locator: The First Book, wooden mannikins
occurrences.motif_label: flood_and_renewal
occurrences.basis: Floodwaters destroy an unsatisfactory prior race, creating narrative space for later human creation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The waters were swollen, and a great flood came upon the mannikins of wood.
Houses crumble, trees throw them down, caverns close before them, and the ruined race is linked to monkeys in the woods.

motifs.label: Death And Rebirth

occurrences.source_title: Deuteronomy
occurrences.passage_locator: Deuteronomy 34:1-12
occurrences.motif_label: death_rebirth
occurrences.basis: Moses' death is followed by Joshua's recognized leadership and wisdom.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Moses the servant of Yahweh died there in the land of Moab... Joshua the son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom.

The father finds the axe under the floor, polishes it, gives it a new handle, sets up divine symbols, and the son is immediately healed.
Because the divine implements tell him hidden causes and treatments, the boy is regarded as a great soothsayer and wizard who could turn death into life.

The hunter wakes, becomes gravely sick, goes a second time to Hades after a few days, and does not return to the land of the living.

The snake-hunter climbs the pine, throws himself down, regains consciousness as a human, and sees an immense ripped-open serpent body nearby.

Well-born is reborn in a potter’s household in Benares; Sakka appears as an old woman with a cart of golden cucumbers, offers them only to the righteous, and leaves them and the cart for Well-born.

Well-born becomes the beautiful daughter of a Titan because of her virtue; her father assembles Titans for a husband choice; Sakka appears as a Titan, she chooses him, and he leads her to the heavenly city.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Cariyā-Piṭaka is described as showing when and in what births Gotama acquired the Ten Great Perfections required for becoming a Buddha.

The first two Perfections receive whole chapters with ten previous-birth examples each, and the third chapter gives fifteen examples for the other eight Perfections; the author suggests the original plan may have been ten Birth Stories for each Perfection.

occurrences.motif_label: Previous-birth sacred biography
occurrences.basis: The bas-reliefs are said to show scenes from the life of Gotama in his last or previous births, and these stories are called Jātakas or Birth Stories.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Buddhist bas-relief carvings on railings around dome-shaped relic shrines at Sānchi, Amaravatī, and Bharhut are described as illustrations of Jātaka Birth Stories, including scenes from Gotama’s last or previous births; some Bharhut carvings have Jātaka titles inscribed over them.

The bas-reliefs are treated as evidence that by the end of the third century B.C. Birth Stories were considered sacred, represented around important Buddhist buildings, and known by the technical name Jātakas.

The verses describe many births, seeking the architect of the desire-like house, addressing the house-builder, breaking rafters, destroying the central support, and arriving at the extinction of evil desire.

occurrences.basis: The conclusion identifies figures across past and present stories, while the passage explains this through character and karma rather than a soul passing from body to body.

occurrences.motif_label: Long quest through many births to Buddhahood
occurrences.basis: The Bodisat comes through vast kalpas and many births, searches for Buddha-making conditions, fulfills Perfections, and proceeds up to Vessantara.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Bodisat is said to have come down through four asaŋkheyyas plus one hundred thousand kalpas, making resolve in the presence of twenty-four Buddhas beginning with Dīpaŋkara; after Kassapa there is no other Buddha besides the present supreme Buddha, and the Bodisat received prophecy from each of the twenty-four Buddhas.

The Bodisat exerts himself according to his resolve at Dīpaŋkara’s feet, searches for Buddha-making conditions, beholds the Perfection of Almsgiving, and comes down through many births fulfilling the Perfections up to Vessantara.

Verses praise rewards of Bodisats destined for Buddhahood: they traverse a long road through vast ages and are not born in hell, between worlds, as hungry ghosts, as small animals, or with certain impairments when born among humans.

occurrences.basis: The Bodisat is reported dead after fainting in extreme penance, Suddhodana refuses the report, and the Bodisat recovers consciousness and stands up.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Bodisat performs uttermost penance with one seed, one grain, or complete fasting; angels infuse sap of life; he becomes skeletal and dark, loses the Thirty-two signs, suffers pain, faints, and falls.

Some angels say Gotama is dead, others compare his state to that of Arahats; a death report reaches Suddhodana, who refuses to believe his son could die before Wisdom, recalling earlier miracles at the Jambu-tree and with Kāḷa Devala.
The Bodisat recovers consciousness and stands; angels report to the king that his son is well, and the king says he knew his son was not dead.

Eusebius says Osiris among the Egyptians represents fruitful power that disappears into earth in sowing and is consumed as food.

occurrences.motif_label: divine spirit transmigrating at the death of its human incarnation
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly states that at the death of a human incarnation the divine spirit may transmigrate, then gives Kaffa, Laosian, Bhotan, Grand Lama, and Dalai Lama examples.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage states that at the death of a human incarnation, the divine spirit sometimes transmigrates into another person.
After the Kaffa pope dies, priests declare that Deòce has passed into the king, who then unites spiritual and temporal power and reigns as god and king.
Before work at salt-pans in a Laosian village, workers sacrifice to a local divinity that is incarnate in a woman and transmigrates into another woman at her death.

In Bhotan, the Dhurma Raja is the spiritual head of government and a perpetual incarnation of deity; after his death the new incarnate god appears in an infant who refuses mother's milk and prefers cow's milk.
Buddhist Tartars believe in many living Buddhas serving as Grand Lamas; when one dies, disciples expect him to reappear as an infant and seek his birthplace.

The Dalai Lama of Lhasa is head of all Lamas, regarded as a living god, and at death his divine and immortal spirit is born again in a child; accounts differ between recognition methods and election by lot.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In Bohemia, young people throw a puppet called Death into water; girls cut a young tree, fasten to it a white-clothed woman-like puppet, and sing: “We carry Death out of the village, / We bring Summer into the village.”

occurrences.motif_label: Sleeping spring bridegroom awakened
occurrences.basis: The Briançon and Russian customs include a sleeper in a spring setting who is awakened by a female participant, with the Briançon figure called the bridegroom of May.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Near Briançon on May Day, a deserted young man is wrapped in green leaves, feigns sleep, is awakened by a girl who would marry him, dances with her, and is called the bridegroom of May; his leaf garment is made into a flowered nosegay.

In the Russian Nerechta custom, girls go to a birch wood, bind a birch and twist its branches into a wreath, kiss through it, enact a sleeper awakened and kissed, make garlands, and throw them into water to read their fate; Frazer suggests the sleeper was probably once a lad.
