occurrences.motif_label: Blood of a slain figure becomes a named stream
occurrences.basis: The blood of Acis, after his murder by Polyphemus, forms a stream bearing his name.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Polyphemus, a man-eating Cyclops blinded and outwitted by Odysseus, loves Galatea; when she prefers Acis, Polyphemus kills Acis with a rock, and Acis' blood forms a named stream.

occurrences.passage_locator: MERCURY. / DIONYSUS (BACCHUS). / BACCHUS OR LIBER. / AIDES (PLUTO).; lines 4246-4341
occurrences.motif_label: Forgetfulness before renewed embodiment
occurrences.basis: The Pythagorean doctrine described here has souls dwell in Elysium, drink Lethe, and then animate other bodies on earth without memory of the past.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Lethe in Elysium is a stream of oblivion; in the described Pythagorean doctrine, shades drink it before animating new earthly bodies after a thousand years.

occurrences.passage_locator: FORTUNA. / ANANKE (NECESSITAS). / MOMUS. / EROS (CUPID, AMOR) AND PSYCHE.; lines 4917-4962
occurrences.motif_label: death-like sleep and awakening by divine beloved
occurrences.basis: The black vapour throws Psyche into death-like sleep, and Eros, her beloved, awakens her with a golden arrow.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After leaving the lower world, Psyche opens the box from curiosity; a dense black vapour comes out and throws her into a death-like sleep.
Eros awakens Psyche with the point of a golden arrow, reproaches her curiosity and folly, persuades Aphrodite to reconcile with her, and induces Zeus to admit her among the immortal gods.

occurrences.passage_locator: ORIGIN OF THE WORLD.--FIRST DYNASTY. / URANUS AND GAEA. (COELUS AND TERRA.) / SECOND DYNASTY. / CRONUS (SATURN).; lines 549-631
occurrences.motif_label: restoration of swallowed siblings
occurrences.basis: Metis's potion causes Cronus to give back the children he swallowed, restoring them to the light of day.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Cronus fears his children may rise against his authority and swallows each child as soon as it is born.
Zeus grows to manhood and, aided by Metis, causes Cronus to drink a potion that makes him give back the swallowed children; the stone is placed at Delphi as a relic.

occurrences.motif_label: healer who reverses death
occurrences.basis: The passage says Asclepias warded off death and restored the dead to life.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Asclepias discovers cures, perfects healing so that he wards off death and restores the dead to life, and is popularly believed to be aided by Medusa's blood given by Pallas-Athene.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VESTALIA. / PART II.--LEGENDS. / CADMUS. / PERSEUS.; lines 6633-6734
occurrences.motif_label: monstrous birth from slain body
occurrences.basis: Pegasus and Chrysaor spring from Medusa's headless trunk after Perseus beheads her.

evidence.quote_or_summary: With helmet, wallet, Hermes' sickle, and winged sandals, Perseus reaches the sleeping Gorgons; avoiding direct sight and using his shield image, he cuts off Medusa's head, from whose trunk Pegasus and Chrysaor spring.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CADMUS. / PERSEUS. / THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE.; lines 7432-7522
occurrences.motif_label: cauldron rejuvenation and deceptive death-rebirth
occurrences.basis: Medea cuts up an old ram, boils it in a cauldron, and produces a young lamb, then uses the demonstration to persuade Pelias' daughters to kill him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Medea befriends Pelias' daughters, claims the art of restoring youth, demonstrates with an old ram boiled in a cauldron from which a young lamb appears, and Pelias dies at the hands of his children.

occurrences.motif_label: ever-renewed food animal
occurrences.basis: Sæhrimnir is slain and eaten daily but comes to life again before the next meal.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Einheriar eat the flesh of Sæhrimnir, cooked by Andhrimnir in Eldhrimnir; the boar is slain daily and comes to life again before the next meal.

occurrences.passage_locator: LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS / INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN; lines 1014-1160
occurrences.motif_label: cyclical battle wounds and restoration
occurrences.basis: The warriors wound one another in combat and are completely healed when the dinner horn sounds.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After feasting, the warriors arm themselves, ride into the courtyard, fight, receive terrible wounds, and are healed when the dinner horn sounds.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS / INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN; lines 1298-1437
occurrences.motif_label: Murdered dead return as avenging animals
occurrences.basis: The souls of murdered peasants are said to assume rat forms and kill their murderer.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A vast swarm of rats, identified as the souls of the murdered peasants, pursues Bishop Hatto to a stone tower in the Rhine, gnaws through its walls, and devours him alive.
The rats attack from all directions and “were sent to do judgment on him.”

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA; lines 1877-1990
occurrences.motif_label: seasonal loss and restoration through divine absence and return
occurrences.basis: Odin's absence brings loss of blessings and winter-like domination by frost-giants; his return after seven months releases the earth and restores blessings.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odin discovers the sacrilege, leaves Asgard with his blessings, and during his absence usurpers take his place while Jotuns bind the earth in cold, strip trees, and cover the earth in white and mist.
After seven months Odin returns, drives usurpers away, forces the frost-giants to release the earth, and again showers blessings upon it.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA; lines 2238-2359
occurrences.motif_label: Life-token flowers foretell death and departure
occurrences.basis: The blue flowers remain fresh through the man's long life and droop before he returns to the cave and disappears.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The shepherd enters a jewelled stalactite cave, sees a silvery central woman with maidens, chooses blue flowers, and Holda gives them with a lifespan condition plus seed to sow.
The bouquet remains fresh through the peasant's long life, then droops; he returns to the glacier doorway, enters the cave, and is never seen again, living under Holda's care according to legend.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA; lines 2238-2359
occurrences.motif_label: Dead or withered wood blooms as sign of pardon
occurrences.basis: The Pope's withered staff blooms, proving Tannhäuser's pardon after repentance.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Pope says Tannhäuser can no more hope for pardon than for the Pope's staff to bud and bloom.
Tannhäuser returns to the Hörselberg and vanishes; messengers then announce his pardon because the withered staff has miraculously borne green leaves.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA; lines 2238-2359
occurrences.motif_label: Magic fountain of youth or renewal
occurrences.basis: Holda owns Quickborn, a magic fountain said to rival the fountain of youth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Holda owns a magic fountain called Quickborn, compared to the fountain of youth, and a chariot for inspecting her domain.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA; lines 2362-2458
occurrences.motif_label: spring renewal after winter
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly frames Ostara as goddess of spring and of Nature's resurrection after winter, with spring festival customs.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Eástre/Ostara is described as a spring goddess identified with Frigga; her feast preserves customs of coloured eggs, flower-crowned Easter-stones, dancing, and bonfires.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR; lines 2611-2730
occurrences.motif_label: Surviving divine sons rule a renewed world
occurrences.basis: Magni and Modi, sons of Thor, are destined to survive their father and the twilight of the gods and rule a new world rising from the ashes of the first.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Thor's wives and children are named; Magni and Modi will survive Thor and the twilight of the gods and rule the new world.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR; lines 2733-2850
occurrences.motif_label: slain animals restored through intact bones and divine implement
occurrences.basis: Thor's goats are killed and eaten, their bones are to be kept intact in the skins, and Thor restores them by striking the skins with Miölnir.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The peasant host is hospitable but poor. Thor slays both goats, cooks them, invites the household to eat, and warns everyone to put all the bones unbroken into the goat skins on the floor.

Thialfi, encouraged by Loki, breaks a bone and sucks out the marrow. In the morning Thor strikes the goat skins with Miölnir, and the goats return alive, one lame. Thialfi admits fault, and the peasant offers Thialfi and Roskva to serve Thor forever.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR; lines 3050-3168
occurrences.motif_label: younger divine generation destined to survive and rule renewed cosmos
occurrences.basis: The gods read Magni's feat as confirming predictions that their descendants will survive them and rule a new heaven and earth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Magni, Thor's very young son, lifts the giant's foot from Thor; the gods read this as proof that descendants will surpass and survive them.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR; lines 3171-3290
occurrences.motif_label: land becomes fruitful after divine victory
occurrences.basis: After Thor defeats his enemy and takes possession of the land, Odin sees green shoots covering the ruins and the land becoming fruitful.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The gods leave ruins behind, return to Asgard, restore Freya’s garments, rejoice over the hammer, and Odin later sees green growth on the conquered land.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR / CHAPTER V: TYR / CHAPTER VI: BRAGI; lines 3722-3817
occurrences.motif_label: slain wise being transformed into inspiration drink
occurrences.basis: Kvasir's blood is collected and mixed with honey to create a drink that gives poetic and enchanting song ability.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Fialar and Galar kill sleeping Kvasir, drain his blood into Od-hroerir, Son, and Boden, and mix the blood with honey to make a beverage that turns its drinker into a poet and charming singer.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR / CHAPTER V: TYR / CHAPTER VI: BRAGI; lines 3819-3966
occurrences.motif_label: Life emerging from deathlike stillness
occurrences.basis: Bragi shows no signs of life until leaving subterranean darkness, then sits up and sings the song of life near the realm of the dwarf of death.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Bragi, child of Odin and Gunlod, is born in the cave; dwarfs give him a magical golden harp and send him out on a vessel; after showing no signs of life, he sits up and sings the song of life while his song reaches heaven and Hel’s realm.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER IV: THOR / CHAPTER V: TYR / CHAPTER VI: BRAGI / CHAPTER VII: IDUN; lines 4135-4274
occurrences.motif_label: divine youth restored by sacred fruit
occurrences.basis: The Æsir eat Idun's apples and recover strength and good looks; the narrator connects this renewal with spring resurrection.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Æsir rejoice at Idun's recovery, eat her apples, regain strength and beauty, and vow to set Thiassi's eyes as a constellation in the heavens.

The narrator explains Idun as vegetation carried off in autumn, Thiassi as wintry wind, Loki as south wind, the seed or swallow as signs of spring, and renewed youth and beauty as Nature's spring resurrection.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CONTENTS / LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS / INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING; lines 456-592
occurrences.motif_label: World fashioned from a slain primordial giant
occurrences.basis: The gods slay Ymir and use his corpse to fashion earth, ocean, hills, vegetation, heavens, and clouds.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Giants wage war against Buri and Börr; Börr marries Bestla; Odin, Vili, and Ve slay Ymir; Ymir's blood causes a deluge in which only Bergelmir escapes by boat with his wife.
After triumphing over their foes, the Æsir begin improving the desolate world and roll Ymir's corpse into the yawning abyss to create the world from its parts.
Ymir's flesh becomes Midgard, his blood or sweat the ocean, bones hills, teeth cliffs, hair vegetation, skull the heavens, and brains clouds; Midgard is centered and hedged by his eyebrows.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VIII / BOOK IX / BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE.; lines 4680-4781
occurrences.motif_label: fatal misadventure of a companion before departure
occurrences.basis: Elpenor dies by falling from the roof, and his soul goes down to Hades just before the group departs toward Hades.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Elpenor, drunk and sleeping on the roof, wakes suddenly, forgets the stairs, falls off the roof, breaks his neck, and his soul goes to Hades.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE. / BOOK XI / THE VISIT TO THE DEAD.88; lines 4876-4967
occurrences.motif_label: ungraspable ghost of a beloved dead relative
occurrences.basis: Odysseus attempts three times to embrace his mother's ghost, but she cannot be clasped and slips away like a dream or phantom.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odysseus tries three times to embrace his mother's ghost, but she slips away like a dream or phantom; he asks whether Proserpine is mocking him with only a phantom.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE. / BOOK XI / THE VISIT TO THE DEAD.88; lines 4969-5068
occurrences.motif_label: death and recurrent return to life
occurrences.basis: Castor and Pollux die and come to life again on alternate days throughout all time by Jove's dispensation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Leda, wife of Tyndarus, bears Castor and Pollux; they lie under the earth yet live, dying and coming to life again on alternate days by Jove's dispensation, and they have divine rank.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE.; lines 1300-1387
occurrences.motif_label: decline and possible renewal of cultural life
occurrences.basis: The passage describes literary decay and asks whether an elixir can restore life and youth to a nation's literature.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says such an age of sciolism and scholasticism may again overtake the literary world; some think the Muse of Literature may move to less exhausted countries and that criticism may wither original genius.
The passage asks whether any "elixir" can "restore life and youth to the literature of a nation" or prevent it becoming enfeebled.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE.; lines 1389-1409
occurrences.motif_label: Revival from the past
occurrences.basis: The passage speaks of seeds of revival and renaissance in the future and rejects the idea that literature will die out.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Recollection of the past contains “many seeds of revival and renaissance in the future.”
The passage says the world is not exhausted and the fear that literature will die out is groundless.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 208-288
occurrences.motif_label: Cycle of reincarnation and restoration of wings
occurrences.basis: Souls choose later lives after a thousand years, may descend into beasts and return to human form, and eventually recover wings.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “After death comes the judgment”; bad souls go under the earth, good souls to heavenly joy, and after a thousand years souls choose another life; some eventually regain wings, and souls may pass into beasts and return to human form.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2636-2763
occurrences.motif_label: transformed humans reborn as singing animals
occurrences.basis: Socrates recounts that humans who died from continuous singing now live again as grasshoppers, singing from birth without hunger or thirst.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates tells that grasshoppers were once humans before the Muses; when song appeared they were delighted, sang continually, forgot food and drink, and died.
The former humans live again as grasshoppers, do not hunger or thirst, sing from birth without eating or drinking, and after death go to the Muses in heaven to report who honors them.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 639-716
occurrences.motif_label: conversion or rebirth into transformed love
occurrences.basis: The pair must be converted or born again before seeing the world transformed into heavenly beauty.

evidence.quote_or_summary: True love of the mind cannot exist between two souls until they are purified from earthly passion; they must pass through trial and conflict and be converted or born again.
After this, the world is transformed into heavenly beauty and a divine idea accompanies their thoughts and actions.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 718-802
occurrences.motif_label: transmigration through human and animal forms
occurrences.basis: The passage describes the soul's after-existence as passing through many forms of humans and animals and later refers to Plato's possible doctrine of transmigration.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The soul's after-existence passes through many forms of humans and animals and is spent regaining the vision, while animal desires of the inferior steed hinder it.
The passage says Plato may have been serious in his reminiscence of a former state of being and perhaps in his doctrine of transmigration.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII. / BOOK IX. / BOOK X.; lines 24427-24481
occurrences.motif_label: death-to-new-life cycle
occurrences.basis: The prophet announces a new cycle of life and mortality in which souls choose new lives.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “Mortal souls, behold a new cycle of life and mortality”; the speech says the souls will choose their genius, the first lot gives first choice, the chosen life becomes destiny, and responsibility rests with the chooser.

There are more lives than souls, including animal lives and human lives in many conditions: tyrannies, poverty, exile, beggary, fame, beauty, strength, ancestry, women's lives, wealth, poverty, disease, health, and mean states.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII. / BOOK IX. / BOOK X.; lines 24483-24572
occurrences.motif_label: choice of reincarnated lives
occurrences.basis: Souls choose new human or animal lives and are later driven upward to birth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A person devoted to sound philosophy may have a happier journey to another life and return; the choices of souls are often based on experiences from previous lives.
The souls of Orpheus, Thamyras, Ajax, and Agamemnon choose the lives of a swan, nightingale, lion, and eagle respectively, with prior resentments and sufferings affecting their choices.

Atalanta chooses under the attraction of athletic fame; Epeus passes into the nature of a woman skilled in arts; Thersites puts on a monkey’s form; Odysseus, last to choose, seeks and gladly chooses a private man’s life without cares.
Men pass into animals, and tame and wild animals change into one another and into corresponding human natures, with good becoming gentle and evil becoming savage.
After rest, at midnight a thunderstorm and earthquake occur, and the souls are driven upward in many ways to their birth, like shooting stars.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 4961-5048
occurrences.motif_label: transmigration cycle measured by number
occurrences.basis: The passage states that 216 is also the period of the Pythagorean Metempsychosis.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The narrator gives reasons for agreeing that 216 is the Platonic number of births: it fits the description, would be familiar to a Greek mathematician, is the cube of 6 and the sum of 3 cubed, 4 cubed, and 5 cubed, relates to the Pythagorean triangle, is the period of Pythagorean Metempsychosis, corresponds to musical scale positions, derives from the cubes of 2 and 3 in the Platonic Tetractys, and the Pythagorean triangle is called the figure of marriage.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 5706-5773
occurrences.motif_label: revival after apparent death
occurrences.basis: Er is supposed dead, placed on a funeral pyre, comes to life again, and recounts what he has seen.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The story of Er is introduced: Er, son of Armenius, is thought killed in battle, remains uncorrupted, is placed on a funeral pyre on the twelfth day, revives, and reports what he saw below.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 5775-5855
occurrences.motif_label: soul transformation into animal and human forms
occurrences.basis: Named souls and other beings change into swans, nightingales, lions, eagles, monkeys, human occupations, and other animal forms.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The souls of Orpheus, Thamyras, Ajax, and Agamemnon choose or enter forms of swan, nightingale, lion, and eagle.
Atalanta chooses an athlete's honours; Epeus a workwoman's nature; Thersites becomes a monkey; Odysseus chooses the neglected private man's life and rejoices.
Men pass into animals, and wild and tame animals change into one another.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 5857-5941
occurrences.motif_label: death and rebirth cycle of souls
occurrences.basis: Souls complete postmortem rites, drink forgetfulness, and are sent to birth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After the souls choose, Lachesis sends each a genius or attendant; they pass under Clotho’s hand and spindle, to Atropos, and beneath the throne of Necessity.

The souls travel in scorching heat to the plain of Forgetfulness, rest by the river Unmindful, and drink water that causes total forgetfulness if drunk beyond the required amount; Er is prevented from drinking.
At midnight thunderstorms and earthquakes occur; souls are driven in different directions like stars to birth; Er awakens in the morning lying on the pyre.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 6123-6207
occurrences.motif_label: Imaginative renewal of the world
occurrences.basis: The imagined higher poetry is said to renew the youth of the world and recover a former age in which the poet was humanity’s teacher and friend.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage imagines poetry as a hymn of divine perfection, renewing the world’s youth, preserving the good, and joining love with knowledge and service.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 6284-6350
occurrences.motif_label: forgetfulness before rebirth
occurrences.basis: Some souls drink from the waters of Forgetfulness, while souls go to birth and Er is kept from drinking.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The narrative includes a thousand-year pilgrimage, Ardiaeus, Er coming to life on the twelfth day, seven days in a meadow, four days to a column of light, a twentieth lot, souls blaming others, waters of Forgetfulness, Er not drinking, Odysseus desiring rest, Er's return to the body, and other souls shooting like stars to birth.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 6419-6504
occurrences.motif_label: Transmigration of souls
occurrences.basis: The doctrine of transmigration is listed among traces of Pythagoreanism in the Republic.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage identifies Pythagorean traces in mystical numbers, the interval between king and tyrant, transmigration, the music of the spheres, and mathematics in education.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 7874-7955
occurrences.motif_label: cyclical destruction and renewal of civilization
occurrences.basis: The passage describes arts discovered and lost, cities overthrown and rebuilt, many destructions of mankind, preservation of a remnant, and the world beginning again after a deluge.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ancient experience is said to suggest cycles in which arts are discovered and lost, cities overthrown and rebuilt, deluges, volcanoes, and convulsions alter the earth, mankind is repeatedly destroyed, a remnant is preserved, and the world begins again after a deluge.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 1320-1353
occurrences.motif_label: return from death or underworld condition
occurrences.basis: Alcestis is granted the privilege of returning alive to earth after laying down her life.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Alcestis, daughter of Pelias, is willing to lay down her life on behalf of her husband when no one else will.
Gods and humans admire Alcestis' noble action, and the gods grant her the privilege of returning alive to earth.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 1320-1353
occurrences.motif_label: choice between long life and glorious death
occurrences.basis: Achilles is told he can avoid death and return home to old age if he does not slay Hector, but he chooses vengeance and death for Patroclus.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Achilles is presented as the beloved of Patroclus; he knows from his mother that he can avoid death, return home, and live to old age if he abstains from slaying Hector.
Achilles gives his life to avenge his friend Patroclus after Patroclus is dead.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 2200-2261
occurrences.motif_label: alternation between flourishing and deathlike lack
occurrences.basis: Love is described as alive and flourishing when in plenty, dead at another moment, and alive again through his father’s nature.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Love is neither mortal nor immortal; he flourishes when in plenty, is dead at another moment, and lives again by his father’s nature. He is neither in want nor wealth and is between ignorance and knowledge.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 2318-2392
occurrences.motif_label: mortal renewal through substitution
occurrences.basis: Mortal nature is described as leaving a new existence in place of the old, while body, soul, and knowledge undergo continual loss and renewal.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Diotima says mortal nature seeks to be everlasting and immortal and attains this by generation, which leaves a new existence in place of the old.
Diotima says the same individual is not absolutely unified but undergoes bodily loss and repair, and that the soul’s qualities also come and go.
Diotima explains recollection as knowledge departing through forgetfulness and being renewed and preserved so that it appears the same though it is new.
Diotima says mortal things are preserved by substitution, unlike the divine, and concludes that universal care for offspring is for the sake of immortality.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 64-148
occurrences.motif_label: Self-sacrificial death for spouse followed by return from the dead
occurrences.basis: Alcestis dies for her husband and is allowed to come again from the dead as recompense for virtue.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Alcestis is presented as a true love who dared to die for her husband and was allowed to return from the dead as recompense for virtue.

occurrences.source_title: The Ramayan of Valmiki
occurrences.passage_locator: Book I, Canto XLIV: The Descent Of Gangá
occurrences.motif_label: ancestral release through sacred water
occurrences.basis: Bhagiratha's whole quest culminates when the river reaches his kinsmen's remains and their spirits attain beatitude.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Bhagiratha leads Gangá through the sea and nether caves to the dust of Sagar's sons, pours the funeral libation, and their spirits gain beatitude and rise to heaven.
Brahmá praises Bhagiratha, says the sons of Sagar have joined the blest, names the river Bhágirathí and Tripathagá, and instructs the king to complete his vow and libations.

occurrences.source_title: The Upanishads
occurrences.passage_locator: Katha-Upanishad, Part First VII-Part Second IV
occurrences.motif_label: death-question wisdom
occurrences.basis: The desired knowledge concerns what becomes of a person after death, and Yama praises Nachiketas as one who longs for wisdom.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Nachiketas asks what becomes of a man after death.
Nachiketas asks for no other boon than the hidden secret of the great Hereafter.
Yama says ignorance and wisdom lead in opposite directions and Nachiketas longs for wisdom.

occurrences.source_title: The Upanishads
occurrences.passage_locator: Katha-Upanishad, Part Second XVIII-XXIII; Part Sixth XVIII
occurrences.motif_label: deathless self wisdom
occurrences.basis: The teaching concerns the Self that is not born, does not die, and is known by the wise.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Self is never born and never dies; it is not slain when the body is slain.
The Self is subtler than the subtle, greater than the great, and dwells in each heart.
The wise know the bodiless Self within perishable bodies and do not grieve.

occurrences.source_title: The Popol Vuh
occurrences.passage_locator: The Second Book, Hero Twins in Xibalba
occurrences.motif_label: death_rebirth
occurrences.basis: The brothers die together, their bones are powdered and submerged, and they reappear in transformed forms.

evidence.locator: The Second Book, staged death and return
evidence.quote_or_summary: The brothers die on a funeral pile, their bones are powdered and thrown into the river, and they reappear like men-fishes and then ragged old men.

occurrences.source_title: An Old Babylonian Version of the Gilgamesh Epic
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION I, Meissner fragment / Sabitum address
occurrences.motif_label: impossible_immortality_quest
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly says the sought life will not be found because death is imposed on mankind and life is kept by the gods.

evidence.locator: INTRODUCTION I, Meissner fragment / Sabitum address
evidence.quote_or_summary: Why, O Gish, does thou run about? / The life that thou seekest, thou wilt not find.

evidence.locator: INTRODUCTION I, Meissner fragment / Sabitum address
evidence.quote_or_summary: When the gods created mankind, / Death they imposed on mankind; / Life they kept in their power.

motifs.label: Royal Legitimacy

occurrences.source_title: Numbers
occurrences.motif_label: royal_legitimacy
occurrences.basis: The oracle uses star and scepter language for Jacob and Israel.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Spirit of God came on him... A star will come out of Jacob. A scepter will rise out of Israel.

occurrences.source_title: The Mabinogion
occurrences.passage_locator: Pwyll Prince of Dyved; encounter with Arawn and year in Annwvyn
occurrences.motif_label: return_with_new_status
occurrences.basis: Pwyll returns from Annwvyn after ruling and gains the title Chief of Annwvyn.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Arawn restores Pwyll's form, Pwyll returns to Dyved, friendship is strengthened, and Pwyll is called Chief of Annwvyn.

occurrences.source_title: The Sayings of Confucius
occurrences.passage_locator: Government and Public Affairs
occurrences.motif_label: moral center of rule
occurrences.basis: The ruler's virtue is treated as an ordering center that draws the community into alignment.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A virtuous ruler is like the Pole-star, which keeps its place while the other stars do homage to it.
Punishment suppresses lawbreaking without shame, while rule by inner self-control preserves moral sense and makes people good.
Government is keeping straight; a good ruler leads people into line and bends them like grass before wind.

occurrences.source_title: The Sayings of Confucius
occurrences.passage_locator: Government and Public Affairs
occurrences.motif_label: public trust above force
occurrences.basis: Food and soldiers may be sacrificed before the confidence of the people, without which rule collapses.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Good government needs food, soldiers, and above all the confidence of the people, without which the state cannot stand.

occurrences.source_title: Persian Literature, Volume 1
occurrences.passage_locator: GUSHTSP, AND THE FAITH OF ZERDUSHT / THE HEFT-KHAN OF ISFENDIYR / CAPTURE OF THE BRAZEN FORTRESS / THE DEATH OF ISFENDIYR; lines 13144-13177
occurrences.motif_label: Royal succession established after the death of an heir
occurrences.basis: After Isfendiyr’s death, Gushtsp summons Bahman and appoints him to succeed to the throne.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Isfendiyr’s bier arrives at Gushtsp’s palace; Gushtsp weeps; the mother and sisters lament and say the death was not by Rustem or Zl but by the Smrgh; the public curses Gushtsp, who stays confined until after the interment.

Gushtsp consults Bashtan who confirms Rustem’s declarations; Gushtsp acquits Rustem and attributes the event to destiny; he summons Bahman and appoints him successor, praising his resemblance to Isfendiyr in verse.

occurrences.source_title: Persian Literature, Volume 1
occurrences.passage_locator: KAI-KS / THE SEVEN LABORS OF RUSTEM / INVASION OF IRN BY AFRSIYB / THE RETURN OF KAI-KS; lines 5019-5036
occurrences.motif_label: Hero returns home after victory and reports to rulers
occurrences.basis: Rustem reports victory by letter to Kai-ks and the party returns home to pay respects to the Persian king.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Rustem and companions fall back to the sporting-grounds; from there Rustem informs Kai-ks by letter of the victory gained.
The party returns home to pay their respects to the Persian king.

occurrences.source_title: Persian Literature, Volume 1
occurrences.passage_locator: INVASION OF IRN BY AFRSIYB / THE RETURN OF KAI-KS / STORY OF SOHRB / THE STORY OF SAIWUSH; lines 8390-8407
occurrences.motif_label: Legitimate succession established by merit and public coronation
occurrences.basis: The passage links Kai-khosru’s demonstrated success to a formal announcement of succession and a coronation with pomp, establishing him as rightful ruler.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Kai-khosru’s expedition against an enchanted castle is compared favorably to Frburz’s; it establishes him in the king’s estimation, and it is announced to princes/nobles/warriors that he will succeed to the throne and be crowned on a fortunate day.
The coronation takes place shortly afterward with great pomp and splendor.

occurrences.source_title: The Poetic Edda
occurrences.passage_locator: RIGSTHULA / THE SONG OF RIG / INTRODUCTORY NOTE / NOTES; lines 8480-8601
occurrences.motif_label: Kingly title/name linked to legitimacy via etymology ('Rig' = king)
occurrences.basis: The notes state the name Rig is based on Old Irish for “king.”

evidence.quote_or_summary: Notes state “Rig” is almost certainly based on Old Irish ri/rig meaning “king.”

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE ASS AND HIS SHADOW / THE FARMER AND HIS SONS / THE DOG AND THE COOK / THE MONKEY AS KING; lines 1823-1836
occurrences.motif_label: unworthy or unwise king
occurrences.basis: The Monkey is made King because he delights the animals, but his immediate capture in a simple trap leads the Fox to challenge his fitness as King of the Beasts.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At a gathering of all the animals, the Monkey dances, delights them, and is made King.
The Monkey goes toward the meat, is caught in the trap, and reproaches the Fox for leading him into danger.
“O Monkey, you call yourself King of the Beasts and haven't more sense than to be taken in like that!”

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE TWO BAGS / THE OXEN AND THE AXLETREES / THE BOY AND THE FILBERTS / THE FROGS ASKING FOR A KING; lines 2135-2152
occurrences.motif_label: Petition to a deity for a ruler
occurrences.basis: The Frogs ask Jupiter to give them a king, and Jupiter assigns rulers to them.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Frogs are discontented because they have no ruler and send a deputation to Jupiter asking him to give them a king.
Jupiter regards the request as foolish, casts a log into the pool where the Frogs live, and says it will be their king.
Jupiter, annoyed at being pestered, sends a Stork to rule over the Frogs.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation

occurrences.basis: When the kings are equal in age, kingdom, army, wealth, renown, country, caste, tribe, and family, the road-precedence question is decided by which king is most righteous; the commentary says goodness is the true measure of greatness.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The charioteer of the king of Benāres compares the kings by age, kingdom, army, wealth, renown, country, caste, tribe, and family, and finds them equal.

Mallika and his charioteer alight, take out the horses, remove their chariot, and make way for the king of Benāres.

The commentary states that the lesson is that justice is noble, evil should be conquered by good, and goodness is the true measure of greatness; it also says the first four lines of the Second Moral appear as Dhammapada verse 223 and that the idea is also found in the Mahā Bhārata.

Strabo is cited for kings worshipped as gods who are kept shut in and remain at home for the most part.

A run of footnotes cites sources on rulers or kings in Loango, the Niger region, Strabo, Sabaean materials, Heraclides, Korea, Tonquin, and Burma, with brief comments on public appearance or palace departure in some notes.

occurrences.basis: Raiatean and Tahitian kings are deified or identified with gods, and Indian kings are described as deities in human form.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Tanatoa, King of Raiatea, is deified by ceremony at the chief temple, worshipped, consulted as an oracle, and offered sacrifices and prayers.
Island kings regularly receive divine honours at accession; the Tahitian king receives a sacred red and yellow feather girdle that identifies him with the gods.
In India every king is described as nearly a present god; Manu is cited as saying even an infant king should not be despised as mortal because he is a great deity in human form.

occurrences.motif_label: weather-controlling sacred ruler
occurrences.basis: Multiple rulers or sacred figures are described as divine, semi-divine, or sanctified and as able to control rain, weather, storms, or related natural conditions.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Spanish conquerors encounter the Chibchas/Muyscas/Mozcas in the Colombian Andes; they are organized into two kingdoms and spiritually linked to the pontiff of Sogamozo or Iraca, whose sanctity is said to make waters, rain, and weather obey him.

The Waganda believe in a god of Lake Nyanza who may dwell in a man or woman; the incarnate god is feared, consulted as an oracle, and believed able to heal or inflict sickness, withhold rain, and cause famine, receiving presents when consulted.
The king of Loango is honored as a god and believed able to grant rain; in December people beg him for rain, and he shoots an arrow into the air from his throne to bring it.
The king of Quiteva is treated as a deity; subjects pray and give gifts to him for rain, fair weather, and relief from winds and storms.

Among the Barotse, an old belief treats the chief as a demigod; people go to the chief’s yard during thunderstorms, kneel to him, and ask him to open the water-pots of heaven and send rain to gardens.

occurrences.motif_label: Ruler responsible for fertility and weather
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly links kings or priest-kings to crop growth, rain, weather, harvest, food, and good seasons.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Among the Antaymours of Madagascar, the king is responsible for crop growth and every misfortune that befalls the people.
In parts of West Africa, if prayers and offerings to the king fail to bring rain, subjects bind him and take him to his forefathers’ grave to obtain rain.
The Banjars credit their king with rain or fine weather, reward him in fine weather, and insult and beat him during long drought or rain until the weather changes.
During a long famine under Swedish king Domalde, chiefs decided he caused the scarcity, slew him for good seasons, and smeared his blood on the gods’ altars.
In King Olaf’s reign, famine was blamed on the king’s sparing sacrifices; the people burned him in his dwelling, “giving him to Odin as a sacrifice for good crops.”
On Niuē, kings were also high priests thought to make food grow; people killed them during scarcity until no one would be king and the monarchy ended.

The Burgundians of old deposed their king if crops failed.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Frazer asks whether the King of the Wood may have descended from a line of kings stripped of political power, but argues against this because the priest of Nemi lived at a forest sanctuary by the lake shore rather than in nearby Aricia.
Frazer argues that the title King of the Wood suggests not ordinary kingship but a king of nature, specifically of the woods, and says departmental kings of nature would be closer analogues.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Namvulu Vumu dwells on a hill at Bomma and is called King of the Rain and Storm.
Some Upper Nile tribes acknowledge Kings of the Rain, Mata Kodou, credited with giving rain at the proper time in the rainy season.
Before the rains, householders go to the King of the Rain and offer a cow so that he may make rain fall soon.
The Alfai is a priestly, hereditary, king-like figure believed able to make rain and drive away locusts; people bring tribute and cultivate a field for him.
In the backwoods of Cambodia are reported two mysterious sovereigns, the King of the Fire and the King of the Water, formerly exchanging presents with the King of Cambodia.
The Kings of Fire and Water reside among the Chréais or Jaray in forest-clad mountains and high plateaux; their functions are purely mystic or spiritual, not political, and they live on offerings.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The offices are hereditary in one or two royal families, but eligible men flee and hide when a vacancy occurs because the dignity is not coveted.
The dignity is confined to the family because it possesses talismans: a still-fresh creeper fruit, an old rattan not dry, and a sword containing a Yan or spirit.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The rule of the sanctuary was that a candidate could succeed to the priesthood only by slaying the priest, and then held office until slain by a stronger or craftier man.
At Nemi no branch of the certain tree might be broken except by a runaway slave; if he succeeded, he could fight the priest and, by killing him, reign as King of the Wood.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The King of the Wood could only be assailed by someone who had plucked the Golden Bough, and his life was safe while the bough or its tree remained uninjured.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Considering his double character as king and priest, relation to the Golden Bough, and the woodland divinity of the grove, the passage provisionally assumes that the King of the Wood was a living incarnation of the tree-spirit, like the May King and Northern European congeners.

The passage compares Cambodian offerings to the mystic Kings of Fire and Water with Italian pilgrims turning from the Latian plain toward the Alban Mountain, home of the mysterious priest of Nemi, the King of the Wood.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Kings or priests in early society are described as supernatural or divine, as responsible for natural calamities, and as liable to punishment for negligence or guilt.
The ruler's person is called the "dynamical centre of the universe" and the "point of support on which hangs the balance of the world."

The Mikado or Dairi is presented as a typical example: spiritual emperor of Japan, incarnation of the sun goddess, and host to all gods for one month each year, during which temples are thought deserted.

occurrences.basis: The Mikado's sacred status is maintained by restrictions on touching ground, exposure to sun and air, bodily grooming, stillness, vessels, and clothing.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The quoted account says the Mikado is carried to avoid touching the ground, protected from open air and sunlight, and not allowed to cut hair, beard, or nails except by nocturnal cleaning treated as theft.

The Mikado formerly sat motionless on the throne with the imperial crown to preserve peace; movement or prolonged gaze was feared to bring disaster, and later the crown itself was placed on the throne as a palladium.
The Mikado's food was prepared in new pots and dishes, which were usually broken; lay use of dishes or garments was feared to cause swelling, inflammation, and pains.
An earlier account repeats that touching the ground was degrading, sun and moon were not permitted to shine on his head, bodily superfluities were not removed, and food was prepared in new vessels.

occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly links a priestly king or pontiff’s life and conduct to wind, atmosphere, crops, the earth, and the world’s continued existence.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Kukulu of Shark Point near Cape Padron lives alone in a wood, may not touch a woman, leave his house, quit his chair, or lie down; if he lay down, wind and navigation would cease; he regulates storms and atmosphere.

Chitomé or Chitombé of Congo is regarded as a god on earth and all-powerful in heaven; receives first-fruits; married people must observe continence during his travels; his natural death is thought to entail the world’s destruction and earth’s annihilation.

The passage generalizes that in Japan and West Africa the order of nature and even the world’s existence are bound up with the king or priest, making him a source of blessing and danger; rain, sunshine, wind, and the earth are attributed to him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Kukulu of Shark Point near Cape Padron lives alone in a wood, may not touch a woman, leave his house, quit his chair, or lie down; if he lay down, wind and navigation would cease; he regulates storms and atmosphere.

Chitomé or Chitombé of Congo is regarded as a god on earth and all-powerful in heaven; receives first-fruits; married people must observe continence during his travels; his natural death is thought to entail the world’s destruction and earth’s annihilation.

The Zapotec high pontiff governs Yopaa, is described as a close parallel to the Mikado, is treated as a god, must not touch the ground, is borne in a palanquin, and causes people to prostrate themselves lest they see his shadow and die.

The divine ruler is hedged in by etiquette, prohibitions, and observances meant not for dignity or comfort but to prevent conduct that could disturb nature and involve ruler, people, and universe in catastrophe.

occurrences.motif_label: dangerous or burdensome sacred kingship
occurrences.basis: Several examples describe kingship as dangerous, unwanted, or an irksome burden that successors evade or rulers shift to others.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Cambodia is said to force the kingships of Fire and Water on reluctant successors, while Savage Island monarchy ended when no one accepted the dangerous distinction.
In parts of West Africa, a secretly chosen successor is seized, bound, and kept in a fetish-house until accepting the crown; one chief is said to have stayed armed to resist enthronement.
Tahitian kings regularly abdicate at a son's birth; the son is proclaimed sovereign and receives the father's homage, perhaps to shift the burdensome restrictions of royalty.

occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly describes nominal sacred or royal figures separated from those exercising real political or military power in Japan, Tonquin, Mangaia, and cited American examples.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Japanese Mikados are described as transferring supreme power to infant children; a Mikado abdicates to a three-year-old son, a usurper seizes sovereignty, and Yoritomo restores the Mikado's nominal power while retaining actual power and founding the Tycoon line.
Later Tycoons are described as becoming palace-bound puppets occupied with ceremonies while the council of state manages government.
In Tonquin, Mack usurps the throne, Tring restores the king but keeps the military dignity; afterward dovas keep title and pomp while chovas wield real political power.
In Mangaia, hereditary kings hold spiritual functions, victorious war-chiefs hold temporal government after royal investiture, and kings receive the best lands and daily food offerings.
The passage says American examples of partitioned authority between an emperor and a pope have already been cited from early Mexico and Colombia.

In Mandalay lattice-palings lined routes where the king might pass; people stayed behind them and were not supposed to look through the holes.

occurrences.basis: The Chitomé, kings of Meroe, king of Unyoro, king of Kibanga, and Zulu king are associated with rules or expectations that a royal or divine figure should die by human action rather than natural decline.

The Ethiopian kings of Meroe are described as worshipped as gods; priests send commands to die by oracle, until Ergamenes disregards the command and kills the priests in the Golden Temple.
In Unyoro the king is to be killed by his wives when seriously ill or aged because of a prophecy about dynastic loss; in Kibanga sorcerers tighten a rope around the dying king's neck.
A Zulu custom is reported in which a king must not have wrinkles or gray hairs; Chaka anxiously seeks hair oil to remove signs of age, since gray hairs would signal the monarch's death.

occurrences.basis: The passage states that the Chitomé's natural death would make the world perish, while in Unyoro a prophecy says the dynasty will lose the throne if the king dies naturally.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Congo pontiff Chitomé is believed to sustain the earth; if he dies naturally the world will perish, so his successor kills him with a rope or club when he is ill and near death.

occurrences.motif_label: Signs of age disqualifying the king
occurrences.basis: The Zulu passage describes wrinkles and gray hairs as marks disqualifying a monarch of a warlike people and as signals that the king must die.

occurrences.motif_label: unblemished body as condition of legitimate kingship
occurrences.basis: Several examples require rulers to lack bodily defect or describe defects as making them unfit to live, reign, or be crowned.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sedanda, afflicted with leprosy, decides to poison himself, nominates a successor, and holds that sovereigns serving as examples should have no bodily defect and cease to deserve life or rule when defects befall them.

Frazer compares the Sofala case to Ethiopian kings, conjecturing that bodily defect or decay prompted execution under priestly oracular authority, and notes that Ethiopian kings were chosen for size, strength, and beauty.
The Sultan of Wadâi is said to require no obvious bodily defect, and a king of Angoy cannot be crowned with any blemish such as a broken or filed tooth or old scar.

occurrences.passage_locator: MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE. / CHAPTER III. KILLING THE GOD.; lines 4750-4806
occurrences.motif_label: fixed-term killing of the sacred ruler
occurrences.basis: The passage presents divine or royal figures whose reign is limited by a fixed term and whose death is required at its end.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Some divine kings or priests are killed only after visible signs of decline, while other peoples fixed a term and killed the king while still vigorous to avoid decay.

In Quilacare, a twelve-year feast honors an idol; the king’s reign lasts from jubilee to jubilee. At the feast he bathes, prays to the idol, mounts a decorated scaffolding, cuts off parts of his body with knives, cuts his throat, and the act is called sacrifice to the idol. A willing successor present at the rite is raised as king.
The Samorin of Calicut formerly had to cut his throat publicly after twelve years; later, a twelve-year jubilee was proclaimed, a tent was pitched, and a feast lasted ten or twelve days.

occurrences.motif_label: succession through regicidal challenge
occurrences.basis: In the modified Samorin custom, a guest who kills the ruler after fighting through the guards succeeds to the empire.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Under the modified Samorin custom, guests could gain the crown by fighting through many guards and killing the Samorin in his tent. In 1695 three attackers were killed, and a young nephew who struck at the Samorin was stopped when a burning brass lamp marred the blow; he too was killed.

occurrences.basis: Both Southern Indian examples are organized around a twelve-year jubilee or feast that marks the end of the ruler’s permitted term or the occasion for lethal challenge.

occurrences.motif_label: annual temporary abdication and nominal sovereignty
occurrences.basis: The Cambodian king abdicates annually for three days while a hereditary temporary king receives sovereignty and performs royal procession.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In Cambodia, the king annually abdicated for three days in Méac, performing no authority, not touching the seals, and not receiving revenues, while the temporary king Sdach Méac reigned.

The temporary Cambodian king’s hereditary office is described; he is processed by mandarins, rides a royal elephant in a royal palanquin, wears a white cap and wooden regalia, receives sovereignty for three days, and processes through palace and capital.

occurrences.passage_locator: MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE. / CHAPTER III. KILLING THE GOD.; lines 4887-4943
occurrences.motif_label: three-day temporary or mock kingship
occurrences.basis: Both described customs install a temporary ruler for three days who exercises or mimics real authority.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In Siam, a temporary king is appointed for three days while the real king remains in the palace; the temporary king’s agents seize goods and arriving ships.

In Upper Egypt at the Coptic solar New Year, when the Nile is generally highest, government is suspended for three days and each town chooses a ruler wearing a fool’s cap, flaxen beard, strange mantle, and wand; he deposes the governor, mounts the throne, and holds tribunal.

occurrences.motif_label: ritual suspension or displacement of normal rule
occurrences.basis: The real Siamese king remains secluded while the temporary king acts; in Upper Egypt the regular government is suspended and the governor is deposed by the mock ruler.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In Siam, a temporary king is appointed for three days while the real king remains in the palace; the temporary king’s agents seize goods and arriving ships.

In Upper Egypt at the Coptic solar New Year, when the Nile is generally highest, government is suspended for three days and each town chooses a ruler wearing a fool’s cap, flaxen beard, strange mantle, and wand; he deposes the governor, mounts the throne, and holds tribunal.

occurrences.passage_locator: MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE. / CHAPTER III. KILLING THE GOD.; lines 4945-5006
occurrences.motif_label: temporary substitute kingship at accession
occurrences.basis: Multiple examples involve a non-final or substitute figure temporarily occupying a throne or royal seat at the beginning of a reign or installation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In Jambi, a commoner occupies the throne for one day at the start of a reign; a tradition about five royal brothers explains the hereditary privilege.
In Bilaspur, after a Rajah’s death, a Brahman eats rice and milk from the dead ruler’s hand, rules for a year, is watched, receives gifts, and is expelled; the Rajah’s spirit is said to enter him.

At a Carinthian prince’s installation, a hereditary peasant sits on a marble stone with a cow and mare nearby, challenges the prince, yields the seat for compensation and tax exemption, and gives the prince a light blow.

occurrences.passage_locator: MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE. / CHAPTER III. KILLING THE GOD.; lines 4945-5006
occurrences.motif_label: transfer of royal spirit or supernatural royal function
occurrences.basis: The Bilaspur Brahman is said to receive the dead Rajah’s spirit, and the passage explicitly states that divine or supernatural royal functions are transferred to temporary substitutes in Cambodian and Siamese examples.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In Bilaspur, after a Rajah’s death, a Brahman eats rice and milk from the dead ruler’s hand, rules for a year, is watched, receives gifts, and is expelled; the Rajah’s spirit is said to enter him.

Frazer states that Cambodian and Siamese examples show transfer of divine or supernatural royal functions to temporary substitutes; the Siamese raised foot, Cambodian rice trampling, and Siamese ploughing/sowing are linked to spirits and harvest abundance.

occurrences.motif_label: ritual exchange for cession of authority
occurrences.basis: In Carinthia, the hereditary peasant yields the marble seat to the prince only after receiving money, animals, and exemption from taxes, and then strikes the prince lightly.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At a Carinthian prince’s installation, a hereditary peasant sits on a marble stone with a cow and mare nearby, challenges the prince, yields the seat for compensation and tax exemption, and gives the prince a light blow.

occurrences.passage_locator: MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE. / CHAPTER III. KILLING THE GOD.; lines 5008-5083
occurrences.motif_label: sacrificial substitute for the king
occurrences.basis: The temporary king or royal substitute is presented as dying in place of the real king, while bearing royal-divine attributes.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Temporary kings in Cambodia and Jambi are said to come from a stock believed akin to the royal family.
Frazer argues that a substitute death for the king must be invested with the king's divine attributes or supernatural functions, as with temporary kings of Siam and Cambodia.

The king's son is described as the best representative of the king's divine character and therefore the most appropriate person to die for the king and people; this is linked to Semitic Western Asia and the Sacaean festival.

occurrences.passage_locator: MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE. / CHAPTER III. KILLING THE GOD.; lines 5085-5132
occurrences.motif_label: soul transmitted to successor at death
occurrences.basis: Multiple examples describe a dying or dead person's soul, breath, rank, or identity being received by a successor, with the conclusion applied to a divine king or priest.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In Nias, succession to a chief can require catching the dying chief's last breath and soul in the mouth or a bag; rivals may crowd around, one candidate used a bamboo tube, and when there is no son the soul is caught in a bag fastened to an image of the deceased.

Among the Takilis or Carrier Indians, a priest catches the deceased's soul in his hands during cremation and transmits it to a successor by throwing his hands toward him and blowing; the recipient takes the deceased's name and rank.
"when the divine king or priest is put to death his spirit is believed to pass into his successor"

occurrences.passage_locator: MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE. / CHAPTER III. KILLING THE GOD.; lines 5135-5218
occurrences.motif_label: ritual transfer of office through combat or successful challenge
occurrences.basis: The King of the Wood holds office until slain by a stronger man, and the King of Calicut can be challenged by candidates at prescribed intervals.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The King of the Wood is described as an incarnation of the tree or vegetation spirit whose valued life is guarded, yet who must be killed by a stronger successor so divine vitality is preserved and transferred.
The King of Calicut is compared with the King of the Wood; he could be attacked once every twelve years, and Frazer conjectures that both rules mitigated an older fixed-term death rule.

occurrences.passage_locator: MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE. / CHAPTER III. KILLING THE GOD.; lines 5220-5303
occurrences.motif_label: Festival King tried and symbolically beheaded
occurrences.basis: In the Königgrätz and Pilsen examples, a King is crowned or invested, subjected to accusation or pursuit, and symbolically decapitated by striking off hats or a crown.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Königgrätz district Whit-Monday custom: a King and Queen are chosen, garlanded, proclaimed, and invested; the King is accused and tried, and if guilty, kneels while stacked hats are struck from his head with a wooden sword as symbolic beheading.

Pilsen district Whit-Monday custom: a bark-dressed mounted King with a gilt-paper crown rides from a green arbour under May-trees, flees pursuit, remains King if uncaught, but if caught is beaten, dismounted, has his crown struck off by the executioner, sinks down, and is carried on a bier.

occurrences.basis: In the Pilsen district, the King remains King for another year if pursuers fail to catch him, but if caught he is beaten, dismounted, and symbolically beheaded.

occurrences.motif_label: transfer of divine life to a vigorous successor
occurrences.basis: The passage says divine life in an aging mortal body is detached and conveyed to a new incarnation by killing the old representative of the god.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Divine life incarnate in a mortal body is said to risk taint, corruption, and enfeeblement as its human medium ages.
The divine spirit is saved from weakness by killing the old representative and conveying the spirit to a new, vigorous incarnation.
The killing of the god's human incarnation is described as "a necessary step to his revival or resurrection in a better form."

occurrences.motif_label: sacred king holds office by surviving combat or flight
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly links kingly or priestly office to proof of bodily vigor through flight, pursuit, or defense against attack.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The northern kings die violent deaths; flight and pursuit are prominent in several customs, and in one case outrunning pursuers preserves life and office for another year.
Frazer compares the northern case with the King of Calicut defending his life every twelve years and the priest of Nemi defending himself against assault at any time.
The life of the god-man is prolonged when a severe contest of fight or flight shows that bodily strength has not decayed, postponing violent death.
Frazer conjectures that the Roman regifugium may originally have been a comparable flight of a divine king who must prove vigor by hand or foot.

Babylonian and Assyrian kings are said to seem also to have been regarded as gods; the oldest royal names on monuments are preceded by a star, described as the mark for “god.”
The note says there is no trace in Babylon and Assyria of temples and priests for the worship of kings.

“Le roi est mort, vive le roi!”

occurrences.motif_label: divine descent supporting rulership
occurrences.basis: Hohodemi’s rule over Japan is linked to descent from Amaterasu, the Sun Goddess.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hohodemi governs Japan, is fourth Mikoto in descent from Amaterasu, and is described as handsome, strong, brave, and the greatest hunter, called the Happy Hunter of the Mountains.

occurrences.motif_label: divine and royal descent identities
occurrences.basis: Hohodemi is identified as grandson of Amaterasu, and the princesses are daughters of Ryn Jin, King of the Sea.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Happy Hunter identifies himself as Hohodemi; Princess Tayotama says he is the grandson of Amaterasu and identifies herself and Tamayori as daughters of Ryn Jin.
Princess Tayotama says her father will be pleased that the grandson of Amaterasu has come down to the bottom of the sea; Tamayori agrees they are honored to welcome him.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE BAMBOO-CUTTER AND THE MOON-CHILD / THE GOBLIN OF ADACHIGAHARA / THE SAGACIOUS MONKEY AND THE BOAR / THE HAPPY HUNTER AND THE SKILLFUL FISHER; lines 4436-4526
occurrences.motif_label: Rival brothers, usurpation, and restoration of rule
occurrences.basis: The Skillful Fisher usurps his brother's position, attempts to kill him, then promises to restore his rights and acknowledge him as Lord of all Japan.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Skillful Fisher had used the lost hook as an excuse to drive out his brother, usurped his place as ruler, and became powerful and rich; he is surprised by the Happy Hunter's return.
The Skillful Fisher only pretends forgiveness, hates his brother, plans to kill him, and follows him in the rice fields with a dagger; the Happy Hunter decides to use the tide jewels.
The Skillful Fisher, frightened and impressed, humbles himself, asks forgiveness, promises to restore his brother's rights, and swears to bow before him as Lord of all Japan.
The Happy Hunter rules without family strife, Japan has peace for a long time, and he prizes the Jewels of the Flow and Ebb of the Tide given by Ryn Jin, the Dragon King of the Sea.

occurrences.motif_label: sacred imperial regalia legitimating royal power
occurrences.basis: The passage connects the three sacred treasures, especially the sword, with the Emperor, Ise, Amaterasu, and imperial descent.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The imperial insignia consist of three sacred treasures: the Mirror of Yata, the Jewel of Yasakami, and the Sword of Murakumo; the sword is later called Kusanagi and treated as a symbol of strength and talisman of invincibility for the Emperor.
The sword was kept at Ise shrines dedicated to Amaterasu, the Sun Goddess from whom the emperors are said to descend; the story is said to explain the sword's change of name to grass-clearing.

occurrences.motif_label: dying enemy confers heroic name
occurrences.basis: The dying Takeru recognizes Prince Yamato's superiority and gives him the new name Yamato Take as bravest man in Yamato.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The dying brigand asks the Prince to wait, asks who he is, and says that one who has overcome both brothers alone must be more than mortal.
The dying Takeru recognizes Yamato's strength, gives him the new name Yamato Take, bequeaths the title as bravest man in Yamato, and dies.

occurrences.motif_label: royal son pacifies land by defeating rebels
occurrences.basis: The Prince is the King's son, sent as avenger of evil, and his victories bring peace and rest to the land and people before royal reward.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Prince identifies himself as the King's son Yamato, sent by his father as avenger of evil to bring death to rebels and end robbery and murder.
The narrator says Yamato Take prevails against the King's foes through wisdom, bodily strength, and craftiness, bringing peace and rest to the land and people.
When Yamato Take returns to the capital, the King praises him, holds a palace feast, gives rare gifts, and loves him more than ever.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The aunt gives him a sword and a handmade bag of flints; the sword is Murakumo, one of the three sacred treasures and part of the Imperial House insignia, and she tells him to use it in his greatest need.

occurrences.motif_label: exile of rightful heirs to the forest
occurrences.basis: The king sends the older princes away to the forest to preserve their lives and later the eldest returns to take the throne by right.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The king refuses, saying the kingdom must go first to the oldest son, then the second, and only after both are dead to the third.
The king fears the queen may harm the older princes and sends them to live in the forest until his death, telling them to return later to reign in the city that is theirs by right.

The three princes live in the forest until the king dies, then return to the palace; the eldest is made king, has his brothers rule with him, and builds a home for the water-sprite in the palace grounds.

occurrences.motif_label: Election and rejection of an animal king
occurrences.basis: The birds assemble to choose a king, initially select the Owl, reject him after objection, and choose the Turtle Dove instead.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The birds gather on a great flat rock, say that humans, beasts, and fish have kings, and decide to choose the Owl as their king.
An old Crow says he does not want the Owl as king, pointing to the Owl's sour look and asking how he would look when angry.
The Crow flies up crying that he does not like it; the Owl follows. "From that time on the Crows and the Owls have been enemies." The birds choose a Turtle Dove as king.

occurrences.motif_label: royal recognition after martial victory
occurrences.basis: After the little bowman defeats the invading army, the king and people name him brave and the king makes him chief of the army.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The little bowman says 'And now to win,' drives the war-elephant into battle, breaks into the enemy camp, drives the foreign king back, and leads the army into the city.
The king and people call the victor the brave little bowman, and the king makes him chief of the army and gives him rich gifts.

"Then they made the poor man king, and set him to rule over them."

evidence.quote_or_summary: Early Italian tribes regarded the deity as spring and agricultural; Romans made him a chief war god, protector, and father of Romulus and Remus.

occurrences.passage_locator: ORIGIN OF THE WORLD.--FIRST DYNASTY. / URANUS AND GAEA. (COELUS AND TERRA.) / SECOND DYNASTY. / CRONUS (SATURN).; lines 549-631
occurrences.motif_label: divine succession war
occurrences.basis: War breaks out between father and son; Zeus defeats Cronus and receives supreme power as successor.

evidence.locator: lines 549-631, armies on Olympus and Othrys
evidence.quote_or_summary: War begins between Cronus and Zeus; Zeus's forces stand on Mount Olympus, while Cronus and his brother-Titans occupy Mount Othrys.
Zeus liberates imprisoned Giants and calls the Cyclops; the Cyclops bring thunderbolts, and the Hecatoncheires hurl them and raise earthquakes.
The battle is marked by towering sea, shaking earth, thunder, lightning, and mist enveloping Cronus and his allies.
Cronus's army is overthrown, his brothers are sent to the lower world, Cronus is banished, and supreme power passes to Zeus; the war is called the Titanomachia.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Janus received the exiled deity kindly and shared his throne with him.
Their united reign was peaceful, happy, and prosperous, and was called the Golden Age.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Pallas-Athene commands Cadmus to sow the dragon's teeth; armed men arise, fight until five remain, and those survivors help Cadmus build Thebes; later noble Theban families claim descent from them.

occurrences.motif_label: Heroic founder and legitimating ancestor
occurrences.basis: Perseus founds Mycenae and Midea, is ancestor of Heracles through Alcmene, and receives heroic honours in multiple places.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Perseus performs funeral rites for Acrisius, exchanges kingdoms with Megapenthes, founds Mycenae and Midea, and gives Medusa's head to Pallas-Athene, who places it on her shield.
Perseus and Andromeda are said to be ancestors of many heroes, especially Heracles through Alcmene; heroic honours are paid to Perseus in Argos, Athens, and Seriphus.

occurrences.motif_label: dispossessed heir departs to reclaim kingdom
occurrences.basis: Jason, son of the displaced king Aeson, leaves Chiron and goes to Iolcus to demand the throne from the usurper Pelias.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Aeson is forced to flee after Pelias usurps Iolcus; Jason is saved, entrusted to Chiron, and trained for ten years in the Centaur’s cave.
Jason desires to regain his paternal inheritance, leaves Chiron, and sets out for Iolcus to demand the kingdom from Pelias.
Pelias entertains Jason, then Jason demands the throne; Pelias consents only if Jason undertakes an expedition for him.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome

occurrences.motif_label: prophetic identifying sign marks threat to ruler
occurrences.basis: Pelias recognizes Jason’s one unshod foot as matching an oracle predicting loss of the kingdom by a man wearing one sandal.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The old woman transforms into Hera, promises to guide and protect Jason, disappears, and Jason notices he has lost one sandal.
At Iolcus, Pelias sacrifices to Poseidon, sees Jason’s unshod foot, and recalls an oracle foretelling loss of his kingdom by a man wearing one sandal.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: PART II.--LEGENDS. / CADMUS. / PERSEUS. / THE ARGONAUTS.; lines 6904-6953
occurrences.motif_label: impossible or dangerous quest imposed as condition for kingship
occurrences.basis: Pelias promises Jason the throne, kingdom, and sceptre if Jason obtains Phryxus’s remains and the Golden Fleece from Colchis.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Pelias entertains Jason, then Jason demands the throne; Pelias consents only if Jason undertakes an expedition for him.
Pelias says Phryxus’s shade appeared in dreams requesting the return of his remains and the Golden Fleece from Colchis, promising Jason throne, kingdom, and sceptre if he succeeds.

occurrences.basis: An oracle declares that Aetes’ life depends on the safe-keeping of the Golden Fleece.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Aetes nailed the fleece in the Grove of Ares and dedicated it to the god of War; after an oracle said his life depended on the fleece, he guarded the grove entrance with an immense dragon that never slept.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After victory, Zeus and his brothers divide the conquered world by lot: Zeus reigns in Heaven, Aides governs the Lower World, Poseidon commands the sea, and Zeus's supremacy is recognized in all three kingdoms.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At the banquet and afterward, Jason explains the expedition; Aetes angrily insists the Fleece is his property, then promises it only if the heroes prove divine origin through a superhuman task.

Pelops sees flames from the royal castle after a lightning strike, flies there with his winged horses, rescues Hippodamia unharmed, marries her, and reigns in Pisa for many years.
