occurrences.motif_label: ransom naming of a royal survivor
occurrences.basis: Podarces is ransomed with Hesione's golden diadem and thereafter bears the name Priam, explained as the ransomed one.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Heracles gives Hesione to Telamon; Hesione chooses to release Podarces and ransoms him with her golden diadem, after which he is called Priam, the ransomed one.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE. / PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES). / BELLEROPHON.; lines 8325-8402
occurrences.motif_label: royal reward through rule and marriage
occurrences.basis: After Bellerophon's victories, Iobates gives him a share in government and his daughter in marriage.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Iobates sets brave Lycians in ambush to destroy Bellerophon, but Bellerophon kills them all; Iobates concludes that he is favored and protected by the gods and stops persecuting him.

Iobates gives Bellerophon rule and his daughter in marriage. Later Bellerophon becomes proud, tries to mount to heaven on Pegasus, and is punished by Zeus, who sends a gadfly; Pegasus throws him, and he wanders in remorse and melancholy.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES). / BELLEROPHON. / THESEUS.; lines 8404-8503
occurrences.motif_label: concealed royal paternity revealed by tokens
occurrences.basis: Aegeus conceals his identity from a future son, leaves sword and sandals as tokens, and later recognizes Theseus by the sword before acknowledging him as heir.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Before departing, Aegeus deposits his sword and sandals beneath a huge rock and tells Aethra to send a future son to Athens with these identity tokens when he can move the stone.
Theseus is born, raised by Pittheus, grows strong, rolls away the stone, and receives the sword and sandals that had lain there for sixteen years.
Before tasting the wine, Theseus draws his sword; Aegeus recognizes the weapon, embraces him, presents him as heir, and banishes Medea.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES). / BELLEROPHON. / THESEUS.; lines 8404-8503
occurrences.motif_label: poisoned banquet averted by recognition
occurrences.basis: Medea arranges poisoned wine for Theseus, but he draws the sword before drinking and is recognized by Aegeus as son and heir.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In Athens, Medea knows through supernatural powers that Theseus is the king's son, fears loss of influence, and arranges poisoned wine at a banquet.
Before tasting the wine, Theseus draws his sword; Aegeus recognizes the weapon, embraces him, presents him as heir, and banishes Medea.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES). / BELLEROPHON. / THESEUS.; lines 8404-8503
occurrences.motif_label: rival kin oppose acknowledged heir
occurrences.basis: The fifty sons of Pallas oppose Theseus after he is acknowledged as rightful heir and plot to kill him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After Theseus is acknowledged as heir, the fifty sons of Pallas expect power, plot his death, but are surprised and destroyed by Theseus.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES). / BELLEROPHON. / THESEUS.; lines 8505-8590
occurrences.motif_label: Heroic succession and civic foundation
occurrences.basis: After Aegeus’ death, Theseus ascends the throne with Athenian approval and unifies Attica under Athens, then renews games and institutes festivals.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Theseus ascends the vacant throne with unanimous Athenian approval, becomes known as a wise prince and legislator, and persuades Attic communities to entrust administration to Athens.
Theseus renews the Isthmian Games and institutes festivals, chiefly the Panathenaea in honor of Athene-Polias.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES). / BELLEROPHON. / THESEUS.; lines 8683-8725
occurrences.motif_label: Political disorder during the hero-king's absence
occurrences.basis: Theseus' prolonged imprisonment leads to revolt, seizure of government by Menesthius, and later restoration and abdication.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Theseus' prolonged absence enables a faction headed by Menesthius to seize supreme power and control the government.
After returning to Athens, Theseus suppresses unrest, expels Menesthius, punishes revolt leaders, and resumes the throne.
Theseus loses the people's support, faces continuing dissension, voluntarily abdicates, and retires to Scyros.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES). / BELLEROPHON. / THESEUS.; lines 8683-8725
occurrences.motif_label: Posthumous return of heroic remains and foundation of honor shrine
occurrences.basis: By the Delphic oracle's command, Theseus' remains are brought back to Athens and a temple is erected in his honor.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Centuries later, by command of the Delphic oracle, Cimon brings Theseus' remains to Athens, where a temple is erected in his honor.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: HERACLES (HERCULES). / BELLEROPHON. / THESEUS. / OEDIPUS.; lines 8727-8823
occurrences.motif_label: monster's riddle solved to free a city and win kingship
occurrences.basis: The Sphinx kills those who fail her riddles; Oedipus solves one, causing her death and gaining the throne and Jocaste.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hera sends the Sphinx as punishment to Thebes; from a rocky height the Sphinx asks riddles and devours those who fail.
After Laius's death, Creon rules and proclaims that kingship and Jocaste's hand will go to whoever solves a Sphinx riddle.
Oedipus enters Thebes, requests a riddle, solves it, and the Sphinx kills herself; Oedipus becomes king and husband of Jocaste.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: BELLEROPHON. / THESEUS. / OEDIPUS. / THE SEVEN AGAINST THEBES.; lines 8825-8917
occurrences.motif_label: sibling conflict over royal legitimacy
occurrences.basis: Eteocles expels Polynices from shared rule, and the later expedition is framed as an effort to recover Polynices' lawful share.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After Oedipus' abdication, Eteocles and Polynices rule Thebes, but Eteocles takes sole power and expels Polynices.
Adrastus gathers chiefs for the expedition; Amphiaraus foresees disaster, warns against the plan, refuses to join, and hides.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THESEUS. / OEDIPUS. / THE SEVEN AGAINST THEBES. / THE EPIGONI.; lines 8979-9016
occurrences.motif_label: conquest followed by contested royal installation
occurrences.basis: After Thebes is entered and plundered, Thersander, son of Polynices and descendant of Cadmus, is placed on the throne his father had contested.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Thebans send ambassadors to prolong negotiations, evacuate by night with wives and children, and the next morning the Argives enter and plunder Thebes, placing Thersander on the throne.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: RHEA (OPS). / DIVISION OF THE WORLD. / THEORIES AS TO THE ORIGIN OF MAN. / THIRD DYNASTY--OLYMPIAN DIVINITIES.; lines 900-984
occurrences.motif_label: Divine patronage of kingship and state order
occurrences.basis: Zeus is founder of kingly power, patron of princes, protector of assemblies, and guardian of the community.

evidence.quote_or_summary: As lord of state-life, Zeus founds kingly power, upholds state institutions, patronizes princes, protects assemblies, and watches over the community.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE SEVEN AGAINST THEBES. / THE EPIGONI. / ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE.; lines 9109-9206
occurrences.motif_label: Divinely sanctioned ancestral claim to rule or land
occurrences.basis: The Heraclidae claim the Peloponnesus as lawful patrimony, grounded in Zeus' will for Heracles' rightful possession.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hyllus, Iolaus, and the brothers leave Athens to invade the Peloponnesus, which they regard as lawful patrimony because Zeus had intended it for Heracles before Hera caused Eurystheus to be born first.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE SEVEN AGAINST THEBES. / THE EPIGONI. / ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE.; lines 9208-9222
occurrences.motif_label: territorial legitimacy through lot and reward
occurrences.basis: After gaining the Peloponnesus, the Heraclidae divide its kingdoms by lot and confer Elis upon Oxylus for his services.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The long-suffering descendants of the great hero succeed and obtain possession of the Peloponnesus.
The Peloponnesus is divided by lot: Argos to Temenus, Lacedaemon to Aristodemus, and Messene to Cresphontes.
In gratitude for Oxylus's services, the Heraclidae confer the kingdom of Elis upon him.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE EPIGONI. / ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE. / THE SIEGE OF TROY.; lines 9224-9321
occurrences.motif_label: Hidden royal child recognized through contest
occurrences.basis: Paris grows up unaware of noble birth, defeats his unknown royal brothers in games, and is recognized as Priam and Hecuba's son.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hecuba dreams she gives birth to a flaming brand; Aesacus interprets this as foretelling a son who will destroy Troy; Paris is exposed on Mount Ida but found and reared by shepherds.
Paris visits funeral games in Troy, defeats his unknown brothers Hector and Deiphobus, is identified by Cassandra, and is joyfully acknowledged by his parents.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE EPIGONI. / ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE. / THE SIEGE OF TROY.; lines 9869-9911
occurrences.motif_label: survivor carries father from fallen city and becomes ancestral hero
occurrences.basis: Aeneas, son of Aphrodite, escapes Troy with his son and father, carries Anchises, leaves for Italy, and becomes ancestral hero of the Roman people.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Aeneas, son of Aphrodite, escapes with his son and father Anchises, carries Anchises on his shoulders, goes to Mount Ida and then Italy, and becomes ancestor-hero of the Romans.

occurrences.motif_label: humane helper rewarded with kingship and prosperity
occurrences.basis: Agnar's humane act and ale-giving are repaid by Odin with the throne and future prosperity.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Geirrod draws his sword to kill the singer, is dismayed by a transformation, falls on the blade, and dies as Odin foretold; Odin then rewards Agnar with the throne and prosperity for his humanity and ale.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS / INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN; lines 1709-1827
occurrences.motif_label: culture-founding conquering ancestor
occurrences.basis: The semi-historical Odin conquers lands, leaves sons on thrones, founds cities, builds a temple, introduces worship, and is later linked to royal descent.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A semi-historical Odin, chief of the Æsir from Asia Minor, migrates into Europe, conquers several lands, leaves sons on thrones, founds Odensö and Sigtuna, builds a temple, and introduces worship.

Ancient poems say Odin's sons become kings of East Saxony, West Saxony, Franconia, Denmark, Norway, and Sweden, and are ancestors of Saxons and northern royal families; another version links Odin and Frigga's seven sons to the Anglo-Saxon heptarchy.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA; lines 2123-2236
occurrences.motif_label: royal ancestry from a goddess
occurrences.basis: Gefjon becomes the ancestress of the royal Danish race of Skioldungs.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Gefjon marries Skiold, one of Odin’s sons, becomes ancestress of the royal Danish Skioldungs, and founds Hleidra or Lethra, a principal sacrificial place for heathen Danes.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR / CHAPTER V: TYR; lines 3369-3493
occurrences.motif_label: sacred weapon confers victory and rulership
occurrences.basis: Cheru declares that possessors of the sacred sword will have victory; the stranger gives it to Vitellius and hails him as emperor, after which the legions proclaim him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Cheru's sword was made by the sons of Ivald, kept sacred in a temple, believed to give victory to its possessors, then disappeared; a prophetess revealed that the Norns decreed its wielder would conquer the world and die by it.
A tall stranger came to Cologne, called Vitellius away from feasting, gave him the sword before Roman soldiers, hailed him as emperor, and the legions took up the cry.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR / CHAPTER V: TYR; lines 3495-3611
occurrences.motif_label: Hidden sacred weapon destined for a conqueror
occurrences.basis: The sword is hidden, prophesied to be found by a world-conqueror, and then claimed by Attila as a warrant for conquest.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An old German soldier retires near the Danube, secretly buries his treasured sword beneath his hut, and says it will be found by the man destined to conquer the world, who will not escape the curse.
Attila discovers the buried sword after it wounds a cow, calls it Cheru’s sword, proclaims conquest, wins battles, and is later killed in bed by Ildico with the same sword.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER IV: THOR / CHAPTER V: TYR / CHAPTER VI: BRAGI / CHAPTER VII: IDUN; lines 4410-4484
occurrences.motif_label: Divine marriage producing royal lineage
occurrences.basis: Skadi’s later union with Odin is said to produce Sæming, first king of Norway and founder of a royal race.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Skadi resumes hunting; one account says she marries Odin and bears Sæming, first king of Norway and founder of a royal race, while other accounts say she marries Uller, the winter-god. She is represented with bow and arrow and accompanied by a wolf-like dog.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS / INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN; lines 880-1012
occurrences.motif_label: Divine protection of princes and heroes
occurrences.basis: Odin is identified as leader and protector of princes and heroes and as the deity who honors selected warriors.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odin is introduced as the highest god, Allfather, god of universal wisdom and victory; he sits in Asgard on Hlidskialf, from which he can overlook the whole world.

Odin is worshipped as god of battle and victory; he sends Valkyrs to choose half of the dead warriors and carry them over Bifröst into Valhalla, where Hermod and Bragi welcome them before Odin's throne.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XX / BOOK XXI / BOOK XXII / BOOK XXIII; lines 10119-10211
occurrences.motif_label: restoration of the hero's appearance
occurrences.basis: After Ulysses is washed, clothed, and beautified by Minerva, he appears stronger and more splendid in his own house before facing Penelope.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Eurynome washes, anoints, and clothes Ulysses; Minerva enhances his stature, strength, hair, and beauty; he sits opposite Penelope and calls her heart hard as iron.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: HENRY FESTING JONES. / THE ODYSSEY / BOOK I / BOOK II; lines 1038-1133
occurrences.motif_label: heir threatened by rivals in the household
occurrences.basis: The suitors discuss Telemachus's possible death and division of his property, while Euryclea warns that they will scheme against him once he leaves.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Suitors say Telemachus may seek friends from Pylos or Sparta, obtain poison, perish far away like his father, and leave property for them to divide.
Euryclea cries, calls Telemachus the one hope of the house, says his father is dead abroad, warns that the wicked suitors will plot against him, and urges him not to cross the barren ocean.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XXI / BOOK XXII / BOOK XXIII / BOOK XXIV; lines 10446-10532
occurrences.motif_label: weapon test reveals rightful hero
occurrences.basis: The suitors cannot string Ulysses' bow, while Ulysses strings it easily and shoots through the iron before reclaiming violent control of his house.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses has his wife offer his bow and iron as a contest for the suitors; none can string the bow, and Telemachus insists that Ulysses receive it despite the suitors' objections.
Ulysses strings the bow with ease and sends his arrow through the iron.

Ulysses pours out his arrows, first kills Antinous, and then the suitors fall thickly; Amphimedon says it was plain that a god was helping as the attackers struck throughout the cloisters and the ground filled with blood.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XXI / BOOK XXII / BOOK XXIII / BOOK XXIV; lines 10624-10722
occurrences.motif_label: Restored household and loyal recognition
occurrences.basis: Dolius and his sons greet Ulysses as restored by heaven, and household members gather around him in due order.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Dolius and his sons arrive for the meal, recognize Ulysses, greet and embrace him; Dolius kisses Ulysses’ hand and says heaven has restored him home.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XXI / BOOK XXII / BOOK XXIII / BOOK XXIV; lines 10724-10815
occurrences.motif_label: returning ruler’s legitimacy confirmed after vengeance
occurrences.basis: Jove states that Ulysses has returned, taken revenge, and should continue to rule under the settlement.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Jove says Ulysses has taken revenge and proposes that the parties swear a solemn covenant, Ulysses continue to rule, the others forget the massacre, and peace and plenty reign.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XXII / BOOK XXIII / BOOK XXIV / FOOTNOTES:; lines 11614-11741
occurrences.motif_label: Weapon-feat test with aligned axes
occurrences.basis: The note reconstructs the feat of shooting through twelve axe-handle holes; in this passage the described focus is the difficult archery feat.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Notes discuss house construction and reconstruct the axe feat: twelve axes in a row, with Ulysses’ arrow passing through all the handle holes.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I / BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS.; lines 1232-1327
occurrences.motif_label: son avenges murdered father
occurrences.basis: Orestes kills Aegisthus, the murderer of his father Agamemnon, and Nestor presents this as a good reason for a man to leave a son behind.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Nestor reports safe returns for some leaders, says Agamemnon died at Aegisthus' hands, and says Orestes killed false Aegisthus, the murderer of his father.
Telemachus says Orestes' name will live because he avenged his father, and wishes heaven would let him take similar vengeance on the wicked suitors who mistreat him and plot his ruin.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I / BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS.; lines 1424-1514
occurrences.motif_label: Public authority signaled by sceptre and ancestral seat
occurrences.basis: Nestor sits on the marble benches formerly associated with Neleus, holding a sceptre as guardian of the public weal, while sons gather around him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At rosy-fingered Dawn, Nestor sits on marble benches formerly used by Neleus, holding a sceptre as guardian of the public weal; his sons and Telemachus gather.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS. / BOOK IV; lines 1561-1661
occurrences.motif_label: royal palace splendour compared with divine dwelling
occurrences.basis: The visitors marvel at the palace's gleam and Telemachus likens it to the palace of Olympian Jove; Menelaus also infers noble descent from the visitors' appearance.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus and Pisistratus are astonished because the house's "splendour was as that of the sun and moon."
Menelaus welcomes them to eat, says he will ask who they are afterward, and says they must descend from sceptre-bearing kings; he gives them a prime piece of roast loin.
Telemachus says the bronze, gold, amber, ivory, and silver make it "like seeing the palace of Olympian Jove."

Menelaus says no one can equal Jove's immortal house, then says he traveled much and suffered hardship for nearly eight years before returning with his fleet through Cyprus, Phoenicia, Egypt, Ethiopia, Sidon, the Erembians, and Libya.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS. / BOOK IV; lines 1762-1847
occurrences.motif_label: Threatened household and expected avenging return
occurrences.basis: Telemachus reports suitors consuming his estate and courting his mother; Menelaus says Ulysses would destroy them if he returned.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus says he came to learn about his father, describes suitors wasting his estate while courting his mother, and asks Menelaus as a suppliant to tell plainly what he saw or heard about Ulysses.

Menelaus is shocked, says the suitors would usurp a brave man's bed, compares them to a hind's young in a lion's lair, says Ulysses would swiftly punish them if he returned, and promises to report what the old man of the sea told him.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS. / BOOK IV; lines 1950-2039
occurrences.motif_label: marriage tie conferring exceptional divine fate
occurrences.basis: Menelaus' future removal to Elysium is explained by his marriage to Helen and his status as Jove's son-in-law.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Proteus says Menelaus will not die in Argos but will be taken to the Elysian plain at the ends of the world, where Rhadamanthus reigns and life is easy; this is because Menelaus married Helen and is Jove's son-in-law.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS. / BOOK IV; lines 2135-2239
occurrences.motif_label: threatened heir ambushed on return
occurrences.basis: Telemachus, son of Ulysses and heir to the house, is targeted for murder as he comes home, and Penelope frames the danger as an attempt to exterminate the family line.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “They are going to try and murder Telemachus as he is coming home from Pylos and Lacedaemon” after seeking news of his father.

Penelope collapses in grief, the maids weep around her, and she laments losing Ulysses and now having her son at the mercy of winds and waves; she orders Dolius to inform Laertes of the threat to their race.
Penelope lies upstairs unable to eat or drink, wonders whether Telemachus will escape, is compared to a trapped lioness surrounded by huntsmen, and falls asleep.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV / BOOK V / BOOK VI / THE MEETING BETWEEN NAUSICAA AND ULYSSES.; lines 2694-2792
occurrences.motif_label: royal founder establishes a protected city and cultic order
occurrences.basis: Nausithous relocates the Phaeacians, surrounds the city with a wall, builds houses and temples, and divides lands; the reigning king Alcinous follows in this royal setting.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses sleeps; Minerva goes to the Phaeacians. The Phaeacians had moved from Hypereia near the Cyclopes to Scheria under Nausithous, who built and divided the city; Alcinous now reigns, and Minerva goes to his house to further Ulysses' return.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VI / THE MEETING BETWEEN NAUSICAA AND ULYSSES. / BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS.; lines 2992-3088
occurrences.motif_label: divine ancestry of a ruling house
occurrences.basis: Alcinous and Arete are linked genealogically to Neptune through Nausithous, and Alcinous rules the Phaeacians.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva points out the house, tells Ulysses to seek Arete, recounts the descent of Alcinous and Arete from Neptune, describes Arete's exceptional honor, and says her goodwill may enable Ulysses' return home.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: PREFACE TO SECOND EDITION / HENRY FESTING JONES. / THE ODYSSEY / BOOK I; lines 494-587
occurrences.motif_label: uncertain lineage of the son
occurrences.basis: Telemachus says his mother tells him he is Ulysses’ son but that a child cannot know his own father; Minerva responds that Penelope has a fine son and that the race will not die out.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus says his mother tells him he is Ulysses’ son, but a child cannot know his father, and he calls his reported father ill-starred.
Minerva says Telemachus’ race will not die out while Penelope has such a son, then asks about the feast and criticizes the guests for their riot and lack of their own provisions.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: PREFACE TO SECOND EDITION / HENRY FESTING JONES. / THE ODYSSEY / BOOK I; lines 589-680
occurrences.motif_label: returning avenger restores threatened household
occurrences.basis: Minerva discusses whether Ulysses will return and take revenge in his own house, and frames the suitors' presence as destructive to the household.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus says the gods have hidden his father more closely than any mortal, that storm-winds carried him off without trace, and that suitors from Dulichium, Same, Zacynthus, and Ithaca are consuming his house while courting his mother.

Minerva says Ulysses is needed at home; if armed as when she first knew him, he would deal with the suitors quickly. She recalls his quest for arrow poison from Ilus and says the suitors would have a short shrift and sorry wedding.

Minerva says heaven will determine Ulysses' return, then advises Telemachus to call an assembly, order the suitors away, send Penelope to her father if she wants remarriage, sail with twenty men to Pylos and Sparta for news, perform rites and build a barrow if Ulysses is dead, and consider killing the suitors; she cites Orestes' fame for killing Aegisthus.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: PREFACE TO SECOND EDITION / HENRY FESTING JONES. / THE ODYSSEY / BOOK I; lines 589-680
occurrences.motif_label: avenging son as model for winning fame
occurrences.basis: Minerva tells Telemachus to show his mettle and invokes Orestes' praised killing of his father's murderer Aegisthus.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva says heaven will determine Ulysses' return, then advises Telemachus to call an assembly, order the suitors away, send Penelope to her father if she wants remarriage, sail with twenty men to Pylos and Sparta for news, perform rites and build a barrow if Ulysses is dead, and consider killing the suitors; she cites Orestes' fame for killing Aegisthus.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: PREFACE TO SECOND EDITION / HENRY FESTING JONES. / THE ODYSSEY / BOOK I; lines 682-759
occurrences.motif_label: contested household and royal legitimacy
occurrences.basis: The passage centers on Telemachus asserting mastery in his own house and discussing whether he can be chief in Ithaca, while suitors challenge or limit that claim.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus tells his mother to let the bard sing, says Jove sends good and evil, mentions the ill-fated return of the Danaans and Ulysses not returning from Troy, then sends her to loom, distaff, servants, and declares himself master in the house.

Telemachus calls the suitors shameless and insolent, tells them to enjoy the present feast without brawling, orders them to meet him in assembly, directs them to feast elsewhere at their own cost, and warns that Jove may reckon with them.

The suitors marvel at Telemachus’s boldness; Antinous prays that Jove never grant him chiefship in Ithaca; Telemachus replies that he would be chief if god wills it and will at least rule his own house and what Ulysses won for him.

Eurymachus says heaven decides who will be chief, acknowledges Telemachus’s mastery over his own house and possessions, asks about the stranger, and Telemachus identifies him as Mentes while knowing inwardly that he had been the goddess.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: ULYSSES LEAVES SCHERIA AND RETURNS TO ITHACA. / BOOK XIV / ULYSSES IN THE HUT WITH EUMAEUS. / BOOK XV; lines 6932-7022
occurrences.motif_label: bird omen confirming royal household power
occurrences.basis: The hawk with a dove is interpreted as divinely sent and as meaning Telemachus will remain powerful and his house will be unmatched in royal standing in Ithaca.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A hawk, called Apollo's messenger, flies by on Telemachus' right holding a dove, and feathers fall between Telemachus and the ship.
Theoclymenus says the bird was sent by a god and means that Telemachus will remain powerful, with no house in Ithaca more royal than his own.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: ULYSSES IN THE HUT WITH EUMAEUS. / BOOK XV / BOOK XVI / ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS.; lines 7025-7122
occurrences.motif_label: hidden lord witnesses disorder in his house
occurrences.basis: Ulysses, present as the stranger, hears of and condemns abuses in his own household and speaks of Ulysses or Ulysses’ son fighting there rather than enduring the disgrace.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses says he is shocked by the suitors’ insolence and declares that if he were as young as Telemachus, or were Ulysses himself, he would rather die fighting in his own house than see strangers mistreated, women servants dragged about, wine wasted, and bread consumed to no purpose.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: ULYSSES IN THE HUT WITH EUMAEUS. / BOOK XV / BOOK XVI / ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS.; lines 7025-7122
occurrences.motif_label: restoration of household honor against many offenders
occurrences.basis: Ulysses’ speech contrasts the rightful household of Ulysses with the suitors’ abuse of strangers, women servants, wine, and bread, and imagines violent resistance even against superior numbers.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses says he is shocked by the suitors’ insolence and declares that if he were as young as Telemachus, or were Ulysses himself, he would rather die fighting in his own house than see strangers mistreated, women servants dragged about, wine wasted, and bread consumed to no purpose.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: ULYSSES IN THE HUT WITH EUMAEUS. / BOOK XV / BOOK XVI / ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS.; lines 7124-7222
occurrences.motif_label: Threatened household and restoration plot
occurrences.basis: Telemachus' estate is being consumed by suitors, and Minerva instructs Ulysses to reveal himself and plan their destruction.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus says there is no enmity with his people, describes a lineage of only sons, and says suitors from nearby islands and Ithaca are consuming his house while courting Penelope and plotting against him.
Minerva tells Ulysses it is time to tell his son, to plan the destruction of the suitors, and to go toward town; she says she will join him and is eager for the fight.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: ULYSSES IN THE HUT WITH EUMAEUS. / BOOK XV / BOOK XVI / ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS.; lines 7224-7319
occurrences.motif_label: restoration of rightful household authority
occurrences.basis: Ulysses, the returned father and master of the house, plans with his son against suitors who occupy the household and waste the estate.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus praises Ulysses' renown but warns that the suitors are numerous, listing fifty-two from Dulichium, twenty-four from Same, twenty from Zacynthus, twelve from Ithaca, and attendants.

Ulysses says the gods will not stay out of the fray, instructs Telemachus to return home, and says the swineherd will bring him disguised as a miserable old beggar; Telemachus must endure seeing him mistreated.
Ulysses tells Telemachus that no one must know he is in the house, not Laertes, Eumaeus, servants, or Penelope, and proposes testing the women and other servants.
Telemachus says he can keep counsel, questions the plan to test all the men immediately, supports proving the women, and refers to needing a sign from Jove.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: ULYSSES IN THE HUT WITH EUMAEUS. / BOOK XV / BOOK XVI / ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS.; lines 7321-7414
occurrences.motif_label: plot against the royal son and heir
occurrences.basis: The suitors plot to kill Telemachus, discuss division of his property, and treat his survival as an obstacle to their plans in Ulysses' household.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Antinous says the gods have saved Telemachus and that the suitors must make an end of him before he can call the Achaeans in assembly.

Antinous proposes seizing Telemachus away from town or on the road, dividing his property, and allowing Penelope and her future husband to keep the house; alternatively, the suitors should cease consuming his goods and compete for Penelope from their own houses.

Amphinomus, described as a leading suitor from Dulichium and of good disposition, says he does not favor killing Telemachus, calls killing one of noble blood heinous, and advises first consulting the oracles of Jove.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XV / BOOK XVI / ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII; lines 7434-7526
occurrences.motif_label: divine favor shown through enhanced appearance
occurrences.basis: Minerva endows Telemachus with divine comeliness so that observers marvel at him as he moves in public.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus goes out spear in hand with two dogs; Minerva gives him divine comeliness; the suitors gather with fair words and malicious hearts, but he avoids them.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XV / BOOK XVI / ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII; lines 7528-7613
occurrences.motif_label: Return of the absent householder to confront usurpers
occurrences.basis: Menelaus frames the suitors as usurping Ulysses' bed and predicts their destruction if Ulysses returns; Theoclymenus says Ulysses is already in Ithaca preparing a reckoning.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Menelaus says the suitors would usurp a brave man's bed and compares them to young animals in a lion's lair; the returning lion will make short work of them, as Ulysses would of the suitors.

Theoclymenus tells Penelope he can divine surely, invokes Zeus, hospitality, and Ulysses' hearth, and says Ulysses is in Ithaca investigating evil deeds and preparing a day of reckoning; he cites an omen seen on the ship.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XV / BOOK XVI / ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII; lines 7615-7715
occurrences.motif_label: household disorder during master's absence
occurrences.basis: The suitors feast in Ulysses' house, Melanthius joins them, and Eumaeus states that servants neglect work when the master's hand is absent.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Melanthius reaches the house, sits among the suitors opposite Eurymachus, and receives meat and bread from servants.
Ulysses praises the house's size and defenses, including a surrounding battlemented wall and double doors, and notes the smell of roast meat and sound of music within.
Eumaeus says Argos belonged to the man who died far away, recalls his former hunting excellence, and says servants neglect work when the master's hand is absent.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: HENRY FESTING JONES. / THE ODYSSEY / BOOK I / BOOK II; lines 762-849
occurrences.motif_label: young heir assumes public role in absent father’s place
occurrences.basis: Telemachus calls the assembly, appears with divine enhancement, and takes his father’s seat while speaking of the absent Ulysses and the danger to his house.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus sends criers to convene the assembly and goes there with spear in hand and two hounds.
Minerva gives Telemachus divine comeliness; people marvel, and he takes his father’s seat while the oldest councillors make way.
Telemachus says he convened the assembly because he is aggrieved; his first misfortune is the loss of his father, who was chief among them and like a father to everyone.
Telemachus says his second misfortune is that suitors press his mother to marry against her will and consume his household’s oxen, sheep, goats, and wine, threatening to ruin the estate.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XVI / ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII / BOOK XVIII; lines 8177-8277
occurrences.motif_label: courtship exchange violated and restored through gifts
occurrences.basis: Penelope contrasts proper wooing, which includes feast animals and gifts, with the suitors' consumption of the household; the suitors then provide costly presents.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Penelope replies that heaven took her beauty when Ulysses sailed to Troy; she recalls his instruction to care for the household and remarry when their son grew a beard; she criticizes the suitors for consuming property instead of following courtship custom with feasts and presents.

Antinous allows Penelope to accept presents but says the suitors will not leave until she marries the best man among them; the suitors bring a decorated dress, gold brooches, a gold and amber chain, earrings, a necklace, and other presents.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XVI / ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII / BOOK XVIII; lines 8279-8350
occurrences.motif_label: Restoration of household authority against disorderly guests
occurrences.basis: Telemachus rebukes the suitors’ disorder in Ulysses’ house, and Amphinomus recognizes that the stranger has come to Telemachus’ house to be dealt with by him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus rebukes the suitors for madness and disorder and tells them that after supper they should go home to bed.
Amphinomus advises the suitors not to take offense and not to do violence to the stranger or to any of Ulysses’ servants, leaving the stranger to Telemachus.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII / BOOK XVIII / BOOK XIX; lines 8353-8450
occurrences.motif_label: restoration of household authority through father and son
occurrences.basis: Telemachus takes charge of household property, helps remove his father’s armour, and is described by Ulysses as no longer in boyhood and able to notice wrongdoing in the house.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus asks Euryclea to shut the women in their room while he moves his father’s armour to the storeroom, and says the stranger will carry the light.

Euryclea bolts the women inside; Ulysses and Telemachus move helmets, shields, and spears; Minerva precedes them with a gold lamp, and Telemachus sees the house glowing as if with fire and says some god has come down from heaven.

Ulysses replies to Melantho, describing his ragged begging state, claiming he was once rich before Jove took all away, and warning her that Ulysses may still come home and that Telemachus is grown enough to notice wrongdoing.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII / BOOK XVIII / BOOK XIX; lines 8452-8531
occurrences.motif_label: righteous rule mirrored by natural abundance
occurrences.basis: Ulysses compares Penelope's fame to that of a blameless king whose virtues cause crops, flocks, fruit trees, fish, and people to flourish.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses praises Penelope and likens her fame to that of a blameless king whose righteous rule brings wheat, barley, fruit, lambs, fish, and good conduct among the people.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII / BOOK XVIII / BOOK XIX; lines 8452-8531
occurrences.motif_label: genealogical legitimation through named rulers and divine contact
occurrences.basis: The claimed identity traces descent through Deucalion to Minos, a ruler said to confer with Jove every nine years.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses replies with a Cretan identity tale: Crete is fertile, has ninety cities and many peoples; Cnossus was ruled by Minos, who conferred with Jove; Minos fathered Deucalion, whose sons were Idomeneus and the claimed Aethon.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: HENRY FESTING JONES. / THE ODYSSEY / BOOK I / BOOK II; lines 851-936
occurrences.motif_label: wasteful suitors consuming the absent lord's household
occurrences.basis: The suitors remain in the house, demand marriage to Penelope, and state that they will continue eating up Telemachus's estate until she chooses one of them.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The suitors say they will not leave their lands or stop consuming the estate until Penelope chooses and marries one of them.
Eurymachus says the suitors fear no man or fortune-telling and will continue eating up Telemachus's estate without paying until Penelope stops keeping them in expectation.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII / BOOK XVIII / BOOK XIX; lines 8788-8861
occurrences.motif_label: marriage contest using the hero’s weapon
occurrences.basis: Penelope announces that suitors must string Ulysses’ bow and shoot through twelve axes; the successful contestant will be the man she follows from the house.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Penelope says dawn will bring the day she leaves Ulysses’ house; she will hold a contest with twelve axes and Ulysses’ bow, following whichever suitor can string the bow and shoot through all twelve axes.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XVII / BOOK XVIII / BOOK XIX / BOOK XX; lines 9045-9146
occurrences.motif_label: Heir asserts household authority against usurping rivals
occurrences.basis: Telemachus declares that the house belongs to Ulysses and has passed to him, and he threatens suitors who abuse guests and property.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus seats Ulysses at a small table with food and wine in a gold cup, warns the suitors not to use gibes or blows, and says the house belongs to Ulysses and has passed to him.

Telemachus tells Ctesippus he would have speared him if he had hit the stranger, says he is now grown enough to understand good and evil, and denounces the suitors for consuming livestock, grain, and wine, insulting guests, and abusing women servants.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XVII / BOOK XVIII / BOOK XIX / BOOK XX; lines 9148-9215
occurrences.motif_label: returning father poised to punish offenders in his house
occurrences.basis: Telemachus watches his father, expecting him to begin an attack upon the suitors who are in Ulysses' house and have brought doom on themselves.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Theoclymenus says he has his own eyes, ears, feet, and understanding mind; he sees mischief overhanging those insulting and plotting ill in Ulysses' house, says none will escape, and goes back to Piraeus, who welcomes him.
“Telemachus gave him no heed, but sat silently watching his father, expecting every moment that he would begin his attack upon the suitors.”

The dinner had been abundant after many sacrifices, but the coming supper is described as gruesome, to be laid before the suitors by a goddess and a brave man because they had brought doom on themselves.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XVIII / BOOK XIX / BOOK XX / BOOK XXI; lines 9218-9315
occurrences.motif_label: Weapon trial determining marriage and household succession
occurrences.basis: Penelope makes marriage depend on stringing Ulysses' bow and shooting through twelve axes; Telemachus frames success with the bow as a way to keep his mother in the household and preserve his father's prizes.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Penelope tells the suitors they abuse the hospitality of the absent owner and declares that whoever strings Ulysses' bow and shoots through twelve axes will be the man she follows from her lawful husband's house.

Telemachus speaks of Penelope as his mother, urges the suitors to proceed with the contest, praises her, and says he will try the bow so that, if he succeeds, he will not allow her to leave with a stranger.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: HENRY FESTING JONES. / THE ODYSSEY / BOOK I / BOOK II; lines 938-1036
occurrences.motif_label: youth measured against parental lineage
occurrences.basis: Minerva evaluates Telemachus’ chance of success by whether he shares the qualities and blood of Ulysses and Penelope.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva tells Telemachus that if he is like his father, Ulysses, he will not be foolish or cowardly, and invokes the blood of Ulysses and Penelope as grounds for hope.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XVIII / BOOK XIX / BOOK XX / BOOK XXI; lines 9416-9503
occurrences.motif_label: weapon test determining status and marriage claim
occurrences.basis: The bow belongs to Ulysses, the suitors cannot string it, and Eurymachus links success or failure with the suitors' public standing and Penelope's courtship.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Eurymachus warms the bow by the fire but cannot string it and laments that the suitors are inferior to Ulysses in strength.
“give me the bow that I may prove the power of my hands among you all”
Eurymachus says the suitors fear gossip that they were too feeble to string the brave man's bow while a beggarly tramp strung it and shot through the iron.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XVIII / BOOK XIX / BOOK XX / BOOK XXI; lines 9505-9596
occurrences.motif_label: weapon trial validates rightful authority
occurrences.basis: Authority over the bow is asserted by Telemachus; Ulysses alone strings the bow and completes the axe shot, proving power associated with the household's rightful line.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus says he alone may give or withhold the bow, sends Penelope to household work, and states that the bow is especially his matter because he is master in the house.
Ulysses strings the bow as easily as a skilled bard strings a lyre; the string sings, the suitors are dismayed, and Jove thunders loudly as an omen.
Ulysses takes an arrow, draws it while seated, and shoots through all the axe handle-holes into the outer courtyard.
Ulysses makes a sign with his eyebrows, and Telemachus arms himself with sword and spear beside his father's seat.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XIX / BOOK XX / BOOK XXI / BOOK XXII; lines 9599-9707
occurrences.motif_label: returning ruler punishes household usurpers
occurrences.basis: Ulysses explicitly identifies himself as returned from Troy and condemns the suitors for occupying his household, wooing his wife, wasting his goods, and plotting against his son and local authority.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses tells the suitors they thought he would not return from Troy, accuses them of wasting his goods, abusing women servants, wooing his wife, and fearing neither God nor man, and says they shall die.
Eurymachus addresses Ulysses, says Antinous led the wrongs, claims Antinous wanted to kill Telemachus and rule Ithaca, and offers fines in oxen, gold, and bronze.
Ulysses refuses any present or future goods and says he will not stay his hand until all the suitors are paid in full; they must fight or try to flee.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XIX / BOOK XX / BOOK XXI / BOOK XXII; lines 9709-9805
occurrences.motif_label: reclaiming the household against armed usurpers
occurrences.basis: Ulysses fights armed suitors in his own house with his son and loyal allies, while opponents threaten to kill father and son and seize property.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After leaving Melanthius in cruel bondage, the allies arm themselves and return to Ulysses; four men stand in the cloister while the suitors remain many in the court.
The suitors raise an uproar; Agelaus warns Mentor not to side with Ulysses and threatens to kill him and absorb his property into Ulysses' property after father and son are killed.
Minerva, angered, scolds Ulysses by recalling his nine years fighting at Troy, his killings there, and the stratagem by which Priam's city was taken.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XIX / BOOK XX / BOOK XXI / BOOK XXII; lines 9807-9908
occurrences.motif_label: returning master punishes household usurpers
occurrences.basis: Ulysses is identified as acting in his own house against suitors who had sought his wife and harmed him during his absence.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses and his companions strike back: Ulysses hits Eurydamas and Agelaus, Telemachus hits Amphimedon and Leocritus, Eumaeus hits Polybus, and the stockman kills Ctesippus after taunting him.
Leiodes catches Ulysses' knees, asks for mercy, says he never wronged the women, tried to stop the others, and was the suitors' sacrificing priest.
Ulysses replies that as sacrificing priest Leiodes must have prayed against his return and for marriage to his wife; Ulysses then kills him with Agelaus' sword.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 1039-1112
occurrences.motif_label: Ideal ruler as living law
occurrences.basis: The passage says that in the Politicus the king’s mind or will is preferred to written law and that he is law personified.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “the mind or will of the king is preferred to the written law; he is supposed to be the Law personified, the ideal made Life.”

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 10460-10547
occurrences.motif_label: usurpation through hidden power and royal conspiracy
occurrences.basis: Gyges uses the ring-enabled opportunity to reach the court, seduce the queen, kill the king, and take the kingdom.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Gyges arranges to be a messenger to court, seduces the queen, conspires with her against the king, kills him, and takes the kingdom.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1100-1178
occurrences.motif_label: divine sanction of rulership
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly mentions the divine right of a monarch and the divine right of kings or governments as a form of authority claim.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says ancient and modern theories have a family likeness to Glaucon’s speculation, including power as the foundation of right and divine right of monarchs or governments.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III.; lines 13507-13621
occurrences.motif_label: divine differentiation of social ranks
occurrences.basis: God is said to mingle different metals into different people, assigning gold to rulers, silver to auxiliaries, and brass or iron to productive classes.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The tale says God framed citizens differently by mingling gold, silver, brass, or iron into them; gold belongs to rulers, silver to auxiliaries, and brass and iron to husbandmen and craftsmen, with rank changes possible in children.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III.; lines 13507-13621
occurrences.motif_label: oracle validating civic hierarchy
occurrences.basis: The tale includes an oracle that the State will be destroyed if a brass or iron man becomes guardian.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The tale cites an oracle saying the State will be destroyed when a man of brass or iron guards it.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 17211-17397
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom as qualification for rulership
occurrences.basis: The passage argues that rulers or guardians should be those who know the truth of each thing and can guard the laws and institutions of the State.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “philosophers only are able to grasp the eternal and unchangeable,” while others “wander in the region of the many and variable”; the speaker asks which class should rule the State.
“Whichever of the two are best able to guard the laws and institutions of our State—let them be our guardians.”

The speaker says a guardian should have eyes, then describes those without knowledge of true being or a clear pattern in the soul as lacking the painter-like vision needed to order laws about beauty, goodness, and justice, and says they are much like blind persons.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1774-1852
occurrences.motif_label: divinely assigned social metals
occurrences.basis: God is said to fashion people from different metals, with gold assigned to rulers, and an oracle forbids rule by brass or iron.

evidence.quote_or_summary: God framed some citizens of gold to rule, others of silver as auxiliaries, and others of brass and iron as husbandmen and craftsmen.
An oracle says “that the State will come to an end if governed by a man of brass or iron.”

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 18013-18130
occurrences.motif_label: royal legitimacy through philosophical or divine inspiration
occurrences.basis: Socrates allows that kings, princes, or royal sons may become fit for rule if divinely inspired with true love of true philosophy.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates states that cities, states, and individuals will not be perfected until philosophers are compelled to care for the State and the State obeys them, or until royal figures are divinely inspired with true love of true philosophy.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 18132-18283
occurrences.motif_label: royal or princely philosopher as possible founder
occurrences.basis: The passage considers whether sons of kings or princes may be philosophers by nature and says one such man with an obedient city could establish the ideal polity.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speakers say that one man with a city obedient to his will would be enough to bring the ideal polity into existence, and that citizens may obey the laws and institutions he imposes.
The speakers ask whether anyone will deny that there may be sons of kings or princes who are philosophers by nature, and whether one such person might escape destruction.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19022-19142
occurrences.motif_label: reluctant righteous rulership
occurrences.basis: The best-governed State is said to be ruled by those most reluctant to govern, who value philosophy, virtue, and wisdom above political ambition.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The pupils may spend most of their time in heavenly light, but will take office as a stern necessity rather than in the manner of present rulers.
The passage contrasts rulers rich in virtue and wisdom with those poor and hungry for private advantage; lovers of rule become rivals and fight.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1996-2074
occurrences.motif_label: state-founding origin myth
occurrences.basis: The passage says every Greek state had an origin myth and that the Platonic republic may have a tale of earthborn men used to support its social order.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Plato adapts mythology like the Homeric poems to the needs of the state, making the Phoenician tale the vehicle of his ideas.
Every Greek state had an origin myth, and the Platonic republic may also have a tale of earthborn men.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 20154-20256
occurrences.motif_label: philosopher-ruler establishes just order
occurrences.basis: True philosopher kings make the constitution possible, despise worldly honors, esteem right, serve justice, and set the city in order.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “Then comes the famous request for a body-guard ... ‘Let not the people’s friend,’ as they say, ‘be lost to them.’”
The more detestable his actions, the more satellites he needs; paid followers or drones from many lands flock to him.
The tyrant robs citizens of slaves, frees them, enrolls them in his bodyguard, and trusts them as friends of his own sort.

occurrences.motif_label: wisdom joined to rulership
occurrences.basis: The passage says political well-being depends on kings becoming philosophers or philosophers becoming kings, linking rule to philosophical knowledge.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “Until, then, kings are philosophers, or philosophers are kings, cities will never cease from ill” and the change is called “the great wave.”
The passage names abstract ideas such as justice, beauty, good, and evil as single realities that appear many in combinations, and says those who recognize these realities are philosophers.

occurrences.motif_label: philosopher ruler establishes ideal polity
occurrences.basis: The passage says perfection requires philosophers to hold office or royal sons to love philosophy, and that one philosopher son of a king could bring the ideal polity into being.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says the many have not seen the unity of ideas and that perfection in states or individuals requires philosophers to hold office or royal sons to be inspired with true love of philosophy.

The passage says the philosopher is a lover of truth; it considers whether a king's son could be a philosopher and concludes that one philosopher royal son with obedient citizens could bring the ideal polity into being.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic

occurrences.motif_label: reluctant wise ruler compelled to serve the community
occurrences.basis: The philosopher trained for knowledge is described as reluctant to rule but compelled to descend and govern for the common good and salvation of the State.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Pleasure and desire are described as leaden weights binding the soul to earth; rulers must be chosen from natures able to ascend to light and knowledge, but must be forced down again among the captives.
The philosopher is told he has been trained to be ruler and king of the hive, must descend into the den, learn to use his eyes in the dark, and rule from waking knowledge for the State's salvation.

The mature figure may take a turn at the helm of State and train others as successors.
The State may come into being when philosopher-kings arise, despise earthly vanities, and serve justice only.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "The number of the interval which separates the king from the tyrant, and royal from tyrannical pleasures, is 729, the cube of 9."
The passage describes Plato as using a progression of numbers and a geometrical figure to express the immeasurable interval between royal and tyrannical life.

occurrences.motif_label: Ruler legitimated by union of command and thought

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage asks whether the ruler or statesman should be a philosopher and states that some figures have united command with thought and reflection.
The passage says mankind has seen bad imitations of the philosopher-statesman, but not a ruler in whom thought and action are perfectly balanced in a constitutional state.

occurrences.motif_label: Divinely authorized universal kingship or empire
occurrences.basis: Dante’s Universal Empire is described as divinely authorized, heir to Rome, and necessary for world peace.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Dante’s De Monarchia is described as a medieval ideal envisioning a Universal Empire, divinely authorized yet distinct from the Papacy, and heir to the Roman Empire through Roman virtues and beneficent rule.

Dante’s claim for Roman world-governance is said to be confirmed by miracles, St. Paul’s appeal to Caesar, Christ’s condemnation by a divinely authorized tribunal, and arguments from divine unity, family or nation, scripture, history, nature, classics, and logic.

Dante sees the world’s misery and no hope of happiness or peace until all nations are included in one empire; the Roman Empire idea is deeply fixed, and the aspiration is for mortal life to pass in freedom and peace.

Bharat tells Bharadvája that Vaśishṭha instructed him to hold the sandals because they would secure Ayodhyá's welfare, and the hermit praises Bharat's just mind.

occurrences.motif_label: path to awakening and release
occurrences.basis: The passage describes a named way that purifies intelligence, ends pain, and frees those who enter it from Mara's bondage.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The best of ways is the eightfold; the best of truths the four words; the best of virtues passionlessness; the best of men he who has eyes to see.

If you go on this way, you will make an end of pain! The way was preached by me, when I had understood the removal of the thorns (in the flesh).
You yourself must make an effort. The Tathagatas (Buddhas) are only preachers. The thoughtful who enter the way are freed from the bondage of Mara.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Kāḷa Devala tells his nephew Nālaka that the child will become a Buddha in thirty-five years and urges him to renounce; Nālaka takes yellow clothes, a pot, shaves his head, takes robes, vows, and goes to the Himālayas as a monk.

occurrences.motif_label: renunciation foretold and imitated
occurrences.basis: The predicted path requires taking vows; Kondanya renounces, and four others take vows in imitation after hearing that the prince has taken vows.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Kondanya leaves all he has, makes the great renunciation, comes to Uruvela, and takes up residence there for spiritual exertion.
Kondanya tells the Brahmans' sons that Siddhattha has taken vows; four follow him into vows, forming the Company of the Five Elders.

occurrences.motif_label: Hair cutting and change of clothing as renunciant transformation
occurrences.basis: The Bodisat cuts off his hair and diadem, rejects royal muslin as unsuitable, receives mendicant requisites, and adopts renunciation garb.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Bodisat judges his locks unsuitable for a mendicant and cuts off his own hair and diadem with his sword, leaving short right-curling hair.

Ghaṭikāra, an archangel and former friend, brings the eight requisites of a mendicant; the Bodisat dresses in the signs of an Arahat and the garb of renunciation and tells Channa to reassure his parents.

occurrences.motif_label: ascetic ordeal as testing struggle
occurrences.basis: The Bodisat undertakes the Great Struggle, practices extreme fasting for six years, is served by attendants, collapses, and later changes course.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Five mendicants, including Kondanya, meet the Bodisat, stay by him for six years, serve him, and repeatedly expect that he will become a Buddha.

The Bodisat performs uttermost penance with one seed, one grain, or complete fasting; angels infuse sap of life; he becomes skeletal and dark, loses the Thirty-two signs, suffers pain, faints, and falls.
The six years' penance becomes widely known; the Bodisat perceives penance is not the way to Wisdom, resumes ordinary food, and regains the Thirty-two signs and gold-like color.

occurrences.motif_label: ritual bathing at a liminal river place
occurrences.basis: After accepting the offering, the Bodisat goes to a named ferry on the Nerañjarā river, descends, bathes, dresses in the garb of Arahats, and then eats the prepared food.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Bodisat rises, leaves the tree on his right hand, carries the vessel to the Nerañjarā river at the Supatiṭṭhita ferry, places it on the bank, descends into the river, and bathes.

evidence.locator: lines 6257 and following passage text supplied
evidence.quote_or_summary: After dressing in the garb of Arahats, he sits facing east, divides the rice into forty-nine balls, eats it without water, and for forty-nine days at the Tree of Wisdom has no other food, bathing, tooth-washing, or natural cravings, living on meditative joys.

occurrences.motif_label: immovable vow before enlightenment
occurrences.basis: The Bodisat vows that his body may dry up but that he will not leave the seat until attaining complete insight.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The eastern place is identified as where all Buddhas sit cross-legged and as unshaken; the grass forms a fourteen-cubit seat, and the Bodisat vows not to leave until complete insight is attained.

occurrences.motif_label: tempting or obstructing adversary before liberation
occurrences.basis: Māra seeks to keep Siddhattha from freeing himself from his dominion and deploys a vast army to overwhelm him as he sits beneath the Bo-tree.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Māra declares he will not let Siddhattha free himself, sounds the war-cry, leads a vast army, mounts an immense elephant, creates a thousand arms, and takes weapons.
Angels of many world-systems praise the Great Being; Sakka, the Nāga king, and Mahā Brahma honor him, but all deities flee when Māra’s army surrounds the Bo-tree seat, leaving the Great Being alone.

occurrences.motif_label: heroic solitude after divine supporters withdraw
occurrences.basis: Divine beings praise and honor the Great Being, but when Māra’s army arrives they flee, leaving him alone.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Angels of many world-systems praise the Great Being; Sakka, the Nāga king, and Mahā Brahma honor him, but all deities flee when Māra’s army surrounds the Bo-tree seat, leaving the Great Being alone.

occurrences.motif_label: Demonic assault overcome by perfected virtue
occurrences.basis: Māra attacks Siddhattha with hosts, elements, weapons, and darkness, but Siddhattha remains seated and relies on perfected virtues.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Māra tells his host to attack Siddhattha from behind; Siddhattha sees the gods have fled, notes he has no relatives to help him, and resolves to use the ten cardinal virtues as shield and sword while meditating on the Ten Perfections.
Māra sends a destructive whirlwind and then a mighty rain and flood, but through the Great Being's goodness the wind cannot shake his robe and the flood cannot wet even a dew-drop-sized place on it.

Māra sends storms of rocks, weapons, charcoal, ashes, sand, and mud; these come with smoke, flame, or heat but become heavenly flowers, sandalwood dust, or heavenly perfume at the future Buddha's feet.

Māra brings fourfold darkness to terrify Siddhattha, but it vanishes before the future Buddha; the passage lists nine failed assaults: wind, rain, rocks, weapons, charcoal, ashes, sand, mud, and darkness.

occurrences.motif_label: Teaching that initiates stages of awakening
occurrences.basis: Multiple named discourses and proclamations cause hearers to attain the First Path, Nirvana, Arahatship, or lay discipleship.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Surrounded by myriads of angels, the Buddha teaches The Foundation of the Kingdom of Righteousness; Kondanya and then the other elders attain the First Path, and all five attain Nirvana after the discourse On the Non-existence of the Soul.
Yasa leaves home, hears “Follow me, Yasa!”, attains the First Path and Arahatship, and his fifty-four companions are received into the order and attain Arahatship.

At Uruvela the Buddha overcomes three ascetic brothers and their thousand disciples by 3,500 miracles, receives them into the Order, establishes them in Arahatship through a discourse on fire, and goes to the Palm-grove near Rajagaha.

The multitude praises the power of the Buddhas; the Buddha says he overcame Kassapa in former ages, utters the Maha Narada Kassapa Jataka, proclaims the Four Truths, and the king with nearly all his retinue attains the First Path.

occurrences.motif_label: miraculous initiation into the Order
occurrences.basis: Those admitted to the Order appear at once with miraculously created robes and bowls, like long-standing Elders.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A messenger with a thousand followers listens to the Sage, attains Arahatship with his retinue, asks to enter the Order, and appears with miraculously created robes and bowls.

occurrences.motif_label: Initiation into the religious order
occurrences.basis: Nanda is received into the Order, and Rāhula is to be received into the Order by Sāriputta.

evidence.quote_or_summary: During coronation, housewarming, and Nanda’s marriage festivals, the Buddha gives Nanda his bowl to carry in order to make him abandon the world. Janapada Kalyāṇī calls after Nanda, who follows the Blessed One to the Wihāra and is received unwillingly into the Order.

Rāhula follows the Blessed One asking for his inheritance. The Blessed One reflects that worldly wealth perishes and says, “I will give him the sevenfold wealth of the Arahats which I obtained under the Bo-tree, and make him the heir of a spiritual inheritance!” He then tells Sāriputta to receive Rāhula into the Order.

occurrences.motif_label: renunciation and initiation into the religious order
occurrences.basis: Great Roadling requests entry into the Order, receives permission, is ordained as a novice, and later becomes a full member.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Great Roadling grows up in his grandfather’s house, goes with him to hear the Buddha preach, turns toward renunciation, asks to enter the Order, and receives his grandfather’s support.
The Teacher has a monk ordain Great Roadling, the monk teaches meditation on the body’s perishability, and Great Roadling later learns scripture, becomes a full member, and attains Arahatship.

occurrences.motif_label: failed novice restored by the teacher
occurrences.basis: Little Roadling is initiated but fails at memorization, is expelled, and is then redirected by the Teacher into a practice that culminates in Arahatship.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Little Roadling is ordained, taught to live by the Ten Commandments, but cannot memorize even one stanza after four months.
The elder brother says Little Roadling is not fit for the discipline and expels him from the monastery.
The Teacher becomes aware of the matter, waits by the gateway, and tells Little Roadling that his profession was under him and that he may stay with him.
The Teacher seats Little Roadling before his apartment, gives him a very white cloth, and tells him to face east and rub it while repeating, 'The removal of impurity.'
When the stanzas are finished, Little Roadling attains Arahatship and the intellectual gifts of an Arahat, by which he understands all the Scriptures.

occurrences.motif_label: Initiatory prohibition tied to mythic action at a well
occurrences.basis: The passage says Eleusinian initiates were forbidden to sit on a well because of the mythic episode in which the searching goddess sits there.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The note says the myths of Isis and Demeter agree because both goddesses, searching for the loved and lost one, sat sad and weary on the edge of a well; Eleusinian initiates were therefore forbidden to sit on a well.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "at the initiation into the Eleusinian mysteries ... the central mystery revealed to the initiated was a reaped ear of corn"

occurrences.motif_label: Concealed green figure discovered and guessed
occurrences.basis: The Thüringen May King hides inside a verdurous frame, is sought out, returned to the village, and guessed by authorities and others.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In Brunswick and Thüringen, a May King is covered with a May-bush or enclosed in a birch-covered wooden frame crowned with birch and flowers; others find him, bring him back, and guess who is inside, paying forfeits for wrong guesses.

occurrences.motif_label: Danger to souls at thresholds or transitions
occurrences.basis: The passage says demons are especially feared by persons who have just entered a new house and describes a house-warming soul-restoration rite.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At an Alfoer house-warming in Celebes, a priest hangs a bag, recites gods through the night, offers egg and rice, and holds the soul-filled bag on each household member's head.

occurrences.basis: Young people undergo a purificatory ceremony and participate in a prescribed festival setting with crowned dogs and a ritual meal.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At the annual festival young people underwent purification, dogs were crowned, and the feast included young kid, wine, and hot cakes on leaves.

occurrences.motif_label: Admission ordeal with confession and vows
occurrences.basis: Visitors to Kalamba undergo a staged sequence before being allowed to reside in the town, including bathing, naked approach, markings, pepper in the eyes, confession, answers, and vows.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Subject chiefs visiting Kalamba for the first time or after rebellion bathe in two brooks over two days, sleep in the open market-place, approach naked, receive white marks from Kalamba, then undergo a pepper ordeal with confession, questions, and vows before residing in town.

occurrences.motif_label: post-initiation soul vulnerability
occurrences.basis: The New South Wales example states that after initiation into tribal mysteries the young man's soul is in a critical state and he must cover his mouth when a woman is present.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In West Timor a speaker covers his mouth with his hand to prevent demon entry and magical harm to the soul; in New South Wales, a recently initiated young man covers his mouth with a rug when a woman is present.

occurrences.motif_label: seclusion of liminal persons
occurrences.basis: The passage describes seclusion at childbirth, puberty, after homicide, at circumcision, and in connection with first war-path status; puberty, circumcision, and first-war examples support an initiation-related reading.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Women at childbirth are described as secluded, with vessels used during seclusion burned; an Eskimo example says shared cups or dishes after confinement require purification by incantations.
North American examples describe puberty dishes reserved for girls, men who have slain enemies using only their own dishes or pipes, and those dishes or pipes being burned after seclusion.
Kafir boys at circumcision live in a special hut; after healing, used vessels, boyish mantles, and the hut are burned. A young Indian brave on first war-path uses vessels no one else may touch.

occurrences.motif_label: initiation blood received by the community
occurrences.basis: Australian initiation examples describe circumcision and tooth extraction blood being received on the bodies of tribesmen rather than falling to the ground.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Frazer generalizes royal blood avoidance to a broader reluctance to shed human blood or let it fall on the ground, citing Cambaluc punishments, Captain Christian’s execution on white blankets, and Australian initiation examples.

occurrences.motif_label: ritual transfer of identity, name, or rank through soul capture
occurrences.basis: The Carrier successor receives the soul through priestly action and takes the deceased person's name and rank.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Among the Takilis or Carrier Indians, a priest catches the deceased's soul in his hands during cremation and transmits it to a successor by throwing his hands toward him and blowing; the recipient takes the deceased's name and rank.

occurrences.motif_label: Gender-restricted ritual procession
occurrences.basis: Women or girls control key ritual actions, while males are barred from participation or limited to antagonistic/disposal roles.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In parts of Lusatia, women in mourning make a straw Death puppet with a white shirt, broom, and scythe, carry it to the village boundary while boys throw stones, tear it apart, then cut a fine tree, hang the shirt on it, and carry it home singing.

In a Saxon village near Hermanstadt, schoolgirls make a corn-sheaf and broomstick Death figure, dress it in a matron’s Sunday clothes, display it, carry it in procession with boys excluded, strip it, and throw the straw bundle to boys, who fling it into a stream.

In the second act, one girl is invested with the clothes and ornaments previously worn by the figure of Death and led in procession with hymns; the ceremony ends with a feast, with boys again excluded.

occurrences.motif_label: ritual reenactment of divine death and return
occurrences.basis: Frazer states that Cretan rites represented Dionysus’s suffering and death in detail and, where the myth included it, enacted his resurrection; he also links Dionysiac mysteries with immortality teaching.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Cretans celebrated a biennial festival representing Dionysus’s sufferings and death in detail, and where resurrection belonged to the myth it was also enacted in the rites.
Frazer cites Plutarch’s consolation to his wife as evidence that the mysteries of Dionysus taught, or revealed, immortality of the soul.
