occurrences.basis: The passage lists girls secluded at puberty in Loango and Macusi treatment of girls at puberty, along with seclusion of women during menstruation and dread of menstruous blood.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Entries mention girls secluded at puberty in Loango, Macusi treatment of girls at puberty, and seclusion of women during menstruation.

occurrences.basis: Purified women called drawers descend into caverns, drive away serpents, and retrieve remains for altar placement.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Women called drawers, after three days of ceremonial purity, descended into the caverns, frightened away serpents by clapping, brought up decayed remains, and placed them on the altar.

occurrences.motif_label: puberty seclusion of girls
occurrences.basis: Several notes describe girls or daughters being confined, shut up in huts, or otherwise secluded at puberty or related life-stage observances.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Note 615 cites New Britain/New Ireland materials: girls wear scented herb wreaths around waist and neck; an old woman or child occupies the lower floor of the cage; confinement may last a month in Powell's account, with longer duration suggested for chiefs' daughters.

The same note says that among the Goajiras of Colombia, rich people keep daughters shut up in separate huts at puberty for one to four years, while poor people can do so only for a fortnight or a month.
Note 620 gives references for caps, hoods, and veils worn by girls at such seasons.

occurrences.basis: The Fiji note says brides being tattooed were kept from the sun and suggests this may relate to the Melanesian custom of secluding girls at puberty.

occurrences.basis: The Brahman boy after sacred-thread investment and Bali boys after tooth filing are both restricted for three days, including avoidance of the sun or confinement in a dark room.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After the ceremony, children born in the past year are carried out and made to touch the serpent skin’s tail; Frazer says this places infants under the tribal god’s protection.
In Senegambia, a python is expected to visit every child of the Python clan within eight days after birth.
The Psylli, called a Snake clan of ancient Africa, exposed infants to snakes, believing snakes would not harm true-born clan children.

occurrences.basis: The Karok rite includes fasting by a ritual specialist, a salmon dance, a prohibition on taking salmon before and after the dance, and equipment restrictions.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Karoks dance for salmon; the Kareya or God-man fasts ten days in the mountains, returns, takes the first salmon, eats some, kindles sacred fire in the sweating-house with the rest, and salmon-taking is forbidden before and for ten days after the dance.

Karok fishermen avoid poles gathered by the river where salmon might have seen them; poles must come from the highest mountain, and reused poles are avoided because old salmon would have told young ones about them.

occurrences.motif_label: Puberty seclusion as initiation ordeal
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly describes girls at puberty being isolated in dark enclosures, subjected to restrictions, and later returned or brought out; one account explicitly calls the Aht retirement an initiatory ordeal.

evidence.quote_or_summary: New Guinea chiefs' daughters are kept indoors in shaded houses; Ot Danom girls are shut in dark raised cells for long periods with only a slave woman attending, later shown the sun, earth, water, trees, and flowers as if newly born, followed by a feast, killing of a slave, and blood-smearing; Ceram girls were shut in dark huts at puberty.

Aht girls are enclosed with mats so neither sun nor fire can be seen, receive water but no food, and are disgraced if they see fire or sun; Thlinkeet or Kolosh girls are confined in blocked huts or cages, fed through a small window, drink from an eagle wing-bone, and wear flapped hats so their gaze does not pollute the sky; Koniag girls remain in constrained kneeling postures in small huts.

Rio de la Plata girls are sewn into hammocks as if dead, leaving a small breathing hole; Chiriguano girls are hoisted in hammocks and later lowered, after which old women with sticks hunt the snake said to have wounded the girl until one says it is killed.

Some Brazilian girls at puberty have hair burned or shaved, are cut with an animal tooth until bloody, have gourd ashes rubbed into wounds, are bound in a hammock for three days without food or drink, avoid ground contact, are carried by a female relation with a live coal, abstain from salt and flesh, are later gashed again, blackened with pigment, and return to ordinary movement.

occurrences.motif_label: puberty seclusion and initiation into womanhood
occurrences.basis: Multiple cases describe girls at puberty or maturity being secluded, restricted, ritually treated, and later reintegrated or considered marriageable.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Among the Macusis, a girl at first signs of puberty is hung in a hammock at the highest point of the hut; by day she remains there, at night she descends, lights a fire, and stays beside it; she fasts and later moves to a compartment in the darkest corner.

The Macusis girl cooks at a separate fire in her own vessel; a magician mutters charms and breathes on her and valuable contacted items; her pots and drinking vessels are broken and buried; after bathing she is beaten by her mother with rods and later is described as clean.

Among the Uaupes, a puberty girl is secluded for a month on little bread and water, beaten by relations and friends with sipo pieces until senseless or dead, possibly repeated, and after licking sipo dipped in prepared meat and fish is considered marriageable.

A Hindu maiden at maturity is kept in a dark room for four days, forbidden to see the sun, regarded as unclean and untouchable, and limited to a diet including boiled rice, milk, sugar, curd, and tamarind without salt.
In Cambodia a girl at puberty is put to bed under a mosquito curtain for a stated period, though shortened periods are often accepted.

Another Cambodian account says a maiden at puberty enters the shade, follows rules such as not being seen by a strange man and not eating flesh or fish, but leaves retirement during eclipses to worship the monster said to catch heavenly bodies between its teeth.

occurrences.basis: The Chontal seeker withdraws to a lonely river or mountain place, prays, sacrifices, sleeps, encounters a visionary animal, offers blood, and receives a nagual companion.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Chontal procedure: a young Indian goes to a lonely place by a river or to a mountain top, prays to the gods, sacrifices a dog or bird, sleeps, sees a jaguar, puma, coyote, crocodile, serpent, or bird, and offers it blood from his body while praying for salt and cacao.
The animal says the first animal met on a later hunt "will be myself, who will always be your companion and nagual."

occurrences.motif_label: initiation through simulated death and revival
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly describes puberty rites as a pretense of killing the lad and bringing him to life again, and calls this a simulation of death and resurrection.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says that among many tribes, especially totemic ones, puberty initiation often includes a pretense of killing a lad and restoring him to life; this is explained as extracting the youth’s soul and transferring it to the totem.

occurrences.motif_label: initiatory death and rebirth
occurrences.basis: Multiple reported rites or beliefs describe novices as killed, buried, swallowed, rendered lifeless, or treated as dead, then revived or returned with adult or initiated status.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Australian examples: Thuremlin kills and restores boys; Bullroarer sound is said to be wizards swallowing and bringing boys up again; the Ualaroi say a ghost kills and revives a boy as a man.
A resurrection ceremony places a disguised old man in a covered grave holding a bush; novices are brought to the grave, a song is sung, the bush moves, and the man rises.
Fijian initiates are shown apparently dead, bloodied men with entrails protruding; at a priest's yell the men rise and run to the river to cleanse themselves of pig blood and entrails.

In Ndembo rites, doctors arrange pretended death and enclosure; after months or years, with fees and feast goods supplied, initiates are brought to life, act ignorant or strange, and receive a special name.

In Ambamba, the fetish priest shakes a calabash; men and lads fall into lifeless torpidity or are carried away by the fetish, later returning without understanding and being re-taught before return to parents.

occurrences.motif_label: initiation through seclusion and instruction
occurrences.basis: Both described rites remove youths from ordinary society, place them under ritual supervision, and return them after instruction or alteration.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At the king’s order a forest place is appointed; youths are brought there weeping, told they must suffer death, dispose of property, and are instructed by initiated persons in a dance called killing and songs praising Belli.
The forest life lasts five or six years in a village with hunting and fishing; other boys may arrive later; women and uninitiated persons are barred from approaching the sacred wood.

After instruction, novices are shut in huts, interact with women bringing food, pretend ignorance of people and customs, wear bird feathers and bark caps, dance the dance of Belli publicly, and are taken to their parents’ houses.

Huskanaw among the Indians of Virginia is described as an initiatory ceremony in which youths are confined alone in the woods for months and receive only an intoxicating root infusion, leading to a period of madness.

The Huskanaw account says the youths drink enough Wysoccan, likened to water of Lethe, to forget parents, possessions, and language; doctors gradually restore them, keepers guard them, and they must relearn speech and recognition, thereby commencing men by forgetting they had been boys.

occurrences.motif_label: ritual death and restoration in initiation
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly describes candidates or boys as apparently killed, knocked down, swallowed, buried, or struck dead and then revived, restored, disgorged, uncovered, or reborn as part of admission to societies or rites.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Among the Naudowessies, Carver saw a candidate kneel before a chief, receive a bean-like object, fall motionless as if shot, then revive after blows and expel the object from his mouth.

Other tribes use animal-skin medicine-bags containing charms; a spirit or breath from the bag is believed able to kill and restore life, and thrusting the bag once fells a man while a second thrust revives him.
At Nootka Sound, a chief fires near his son's ear; the son falls as if killed, women lament, armed people enter, and two wolf-skin masked figures moving like beasts carry the prince away.

The Toukaway Indians have a wolf-totem ceremony in which wolf-skin men run on all fours, howl, dig up a living buried tribesman, give him bow and arrows, and tell him to act as wolves do; Frazer compares it to Australian grave-resurrection rites.
On Rook, masked dancers demand boys, make them creep between their legs, announce that Marsaba has eaten the boys and will only disgorge them after receiving pigs, taro, and other provisions.

In New Britain, boys are initiated into the Duk-duk association by a cane blow from Tubuvan supposed to kill them; Tubuvan and Duk-duk are concealed performers representing cassowaries, female and male respectively, whom women may not see.

occurrences.motif_label: puberty initiation of boys into adult or secret society status
occurrences.basis: Both described rites center on boys at the proper age or puberty undergoing formal ceremonies, seclusion, instruction, and admission to a social-religious association.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Among the Galela and Tobelorese, boys undergo a form of initiation involving a pretence of being begotten anew; a shed and feast are prepared, red-coloring materials are worked into powder, each boy’s name is called, vessels are filled with water, and the boys are smeared with red water representing blood.

In western Ceram, boys at puberty enter the Kakian association, described as religious and social, with initiation of young men as a chief object; the Kakian house is a dark oblong wooden shed in the forest, and boys are conducted there blindfolded by two sponsors or guardians, followed by kin.

The boys stay in the Kakian house five or nine days, sit in darkness hearing trumpets, musket shots, and swords, bathe daily, are smeared with yellow dye to look swallowed by the devil, receive thorn-tattooed crosses, sit motionless, and hear rules, secrecy warnings, behavioral instruction, and tribal traditions through a trumpet voice imitating spirits.

occurrences.motif_label: Initiation as simulated death and restoration
occurrences.basis: The lads are mourned, announced as restored to life, return from spirit-land, and are then treated as transformed initiates.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Mothers and sisters mourn; sponsors return announcing the devil restored the lads to life through priests' intercession, arriving fainting and mud-daubed like nether-world messengers.
Each lad receives a feathered stick from the priest, said to have been given by the devil at restoration and to serve as a token that the lads have been in spirit-land.
The returning lads totter, enter backward or by the back door, hold plates upside down, remain dumb, communicate by signs, and are taught common acts as newborn children.
The boys face food and hair-combing taboos; the high priest later cuts a crown lock in the forest; after the rites they are deemed men and may marry.

occurrences.motif_label: Initiate as newborn child
occurrences.basis: The sponsors must teach common acts of life to the lads as if they were newborn children, and Frazer explicitly frames initiation as new birth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The returning lads totter, enter backward or by the back door, hold plates upside down, remain dumb, communicate by signs, and are taught common acts as newborn children.

Frazer says death-and-resurrection or new-birth simulation at initiation has left traces elsewhere and cites Brahman sacred-thread investiture and Manu's statements about first, second, and third births.

occurrences.motif_label: Purification before sacred festival
occurrences.basis: Participants fast, abstain from pleasures, use an emetic purifying medicine, keep silence, and the high priest undergoes triple immersion before officiating.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The crier commands a three-day fast, abstinence, purification medicine, and silence; the people take a red emetic liquor from the so-called root of blood.
The high priest stands at the temple threshold, must plunge three times into the Mississippi before presiding, and holds two pieces of dry wood.

Ground entry says sacred persons, girls at puberty, and sacred things may not touch the ground.

occurrences.motif_label: fear test by monstrous being
occurrences.basis: The Dragon King waits in serpent-dragon shape to find a brave man; Hidesato proves fearless by walking over the dragon instead of fleeing.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hidesato is alarmed but chooses not to turn back; he walks over the dragon’s body and between its coils without looking backward.
The Dragon King says the centipede has found his home and carries off his family night after night; he waited in serpent-dragon shape for a brave human, and Hidesato is the first not to flee.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE TONGUE-CUT SPARROW / THE STORY OF URASHIMA TARO, THE FISHER LAD / THE FARMER AND THE BADGER / THE ADVENTURES OF KINTARO, THE GOLDEN BOY; lines 1697-1832
occurrences.motif_label: test of strength with mysterious stranger
occurrences.basis: A woodcutter who has secretly observed Kintaro enters the cottage and challenges him to a right-hand strength contest that ends in a draw.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A woodcutter standing on a rock sees Kintaro uproot the tree, thinks he is no ordinary child, and follows the party after they cross.
A voice outside asks to join the next wrestling match; the old woodcutter enters the cottage, surprising Kintaro and Yama-uba, and proposes a test of strength.
Kintaro and the woodcutter grasp right hands and try to bend each other's arm; after a long contest the woodcutter declares it a draw.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE TONGUE-CUT SPARROW / THE STORY OF URASHIMA TARO, THE FISHER LAD / THE FARMER AND THE BADGER / THE ADVENTURES OF KINTARO, THE GOLDEN BOY; lines 1834-1943
occurrences.motif_label: initiation into warrior status through patronage
occurrences.basis: Kintaro is presented to a powerful lord, made a vassal, later becomes Chief of the Four Braves, and tests his sword against a monster.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sadamitsu brings Kintaro to Lord Minamoto-no-Raiko, tells his story, and Raiko makes Kintaro one of his vassals.
Raiko’s army includes the elite Four Braves; after Kintaro grows up, Raiko makes him their chief. News then arrives of a cannibal monster, and Raiko orders Kintaro to rescue the people.
Kintaro surprises the monster in its den, cuts off its great head, and carries it back in triumph to his master.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE STORY OF URASHIMA TARO, THE FISHER LAD / THE FARMER AND THE BADGER / THE ADVENTURES OF KINTARO, THE GOLDEN BOY / THE STORY OF THE MAN WHO DID NOT WISH TO DIE; lines 2251-2371
occurrences.motif_label: Supernatural guide evaluates the seeker
occurrences.basis: Jofuku appears in a luminous cloud, judges Sentaro's desire selfish, and explains why he is unfit for hermit discipline.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sentaro prays at Jofuku's shrine for seven days; at midnight on the seventh day the inner shrine opens and Jofuku appears in a luminous cloud.
Jofuku calls Sentaro's wish selfish and describes hermit life as austere, world-renouncing, desire-free, and eventually able to ride a crane or carp and walk on water.
Jofuku says Sentaro is idle and unsuited to hermit life, but will be helped by being sent to the country of Perpetual Life, where people live forever.

occurrences.motif_label: Austerity as path to supernatural lightness
occurrences.basis: Jofuku says hermits follow strict rules, cut themselves off from the world, become free from earthly desire, and gain abilities such as riding a crane or carp and walking on water.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Jofuku calls Sentaro's wish selfish and describes hermit life as austere, world-renouncing, desire-free, and eventually able to ride a crane or carp and walk on water.

occurrences.motif_label: dream ordeal as moral test
occurrences.basis: Sentaro's frightening adventure is revealed as a dream allowed by Jofuku, including the sea and shark, to test whether his desire for death was real.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sentaro wakes from his own screams and finds he had slept during prayer before the shrine; the adventures were only a wild dream.
The messenger says Jofuku sent him, allowed Sentaro to see the land of Perpetual Life in a dream, and tested him by letting him drop into the sea and sending a shark to swallow him.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE FARMER AND THE BADGER / THE ADVENTURES OF KINTARO, THE GOLDEN BOY / THE STORY OF THE MAN WHO DID NOT WISH TO DIE / THE BAMBOO-CUTTER AND THE MOON-CHILD; lines 3062-3176
occurrences.motif_label: childhood threshold rite
occurrences.basis: The girl's first obi at age three is explicitly described as a sign that she crossed the threshold of girlhood and left infancy behind.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The daughter's growth is marked by a temple visit at thirty days old, a dolls festival, and a first scarlet-and-gold obi on her third birthday, described as crossing from infancy into girlhood.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE JELLY FISH AND THE MONKEY / THE QUARREL OF THE MONKEY AND THE CRAB / THE WHITE HARE AND THE CROCODILES / THE STORY OF PRINCE YAMATO TAKE; lines 5705-5811
occurrences.motif_label: young royal hero commissioned to restore order
occurrences.basis: Yamato has just reached manhood at sixteen and is sent by his father to subdue rebels, beginning a dangerous expedition.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The realm is troubled by outlaw brothers Kumaso and Takeru; Keiko orders sixteen-year-old Yamato to subdue them, and Yamato receives the command joyfully and without fear.
Before leaving, Yamato prepares with followers, prays at Ise, takes leave of his aunt Princess Yamato, and receives from her a gorgeous robe as a keepsake and good-luck aid.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE QUARREL OF THE MONKEY AND THE CRAB / THE WHITE HARE AND THE CROCODILES / THE STORY OF PRINCE YAMATO TAKE / MOMOTARO, OR THE STORY OF THE SON OF A PEACH; lines 6510-6645
occurrences.motif_label: Courage test at a water threshold
occurrences.basis: At the sea, the animals are daunted; Momotaro rebukes them as cowards and threatens to go alone, after which they beg to continue and gain courage.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After traveling through valleys and hills, the party reaches the shore of the North-Eastern Sea; the animals have never seen the sea and wonder how to cross to the Island of Devils.
Momotaro notices the animals are daunted, calls them cowards, threatens to discharge them and go alone, and the dog, monkey, and pheasant beg him to take them along.

occurrences.motif_label: hero accepts a public challenge to enter a feared place
occurrences.basis: Watanabe accepts Hojo’s challenge, rides out in dangerous weather, and tests the rumor at the gate to preserve his honor.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hojo proposes that Watanabe prove the matter by going to the gate himself; Watanabe accepts because he cannot bear being thought afraid.
Watanabe buckles on his sword, armor, and helmet; his comrades write their names on paper, which he says he will put on the Gate of Rashomon as proof of his visit.
Watanabe rides out on a moonless, starless, stormy night with heavy rain and howling wind; his companions wait by the charcoal fire and wonder whether he will meet an Oni.

occurrences.passage_locator: ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE. / THE SIEGE OF TROY. / RETURN OF THE GREEKS FROM TROY.; lines 10201-10297
occurrences.motif_label: dangerous song resisted by binding and blocked hearing
occurrences.basis: Odysseus hears the Sirens' song while tied to the mast, while his crew's ears are stopped with wax to prevent them from hearing it.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Circe has warned Odysseus not to listen to the Sirens. To protect the crew, he fills their ears with wax; to hear the song himself, he has his companions lash him to the mast and orders them not to release him.
The Sirens sit on their island and sing alluringly; Odysseus begs to be released, but the sailors keep him bound until the island is out of sight, saving his life.

occurrences.motif_label: mystery festival rites
occurrences.basis: The Greek festivals section includes the Eleusinian Mysteries.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The festival sections list Greek festivals including the Eleusinian Mysteries, Thesmophoria, Dionysia, Panathenaea, and Daphnephoria, and Roman festivals including Saturnalia, Cerealia, and Vestalia.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: PALLAS-ATHENE (MINERVA). / MINERVA. / THEMIS. / VESTA.; lines 1776-1867
occurrences.motif_label: Secret initiation into sacred rites
occurrences.basis: The Eleusinian Mysteries are described as rites for favoured initiates, with Celeus and his family first initiated.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Eleusinian Mysteries are said to have been instituted by Demeter; the passage cautiously describes possible teachings for initiates, including a seasonal explanation of the myth.
Celeus and his family are first initiated; Celeus becomes high-priest; Triptolemus and Celeus's daughters assist; the Athenians celebrate the Mysteries every five years by torchlight.

occurrences.passage_locator: FORTUNA. / ANANKE (NECESSITAS). / MOMUS. / EROS (CUPID, AMOR) AND PSYCHE.; lines 4825-4914
occurrences.motif_label: Lost divine beloved sought through wandering and trials
occurrences.basis: After Eros departs, Psyche wanders over the world searching for him and undergoes hard tasks with hidden aid.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Psyche approaches Eros at night with lamp and dagger, sees his beautiful form, accidentally drops burning oil on him, and Eros wakes, reproaches her, spreads his wings, and leaves.
Psyche wanders over the world searching for Eros, appeals to Aphrodite, receives hard tasks, and is aided by invisible beneficent beings sent by Eros.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: FORTUNA. / ANANKE (NECESSITAS). / MOMUS. / EROS (CUPID, AMOR) AND PSYCHE.; lines 4917-4962
occurrences.motif_label: ordeal purification before divine reunion
occurrences.basis: Psyche undergoes severe penance and trials before being reunited with Eros and admitted among the immortal gods; the passage explicitly presents the myth as an allegory of the soul purified by suffering before reunion with divine essence.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Psyche undergoes severe penance; Aphrodite orders her to descend into the underworld and obtain from Persephone a box containing charms of beauty.
Eros awakens Psyche with the point of a golden arrow, reproaches her curiosity and folly, persuades Aphrodite to reconcile with her, and induces Zeus to admit her among the immortal gods.
The reunion is celebrated by the Olympian deities; the Graces shed perfume, the Hours sprinkle roses, Apollo plays his lyre, and the Muses sing.
"This myth would appear to be an allegory" of the soul being purified by earthly sorrows and sufferings before reunion with divine essence.

occurrences.passage_locator: LIBITINA. / LAVERNA. / COMUS. / THE CAMENAE.; lines 5955-5976
occurrences.motif_label: Religious initiation by a female divine or nymphic instructor
occurrences.basis: Egeria is said to have initiated Numa Pompilius in forms of religious worship that he then introduced among his people.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Egeria is said to have initiated Numa Pompilius in forms of religious worship that he introduced among his people.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: TEMPLES. / STATUES. / ALTARS. / PRIESTS.; lines 6182-6199
occurrences.motif_label: ritual purity through restricted marriage or celibacy
occurrences.basis: Priests and priestesses may marry only once, and some voluntarily adopt celibacy.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Priests and priestesses may marry, but not a second time; some voluntarily adopt celibacy.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: AUGURS. / FESTIVALS. / GREEK FESTIVALS. / ELEUSINIAN MYSTERIES.; lines 6361-6392
occurrences.motif_label: initiation into sacred mysteries
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly describes initiation into solemn rites, preparatory Lesser Mysteries, Greater Mysteries, instruction of initiates, and strict secrecy.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Priests taught initiates secret moral meanings drawn from Demeter and Persephone myths, with immortality of the soul named as the most important belief taught.
Initiation into the rites was originally restricted to Athenians, involved awe-inspiring ceremonies, and imposed secrecy whose violation was punishable by death.
Initiation into the Lesser Mysteries served as preparation for the Greater Mysteries.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: GREEK FESTIVALS. / ELEUSINIAN MYSTERIES. / THESMOPHORIA. / DIONYSIA.; lines 6394-6446
occurrences.motif_label: women-only sacred festival
occurrences.basis: The Thesmophoria is described as an exclusively female festival honoring Demeter, a goddess associated here with marriage, social institutions, and agriculture.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Thesmophoria was a festival honoring Demeter as presiding over marriage and social institutions resulting from agriculture.
This festival was celebrated exclusively by women.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: GREEK FESTIVALS. / ELEUSINIAN MYSTERIES. / THESMOPHORIA. / DIONYSIA.; lines 6394-6446
occurrences.motif_label: ecstatic nocturnal mountain initiation
occurrences.basis: Women called Menades or Bacchantes are initiated into mystic observances and gather by night on mountain sides with torches and thyrsi in religious frenzy.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Some Dionysian festivals included mystic observances into which only women called Menades or Bacchantes were initiated.
The initiated women wore fawn-skins and assembled by night on mountain sides, with some carrying blazing torches and others thyrsi.
The women shouted, clapped, danced wildly, entered frenzy, and tore apart the sacrificial animal brought to Dionysus.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: GREEK FESTIVALS. / ELEUSINIAN MYSTERIES. / THESMOPHORIA. / DIONYSIA.; lines 6394-6446
occurrences.motif_label: state suppression of ecstatic mystery rites
occurrences.basis: The Bacchanalia are described as mystic rites introduced into Rome and later prohibited by state authorities after alleged excesses.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The rites were introduced into Rome as Bacchanalia; men also joined, but state authorities later prohibited them because of reported excesses.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: ROMAN FESTIVALS. / SATURNALIA. / CEREALIA. / VESTALIA.; lines 6521-6561
occurrences.motif_label: ritual purity vow and severe punishment
occurrences.basis: The Vestal Virgins undergo a staged term of religious training and service and are vowed to chastity, with violation punished by burial alive.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Vestals' office lasts thirty years: ten years of initiation, ten of performing duties, and ten of instructing novices.
The Vestals are vowed to chastity; violation is punished by being buried alive.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VESTALIA. / PART II.--LEGENDS. / CADMUS. / PERSEUS.; lines 6633-6734
occurrences.motif_label: heroic departure for monster-slaying quest
occurrences.basis: Perseus leaves on an expedition to slay Medusa and must gain special equipment and knowledge before confronting the Gorgons.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Polydectes joins Danae, educates Perseus as a hero, and encourages him toward a deed; the slaying of Medusa is chosen for greatest renown.
Perseus needs winged sandals, a magic wallet, and Aides' helmet from the Nymphs; guided by Hermes and Pallas-Athene, he takes the Graeae's single eye and tooth until they give directions.

With helmet, wallet, Hermes' sickle, and winged sandals, Perseus reaches the sleeping Gorgons; avoiding direct sight and using his shield image, he cuts off Medusa's head, from whose trunk Pegasus and Chrysaor spring.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: PART II.--LEGENDS. / CADMUS. / PERSEUS. / THE ARGONAUTS.; lines 6904-6953
occurrences.motif_label: hero trained in youth by non-parental mentor
occurrences.basis: Jason is entrusted to Chiron and spends ten years in the Centaur’s cave learning useful and warlike arts.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Aeson is forced to flee after Pelias usurps Iolcus; Jason is saved, entrusted to Chiron, and trained for ten years in the Centaur’s cave.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CADMUS. / PERSEUS. / THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE.; lines 7050-7143
occurrences.motif_label: Trial by compulsory contest with a local king
occurrences.basis: Amycus requires strangers to box before leaving, and Pollux serves as the heroes' champion.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In the country of the Bebrycians, King Amycus requires a boxing match; Pollux is chosen as champion and the contest is fatal to Amycus.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CADMUS. / PERSEUS. / THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE.; lines 7145-7238
occurrences.motif_label: Dangerous threshold passage tested by a bird
occurrences.basis: The crew must pass between clashing rocks and first sends a dove to test whether the path can be crossed safely.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Argonauts hear a tremendous crash caused by the Symplegades, two great rocky islands that float in the sea and repeatedly meet and separate.

Following Phineus' advice, Typhus steers while Euphemus releases a dove; when it passes through the rocks with some tail feathers lost, the Argonauts row through safely, and the Symplegades later become permanently fixed.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CADMUS. / PERSEUS. / THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE.; lines 7145-7238
occurrences.motif_label: Superhuman trial imposed by a king
occurrences.basis: Aetes promises the Fleece only if the heroes demonstrate divine origin by performing a task requiring superhuman power.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At the banquet and afterward, Jason explains the expedition; Aetes angrily insists the Fleece is his property, then promises it only if the heroes prove divine origin through a superhuman task.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CADMUS. / PERSEUS. / THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE.; lines 7240-7332
occurrences.motif_label: Impossible tasks overcome through magical helper
occurrences.basis: Jason faces lethal tasks set by Aetes and succeeds through Medea's magic salve, instructions, and potion.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Aetes' task requires Jason to yoke fire-breathing oxen, plough Ares' field, sow poisonous dragon's teeth, and destroy the armed men that arise.
Medea and Jason confess mutual attachment; she gives him protective magic salve and tells him to make the armed men fight over a rock; Jason promises to take her as wife.
Relying on Medea's magic, Jason seizes and yokes the oxen, ploughs the stony ground, and sows a helmet full of dragon's teeth.
Armed men spring from the furrows; Jason throws a rock among them, they attack one another, and he kills them all.
Medea casts potion drops on the dragon, causing deep sleep; Jason climbs the tree, secures the Fleece, and they depart on the Argo.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE. / PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES).; lines 7587-7685
occurrences.motif_label: heroic moral initiation through choice
occurrences.basis: Heracles withdraws to a lonely forest place to decide how to use his powers, hears competing speeches from Vice and Virtue, and chooses Virtue.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Heracles goes to a secluded forest to decide how to use his powers; two beautiful females appear, identified as Vice and Virtue, with contrasting appearance and bearing.
Vice promises that his life shall be "one round of pleasure and enjoyment" without physical or mental exertion.
Virtue says that the gods grant no good and desirable thing "that is not earned by labour."
Heracles listens to both speakers and decides to follow Virtue, honor the gods, and devote his life to his country.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE. / PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES).; lines 7687-7783
occurrences.motif_label: oracle-bounded servitude through labors
occurrences.basis: Heracles is commanded to undertake difficult tasks, consults Delphi, and learns that ten tasks will end his servitude.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Eurystheus, king of Mycenae, commands Heracles to undertake difficult tasks; Zeus tells Heracles not to rebel against the Fates; Delphi says ten tasks will end the servitude.
Hera's influence turns Heracles' melancholy into madness, during which he kills his children; after regaining reason he withdraws, grieves, and decides that work will help him begin the tasks.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE. / PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES).; lines 8076-8168
occurrences.motif_label: initiation before perilous descent
occurrences.basis: Before descending, Heracles is initiated into the Eleusinian Mysteries and receives necessary information from priests.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After initiation into the Eleusinian Mysteries and priestly instruction, Heracles goes to the opening at Taenarum; Hermes conducts his descent, shades flee, and Hermes stops him from striking Medusa's shadow.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE. / PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES).; lines 8170-8264
occurrences.motif_label: hero's temporary servitude as expiation
occurrences.basis: Heracles submits to being sold as a slave for three years, and the purchase price is assigned as compensation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Pythia commands Heracles to expiate the crime by being sold by Hermes for three years as a slave, with the price given to Eurytus as compensation.
Heracles submits, is conducted by Hermes to Omphale of Lydia, is bought for three talents, and later performs strong and courageous services for Omphale, including clearing robbers.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE. / PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES). / BELLEROPHON.; lines 8325-8402
occurrences.motif_label: dangerous tasks used as indirect execution
occurrences.basis: Iobates cannot bring himself to kill Bellerophon as a guest and instead sends him on perilous enterprises likely to cause his death.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After reading the letter, Iobates is horrified but decides to send Bellerophon on dangerous enterprises because he cannot kill a guest he esteems.
Iobates first sends Bellerophon to kill the Chimaera, described as a monster devastating the country, with lion, goat, and dragon body parts and flames issuing from its jaws.
Iobates sends Bellerophon against the Solymans and then the Amazons; Bellerophon returns victorious from both conflicts.
Iobates sets brave Lycians in ambush to destroy Bellerophon, but Bellerophon kills them all; Iobates concludes that he is favored and protected by the gods and stops persecuting him.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES). / BELLEROPHON. / THESEUS.; lines 8404-8503
occurrences.motif_label: strength test before receiving identity tokens
occurrences.basis: Theseus must be old enough and strong enough to move the stone before learning his father's identity and taking the sword and sandals.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Before departing, Aegeus deposits his sword and sandals beneath a huge rock and tells Aethra to send a future son to Athens with these identity tokens when he can move the stone.
Theseus is born, raised by Pittheus, grows strong, rolls away the stone, and receives the sword and sandals that had lain there for sixteen years.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES). / BELLEROPHON. / THESEUS.; lines 8404-8503
occurrences.motif_label: hero chooses perilous departure route
occurrences.basis: Theseus leaves for Athens and deliberately chooses the dangerous land route over the safe sea route to prove himself by feats of valour.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Though urged to use the safe sea route, Theseus chooses the dangerous land road to Athens in order to emulate Heracles and distinguish himself by valour.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE EPIGONI. / ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE. / THE SIEGE OF TROY.; lines 9323-9415
occurrences.motif_label: Choice between long obscure life and brief heroic glory
occurrences.basis: A prophecy gives Achilles the alternatives of a long inglorious life or a brief victorious heroic career ending in death.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Achilles is son of Peleus and Thetis; Thetis dips him in the Styx, leaving only his right heel vulnerable, and later hides him on Scyros after a prophecy about his fate.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE EPIGONI. / ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE. / THE SIEGE OF TROY.; lines 9323-9415
occurrences.motif_label: Hidden necessary warrior revealed by martial test
occurrences.basis: Achilles is required for Troy's capture and is revealed when weapons and martial music provoke him to seize the arms.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Calchas reveals Achilles' concealment; Odysseus, disguised as a merchant, uses trinkets, weapons, and martial music to identify him; Achilles joins with Patroclus, Myrmidons, and fifty ships.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I / BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS.; lines 1136-1230
occurrences.motif_label: divine guide gives courage and instruction
occurrences.basis: Minerva leads Telemachus, instructs him to question Nestor, and gives him courage to speak.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva leads the way and Telemachus follows her.
Minerva tells Telemachus not to be shy, because he has taken the voyage to learn where his father is buried and how he came to his end, and tells him to ask Nestor for the truth.
Minerva answers that instinct and heaven will prompt Telemachus, and that the gods have been with him since birth.
Telemachus answers boldly because Minerva has given him courage to ask about his father and gain a good name.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I / BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS.; lines 1232-1327
occurrences.motif_label: young heir urged to prove himself
occurrences.basis: Nestor urges Telemachus to show his mettle and make a name, and Telemachus expresses desire to act against the suitors.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "show your mettle and make yourself a name in story."
Telemachus says Orestes' name will live because he avenged his father, and wishes heaven would let him take similar vengeance on the wicked suitors who mistreat him and plot his ruin.
Nestor recalls hearing that Telemachus' mother has many suitors who are ill-disposed toward him and make havoc of his estate; he asks whether Telemachus submits or lacks public and heavenly support.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV / BOOK V / BOOK VI / THE MEETING BETWEEN NAUSICAA AND ULYSSES.; lines 2694-2792
occurrences.motif_label: marriageable maiden sent to water for cleansing and preparation
occurrences.basis: Minerva connects Nausicaa's washing day with approaching marriage and suitors; Nausicaa leads maids to wash clothes, bathe, and anoint themselves by water.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva tells Nausicaa that her clothes are disordered, that she will soon be married, and that she should ask for a wagon and mules to carry clothing to the washing-cisterns at daybreak.
At the waterside the women unharness the mules, wash clothes in pure water, lay them by the sea, bathe and anoint themselves, eat by the stream, then remove veils and play ball while Nausicaa sings.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV / BOOK V / BOOK VI / THE MEETING BETWEEN NAUSICAA AND ULYSSES.; lines 2882-2972
occurrences.motif_label: Purification and re-clothing of the distressed stranger
occurrences.basis: Ulysses moves from brine-covered exposure to washing, anointing, and receiving new clothes before approaching society.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The maids stop fleeing, seat Ulysses in shelter, bring a shirt, cloak, and golden cruse of oil, and tell him to wash in the stream.
Ulysses asks the women to stand aside so he can wash and says he is ashamed to strip before them.
Ulysses washes brine from his back, shoulders, and hair, anoints himself with oil, and puts on the clothes given by the girl.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV / BOOK V / BOOK VI / THE MEETING BETWEEN NAUSICAA AND ULYSSES.; lines 2882-2972
occurrences.motif_label: Liminal waiting outside the city before entry
occurrences.basis: Ulysses must wait in Minerva's grove outside town before crossing gates and courts to approach the royal household.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Nausicaa tells Ulysses to wait at a roadside poplar grove dedicated to Minerva, with a well, meadow, and her father's garden ground nearby.

evidence.locator: lines 2970-2972 and following passage text in supplied range
evidence.quote_or_summary: Nausicaa instructs Ulysses to ask for Alcinous's house, pass through gates and courts, approach her mother by the fire as she spins purple wool, clasp her knees, and gain hope of returning home.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VI / THE MEETING BETWEEN NAUSICAA AND ULYSSES. / BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS.; lines 3176-3259
occurrences.motif_label: shipwrecked stranger aided by maiden
occurrences.basis: After storm and exposure, Ulysses asks Alcinous's daughter for aid; she gives him bread, wine, washing, and clothes.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Neptune raises a storm; the sea breaks the raft, and Ulysses swims toward shore.
Ulysses avoids a rocky landing, swims to a sheltered river, exits the water, and gathers his senses.
At nightfall Ulysses enters a thicket, covers himself with leaves, and sleeps deeply until afternoon.
Ulysses wakes and sees the daughter and maid servants on the beach; he asks the daughter for aid.
The daughter gives Ulysses bread, wine, washing in the river, and the clothes he is wearing.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: THE MEETING BETWEEN NAUSICAA AND ULYSSES. / BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS. / BOOK VIII; lines 3295-3396
occurrences.motif_label: public testing and display through athletic games
occurrences.basis: Alcinous proposes athletic sports so the guest may report Phaeacian excellence in boxing, wrestling, jumping, and running; many competitors gather for prizes.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Only Alcinous notices Ulysses' distress and sighs; he says the feast and minstrelsy have been sufficient and proposes athletic sports so the guest may later report Phaeacian excellence.
A servant hangs up Demodocus' lyre and leads him out with the chief Phaeacians toward the sports; a crowd follows, and many named competitors, including Euryalus and Alcinous' three sons, compete.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VIII / BOOK IX / BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE.; lines 4399-4490
occurrences.motif_label: expedition chosen by lot toward dangerous house
occurrences.basis: The crew is divided into companies; lots are cast in a helmet, and Eurylochus leads twenty-two men to Circe's house.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Lots are cast in a helmet; the lot falls to Eurylochus, who departs with twenty-two men while both groups weep.
Eurylochus's party reaches Circe's house, built of cut stones in the middle of the forest on a site visible from far away.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VIII / BOOK IX / BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE.; lines 4492-4586
occurrences.motif_label: hero resists witchcraft and compels the enchantress to negotiate
occurrences.basis: Following Mercury's instructions, Odysseus withstands Circe's drug and wand, threatens her with a sword, and receives her recognition and proposal of trust.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Mercury explains that Circe will drug a drink but the herb will block her spells; he tells Odysseus to draw his sword when she strikes with her wand and to make her swear not to plot further harm.

Odysseus reaches Circe's gates, enters when she invites him, sits on a silver-inlaid seat, and drinks from a drugged golden goblet; Circe strikes him with her wand and orders him to the pigstye, but the charm fails.

Odysseus rushes at Circe with his drawn sword; she screams, clasps his knees, asks who he is, says no man has resisted her drug before, identifies him as Ulysses foretold by Mercury, and asks him to sheathe his sword and go to bed so they may make friends and trust each other.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE. / BOOK XI / THE VISIT TO THE DEAD.88; lines 4876-4967
occurrences.motif_label: journey to a land ignorant of the sea
occurrences.basis: Odysseus must carry an oar inland until people no longer recognize it as an oar, then plant it and perform sacrifice.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odysseus must carry a well-made oar to a country where people do not know the sea, ships, or oars; when a wayfarer calls it a winnowing shovel, he must plant it and sacrifice a ram, bull, and boar to Neptune.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XI / THE VISIT TO THE DEAD.88 / BOOK XII / THE SIRENS, SCYLLA AND CHARYBDIS, THE CATTLE OF THE SUN.; lines 5422-5511
occurrences.motif_label: Self-binding to withstand temptation
occurrences.basis: Ulysses arranges to be bound to the mast and orders tighter bonds if he asks for release, allowing controlled exposure to the Sirens' song.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses tells the men Circe's prophecies, including the warning to avoid the Sirens who sing in a field of flowers; he says he alone may hear them and orders himself bound upright to the mast, tighter if he asks release.
At the Sirens' island the wind falls calm; the crew rows, Ulysses softens wax in the sun and stops the men's ears, and the men bind him hands and feet to the mast while rowing onward.
Ulysses longs to hear more and signals for release; the crew rows faster, and Eurylochus and Perimedes bind him more strongly until the Sirens are out of hearing, then remove the wax and unbind him.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XV / BOOK XVI / ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII; lines 7615-7715
occurrences.motif_label: abused disguised hero restrains vengeance
occurrences.basis: Ulysses is insulted and kicked, considers killing or beating Melanthius, but chooses endurance and self-control.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Melanthius mocks Ulysses as a miserable beggar, calls him unfit for honorable gifts or work, and says stools will be thrown at him if he approaches Ulysses' house.
Melanthius kicks Ulysses on the hip; Ulysses stands firm, considers retaliation, and decides to endure it and restrain himself.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: HENRY FESTING JONES. / THE ODYSSEY / BOOK I / BOOK II; lines 762-849
occurrences.motif_label: young heir assumes public role in absent father’s place
occurrences.basis: Telemachus calls the assembly, appears with divine enhancement, and takes his father’s seat while speaking of the absent Ulysses and the danger to his house.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus sends criers to convene the assembly and goes there with spear in hand and two hounds.
Minerva gives Telemachus divine comeliness; people marvel, and he takes his father’s seat while the oldest councillors make way.
Telemachus says he convened the assembly because he is aggrieved; his first misfortune is the loss of his father, who was chief among them and like a father to everyone.
Telemachus says his second misfortune is that suitors press his mother to marry against her will and consume his household’s oxen, sheep, goats, and wine, threatening to ruin the estate.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XVI / ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII / BOOK XVIII; lines 8177-8277
occurrences.motif_label: coming-of-age marker governing remarriage
occurrences.basis: Penelope recalls Ulysses' instruction that she may marry when their son grows a beard.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Penelope replies that heaven took her beauty when Ulysses sailed to Troy; she recalls his instruction to care for the household and remarry when their son grew a beard; she criticizes the suitors for consuming property instead of following courtship custom with feasts and presents.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII / BOOK XVIII / BOOK XIX; lines 8705-8786
occurrences.motif_label: youthful animal encounter leaves identifying mark
occurrences.basis: A boar hunt on Parnassus results in a deep wound above Ulysses’ knee, and that wound later becomes the scar by which he is known.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At dawn the sons of Autolycus go hunting with hounds, Ulysses accompanies them with a long spear, and they reach a mountain dell and the dense lair of a huge boar on Parnassus.
The boar rushes out with raised bristles and flashing eyes, wounds Ulysses above the knee, and is then struck through the right shoulder by Ulysses’ spear and dies.
Euryclea recognizes Ulysses by holding his scarred limb, drops his foot into the bath so that the water spills, and tells him she knows he is Ulysses after touching him.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XIX / BOOK XX / BOOK XXI / BOOK XXII; lines 9709-9805
occurrences.motif_label: hero tested before final victory
occurrences.basis: Minerva deliberately withholds full victory so that Ulysses' and Telemachus' prowess may be further proved during the conflict.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva does not give full victory yet, wishing to further prove the prowess of Ulysses and Telemachus; she flies to a rafter in the form of a swallow.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 1190-1207
occurrences.motif_label: initiation and uninitiated misunderstanding
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly contrasts those with sympathy for mysticism against the uninitiated, who misread the dialogues as poetic dreams.

evidence.quote_or_summary: No one can duly appreciate the dialogues of Plato, especially the Phaedrus, Symposium, and parts of the Republic, without sympathy with mysticism.
To the uninitiated, the writings may appear to be dreams of a poet disguised as a philosopher.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 208-288
occurrences.motif_label: Mystic initiation into blessed heavenly sights
occurrences.basis: The soul is said to have celebrated holy mysteries and beheld blessed apparitions in pure light.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The philosopher recollects knowledge gained among the gods when seeing earthly beauty; the soul once beheld mysteries in pure light before being entombed in the body and is compared to a bird eager to leave its cage.

The corrupted nature rushes toward sensual pleasure; the true mystic beholds a god-like form with delight, the wing begins to grow again, the beloved is a physician, and love is called dove or winged one by immortals.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2096-2186
occurrences.motif_label: ritual purification and release from ancestral guilt
occurrences.basis: Madness, holy prayers, rites, inspired utterances, purifications, and mysteries are said to deliver families from plagues and woes caused by ancient blood-guiltiness.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Where plagues and great woes arise in families from ancient blood-guiltiness, madness with holy prayers, rites, inspired utterances, purifications, and mysteries provides deliverance and release from calamity.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2323-2387
occurrences.motif_label: mystery initiation through recollection
occurrences.basis: The one who rightly uses memories of divine realities is initiated into perfect mysteries and becomes truly perfect.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The philosopher recollects the things the soul saw while following God; the philosopher's mind has wings and is initiated into perfect mysteries through these memories.
Philosophers once followed Zeus and others followed other gods; they saw beauty shining, a blessed mystery, and calm apparitions in pure light before later evils.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2389-2457
occurrences.motif_label: Initiated vision of otherworldly beauty
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly contrasts the uninitiated or corrupted person with the recently initiated spectator who has seen many glories in the other world.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The uninitiated or corrupted person does not easily rise to true beauty, while the recently initiated spectator has seen many glories in the other world.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2459-2497
occurrences.motif_label: initiation into mysteries of true love
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly calls the inspired lover’s process an initiation into the mysteries of true love.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The inspired lover’s desire is “fair and blissful” to the beloved and is called “the initiation ... into the mysteries of true love.”

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2499-2549
occurrences.motif_label: discipline and taming of unruly desire
occurrences.basis: The unruly horse repeatedly resists control but is eventually punished, humbled, and made to follow the charioteer's will.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The unruly horse reproaches the charioteer and fellow horse, then repeatedly fights, neighs, and drags them toward the beloved.
The charioteer violently restrains the wild horse, wounds its mouth, forces it down, punishes it, and after several repetitions it becomes tamed and humbled.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 290-374
occurrences.motif_label: Taming the unruly impulse before the beloved
occurrences.basis: The charioteer repeatedly restrains and subdues the unruly steed, after which the lover's soul follows the beloved in modesty and holy fear.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A charioteer and two steeds, one noble and one ill-looking, are described as a figure of the soul approaching the vision of love.

The evil steed rushes forward; the charioteer pulls back, uses bit and reins, causes pain and blood, and eventually tames and humbles the steed so the lover follows the beloved with modesty and holy fear.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 3061-3191
occurrences.motif_label: divine madness as release from ordinary custom
occurrences.basis: The passage contrasts madness from human infirmity with divine release of the soul from custom and convention, then names prophetic, initiatory, poetic, and erotic forms.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates states that there are two kinds of madness: one from human infirmity and one a divine release of the soul from custom and convention.
Divine madness is divided into prophetic, initiatory, poetic, and erotic forms, associated respectively with Apollo, Dionysus, the Muses, and Aphrodite with Eros.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 639-716
occurrences.motif_label: purification through trial before sacred union
occurrences.basis: The passage describes purification from earthly passion through trial and conflict before true love can exist between two souls.

evidence.quote_or_summary: True love of the mind cannot exist between two souls until they are purified from earthly passion; they must pass through trial and conflict and be converted or born again.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 886-959
occurrences.motif_label: spiritual combat resolved by rational mastery
occurrences.basis: The passage describes a spiritual combat in which the rational soul becomes victor and master of both steeds.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage distinguishes lower and higher love, describes higher love as contemplating forms with religious awe, compares the opposition to flesh and spirit in St. Paul, and mentions the rational soul mastering both steeds in spiritual combat.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 10460-10547
occurrences.motif_label: being versus seeming in moral trial
occurrences.basis: The just man must be truly just while seeming unjust and being thought worst until death, so that he is put to the proof.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The just man is placed beside him as noble and simple, wishing to be rather than seem good, clothed in justice only, thought worst while being best, and continuing so until death.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 10635-10722
occurrences.motif_label: Mysteries redeeming the living and the dead from underworld pains
occurrences.basis: Rites called mysteries are said to serve the living and dead, redeem people from the pains of hell, and answer fear of suffering in the world below.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Books attributed to Musaeus and Orpheus are used for rituals persuading people and cities that sacrifices and amusements can make expiations and atonements for the living and dead; these mysteries redeem from pains of hell.

A fear is raised that there is a world below where people or descendants suffer for unjust deeds; the reply invokes mysteries and powerful atoning deities, supported by cities and poets or prophets called children of the gods.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 11286-11457
occurrences.motif_label: education as formation of the heroic guardian
occurrences.basis: The passage frames the education of guardians as the education of heroes, beginning with music, literature, and early formative stories.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The dialogue asks how the guardians are to be reared and educated, calls the coming account the education of heroes, and divides traditional education into gymnastic for the body and music for the soul.
Music includes literature; literature may be true or false; children first receive stories that are mainly fictitious before they are old enough for gymnastics.
"the beginning is the most important part of any work... for that is the time at which the character is being formed"

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 11286-11457
occurrences.motif_label: restricted sacred knowledge in mystery setting
occurrences.basis: Objectionable stories of gods are to be buried in silence or, if necessary, heard only by a chosen few in a mystery accompanied by an extraordinary sacrificial victim.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage names Hesiod's stories of Uranus, Cronus, and the suffering Cronus's son inflicted on him, and says such stories should be silenced or restricted to a chosen few in a mystery with an extraordinary victim rather than a common Eleusinian pig.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III.; lines 12275-12403
occurrences.motif_label: imitation forming character
occurrences.basis: The speaker argues that imitations beginning in youth become habits and second nature affecting body, voice, and mind, and therefore guardians must imitate only suitable virtues.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Guardians are to dedicate themselves to maintaining freedom in the State; if they imitate, they should imitate only courageous, temperate, holy, free, and similar characters, because repeated imitation becomes habit and second nature affecting body, voice, and mind.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III.; lines 12788-12962
occurrences.motif_label: disciplined initiation of guardians
occurrences.basis: Young guardians undergo lifelong training in music, gymnastic, sobriety, endurance, and regulated diet for their role.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Gymnastic is to follow music, begin early, continue through life, and be guided by the principle that the good soul improves the body as far as possible.
The guardians must abstain from intoxication, and their food is considered because they train for the great contest of all.

Ordinary athletes are criticized as sleepy and fragile; warrior athletes should be like wakeful dogs, keen in sight and hearing, and able to endure changes of water, food, summer heat, and winter cold on campaign.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III.; lines 13350-13505
occurrences.motif_label: Testing and initiation of future guardians
occurrences.basis: Candidates are watched from youth through maturity and subjected to trials involving forgetfulness, deception, toils, pains, conflicts, terrors, and pleasures; only those who emerge victorious and pure are appointed to the higher role.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Candidates are watched from youth and made to perform actions likely to cause forgetfulness or deception; those who remember and are not deceived are selected, failures rejected, with further proof through toils, pains, and conflicts.

Candidates are tested with terrors and pleasures, like colts tested amid noise and tumult and more thoroughly than gold in a furnace; whoever passes at every age, victorious and pure, is appointed ruler and guardian and honored in life and death, while failures are rejected.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III.; lines 13350-13505
occurrences.motif_label: Purification through ordeal
occurrences.basis: The candidate who passes tests at every age is said to come out of the trial victorious and pure, with testing compared to gold proved in a furnace.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Candidates are tested with terrors and pleasures, like colts tested amid noise and tumult and more thoroughly than gold in a furnace; whoever passes at every age, victorious and pure, is appointed ruler and guardian and honored in life and death, while failures are rejected.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1336-1415
occurrences.motif_label: Restricted tale disclosed only through mystery and sacrifice
occurrences.basis: Improper divine tales are said, if spoken at all, to belong in a mystery after sacrifice rather than in ordinary instruction of the young.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Homer and Hesiod are criticized for improper divine stories about Uranus and Saturn, Zeus, Hephaestus, divine strife, and family violence; such stories may have mystical interpretation but youth cannot understand allegory.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV.; lines 13923-14069
occurrences.motif_label: Formation of character through ordered initiation into practice
occurrences.basis: Youth are to be trained from the first through ordered play and music so that their future actions and civic character are shaped by order.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Youth should be trained from the first in a stricter system, because lawless amusements make lawless youths who cannot become well-conducted and virtuous citizens.

evidence.locator: lines 13923-14069, good beginning in play and music
evidence.quote_or_summary: A good beginning in play, aided by music, produces a habit of order that accompanies all actions and can raise fallen places in the State.

evidence.locator: lines 13923-14069, manners not legislated in detail
evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage lists respect before elders, honour to parents, dress, hair, deportment, and manners, and says precise written enactments about such matters are unlikely to last.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1417-1481
occurrences.motif_label: sacrifice before mysteries
occurrences.basis: The passage mentions offering an almost unprocurable victim when impure mysteries are to be celebrated.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage lists humorous but serious examples: Glaucon's disappointment at the 'city of pigs,' the guardian illustrated by the dog, an almost unprocurable victim for impure mysteries, and the behavior of Zeus to his father and Hephaestus to his mother.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1543-1614
occurrences.motif_label: purification of myth for civic courage
occurrences.basis: The passage frames the removal of certain religious and poetic tales as a means to banish fear and educate youth toward courage, temperance, and obedience.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Religion is to be purified to banish fear of death; poets are asked not to abuse hell and to remove untrue and discouraging tales about the world below.

Examples to be removed include Achilles's words about serving rather than ruling the dead, squalid mansions, shadows, souls beneath the earth like smoke or bats, Cocytus, Styx, ghosts, sapless shades, and Tartarean terms; such tales are not proper food for soldiers.

Youth must be temperate; temperance is self-control and obedience to authority. Homer sometimes teaches silent awe of leaders but elsewhere uses abusive drunken language that will not teach self-control.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V.; lines 16290-16451
occurrences.motif_label: Youth initiated into adult warfare by supervised spectatorship
occurrences.basis: Children strong enough are taken to war to observe the work they will later do, help in war, and learn under experienced veterans.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Children strong enough are to accompany expeditions, look on at their future work, help in war, and wait upon fathers and mothers; potters' boys are used as an analogy.
The first step is 'to make our children spectators of war' while securing them against danger.
Children are to be placed under experienced veterans who will be 'their leaders and teachers.'

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V.; lines 16613-16748
occurrences.motif_label: ordeal of the third wave
occurrences.basis: Socrates describes the next and most difficult proposal as the third, greatest, and heaviest wave to be faced in discussion.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says the interlocutor is bringing upon him the 'third' wave, 'the greatest and heaviest.'

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1774-1852
occurrences.motif_label: tested guardians through ordeals
occurrences.basis: Future guardians are tried through danger, pleasure, and other pressures and must emerge victorious and unstained, like refined gold.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Guardians must be tested “like gold in the refiner’s fire,” passing through danger and pleasure without stain.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 17902-18011
occurrences.motif_label: Lifelong initiation into wisdom
occurrences.basis: The speaker prescribes age-appropriate philosophical education, bodily preparation, increasing exercise of the soul, and later freedom oriented toward happiness in this life and another.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker proposes age-suited education: early philosophy, bodily training, later gymnastics of the soul, and freedom after civic and military duties, ending in happiness here and another life.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 18285-18436
occurrences.motif_label: probation before entrusted rule
occurrences.basis: The aspirant must undergo tests involving labours, dangers, pleasures, and knowledge before sharing office or command.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The interlocutors agree that higher education and command require both qualities and that such a class is rarely found.
“The aspirant must not only be tested in those labours and dangers and pleasures... he must be exercised also in many kinds of knowledge.”

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 18781-18911
occurrences.motif_label: Painful initiation into clearer vision
occurrences.basis: The liberated prisoner undergoes compulsion, pain, disorientation, gradual acclimation, and eventual understanding of the sun's role.

evidence.quote_or_summary: When a prisoner is liberated and compelled to stand, turn, walk, and look toward the light, he suffers pain, is distressed by glare, and is perplexed when shown the objects.
The prisoner grows accustomed to the upper world, first seeing shadows, then reflections in water, then objects, then moon, stars, and the night sky.
Last of all, the prisoner can see the sun itself, not merely its reflection in water, and contemplate it in its own place.
The prisoner reasons that the sun gives seasons and years, guards the visible world, and is in a certain way the cause of what he and his fellows had seen.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 18913-19020
occurrences.motif_label: Initiatory turning or conversion of the whole soul
occurrences.basis: Learning is described as a gradual turning of the whole soul toward being and the good, not as the external insertion of knowledge.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker says certain educators are wrong when they claim to put knowledge into the soul as if putting sight into blind eyes.
The capacity of learning exists in the soul already; the whole soul must turn from becoming toward being and learn to endure the sight of the good.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 18913-19020
occurrences.motif_label: Purification from downward-dragging pleasures
occurrences.basis: The passage imagines youthful natures severed from sensual pleasures that act like leaden weights and redirected toward truth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage imagines youthful natures severed from sensual pleasures such as eating and drinking, which are compared to leaden weights that drag the soul’s vision downward.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19022-19142
occurrences.motif_label: initiation through turning of the soul
occurrences.basis: The process of producing guardians is described as a transformation from near-night to the true day of being, effected by the turning around of the soul.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "brought from darkness to light,—as some are said to have ascended from the world below to the gods"
The process is not the turning over of an oyster-shell but the turning around of a soul from a day little better than night to the true day of being, called the ascent from below and true philosophy.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19468-19613
occurrences.motif_label: ordered initiation through sciences
occurrences.basis: The dialogue lays out a sequence of studies—geometry, solid geometry, and astronomy—through which learners are guided toward higher knowledge.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says the city’s inhabitants should learn geometry, which also brings military advantages and quickness of apprehension.
Socrates corrects the order of studies: plane geometry should be followed by solid geometry before astronomy; he says neglected studies need state support, directors, and earnest search.
The interlocutor says astronomy “compels the soul to look upwards” and leads from “this world to another.”

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19738-19854
occurrences.motif_label: Cave or underground confinement and release
occurrences.basis: Prisoners are confined in an underground den, released from chains, and guided through a sequence of increasingly clear perceptions.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage describes prisoners released from chains, moved from shadows to images and light, ascending from an underground den to the sun, and first seeing images in water; firelight is contrasted with the sun.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19856-19996
occurrences.motif_label: disciplined initiation into higher knowledge
occurrences.basis: Future rulers are to undergo a demanding education in questioning, bodily exercise, intellectual discipline, and youthful toil before being fit for authority.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Future rulers of the ideal State must not be without reason and must receive an education enabling skill in asking and answering questions.
The selected natures should be sure, brave, noble, generous, keen, quick to learn, possessed of memory, tireless, and able to endure bodily and intellectual discipline.
The speaker says the future selection should not be of old men; youth is the time for extraordinary toil.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19998-20152
occurrences.motif_label: Staged initiation through education and trials
