occurrences.basis: The passage lays out age-graded preparation, testing through labours, lessons, dangers, gymnastics, selection at twenty, and further selection at thirty before dialectic.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Children are to be taken on horseback to see battle and, if no danger is present, brought close like young hounds to taste blood.
The same practice is proposed for labours, lessons, and dangers; those most at home in all are enrolled in a select number.
After necessary gymnastics, selected twenty-year-olds are promoted and their sciences are brought together so they can see their relation to each other and to true being.
At thirty, the most comprehensive and steadfast candidates are selected and tested by dialectic to learn who can give up sight and the other senses and attain absolute being with truth.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 20154-20256
occurrences.motif_label: staged philosophical initiation through education and testing
occurrences.basis: The passage lays out a sequence of selected trainees, years of study, descent into practical offices, testing under temptation, and final qualification at age fifty.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Disciples of philosophy are to be orderly and steadfast, not chance aspirants or intruders.
Philosophy is proposed to replace gymnastics and be pursued diligently, earnestly, and exclusively for five years.
After five years, trainees are to be 'sent down again into the den' and compelled to hold military or other offices, so their firmness under temptation can be tried.
The practical stage of life is said to last fifteen years.
At fifty, those who survive and distinguish themselves must 'raise the eye of the soul' to the universal light and behold the absolute good.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 20154-20256
occurrences.motif_label: new generation separated for formation under ideal laws
occurrences.basis: The rulers send older inhabitants away, take the children, and train them in the rulers’ habits and laws to establish the constitution.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The rulers send inhabitants older than ten into the country, take the children, and train them in the rulers’ habits and laws so the State may attain happiness.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII.; lines 21268-21405
occurrences.motif_label: inverted initiation into disorderly pleasures
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly says the soul is being initiated in great mysteries, after which vices return with ceremonial praise and the young man enters libertinism.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The soul is emptied and swept clean while being initiated in great mysteries; garlanded vices return and are praised with favorable names; the young man moves into libertinism of unnecessary pleasures.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VI. / BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII. / BOOK IX.; lines 22998-23129
occurrences.motif_label: education installs an inner guardian
occurrences.basis: Children are not allowed freedom until cultivation establishes a guardian and ruler in their hearts analogous to civic constitution.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Law is called the ally of the whole city; children are governed until cultivation of the higher element establishes a guardian and ruler in their hearts.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 2829-2913
occurrences.motif_label: martial initiation of youths through controlled exposure to battle
occurrences.basis: Young warriors observe battle, are trained to ride, and are supervised by veterans while learning warfare.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Parents take children to look on at battle, compared with potters’ boys learning by watching the wheel; the sight of young ones encourages bravery.
“they should have wings—that is to say, swift and tractable steeds”

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 3256-3342
occurrences.motif_label: Testing and purification of future guardians
occurrences.basis: Guardians and aspirants are tested through pleasures, pains, dangers, and knowledge before receiving honour.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Guardians are to be tested in the “refiner’s fire of pleasures and pains” and rewarded if pure.
The speaker says the guardians must be philosophers, despite the difficulty of combining necessary qualities, and must be tested in pleasures, dangers, and highest knowledge.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 3736-3821
occurrences.motif_label: education as conversion or turning of the soul
occurrences.basis: The passage says the soul already has sight and requires turning toward the light; cutting away weights of pleasure and desire allows intelligence to behold truth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The parable teaches that instruction does not give eyes to the blind; the soul's faculty of sight is already present and must be turned toward light, which is called conversion.

Pleasure and desire are described as leaden weights binding the soul to earth; rulers must be chosen from natures able to ascend to light and knowledge, but must be forced down again among the captives.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 3983-4011
occurrences.motif_label: Initiatory restriction of higher knowledge
occurrences.basis: The speaker says Glaucon cannot follow and that absolute truth is not revealed to one not disciplined in previous sciences.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “Dear Glaucon, you cannot follow me here. There can be no revelation of the absolute truth” without discipline in prior sciences.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 4013-4089
occurrences.motif_label: staged initiation through tests and selections
occurrences.basis: The passage lays out sequential ages, selections, gymnastic and intellectual trials, dialectical training, and practical experience before full rulership.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Disciples must be young; youth is the time of study, and early learning should be play that detects natural bent.
After bodily training, at twenty a selection is made; the sciences learned in fragments are brought into relation with each other and with true being.
At thirty, a further selection is made of those able to withdraw from the world of sense into the abstraction of ideas.
The second gymnastic training of the soul lasts about five or six years from thirty; afterward the student goes down into the den, commands armies, and gains life experience for fifteen years.
At fifty the student returns to the end of all things, lifts his eyes to the idea of good, and orders life after that pattern.
The mature figure may take a turn at the helm of State and train others as successors.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 4241-4307
occurrences.motif_label: distorted sight after crossing between worlds
occurrences.basis: Two forms of disordered eyesight are described, one from transfer from darkness to day and one from descent into the den.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage symbolizes two kinds of disordered eyesight: the captive transferred from darkness to day and the heavenly messenger who voluntarily descends into the den for the good of fellow-men.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 4571-4620
occurrences.motif_label: corruption through initiation into pleasures
occurrences.basis: The youth is introduced by wild companions to new pleasures after tasting the drone’s honey and passes from necessary to unnecessary pleasures.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “The youth who has had a miserly bringing up, gets a taste of the drone’s honey; he meets with wild companions, who introduce him to every new pleasure.”
False spirits shut the castle gates, win the battle, ally with desires, banish modesty and temperance, and bring back vices crowned with garlands under new names.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 5775-5855
occurrences.motif_label: choice of next life by lot and moral discernment
occurrences.basis: Souls receive lots, view possible lives, and are warned that wise understanding is needed to choose well and avoid evil.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “A new period of mortal life has begun”; souls may choose, and “the responsibility of choosing is with you—God is blameless.”
The interpreter casts lots among the souls, each takes the lot near him, and many more samples of lives than souls are laid before them.
The samples include human and animal lives, tyrannies ending in misery and exile, famous lives of men and women, and mixed conditions of wealth, poverty, sickness, and health.
The passage states that education should teach refusal of evil, choice of good, knowledge of life's combinations, and selection of the life that makes the soul better.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 6123-6207
occurrences.motif_label: Beauty guiding the soul toward reason
occurrences.basis: The passage quotes or paraphrases Plato’s idea that beauty may imperceptibly draw the soul from childhood into harmony with reason.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Plato is said not to seriously expel poets but to protest poetic unreality; readers may become what they read; beauty is compared to a breeze drawing the soul toward reason.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 7233-7307
occurrences.motif_label: Initiatory second education into contemplation
occurrences.basis: Older soldiers enter a second novitiate of study and contemplation, and guardians undergo a second education toward higher knowledge and legislation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: War and philosophy are the permitted interests; when citizens are too old to be soldiers, they retire from active life to a second novitiate of study and contemplation.
The second education is directed toward higher knowledge and aims to make already good citizens into good legislators.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 7478-7558
occurrences.motif_label: protective formation of youth in a purified environment
occurrences.basis: The young are to be raised away from harmful sights and sounds in a healthy atmosphere, gradually learning temperance, endurance, and balanced bodily and mental development.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The young are to grow up in happy, healthy surroundings, away from sights or sounds harmful to character or taste, with impressions of truth and goodness wafted to them.
Education is harmonious growth, teaching temperance and endurance while body and mind develop in equal proportions; simplicity is the rule of life.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 7708-7783
occurrences.motif_label: staged initiation toward higher knowledge or beauty
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly says beauty in the Symposium is attained by stages of initiation and the good by regular gradations of knowledge.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Idea of good is represented in the Symposium as beauty and is supposed to be attained there by stages of initiation, as here by regular gradations of knowledge.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 7785-7872
occurrences.motif_label: ignorance in the Den and need for self-knowledge
occurrences.basis: Most people are described as living contentedly in the Den while lacking teachers who would expose ignorance and prompt self-knowledge.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says most men are destined for ‘the Den,’ lack teachers such as Socrates or Christ who would expose ignorance or sin, struggle to receive self-knowledge, while a few receive a second life from great teachers and light a candle from the fire of genius.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 1439-1491
occurrences.motif_label: trial of lover and beloved
occurrences.basis: Custom is said to test both lover and beloved through contests, trials, pursuit, flight, and time before their character is revealed.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Custom has both kinds proven, encourages some to pursue and others to flee, and tests lover and beloved in contests and trials until their classes are shown.
Hasty attachment is dishonourable because time is the true test of this and most other things.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 2318-2392
occurrences.motif_label: instruction in the mysteries of love
occurrences.basis: A teacher instructs an ignorant learner in the object, cause, and mysteries of love, using questions and explanations.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Diotima asks Socrates what lovers pursue; Socrates replies that he does not know and came to learn from her.
“The object which they have in view is birth in beauty, whether of body or soul.”

Diotima describes animals, birds, and beasts as agonized by procreative desire, seeking union, caring for offspring, and enduring danger, hunger, or death for their young; Socrates asks to be taught the cause and mysteries of love.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 2394-2475
occurrences.motif_label: Initiation into hidden mysteries of love
occurrences.basis: Diotima explicitly distinguishes lesser mysteries from greater hidden mysteries and frames Socrates as one who may or may not attain them.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Diotima says these are the lesser mysteries of love and introduces greater and more hidden mysteries that Socrates may or may not attain.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 2394-2475
occurrences.motif_label: Teacher-guided path to revelation
occurrences.basis: A guide or instructor directs the seeker, and Diotima presents a path culminating in a revealed vision of a single science of beauty.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Diotima says these are the lesser mysteries of love and introduces greater and more hidden mysteries that Socrates may or may not attain.

The seeker begins with one beautiful form, advances to all beautiful forms, beauty of mind, laws and institutions, sciences, the vast sea of beauty, and the final vision of the science of beauty everywhere.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 2477-2569
occurrences.motif_label: initiatory instruction leading to final vision
occurrences.basis: The seeker is instructed in love, follows an ordered sequence, and at the end suddenly perceives wondrous beauty.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The instructed lover finally perceives an everlasting, changeless, absolute beauty distinct from bodily parts, speech, knowledge, animals, heaven, earth, or any place.
"begin from the beauties of earth and mount upwards ... using these as steps only" toward the notion and essence of absolute beauty.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 2653-2699
occurrences.motif_label: initiation through painful self-recognition
occurrences.basis: Socrates' speech makes the speaker confess neglect of his soul, feel shame, and struggle between moral insight and love of popularity.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates brings the speaker to feel he can hardly endure his life; unless he shuts his ears and flees as from a siren's voice, he fears he would grow old sitting at Socrates' feet.
Socrates makes the speaker confess he neglects his soul while attending to Athenian affairs; the speaker says Socrates uniquely makes him ashamed, though popularity overcomes him when he leaves.
The speaker says he has often wished Socrates dead, yet knows he would be more sorry than glad if Socrates died, leaving him at his wit's end.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 2701-2761
occurrences.motif_label: Restricted disclosure before initiated or sympathetic hearers
occurrences.basis: The speaker says only fellow sufferers can understand his agony and tells profane or unmannered persons to close their ears.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker invokes 'In vino veritas,' says he has felt the serpent's sting, and calls philosophy's pang more violent than any serpent's tooth.

The speaker names Phaedrus, Agathon, Eryximachus, Pausanias, Aristodemus, Aristophanes, and Socrates as having the same madness and passion in longing after wisdom, then tells attendants and profane persons to close their ears.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 2763-2834
occurrences.motif_label: temptation resisted by self-restraint
occurrences.basis: Alcibiades attempts to captivate Socrates, but Socrates remains superior to the solicitation, and Alcibiades awakens as from the couch of a father or elder brother.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Alcibiades thinks his words have wounded Socrates like arrows, wraps his coat around him, lies under Socrates' threadbare cloak in winter, and says nothing more happened before he awoke as from the couch of a father or elder brother.

Alcibiades reflects on rejection and says he wondered at Socrates' temperance, self-restraint, manliness, wisdom, and endurance; he compares Socrates' resistance to money to Ajax being unwounded by steel.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 320-409
occurrences.motif_label: initiation into greater mysteries
occurrences.basis: Diotima explicitly says she will initiate the listener into the greater mysteries, leading toward a final vision of beauty.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Diotima announces initiation into the greater mysteries: the lover proceeds from one fair form to many, to beautiful minds, laws, institutions, sciences, and finally universal beauty, beheld by the mind’s eye, producing virtue, wisdom, divine friendship, and immortality.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 677-763
occurrences.motif_label: prophetic female teacher reveals the mystery of love
occurrences.basis: Diotima, a prophetess with sacred and superhuman character, is described as teaching Socrates the art and mystery of love.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Diotima, prophetess of Mantineia, teaches Socrates the art and mystery of love, love as philosophy, and the transformation of human want from procreation to intellectual desire; comparisons are made with Christian, medieval, and Dantean love.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 765-833
occurrences.motif_label: victory over bodily temptation
occurrences.basis: Socrates is represented as a saint who wins an Olympian victory over temptations of human nature.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates is represented as a saint who has won 'the Olympian victory' over the temptations of human nature.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 765-833
occurrences.motif_label: mentor-beloved educational bond
occurrences.basis: The passage describes youths attached or entrusted to elder men for training in manly exercises and virtue.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In Greek states, especially Sparta and Thebes, an honourable attachment of youth to elder man is described as part of education.
A young person is described as entrusted by parents to an elder friend expected to train him in manly exercises and virtue.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 835-921
occurrences.motif_label: education through elder-youth bond
occurrences.basis: The passage describes an elder friend's attachment to a beloved youth as part of education in Thebes and Lacedemon, with parental encouragement under honourable conditions.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage describes Theban and Lacedemonian elder-youth attachment as educational when not licentious, mentions Epaminondas and companions, discusses kiss or embrace as salutation custom, and compares later Romans, Celts, and Persians.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 923-996
occurrences.motif_label: philosophical ascent through stages
occurrences.basis: The passage describes movement from this world to another through steps or stages, from sense particulars to universals, and through higher degrees of initiation to the vision of beauty.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Phaedo is compared with the Symposium; unlike Phaedo and Phaedrus, the Symposium has no break between this world and another but rises through steps from sense particulars to universals and a single science.
The passage describes a language of mysteries with higher degrees of initiation leading to a perfect vision of eternal, absolute, divine beauty beyond limits of space and time.

occurrences.source_title: The Song Celestial; Or, Bhagavad-Gita
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER II
occurrences.motif_label: battlefield_revelation
occurrences.basis: A teaching about life, grief, duty, and action is delivered after Arjuna's refusal in the space between the opposing armies.

evidence.quote_or_summary: And sighing,"I will not fight!" held silence then.
While the Prince wept despairing 'twixt those hosts, Krishna made answer in divinest verse:
Life cannot slay. Life is not slain!
This Life within all living things, my Prince! Hides beyond harm; scorn thou to suffer, then, For that which cannot suffer. Do thy part!
If, knowing thy duty and thy task, thou bidd'st Duty and task go by--that shall be sin!
Therefore, arise, thou Son of Kunti! brace Thine arm for conflict, nerve thy heart to meet-- As things alike to thee--pleasure or pain, Profit or ruin, victory or defeat:

occurrences.source_title: The Song Celestial; Or, Bhagavad-Gita
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER XI
occurrences.motif_label: cosmic_vision
occurrences.basis: Arjuna receives divine sight and sees the universe gathered into one vast manifested form.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Fain would I see, As thou Thyself declar'st it, Sovereign Lord! The likeness of that glory of Thy Form Wholly revealed.
Thou canst not!--nor, with human eyes, Arjuna! ever mayest! Therefore I give thee sense divine. Have other eyes, new light!
Out of countless eyes beholding, Out of countless mouths commanding, Countless mystic forms enfolding In one Form:
So did Pandu's Son behold All this universe enfold All its huge diversity Into one vast shape,

occurrences.source_title: The Upanishads
occurrences.passage_locator: Katha-Upanishad, Part First VII-Part Second IV
occurrences.motif_label: initiation by death teacher
occurrences.basis: Nachiketas crosses into Death's abode, passes a test of temptations, and receives instruction from Yama.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Nachiketas went to Death's abode and waited without food or drink for three days.
Yama offers long life, wealth, rulership, chariots, music, and other difficult-to-obtain desires.
Nachiketas calls these pleasures fleeting and tells Death to keep chariots, dance, and music.
Yama teaches that the good and pleasant differ, and the wise prefer the good.
Yama says ignorance and wisdom lead in opposite directions and Nachiketas longs for wisdom.

occurrences.source_title: The Upanishads
occurrences.passage_locator: Katha-Upanishad, Part Second XVIII-XXIII; Part Sixth XVIII
occurrences.motif_label: liberation through death-taught knowledge
occurrences.basis: Nachiketas acquires wisdom taught by the Ruler of Death and becomes free from impurity and death.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Nachiketas acquired wisdom taught by the Ruler of Death and became free from impurity and death.

occurrences.source_title: The Popol Vuh
occurrences.passage_locator: The Second Book, Hero Twins in Xibalba
occurrences.motif_label: underworld_trial
occurrences.basis: The twins descend to Xibalba and pass a series of named houses, rivers, decoys, heat, cold, animal, and weapon dangers.

evidence.locator: The Second Book, entrance to Xibalba
evidence.quote_or_summary: The twins cross the river of blood and river Papuhya, expose wooden decoys, avoid the red-hot stone, pass the House of Gloom, and beat the Xibalbans at ball.
The twins survive the House of Lances, House of Cold, House of Tigers, and House of Fire through helpers and stratagems.

evidence.locator: The Second Book, House of Bats
evidence.quote_or_summary: Hun-Ahpu is beheaded by Camazotz in the House of Bats, but the brothers later emerge uninjured from all the ordeals.

occurrences.source_title: An Old Babylonian Version of the Gilgamesh Epic
occurrences.passage_locator: PENNSYLVANIA TABLET, TRANSLATION, Col. I-Col. III
occurrences.motif_label: civilization_boundary_initiation
occurrences.basis: Enkidu moves from field, cattle, and mountain associations into clothing, food, wine, grooming, and protection of shepherds.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Enkidu forgets his birthplace after the woman; she tells him to leave roaming with cattle, go to Erech and Eanna, clothes him, and leads him by the hand.
Eat food, O Enkidu, / The provender of life! / Drink wine, the custom of the land!

occurrences.source_title: Persian Literature, Volume 1
occurrences.passage_locator: Birth of Rustem; Simurgh aid, prodigious growth, and the white elephant feat
occurrences.motif_label: first_beast_slaying_as_initiation
occurrences.basis: Rustem's night encounter with the rampaging white elephant functions as an early ordeal that proves his public heroic power.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The white elephant at Sistan gets loose by night, crushes people, and cannot be held back while Rustem forces his way past the guards.
Rustem faces the elephant, bends his iron mace with the blow, kills it in the dust, and receives Zal's amazed praise.

occurrences.source_title: The Confessions of Al Ghazzali
occurrences.passage_locator: The Confessions of Al Ghazzali, Sufism
occurrences.motif_label: theory crossed into initiation
occurrences.basis: The passage marks a threshold where intellectual knowledge must become practice, ecstasy, and moral transformation.

evidence.locator: The Confessions of Al Ghazzali, Sufism, lines 920-954
evidence.quote_or_summary: Al Ghazzali says Sufism requires theory joined to practice and consists in experiences rather than definitions.

occurrences.source_title: The Mystics of Islam
occurrences.passage_locator: The Mystics of Islam, The Path
occurrences.motif_label: mapped interior pilgrimage
occurrences.basis: Sufi spiritual life is described as a journey, pilgrimage, path, and ascent with stages.

evidence.locator: The Mystics of Islam, The Path, lines 796-837
evidence.quote_or_summary: Nicholson presents Sufi spiritual life as a journey or pilgrimage through stages and states toward gnosis, truth, and union with Reality.

occurrences.source_title: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer
occurrences.passage_locator: Chuang Tzu, Chapter II, butterfly dream
occurrences.motif_label: dream transformation
occurrences.basis: The speaker moves between human and butterfly identity through dream and questions which identity is primary.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Chuang Tzu dreams he is a butterfly and then questions whether he is a man dreaming a butterfly or a butterfly dreaming a man.

occurrences.source_title: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer
occurrences.passage_locator: Chuang Tzu, Chapter II, Great Awakening
occurrences.motif_label: waking and dream as reversible states
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly reverses the apparent hierarchy between dream and waking.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says dreamers do not know they dream and that the Great Awakening reveals this life as a great dream.

occurrences.source_title: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
occurrences.passage_locator: Tao Teh King, Ch. 43.1-2
occurrences.motif_label: soft overcomes hard
occurrences.basis: The passage directly contrasts the softest thing with the hardest and says the softest overcomes.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The softest thing in the world overcomes the hardest; what has no substantial existence enters where there is no crevice; the passage connects this with "doing nothing" and "non-action."

occurrences.source_title: Persian Literature, Volume 1
occurrences.passage_locator: Persian Literature, Volume 1 / PERSIAN LITERATURE / SPECIAL INTRODUCTION; lines 68-154
occurrences.motif_label: Welding of dual cultural forces (Hellenic and Semitic) as defining signature
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly frames Persian history and literature as shaped by two forces (Hellenic and Semitic) whose “welding together” defines Persia.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The author argues Persian literature’s appeal comes from shared underlying forces with modern civilization: Hellenic influence (love of beauty) and Semitic influence (moral/religious tone). These two forces are said to have operated in Persia; the Avesta’s religion is said to resemble that of the Old and New Testaments; European writers are said to have re-sung Persian masterpieces for modern audiences.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE GOOSE THAT LAID THE GOLDEN EGGS / THE CAT AND THE MICE / THE MISCHIEVOUS DOG / THE CHARCOAL-BURNER AND THE FULLER; lines 1002-1013
occurrences.motif_label: white and black occupational contrast
occurrences.basis: The fuller's whitening work is explicitly opposed to the blackening effect of the charcoal-burner's charcoal.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The fuller refuses: "everything I take such pains to whiten would be blackened in no time by your charcoal."

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE LION AND THE MOUSE / THE CROW AND THE PITCHER / THE BOYS AND THE FROGS / THE NORTH WIND AND THE SUN; lines 1255-1283
occurrences.motif_label: contest of opposed personified natural powers
occurrences.basis: The North Wind and the Sun are personified as rivals claiming superior strength and testing their powers on the traveller.

evidence.locator: lines 1265-1269, THE NORTH WIND AND THE SUN
evidence.quote_or_summary: The North Wind and the Sun dispute which is stronger and agree to test their powers on a traveller by seeing who can strip him of his cloak first.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE BOYS AND THE FROGS / THE NORTH WIND AND THE SUN / THE MISTRESS AND HER SERVANTS / THE GOODS AND THE ILLS; lines 1301-1320
occurrences.motif_label: personified opposition of good and harm
occurrences.basis: The passage presents Goods and Ills as opposing personified forces in human affairs, initially balanced and later unevenly distributed.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In the youth of the world, Goods and Ills entered human concerns equally, so Goods did not make humans wholly blessed and Ills did not make them wholly miserable.
Because of mankind’s foolishness, Ills multiplied and strengthened until they seemed likely to drive Goods out of human affairs and banish them from earth.
The fable concludes that earth is full of Ills, which come and go freely, while Goods come one by one from heaven and are seldom seen.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE BLACKAMOOR / THE TWO SOLDIERS AND THE ROBBER / THE LION AND THE WILD ASS / THE MAN AND THE SATYR; lines 2597-2608
occurrences.motif_label: same action used for opposite effects
occurrences.basis: The man's breath is used first to warm cold hands and then to cool hot porridge, creating a hot/cold opposition around one act.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In winter, the satyr saw the man blowing on his hands; the man explained that he was warming his hands.
At supper, both had steaming hot bowls of porridge; the man blew on his porridge and explained that he was cooling it.
"I can't be friends with a man who blows hot and cold with the same breath."

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE HORSE AND HIS RIDER / THE GOAT AND THE VINE / THE TWO POTS / THE OLD HOUND; lines 2835-2859
occurrences.motif_label: Unequal companions make unsafe friends
occurrences.basis: The fable contrasts a fragile earthenware pot with a stronger brass pot and explicitly concludes that equals make the best friends.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Two pots, one earthenware and one brass, are carried away down a river in flood.
The brass pot urges the other to stay close for protection; the earthenware pot asks him not to come near because a touch would break him.
"Equals make the best friends."

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE LION AND THE ASS / THE PROPHET / THE HOUND AND THE HARE / THE LION, THE MOUSE, AND THE FOX; lines 2941-2963
occurrences.motif_label: ambiguous friend-or-enemy behavior
occurrences.basis: The hound alternates between threatening and playful acts, and the hare frames this as a contradiction between friend and enemy; the moral calls such conduct playing double.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A young hound starts and catches a hare, then alternates between snapping at her as if to kill and letting go to frisk as if playing.
"If you are my friend, why do you bite me? If you are my enemy, why do you play with me?"
"He is no friend who plays double."

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE SICK MAN AND THE DOCTOR / THE TRAVELLERS AND THE PLANE-TREE / THE FLEA AND THE OX / THE BIRDS, THE BEASTS, AND THE BAT; lines 3504-3515
occurrences.motif_label: double allegiance punished by exclusion
occurrences.basis: After occupying both sides during the conflict, the Bat is named double-faced and rejected by both groups.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “neither the Birds nor the Beasts would have anything to do with so double-faced a traitor”
“he remains to this day a solitary outcast from both”

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE TRAVELLERS AND THE PLANE-TREE / THE FLEA AND THE OX / THE BIRDS, THE BEASTS, AND THE BAT / THE MAN AND HIS TWO SWEETHEARTS; lines 3518-3528
occurrences.motif_label: opposed partners produce total loss
occurrences.basis: Two paired figures act from opposite age preferences: one removes dark hairs to make the man older, and the other removes grey hairs to make him younger; together they leave him bald.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The older sweetheart dislikes having a lover who looks younger than herself and pulls out his dark hairs to make him look old.
The younger sweetheart dislikes the man looking older than herself and pulls out his grey hairs to make him look young.
“Between them, they left not a hair in his head, and he became perfectly bald.”

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE ASS AND THE MULE / BROTHER AND SISTER / THE HEIFER AND THE OX / THE KINGDOM OF THE LION; lines 3723-3734
occurrences.motif_label: weak and strong reconciled
occurrences.basis: The hare explicitly contrasts the weak and the strong and welcomes their fearless coexistence.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The hare says: "the weak take their place without fear by the side of the strong."

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: HONORARY SECRETARIES. / INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA.; lines 1011-1094
occurrences.motif_label: sun and moon exchange roles and genders
occurrences.basis: A female night-luminary exchanges with a male luminary, resulting in a female sun and male moon.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A female luminary formerly came out at night but, shocked by outdoor immoralities, exchanged with the male luminary; now the sun is female and the moon male.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: HONORARY SECRETARIES. / INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA.; lines 902-1009
occurrences.motif_label: Contest determines rule of the world
occurrences.basis: Good and bad gods dispute world government and agree that first sight of the sunrise will decide who rules.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After the Creator finishes the world, good/brilliant and bad gods dispute rule; they agree that first sight of sunrise decides possession; the fox-god looks west, sees the sunrise's refulgence, and the brilliant gods rule.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 1 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER I. THE KING OF THE WOOD. / MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE.; lines 3112-3185
occurrences.motif_label: person as visible body plus inner double
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly describes a person as two in one, with a visible body and an invisible little body, and reports similar beliefs in a little body or model-like soul.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A missionary says he is two in one, with a visible great body and an invisible little body that flies away at death; some Australian interlocutors reply that they too have a little body in the breast and give different answers about its destination after death.
Frazer reports Huron and Eskimo beliefs that the soul resembles the body, and a Nias belief that souls are measured by weight or length before birth, with life span related to soul length.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS; lines 1279-1324
occurrences.motif_label: Sacred animal treated as taboo or unclean
occurrences.basis: The pig is described as both sacred and unclean, with the author framing this ambiguity as taboo where sanctity and uncleanness are not differentiated.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At Hierapolis pigs were neither sacrificed nor eaten; touching a pig caused uncleanness for the day; people differed on whether pigs were unclean or sacred, which the passage identifies with taboo.
The passage describes Jewish attitudes to pigs as ambiguous: Greeks could not decide whether Jews worshipped or abominated swine, since they might neither eat nor kill them.

The passage says some Jews met secretly in gardens to eat swine and mice as a religious rite and interprets this as an ancient sacramental eating of divine animals; it concludes that so-called unclean animals were originally sacred.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: CONTENTS / NOTE. OFFERINGS OF FIRST-FRUITS. / INDEX. / FOOTNOTES; lines 13729-13864
occurrences.motif_label: ritual contest between good and evil forces
occurrences.basis: The Chukma funeral contest explicitly divides participants into sides representing good spirits and powers of evil, with victory arranged for the good side.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Among the Chukmas, a priest's body is conveyed to cremation on a car; ropes are attached, two equal groups pull in opposite directions, one side represents good spirits and the other evil powers, and the good side is arranged to win.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS; lines 1422-1506
occurrences.motif_label: Sacrificial victim as both god and god’s enemy
occurrences.basis: The passage argues that the pig was originally Osiris or the corn-spirit but later reinterpreted as Typhon or Osiris’s enemy.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says a being regarded with mixed feelings may become a god or devil; in Egypt the pig came to be viewed as an embodiment of Set or Typhon, enemy of Osiris.
The passage argues that an animal killed solemnly once and only once in the year is generally divine, spared the rest of the year as a god and slain in the character of a god.

The passage argues that the pig sacrificed once a year to Osiris was originally a god and was Osiris, later distinguished from and opposed to Osiris; the sacrifice took place on the day tradition said Osiris was killed.

The killing of the pig is described as an annual representation of the killing of Osiris, compared with Thesmophoria pigs representing Proserpine’s descent and with European harvest killings of animals as representatives of the corn-spirit.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE STORY OF URASHIMA TARO, THE FISHER LAD / THE FARMER AND THE BADGER / THE ADVENTURES OF KINTARO, THE GOLDEN BOY / THE STORY OF THE MAN WHO DID NOT WISH TO DIE; lines 2373-2477
occurrences.motif_label: inverted values in a deathless land
occurrences.basis: Sentaro values escape from death, while the deathless islanders value death and consume poisons as desirable goods.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Unlike Sentaro, the islanders long for death as desirable because they are tired of long life and desire the happy land called Paradise.
Foods poisonous elsewhere are treated as desirable; rich people buy poisons hoping to die, but poisons have no harmful effect, and poisonous globe-fish and Spanish-fly sauces are sold as food.
Sentaro at first delights in life without death, but after business troubles and three hundred years of monotony he grows tired and longs for his homeland.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE BAMBOO-CUTTER AND THE MOON-CHILD / THE GOBLIN OF ADACHIGAHARA / THE SAGACIOUS MONKEY AND THE BOAR / THE HAPPY HUNTER AND THE SKILLFUL FISHER; lines 3899-4008
occurrences.motif_label: brothers with paired domains and occupations
occurrences.basis: The passage sets up two brothers with contrasted spheres: mountains and hunting for the younger brother, sea and fishing for the elder brother.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hohodemi governs Japan, is fourth Mikoto in descent from Amaterasu, and is described as handsome, strong, brave, and the greatest hunter, called the Happy Hunter of the Mountains.
Hohodemi’s elder brother is a surpassingly skillful fisher called the Skillful Fisher of the Sea, and the brothers pursue their respective occupations happily.
The Happy Hunter proposes that the brothers change occupations: the elder brother should hunt in the mountains while he fishes in the sea.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE STORY OF PRINCE YAMATO TAKE / MOMOTARO, OR THE STORY OF THE SON OF A PEACH / THE OGRE OF RASHOMON / HOW AN OLD MAN LOST HIS WEN; lines 7364-7483
occurrences.motif_label: Elemental opposition of fire and water
occurrences.basis: The passage contrasts Shikuyu as master of fire with Kokai as master of water, and the conflict turns on fire-associated countermeasures against magically raised floods.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Shikuyu lives at the South Pole because he burns everything except ice and snow; he is a thirty-foot giant and master of all fire, just as Kokai is master of water.
Kokai boasts that he can extinguish the Fire King, raises floods as high as mountains by incantation, and Shikuyu has the soldiers scatter ashes that turn the water into stiff mud.

occurrences.motif_label: contrast of wisdom and folly
occurrences.basis: The title 'The Wise and the Foolish Merchant' explicitly juxtaposes wise and foolish figures.

evidence.quote_or_summary: X THE WISE AND THE FOOLISH MERCHANT

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VENUS. / HELIOS (SOL). / EOS (AURORA). / PHOEBUS-APOLLO.; lines 2200-2277
occurrences.motif_label: Dual beneficent and destructive solar power
occurrences.basis: Apollo’s rays bring growth, health, and pasture, but also disease, sudden death, and pestilence.

evidence.locator: lines 2200-2277; Apollo passage, beneficial rays paragraph
evidence.quote_or_summary: Apollo’s warm and gentle rays bring joy to nature, health and prosperity to humans, disperse vapours, ripen grain, and bloom flowers.

evidence.locator: lines 2200-2277; Apollo passage, death and pestilence paragraph
evidence.quote_or_summary: Apollo’s fierce rays can spread disease and sudden death; he and Artemis share the death function; in the Iliad he sends pestilence into the Greek camp with death-bringing arrows.
Apollo protects shepherds because he warms fields and meadows and gives rich pastures to flocks.
Apollo is regarded as god of healing because the sun’s temperate heat invigorates humans and animals and promotes medicinal herbs and plants needed to cure diseases.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VENUS. / HELIOS (SOL). / EOS (AURORA). / PHOEBUS-APOLLO.; lines 2365-2439
occurrences.motif_label: Opposed arrows producing love and aversion
occurrences.basis: Eros uses two darts of different materials and opposite effects: gold inspires love, lead creates aversion.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Apollo mocks Eros after killing Python; Eros takes a golden dart that inspires love and a leaden dart that creates aversion, striking Apollo with the first and Daphne with the second.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: SELENE (LUNA). / ARTEMIS (DIANA). / ARCADIAN ARTEMIS. / EPHESIAN ARTEMIS.; lines 2926-2974
occurrences.motif_label: Twofold goddess of love and heavenly light
occurrences.basis: Metra is explicitly described as a twofold divinity whose phases are all-pervading love and the light of heaven.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Metra is described as a twofold divinity representing all-pervading love and the light of heaven; Greek settlers connected her with Artemis as Selene because of celestial light.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: PART I.--MYTHS. / INTRODUCTION. / ORIGIN OF THE WORLD.--FIRST DYNASTY. / URANUS AND GAEA. (COELUS AND TERRA.); lines 436-525
occurrences.motif_label: paired cosmic oppositions of light and darkness
occurrences.basis: The passage contrasts Uranus and Gaea's light and earth imagery with Erebus and Nyx as Darkness and Night, and describes Dawn and Daylight as children of Uranus and Nyx.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Erebus and Nyx are described as offspring of Chaos; Erebus is Darkness ruling a lower world without daylight, and Nyx represents Night.
Uranus is united with Nyx as god of light, producing Eos and Hemera; Nyx is also married to Erebus.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: ERINYES, EUMENIDES (FURIAE, DIRAE). / MOIRAE OR FATES (PARCAE). / NEMESIS. / NYX (NOX).; lines 4548-4560
occurrences.motif_label: darkness preceding light
occurrences.basis: Nyx and Erebus produce Aether and Hemera, and the passage explicitly explains this as meaning darkness always precedes light.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Nyx is united to Erebus; their children are Aether and Hemera, indicating that "darkness always precedes light."

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: MOIRAE OR FATES (PARCAE). / NEMESIS. / NYX (NOX). / THANATOS (MORS) AND HYPNUS (SOMNUS).; lines 4562-4601
occurrences.motif_label: Divine twin brothers personifying paired states
occurrences.basis: The passage identifies Death and Sleep as twin brothers, children of Nyx, and contrasts their paired but opposed reception among mortals.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Thanatos and Hypnus are twin brothers, children of Nyx, dwelling in the realm of shades; Thanatos is feared and hated by mortals, while Hypnus is loved and welcomed.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: NEMESIS. / NYX (NOX). / THANATOS (MORS) AND HYPNUS (SOMNUS). / MORPHEUS.; lines 4603-4614
occurrences.motif_label: Dual gate distinction between false and true dreams
occurrences.basis: The House of Dreams has two gates with opposed functions: ivory for deceptive visions and horn for fulfilled dreams.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Homer describes the House of Dreams as having two gates: ivory for deceptive and flattering visions, and horn for dreams that are fulfilled.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: ASCLEPIAS (AESCULAPIUS). / AESCULAPIUS. / ROMAN DIVINITIES. / JANUS.; lines 5712-5790
occurrences.motif_label: two-faced temporal duality
occurrences.basis: Janus is represented with two faces looking in opposite directions, explained as one face looking to the past and the other to the future.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Janus is usually represented with two faces; as door-keeper of heaven he stands with a key and a rod or sceptre.

Janus is said to have been an ancient Italian king deified after wise rule; Saturn, identified with Greek Cronus, gave him knowledge of past and future events, explaining his two opposite-facing faces.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: JANUS. / FLORA. / ROBIGUS. / POMONA.; lines 5806-5825
occurrences.motif_label: beneficent and destructive plant divinities in opposition
occurrences.basis: Robigus is described as an antagonistic divinity in opposition to Flora and as destructive to tender herbs.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Robigus is described as an antagonistic divinity opposed to Flora, a worker of evil who delights in destroying tender herbs by mildew.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: ROBIGUS. / POMONA. / VERTUMNUS. / PALES.; lines 5846-5863
occurrences.motif_label: dual-gender divinity of pastoral fertility
occurrences.basis: Pales is represented sometimes as male and sometimes as female, with related pastoral and fertility domains.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Pales is a very ancient Italian divinity represented sometimes as male and sometimes as female.
As a male divinity, Pales is particularly the god of shepherds and flocks.
As a female deity, Pales presides over husbandry and the fruitfulness of herds.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: LAVERNA. / COMUS. / THE CAMENAE. / GENII.; lines 5978-6004
occurrences.motif_label: opposed good and evil spiritual influences shaping fate
occurrences.basis: A beneficent genius and an evil genius are described as antagonistic influences whose conflict affects the individual’s fate.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A second evil genius was believed to instigate wrong-doing, oppose the beneficent genius, and influence the individual’s fate through this conflict.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: STATUES. / ALTARS. / PRIESTS. / SACRIFICES.; lines 6201-6287
occurrences.motif_label: differentiated offerings by divine realm and deity
occurrences.basis: The passage distinguishes white victims for Olympian divinities and black victims or blood libation for lower-world gods, and gives deity-specific offerings for Demeter and Dionysus.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Every sacrifice includes salt and a libation, usually wine in a full cup; sacrifices to infernal gods use blood in the libation cup.
Olympian divinities receive white animals, while gods of the lower world receive black animals.
Public sacrifices consider the deity's individuality: a sow is offered to Demeter because it roots seed-corn, and a goat to Dionysus because it damages vineyards.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE. / PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES).; lines 8170-8264
occurrences.motif_label: role reversal of heroic arms and feminine labor
occurrences.basis: Omphale wears Heracles' lion skin and helmet while Heracles wears female garments and spins wool at her feet.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Omphale learns her slave is Heracles, frees him, offers marriage and kingdom, and in her palace wears his lion skin and helmet while he wears female garments and spins wool.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CONTENTS / LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS / INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING; lines 328-454
occurrences.motif_label: Creation through opposed cold and heat
occurrences.basis: The world-origin sequence is framed around Nifl-heim's ice and Muspells-heim's fire acting on each other in the abyss.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Northern climate and scenery are said to shape religious belief; Icelanders are said to imagine creation from a strange mixture of fire and ice.
Nifl-heim lies north of the abyss; Hvergelmir supplies twelve Elivagar streams whose waters freeze into ice-blocks and fall into the abyss.
Muspells-heim lies south of the abyss as a fiery realm guarded by Surtr, who sends sparks that melt ice-blocks below.

Steam becomes hoarfrost as heat and cold interact; Ymir or Orgelmir comes to life amid ice-blocks, is born of rime, and is called an ice-giant. The quoted Eddic passage says there was no sand, sea, earth, heaven, or grass, only chaos.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CONTENTS / LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS / INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING; lines 456-592
occurrences.motif_label: Conflict of gods and giants as opposing forces
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly frames gods and giants as opposite forces and describes their long war.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Giants wage war against Buri and Börr; Börr marries Bestla; Odin, Vili, and Ve slay Ymir; Ymir's blood causes a deluge in which only Bergelmir escapes by boat with his wife.

occurrences.basis: Sun and Moon are chased by wolves whose goal is to swallow them and restore primeval darkness; eclipses are linked to temporary overtaking.

evidence.locator: lines 594-736, section 'The Wolves Sköll and Hati'
evidence.quote_or_summary: Sköll and Hati pursue Sun and Moon, sometimes try to swallow them and cause eclipses; human noise makes them release the orbs; the passage connects the pursuit with final doom at Ragnarok.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CONTENTS / LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS / INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING; lines 594-736
occurrences.motif_label: Apocalyptic struggle of opposing forces
occurrences.basis: The passage frames good and evil, death and life, as moving toward a final struggle at Ragnarok and states the gods are doomed to perish with the world.

evidence.locator: lines 594-736, section 'The Wolves Sköll and Hati'
evidence.quote_or_summary: Sköll and Hati pursue Sun and Moon, sometimes try to swallow them and cause eclipses; human noise makes them release the orbs; the passage connects the pursuit with final doom at Ragnarok.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CONTENTS / LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS / INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING; lines 594-736
occurrences.motif_label: Personified seasonal opposition
occurrences.basis: Summer and Winter are made rulers of seasons and are described as enemies with opposed dispositions.

evidence.locator: lines 594-736, paragraph on time divisions and seasons
evidence.quote_or_summary: The gods appoint divisions of the day and make Summer and Winter rulers of the seasons; Summer is gentle and loved, while Winter is his deadly enemy and linked to icy wind.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CONTENTS / LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS / INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING; lines 594-736
occurrences.motif_label: Creation and division of chthonic dwarfs and light elves
occurrences.basis: Creatures from Ymir's flesh are formed by the gods and separated into dark underground dwarfs and fair elves dwelling between heaven and earth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Maggot-like creatures breed in Ymir's flesh; the gods give them forms and intelligence, sending dark dwarfs underground to Svart-alfa-heim and fair elves to Alf-heim between heaven and earth.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CONTENTS / LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS / INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING; lines 865-877
occurrences.motif_label: war of divine clans followed by reconciliation
occurrences.basis: The passage presents two divine groups, Æsir and Vanas, first in conflict and then reconciled through peace.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Æsir are original inhabitants of heaven; the Vanas are also recognized divinities, associated with sea and wind, dwelling in Vana-heim and ruling their realms.
Before the golden palaces in Asgard are built, a dispute arises between the Æsir and Vanas; they fight using rocks, mountains, and icebergs as missiles.
The two sides conclude that unity brings strength, compose their differences, make peace, and ratify the treaty by exchanging hostages.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XXII / BOOK XXIII / BOOK XXIV / FOOTNOTES:; lines 11278-11377
occurrences.motif_label: boundary or transition marked by night and day
occurrences.basis: The note cites the phrase that the ways of night and day are near.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The note translates a phrase as saying that the ways of night and day are near and discusses amber-route and Sacred Way interpretations.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE. / BOOK XI / THE VISIT TO THE DEAD.88; lines 5070-5169
occurrences.motif_label: treacherous spouse versus faithful spouse at homecoming
occurrences.basis: Agamemnon condemns Clytemnestra for murdering him and contrasts her with Penelope, whom he calls admirable and unlikely to murder Ulysses.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Agamemnon says Cassandra screamed as Clytemnestra killed her; he lay dying with a sword in his body, and Clytemnestra did not close his lips or eyes.
Agamemnon advises Ulysses not to tell even his wife everything, but says Penelope is admirable and unlikely to murder him; he expects Ulysses and his grown son to have a joyful meeting.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 1039-1112
occurrences.motif_label: Union of inward and outward person
occurrences.basis: The cited prayer asks for beauty in the inward soul and for the inward and outward person to be at one.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “Give me beauty in the inward soul, and may the inward and outward man be at one.”

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 154-206
occurrences.motif_label: Winged soul chariot ascending or falling
occurrences.basis: The soul is figured as a charioteer with winged steeds, including mortal and immortal components, and is described as soaring upward or dropping to earth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: All soul is immortal and source of motion; its form is figured as a charioteer with a pair of winged steeds; divine steeds are immortal, while the human pair includes one mortal and one immortal; the immortal soul soars heavenward and the mortal drops plumes to earth.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 1781-1894
occurrences.motif_label: Inner duality of reason and desire
occurrences.basis: The passage presents two ruling principles in each person, one desire for pleasure and the other opinion aspiring to the best, sometimes in harmony and sometimes at war.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The embedded speech distinguishes natural desire for pleasure from acquired opinion aspiring after the best; when reason-led opinion rules it is temperance, and when reasonless desire rules and drags toward pleasure it is excess.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2188-2244
occurrences.motif_label: soul as charioteer with opposed horses
occurrences.basis: The human chariot team contains one noble and one ignoble horse, creating a divided pair that troubles the driver.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The soul's nature is presented in a figure of a charioteer and a pair of winged horses; divine teams are noble, while the human team contains one noble and one ignoble horse.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2499-2549
occurrences.motif_label: divided soul in internal conflict
occurrences.basis: The soul is represented as a composite of opposed horses and a charioteer, with one horse obedient and the other unruly.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker says each soul is divided into three: two horses and a charioteer.
The right-hand horse is white, well-formed, honorable, modest, temperate, and guided without the whip.
The other horse is crooked, dark, insolent, proud, deaf, and hardly yields to whip and spur.
When the charioteer beholds love, the obedient horse refrains, but the other horse forces the group toward the beloved and the joys of love.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2551-2634
occurrences.motif_label: Dual conflict within the soul
occurrences.basis: The soul is described through opposing elements: wanton steeds pressing toward desire and charioteer or fellow-steed arguing from shame and reason; later the vicious elements are enslaved and virtuous elements emancipated.

evidence.quote_or_summary: When the lovers meet, the wanton steed of the lover seeks pleasure, the wanton steed of the beloved is full of uncomprehended passion, and the fellow-steed and charioteer oppose with shame and reason.

If self-control, order, and philosophy prevail, the pair live in happiness and harmony, master themselves, enslave vicious elements, emancipate virtuous elements, and become light and winged for flight.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 290-374
occurrences.motif_label: Chariot-team as image of the divided soul
occurrences.basis: The charioteer and two steeds are explicitly called a figure of the soul, with one obedient and one unruly element.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A charioteer and two steeds, one noble and one ill-looking, are described as a figure of the soul approaching the vision of love.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 3061-3191
occurrences.motif_label: right and left division of a single power into opposed forms
occurrences.basis: Socrates compares division to a body split into left and right sides and applies this to evil left-handed love and divine right-sided love.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates explains division by natural joints and compares it to a body divided into left and right sides; one discourse found evil left-handed love, while the other found divine love on the right side and praised it as author of the greatest benefits.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 3663-3779
occurrences.motif_label: Distinguishing dream from reality
occurrences.basis: Socrates says failure to know justice, injustice, good, and evil leaves a writer unable to distinguish dream from reality.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says that lacking knowledge of justice, injustice, good, and evil, and being unable “to distinguish the dream from the reality,” is disgraceful in a writer.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 3781-3808
occurrences.motif_label: Inner and outer harmony sought through prayer
occurrences.basis: Socrates prays for beauty in the inward soul and for the outward and inward man to be at one.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “Beloved Pan, and all ye other gods who haunt this place, give me beauty in the inward soul; and may the outward and inward man be at one.”

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 549-637
occurrences.motif_label: higher and lower love
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly distinguishes two loves: higher and lower, holy and unholy, mind and body.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says Socrates or Archilochus would need to sing a palinode for injustice done to lovely Helen, then states that there are “two loves, a higher and a lower, holy and unholy, a love of the mind and a love of the body.”

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 63-152
occurrences.motif_label: opposition of reason and desire
occurrences.basis: Socrates' account identifies two principles in everyone, reason and desire, usually at war with one another.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says all people have two opposed principles, reason and desire; rational victory is temperance, irrational victory is intemperance or excess.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 718-802
occurrences.motif_label: chariot allegory of the divided soul
occurrences.basis: The soul is imaged as a charioteer with two winged steeds, with the horses representing opposed or differing impulses and the charioteer representing reason.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage turns to the image of the souls of gods and humans as two winged steeds and a charioteer.

The charioteer is identified with reason, the black horse with sensual or concupiscent nature, and the white horse with rational impulse and virtues such as honour, modesty, temperance, and true glory.

The moral or spiritual element is represented by an immortal steed that sides with reason, though reason and this element are dragged by furious desire; the way of philosophy is described as abstinence from bodily delights.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 886-959
occurrences.motif_label: opposed lower and higher forms of love
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly contrasts lower and higher love and says the two are opposed though not absolutely separated.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage distinguishes lower and higher love, describes higher love as contemplating forms with religious awe, compares the opposition to flesh and spirit in St. Paul, and mentions the rational soul mastering both steeds in spiritual combat.
Love is represented as a great power of nature with many forms and two principal ones; the two forms are opposed but not absolutely separate and can transform into one another.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 886-959
occurrences.motif_label: spiritual combat resolved by rational mastery
occurrences.basis: The passage describes a spiritual combat in which the rational soul becomes victor and master of both steeds.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage distinguishes lower and higher love, describes higher love as contemplating forms with religious awe, compares the opposition to flesh and spirit in St. Paul, and mentions the rational soul mastering both steeds in spiritual combat.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS. / THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I.; lines 10055-10189
occurrences.motif_label: Moral duality of just and unjust
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly contrasts just/unjust, wise/ignorant, good/evil, friendship/enmity, and harmony/division.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates elicits that the just is like the wise and good and the unjust like the evil and ignorant; Thrasymachus admits this reluctantly, perspiring and blushing.
“injustice creates divisions and hatreds and fighting, and justice imparts harmony and friendship”
Injustice among two people, in a city, army, family, other body, or single person is said to produce quarrel, disunity, incapacity for united action, and enmity toward self and the just.
Socrates obtains agreement that the gods are just; from this he concludes that the unjust is enemy of the gods and the just is their friend, while Thrasymachus declines to oppose him.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS. / THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I.; lines 10191-10359
occurrences.motif_label: opposition of justice and injustice
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly contrasts justice with injustice, good soul with evil soul, living well with living ill, and happiness with misery.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says unjust people acting together must retain some justice; wholly unjust people would injure one another and be incapable of action.
The soul is said to have an excellence; an evil soul rules badly and a good soul rules well; justice is admitted as the soul’s excellence and injustice as its defect.
The speakers agree that the just soul and just man live well, that living well is blessed and happy, and that the unjust man is miserable; injustice is not more profitable than justice.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 10460-10547
occurrences.motif_label: paired moral opposites tested to extremes
occurrences.basis: The passage constructs an entirely just man and an entirely unjust man, places them side by side, and asks for judgment about which is happier.

evidence.quote_or_summary: To judge the just and unjust lives, the passage says the two must be isolated, each fully equipped for the work of his respective life.
The unjust man is compared to a master craftsman and must be able to hide wrongdoing, seem just, speak effectively if exposed, and rely on courage, strength, money, and friends.
The just man is placed beside him as noble and simple, wishing to be rather than seem good, clothed in justice only, thought worst while being best, and continuing so until death.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 10980-11113
occurrences.motif_label: plain healthy life contrasted with fevered luxury
occurrences.basis: Socrates contrasts the simple, healthy constitution with a luxurious State described as at fever-heat.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The simple city produces food, clothes, shoes, and houses; citizens work seasonally, eat bread and cakes, recline on simple bedding, drink wine, wear garlands, hymn the gods, converse, and limit family size according to means.

Socrates adds relishes and plain foods including salt, olives, cheese, roots, herbs, figs, peas, beans, myrtle-berries, and acorns roasted at the fire, with moderate drinking and expected peace, health, old age, and inheritance of similar life by children.
Glaucon says this would feed a city of pigs and asks for ordinary comforts: sofas, tables, sauces, and sweets in the modern style.

Socrates says the question is how a luxurious State is created; he calls the simple constitution true and healthy, and the luxurious State a State at fever-heat with added furniture, dainties, perfumes, incense, courtesans, cakes, painters, embroiderers, gold, ivory, and many materials.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1100-1178
occurrences.motif_label: mixed good and evil in human nature
occurrences.basis: The passage says human nature oscillates between good and evil and that individual character cannot be explained simply by evil because good counteracts it.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says human nature oscillates between good and evil and warns against explaining all action by worse motives, using images of alloy, shadow, and self-interest.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 11115-11284
occurrences.motif_label: Union of opposed qualities in the ideal guardian
occurrences.basis: The good guardian must combine great spirit with gentleness, being dangerous to enemies and gentle to friends, despite the apparent contradiction.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Guardians “ought to be dangerous to their enemies, and gentle to their friends,” otherwise they will destroy themselves.
Socrates asks how to find a gentle nature with great spirit; the combination appears contradictory, and without both qualities the good guardian seems impossible.
Socrates, in perplexity, says they have lost sight of the image before them and asserts that natures gifted with the opposite qualities do exist.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 11459-11608
occurrences.motif_label: Good deity not author of evil
occurrences.basis: The speakers distinguish good from evil causation and state that God is cause of good only, with evil causes to be sought elsewhere.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The argument states that God must be represented as truly good; what is good does not hurt or cause evil; therefore God is cause of good only, not of most human evils.
“God is not the author of all things, but of good only.”

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 11459-11608
occurrences.motif_label: Conflict among gods and divine kin as prohibited model
occurrences.basis: The passage names wars in heaven, divine plots, fights, and quarrels among gods and relatives as stories to exclude because they would model civic conflict.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speakers say future guardians should not be told of wars in heaven, divine plots and fights, battles of giants, or quarrels of gods and heroes with friends and relatives.
The passage excludes stories of Hephaestus binding Hera, Zeus throwing Hephaestus for taking her part, and the battles of the gods in Homer, whether allegorical or not.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1180-1263
occurrences.motif_label: duality of State and individual
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly pairs and contrasts State and individual, ethics and politics, and collective and individual action.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says Plato preserves Greek thought by beginning with the State and proceeding to the individual; early persons are citizens of a prior State rather than isolated moral individuals.

The passage describes a confusion or identification of individual and State, ethics and politics; the good man and good citizen coincide only in the perfect State, achieved through education from within.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III.; lines 12405-12538
occurrences.motif_label: two opposed modes of speech
occurrences.basis: The passage divides speech and poetry into restrained narration with slight imitation and a changeful mimetic mode using many voices, gestures, harmonies, and rhythms.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A worse character is described as ready to imitate anything, including thunder, wind, hail, wheels, pulleys, instruments, and animal sounds, with little narration.

The two styles differ in simplicity and change: one keeps nearly the same harmony and rhythm, while the other requires all sorts of harmonies and rhythms; all poetry and verbal expression fall into these styles or their mixture.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III.; lines 12788-12962
occurrences.motif_label: harmonious union of beautiful soul and beautiful form
occurrences.basis: The passage presents soul and bodily form as harmonizing in one mould and later contrasts true harmonious love with intemperate pleasure.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A beautiful soul harmonizing with a beautiful form in one mould is called the fairest and loveliest sight.
Excess pleasure is separated from temperance and virtue; sensual love is called especially keen and mad, while true love is love of beauty and order, temperate and harmonious.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III.; lines 12964-13082
occurrences.motif_label: Simplicity as the source of health and temperance
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly contrasts simplicity with complexity and connects simplicity to temperance of soul and bodily health.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Complexity is said to engender licence and disease; simplicity in music produces temperance in the soul, and simplicity in gymnastic produces bodily health.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III.; lines 13198-13348
occurrences.motif_label: dual principles requiring harmony
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly names two principles of human nature, the spirited and the philosophical, and presents two corresponding arts that tune them into harmony.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The philosophical quality gives gentleness if rightly educated; guardians should have both qualities in harmony, making the soul temperate and courageous.
