“there are two principles of human nature, one the spirited and the other the philosophical,” and a god has given two arts so that the principles may be harmonized like instrument strings.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV.; lines 13653-13780
occurrences.motif_label: paired extremes corrupting the community
occurrences.basis: Wealth and poverty are paired as opposing conditions that both cause deterioration, discontent, and civic danger.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates identifies wealth and poverty as two causes of the deterioration of arts, beginning with the example that a rich potter becomes less diligent.
Socrates says that a poor potter lacks money for tools or instruments and therefore cannot work or teach sons and apprentices equally well.
Socrates calls wealth and poverty new evils to be watched against: wealth produces luxury and indolence, poverty produces meanness and viciousness, and both produce discontent.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV.; lines 13782-13921
occurrences.motif_label: unity of the ordered community against internal division
occurrences.basis: The passage contrasts the proposed one self-sufficing state with other cities divided into poor and rich factions at war with one another.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “any city, however small, is in fact divided into two, one the city of the poor, the other of the rich”
The speaker says the state should increase only so far as is consistent with unity, and guardians should account the city neither large nor small but one and self-sufficing.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV.; lines 14244-14387
occurrences.motif_label: dual principles within person and polity
occurrences.basis: The human soul and the State are both described through a relation between better and worse parts, with order depending on the better ruling the worse.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker explains that a human soul contains a better and a worse principle; one is master of oneself when the better controls the worse, and enslaved to self when the worse overwhelms the better.
The newly-created State is said to be master of itself if temperance and self-mastery mean the rule of the better part over the worse.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV.; lines 14689-14843
occurrences.motif_label: division of the soul by opposing impulses
occurrences.basis: The passage treats attraction and repulsion as opposites, then argues that a thirsty soul drawn toward drink and pulled away from drink must involve different principles.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker asks whether “assent and dissent, desire and aversion, attraction and repulsion” are opposites, and the respondent agrees.

If something pulls a thirsty soul away from drink, the speaker says it must be different from the thirsty principle that draws the soul to drink, since the same thing cannot act in contrary ways about the same object at the same time and in the same part.

evidence.locator: line 14843 and following sentence in supplied passage
evidence.quote_or_summary: The respondent agrees that “a man” may be thirsty and “yet unwilling to drink.”

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1483-1541
occurrences.motif_label: coexistence of popular worship and philosophical religion
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly contrasts poetic tradition, temple worship, and philosophical religion as coexisting forms.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Two forms of religion are described as existing side by side: poetic tradition and customary temple worship.
The philosopher's religion is described as dwelling in ideas while still offering a cock to Aesculapius and praying at sunrise.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1483-1541
occurrences.motif_label: inner falsehood opposed to outward or poetic deception
occurrences.basis: The 'lie in the soul' is contrasted with the 'lie in words,' distinguishing corruptive ignorance from verbal or literary accommodation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The lie in the soul is described as a true lie: corruption of highest truth and deception of the highest part of the soul, with examples involving false claims about God and knowledge.
The lie in words is contrasted as deception in play, poem, allegory, figure of speech, or accommodation, useless to gods but sometimes useful to humans.
Socrates answers the question about deceiving a madman and contrasts God and man; God is Truth, while mankind may appear partial or false.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV.; lines 14845-14992
occurrences.motif_label: Inner conflict among parts of the soul
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly describes conflict between reason, appetite, and spirit, including the Leontius example and the statement that anger goes to war with desire.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker distinguishes a soul-principle that bids a man to drink from a stronger forbidding principle, then names the reasoning element rational and the loving, hungering, thirsting element irrational or appetitive.

Leontius, son of Aglaion, comes from the Piraeus under the north wall, sees dead bodies at the place of execution, struggles between desire and abhorrence, covers his eyes, then forces them open and runs to look.
The tale is interpreted to mean that anger can go to war with desire; the speaker also compares inner struggle to factions in a State and says spirit sides with reason against violent desires.

The passage argues that passion or spirit is a third element, distinct from desire and reason, naturally auxiliary to reason; children, brute animals, and a Homeric line about smiting the breast and rebuking the soul are cited.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V.; lines 15528-15704
occurrences.motif_label: male-female duality examined through shared civic nature
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly contrasts male and female sex while arguing that sex difference alone does not determine civic education, administration, or guardianship.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker says pursuits should be assigned by actual fitness; bearing and begetting children alone do not prove women should receive a different education from men, so guardian wives should share guardian pursuits.

The speaker says there is no special faculty of state administration belonging to a woman as woman or a man by sex; gifts of nature are diffused in both, and the pursuits of men are also pursuits of women.

The speaker says one woman may have the guardian temper; men and women alike possess guardian-making qualities; qualified women are to be selected as companions and colleagues of similar men, and same natures should have same pursuits.
The speaker says the same education that makes a man a good guardian will make a woman a good guardian, because their original nature is the same.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1616-1687
occurrences.motif_label: paired war and peace harmonies
occurrences.basis: Dorian and Phrygian harmonies are retained as a pair, one for war and courage and the other for peace, obedience, instruction, or religious feeling.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Lamenting and convivial harmonies are banished; Dorian and Phrygian remain, one for war and courage and the other for peace, obedience, instruction, or religious feeling.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V.; lines 16453-16611
occurrences.motif_label: War versus domestic discord
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly distinguishes internal/domestic discord from external/foreign war and aligns each with different relationships of friend and enemy.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker distinguishes discord as internal and domestic from war as external and foreign.

The Hellenic race is described as united by blood and friendship, while barbarians are alien and strange; Hellenic conflict is discord among natural friends, whereas conflict with barbarians is war against natural enemies.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V.; lines 16613-16748
occurrences.motif_label: discord among friends resolved by correction
occurrences.basis: The passage contrasts discord among friends with war against enemies and prescribes correction rather than destruction.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Differences are described as discord, a quarrel among friends; the citizens will use friendly correction and will not enslave or destroy opponents.
The guardians are to enact a law against devastating Hellenic lands or burning Hellenic houses, because guilt belongs to a few while the many are friends.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V.; lines 16886-17066
occurrences.motif_label: Duality and mediation between opposed states
occurrences.basis: The dialogue repeatedly contrasts one and many, dream and waking, knowledge and opinion, being and not-being, and proposes an intermediate between knowledge and ignorance.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Just and unjust, good and evil, and every other class are said to be one singly but to appear many through combinations with actions, things, and one another.

The passage contrasts the dreamer, who puts a copy in place of the real object, with one who recognizes absolute beauty and distinguishes the idea from participating objects; the latter is called wide awake.

The dialogue argues that something that is can be known, what is utterly non-existent is unknown, and any intermediate between being and not-being would correspond to an intermediate between knowledge and ignorance.
Knowledge and opinion are both treated as faculties, but the respondent says infallible knowledge cannot be identified with opinion, which errs; their distinct powers imply distinct spheres.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1689-1772
occurrences.motif_label: Moral duality of simplicity and luxury
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly contrasts simple music, diet, and medicine with deforming art, strong drink, gluttony, luxurious cookery, legalism, and excessive medical care.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Artists and poets are warned against unseemliness; sculpture, painting, and music must conform to simplicity; guardians should grow among health and beauty, and music enters the innermost soul to shape the sense of beauty and deformity.

The passage turns from music to gymnastics, says soul is related to body as cause to effect, requires guardians to abstain from strong drink, and describes warrior athletes as wide-awake dogs hardened to changes of food and climate.
Homer is cited as feeding heroes on roast meat only, without fish, boiled meats, pots and pans, or sweet sauces; luxurious cookery, confections, courtezans, and certain melodies are forbidden.
Gluttony and intemperance are said to fill a town with doctors and pleaders; needing outside justice and taking pride in legal twists are presented as signs of bad education.

Asclepius is said to avoid prolonged disease-care because citizens in a well-ordered state have no leisure to be ill; he and his sons cure honest diseases and wounds but refuse intemperate and worthless subjects.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V.; lines 17068-17208
occurrences.motif_label: Duality of opposed predicates in sensible things
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly describes manifold things as bearing opposite predicates, such as beautiful and ugly, just and unjust, or being and not-being.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker addresses the lover of beautiful sights who rejects absolute beauty; the discussion states that beautiful, just, holy, great, small, heavy, and light things may also be described by opposite names, and compares individual objects to riddles with double sense.
The many ideas about beautiful and other things are said to be tossed in a region half-way between pure being and pure not-being; this intermediate flux is assigned to opinion.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 17211-17397
occurrences.motif_label: turning desire from bodily pleasures toward the soul
occurrences.basis: The speaker contrasts pleasures of the soul with bodily pleasure and uses the image of a stream drawn into another channel.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker says strong desires in one direction are weaker in others, like a stream drawn into another channel; the true philosopher’s desires are drawn toward knowledge and pleasures of the soul rather than bodily pleasure.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 18617-18744
occurrences.motif_label: dual ordering of visible and intelligible realms
occurrences.basis: The passage distinguishes two ruling powers, visible and intellectual worlds, and a divided line with corresponding subdivisions.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker asks the listener to imagine two ruling powers, one over the intellectual world and one over the visible, and to fix the distinction between visible and intelligible in mind.
A line is to be cut into two unequal parts, and each part divided again in the same proportion, with main divisions answering to visible and intelligible spheres and their relative clarity.
The sections have different degrees of truth; copy is to original as opinion is to knowledge.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 18781-18911
occurrences.motif_label: Shadow-world contrasted with real objects
occurrences.basis: The den presents a contrast between shadows taken as truth and later-seen objects and sunlight treated as clearer vision.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The prisoners see only their own shadows, one another's shadows, and the shadows of the carried objects.
If the prison had an echo, prisoners would think a passer-by's spoken voice came from the passing shadow; the truth for them would be only shadows of images.
When a prisoner is liberated and compelled to stand, turn, walk, and look toward the light, he suffers pain, is distressed by glare, and is perplexed when shown the objects.
Last of all, the prisoner can see the sun itself, not merely its reflection in water, and contemplate it in its own place.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19144-19306
occurrences.motif_label: perplexing opposites prompting higher inquiry
occurrences.basis: Opposed qualities such as great/small, hard/soft, and light/heavy are presented as sensory intimations that perplex the soul and require explanation by thought.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker distinguishes sense-objects that do not invite thought from those that do, saying that some sensations are adequate while others are untrustworthy and demand inquiry.

The speaker asks whether sight and touch adequately perceive great and small, thick and thin, hard and soft, light and heavy; the soul is said to be perplexed by the same thing being indicated through opposed qualities.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19468-19613
occurrences.motif_label: upward and downward orientation as epistemic contrast
occurrences.basis: The interlocutor presents astronomy as upward movement from this world to another, while Socrates opposes this with the claim that it may make people look downward.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The interlocutor says astronomy “compels the soul to look upwards” and leads from “this world to another.”
Socrates says those who elevate astronomy into philosophy seem to make people “look downwards and not upwards.”

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19615-19736
occurrences.motif_label: duality of sight and hearing as parallel disciplines
occurrences.basis: Astronomy and harmony are compared as sister sciences, one related to eyes and stars, the other to ears and harmonious motions.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The second science is related to ears as the first is to eyes; eyes look at stars, ears hear harmonious motions, and these are called sister sciences by the Pythagoreans.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19856-19996
occurrences.motif_label: appearance versus truth
occurrences.basis: The passage contrasts opinion with science, shadow with knowledge, and dreaming or slumbering with being awake to truth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Knowledge of the good requires rational definition and answering objections by truth; without it one apprehends only a shadow by opinion, dreams and slumbers in life, and then arrives at the world below.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII.; lines 20259-20385
occurrences.motif_label: city mirrors the soul
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly connects forms of government with dispositions of individual minds and says states grow out of human characters.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "States are as the men are; they grow out of human characters."

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII.; lines 20387-20491
occurrences.motif_label: discord born from mixture of unequal groups
occurrences.basis: Opposed metal groups are drawn different ways, battle, divide property, and create a regime marked by war and watchfulness.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Iron is mingled with silver and brass with gold, producing dissimilarity, inequality, irregularity, hatred, and war; the Muses call this the stock from which discord has sprung.

When discord arises, iron and brass pursue money, land, houses, gold, and silver, while gold and silver races incline toward virtue and the ancient order because they have true riches in their own nature.
The groups battle, then agree to distribute land and houses among individual owners; they enslave former friends and maintainers as subjects and servants and keep watch against them.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII.; lines 20493-20627
occurrences.motif_label: Divided inner life shaped by opposing influences
occurrences.basis: The youth is drawn opposite ways between the father's rational influence and other influences encouraging passion and appetite.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The young man hears and sees these things, compares his father with others, and is drawn opposite ways as the father nourishes the rational principle while others encourage the passionate and appetitive.
Because he is not originally bad but has bad company, the youth is brought to a middle point and gives the inner kingdom to contentiousness and passion, becoming arrogant and ambitious.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII.; lines 20629-20813
occurrences.motif_label: divided city of rich and poor
occurrences.basis: The oligarchical state is explicitly described as not one but two states, poor and rich, occupying the same place and conspiring against each other.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “such a State is not one, but two States, the one of poor, the other of rich men; and they are living on the same spot and always conspiring against one another.”

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 2076-2139
occurrences.motif_label: inner duality of higher and lower principles
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly frames human nature as divided between higher and lower principles, mind and body, reason and desire, and opposed tendencies.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage asks how far mind can control body, whether they are antagonistic or harmonious, describes higher and lower principles that may take up arms or reconcile, and says the body may become the mind’s ally or instrument.
One tendency says, ‘Drink’; another says, ‘Do not drink; it is not good for you,’ followed by remarks on rightful superiority, responsibility for health, and limited human freedom.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII.; lines 20815-20973
occurrences.motif_label: Inner enthronement of appetite over reason
occurrences.basis: The passage presents the person as an internal polity in which the covetous element becomes king and reason and spirit are subordinated.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "seat the concupiscent and covetous element on the vacant throne" and let it "play the great king within him, girt with tiara and chain and scimitar"
Reason and spirit are made to sit obediently on either side of the covetous sovereign and are directed toward turning smaller sums into larger ones and admiring riches and rich men.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII.; lines 20815-20973
occurrences.motif_label: Divided self as two persons
occurrences.basis: The miser is explicitly described as at war with himself and as two men rather than one.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "The man, then, will be at war with himself; he will be two men, and not one"

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII.; lines 21107-21266
occurrences.motif_label: political order mirrored in the individual soul
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly moves from the democratic city to the democratic individual and compares change in the city with change in the young man's soul.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker turns from the state to the individual and asks how the corresponding man comes into being.
The speaker compares the young man's change to change in the city, where an external alliance helps one internal division; similarly, external desires assist kindred internal desires.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII.; lines 21107-21266
occurrences.motif_label: inner civil war of desires
occurrences.basis: The young man's soul is described as divided into opposing factions, and he is said to go to war with himself.

evidence.quote_or_summary: If father or kindred support the oligarchical principle by advice or rebuke, faction and counter-faction arise in the soul and the young man goes to war with himself.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII.; lines 21407-21561
occurrences.motif_label: Excess liberty reverses into slavery and tyranny
occurrences.basis: The speaker states that excessive increase causes reaction in the opposite direction and that extreme liberty passes into extreme slavery and tyranny.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker says the same disease that ruins oligarchy ruins democracy, that excess causes reaction in the opposite direction in seasons and living things, and that excess liberty passes into excess slavery and tyranny.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 2141-2228
occurrences.motif_label: Duality within the city: rich and poor as hostile nations
occurrences.basis: Other states are described as not truly one state but many, because each contains two hostile nations, rich and poor.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Other states are called many in one because each contains two hostile nations, rich and poor, which can be set against each other; the true State remains mighty while faithful to its principles.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VI. / BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII. / BOOK IX.; lines 21842-21983
occurrences.motif_label: Conflict between rational and irrational principles in the soul
occurrences.basis: The passage contrasts reason with appetites and passion, and describes pacifying two irrational principles while rousing reason.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker says unlawful unnecessary appetites exist in everyone, but in some they are controlled by laws, reason, and better desires.
“when the reasoning and human and ruling power is asleep; then the wild beast within us... goes forth to satisfy his desires”
The temperate person awakens rational powers before sleep, moderates appetites, pacifies passion, rouses reason, and thereby comes nearest to truth and is least likely to suffer lawless visions.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VI. / BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII. / BOOK IX.; lines 21985-22135
occurrences.motif_label: inner tyranny of desire
occurrences.basis: The passage presents a structured analogy between the soul ruled by Love and desires and a city ruled by a tyrant; the inner ruler leads a rabble to lawless acts.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After parental property fails, pleasures swarm in the soul; old judgments are overthrown by passions that are Love's bodyguard. Love is tyrant and king, leading him to housebreaking, theft, temple robbery, murder, forbidden food, and other horrid acts, making waking reality what had been dream.
When the noxious class and their followers become numerous and aware of their strength, aided by popular infatuation, they choose the one with most tyrant in his soul and create him tyrant.
If resisted, the tyrant beats the people as he began by beating father and mother, and keeps his fatherland or motherland subject to young retainers.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VI. / BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII. / BOOK IX.; lines 21985-22135
occurrences.motif_label: dream transgression made waking life
occurrences.basis: The man becomes in waking reality what he had formerly been only rarely in dream, and the worst man is summarized as the waking reality of what was dreamed.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After parental property fails, pleasures swarm in the soul; old judgments are overthrown by passions that are Love's bodyguard. Love is tyrant and king, leading him to housebreaking, theft, temple robbery, murder, forbidden food, and other horrid acts, making waking reality what had been dream.

Such men associate with flatterers or tools, are always masters or servants and never friends, lack true freedom and friendship, are treacherous and unjust, and the worst man is the waking reality of what was dreamed.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VI. / BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII. / BOOK IX.; lines 22137-22315
occurrences.motif_label: Macrocosm and microcosm of political order and soul
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly states a parallel between State and individual, treating the condition of the city and the condition of the soul as corresponding forms.

evidence.locator: 22137-22315; opening comparison of men and states
evidence.quote_or_summary: The speakers agree that the tyrannical man resembles the tyrannical State, the democratic man resembles the democratic State, and so on.
The city governed by a tyrant is described as completely enslaved; only a few are free or masters, while the people generally and the best of them are degraded and enslaved.

evidence.locator: 22137-22315; soul likened to the tyrannical State
evidence.quote_or_summary: The tyrannical man's soul is said to be full of meanness and vulgarity, with the best elements enslaved and a small ruling part that is the worst and maddest.
The tyrannical city and tyrannical soul are described as poor, insatiable, fearful, and marked by lamentation, sorrow, groaning, pain, passions, and desires.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VI. / BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII. / BOOK IX.; lines 22824-22996
occurrences.motif_label: just king contrasted with tyrant
occurrences.basis: The passage contrasts the king and tyrant as opposite extremes in relation to true pleasure, pain, law, order, and justice.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The tyrant is said to live at the greatest distance from true or natural pleasure, while the king lives at the least distance and therefore most pleasantly.
The speaker describes three pleasures, places the tyrant far beyond spurious pleasure, and calculates that the king lives 729 times more pleasantly than the tyrant.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VI. / BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII. / BOOK IX.; lines 22998-23129
occurrences.motif_label: soul as composite creature
occurrences.basis: The human creature is represented as containing a man, a many-headed monster, and a lion or spirited animal whose relations determine justice or vice.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The unjust position is described as feeding the multitudinous monster, strengthening the lion, weakening the man, and letting the parts fight, bite, and devour one another.

The just position gives mastery to the man within, treats the many-headed monster like a husbandman cultivating gentle qualities and restraining wild ones, and makes the lion-heart an ally in uniting the parts.

Intemperance is tied to the multiform monster being too much at large; pride and bad temper to the lion and serpent element growing disproportionately; luxury and softness to weakening the same creature.
Flattery, meanness, and mean employments are explained through subordination of the spirited animal to the unruly monster, including the image of a lion becoming a monkey.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII. / BOOK IX. / BOOK X.; lines 23168-23363
occurrences.motif_label: appearance versus reality
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly contrasts forms or true existence with crafted objects and painted or mirrored appearances.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speakers begin an inquiry into imitation; the main speaker says things with a common name correspond to a form, using beds and tables as examples, and says artisans make particular objects but not the ideas themselves.

The speaker proposes that by turning a mirror around one could quickly make the sun, heavens, earth, oneself, animals, plants, and other things, but the respondent says these would be appearances only.
The painter is described as another creator of appearances whose created bed is not a real bed.
The passage identifies three beds and three corresponding artists: the bed in nature made by God, the bed made by the carpenter, and the bed made by the painter.
The painter is designated as "the imitator of that which the others make" and as "third in the descent from nature."

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 2331-2410
occurrences.motif_label: ordered harmony of higher and lower parts
occurrences.basis: Temperance is described through the relation of better and worse principles and through the harmonious attunement of upper, middle, and lower classes.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Temperance is described as mastery of the worse by the better and as harmony diffused through the city, attuning upper, middle, and lower classes like strings of an instrument.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII. / BOOK IX. / BOOK X.; lines 23653-23817
occurrences.motif_label: divided soul with opposed principles
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly distinguishes rational and irrational principles in the soul and states that being drawn in opposite directions implies two distinct principles.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The part of the soul that trusts measure and calculation is called better; the part opposed to them is called an inferior principle.
A principle of law and reason bids resistance to sorrow while a feeling of misfortune forces indulgence; opposite directions imply distinct principles.
The principle that inclines people to recollect troubles and lament, never having enough of them, is called irrational, useless, and cowardly.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII. / BOOK IX. / BOOK X.; lines 23819-23921
occurrences.motif_label: reason governing passion
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly opposes law and reason to pity, laughter, lust, anger, pain, and pleasure, and says passions should be controlled for happiness and virtue.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker says the same pattern holds for ridicule: laughter restrained by reason is released at comedy and may lead the spectator to comic behavior at home.
The speaker extends the claim to lust, anger, desire, pain, and pleasure, saying poetry feeds and waters passions rather than drying them up, letting them rule when they ought to be controlled.
The speaker warns that if the honeyed muse enters in epic or lyric verse, pleasure and pain rather than law and reason will rule the State.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII. / BOOK IX. / BOOK X.; lines 24305-24376
occurrences.motif_label: right and left paths differentiated by moral status
occurrences.basis: The just are directed to the right-hand heavenly way while the unjust are directed to the left-hand lower way.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The judges send the just upward to the right and the unjust downward to the left; the souls bear symbols or sentences of their deeds.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 2456-2517
occurrences.motif_label: Opposing impulses within one person
occurrences.basis: The thirst example contrasts animal desire with rational restraint, and the Leontius story contrasts desire to see with abhorrence.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "the animal one saying ‘Drink;’ the rational one, which says ‘Do not drink.’"
Leontius comes up from the Piraeus outside the north wall and passes dead bodies lying by the executioner.
"at first he turned away and shut his eyes, then, suddenly tearing them open" and addressed them: "Take your fill, ye wretches, of the fair sight."

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 2519-2584
occurrences.motif_label: Harmony versus disorder of the soul
occurrences.basis: The passage opposes justice and injustice, virtue and vice, health and disease, and harmony and insubordination in the soul.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage explains justice through each principle doing its own business and says justice binds together the three chords of the soul and acts harmoniously.
The passage calls injustice the insubordination of inferior elements, compares it to disease in the body, and describes virtue as health and beauty of the soul and vice as disease and deformity.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 253-329
occurrences.motif_label: duality resolved into unity
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly presents paired structures—two parts of the work, justice and State as two faces of one truth, soul and body, idea and reality, inner and external kingdom—while emphasizing their blending or attempted unification.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Books I-IV are said to describe a State in accordance with Hellenic religion and morality; Books V-X transform it into an ideal kingdom of philosophy, and the two viewpoints are opposed though veiled by Plato's genius.
"the two blend in one, and are two faces of the same truth; for justice is the order of the State, and the State is the visible embodiment of justice"

The passage describes justice and the State through analogies: soul and body, idea and reality, inner kingdom and external kingdom, heavenly house reduced to earthly building, and warp and woof in a texture.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 2586-2659
occurrences.motif_label: ordered inner division of the soul
occurrences.basis: The passage describes the soul as divided into rational, irascible, and concupiscent elements, with the irascible element both irrational and inclined toward reason.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Plato's psychology is described as dividing the soul into rational, irascible, and concupiscent elements, a division retained by Aristotle and later ethical writers.
The irascible faculty is described through righteous indignation, spirit, passion, and courage; though irrational, it inclines to side with the rational element.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 2661-2743
occurrences.motif_label: shared education for women and men guardians
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly argues that women and men with the same relevant natures should share education in music, gymnastics, and war.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says guardians are like watch-dogs; male and female dogs share employments, so women with the same employments as men need the same education in music, gymnastics, and war, though this may provoke jokes about riding, weapons, and naked exercise.

Socrates argues that differences may be nominal or partial, comparing bald and hairy people, male and female physicians, and physician versus carpenter; he says begetting and bearing children do not prove distinct educations and that aptitudes are found among both sexes.
Socrates concludes that women of the right nature should receive the same education, be colleagues of the guardians, and share war and defense of the country; those who laugh are called foolish.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 2661-2743
occurrences.motif_label: partial difference versus true difference of nature
occurrences.basis: Socrates distinguishes accidental differences such as bald and hairy or male and female physician from differences that entail different work, such as physician and carpenter.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates argues that differences may be nominal or partial, comparing bald and hairy people, male and female physicians, and physician versus carpenter; he says begetting and bearing children do not prove distinct educations and that aptitudes are found among both sexes.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 2829-2913
occurrences.motif_label: dual distinction between civil discord and foreign war
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly divides war into civil and foreign types and treats Hellenic war as discord within a family.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “war is of two kinds, civil and foreign”

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 2915-3003
occurrences.motif_label: duality of being and not-being
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly opposes being and not-being and places opinion in an intermediate region that partakes of both.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Knowledge is of what is, ignorance of what is not, and opinion concerns a third thing that both is and is not; opinion and knowledge are distinct faculties with distinct objects.
Opinion lies between knowledge and ignorance and is “darker than the one and brighter than the other.”
The old riddle says: “A man and not a man shot and did not shoot a bird and not a bird with a stone and not a stone.”

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 3256-3342
occurrences.motif_label: Dual division of visible and intelligible realms
occurrences.basis: The passage distinguishes two corresponding worlds, visible and intelligible, under the image of a divided line.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Two suns or principles are paired with two worlds, visible and intelligible, represented by a line divided into unequal and subdivided parts.
The lower visible sphere contains shadows and reflections, while the upper visible sphere contains real objects of nature or art.
The intelligible sphere includes mathematics, where the mind works with figures and numbers and uses hypotheses.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 331-413
occurrences.motif_label: false teachers and evil rulers opposed to the ideal order
occurrences.basis: The passage contrasts divine and human perfection with poets, sophists, and tyrants described as false teachers and evil rulers.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Republic is described as a vehicle of several great truths represented in the State, with an explicit comparison to Jewish prophetic images and with themes of good, justice, education, false teachers, evil rulers, the world, and a heavenly kingdom as pattern.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 3589-3670
occurrences.motif_label: Hierarchy from shadow to reason
occurrences.basis: The divided line arranges shadows, objects, understanding, and reason in a hierarchy from lower perception to higher certainty.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The line is described as reaching from unity to infinity, divided and subdivided; the passage also mentions shadows, images, faith, understanding, and reason.
True knowledge is described as whole and at rest; understanding is incomplete and in motion, while ideas are called images and hypotheses until connected with the idea of good.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 3822-3899
occurrences.motif_label: Duality of visible and intelligible
occurrences.basis: The passage contrasts sense perception with mind, visible objects with intelligible being, and becoming with being.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage asks for the way “from darkness to light” and describes philosophy as “the conversion of a soul from night to day, from becoming to being.”

The passage explains that certain sensible things stimulate the mind by presenting contrast and relation, such as three fingers, great and small, one and more than one, and visible versus intelligible.
Geometry is introduced as the second branch of education; Glaucon notes its military usefulness, but the speaker says its higher use is contemplation of the idea of good and true being.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 3901-3981
occurrences.motif_label: Duality of sense and intellect
occurrences.basis: The passage opposes bodily eye and soul’s eye, visible heavens and divine Original, empirical hearing and unheard numerical harmony, and sense and pure intellect.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Astronomy is proposed; Glaucon names practical uses; Socrates says education is not merely useful information but a purification of the eye of the soul by which truth is seen.

The heavens are described as the embroidery of a copy below the divine Original; their visible beauty can illustrate but cannot yield exact equality or numerical relations because matter disturbs symmetry.
Musicians put ears in place of minds; empirics dispute notes and manipulate lyre strings; Pythagorean harmonists investigate heard consonances but not unheard numerical harmony found in problems.
Dialectic is compared with the effort of sight moving from shadows to the images that gave the shadows, and is said to withdraw from sense toward contemplation of the idea of good.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 4309-4393
occurrences.motif_label: political order mirrored in individual nature
occurrences.basis: The passage says that five States correspond to five human natures in individuals and proceeds from forms of government to matching types of people.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The four notable inferior constitutions are Lacedaemonian or Cretan, oligarchy, democracy, and tyranny; tyranny is the disease or death of government; States are of flesh and blood, so five States correspond to five human natures.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 4478-4569
occurrences.motif_label: divided city or divided polity
occurrences.basis: The oligarchical state is explicitly described as two struggling nations, the rich and the poor, within one state.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The oligarchical state is described as two nations, rich and poor, struggling together; the rich fear arming the poor and resist paying for defenders.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 4571-4620
occurrences.motif_label: divided soul as opposed factions
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly describes opposed alliances and factions within the individual, with violent conflict between order and disorder.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “The youth who has had a miserly bringing up, gets a taste of the drone’s honey; he meets with wild companions, who introduce him to every new pleasure.”

The passage describes allies on both sides, with temptations and passions opposed to reason, parents, and friends; passions seize the Acropolis, glossed as the soul, and falsehoods and illusions ascend.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 4623-4685
occurrences.motif_label: Excess turning into its opposite
occurrences.basis: The passage states a law of contraries in which excess freedom passes into excess slavery.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Excess freedom passes into excess slavery; rogues and paupers are compared to drones with and without stings, to phlegm and bile, and the legislator to a physician or bee-master keeping drones from the hive.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 4687-4772
occurrences.motif_label: excessive liberty turns into slavery
occurrences.basis: The passage says the people pass from fear of slavery into slavery and that disordered liberty becomes the worst servitude.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “the people have jumped from the fear of slavery into slavery, out of the smoke into the fire.”

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 4774-4869
occurrences.motif_label: divided community as two nations in one
occurrences.basis: The passage notes the description of two nations in one becoming increasingly divided in Greek Republics.

evidence.locator: lines 4867-4869 and following listed remarks in supplied passage
evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage notes that Book VIII uses many metaphors, including two nations in one, equality among unequals, the free ways of men and animals, foreign mercenaries, and universal mistrust.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 4871-4959
occurrences.motif_label: duality of perfect divine cycle and imperfect human cycle
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly contrasts a perfect or cyclical divine number with a human or imperfect number concerning births and generations.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Plato is said to speak of a perfect or cyclical divine number and a human or imperfect number; the latter concerns generations or births and presides over them like stars or Pythagorean numerical figures, probably as the number 216.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 5050-5130
occurrences.motif_label: duality of perfect divine order and imperfect human generation
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly contrasts divine creation as perfect with human generation as imperfect, each represented by different kinds of number.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says Plato used a numerical symbol, retained much Pythagorean spirit, and contrasted perfect divine creation presided over by a cyclical number with imperfect human generation presided over by imperfect numbers.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 5050-5130
occurrences.motif_label: reason restraining lawless appetites
occurrences.basis: The passage contrasts reason and law with unlawful appetites that awaken when reasoning powers sleep.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Book IX begins with inquiry into the tyrannical man and then describes unlawful appetites, which can be weakened by reason and law but wake when reason sleeps.
A temperate man who has prepared himself with reason and self-knowledge before sleep has less abnormal visions; even good men have a wild-beast nature that appears in sleep.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 5132-5213
occurrences.motif_label: enslavement of the better part by the worse
occurrences.basis: The soul and State are described in terms of bad freedom and good slavery, with the better part enslaved to the worse.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The judge compares individual and State: both have little freedom and much slavery; the better part is enslaved to the worse; the public tyrant is still more miserable.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 5331-5398
occurrences.motif_label: inner conflict between beast and higher self
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly contrasts the beast with the man or God in man, and defines noble and ignoble conduct by which part rules the other.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Injustice feeds the beasts and starves the man; justice strengthens the man, nourishes the gentle principle, allies with the lion heart, restrains the many-headed hydra, and brings the parts into unity.
The noble subjects the beast to the man or God in man; selling the diviner part for wealth is compared with selling children to brutal men and with Eriphyle selling her husband’s life for a necklace.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 5400-5481
occurrences.motif_label: moral distance between king and tyrant
occurrences.basis: The king and tyrant are contrasted through the interval of 729 and through royal versus tyrannical pleasures.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "The number of the interval which separates the king from the tyrant, and royal from tyrannical pleasures, is 729, the cube of 9."
The passage describes Plato as using a progression of numbers and a geometrical figure to express the immeasurable interval between royal and tyrannical life.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 5541-5616
occurrences.motif_label: divided soul under conflicting influences
occurrences.basis: The passage describes opposed influences within a person: feeling and sorrow on one side, reason and law on the other.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage contrasts sorrowful feeling with reason and law, which enjoin patience; it advises seeking a rational cure rather than lamenting.
The poet is compared with the painter as producing a lesser truth and engaging the inferior part of the soul, indulging feeling and weakening reason.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 5618-5704
occurrences.motif_label: Duality of body and immortal soul
occurrences.basis: The passage distinguishes body and soul, treating bodily destruction as unlike the soul’s condition and arguing that the soul is immortal and everlasting.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage argues that all things have inherent good and evil; the soul’s corruptions include injustice, intemperance, and cowardice, but these do not destroy it as disease destroys the body.
The body and soul are distinguished; bodily evils such as disease or violence cannot destroy the soul unless they make it unholy and unjust, which is denied.
Because neither internal nor external evil destroys the soul, it is called immortal and everlasting; souls are said to remain the same in number, neither diminishing nor increasing.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 5943-6033
occurrences.motif_label: opposition of appearance and truth
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly opposes appearances, sense, particulars, and opinion to truth, universals, reasoning, and abstract ideas.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Plato introduces objections that the poet or painter is an imitator, removed from truth and producing appearances; the analysis contrasts this with modern views of art and mentions Pheidias's Zeus or Athene.
Plato rejoices in banishing poets, associates them with inferior faculties, treats Homer and Hesiod as no rule of life, and is described as opposing poetry to philosophy, sense to abstract ideas.

The passage says Scripture opposes seen to unseen things and that Plato similarly opposes particulars of sense to universals and ideas; it then critiques Plato's treatment of particulars and universals.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 6209-6282
occurrences.motif_label: immortal soul opposed to body
occurrences.basis: The passage describes an argument resting on absolute dualism of soul and body and on the soul's resistance to destruction.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The argument for immortality is said to rest on absolute dualism of soul and body; vice is the soul's proper evil, and Plato is said to waver between an original soul to be restored and a character formed by training and education.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 6668-6744
occurrences.motif_label: gender duality reworked as shared civic training
occurrences.basis: The passage frames men and women as a paired contrast and summarizes Plato's argument that both should share occupations, training, education, and civic roles.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says community of property was less difficult for Plato and Aristotle than community of wives and children, and that Plato proposed same occupations, training, and education for men and women.

The passage reports objections about different natures and division of labour, then says Plato answered that men and women differ organically only in begetting and bearing children, and that natural gifts are scattered among both sexes.

The passage says Plato's ideal woman is companion of the man, sharing the toils of war, cares of government, and bodily and mental exercises, while losing as far as possible the incidents of maternity and female sex characteristics.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 6824-6912
occurrences.motif_label: Mind-body duality in social order
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly contrasts body and mind, animal and human, physical and moral, and argues against separating body and mind in marriage.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage contrasts humans with animals; says humans are not bred for physical utility; calls for marriage of minds and bodies; states that Plato’s arrangement removes parental knowledge, family affection, and private children; and notes that nobler animals protect offspring and remain faithful.
The passage questions placing life on a physical basis, prioritizes the moral, human, and rational, and says mind, reason, duty, conscience, truth, and mental health cannot be excluded.

The passage says Plato separated body and mind in marriage, contradicted his idealism, opposed the family sentiment of Hellas, may have been misled by Sparta, and would make one family from all families by selecting the finest men and women for breeding.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 6989-7077
occurrences.motif_label: human moral duality
occurrences.basis: The passage describes humans as moving between good and evil and warns against ungoverned passions.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage contrasts reformers who isolate the animal part of human nature with the speaker's view of humans as many-sided, moving between good and evil, and striving to rise above themselves.
The passage warns of a condition in which human passions are controlled by no divine or human authority, with no shame, decency, or higher affection sanctifying natural instincts.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 7309-7390
occurrences.motif_label: Personal and impersonal forms of the divine
occurrences.basis: The passage contrasts Hebrew, Greek, Christian, and modern conceptions of God, the Idea of Good, and divine perfection in personal or impersonal form.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Hebrew prophet is said to believe faith in God enables governance, while the Greek philosopher imagines contemplation of the good makes a legislator; both find repose in divine perfection.
The passage notes that the Timaeus lacks mention of the idea of good and the Republic lacks mention of the divine Creator, then asks how they are related.
The passage suggests the Idea of Good is another mode of conceiving God, contrasting Greek philosophical abstraction with Christian or modern difficulty in treating abstraction as real.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 7392-7476
occurrences.motif_label: state as individual analogy
occurrences.basis: The passage describes Plato as assimilating the state to the individual and looking for parallels between state succession and individual lives.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Plato assimilates the state to the individual, does not distinguish ethics from politics, and treats a state as most itself when it resembles one man with uniform citizens.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 7560-7638
occurrences.motif_label: body subordinated to mind
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly distinguishes body and mind and describes the body as servant of the mind, with lower subject to higher.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Music and gymnastic are both said to improve the mind; the body is described as the servant of the mind, and other Greek writers are contrasted with Plato on Spartan discipline.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 8057-8096
occurrences.motif_label: Communal unity as ideal polity
occurrences.basis: The highest state is defined by the removal of private individuality and by common property, family relations, emotional responses, and civic judgment, producing maximal unity.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The highest state is described by the saying “Friends have all things in common,” including communion of women, children, and property, with private and individual life banished and common praise, blame, joy, and sorrow.
No other principle is said to constitute a state more exalted in virtue; a state inhabited by Gods or sons of Gods would make them blessed, and this state is to be treated as the pattern.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 8057-8096
occurrences.motif_label: Primitive innocence contrasted with civilized knowledge
occurrences.basis: The Statesman myth contrasts a state of innocence with a state like the present, possessing art and science and distinguishing good from evil.

evidence.quote_or_summary: As in the Republic, the Statesman has a myth, but it describes a former rather than future existence of mankind; it asks whether a state of innocence or one with art, science, and moral distinction is preferable, and gives no answer.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 8098-8150
occurrences.motif_label: dual civic body within one polity
occurrences.basis: The passage contrasts public talk about two Suns with Cicero’s interest in the two nations in one that divided Rome.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Cicero turns from heavenly phenomena to civil and political life, preferring discussion of Rome’s two nations in one; speaking as Scipio, he avoids assuming too much the character of a teacher.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 8152-8239
occurrences.motif_label: Dual sacred and worldly kingdoms
occurrences.basis: Augustine is said to trace the kingdom of God and the kingdoms of the world as parallel histories into an ideal future.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Augustine traces the kingdom of God in Jewish scripture and the kingdoms of the world in gentile writers into an ideal future, treating heathen mythology, Sybilline oracles, Plato’s myths, and Neo-Platonist dreams as factual.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 837-921
occurrences.motif_label: Opposition of justice and injustice
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly structures the inquiry as a contrast between just and unjust, virtue and vice, wisdom and folly, skill and unskill, strength and weakness, and happiness and unhappiness.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage turns to Thrasymachus's assertion that injustice is more gainful than justice; he is led to say that injustice is virtue and justice vice.
Socrates is said to be weaving a net around Thrasymachus and uses the analogy of musician, doctor, and skilled artist to compare the just with the skilled and the unjust with the unskilled.
“A house that is divided against itself cannot stand”; the passage also says Thrasymachus perspired and blushed, and that injustice requires a remnant of justice for united action.
The passage asks whether the just or unjust person is happier and answers that happiness is the end of the soul and justice the soul's excellence by which happiness is attained.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 8572-8629
occurrences.motif_label: paired future hopes: world-future and otherworld-future
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly presents two ideals, one concerning the human race in this world and the other concerning the individual in another world.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Two ideals are introduced: the future of the human race in this world and the future of the individual in another; one realizes present life, while the other abnegates and transcends it.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 923-1012
occurrences.motif_label: moral harmony opposed to discord
occurrences.basis: The passage contrasts harmony of soul and body with evil as discord and dissolution.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “The harmony of the soul and body, and of the parts of the soul with one another” is called the Hellenic mode of conceiving human perfection.
In the epilogue with Thrasymachus, Plato argues that evil is not strength but discord and dissolution.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS. / THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I.; lines 9637-9730
occurrences.motif_label: opposition of justice and injustice
occurrences.basis: The passage presents justice and injustice as opposed principles, with Thrasymachus assigning loss and service to justice and profit, strength, freedom, and mastery to injustice.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Thrasymachus contrasts shepherds or neatherds and rulers, then states that justice is another's good, the interest of the ruler and stronger, while subjects serve that interest.
Thrasymachus says the just person loses and the unjust person gains in contracts, taxes, public receipts, and public office.

Thrasymachus describes tyranny as the highest injustice, taking property by fraud and force, including sacred and profane, public and private things, and enslaving citizens; such a person is called happy and blessed when successful.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS. / THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I.; lines 9862-10053
occurrences.motif_label: Opposed moral pairs: justice and injustice, good and bad, wise and foolish
occurrences.basis: The argument is structured through paired oppositions: justice versus injustice, virtue versus vice, wisdom versus foolishness, knowledge versus ignorance, and like versus unlike.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "You say that perfect injustice is more gainful than perfect justice?" Thrasymachus answers that this is what he says.
Thrasymachus rejects the expected classification of justice as virtue and injustice as vice, calling justice "sublime simplicity" and injustice "discretion."
The speaker says he is amazed that Thrasymachus classes injustice with wisdom and virtue, and observes that Thrasymachus attributes to the unjust qualities previously attributed to the just.

Through questions and answers, the just person is described as not seeking more than another just person but seeking more than the unjust; the unjust person is described as claiming more than the just and striving for more than all, including other unjust persons.

The speaker generalizes to knowledge and ignorance: the knowledgeable person would not wish to say or do more than another knowledgeable person in the same case, while the ignorant person would desire more than both the knowing and the ignorant.
The exchange concludes that the wise and good will not desire to gain more than their like but more than their opposite, whereas the bad and ignorant will desire more than both.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 1355-1438
occurrences.motif_label: two opposed forms of a divine power
occurrences.basis: The passage divides Aphrodite and Love into heavenly and common forms and builds the argument on this paired contrast.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Pausanias says Love should not be praised indiscriminately and that, since there is more than one Love, the speaker must determine which Love is to be praised.

Pausanias says Love is inseparable from Aphrodite; there are two Aphrodites and therefore two Loves: heavenly Aphrodite, daughter of Uranus with no mother, and common Aphrodite, daughter of Zeus and Dione.
The Love from common Aphrodite is described as common, undiscriminating, bodily, directed toward women as well as youths, and careless about noble accomplishment.
The Love from heavenly Aphrodite is described as from the male only, without wantonness, turning toward males of valiant and intelligent nature, and seeking faithful lifelong companionship.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 1439-1491
occurrences.motif_label: dual classification of love as noble or base
occurrences.basis: The passage opposes honourable and dishonourable pursuit, good and evil lovers, and body-directed versus soul- or disposition-directed love.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker says the matter is not simple: practices are honourable when followed honourably and dishonourable when followed dishonourably.
The evil or vulgar lover loves the body rather than the soul; because the loved thing is unstable, he flies away when youth's bloom is over.
The love of noble disposition is lifelong because it becomes one with the everlasting.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 1493-1543
occurrences.motif_label: dual forms of love from two goddesses
occurrences.basis: The passage contrasts heavenly love associated with a heavenly goddess and other loves as offspring of a common goddess.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Acceptance for the sake of virtue is noble; this love is called heavenly, of the heavenly goddess, and valuable to individuals and cities; other loves are offspring of the common goddess.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 150-231
occurrences.motif_label: dual love divided into higher and lower forms
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly distinguishes two loves: heavenly and earthly, noble and coarse, good and bad.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Pausanias says Phaedrus should distinguish heavenly and earthly love; he identifies two Aphrodites and contrasts their associated loves.
Eryximachus agrees there are two loves, extends them to animals, plants, and the body, and describes medicine, other arts, music, and Heracleitus' harmony of opposites in relation to reconciliation.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 150-231
occurrences.motif_label: divine doublet grounding ethical distinction
occurrences.basis: The two loves are explicitly linked to two Aphrodites with different genealogies and qualities.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Pausanias says Phaedrus should distinguish heavenly and earthly love; he identifies two Aphrodites and contrasts their associated loves.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 150-231
occurrences.motif_label: reconciliation of opposites through love
occurrences.basis: Medicine, arts, music, and bodily processes are described as reconciling conflicting elements and producing harmony after opposition.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Eryximachus agrees there are two loves, extends them to animals, plants, and the body, and describes medicine, other arts, music, and Heracleitus' harmony of opposites in relation to reconciliation.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 150-231
occurrences.motif_label: seasonal harmony and disorder
occurrences.basis: The passage applies harmony and disagreement to seasons and paired qualities such as moist/dry and hot/cold, with disease arising from disorder.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage applies harmony and disagreement to seasons, elemental pairs, heavenly bodies, divination, piety and impiety, and friendship with gods and humans.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 1545-1608
occurrences.motif_label: duality of love
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly distinguishes two loves: healthy and diseased, fair and foul, heavenly and vulgar.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Eryximachus says Pausanias distinguished two kinds of love, and adds that double love exists in bodies, animals, productions of the earth, and all that is; love is a universal deity over divine and human things.
The human body is said to have two unlike loves and desires, healthy and diseased; medicine concerns knowing bodily loves and desires and how to satisfy or refuse them.

In practical music and education, the speaker repeats the distinction between fair heavenly love connected with Urania and vulgar Polyhymnia, urging temperance and circumspection so pleasure does not become licentiousness or disease.
Eryximachus infers that in music, medicine, and all things human and divine, both loves are present and should be noted.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 1610-1659
occurrences.motif_label: Dual loves as ordering and disordering powers
occurrences.basis: The passage contrasts harmonious or good love with wanton or evil love across seasons, ritual life, piety, and human-divine relations.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The seasons contain both principles; harmonious blending of hot/cold and moist/dry brings health and plenty, while wanton love brings pestilence, disease, hoar-frost, hail, and blight.
Sacrifices and divination are described as the art of communion between gods and men; divination is called “the peacemaker of gods and men.”
Good love perfected with temperance and justice has great power, produces happiness and harmony, and makes humans friends with gods and one another.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 1661-1745
occurrences.motif_label: primordial doubled beings split into halves
occurrences.basis: The passage states that humans were originally doubled round beings and that Zeus cut them in two, producing the present divided human condition.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Original human nature is said to have had three sexes: man, woman, and Androgynous; primeval humans were round and had four hands, four feet, two faces on one head, four ears, two sexual organs, and corresponding parts.
Zeus proposes to humble humans by cutting them in two, decreasing their strength, increasing their numbers, and threatening further division if they remain insolent.
The speaker states that ancient desire reunites original nature, makes one out of two, and heals the human condition.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 1746-1831
occurrences.motif_label: Separated halves seeking reunion
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly describes people as halves of an original whole who seek their own true loves and a return to their primeval nature.

evidence.quote_or_summary: When one meets the other half of himself, the pair are absorbed in love, friendship, and intimacy, remain together, and feel an intense yearning of the soul beyond ordinary intercourse.

The speaker says the wish to become one expresses an ancient need: humans were once one and whole; God dispersed them because of wickedness; further disobedience could cause further splitting, like profile figures or tallies.

The speaker exhorts piety, calls Love lord, minister, and greatest benefactor, says Love leads people back to their own nature, and promises restoration, healing, happiness, and blessedness if humans are pious.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 1833-1883
occurrences.motif_label: youthful benevolent deity opposed to age
occurrences.basis: Agathon presents Love as youngest and ever youthful, fleeing and hating Age, with youth and love moving together.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Agathon says Love is the fairest and best, the youngest of the gods, flees Age, and lives and moves with youth.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 1833-1883
occurrences.motif_label: divine violence replaced by peaceful rule
occurrences.basis: Agathon contrasts earlier chaining, mutilation, and violence among gods under Necessity with peace and sweetness in heaven under Love’s rule.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Agathon denies that Love is older than Iapetus and Kronos; he says ancient divine acts reported by Hesiod and Parmenides were done by Necessity, and that Love would have prevented chaining, mutilation, and violence, bringing peace and sweetness in heaven.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 1885-1974
occurrences.motif_label: love conquers war
occurrences.basis: The God of War is described as captive and servant, while Love is lord and master through the love of Aphrodite.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The God of War is described as no match for Love: he is captive, Love is lord, and the love of Aphrodite masters him.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 2102-2198
occurrences.motif_label: intermediate being between opposed states
occurrences.basis: Diotima says right opinion stands between wisdom and ignorance and that Love is between fair and foul, good and evil.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Diotima argues that Love is neither fair nor good, but not therefore foul or evil; she gives right opinion as a mean between wisdom and ignorance and places Love in a mean between opposites.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 2200-2261
occurrences.motif_label: being defined by a mean between opposites
occurrences.basis: Love is repeatedly placed between mortal and immortal, divine and mortal, poverty and plenty, ignorance and knowledge, life and death, and wisdom and foolishness.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Diotima says Love is neither mortal nor immortal, but a great daimon between divine and mortal; he conveys prayers and sacrifices to gods and divine commands and replies to humans, spanning the chasm between them.

Love is neither mortal nor immortal; he flourishes when in plenty, is dead at another moment, and lives again by his father’s nature. He is neither in want nor wealth and is between ignorance and knowledge.
