Diotima says lovers of wisdom are those between the wise and the foolish; Love is one of them because wisdom is beautiful and Love is of the beautiful. His father is wealthy and wise, his mother poor and foolish.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 2263-2316
occurrences.motif_label: rejected search for the other half
occurrences.basis: The passage cites the idea that lovers seek their other half but explicitly qualifies or rejects it unless the half or whole is good.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Diotima notes the saying that lovers seek their other half, but says they seek neither half nor whole unless it is good, adding that people would discard even their own hands or feet if evil.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 233-318
occurrences.motif_label: Primordial composite humanity divided into sexes
occurrences.basis: The passage presents human nature as originally three-sexed and round, later cut into halves by Zeus.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says human nature originally had three sexes and that the original beings were round, with four hands, four feet, and two faces.
Zeus proposes cutting the beings in two so that their strength is halved and sacrifices are doubled.
Zeus splits them, and Apollo is told to turn their faces, rearrange their bodies, remove wrinkles, and tie the skin at the navel.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 2836-2933
occurrences.motif_label: hidden wisdom inside a ridiculous exterior
occurrences.basis: Socrates’ speech is described as ridiculous at first and clothed in satyr-like language, but when opened it contains divine, virtuous meaning.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates’ words are likened to Silenus images that open: outwardly ridiculous and satyr-like, speaking of ordinary trades and animals, but inwardly full of meaning, divine quality, and images of virtue.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 2836-2933
occurrences.motif_label: Silenus or satyr-like wise figure
occurrences.basis: Alcibiades says Socrates’ closest likeness is Silenus and the satyrs, and that this figure represents both Socrates and his words.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Alcibiades says Socrates is absolutely unlike any human being, unlike comparisons among famous men, and has no likeness except the earlier figure of Silenus and the satyrs.

Socrates’ words are likened to Silenus images that open: outwardly ridiculous and satyr-like, speaking of ordinary trades and animals, but inwardly full of meaning, divine quality, and images of virtue.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 320-409
occurrences.motif_label: mixed parentage producing a dual-natured figure
occurrences.basis: Love’s parentage from Plenty and Poverty explains his alternating fullness and deprivation and his mixture of poverty and resourcefulness.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Diotima answers that Love is the son of Plenty and Poverty, shares both natures, is poor and squalid yet bold and resourceful, and stands between ignorance and knowledge like the philosopher.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 411-502
occurrences.motif_label: Cosmic duality through opposites
occurrences.basis: Male and female are set alongside odd and even and finite and infinite in the Pythagorean list of opposites.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage discusses gender, sex in plants, elemental affinities, marriages of earth and heaven, Love as a mythic personage and cause of creation, and male/female among Pythagorean opposites.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 593-675
occurrences.motif_label: dual forms of Love
occurrences.basis: Pausanias distinguishes elder and younger Love and evaluates loves according to their manner of performance.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Pausanias is described as upholder of male loves, appealing to mythology, distinguishing elder and younger Love, and defending such loves as motives to virtue and philosophy.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 593-675
occurrences.motif_label: harmony of opposites after discord
occurrences.basis: Eryximachus explains Love through harmony after discord and harmony in soul, body, heaven, and earth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Eryximachus treats Love as the good physician, extends love and strife to body and mind, explains harmony of opposites as harmony after discord, and summarizes Love as harmony in soul, body, heaven, and earth.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 593-675
occurrences.motif_label: divided beings seeking reunion
occurrences.basis: Aristophanes' account is summarized as teaching that humans cannot exist in isolation, must be reunited to be perfected, and anticipate an ideal union.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage identifies three principles in Aristophanes' jest: humans cannot exist in isolation, must be reunited to be perfected, Love mediates divided human nature, and worldly loves anticipate an unrealized ideal union.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 677-763
occurrences.motif_label: union of reason and passion
occurrences.basis: The passage describes reason and passion as apparently antagonistic, while the Symposium's theme is the 'passion of the reason' and the union of spiritual and fleshly aspects.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage connects the Symposium with Neoplatonism and so-called Eastern mysticism, describes reason and passion as apparently antagonistic, calls the theme the 'passion of the reason,' and uses the image of truth's light and desire's warmth.

The passage describes arrival at a vision of the eternal, the idea as love or truth, the lover of wisdom as spectator of all time and existence, and a mystery uniting spiritual and fleshly, moral and intellectual faculties.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 835-921
occurrences.motif_label: coexistence of good and evil
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly states that good and evil are linked in human nature and exist side by side, reinforced by the harvest image.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "good and evil are linked together in human nature" and, in the parable, "they grow together unto the harvest."

occurrences.source_title: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
occurrences.passage_locator: Theogony ll. 116-138
occurrences.motif_label: night-day differentiation
occurrences.basis: Night gives birth to Aether and Day after union with Erebus.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "From Chaos came forth Erebus and black Night; but of Night were born Aether and Day, whom she conceived and bare from union in love with Erebus."

occurrences.source_title: An Old Babylonian Version of the Gilgamesh Epic
occurrences.passage_locator: PENNSYLVANIA TABLET, TRANSLATION, Col. I-Col. III
occurrences.motif_label: dream_portending_counterpart
occurrences.basis: The dreams are interpreted as announcing a figure like Gish, and the second dream presents that figure as a beloved brother-like likeness.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Some one, O Gish, who like thee / In the field was born and / Whom the mountain has reared
My likeness I have seen in the streets / Of Erech of the plazas ... I loved him as a woman, / I embraced him.

occurrences.source_title: An Old Babylonian Version of the Gilgamesh Epic
occurrences.passage_locator: PENNSYLVANIA TABLET, TRANSLATION, Col. I-Col. III
occurrences.motif_label: rival_counterpart
occurrences.basis: Gish dreams of a likeness he embraces as a brother, and the passage frames Enkidu as someone like Gish before their later meeting.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Some one, O Gish, who like thee / In the field was born and / Whom the mountain has reared
My likeness I have seen in the streets / Of Erech of the plazas ... I loved him as a woman, / I embraced him.

motifs.label: Trickster At The Boundary

occurrences.source_title: The Poetic Edda
occurrences.passage_locator: NOTES / ALVISSMOL / THE BALLAD OF ALVIS / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 7663-7805
occurrences.motif_label: Deceptive delay/trick used against a knowledgeable other; daylight ‘catches’ the dwarf
occurrences.basis: Thor explicitly says he must betray Alvis with “treacherous wiles” and announces that day has caught him when the sun shines in the hall.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Thor remarks that he has never seen more “wealth of wisdom” in one breast, but says he must betray Alvis with treacherous wiles; he declares that day has caught the dwarf and notes that the sun shines in the hall.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE MISCHIEVOUS DOG / THE CHARCOAL-BURNER AND THE FULLER / THE MICE IN COUNCIL / THE BAT AND THE WEASELS; lines 1032-1046
occurrences.motif_label: survival through shifting social category
occurrences.basis: The bat escapes danger by presenting itself under one category when birds are threatened and another when mice are threatened.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Weasel says he cannot release the bat because he is "an enemy of all birds on principle."
The bat says it is not a bird but a mouse; the weasel accepts this and lets it go.
The second weasel says, "I never let a mouse go by any chance."
The bat says it is not a mouse but a bird; the second weasel accepts this and lets it go.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE MICE IN COUNCIL / THE BAT AND THE WEASELS / THE DOG AND THE SOW / THE FOX AND THE CROW; lines 1049-1070
occurrences.motif_label: flattery used to obtain food
occurrences.basis: The Fox flatters the Crow's appearance and voice so that she caws and drops the cheese, which the Fox takes.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Crow sits on a branch of a tree with cheese in her beak; a Fox sees her and plans how to get the cheese.
The Fox stands below the tree, praises the Crow's beauty and plumage, and says she would be Queen of the Birds if her voice matched her looks.
The flattered Crow caws; the cheese falls; the Fox snatches it and says she has a voice but lacks wits.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE HORSE AND THE GROOM / THE WOLF AND THE LAMB / THE PEACOCK AND THE CRANE / THE CAT AND THE BIRDS; lines 1100-1120
occurrences.motif_label: Villainous disguise exposed by prudent victims
occurrences.basis: The Cat disguises himself as a doctor to approach sick Birds, but they refuse him entry; the moral states that disguise cannot deceive the wise.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Cat hears that Birds in an aviary are ailing.
The Cat gets himself up as a doctor, takes medical instruments, and presents himself at the door.
The Birds answer that they will do well when they have seen the last of the Cat, and they do not let him in.
A villain may disguise himself, but he will not deceive the wise.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE PEACOCK AND THE CRANE / THE CAT AND THE BIRDS / THE SPENDTHRIFT AND THE SWALLOW / THE OLD WOMAN AND THE DOCTOR; lines 1138-1159
occurrences.motif_label: deceptive healer steals from patient
occurrences.basis: A doctor charged with curing the woman removes goods from her house during his treatment visits.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The old woman is nearly blind from eye disease and agrees before witnesses to pay a high fee if the doctor cures her, with no payment if he fails.
The doctor prescribes treatment and, on each visit, takes an article from the house until the final visit, when the cure is complete and nothing is left.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE OLD WOMAN AND THE DOCTOR / THE MOON AND HER MOTHER / MERCURY AND THE WOODMAN / THE ASS, THE FOX, AND THE LION; lines 1202-1219
occurrences.motif_label: cunning animal trickster at a dangerous boundary
occurrences.basis: The Fox uses cunning speech and manipulation at the moment of encounter with the Lion and at the hidden pit, crossing from partnership to betrayal.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Fox whispers to the Lion: "I'll manage that you shall get hold of the Ass ... if you'll promise to let me go free."
The Fox rejoins the Ass and leads him by a hidden pit dug by a hunter as a trap for wild animals; the Ass falls into it.
When the Ass is caught and unable to escape, the Lion turns first to the Fox, kills him, and then feasts on the Ass.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE MISTRESS AND HER SERVANTS / THE GOODS AND THE ILLS / THE HARES AND THE FROGS / THE FOX AND THE STORK; lines 1342-1353
occurrences.motif_label: reciprocal trick at a meal
occurrences.basis: One host uses a serving vessel suited to himself but not to the guest; the guest later repeats the pattern with a different vessel that reverses who can eat.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “A Fox invited a Stork to dinner,” where the only fare is “a large flat dish of soup.”
The Fox laps up the soup, while the Stork with her long bill cannot partake; the Fox is amused by her distress.
The Stork later invites the Fox and sets before him a pitcher with a long narrow neck, into which she can easily put her bill.
The Stork enjoys her dinner, while the Fox sits hungry and helpless because he cannot reach the vessel’s contents.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE GOODS AND THE ILLS / THE HARES AND THE FROGS / THE FOX AND THE STORK / THE WOLF IN SHEEP'S CLOTHING; lines 1356-1366
occurrences.motif_label: predator disguised among prey
occurrences.basis: The wolf crosses into the flock by wearing a sheepskin, using disguise to breach the boundary between predator and prey.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The wolf resolves to disguise himself to prey on sheep undetected; he clothes himself in a sheepskin and slips among the sheep at pasture.
The shepherd is completely deceived, and when the flock is penned for the night the wolf is shut in with the rest.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE ASS AND THE LAP-DOG / THE FIR-TREE AND THE BRAMBLE / THE FROGS' COMPLAINT AGAINST THE SUN / THE DOG, THE COCK, AND THE FOX; lines 1484-1507
occurrences.motif_label: clever prey redirects predator to hidden ally
occurrences.basis: The Cock avoids the Fox's lure by directing him to the Dog hidden in the tree trunk, resulting in the Fox's death.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At daybreak the Cock crows; a Fox hears him and wants to make a breakfast of him.
The Fox says he would like "to make the acquaintance of one who has such a beautiful voice."
The Cock replies, "Would you just wake my porter who sleeps at the foot of the tree? He'll open the door and let you in."
The Fox raps on the trunk; the Dog rushes out and tears him in pieces.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE BLIND MAN AND THE CUB / THE BOY AND THE SNAILS / THE APES AND THE TWO TRAVELLERS / THE ASS AND HIS BURDENS; lines 1671-1689
occurrences.motif_label: repeated trick backfires
occurrences.basis: The ass repeats a stratagem that once made its load lighter, but the master’s countermeasure turns the same action into a heavier burden.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The master buys more salt; at the stream, the ass lies down and again rises with a lighter load.
The master detects the trick, returns again, buys many sponges, and loads them on the ass.
When the ass lies down in the stream again, the sponges absorb water, and the ass rises with a larger burden than before.
“You may play a good card once too often.”

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE APES AND THE TWO TRAVELLERS / THE ASS AND HIS BURDENS / THE SHEPHERD'S BOY AND THE WOLF / THE FOX AND THE GOAT; lines 1709-1730
occurrences.motif_label: trickster escapes by deceiving another into danger
occurrences.basis: The Fox, trapped in the well, persuades the Goat to enter, uses the Goat’s body and horns to cross out of the well, and then abandons him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Fox is unable to get out of a well; a thirsty Goat comes by and asks whether the water is good.
“it's the best water I ever tasted in all my life. Come down and try it yourself.”
The Fox proposes that the Goat stand on his hind legs with forelegs against the well so the Fox can climb on his back and horns, promising to help the Goat afterward.
The Goat complies; the Fox climbs over the Goat and out of the well, then walks away.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE ASS AND HIS SHADOW / THE FARMER AND HIS SONS / THE DOG AND THE COOK / THE MONKEY AS KING; lines 1823-1836
occurrences.motif_label: trickster exposes a foolish ruler
occurrences.basis: The Fox uses a baited trap and deferential royal language to expose the Monkey's lack of sense after his elevation to kingship.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Fox is disgusted by the Monkey's promotion, finds a trap with meat in it, takes the Monkey there, and presents the meat as a morsel reserved for the King.
The Monkey goes toward the meat, is caught in the trap, and reproaches the Fox for leading him into danger.
“O Monkey, you call yourself King of the Beasts and haven't more sense than to be taken in like that!”

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE LAMP / THE OWL AND THE BIRDS / THE ASS IN THE LION'S SKIN / THE SHE-GOATS AND THEIR BEARDS; lines 1931-1952
occurrences.motif_label: deception by animal disguise exposed by voice
occurrences.basis: The ass crosses an apparent identity boundary by wearing a lion's skin, deceives observers, and is recognized when he brays.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An ass finds a lion's skin and dresses himself in it.
The disguised ass frightens everyone he meets; men and beasts think he is a lion and flee.
After the ass brays in triumph, the fox hears him and recognizes him as the ass, saying he would have been afraid if he had not heard the voice.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE MOUSE, THE FROG, AND THE HAWK / THE BOY AND THE NETTLES / THE PEASANT AND THE APPLE-TREE / THE JACKDAW AND THE PIGEONS; lines 2059-2072
occurrences.motif_label: disguise to enter another group
occurrences.basis: The jackdaw deliberately alters his appearance to cross into the pigeon flock and gain access to their food.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A jackdaw watches well-fed pigeons in a farmyard, envies them, and decides to disguise himself to share their food.
The jackdaw paints himself white from head to foot and joins the pigeon flock.
As long as the jackdaw remains silent, the pigeons do not suspect that he is not one of them.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE TORTOISE AND THE EAGLE / THE KID ON THE HOUSETOP / THE FOX WITHOUT A TAIL / THE VAIN JACKDAW; lines 2249-2266
occurrences.motif_label: deceptive crossing of status by disguise
occurrences.basis: The Jackdaw attempts to cross from an unlikely candidate to king-elect by fastening other birds' feathers to himself.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Jackdaw, believing his ugly plumage will prevent his selection, waits until the others leave, picks up gaudy dropped feathers, and fastens them to his body.
On the appointed day, the birds assemble before Jupiter's throne; after reviewing them, Jupiter is about to make the Jackdaw king.
The other birds set upon the king-elect, strip him of the borrowed plumes, and reveal him as a Jackdaw.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE LION AND THE ASS / THE PROPHET / THE HOUND AND THE HARE / THE LION, THE MOUSE, AND THE FOX; lines 2941-2963
occurrences.motif_label: mocking onlooker challenges dignity of the powerful
occurrences.basis: The fox, as an observing animal, jokes that the lion is afraid of the mouse, prompting the lion's defensive reply.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A fox jokes that he has seen a lion afraid of a mouse; the lion testily denies fear and says the mouse's bad manners are what he cannot stand.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE LION, THE MOUSE, AND THE FOX / THE TRUMPETER TAKEN PRISONER / THE WOLF AND THE CRANE / THE EAGLE, THE CAT, AND THE WILD SOW; lines 2991-3013
occurrences.motif_label: Deceiver creates mutual fear between neighbors
occurrences.basis: The Cat moves between the Eagle's nest and the Sow's home, telling each that the other is dangerous, causing both to remain immobilized while the Cat benefits.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Cat, described as cunning, tells the Eagle that the Sow intends to uproot the tree and devour the Eagle's and Cat's families.
The Cat tells the Sow that the Eagle is waiting for a chance to carry off one of the little pigs to feed her brood.
After frightening both animals, the Cat returns to her hole, pretends to be afraid, stays hidden by day, and goes out unseen at night to get food for her kittens.
The Eagle is afraid to leave her nest, and the Sow is afraid to leave the roots; both they and their families starve, and their bodies supply food for the Cat's growing family.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE WOLF AND THE SHEPHERD / THE FARMER AND THE STORK / THE CHARGER AND THE MILLER / THE GRASSHOPPER AND THE OWL; lines 3295-3312
occurrences.motif_label: deception through flattery
occurrences.basis: The owl deliberately uses pleasing words, praise, and an attractive offer to lure the grasshopper into danger.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The owl decides to use a trick, praises the grasshopper's song as like Apollo's lyre, says she has nectar from Minerva, and invites him to join her.
The grasshopper is flattered by the praise and tempted by the delicious drink, so he agrees to come in.
Once the grasshopper is inside the hollow where the owl sits, she pounces on him and eats him.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE ASS, THE COCK, AND THE LION / THE BELLY AND THE MEMBERS / THE BALD MAN AND THE FLY / THE ASS AND THE WOLF; lines 3426-3441
occurrences.motif_label: feigned injury used to escape a predator
occurrences.basis: The Ass pretends to be lame and invents a thorn so that the Wolf lowers his guard, allowing the Ass to injure him and escape.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Ass pretends to be very lame and hobbles painfully.
The Ass says he became lame after going through a hedge and treading on a thorn.
The Ass asks the Wolf to remove the thorn with his teeth so it will not stick in the Wolf's throat when the Wolf eats him.
The Wolf agrees, tells the Ass to lift his foot, and focuses entirely on getting out the thorn.
The Ass suddenly kicks the Wolf in the mouth, breaks his teeth, and gallops away.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE SICK MAN AND THE DOCTOR / THE TRAVELLERS AND THE PLANE-TREE / THE FLEA AND THE OX / THE BIRDS, THE BEASTS, AND THE BAT; lines 3504-3515
occurrences.motif_label: opportunistic shifting allegiance
occurrences.basis: The Bat crosses between opposed parties according to which side is winning, rather than committing to one group.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Bat does not definitely choose a party; he joins the Birds when their side prospers and the Beasts when they gain the upper hand.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE STAG AND THE VINE / THE LAMB CHASED BY A WOLF / THE ARCHER AND THE LION / THE WOLF AND THE GOAT; lines 3649-3658
occurrences.motif_label: trickster speech at a boundary
occurrences.basis: The Wolf uses persuasive speech across the high-low separation between himself and the Goat, attempting to move her from safety into danger.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Wolf sees a Goat browsing on scanty herbage at the top of a steep rock and is unable to get at her.
“You are risking your life up there… come down here, where you will find plenty of better food.”
“It's little you care whether I get good grass or bad… what you want is to eat me.”

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE CAGE-BIRD AND THE BAT / THE ASS AND HIS PURCHASER / THE KID AND THE WOLF / THE DEBTOR AND HIS SOW; lines 3889-3904
occurrences.motif_label: implausible sales boast exposed by a sharper retort
occurrences.basis: The debtor makes a market claim about the sow’s festival-specific offspring, and the creditor answers with an even more absurd claim, exposing or amplifying the deception.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The debtor takes his only sow to market to sell; the creditor is present; a buyer asks whether the sow produces good litters.
“she produces females at the Mysteries and males at the Panathenea.”
“at the Dionysia this Sow has kids!”

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE MULE / THE HOUND AND THE FOX / THE FATHER AND HIS DAUGHTERS / THE THIEF AND THE INNKEEPER; lines 3977-4004
occurrences.motif_label: theft by deceptive performance
occurrences.basis: The thief obtains the coat by staging yawns and wolf-like howls and persuading the innkeeper to act out of fear.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The thief sits beside the innkeeper, talks with him, then yawns and howls like a wolf; the innkeeper asks what is wrong.
The thief claims that when he has “yawned three times” he becomes “a ravening wolf” and attacks men’s throats.
After a second yawn and howl, the innkeeper believes the thief and is terrified at the prospect of facing a wolf.
As the thief begins a third yawn, the innkeeper fears being eaten, slips out of his coat, bolts inside, locks the door, and the thief leaves with the coat.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE ANT / THE FROGS AND THE WELL / THE CRAB AND THE FOX / THE FOX AND THE GRASSHOPPER; lines 4091-4117
occurrences.motif_label: predator uses flattery to lure prey
occurrences.basis: The fox explicitly tries to get the grasshopper down by a trick, praising her song and asking her to descend.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A fox hears the grasshopper and thinks she would make a dainty morsel.
The fox tries to get the grasshopper down by a trick, praising her song and asking her to descend so he can meet the owner of the voice.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE FROGS AND THE WELL / THE CRAB AND THE FOX / THE FOX AND THE GRASSHOPPER / THE FARMER, HIS BOY, AND THE ROOKS; lines 4120-4139
occurrences.motif_label: coded speech deceives listeners
occurrences.basis: The farmer deliberately substitutes an indirect signal for the word the birds understand, allowing him to attack before they flee.

evidence.quote_or_summary: When the farmer asks for the sling, the starlings understand and warn the rooks; the farmer decides to say “humph” instead of “sling” and tells the boy to hand him the sling quickly.
The flock returns, the farmer says “Humph,” the starlings do not notice, and he slings stones among them, hitting birds before they escape.
A rook warns the cranes not to go near men because “They have a way of saying one thing and meaning another.”

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE BEE-KEEPER / THE WOLF AND THE HORSE / THE BAT, THE BRAMBLE, AND THE SEAGULL / THE DOG AND THE WOLF; lines 4373-4389
occurrences.motif_label: escape from predator by persuading delay
occurrences.basis: The dog avoids immediate death by persuading the wolf to postpone eating him, then relocates to a safe place.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The dog begs for his life and says he is thin and would make a poor meal at present.
The dog says his master will hold a feast, after which scraps and pickings will make him fat enough to eat.
The wolf considers the proposal good and leaves.
Later the wolf returns to the farmyard and finds the dog lying out of reach on the stable roof.
The dog answers that if the wolf ever catches him lying by the gate again, he should not wait for a feast.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE DOG AND THE WOLF / THE WASP AND THE SNAKE / THE EAGLE AND THE BEETLE / THE FOWLER AND THE LARK; lines 4429-4440
occurrences.motif_label: deceptive explanation concealing a trap
occurrences.basis: The fowler answers the lark’s question with the false claim that he is founding a city, hides, and then captures her when she is caught in the nets.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “I am engaged in founding a city,” said he, and then withdrew and concealed himself nearby.
The lark hopped onto the nets to get the bait and became entangled in the meshes.
The fowler ran up quickly and captured the lark.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE WEASEL AND THE MAN / THE PLOUGHMAN, THE ASS, AND THE OX / DEMADES AND HIS FABLE / THE MONKEY AND THE DOLPHIN; lines 4496-4514
occurrences.motif_label: Boundary-crossing pretender punished
occurrences.basis: The Monkey attempts to pass as an Athenian human of high status while being carried between sea and shore, and the deception results in drowning.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Dolphin sees the Monkey, supposes him to be a man, takes him on his back, and swims toward shore.
The Monkey replies that he is Athenian and says he comes from a very distinguished family.
The Monkey thought he was referring to some high official or other, and replied, "Oh, yes, he's a very old friend of mine."
Detecting the Monkey's hypocrisy, the Dolphin dives below the surface, and the Monkey is quickly drowned.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE WOLF AND HIS SHADOW / THE PLOUGHMAN AND THE WOLF / MERCURY AND THE MAN BITTEN BY AN ANT / THE WILY LION; lines 4663-4678
occurrences.motif_label: deceiver persuades victim to surrender protection
occurrences.basis: The lion cannot safely use force, so he uses flattery to induce the bull to remove the horns that protect him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The lion does not dare attack because he fears the bull's sharp horns.
Hunger compels the lion to act; since force does not promise success, he decides to use artifice.
The lion approaches the bull in a friendly fashion and praises his figure, head, shoulders, and thighs.
The lion asks why the bull wears ugly horns and says he would do better without them.
The bull is foolishly persuaded by the lion's flattery to have his horns cut off.
After losing his only means of defense, the bull falls easy prey to the lion.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE WOLF AND HIS SHADOW / THE PLOUGHMAN AND THE WOLF / MERCURY AND THE MAN BITTEN BY AN ANT / THE WILY LION; lines 4663-4678
occurrences.motif_label: force replaced by cunning
occurrences.basis: The lion determines to use artifice because direct force does not promise success against the horned bull.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The lion does not dare attack because he fears the bull's sharp horns.
Hunger compels the lion to act; since force does not promise success, he decides to use artifice.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE WILY LION / THE PARROT AND THE CAT / THE STAG AND THE LION / THE IMPOSTOR; lines 4698-4726
occurrences.motif_label: deceptive bargain with the gods returned against the deceiver
occurrences.basis: The man attempts to satisfy a vow with symbolic substitutes while claiming full discharge, and the gods respond with an apparent opportunity that leads to his enslavement.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Having no ox, the man makes one hundred small oxen from tallow and offers them on an altar.
"Ye gods, I call you to witness that I have discharged my vow."
The gods send the man a dream telling him to go to the seashore to fetch one hundred crowns he will find there.
At the shore the man meets robbers, who seize him, carry him off, and sell him as a slave for one hundred crowns.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE GNAT AND THE LION / THE FARMER AND HIS DOGS / THE EAGLE AND THE FOX / THE BUTCHER AND HIS CUSTOMERS; lines 4831-4844
occurrences.motif_label: technical truth used to conceal theft
occurrences.basis: The two men divide possession and action so that one can deny having the meat while the other can deny taking it, using evasive speech to conceal a theft.

evidence.quote_or_summary: While the butcher's back is turned, one man snatches a joint and puts it under the other's cloak where it cannot be seen.
"the one who had taken it said he hadn't got it, and the one who had got it said he hadn't taken it"
"Prevarication often amounts to perjury."

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE EAGLE AND THE FOX / THE BUTCHER AND HIS CUSTOMERS / HERCULES AND MINERVA / THE FOX WHO SERVED A LION; lines 4863-4875
occurrences.motif_label: failed theft punished by guardians
occurrences.basis: The fox attempts to steal a lamb from a guarded flock and is punished when the shepherd sets dogs on him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The fox tries to steal a lamb from a flock, but the shepherd sees him and sets dogs on him.
The hunter becomes the hunted and is soon caught and killed by the dogs.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: HERCULES AND MINERVA / THE FOX WHO SERVED A LION / THE QUACK DOCTOR / THE LION, THE WOLF, AND THE FOX; lines 4902-4921
occurrences.motif_label: slanderer punished by the target's counter-speech
occurrences.basis: The Wolf's accusation endangers the Fox, but the Fox's speech redirects the Lion's anger and causes the Wolf's death.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Wolf, seeking to settle old scores, tells the Lion that the Fox has not visited and does not care whether the Lion is well or ill.
The Fox enters, hears the Wolf's final words, and faces the Lion's displeasure, then asks to explain his absence.
“you must flay a Wolf and wrap yourself in his skin while it is still warm”
The Lion turns to the Wolf and kills him with one blow of his paw to try the Fox's prescription.
“That's what comes of stirring up ill-will.”

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE HORSE AND THE STAG / THE FOX AND THE BRAMBLE / THE FOX AND THE SNAKE / THE LION, THE FOX, AND THE STAG; lines 5083-5122
occurrences.motif_label: Trickster lures prey to a predator
occurrences.basis: The Fox acts as intermediary for the Lion and twice persuades the Stag to enter the Lion's den through deceptive speech.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Lion lies sick in his den, asks his friend the Fox to lure the big Stag from the wood, and says he wants the Stag's heart and brains for dinner.
The Fox tells the Stag that the Lion is near death and has appointed him successor over the beasts; the flattered Stag follows the Fox to the den unsuspectingly.
The Fox tries again; the Stag threatens him with his horns, but the Fox claims the Lion meant to whisper royal secrets and may appoint the wolf king unless the Stag returns.
The Stag is persuaded to return; the Lion overpowers him and feasts on the carcass while the Fox secretly steals the brains.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE HORSE AND THE STAG / THE FOX AND THE BRAMBLE / THE FOX AND THE SNAKE / THE LION, THE FOX, AND THE STAG; lines 5083-5122
occurrences.motif_label: Cunning servant steals the coveted portion
occurrences.basis: After helping the Lion obtain the Stag, the Fox steals the brains as his own reward and verbally deflects the Lion's search.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Stag is persuaded to return; the Lion overpowers him and feasts on the carcass while the Fox secretly steals the brains.
The Fox says it is useless to look for the brains because “a creature who twice walked into a Lion's den can't have got any.”

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE RUNAWAY SLAVE / THE HUNTER AND THE WOODMAN / THE SERPENT AND THE EAGLE / THE ROGUE AND THE ORACLE; lines 5195-5207
occurrences.motif_label: trickster's plan turned back on himself
occurrences.basis: The rogue's proposed deception depends on his own later action, and the oracle's answer makes that responsibility explicit.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A rogue wagers that he can prove the Oracle at Delphi untrustworthy by procuring a false reply.
If the oracle says the bird is dead, he will show it alive; if the oracle says it is alive, he will wring its neck and show it dead.
"whether the thing that you hold in your hand be alive or dead is a matter that depends entirely on your own will."

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE WOMAN AND THE FARMER / PROMETHEUS AND THE MAKING OF MAN / THE SWALLOW AND THE CROW / THE HUNTER AND THE HORSEMAN; lines 5305-5317
occurrences.motif_label: trickery through false purchase
occurrences.basis: The horseman gains possession of the hare by offering to buy it and then flees without completing the transaction.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The hunter meets a man on horseback, who observes the catch and offers to buy it.
The hunter agrees, but once the horseman has the hare, he spurs his horse and leaves at full gallop.
The hunter runs after the horseman briefly, realizes he has been tricked, and gives up trying to overtake him.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE HORSE AND THE ASS / THE FOX AND THE GRAPES / THE GOOSE THAT LAID THE GOLDEN EGGS / THE CAT AND THE MICE; lines 967-984
occurrences.motif_label: predator feigns harmlessness to lure prey
occurrences.basis: The cat uses a trick, pretending to be dead in order to coax the mice out of their holes.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The cat says she must coax the mice out by a trick, climbs the wall, hangs by her hind legs from a peg, and pretends to be dead.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA. / II.--MORAL TALES.; lines 1391-1474
occurrences.motif_label: feigned death used to capture animals
occurrences.basis: Panaumbe pretends to be dead so foxes approach and weep; he then kills them and becomes rich.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Panaumbe takes a bludgeon, feigns death, is mourned by approaching foxes, kills them, spares one after breaking its leg, carries the others home, and becomes rich through their flesh and skins.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA. / II.--MORAL TALES.; lines 1391-1474
occurrences.motif_label: failed imitation of a successful trick
occurrences.basis: Penaumbe repeats Panaumbe's method, but prior knowledge from the injured fox makes the trick fail and leads to Penaumbe's miserable death.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Penaumbe asks how Panaumbe became rich; Panaumbe offers to instruct him at dinner, but Penaumbe says he has heard it already, urinates against the door-sill, and leaves.
Penaumbe calls the foxes as Panaumbe did and feigns death; a limping fox remembers a previous event and tells the foxes to weep farther away, so Penaumbe cannot kill any and later dies miserably.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA. / II.--MORAL TALES.; lines 1391-1474
occurrences.motif_label: body opening mistaken for a cavern to trap prey
occurrences.basis: Sea creatures mistake Panaumbe's exposed anus for a rocky cavern, enter it, and are trapped for food and sale.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In the next tale, Panaumbe sits at the seashore and exposes his anus; whales, salmon, and other fish mistake it for a cavern, enter, and are carried home, released into a closed house, caught, eaten or sold, making Panaumbe rich.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA. / II.--MORAL TALES.; lines 1476-1571
occurrences.motif_label: successful trickster contrasted with failed imitator
occurrences.basis: Panaumbe's deceptive actions bring wealth, while Penaumbe's imitations bring death; the crow and narrator explicitly distinguish cleverness from foolishness.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Penaumbe, after hearing how Panaumbe became rich, goes to the sea-shore, takes beings into his body, seals his house, releases what turn out to be poisonous insects, and is stung to death.
At a divided path, an old crow on a tree calls Panaumbe clever; he chooses the narrow left path, the sea-lion gets stuck, and Panaumbe kills it, takes its flesh and skin, and becomes rich.
Penaumbe goes to the sea-shore, repeats the lice-picking deception on a sea-lion, eats flesh and fat from its head, and is pursued after the sea-lion discovers that only bone remains.

At the divided path, the old crow calls Penaumbe a fool; he takes the broad right road, the sea-lion catches and eats him, and the narrator says he might have become rich if he had listened to advice.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA. / II.--MORAL TALES.; lines 1476-1571
occurrences.motif_label: deceptive service to an animal becomes predation and pursuit
occurrences.basis: Both men lure a sea-lion by promising lice-picking, but instead eat flesh and fat from its head; the injured sea-lion then pursues them.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Panaumbe sees a sea-lion, calls it by offering to pick lice from its head, pretends to do so while eating its flesh and fat, and is pursued when the sea-lion discovers the injury.
Penaumbe goes to the sea-shore, repeats the lice-picking deception on a sea-lion, eats flesh and fat from its head, and is pursued after the sea-lion discovers that only bone remains.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA. / II.--MORAL TALES. / IV.--MISCELLANEOUS TALES.; lines 2006-2100
occurrences.motif_label: trickster fabricates sacred animal sign
occurrences.basis: The rascal plants rice to mimic bird dung and claims a divine peacock is nesting in the pine tree.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In 'The Clever Deceiver,' a rascal goes to the mountains, climbs a thick pine-tree, sticks rice on its branches to look like bird dung, and tells the chief that a divine peacock nests there.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA. / II.--MORAL TALES. / IV.--MISCELLANEOUS TALES.; lines 2006-2100
occurrences.motif_label: false fire alarm used in deception
occurrences.basis: The rascal falsely tells the chief that his house is on fire, frightening him away.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The chief sees the false bird-dung signs and asks the rascal to climb for the divine peacock; midway up the tree, the rascal claims the chief's house seems to be on fire and then says it is already burned down.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: AUDITORS. / LOCAL SECRETARIES. / HONORARY SECRETARIES. / INTRODUCTION.; lines 209-263
occurrences.motif_label: cunning fox deity from fox mythology
occurrences.basis: The passage calls the Fox-god cunning and links him to Japanese fox mythology.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says the cunning Fox-god comes from Japanese fox mythology, and that looking for the sunrise in the west belongs to the Japanese Wager of the Phoenix, whose Phoenix is derived from China.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA. / II.--MORAL TALES. / IV.--MISCELLANEOUS TALES.; lines 2102-2199
occurrences.motif_label: trickster escapes execution through substitution
occurrences.basis: The rascal uses deceptive speech to escape his own drowning and causes others to be bound and drowned instead.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The rascal tells the blind man that if he unties him and obeys him, he will pray to the gods and the man's eyes will open.
The blind old man unties the mat; the rascal tells him to remove his clothes, then puts him naked into the mat, ties it, takes the clothes, and hides.
The servants return, accuse the bound person of deceit, ignore the blind old man's plea, and throw him into the river.
The rascal wears the old man's beautiful clothes and tells the chief that a river goddess loved him, caused his misdeeds, and wished to marry his spirit.
Seeing the clothes and believing the rascal, the chief has himself tied in a mat and thrown into the river, where he drowns.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: HONORARY SECRETARIES. / INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA.; lines 485-608
occurrences.motif_label: Deceptive animal trick causes bodily injury
occurrences.basis: The rat steals the owl's food and gives instructions that lead the owl to slide onto a sharp gimlet.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The rat steals the owl's saved food, apologizes, gives instructions to set a gimlet point-up under a tree, and the owl is injured after sliding down the tree.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: HONORARY SECRETARIES. / INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA.; lines 610-713
occurrences.motif_label: Shape-shifting animal trickster outwitted by a human
occurrences.basis: Foxes plan a deception using human and horse shapes, but a man overhears the plan, impersonates one fox, and profits by selling the transformed fox.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In the fox tale, a man gathering bark in the mountains overhears two foxes speaking human language and planning a profit-making scheme in which one becomes a horse and the other a man who sells it.
The man returns, imitates the fox's voice, induces the fox in the hole to become a large chestnut horse, takes it to a rich village, and barters it for food and precious things.
The horse's owner keeps it indoors and feeds it grass; because it is really a fox it wants fish, weakens, escapes through a window, and the two foxes become angry at the man.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: HONORARY SECRETARIES. / INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA.; lines 715-800
occurrences.motif_label: Trickster-like counterfeit human village
occurrences.basis: The mole-god creates a place like a human village, disguises himself, and populates it with birds in human shape so the foxes believe it is human.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The mole-god sees the foxes, creates a human-like village, disguises himself as a very old man, makes treasures, garments, and food, and gives crows and other birds human shape as village householders.
The foxes arrive in human shape, think the place is a human village, trade their goods, watch the village dance, see bird-villagers fly upward, eat mulberries and grapes, and go home.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: HONORARY SECRETARIES. / INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA.; lines 802-900
occurrences.motif_label: Trickster distraction enables recovery of an object
occurrences.basis: The fox-cub and puppy use human forms and dancing antics to amuse and distract the ogre while the rat retrieves the charm.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The fox-cub becomes a little boy and the puppy a little girl; they dance and perform antics that amuse the ogre, though he remains suspicious and intends to kill them later.
The rat nibbles into the box, retrieves the charm, and escapes through the ground passage; the boy and girl disappear, and the ogre chooses not to pursue because he has been taken in by a fox.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: HONORARY SECRETARIES. / INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA.; lines 902-1009
occurrences.motif_label: Trickster fox defeats or evades stronger opponents
occurrences.basis: Fox figures use deception, concealment, or unexpected tactics against the otter, monkey, tiger, and rival gods' expectations.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The otter loses salt in the river; the monkey's children die after dancing in a tree; the monkey and otter blame the fox's wiles; the fox feigns deadly boils with bean paste; the monkey goes across the sea to Japan, explaining the absence of monkeys in Aino-land.

In 'The Fox and the Tiger' No. I, the tiger proposes a race from the top to the bottom of the world for lordship; the fox rides the tiger's tail and reaches the far end first; the tale explains the absence of tigers in Aino-land.

In No. II, the tiger proposes a roaring contest for chieftainship of the world; the fox hides his head in a hole to protect his ears; the tiger's second effort bursts his inside; the tale explains the absence of tigers and the craft and eloquence of foxes.

After the Creator finishes the world, good/brilliant and bad gods dispute rule; they agree that first sight of sunrise decides possession; the fox-god looks west, sees the sunrise's refulgence, and the brilliant gods rule.

occurrences.motif_label: deceiver deceived by the same kind of trick
occurrences.basis: The Jetavana robe-maker deceives others with old-rag robes and is then outwitted by a village robe-maker using an old-rag robe.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Jetavana robe-maker prepares attractive robes from old cloth, trades them for new cloth, and the worn places are revealed when the robes are washed in warm water.
A country-village robe-maker who also cheats people hears of the Jetavana robe-maker and thinks it would be good to outwit him.
The village robe-maker makes a fine robe from old clothes, exchanges it for new cloths, and the Jetavana robe-maker later discovers it is made of rags.

occurrences.motif_label: predator plans deception of vulnerable animals at a shrinking water source
occurrences.basis: A crane at a pond with diminishing water thinks of outwitting the fish and making prey of them.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Long ago the Bodisat is born as a tree genius near a lotus pond; during the dry season a crane sees many fish in a pond with little water and plans to outwit and prey on them.
The fish ask the crane why he sits lost in thought; the crane replies that he is thinking about them.

occurrences.motif_label: deceptive rescuer revealed as predator
occurrences.basis: The crane presents himself as helping the fish escape a poor pond but secretly transports them to a tree to kill and eat them.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The crane says the pond has little water and food and offers to carry the fish to a large lotus-covered pond; the fish suspect he means to eat them, but he denies it and proposes a test.
The crane takes the old purblind fish first to a Varaṇa-tree, kills and eats it, throws its bones away, then repeats this with all the fish.

occurrences.motif_label: villain outwitted by intended victim
occurrences.basis: The crab anticipates the crane’s possible deception, uses his claws to gain control, and kills the crane when the plot is exposed.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The crane invites the crab; the crab doubts being carried in the beak, plans to kill the crane if deceived, and grips the crane’s neck with his claws before departure.

The crane turns toward the Varaṇa-tree, shows the crab the heap of fish-bones, and says he will devour him; the crab threatens to cut off the crane’s head, forces him to land at the pond, then cuts through his neck and enters the water.
The Genius in the Varaṇa-tree praises the event and says: “The villain, though exceeding clever, / Shall prosper not by his villany.”

occurrences.basis: The index describes Māra as the Buddhist Satan, a tempter of Gotama with sovereignty, and an opponent in conflict with the Buddha.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The index identifies Māra as the Buddhist Satan, says he tempts Gotama with sovereignty, notes conflict between the Buddha and Māra, mentions Māra’s daughters, and lists Māra as tempter.

occurrences.basis: Sakka is indexed as serving the Buddha and also tempting a mortal.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Sakka entry says he serves the Buddha, places the Buddha’s hair in a dāgaba in heaven, has a throne that feels hot, is born as the Bodisat, tempts a mortal, and gives presents.

occurrences.motif_label: divine practical joke or temptation
occurrences.basis: Sakka is described as engaging in practical joking by which he tempted people, though also as beneficent.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sakka is described as a gentle god, not immortal, capable of remembering a former birth, sometimes succeeded by a deserving human, and given to practical joking that tempted people.

occurrences.motif_label: Animal disguise creates mistaken identity
occurrences.basis: The hawker dresses an ass in a lion’s skin and the watchmen avoid it because they believe it is a lion.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A hawker travels with goods carried by an ass; when he unloads it, he dresses the ass in a lion’s skin and releases it into rice and barley fields, where watchmen avoid it because they take it for a lion.

occurrences.motif_label: Tempter obstructs the sacred departure
occurrences.basis: Māra arrives with the intention of stopping the Bodisat at the moment of departure and then follows him watching for moral faults.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Māra comes intending to stop the Bodisat, stands in the air, and says the wheel of empire will appear in seven days and make him sovereign over the four continents and two thousand adjacent isles.
The Bodisat identifies Māra, rejects sovereignty, declares his intention to become a Buddha, and Māra resolves to follow him like a shadow watching for lust, anger, or malice.

occurrences.motif_label: deceptive supernatural encounter at a boundary place
occurrences.basis: The demon inhabiting the desert creates a misleading wet appearance and greets the caravan chief after planning to make the group discard their water.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The desert demon thinks: “I will make these fellows throw away the water they have brought... I will eat them every one!”
The demon creates a beautiful carriage drawn by milk-white bulls and approaches with ten or twelve armed demons; he and his attendants appear wet, muddy, and adorned with water-lilies and lotuses.
Because of a headwind, the merchant rides at the front; the demon turns his carriage aside, greets him kindly, and asks where he is going.

occurrences.motif_label: Demon deceives travelers into discarding life-sustaining water
occurrences.basis: A demon falsely claims that water is plentiful ahead and tells the first merchant to pour away his water, which leads to the caravan's destruction.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The demon appears with lotus wreaths, water-lilies, lotus stalks, dirt, water, and mud, and claims that beyond the green forest the country has rain, full pools, and lotus ponds.

The demon asks about the carts, identifies the heavy last cart as carrying water, tells the merchants to break the pots and pour the water away, and the foolish merchant does so without saving even a cupful.
There is no water ahead; the men become weary, stop at sunset, arrange the wagons in a circle, tie the oxen to the wheels, and lack water for oxen and rice-cooking.
At night's end demons come from their city, kill all the men and oxen, eat their flesh, leave bones behind, and the five hundred loaded carts remain.

occurrences.motif_label: shape-shifting water demon lures traveler
occurrences.basis: The demon takes the form of a woodman and tries to entice the Bodisat into the lake with bathing, drinking, lotus food, and flowers.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The demon assumes a woodman's form and invites the Bodisat to enter the lake, bathe, drink, eat lotus stalks, and pick flowers; the Bodisat recognizes him as the captor.

occurrences.motif_label: Monster exploits a loophole or condition to obtain prey
occurrences.basis: The goblin is bound by a specific sneeze condition and raises dust to create the condition for eating the travelers.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After serving the King of the Goblins, the goblin is permitted to eat any man who sneezes in the house, unless another person says a blessing and the sneezer replies reciprocally.
The travelers rest, cook on a fire of sticks, and prepare to sleep; the hungry goblin waits, then raises fine dust until the father sneezes.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Giant Crab, and Other Tales from Old India / WARNING / CONTENTS / THE GIANT CRAB; lines 134-220
occurrences.motif_label: Coordinated deception frees a captive from a monster
occurrences.basis: The elephant's wife feigns attraction to the crab so that he releases her husband, allowing the elephant to kill him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At the lake, the elephant pair goes farthest into the water; as the herd begins to leave, the elephant feels a powerful nip on his leg from the crab.
The crab sees Mrs. Elephant, is attracted to her, and asks whether she will give him a kiss.
Mrs. Elephant pretends to be pleased and tempting; the crab lets go of the elephant and crawls toward her.
The elephant has endured the pain silently; the passage states the situation was part of their trick, and when his leg is free he trumpets and jumps on the crab's back.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE PIOUS WOLF / BIRDS OF A FEATHER / SPEND A POUND TO WIN A PENNY / THE CUNNING CRANE AND THE CRAB; lines 1648-1775
occurrences.motif_label: false rescue by a predator
occurrences.basis: The crane presents himself as a helper who will carry the fish to safety, but he is actually using the journey to kill and eat them.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The crane eats fish when he can, sees the fish gasping in the little pool, and thinks of a trick to get them without trouble.
“I know a beautiful lake close by... and if you like I will carry you there.”
The crane carries the one-eyed fish away again, lays him in a tree cleft, pecks out his eye, kills and eats him, and drops his bones under the tree.
The crane returns for more fish, falsely says the first fish is happy, and repeats the killing until every fish has been eaten.
“Just look at that heap of bones under yon tree!... I ate them, and I'm going to eat you!”

occurrences.source_title: The Giant Crab, and Other Tales from Old India
occurrences.passage_locator: THE PIOUS WOLF / BIRDS OF A FEATHER / SPEND A POUND TO WIN A PENNY / THE CUNNING CRANE AND THE CRAB; lines 1648-1775
occurrences.motif_label: deceiver caught by his own trick
occurrences.basis: The crane’s transport scheme is turned against him when the crab demands to grip his neck, making the predator vulnerable and leading to his death.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The crab asks how he will be carried, rejects relying only on the crane’s beak, and says he will hold the crane’s neck with his claws; the crane agrees.
The crab nips the crane’s neck; the crane becomes frightened and begs forgiveness; the crab tells him to put him in the lake.
The crane sets the crab on the lakeside mud; once safe, the crab cuts off the crane’s head and lives happily in the lake afterward.

occurrences.source_title: The Giant Crab, and Other Tales from Old India
occurrences.passage_locator: THE GREAT YELLOW KING AND HIS PORTER / THE QUAIL AND THE FALCON / PRIDE MUST HAVE A FALL / THE BOLD BEGGAR; lines 2108-2152
occurrences.motif_label: Trickster gains food by deceptive access
occurrences.basis: The man crosses from spectator to recipient of the royal meal by crying out that he has news, feigning distress, and then revealing the practical result of his ruse.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A man who wants a taste of the king's food runs toward the watching crowd shouting 'News!', gains access, and falls before the king as if faint with hunger.
The king says to give the man food; the attendants seat him, and the king feeds him from his own dish and gives him wine until he has eaten a large meal.
When the king asks for the news, the man replies that an hour ago he was hungry and now he is not.
The people are shocked; the king laughs, calls him bold, lets him go free with a warning, and the man leaves happy in the success of his trick.

occurrences.source_title: The Giant Crab, and Other Tales from Old India
occurrences.passage_locator: WARNING / CONTENTS / THE GIANT CRAB / THE HYPOCRITICAL CAT; lines 223-284
occurrences.motif_label: Predator disguised as a holy ascetic
occurrences.basis: The cat uses a display of holiness and ascetic claims to gain the rats’ trust while secretly eating them.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A troop of rats lives in holes by a river side; a cat sees them, wants to eat them, and decides not to attack all at once because many would escape and he is not strong enough.
The cat stands early in the morning near the rats’ holes, facing the sun, snuffing the air, and standing on one leg.
The rats question the cat; he says his name is Holy, says the earth could not bear his weight on all four legs, claims to feed on air, and says he faces the sun to worship it.
The rats think the cat is pious and thereafter bow to him one by one when they start out in the morning.
As the rats file past, the cat waits for the last one, pounces on the hindmost, eats him quickly, and resumes standing on one leg while licking his lips.

occurrences.source_title: The Giant Crab, and Other Tales from Old India
occurrences.passage_locator: PRIDE MUST HAVE A FALL / THE BOLD BEGGAR / THE JACKAL WOULD A-WOOING GO / THE LION AND THE BOAR; lines 2268-2355
occurrences.motif_label: protective disguise through filth
occurrences.basis: The boar covers himself in mud so thoroughly that the lion refuses contact and departs.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The boar loses his conceit, and an old wise boar advises him to roll in mud because lions are clean beasts and dislike dirt.
The boar rolls in dirty places until he is "like a big cake of dirt."
At the lake the lion smells the dirty boar, reacts with disgust, says the boar has saved his life, and refuses to touch him.

occurrences.source_title: The Giant Crab, and Other Tales from Old India
occurrences.passage_locator: THE BOLD BEGGAR / THE JACKAL WOULD A-WOOING GO / THE LION AND THE BOAR / THE GOBLIN CITY; lines 2358-2435
occurrences.motif_label: enchanted false settlement concealing danger
occurrences.basis: The goblins make magical shapes of ordinary rural life to keep the shipwrecked sailors from being frightened away.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A ship is wrecked near the goblin city; five hundred sailors are cast ashore, and the she-goblins bring them food, dry clothes, and an invitation into the city.
The goblins use magic to create appearances of ploughmen, shepherds, huntsmen, hounds, and quiet country life so the sailors will feel safe.

occurrences.passage_locator: CONTENTS / THE GIANT CRAB / THE HYPOCRITICAL CAT / THE CROCODILE AND THE MONKEY; lines 287-410
occurrences.motif_label: Deceptive river crossing as trap
occurrences.basis: The crocodile turns a promised crossing over water into a predatory trap, but the boundary-crossing is reversed to the monkey’s advantage.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Mr. Crocodile calls to the monkey, describes abundant fruit on the far side of the river, and offers to carry him across on his back.
During the crossing, the crocodile sinks and tells the monkey that his wife wants the monkey’s heart to eat.
The monkey leaps off, climbs the fig-tree, eats figs, mocks the crocodile for thinking a creature keeps its heart in a tree, and the crocodile returns to his wife feeling foolish.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE GIANT CRAB / THE HYPOCRITICAL CAT / THE CROCODILE AND THE MONKEY / THE AXE, THE DRUM, THE BOWL, AND THE DIAMOND; lines 413-505
occurrences.motif_label: clever weak figure defeats stronger magical antagonist
occurrences.basis: The young man uses the diamond, tree position, and dropped nuts to provoke and trap the pig-magician before killing him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The man tests whether the diamond caused the miracle by wishing himself down and then back up into the tree, confirming that it is magical.
The pig wakes after the man drops a nut on its nose; it is explained that the pig is really a wicked great magician in pig shape, and that all his power lies in the diamond.
The pig rages below the tree; the man drops more nuts; the pig charges and sticks its tusks in the trunk, after which the man descends and kills it with a stone.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE CROCODILE AND THE MONKEY / THE AXE, THE DRUM, THE BOWL, AND THE DIAMOND / THE WISE PARROT AND THE FOOLISH PARROT / THE DISHONEST FRIEND; lines 826-894
occurrences.motif_label: counter-deception exposes prior deception
occurrences.basis: The plough owner uses a similarly impossible hawk claim to expose the dishonest friend's impossible rat claim.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The owner takes the friend's son for a walk, leaves him safely with another friend, then tells the father that a hawk carried him off.
The father brings the case before the judge, accusing the man; the judge questions the claim that a hawk could carry off a boy.
The plough owner asks who ever heard of a rat eating a plough and explains the earlier events; the judge sees that the complainant cheated him.

occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE. / CHAPTER III. KILLING THE GOD. / FOOTNOTES; lines 12768-12923
occurrences.motif_label: detection of a crop-damaging field being
occurrences.basis: The Rush-cutter is detected by a prescribed threshing action, and an arriving stranger is identified as the dreaded field being.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In Thuringia the dreaded Rush-cutter walked through fields on St. John's Day with sickles tied to his ankles, cutting avenues in the corn; seven bundles of brushwood were silently threshed, and the stranger appearing at the barn door was the Rush-cutter.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS; lines 5484-5571
occurrences.motif_label: trickster exploits a hidden vulnerability
occurrences.basis: Loki, called the mischief-maker, uses disguise and information about the omitted mistletoe to bring about Balder’s death through Hödur.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Loki disguises himself as an old woman, learns from Frigg that mistletoe was too young to swear, pulls the mistletoe, and gives it to blind Hödur while directing him to throw it at Balder.
Hödur throws the mistletoe as directed; it pierces Balder, who falls dead; the gods are speechless and then weep bitterly.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: MY LORD BAG OF RICE / THE TONGUE-CUT SPARROW / THE STORY OF URASHIMA TARO, THE FISHER LAD / THE FARMER AND THE BADGER; lines 1208-1299
occurrences.motif_label: captive trickster gains release through false promise
occurrences.basis: The bound badger manipulates the wife’s pity with promises that he will not escape and will help with her labor, then immediately attacks her once freed.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The badger, hanging upside down, speaks gently to the tired wife, offers to pound barley for her, promises not to escape, and is untied by her out of pity.
After being given the wooden pestle, the badger attacks the wife, kills her, cuts her up, makes soup of her, and waits for the farmer’s return.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: MY LORD BAG OF RICE / THE TONGUE-CUT SPARROW / THE STORY OF URASHIMA TARO, THE FISHER LAD / THE FARMER AND THE BADGER; lines 1301-1411
occurrences.motif_label: trickster revenge through deceptive friendship
occurrences.basis: The rabbit repeatedly poses as the badger's friend or helper while arranging harmful traps and false remedies.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The rabbit plans punishment, finds the badger hiding in his den, invites him to cut grass on the hills, and the badger trusts him and goes along.

On the way home, the rabbit makes the badger walk first, ignites his bundle of grass with flint and steel, explains the noises as Crackling Mountain and Burning Mountain, and the badger runs home with his back burned.
The rabbit says he will bring medicine, makes an ointment from sauce and red pepper, warns it will hurt but calls it wonderful medicine, applies it to the badger's back, and the badger howls in pain.
After the badger recovers, the rabbit thinks of another plan to kill him, talks about fishing, agrees to take the badger, and builds two boats, one of wood and one of clay.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: MY LORD BAG OF RICE / THE TONGUE-CUT SPARROW / THE STORY OF URASHIMA TARO, THE FISHER LAD / THE FARMER AND THE BADGER; lines 1413-1523
occurrences.motif_label: animal helper avenges murder through deception
occurrences.basis: The rabbit deceives the badger with a clay boat and kills him as vengeance for the old woman’s murder.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The rabbit keeps the wooden boat, gives the badger the clay boat, proposes a rowing race, refuses help when the clay dissolves, says he is avenging the old woman’s murder, strikes the badger, and the badger sinks.
The rabbit tells the old farmer that the badger has been killed; the farmer thanks him, says he can again sleep and eat, and invites the rabbit to share his home as a friend.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE STORY OF THE MAN WHO DID NOT WISH TO DIE / THE BAMBOO-CUTTER AND THE MOON-CHILD / THE GOBLIN OF ADACHIGAHARA / THE SAGACIOUS MONKEY AND THE BOAR; lines 3796-3896
occurrences.motif_label: Threatened animal avoids slaughter through a stratagem
occurrences.basis: The monkey learns he is to be killed and, with the boar's plan, uses a staged rescue to make the owners spare him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The monkey overhears the conversation, realizes he is to be killed, laments his master's cruelty, and thinks of seeking the wild boar's counsel.
The monkey goes to the forest, finds the boar, praises his wisdom, and asks what to do about being sold to the butcher.
The boar, pleased by flattery, proposes to seize the master's infant child so that the monkey can rescue it and win the parents' pity.
The parents admire the monkey's conduct and are grateful when it brings the child safely back.
The wife argues that the monkey saved their child; the husband agrees to send the butcher away and feed the monkey too.
The butcher is sent away with an order for boar meat, and the monkey is petted, lives peacefully, and is never struck again.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE STORY OF THE MAN WHO DID NOT WISH TO DIE / THE BAMBOO-CUTTER AND THE MOON-CHILD / THE GOBLIN OF ADACHIGAHARA / THE SAGACIOUS MONKEY AND THE BOAR; lines 3796-3896
occurrences.motif_label: Feigning heroic rescue to gain protection
occurrences.basis: The boar's abduction creates a crisis in which the monkey can appear as the child's rescuer and thereby avoid being sold to the butcher.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The boar, pleased by flattery, proposes to seize the master's infant child so that the monkey can rescue it and win the parents' pity.
The boar carries the child through the gate; the mother cries out, wakes her husband, and the parents see the monkey running after the thief.
The parents admire the monkey's conduct and are grateful when it brings the child safely back.
The wife argues that the monkey saved their child; the husband agrees to send the butcher away and feed the monkey too.
