occurrences.passage_locator: THE SAGACIOUS MONKEY AND THE BOAR / THE HAPPY HUNTER AND THE SKILLFUL FISHER / THE STORY OF THE OLD MAN WHO MADE WITHERED TREES TO FLOWER / THE JELLY FISH AND THE MONKEY; lines 4819-4939
occurrences.motif_label: trickery proposed as substitute for force
occurrences.basis: The chief steward says strength or dexterity will not catch a monkey and that the jelly fish must play a trick.

evidence.locator: lines 4819-4939, jelly fish’s hesitation and advice to trick
evidence.quote_or_summary: The jelly fish says he has no experience catching monkeys; the steward replies that strength will not work and that the only way is to trick one.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE SAGACIOUS MONKEY AND THE BOAR / THE HAPPY HUNTER AND THE SKILLFUL FISHER / THE STORY OF THE OLD MAN WHO MADE WITHERED TREES TO FLOWER / THE JELLY FISH AND THE MONKEY; lines 4941-5079
occurrences.motif_label: animal lured across a boundary by deceptive invitation
occurrences.basis: The steward directs the jelly fish to lure the monkey from his island to the sea palace by praising its wonders, and the jelly fish carries him over the sea.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The chief steward tells the jelly fish to befriend a monkey, praise the Dragon King's Palace and sea wonders, and carry the monkey on his back because monkeys do not swim.
The jelly fish introduces himself as kurage, servant of the Dragon King, and describes the palace, sea garden, coral trees, and jewel-like fruits until the monkey descends the tree while listening.
The jelly fish invites the monkey to visit the palace, offers to carry him because he cannot swim, and skims through the waves with the monkey on his back.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE SAGACIOUS MONKEY AND THE BOAR / THE HAPPY HUNTER AND THE SKILLFUL FISHER / THE STORY OF THE OLD MAN WHO MADE WITHERED TREES TO FLOWER / THE JELLY FISH AND THE MONKEY; lines 5081-5179
occurrences.motif_label: Trickster escapes death by verbal deception
occurrences.basis: The monkey avoids being taken to the Sea King’s Palace and losing his life by persuading the jelly fish to return him to the island with a false story about his liver.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The monkey says monkeys can spare livers, claims to have several, and says he left them hanging on a pine tree.
The jelly fish believes the monkey, is disappointed that the monkey has no liver with him, and turns back toward Monkey Island after the monkey promises to retrieve one.
At the shore, the monkey lands, climbs into the pine tree, rejoices at being safe, and sends compliments to the Dragon King.
The monkey says he cannot afford to lose his liver, admits the promise was false, explains that he deceived the jelly fish to avoid death at the Sea King’s Palace, and mocks him from the tree.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE HAPPY HUNTER AND THE SKILLFUL FISHER / THE STORY OF THE OLD MAN WHO MADE WITHERED TREES TO FLOWER / THE JELLY FISH AND THE MONKEY / THE QUARREL OF THE MONKEY AND THE CRAB; lines 5182-5293
occurrences.motif_label: deceptive exchange of present food for promised future gain
occurrences.basis: The monkey uses persuasive speech about the future value of a seed to obtain the crab's immediately edible dumpling.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The monkey and crab play along a river bank; the crab finds a rice-dumpling, the monkey finds a hard persimmon seed, and the monkey envies the dumpling and proposes an exchange.
The monkey persuades the crab that the seed can grow into a fruit-bearing tree; the crab agrees to exchange, the monkey eats the dumpling, and the crab plants the seed.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE HAPPY HUNTER AND THE SKILLFUL FISHER / THE STORY OF THE OLD MAN WHO MADE WITHERED TREES TO FLOWER / THE JELLY FISH AND THE MONKEY / THE QUARREL OF THE MONKEY AND THE CRAB; lines 5182-5293
occurrences.motif_label: helper betrays the one who requested help
occurrences.basis: The crab asks the monkey to help pick fruit, but the monkey eats the ripe fruit himself and gives the crab none.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The crab cannot climb the tree and seeks the monkey's help; when the monkey hears the tree bears fruit, he devises a plan to get the persimmons for himself.
The monkey climbs the tree, eats the best and ripest persimmons, and gives none to the hungry crab waiting below.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE STORY OF THE OLD MAN WHO MADE WITHERED TREES TO FLOWER / THE JELLY FISH AND THE MONKEY / THE QUARREL OF THE MONKEY AND THE CRAB / THE WHITE HARE AND THE CROCODILES; lines 5455-5593
occurrences.motif_label: trickster obtains a sea crossing by deceiving animals
occurrences.basis: The hare uses deception to make crocodiles form a bridge over the sea, enabling him to cross from Oki to Inaba.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The hare sees a crocodile near the island and thinks that he will try to get what he wants by a trick rather than by asking a favor.
At the hare's request, the crocodile summons many crocodiles, who arrange themselves in the water to form a bridge between Oki and Inaba.
The hare asks permission to walk over the crocodiles' backs to count them, then hops from back to back and crosses to Inaba.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE STORY OF THE OLD MAN WHO MADE WITHERED TREES TO FLOWER / THE JELLY FISH AND THE MONKEY / THE QUARREL OF THE MONKEY AND THE CRAB / THE WHITE HARE AND THE CROCODILES; lines 5455-5593
occurrences.motif_label: boast exploited by a trickster
occurrences.basis: The hare prompts the crocodile to boast about the number of crocodiles and uses that boast to induce the crocodiles to line up across the sea.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The hare greets the crocodile, plays with him, and asks whether the crocodiles are more numerous than the hares; the crocodile boasts that crocodiles in the sea far outnumber hares.
At the hare's request, the crocodile summons many crocodiles, who arrange themselves in the water to form a bridge between Oki and Inaba.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE STORY OF THE OLD MAN WHO MADE WITHERED TREES TO FLOWER / THE JELLY FISH AND THE MONKEY / THE QUARREL OF THE MONKEY AND THE CRAB / THE WHITE HARE AND THE CROCODILES; lines 5595-5702
occurrences.motif_label: deceiver punished and repents
occurrences.basis: The hare admits deceiving the crocodiles, is told its suffering is the consequence of that deceit, and says it has repented.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A kind man carrying a great bag stops; the hare tells how it tricked crocodiles into making a bridge, mocked them, was revenged upon, and was later deceived by men like the present helper.
The man says the hare's suffering was the consequence of deceiving the crocodiles; the hare says it has repented and asks how to be cured.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE JELLY FISH AND THE MONKEY / THE QUARREL OF THE MONKEY AND THE CRAB / THE WHITE HARE AND THE CROCODILES / THE STORY OF PRINCE YAMATO TAKE; lines 5705-5811
occurrences.motif_label: cross-dressed disguise used as battle stratagem
occurrences.basis: Yamato avoids direct combat, disguises himself as a woman with his wife's help, and approaches the enemy camp alone with a hidden dagger.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Yamato judges open battle in the impassable country unwise, decides to use stratagem and surprise, and orders his army to halt.
Ototachibana helps Yamato put on the robe, let down his hair, add her comb and jewels, and inspect the result in a mirror; the disguise appears to make him look like a beautiful lady.
"Thus completely disguised, he set out for the enemy’s camp alone." A sharp dagger is hidden in the folds of his silk gown.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE JELLY FISH AND THE MONKEY / THE QUARREL OF THE MONKEY AND THE CRAB / THE WHITE HARE AND THE CROCODILES / THE STORY OF PRINCE YAMATO TAKE; lines 5813-5924
occurrences.motif_label: hero defeats enemies through disguise and deception
occurrences.basis: The Prince enters an enemy tent disguised as a woman, disarms suspicion through service and charm, and kills the rebel chiefs.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Kumaso and Takeru sit in their tent discussing the King's son's army; Prince Yamato approaches in the disguise of a beautiful woman in sumptuous garments, unrecognized by them.
Kumaso admires the apparent woman, invites the disguised Prince to sit and serve wine, and drinks cup after cup until overcome.
At the chosen moment, the Prince throws down the wine jar, seizes Kumaso, and stabs him to death with a dagger hidden in his breast.
Takeru tries to escape but Prince Yamato catches him by his garments and stabs him, leaving him dying.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE JELLY FISH AND THE MONKEY / THE QUARREL OF THE MONKEY AND THE CRAB / THE WHITE HARE AND THE CROCODILES / THE STORY OF PRINCE YAMATO TAKE; lines 5926-6019
occurrences.motif_label: treacherous host lures hero into deadly trap
occurrences.basis: The governor feigns hospitality, proposes a hunt, and uses the hunt to trap Yamato Take in fire.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Yamato Take marches through Owari to Suruga, where the governor feigns warm hospitality and proposes a deer hunt.
The governor leads Yamato Take to a high-grass plain as a trap; fire breaks out around him on all sides, and the prince realizes the hunt was a trick intended to lure him like a wild beast.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE WHITE HARE AND THE CROCODILES / THE STORY OF PRINCE YAMATO TAKE / MOMOTARO, OR THE STORY OF THE SON OF A PEACH / THE OGRE OF RASHOMON; lines 6883-6997
occurrences.motif_label: deceptive visitor gains entry by claiming intimate kinship or household ties
occurrences.basis: The visitor arrives at the porch at night, claims to be Watanabe's old nurse, and uses that claim to obtain access and persuade him to show the arm.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At night someone knocks at the porch; the servant finds a respectable-looking old woman who says she was Watanabe's nurse when he was a baby, and Watanabe has her shown in.
The old woman insists that, as his old nurse, she should be allowed to see the arm, and asks whether Watanabe suspects her of being a spy sent by the ogre.
Watanabe gives in, leads her to his room, shuts the door, opens the heavy lid of the box, and calls her near to look in without removing the arm.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE STORY OF PRINCE YAMATO TAKE / MOMOTARO, OR THE STORY OF THE SON OF A PEACH / THE OGRE OF RASHOMON / HOW AN OLD MAN LOST HIS WEN; lines 7122-7243
occurrences.motif_label: Human encounter with demons at twilight by a hollow tree
occurrences.basis: The neighbor hides in a hollow tree near sunset and emerges among demons holding a feast with dance and song.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The wife rejoices at the removal; a wicked neighbor with a left-cheek wen hears the story, asks for details, and is told to hide near the hollow tree around sunset.
The neighbor hides in the hollow tree; the demons arrive at twilight for a feast, and he comes before the Oni when the chief asks why the old man has not appeared.

occurrences.source_title: Jataka tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE KING'S WHITE ELEPHANT / THE OX WHO ENVIED THE PIG / GRANNY'S BLACKIE / THE CRAB AND THE CRANE; lines 1523-1623
occurrences.motif_label: false rescue used for predation
occurrences.basis: The crane offers to save the fishes from the drying pond by carrying them to water, but uses the offer to isolate and eat them.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The tale opens in a dry summer with little rain. Animals, especially fishes in a very low pond, suffer for want of water; a crane watches them and offers to carry them to a deep-woods pond with water, food, and shade.

After hearing the report, the fishes want to go. The crane carries them away one by one, not to the pool, but to a hidden place in the woods, where he eats them until all the fishes in the pond are gone.

occurrences.source_title: Jataka tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE KING'S WHITE ELEPHANT / THE OX WHO ENVIED THE PIG / GRANNY'S BLACKIE / THE CRAB AND THE CRANE; lines 1523-1623
occurrences.motif_label: partial truth creates fatal trust
occurrences.basis: The crane shows a real pond to the big fish and returns him, causing the other fishes to trust the crane before he eats them.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A little fish says the crane may want to eat the fishes one by one. The crane replies that they may send a trusted fish with him to see the pond and return.
A big fish goes with the crane, sees the cool, shady, larger, full pond, returns to the little pond, and tells the other fishes about it.

After hearing the report, the fishes want to go. The crane carries them away one by one, not to the pool, but to a hidden place in the woods, where he eats them until all the fishes in the pond are gone.

occurrences.source_title: Jataka tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE KING'S WHITE ELEPHANT / THE OX WHO ENVIED THE PIG / GRANNY'S BLACKIE / THE CRAB AND THE CRANE; lines 1523-1623
occurrences.motif_label: intended victim outwits predator
occurrences.basis: The crab requires a hold on the crane's neck before traveling and kills the crane when the crane reveals his intent to eat him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The crab says he cannot ride on the crane's back and asks to hold the crane's neck with his claws. The crane knows crabs have a tight grip and dislikes the idea, but agrees because he is hungry.

At the place where the crane had eaten the fishes, the crane tells the crab to let go and walk. The crab sees no pond, only a pile of fish bones. The crane admits that the crab's shell will be all that remains if he lets go.
The crab pinches the crane's neck so that the crane's head falls off, then says the crane's bones, not the crab's shell, will dry with the fishes' bones.

occurrences.source_title: Jataka tales
occurrences.passage_locator: XVIII WHY THE OWL IS NOT KING OF THE BIRDS          90 / PUBLISHER'S NOTE / THE MONKEY AND THE CROCODILE / PART I; lines 203-280
occurrences.motif_label: Clever prey escapes predator through deceptive speech
occurrences.basis: The monkey avoids being killed by inventing the claim that his heart is in the tree, leading the crocodile to return him to safety.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The crocodile says he will kill the monkey by keeping him underwater because his mother wants monkey-heart.
The monkey says that if the crocodile had told him, he could have brought his heart; he then claims he left it in the tree and asks to return for it.
The crocodile refuses to go first to the fruit island and instead takes the monkey straight back to the tree to get his heart.
The monkey jumps to the riverbank, runs up the tree, and calls down: "My heart is way up here! If you want it, come for it, come for it!"

occurrences.source_title: Jataka tales
occurrences.passage_locator: XVIII WHY THE OWL IS NOT KING OF THE BIRDS          90 / PUBLISHER'S NOTE / THE MONKEY AND THE CROCODILE / PART I; lines 203-280
occurrences.motif_label: Predator lures victim across a dangerous boundary
occurrences.basis: The crocodile uses the promise of transport across the river to ripe fruit as a lure, then reveals the intent to kill the monkey in the water.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The young crocodile decides to get the monkey who lives in the big tree and wants to go across the river to the island with ripe fruit.
The crocodile calls to the monkey to come to the island, and when the monkey says he cannot swim, the crocodile offers to carry him on his back.
Because the monkey is greedy for ripe fruit, he jumps onto the crocodile's back.
The crocodile dives with the monkey on his back; the monkey goes underwater, is afraid to let go, and later sputters and chokes.
The crocodile says he will kill the monkey by keeping him underwater because his mother wants monkey-heart.

occurrences.source_title: Jataka tales
occurrences.passage_locator: PUBLISHER'S NOTE / THE MONKEY AND THE CROCODILE / PART I / PART II; lines 283-355
occurrences.motif_label: Clever animal escapes a predator's ambush
occurrences.basis: The monkey detects the crocodile's ambush at a river crossing, deceives the predator, and crosses to safety by using the crocodile's body.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The crocodile watches the monkey cross, plans to catch him returning at night, swims about watching him, and later lies still on the rock.
At night the monkey stops, notices the rock seems too high, infers the crocodile is on it, and calls repeatedly to the rock.
The crocodile thinks the rock answers the monkey at night and answers in place of the rock.
The monkey identifies the crocodile; the crocodile says he is waiting to eat him; the monkey says there is no other way home and asks the crocodile to open his mouth wide.
The monkey knows crocodiles shut their eyes when they open their mouths wide; the crocodile lies with mouth open and eyes shut.
The monkey does not jump into the crocodile's mouth; he lands on the crocodile's head, springs to the bank, and goes up into his tree.

occurrences.source_title: Jataka tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE MONKEY AND THE CROCODILE / PART I / PART II / HOW THE TURTLE SAVED HIS OWN LIFE; lines 357-400
occurrences.motif_label: trickster-like survival by speech
occurrences.basis: The turtle’s speech manipulates the boundary between apparent danger and actual safety, resulting in its escape into water.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The turtle asks what it has done to deserve such a dreadful thing and says, “to throw me into the lake! Don’t speak of such a cruel thing!”
The turtle laughs as it slides down the river to its old home and says, “those people do not know how safe I am in the water!”

occurrences.source_title: Jataka tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE QUARREL OF THE QUAILS / THE MEASURE OF RICE / THE FOOLISH, TIMID RABBIT / THE WISE AND THE FOOLISH MERCHANT; lines 948-1073
occurrences.motif_label: deceptive supernatural stranger on the road
occurrences.basis: A demon at the desert crossing assumes a human guise, fabricates environmental signs, and misleads travelers about the road ahead.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A wicked desert demon plans to make the merchant empty the jars, changes into a noble gentleman, summons a carriage and ten armed demon attendants, and creates wet signs on the carriage, oxen, clothing, and hair.

evidence.locator: lines 1000-1022, false report of water ahead
evidence.quote_or_summary: The disguised demon claims that the dark streak ahead is a forest with ponds and frequent rain, asks about the carts, and advises the merchant to empty the water-jars because they are no longer needed.
The wise man knew the man was a demon because he cast no shadow; he says they do not throw away water until they see more.

occurrences.source_title: More Jataka Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE STOLEN PLOW / THE LION IN BAD COMPANY / XVIII / THE WISE GOAT AND THE WOLF; lines 1308-1379
occurrences.motif_label: Predator's deceptive lure and counter-trick
occurrences.basis: The wolves use false mourning and false friendship to lure the goat, while the goat answers with her own deceptive claim about bringing dogs.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The male wolf tells his mate to say he is dead and ask the goat to help bury him, intending to spring up and bite the goat.
Hungry again, the wolves make another attempt: the female wolf says the goat's coming helped her mate recover and invites the goat to come talk and be friends.
The goat recognizes another trick and says she will come with friends: two hounds, Old Gray and Young Tan, the large dog Four-Eyes, and each dog's mate.
The wolf runs back to her mate after hearing this, and the goat never sees either wolf again.

occurrences.source_title: More Jataka Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: XXI THE ELEPHANT AND THE DOG / THE GIRL MONKEY AND THE STRING OF PEARLS / THE THREE FISHES / THE TRICKY WOLF AND THE RATS; lines 307-358
occurrences.motif_label: predator deceives victims by false helplessness
occurrences.basis: The wolf uses a deceptive performance of lameness and harmless air-eating to gain the rats' sympathy and access to them.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Big Rat is chief over many rats in the forest; a wolf sees the troop, wants to catch and eat them, and stands on his hind legs near their home.
The Chief Rat asks why the wolf stands on hind legs and keeps his mouth open; the wolf says he is lame and that he lives only on air.
The Chief Rat pities the wolf and visits with the other rats morning and night; as they leave, the wolf eats the last rat and wipes his lips.

occurrences.source_title: More Jataka Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE GIRL MONKEY AND THE STRING OF PEARLS / THE THREE FISHES / THE TRICKY WOLF AND THE RATS / THE WOODPECKER, TURTLE, AND DEER; lines 360-453
occurrences.motif_label: hunter outwitted by prey animals
occurrences.basis: The Woodpecker blocks the hunter's exits, and the Deer shows himself to lure the hunter away before returning to free the Turtle.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The hunter comes out with a knife; the Woodpecker flies at his face at the front door and then again at the back door, making him turn back twice.
The Deer sees the Turtle has been taken, decides to save him, lets the hunter see him, and leads the hunter into the forest while staying just out of reach.
The Deer slips away, returns by another route, hears the Turtle call from a bag hanging on a tree, lifts the bag with his horns, throws it down, tears it open, and frees him.

occurrences.source_title: More Jataka Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE WOODPECKER, TURTLE, AND DEER / THE GOLDEN GOOSE / THE STUPID MONKEYS / THE CUNNING WOLF; lines 552-594
occurrences.motif_label: feigned death used as a hunting trick
occurrences.basis: The man lies by the lake pretending to be dead so that he may kill one of the animals for supper.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The man takes a club to the lake where animals come to drink and lies down with the club in hand, pretending to be dead.
The wolf says the man would not have pulled back if dead and says, "You pretend you are dead so that you may kill one of us for your supper."

occurrences.source_title: More Jataka Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE WOODPECKER, TURTLE, AND DEER / THE GOLDEN GOOSE / THE STUPID MONKEYS / THE CUNNING WOLF; lines 552-594
occurrences.motif_label: counter-trick defeats the original trick
occurrences.basis: The man admits that he tried to trick the animals but that the cunning Wolf played a better trick on him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The man tells his friends that he tried to get meat by tricking the animals, "but the cunning Wolf played a better trick on me."

occurrences.source_title: More Jataka Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE PENNY-WISE MONKEY / THE RED-BUD TREE / THE WOODPECKER AND THE LION / THE OTTERS AND THE WOLF; lines 722-771
occurrences.motif_label: animal trickster-like opportunist
occurrences.basis: The wolf opportunistically intervenes in the otters' dispute and keeps the valuable middle part while framing it as payment.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The otters address the wolf and ask him to divide the fish because they cannot agree.
The wolf cuts off the tail for one otter, gives the head to the other, and takes the large middle part for himself.
The wolf is pleased, brings the fish toward home, and tells his mate he took it as payment for settling the otters' quarrel.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE. / THE SIEGE OF TROY. / RETURN OF THE GREEKS FROM TROY.; lines 10012-10108
occurrences.motif_label: Hero trapped in monster's cave escapes by cunning
occurrences.basis: Odysseus is trapped in Polyphemus' cave, uses wine, the false name Noman, blinding, and concealment beneath sheep to escape a stronger hostile giant.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odysseus considers killing the sleeping giant but remembers that the cave is blocked by the rock and begins devising an escape plan.
Odysseus offers Polyphemus wine from a goat-skin, says his name is Noman, and Polyphemus says he will eat Noman last.
While Polyphemus sleeps from the wine, Odysseus and his companions heat a piece of the giant's olive-staff in the fire and blind him with it.
Polyphemus' reply to the other Cyclops is: "Noman has injured me"; they conclude he is tricking them and leave.
Polyphemus opens the cave and feels among the sheep; Odysseus has tied companions beneath sheep and escapes himself by clinging to the finest ram.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: MARS. / NIKE (VICTORIA). / VICTORIA. / HERMES (MERCURY).; lines 3746-3817
occurrences.motif_label: trickster-boundary deity
occurrences.basis: Hermes combines boundary-crossing offices—messenger among gods, conductor of shades, god of travellers and roads—with cunning, theft, disguise, and evasion of detection.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hermes is described as messenger and ambassador of the gods, conductor of shades to Hades, patron of youth and athletics, inventor of the alphabet, teacher of interpreting foreign languages, and cunning attendant of Zeus when Zeus travels on earth disguised as a mortal.
Hermes is worshipped as god of eloquence, prosperity of flocks and herds, protector of merchants, patron of artifice and cunning, god of thieves, and patron of those who live by their wits.

Hermes is presented as god of travellers, punisher of those who refuse aid to wayfarers, guardian of streets and roads, associated with Hermae at cross-roads and public places, giver of wealth and good luck, and presider over dice learned from Apollo.
Hermes reaches Pieria at sunset, separates fifty oxen from the herd, uses myrtle-twig sandals to avoid detection, and is seen by Battus, whom he bribes with a cow to keep silent.
Hermes tests Battus by pretending to leave, assuming the form of Admetus, and offering two oxen if Battus reveals the thief; Battus gives the information.

Hermes changes Battus into touchstone for treachery and avarice, sacrifices two oxen to himself and the gods, conceals the rest in a cave, extinguishes the fire, throws his twig shoes into the river Alpheus, and returns to Cyllene.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: MARS. / NIKE (VICTORIA). / VICTORIA. / HERMES (MERCURY).; lines 3819-3892
occurrences.motif_label: trickster crossing divine boundaries
occurrences.basis: Hermes deceives Apollo and Zeus as a newborn, steals divine property, serves as messenger, and mediates between living and dead.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Apollo discovers the robber, confronts Maia and the infant Hermes, brings Hermes before Zeus, and Zeus orders Hermes to show Apollo where the cattle are hidden.
Zeus gives Hermes a winged silver cap and winged feet and appoints him herald of the gods and conductor of shades to Hades.
As conductor of shades, Hermes is invoked by the dying for safe passage across the Styx, can bring departed spirits back, and mediates between living and dead.
The passage lists Hermes' amusing divine tricks, including taking sacred attributes from Athene, Aphrodite, Artemis, and Ares; his victims forgive him because of his dexterity and good humour.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: ANANKE (NECESSITAS). / MOMUS. / EROS (CUPID, AMOR) AND PSYCHE. / HYMEN.; lines 4964-4987
occurrences.motif_label: disguise enables access to beloved and rescue opportunity
occurrences.basis: Hymen disguises himself as a girl to accompany the maidens, placing him in a position to survive the abduction and kill the pirates.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hymen disguises himself as a girl and joins maidens, including his beloved, traveling from Athens to Eleusis for a festival of Demeter.
Pirates surprise the travelers, carry them to a desert island, drink deeply, and fall into heavy sleep.
Hymen seizes the opportunity, kills the pirates, and sails to Athens.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: ORIGIN OF THE WORLD.--FIRST DYNASTY. / URANUS AND GAEA. (COELUS AND TERRA.) / SECOND DYNASTY. / CRONUS (SATURN).; lines 549-631
occurrences.motif_label: mother saves child through substitution trick
occurrences.basis: Rhea saves Zeus by wrapping a stone in baby-clothes so Cronus swallows the stone instead of the infant.

evidence.locator: lines 549-631, Rhea's substitution of the stone
evidence.quote_or_summary: Rhea appeals to Uranus and Gaea, wraps a stone in baby-clothes, and Cronus swallows it without noticing the deception.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: NAPAEAE AND OREADES. / THE WINDS. / PAN (FAUNUS). / FAUNUS.; lines 5585-5598
occurrences.motif_label: wild-place spirit who frightens solitary travellers
occurrences.basis: Faunus is presiding spirit of woods and fields and shares the faculty of alarming travellers in solitary places.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Like Pan, Faunus possesses prophecy, presides over woods and fields, and can alarm travellers in solitary places.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE WINDS. / PAN (FAUNUS). / FAUNUS. / THE SATYRS.; lines 5600-5633
occurrences.motif_label: ritual animal disguise as explanation for mythic beings
occurrences.basis: The passage reports that rural participants at Dionysian festivals wore goat and other animal skins and used the disguise for playful tricks and excesses, and that some authorities connect this to the conception of Satyrs.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At Dionysian festivals, rural shepherds and peasants dress in goat and other animal skins, use the disguise for playful tricks and excesses, and some authorities connect this to the conception of Satyrs.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: ASCLEPIAS (AESCULAPIUS). / AESCULAPIUS. / ROMAN DIVINITIES. / JANUS.; lines 5712-5790
occurrences.motif_label: threshold deity presiding over beginnings
occurrences.basis: Janus presides over beginnings and over gates, doors, and entrances, including heavenly and earthly thresholds.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Janus presided over beginnings: years, months, seasons, and human enterprises; auspicious beginnings explain his high estimation.
Janus appears as an ancient Italian sun-god who opens and closes the gates of heaven and presides over gates and entrances on earth.
As guardian of gates and doors, Janus protected the home; small shrines over house doors contained a two-faced image of the god.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CONSUS. / LIBITINA. / LAVERNA. / COMUS.; lines 5940-5953
occurrences.motif_label: Divine patronage of theft and fraud
occurrences.basis: Laverna presides over thieves, artifice, and fraud, linking a divine figure to deception and illicit boundary-crossing behavior.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Laverna is the presiding goddess of thieves, artifice, and fraud; she has an altar near the Porta Lavernalis and a sacred grove on the Via Salavia.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE. / PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES).; lines 8076-8168
occurrences.motif_label: trickster escape from imposed cosmic burden
occurrences.basis: Heracles feigns assent to Atlas' proposal and tricks Atlas into resuming the heavens before departing.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Heracles follows Prometheus' advice; Atlas puts the dragon to sleep, outwits the Hesperides, brings three golden apples, tries to leave Heracles bearing the heavens, and is tricked into resuming his load.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: SATURN. / RHEA (OPS). / DIVISION OF THE WORLD. / THEORIES AS TO THE ORIGIN OF MAN.; lines 832-898
occurrences.motif_label: deceptive establishment of sacrificial portions
occurrences.basis: Prometheus arranges the ox portions deceptively at Mecone, leading Zeus to choose the bones for the divine portion.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Because humans multiply, the gods convene an assembly at Mecone to settle sacrifices and worship; Prometheus divides an ox into bones hidden by fat and edible parts hidden under skin and stomach.
Zeus, pretending to be deceived but understanding the trick, chooses the bones and in anger refuses mortals the gift of fire.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE EPIGONI. / ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE. / THE SIEGE OF TROY.; lines 9323-9415
occurrences.motif_label: Reluctant hero compelled by exposure of disguise or ruse
occurrences.basis: Odysseus attempts to avoid the expedition by feigning madness, but Palamedes exposes the ruse and forces his participation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odysseus is reluctant to leave Ithaca and feigns madness; Palamedes detects the ruse, causing Odysseus to join, and Odysseus later seeks revenge.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE EPIGONI. / ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE. / THE SIEGE OF TROY.; lines 9776-9867
occurrences.motif_label: Disguised infiltration of an enemy city
occurrences.basis: Odysseus self-inflicts wounds, disguises himself as an old mendicant, and enters Troy to learn the Palladium's location.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odysseus wounds and disguises himself as an old beggar, enters Troy to find the Palladium, is recognized only by Helen, and gains her as an ally.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA; lines 1992-2120
occurrences.motif_label: trickery at a divine threshold
occurrences.basis: Frigga anticipates Odin's plan, alters his sleeping orientation, and uses disguise and naming custom to secure victory for her supplicants.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odin avoids choosing immediately and says he will give victory to those whom his eyes first rest upon in the morning.
Odin expects to face the Vandals when he wakes, but Frigga turns his couch while he sleeps and sends instructions to the Winilers about the dawn arrangement.
"Take thou thy women-folk, / Maidens and wives... / Over your lips / Plait long tresses with cunning"
Odin wakes, sees the armed host, asks what Longbeards they are, and Frigga says he has given them a new name and must give a baptismal gift.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR; lines 2611-2730
occurrences.motif_label: Trickster shapechanger forced to make restitution
occurrences.basis: Loki is identified as the plotter behind Sif's shorn hair, changes form to evade Thor, and is compelled to promise restoration.

evidence.locator: lines 2611-2730; Sif shorn and Thor pursues Loki
evidence.quote_or_summary: Thor finds Sif shorn, suspects Loki, pursues him despite shapechanging, seizes him, and releases him only after Loki promises new hair.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR; lines 2733-2850
occurrences.motif_label: trickster in animal disguise sabotages sacred craftwork
occurrences.basis: Loki assumes the form of a gadfly and interferes with the dwarfs' forging by stinging Brock, causing the hammer's short handle.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sindri puts more gold on the fire and leaves Brock to blow the bellows; Loki, disguised as a gadfly, stings Brock, but Brock continues until Sindri draws out the ring Draupnir, which produces eight rings every ninth night and is called an emblem of fertility.

A lump of iron is cast in the flames; Loki again appears as a gadfly and stings Brock above the eye until blood blocks his sight. Brock briefly raises his hand, and the resulting hammer is short in the handle.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR; lines 2942-3047
occurrences.motif_label: deceptive trials against personified and cosmic forces
occurrences.basis: Utgard-Loki reveals that the contests were magical deceptions against wild fire, thought, the ocean, the Midgard snake, and old age.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Utgard-Loki tells the gods he used magic, identifies himself as Skrymir, and says a mountain protected his head from Thor's blows, with clefts in it showing Thor's strength.
Utgard-Loki explains the hidden identities of the contests: Logi as wild fire, Hugi as thought, the drinking horn as connected to the ocean, the cat as the Midgard snake, and Elli as old age.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR; lines 3050-3168
occurrences.motif_label: gendered disguise to enter giant realm and recover stolen object
occurrences.basis: Thor dresses as Freya and Loki as a handmaiden to travel to Jötun-heim and recover the hammer.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Heimdall advises disguise; Thor wears Freya's clothes, necklace, and veil, while Loki dresses as a handmaiden, and they depart for Jötun-heim.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR; lines 3171-3290
occurrences.motif_label: trickster speech sustains a dangerous deception
occurrences.basis: Loki repeatedly explains suspicious behavior to Thrym and later persuades Thor to travel to Geirrod under false pretenses.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Thrym welcomes the party; Thor, as the bride, eats and drinks enormous amounts; Loki explains the bride’s behavior, gaze, and inattention as signs of love.

Geirrod recognizes the bird as a god in disguise, cages Loki without food or drink, and releases him when Loki promises to bring Thor without hammer, belt, or gauntlet; Loki then persuades Thor to visit.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR / CHAPTER V: TYR; lines 3495-3611
occurrences.motif_label: Monstrous offspring of a boundary-crossing union
occurrences.basis: Loki secretly marries a giantess in Jötun-heim, and their children are monstrous beings who threaten the gods.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Loki and Angur-boda have Fenris, Hel, and Iörmungandr; the monsters grow too large for their cave, and Odin sends Hel to Nifl-heim and Iörmungandr to the sea, where the serpent encircles the earth.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR / CHAPTER V: TYR / CHAPTER VI: BRAGI; lines 3722-3817
occurrences.motif_label: disguised deity seeks precious knowledge-drink by guile and labor
occurrences.basis: Odin disguises himself, travels to Jötun-heim, uses the name Bolwerk, works for Baugi, and participates in a plan to reach the guarded mead by boring into the mountain.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odin, already wise from runic lore and Mimir's fountain, learns of the draught's power, becomes anxious to obtain it, dons hat and cloak, and travels to Jötun-heim, where he sees nine thralls making hay.
At Baugi's house, Odin uses the name Bolwerk and agrees to do the work of nine thralls all summer in return for one draught of Suttung's magic mead; he completes the harvest work.
When winter comes, Baugi hesitates to ask Suttung openly and says he will try guile; Bolwerk and Baugi go to the mountain, and Odin produces the auger Rati so Baugi can bore a hole into the cave.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR / CHAPTER V: TYR / CHAPTER VI: BRAGI; lines 3722-3817
occurrences.motif_label: self-destruction of laborers through desired object
occurrences.basis: After Odin throws the whetstone, the nine thralls fight over it and wound one another with their sharpened scythes.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odin sharpens the nine thralls' scythes with a whetstone, throws the whetstone, and the thralls, competing for it, wound one another and fight until dead or mortally wounded.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER IV: THOR / CHAPTER V: TYR / CHAPTER VI: BRAGI / CHAPTER VII: IDUN; lines 3991-4133
occurrences.motif_label: trickster lures guardian beyond protected boundary
occurrences.basis: Loki deceives Idun into leaving Asgard, and once outside the heavenly abode she is seized by Thiassi.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Loki conceals the condition of release, later deceives Idun with a story about similar apples, leads her from Asgard with a crystal dish of fruit, and Thiassi seizes her on eagle wings and carries her to Thrymheim.

Investigation reveals Idun was last seen with Loki; Odin calls Loki to account, and Loki admits betraying her into the storm giant's power; the accompanying poem calls Loki a traitor who led Idun to Jötun power.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER IV: THOR / CHAPTER V: TYR / CHAPTER VI: BRAGI / CHAPTER VII: IDUN; lines 4277-4407
occurrences.motif_label: Trickster appeases dangerous claimant through comedy
occurrences.basis: Loki uses grotesque antics with a goat to make the angry Skadi smile, softening her before negotiations continue.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Skadi, Thiassi’s daughter and goddess of winter, comes in armor and winter gear to demand satisfaction for her father’s death; the gods offer a fine, she demands a life, and Loki’s goat antics make her smile.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XXII / BOOK XXIII / BOOK XXIV / FOOTNOTES:; lines 11174-11276
occurrences.motif_label: trickster-associated deity invoked for usefulness
occurrences.basis: Mercury is described as a god of thievishness and rascality and as the god likely to be useful to the Phaeacians.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The note says the final drink-offering should have gone to Jove or Neptune; it also says Echeneus proposes a drink-offering to Jove and characterizes Mercury as the god of thievishness and rascality likely to be useful to the Phaeacians.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS. / BOOK IV; lines 1762-1847
occurrences.motif_label: Disguised infiltration of the enemy city
occurrences.basis: Ulysses adopts wounds, bruises, and rags, enters Troy unrecognized, obtains information, and returns to the Achaean camp.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Helen says Ulysses disguised himself with wounds, bruises, and rags, entered Troy as if a menial or beggar, was recognized by her, received her oath of secrecy, killed Trojans, and obtained information before returning to the Argive camp.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VI / THE MEETING BETWEEN NAUSICAA AND ULYSSES. / BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS.; lines 2992-3088
occurrences.motif_label: concealed passage through a potentially hostile city
occurrences.basis: Ulysses passes through the city unseen because Minerva covers him with mist or darkness while he crosses among Phaeacians who dislike strangers.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses goes toward town; Minerva surrounds him with thick mist and appears as a little girl carrying a pitcher; Ulysses asks for Alcinous' house.
Minerva promises to show the way, tells Ulysses not to speak, look at anyone, or ask questions, and describes the Phaeacians as stranger-wary seafarers with swift ships.
Minerva leads; Ulysses follows unseen through the city in a cloud of darkness and admires the harbours, ships, assembly places, walls, and palisade.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VI / THE MEETING BETWEEN NAUSICAA AND ULYSSES. / BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS.; lines 3090-3174
occurrences.motif_label: divine concealment of hero entering a court
occurrences.basis: Ulysses crosses the threshold and passes through the palace hidden by darkness provided by Minerva until he reaches the royal couple.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses looks about, crosses the threshold, and passes through the court hidden by Minerva's cloak of darkness while Phaeacian chiefs make offerings to Mercury.
Ulysses reaches Arete and Alcinous, lays hands upon the queen's knees, the miraculous darkness falls away, and those present are surprised to see him.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: THE MEETING BETWEEN NAUSICAA AND ULYSSES. / BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS. / BOOK VIII; lines 3698-3785
occurrences.motif_label: deceptive object crossing a city boundary with hidden warriors
occurrences.basis: The wooden horse is brought into the Trojan fortress by the Trojans and contains hidden Argives who later emerge to sack the city.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses praises Demodocus's accuracy about the Achaeans' return and asks him to sing of the wooden horse made by Epeus with Minerva's help and filled with the men who sacked Troy.
The bard begins with Argives setting fire to their tents and sailing away while others wait hidden with Ulysses inside the horse in the Trojan assembly place.
The Trojans have drawn the horse into their fortress and debate whether to break it up, throw it down from the rock, or keep it as an offering to the gods.
The city is described as doomed once it takes in the horse, which contains the bravest Argives waiting to bring death and destruction to the Trojans.
Demodocus sings of the Achaeans emerging from the horse, sacking Troy, and Ulysses with Menelaus fighting fiercely at Deiphobus's house and winning by Minerva's help.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS. / BOOK VIII / BOOK IX; lines 3996-4072
occurrences.motif_label: Cunning speech against a dangerous captor
occurrences.basis: Ulysses avoids revealing the ship's location by lying about its wreck and later remains trapped behind the cave boundary while scheming revenge.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Cyclops calls Ulysses foolish, denies fearing the gods or Jove, claims Cyclopes are stronger, and asks where the ship is fastened.
Ulysses says he was too cunning to be caught and lies that Neptune wrecked the ship on rocks, leaving only the present men alive.
The Cyclops seizes two men, kills and eats them, drinks milk, sleeps among the sheep, and Ulysses refrains from stabbing him because the stone would trap them.
At dawn the Cyclops lights the fire, milks the animals, eats two more men, moves and replaces the stone, drives the sheep to the mountain, and Ulysses plans revenge.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS. / BOOK VIII / BOOK IX; lines 4074-4168
occurrences.motif_label: weaker captive defeats stronger monster by stratagem
occurrences.basis: Odysseus is trapped with a powerful cannibal captor and uses prepared concealment, wine, and a false name to make the blinding possible and prevent effective rescue.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odysseus cuts about six feet from the Cyclops' green olive-wood club, has it smoothed, points and chars it, and hides it under dung in the cave.
Odysseus approaches Polyphemus with an ivy-wood bowl of black wine, saying it was meant as a drink-offering in hope that Polyphemus would show compassion and send him home.
"my name is Noman"
Odysseus heats the beam in the embers, encourages his men, and together they drive and rotate the red-hot sharp end into the Cyclops' eye.
Polyphemus says that Noman is killing him by fraud and no man by force; the other Cyclopes answer that if no man attacks him he must be ill, advise prayer to Neptune, and depart.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS. / BOOK VIII / BOOK IX; lines 4074-4168
occurrences.motif_label: intoxication of dangerous host or captor
occurrences.basis: Odysseus gives Polyphemus wine repeatedly until it takes hold of him, enabling the subsequent attack during sleep.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odysseus approaches Polyphemus with an ivy-wood bowl of black wine, saying it was meant as a drink-offering in hope that Polyphemus would show compassion and send him home.
Polyphemus drinks, delights in the wine, asks for more, asks Odysseus' name, and says he wants to give him a present.
After Odysseus fills the bowl three times, the wine affects Polyphemus; he reels, falls backward, sleeps deeply, and vomits wine and human flesh.
Odysseus heats the beam in the embers, encourages his men, and together they drive and rotate the red-hot sharp end into the Cyclops' eye.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS. / BOOK VIII / BOOK IX; lines 4074-4168
occurrences.motif_label: false name blocks recognition and aid
occurrences.basis: Odysseus' name 'Noman' causes Polyphemus' cry for help to be understood as saying that no man is attacking him, so the neighboring Cyclopes leave.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "my name is Noman"
The other Cyclopes ask whether anyone is carrying off sheep or trying to kill Polyphemus by fraud or force.
Polyphemus says that Noman is killing him by fraud and no man by force; the other Cyclopes answer that if no man attacks him he must be ill, advise prayer to Neptune, and depart.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS. / BOOK VIII / BOOK IX; lines 4170-4268
occurrences.motif_label: Escape through concealment beneath animals
occurrences.basis: Ulysses saves himself and his companions by hiding beneath sheep and a ram so the blinded Cyclops cannot detect them.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses devises a plan: male sheep with heavy black fleece are bound in threes, with a man under the middle sheep; Ulysses hides under the belly of a fine ram by gripping its fleece.
At morning the male sheep go out, the ewes wait to be milked, and Polyphemus feels the backs of the sheep without discovering the hidden men underneath.
Polyphemus addresses the ram and says his master has lost his eye because “wicked Noman and his horrid crew” blinded him.
After the ram leaves the cave area, Ulysses gets out, frees his companions, drives the sheep to the ship, silences mourning, and orders the crew to put out to sea.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XII / THE SIRENS, SCYLLA AND CHARYBDIS, THE CATTLE OF THE SUN. / BOOK XIII / ULYSSES LEAVES SCHERIA AND RETURNS TO ITHACA.; lines 5921-5999
occurrences.motif_label: Mutual craft and strategic deception
occurrences.basis: Ulysses invents a lying story, and Minerva remarks that both she and Ulysses can deceive upon occasion.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses is glad to find himself in his own country but does not speak the truth and makes up a lying story.
Minerva smiles, caresses Ulysses, takes the form of a fair, stately, wise woman, and says only an exceptionally shifty liar could surpass him; she says both of them can deceive when needed.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XII / THE SIRENS, SCYLLA AND CHARYBDIS, THE CATTLE OF THE SUN. / BOOK XIII / ULYSSES LEAVES SCHERIA AND RETURNS TO ITHACA.; lines 6001-6093
occurrences.motif_label: Hero disguises identity before reclaiming household
occurrences.basis: Minerva disguises Ulysses so no human will know him before he goes among the suitors, wife, son, and loyal servant.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva promises to stay attentive, predicts bloodshed among those consuming Ulysses' substance, and says she will disguise him so no human being will know him.
Minerva tells disguised Ulysses to go to the loyal swineherd near Raven rock and the fountain Arethusa while she goes to Sparta to see Telemachus with Menelaus.
Minerva touches Ulysses with her wand, wrinkles and withers his body, removes his yellow hair, blears his eyes, gives him filthy tattered clothing, a deer skin, a staff, and a holed wallet.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XIII / ULYSSES LEAVES SCHERIA AND RETURNS TO ITHACA. / BOOK XIV / ULYSSES IN THE HUT WITH EUMAEUS.; lines 6196-6288
occurrences.motif_label: unrecognized or self-concealing returner tells an alternate life story
occurrences.basis: Ulysses is present in the hut while speaking of Ulysses' return in the third person and then gives a detailed Cretan autobiographical account as the old stranger.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses swears by king Jove, the rites of hospitality, and Ulysses' hearth that Ulysses will return within the year and take vengeance on those mistreating his wife and son; he refuses reward until this occurs.

Ulysses begins by saying he could tell his sorrows for twelve months, then claims to be Cretan, son of Castor son of Hylax and a purchased slave concubine, once honored like legitimate brothers, later given little inheritance, enriched through marriage, and inclined to war, ships, weapons, ambushes, and foreign expeditions before Troy.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XIII / ULYSSES LEAVES SCHERIA AND RETURNS TO ITHACA. / BOOK XIV / ULYSSES IN THE HUT WITH EUMAEUS.; lines 6290-6372
occurrences.motif_label: deceiver attempts to sell traveler into slavery
occurrences.basis: The Phoenician persuades the speaker into travel and secretly intends to sell him as a slave in Libya.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After seven years in Egypt, a Phoenician described as cunning persuades the speaker to go to Phoenicia and later places him on a ship for Libya under a false pretense, intending to sell him as a slave.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XIII / ULYSSES LEAVES SCHERIA AND RETURNS TO ITHACA. / BOOK XIV / ULYSSES IN THE HUT WITH EUMAEUS.; lines 6466-6544
occurrences.motif_label: Clever tale obtains needed cloak
occurrences.basis: Ulysses tells a story about a prior clever stratagem that obtained a cloak, and the present telling leads Eumaeus to provide clothing and bedding.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses thinks he will see whether Eumaeus will take off his own cloak and give it to him or make one of his men give him one.

Ulysses, described as crafty and valiant, tells the man to keep quiet, then says he has had a dream and asks someone to tell Agamemnon to send more men; Thoas leaves his cloak and runs to the ships, and the speaker takes the cloak until morning.

Eumaeus praises the story and says the old man will lack neither clothing nor other reasonable needs for the present, though the next morning he must wear his old rags again until Ulysses’ son can provide cloak and shirt.
Eumaeus makes a bed for Ulysses from goatskins and sheepskins before the fire and covers him with a heavy cloak kept for unusually bad weather.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: ULYSSES LEAVES SCHERIA AND RETURNS TO ITHACA. / BOOK XIV / ULYSSES IN THE HUT WITH EUMAEUS. / BOOK XV; lines 6834-6930
occurrences.motif_label: Secret oath, deception, and boundary-crossing theft
occurrences.basis: The traders seduce the servant; she demands an oath, commands secrecy, plans to evade her master, take gold, and abduct a child by ship.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Cunning Phoenician traders, described as great mariners, arrive in a freighted ship; they get hold of and seduce a tall Phoenician servant while she is washing near their ship.
The woman says she will gladly go if the men swear a solemn oath that they will do her no harm by the way, and they swear as instructed.

After the oath, the woman tells the traders not to speak to her in public or at the well, lest her master suspect, imprison her, and have them killed; she tells them to buy and load quickly and send word.

evidence.locator: lines 6834-6930, planned theft and child abduction
evidence.quote_or_summary: The woman says she will bring as much gold as she can and, as nurse to the young son of the house, will carry him off in the ship so the traders can sell him in foreign parts.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XV / BOOK XVI / ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII; lines 7528-7613
occurrences.motif_label: Disguised return in lowly appearance
occurrences.basis: Ulysses travels toward the city in rags, with a shabby wallet and staff, looking like a broken-down old tramp while his identity as master is known to the narration.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses throws a shabby tattered wallet over his shoulders, receives a stick from Eumaeus, and follows him in rags, looking like a broken-down old tramp leaning on a staff.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: HENRY FESTING JONES. / THE ODYSSEY / BOOK I / BOOK II; lines 762-849
occurrences.motif_label: cunning weaving delays unwanted remarriage
occurrences.basis: Antinous describes Telemachus’s mother as artful and says she used a large piece of needlework for Laertes’ pall as a reason to delay marriage.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Antinous calls Telemachus insolent, denies the suitors are to blame, and says Telemachus’s mother is artful and has deceived the suitors for nearly four years.
Antinous says Telemachus’s mother set up a great tambour frame in her room and began a very large piece of fine needlework.
Antinous reports that she asked the suitors not to press her to marry until she had completed a pall for Laertes against the time of his death.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XV / BOOK XVI / ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII; lines 7717-7818
occurrences.motif_label: Hostile rejection of the disguised stranger
occurrences.basis: Ulysses begs as though he were a real beggar, while Antinous abuses the swineherd for bringing him and threatens Ulysses with a stool.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses goes around from left to right, stretching out his hands as though a real beggar; some suitors pity him and ask who he is and where he came from.
Antinous abuses the swineherd for bringing the man to town and complains that tramps and beggars waste the master's property.
Antinous replies harshly, draws the stool from under his feet as if to throw it at Ulysses, while the other suitors give food and fill Ulysses's wallet.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XVI / ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII / BOOK XVIII; lines 7971-8072
occurrences.motif_label: threshold contest for household access
occurrences.basis: The conflict begins at the doorway, concerns which beggar may remain in or near the house, and is framed by the suitors as a contest over food and table access.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Book XVIII opens with a common tramp named Arnaeus, called Irus, who begs around Ithaca and insults Ulysses, trying to drive him from the doorway of his own house.

Antinous laughs and urges the suitors to set the stranger and Irus fighting; the suitors gather laughing, and Antinous offers the victor blood-and-fat goats' paunches at the fire, access to the table, and exclusion of other beggars.
Ulysses drags Irus by the foot to the outer court by the gate-house, props him against the wall, puts his staff in his hands, and warns him not to make himself king of the beggars again.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XVI / ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII / BOOK XVIII; lines 8177-8277
occurrences.motif_label: disguised return to the household
occurrences.basis: The narrator names Ulysses while he remains in the hall as the stranger who has defeated Irus and offers menial service among the suitors.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus tells Penelope that the stranger defeated Irus and wishes Jove, Minerva, and Apollo would make all the suitors as helpless as Irus at the outer gate.
The narrator says Ulysses was glad to hear Penelope trying to get presents from the suitors and flattering them with fair words that he knew she did not mean.
Ulysses tells the maids, servants of long-absent Ulysses, to go to Penelope and says he will hold the light for the suitors, adding that he can endure much.
Ulysses scowls at Melantho, calls her a vixen, and threatens to tell Telemachus what she has said.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XVI / ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII / BOOK XVIII; lines 8177-8277
occurrences.motif_label: cunning speech used to obtain gifts
occurrences.basis: The narrator says Ulysses is glad because Penelope is extracting presents from the suitors by flattering them with words she does not mean.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The narrator says Ulysses was glad to hear Penelope trying to get presents from the suitors and flattering them with fair words that he knew she did not mean.

Antinous allows Penelope to accept presents but says the suitors will not leave until she marries the best man among them; the suitors bring a decorated dress, gold brooches, a gold and amber chain, earrings, a necklace, and other presents.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII / BOOK XVIII / BOOK XIX; lines 8452-8531
occurrences.motif_label: weaving stratagem to delay unwanted marriage
occurrences.basis: Penelope invents a delaying device by publicly weaving a pall and secretly undoing the work at night until the deception is exposed.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Penelope describes setting up a large frame, claiming she must finish a pall for Laertes before remarriage, working by day, and undoing the stitches by torchlight at night for three years.
Penelope says maids betrayed her, suitors caught her and forced her to finish, and now she faces pressure from parents while her son resents the wasting of his estate.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII / BOOK XVIII / BOOK XIX; lines 8452-8531
occurrences.motif_label: disguised returner under false identity
occurrences.basis: Ulysses is present as a stranger, avoids his true ancestry, and supplies a detailed alternate Cretan identity as Aethon.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses asks Penelope not to seek his race and family, saying such memories would increase his sorrow and that continual grieving in another's house is improper.
Penelope asks the stranger to tell who he is and where he comes from, saying he cannot be the son of an oak or a rock.

Ulysses replies with a Cretan identity tale: Crete is fertile, has ninety cities and many peoples; Cnossus was ruled by Minos, who conferred with Jove; Minos fathered Deucalion, whose sons were Idomeneus and the claimed Aethon.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: HENRY FESTING JONES. / THE ODYSSEY / BOOK I / BOOK II; lines 851-936
occurrences.motif_label: weaving deception used to delay remarriage
occurrences.basis: Penelope's daily weaving and nightly unweaving deceives the suitors for three years and delays the demanded marriage choice.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Penelope was seen "working on her great web all day long," and at night she would "unpick the stitches again by torchlight."
The ruse lasted three years; in the fourth year a maid disclosed it, and the suitors caught Penelope undoing her work, forcing her to finish.
The suitors' answer is: "Send your mother away, and bid her marry" according to her and her father's choice.

occurrences.motif_label: trickster ancestor and divine patronage
occurrences.basis: Autolycus, Ulysses’ grandfather, is described as accomplished in theft and perjury and as endowed by Mercury because of offerings.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Autolycus is described as the most accomplished thief and perjurer; Mercury endowed him with this gift and enjoyed his companionship because of offerings of thigh bones of goats and kids.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XVIII / BOOK XIX / BOOK XX / BOOK XXI; lines 9416-9503
occurrences.motif_label: crafty marginal challenger requests the elite test object
occurrences.basis: Ulysses is described as speaking craftily and asks to try the bow; the suitors treat him as a beggar or stranger and react angrily.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Servants wash guests' hands, pages mix wine and water, drink-offerings are made, and Ulysses craftily begins to speak.
“give me the bow that I may prove the power of my hands among you all”

The suitors are angered; Antinous rebukes Ulysses, tells of wine causing Centaur Eurytion's madness, wrongdoing, mutilation, and war with centaurs, and threatens to send Ulysses to deadly king Echetus.
Eurymachus says the suitors fear gossip that they were too feeble to string the brave man's bow while a beggarly tramp strung it and shot through the iron.

occurrences.motif_label: Appearance of virtue concealing deceit
occurrences.basis: The youth is imagined turning to appearance, putting on the show of virtue, and trailing the fox of Archilochus behind him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A lively youth is imagined asking whether to make justice his high tower or fortify himself with crooked deceit; he resolves to turn to appearance, show virtue, and trail the fox of Archilochus.

occurrences.motif_label: magical invisibility enabling concealed transgression
occurrences.basis: The ring’s power makes Gyges invisible; the argument links such undetected power with theft, sexual access, killing, release of prisoners, and godlike freedom among humans.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Gyges finds that “when he turned the collet inwards he became invisible, when outwards he reappeared.”

The argument imagines two such rings for the just and unjust; with safe invisibility, a person could steal, enter houses, have sexual access, kill or release prisoners, and be like a god among humans.

occurrences.motif_label: guardian as thief
occurrences.basis: Socrates argues that the skill that makes someone a good keeper also makes him a good thief, and applies this to the just man and to Homeric Autolycus.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates infers that a good keeper is a good thief and cites Homer on Autolycus: “excellent above all men in theft and perjury.”
Socrates says Polemarchus, Homer, and Simonides agree that justice is an art of theft for helping friends and harming enemies; Polemarchus denies this and says he no longer knows what he said.

occurrences.motif_label: trickster at sacrificial boundary
occurrences.basis: Prometheus uses deceptive food portions in a divine-human dispute that explains altar practice.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "For when the gods and mortal men had a dispute at Mecone... Prometheus was forward to cut up a great ox and set portions before them, trying to befool the mind of Zeus."
"Zeus... saw and failed not to perceive the trick... and because of this the tribes of men upon earth burn white bones to the deathless gods upon fragrant altars."

evidence.locator: The Second Book, entrance to Xibalba

evidence.locator: The Second Book, staged death and return
evidence.quote_or_summary: The brothers die on a funeral pile, their bones are powdered and thrown into the river, and they reappear like men-fishes and then ragged old men.

evidence.locator: The Second Book, defeat of Xibalba
evidence.quote_or_summary: After demonstrating killing and restoring, the twins kill the Xibalban princes at their request and do not resuscitate them.

An Aino fisherman is blown about for six nights, reaches land, follows a pleasant rivulet to a populous place, and enters the house of an old chief of very divine aspect who hosts him.

Within a week Sumedha attains the eight Attainments, five Supernatural Faculties, and supernatural knowledge; verses 38-39 say he gave many thousand millions of wealth to rich and poor, went to Himavanta, and made a hermitage and leafy hut near Dhammaka.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Tissa appears ninety-two world-cycles ago. Tissa’s city, family, disciples, Asana Bo-tree, height, and lifespan are listed.

Phussa appears in the same Maṇḍakalpa. The Bodisat is born as warrior-chief Vijitavī, lays aside his kingdom, takes vows under the Teacher, learns the three Piṭakas, preaches the Law, fulfills the Perfection of Morality, and receives a prophecy. Phussa’s city, family, disciples, Āmalaka Bo-tree, height, and lifespan are listed.

Vessabhū appears after Sikhin. The Bodisat is born as king Sudassana, gives robes and other things to the Order with the Buddha at their head, takes vows, becomes righteous in conduct, meditates on the Buddha, and receives a prophecy. Vessabhū’s city, family, disciples, Sal Bo-tree, height, and lifespan are listed.

“My good Kanthaka, do thou save me this once to-night; so that I, having become a Buddha by your help, shall save the world of men, and that of angels too.”
At the city gate, guards have been set by the king; the Bodisat, Channa, and Kanthaka each contemplate leaping the rampart if needed, but the angel residing at the gate opens it.
The Bodisat leaves the city on the full-moon day of Āsāḷhi; when he wishes to gaze back, the earth revolves like a potter’s wheel, and a spot is fixed for the Kanthaka-Nivattana Cetiya.

At the river, Channa names it Anomā; the Bodisat says his renunciation will also be called Anomā, and Kanthaka leaps across the broad river.
On the sandy beach, the Bodisat tells Channa to return with his ornaments and Kanthaka because he will become a hermit; Channa asks to join him, but the Bodisat refuses three times.

At dawn he takes robe and bowl, travels halfway, meets the Hindu mendicant Upaka, announces how he became a Buddha, and arrives near Benares that evening.

During coronation, housewarming, and Nanda’s marriage festivals, the Buddha gives Nanda his bowl to carry in order to make him abandon the world. Janapada Kalyāṇī calls after Nanda, who follows the Blessed One to the Wihāra and is received unwillingly into the Order.

Makhā Deva resolves to leave the world that day, grants the barber a valuable village, tells his eldest son to assume sovereignty, and says he will enter religious life in Makhā Deva's Mango-park.

Makhā Deva gives up sovereignty, becomes a hermit in the Mango-grove, practices goodwill and meditation for eighty-four thousand years, is born in Brahma heaven, later becomes King Nimi in Mithilā, reunites his family, becomes a hermit again, and returns to Brahma heaven.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The old Bodisat tells his sons to lead their herds to the mountainous part of the forest during the growing crops and return when the crops are cut.

Brownie does not know proper travel times and leads his herd early and late, at dawn and evening twilight, past village gates; men kill many deer, and he returns to the forest with diminished numbers.
Beauty is described as learned, clever, and resourceful; he avoids village gates, does not travel by day, dawn, or twilight, travels at midnight, and reaches the forest without losing any animal.
After four months and after the crops are cut, Brownie loses the rest of his herd and arrives alone, while Beauty comes to his parent with all five hundred deer.

She asks her parents to let her be ordained; they refuse, saying the family is wealthy and she is their only daughter.
Her husband says that if she thinks the body sinful she should become a nun; he grants leave, makes a costly donation, and has her admitted among the nuns connected with Devadatta.

evidence.quote_or_summary: One story says Orestes instituted Diana’s worship at Nemi after killing Thoas, fleeing with his sister to Italy, and bringing the image of Tauric Diana.

occurrences.motif_label: soul departure at death or danger
occurrences.basis: The soul is said to fly away at death or to escape during sickness, yawning, dying, childbirth, danger, marriage, or festivals.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A missionary says he is two in one, with a visible great body and an invisible little body that flies away at death; some Australian interlocutors reply that they too have a little body in the breast and give different answers about its destination after death.
The soul is commonly supposed to escape by natural openings of the body, especially the mouth and nostrils.

Examples include fish-hooks attached to a sick man in Celebes, a Haida medicine-man’s hollow bone for bottling souls, Marquesans holding a dying man’s mouth and nose, Hindus snapping thumbs during yawning, and Itonamas sealing a dying person’s eyes, nose, and mouth.

Childbirth precautions in Celebes and among Alfoers include tying a band around the expectant mother, closing household openings, stopping chinks, tying animal mouths, and requiring people in the house to keep their mouths shut.
Frazer states that the soul is often conceived as a bird ready to fly; Malay, Javanese, Batta, and South Celebes examples use rice to attract, keep, or detain the soul during vulnerable occasions.

occurrences.motif_label: Wandering soul absent from sleeping body
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly describes the soul leaving the body during sleep, with danger if it is detained and cannot return.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A sleeper's soul is said to wander from the body and visit dream places; if the soul is permanently detained, the person dies.
The passage gives dangers to the sleeper's soul: fighting another sleeper's soul, or being carried off by the soul of a recently deceased person, as feared in the Aru Islands.
The passage states that many people avoid waking a sleeper because the absent soul may not return in time; if waking is necessary, it should be gradual.

occurrences.motif_label: involuntary departure or extraction of the soul
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly states that the soul's departure is not always voluntary and may be extracted by ghosts, demons, or sorcerers, then gives examples of living souls leaving or being carried off.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "The departure of the soul is not always voluntary. It may be extracted from the body against its will by ghosts, demons, or sorcerers."

Karen funeral practices include tying children during a passing funeral, using split bamboo and sticks at the grave to show souls how to climb out, avoiding burying souls with bamboos, carrying the bamboos away, and using three branch-hooks while calling the spirit to prevent it from remaining with the dead.

In Keisar people avoid graves at night lest ghosts catch the passer-by's soul. Key Islanders believe unfed forefathers can make people sick by detaining their souls, so food is laid on graves while ancestors are asked to let the sick person's soul return or drive it home.

In Bolang Mongondo sickness is ascribed to ancestral spirits carrying off the patient's soul. Priestesses acting as physicians use a cloth doll on a spear, dance and charms, colored cloths, head-wrapping, pursuit around the house, and restoration of the recaptured soul to a sick boy.

occurrences.motif_label: Expulsion or removal of a harmful or dangerous figure from the community
occurrences.basis: The customs include carrying out Death, carrying figures out of the village, throwing them into water, and carrying the metsik across the village boundary; one speech says Carnival was condemned because he had done harm.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Frazer says two kindred sets of European peasant spring observances have the simulated death of a divine or supernatural being as a leading feature: “Burying the Carnival” and “Driving or carrying out Death,” chiefly known on German and Slavonic ground.

At Braller, a straw-man on a sledge is accompanied by disguised mourners and a procession, tried under a tree, sentenced to death, captured by two girls after attempted rescue, hanged on a tree, and mourned by the disguised old men; an official says Carnival was condemned because he had done harm.

In Altdorf and Weingarten a straw Fool is carried and thrown into water; elsewhere a living Fool representative is thrown into water; at Balwe a straw-man is thrown into the river amid rejoicing and called “Burying the Carnival.”

Esthonians make a straw figure called metsik or wood-spirit, dress it as male one year and female the next, carry it across the village boundary with joyful cries, fasten it to a tree in the wood, and believe the ceremony protects against misfortune.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says Adonis spends half or a third of the year in the lower world and the rest in the upper world, and Frazer interprets this as vegetation or corn buried in earth and reappearing above ground.
