evidence.quote_or_summary: An eyewitness sees a procession of fifty men go westward, led by a painted, shell-bedecked priest and followed by the torch-bearing Shu-lu-wit-si, or God of Fire.
“They are going,” said he, “to the city of the Ka-ka and the home of our others.”

Four days later the men return at sunset, costumed and masked, each bearing a basket of living turtles; the turtles are carried tenderly, some wrapped in blankets and likened to little children on pilgrims’ backs.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS; lines 3546-3619
occurrences.motif_label: released carrier removes harm by departure
occurrences.basis: The swallow, cleansing bird, straw kite, expelled Brahman, and freed buffalo calf all remove or bear away a harmful burden through release, departure, or banishment.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Batta ceremony for a childless woman: sacrifice of three grasshoppers and release of a swallow with a prayer that the curse fall on the bird and fly away.
At Jewish cleansing of a leper or a house suspected of leprosy taint, a bird is let fly away.
Miaotse ceremony when the eldest son reaches seven: the father makes a straw kite and lets it fly in the desert bearing away evil.
In Travancore, a holy Brahman embraces a dangerously ill Rajah, undertakes to bear his sins and diseases, and is sent away from the country forever.
Among the Badagas, the sins of a deceased person are laid on a buffalo calf after a confession; the calf is set free and not used for common purposes.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS; lines 4789-4872
occurrences.motif_label: ritual expulsion beyond community boundaries
occurrences.basis: Mamurius Veturius is driven out of the city, and the passage explains this as necessary for a scapegoat who carries a burden away.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In Rome each 14 March a skin-clad man called Mamurius Veturius, 'the old Mars,' was led through the streets, beaten with long white rods, and driven out near the start of the old Roman year.

The passage says the representative of the god in the Roman ceremony appears to have been both vegetation deity and scapegoat; as scapegoat he must be driven beyond the boundaries to carry his burden away, and Mamurius Veturius appears to have been driven to the land of the Oscans.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS; lines 7733-7804
occurrences.motif_label: departure from community and return after transformation
occurrences.basis: Belli-Paaro youths are taken to the forest and later returned to parents; Huskanaw youths are confined in the woods and later brought back into towns under supervision.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At the king’s order a forest place is appointed; youths are brought there weeping, told they must suffer death, dispose of property, and are instructed by initiated persons in a dance called killing and songs praising Belli.

After instruction, novices are shut in huts, interact with women bringing food, pretend ignorance of people and customs, wear bird feathers and bark caps, dance the dance of Belli publicly, and are taken to their parents’ houses.

Huskanaw among the Indians of Virginia is described as an initiatory ceremony in which youths are confined alone in the woods for months and receive only an intoxicating root infusion, leading to a period of madness.

The Huskanaw account says the youths drink enough Wysoccan, likened to water of Lethe, to forget parents, possessions, and language; doctors gradually restore them, keepers guard them, and they must relearn speech and recognition, thereby commencing men by forgetting they had been boys.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: COMPILED BY / PREFACE / JAPANESE FAIRY TALES / MY LORD BAG OF RICE; lines 151-260
occurrences.motif_label: armed hero departs seeking adventure
occurrences.basis: Hidesato deliberately arms himself and goes out in search of adventures.

evidence.locator: lines 151-260, opening of 'My Lord Bag of Rice'
evidence.quote_or_summary: Hidesato, also called Tawara Toda, is introduced as a brave warrior who arms himself with swords, bow, and quiver and sets out seeking adventure.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE TONGUE-CUT SPARROW / THE STORY OF URASHIMA TARO, THE FISHER LAD / THE FARMER AND THE BADGER / THE ADVENTURES OF KINTARO, THE GOLDEN BOY; lines 1577-1695
occurrences.motif_label: Hidden noble mother and child in mountain exile
occurrences.basis: Kintaro's mother, whose high rank is unknown to local woodcutters, flees to the mountains after her husband's death and raises the child there.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Kintoki marries, falls into disgrace, dies, and his widow flees to the Ashigara Mountains, where she gives birth to Kintaro, the Golden Boy.
Kintaro's great strength is emphasized: by age eight he cuts trees like woodcutters, receives a large ax, is called Wonder-child, and smashes rocks and stones.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE TONGUE-CUT SPARROW / THE STORY OF URASHIMA TARO, THE FISHER LAD / THE FARMER AND THE BADGER / THE ADVENTURES OF KINTARO, THE GOLDEN BOY; lines 1834-1943
occurrences.motif_label: departure from mountain home to enter heroic service
occurrences.basis: Kintaro leaves his mother and animal companions in the mountains to travel with Sadamitsu to the Capital and enter Lord Raiko’s service.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Kintaro’s mother rejoices at the chance for him to become a samurai, entrusts him to Sadamitsu, and Kintaro exclaims with joy that he will go with the general.
Sadamitsu decides to leave for the Capital with Kintaro; Yama-uba is sad but hides her grief, and Kintaro promises to remember and care for her when he becomes a knight.
Kintaro’s tamed animals—the bear, deer, monkey, and hare—come to see him off, follow him to the foot of the mountain, and climb a tree to watch him disappear from sight.
Sadamitsu brings Kintaro to Lord Minamoto-no-Raiko, tells his story, and Raiko makes Kintaro one of his vassals.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE TONGUE-CUT SPARROW / THE STORY OF URASHIMA TARO, THE FISHER LAD / THE FARMER AND THE BADGER / THE ADVENTURES OF KINTARO, THE GOLDEN BOY; lines 2053-2152
occurrences.motif_label: innocent girl ordered taken to wild mountains for execution
occurrences.basis: Terute orders a servant to take Hase-Hime to the Hibari Mountains, the wildest part of the country, and kill her there.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Taking advantage of her husband’s absence, Terute orders an old servant to take Hase-Hime to the Hibari Mountains, described as the wildest part of the country, and kill her there.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE STORY OF URASHIMA TARO, THE FISHER LAD / THE FARMER AND THE BADGER / THE ADVENTURES OF KINTARO, THE GOLDEN BOY / THE STORY OF THE MAN WHO DID NOT WISH TO DIE; lines 2251-2371
occurrences.motif_label: Departure to a deathless realm by magical conveyance
occurrences.basis: Jofuku sends Sentaro to the country of Perpetual Life on a paper crane that grows, rises into the air, and flies over mountains and out to sea.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Jofuku says Sentaro is idle and unsuited to hermit life, but will be helped by being sent to the country of Perpetual Life, where people live forever.
Jofuku gives Sentaro a paper crane; Sentaro sits on it, it grows large enough to ride, spreads its wings, rises, and flies over mountains toward the sea.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE STORY OF URASHIMA TARO, THE FISHER LAD / THE FARMER AND THE BADGER / THE ADVENTURES OF KINTARO, THE GOLDEN BOY / THE STORY OF THE MAN WHO DID NOT WISH TO DIE; lines 2373-2477
occurrences.motif_label: magical departure to a distant otherworldly land
occurrences.basis: Sentaro is carried thousands of miles by a paper crane to the country of Perpetual Life.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sentaro becomes accustomed to a swift flight on a paper bird; after several days they reach an island, and the crane folds itself into his pocket.
Sentaro explores the strange prosperous country, takes hotel lodgings, and receives help from the proprietor to become a resident in the country of Perpetual Life.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE FARMER AND THE BADGER / THE ADVENTURES OF KINTARO, THE GOLDEN BOY / THE STORY OF THE MAN WHO DID NOT WISH TO DIE / THE BAMBOO-CUTTER AND THE MOON-CHILD; lines 3062-3176
occurrences.motif_label: departure of a family member on a difficult journey
occurrences.basis: The father is summoned to the capital, prepares for a long and arduous journey, and leaves his wife and child behind.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The father is summoned to the capital; the text describes travel from Matsuyama to Kyoto as difficult, with rough roads and long walking distances.

The wife anxiously helps her husband prepare; she cannot accompany him because the distance is too great and her duty is to care for the home. The husband asks her to care for everything, especially their daughter.
The father struggles emotionally to leave, exits through the garden gate, and the wife carries the child to the gate to watch him until he vanishes in the distance.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE ADVENTURES OF KINTARO, THE GOLDEN BOY / THE STORY OF THE MAN WHO DID NOT WISH TO DIE / THE BAMBOO-CUTTER AND THE MOON-CHILD / THE GOBLIN OF ADACHIGAHARA; lines 3614-3738
occurrences.motif_label: lost traveler enters haunted place at nightfall
occurrences.basis: The priest loses his way on the haunted plain at sunset and seeks shelter at the cottage.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At sunset a Buddhist pilgrim priest, walking from shrine to shrine, comes to the plain after losing his way; he is tired, hungry, and seeking lodging in late autumn cold.
The priest sees a clump of trees and a single ray of light, reaches a miserable cottage with broken fence and worn screens, and sees an old woman spinning by an old lantern.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: PREFACE / JAPANESE FAIRY TALES / MY LORD BAG OF RICE / THE TONGUE-CUT SPARROW; lines 396-507
occurrences.motif_label: departure to seek lost or injured companion
occurrences.basis: The old man decides to search for the sparrow and sets out over hills and through woods calling for her.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The old man asks how she could be so cruel, is distressed for Suzume San, weeps after his wife sleeps, and decides to look for the sparrow the next day.
He starts “over the hills and through the woods,” stopping at bamboo clumps to call, “Where, oh where does my tongue-cut sparrow stay?”

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: PREFACE / JAPANESE FAIRY TALES / MY LORD BAG OF RICE / THE TONGUE-CUT SPARROW; lines 509-612
occurrences.motif_label: journey out and return home with a gift
occurrences.basis: The old man travels to find the sparrow, enters her hidden home in the bamboo grove, receives a gift, and returns home.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The old man reaches a bamboo wood, finds his sparrow waiting, hears her speak, sees that a new tongue has grown, and realizes she is a fairy rather than a common bird.
The sparrow leads the old man to a beautiful house in the bamboo grove, furnished with fine mats, silk and crape cushions, vases, lacquer boxes, and tokonoma alcoves.

The old man says he must return home; the Lady Sparrow offers him one of two boxes, large or small, and he chooses the smaller because he is too old and feeble to carry the larger one. The sparrows help him leave with it.
The old man comes home late, finds his wife angry, tells her of his visit to the sparrow’s house, and they sit down to open the box.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE JELLY FISH AND THE MONKEY / THE QUARREL OF THE MONKEY AND THE CRAB / THE WHITE HARE AND THE CROCODILES / THE STORY OF PRINCE YAMATO TAKE; lines 5705-5811
occurrences.motif_label: young royal hero commissioned to restore order
occurrences.basis: Yamato has just reached manhood at sixteen and is sent by his father to subdue rebels, beginning a dangerous expedition.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The realm is troubled by outlaw brothers Kumaso and Takeru; Keiko orders sixteen-year-old Yamato to subdue them, and Yamato receives the command joyfully and without fear.
Before leaving, Yamato prepares with followers, prays at Ise, takes leave of his aunt Princess Yamato, and receives from her a gorgeous robe as a keepsake and good-luck aid.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE JELLY FISH AND THE MONKEY / THE QUARREL OF THE MONKEY AND THE CRAB / THE WHITE HARE AND THE CROCODILES / THE STORY OF PRINCE YAMATO TAKE; lines 5926-6019
occurrences.motif_label: heroic departure on royal military mission
occurrences.basis: Yamato Take leaves the capital at royal command to lead an army east against rebels.

evidence.quote_or_summary: News arrives of rebellion in the eastern provinces; Yamato Take offers to lead the army, and the King reluctantly agrees because of the prince’s exceptional bravery and strength.
The King gives Yamato Take the Eight-Arms-Length-Spear of the Holly Tree, compared to a royal standard or banner, and the prince departs east with his army.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE JELLY FISH AND THE MONKEY / THE QUARREL OF THE MONKEY AND THE CRAB / THE WHITE HARE AND THE CROCODILES / THE STORY OF PRINCE YAMATO TAKE; lines 6021-6126
occurrences.motif_label: dangerous sea crossing
occurrences.basis: The expedition attempts to cross from Idzu to Kadzusa by boat and is endangered by the storm at sea.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “This is not the sea! This is only a brook! ... I could jump this if I would.”
After they embark, the sky clouds, a storm arises, waves rise high, and the boat carrying Yamato Take, Ototachibana, and the men is violently tossed.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE JELLY FISH AND THE MONKEY / THE QUARREL OF THE MONKEY AND THE CRAB / THE WHITE HARE AND THE CROCODILES / THE STORY OF PRINCE YAMATO TAKE; lines 6128-6233
occurrences.motif_label: hero’s safe passage through another’s sacrifice
occurrences.basis: Yamato Take reaches the opposite shore safely and later attributes this to his wife’s willing sacrifice.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ototachibana leaps into the sea, disappears in the waves, the storm ceases, the sea becomes calm, and the sea gods are said to be appeased.
Yamato Take reaches the opposite shore safely and later conquers the Eastern Barbarians, identified as the Ainu.
Yamato Take ascribes his safe landing to his wife’s faithful sacrifice and remembers her goodness and love.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE QUARREL OF THE MONKEY AND THE CRAB / THE WHITE HARE AND THE CROCODILES / THE STORY OF PRINCE YAMATO TAKE / MOMOTARO, OR THE STORY OF THE SON OF A PEACH; lines 6371-6508
occurrences.motif_label: heroic departure from home for a dangerous expedition
occurrences.basis: Momotaro requests permission to leave his old parents and home in order to attack the devils' island stronghold, promising to return.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Momotaro asks his old father for a request before repaying his kindness; he asks to go away at once, and says he will come back.

evidence.locator: lines 6371-6508, Momotaro explains the Island of Devils
evidence.quote_or_summary: Momotaro describes a sea island northeast of Japan as the stronghold of devils who invade, kill, rob, carry off goods, disobey the Emperor, and eat some captives.
The old man says he will not hinder Momotaro and tells him to go to the island, destroy the demons, and bring peace to the land.
The two old people tearfully say farewell and expect Momotaro to return victorious; Momotaro says goodbye and leaves the house.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE QUARREL OF THE MONKEY AND THE CRAB / THE WHITE HARE AND THE CROCODILES / THE STORY OF PRINCE YAMATO TAKE / MOMOTARO, OR THE STORY OF THE SON OF A PEACH; lines 6510-6645
occurrences.motif_label: Voyage across water to a monster stronghold
occurrences.basis: The party boards a small ship, crosses the sea, watches for the demons’ island, and reaches the castle stronghold of the devils.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After traveling through valleys and hills, the party reaches the shore of the North-Eastern Sea; the animals have never seen the sea and wonder how to cross to the Island of Devils.

Momotaro obtains a small ship; the four sail in fair weather, the animals become accustomed to the water, they watch for the demons’ island, and Momotaro longs to kill the monsters who harmed his country.

The travelers see land with a large castle on a precipitous shore; Momotaro recognizes the devils’ stronghold, thinks about the attack, and orders the pheasant to fly to the castle and engage the demons.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE WHITE HARE AND THE CROCODILES / THE STORY OF PRINCE YAMATO TAKE / MOMOTARO, OR THE STORY OF THE SON OF A PEACH / THE OGRE OF RASHOMON; lines 6755-6881
occurrences.motif_label: hero accepts a public challenge to enter a feared place
occurrences.basis: Watanabe accepts Hojo’s challenge, rides out in dangerous weather, and tests the rumor at the gate to preserve his honor.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hojo proposes that Watanabe prove the matter by going to the gate himself; Watanabe accepts because he cannot bear being thought afraid.
Watanabe buckles on his sword, armor, and helmet; his comrades write their names on paper, which he says he will put on the Gate of Rashomon as proof of his visit.
Watanabe rides out on a moonless, starless, stormy night with heavy rain and howling wind; his companions wait by the charcoal fire and wonder whether he will meet an Oni.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: JAPANESE FAIRY TALES / MY LORD BAG OF RICE / THE TONGUE-CUT SPARROW / THE STORY OF URASHIMA TARO, THE FISHER LAD; lines 728-854
occurrences.motif_label: departure alone over water before supernatural encounter
occurrences.basis: Urashima goes out in his boat, leaves other fishing boats behind, drifts far over the blue waters, and then hears a non-human voice.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The next morning Urashima goes out in his boat, passes the other fishing boats, drifts far over the blue waters, and thinks about wishing for thousands of years of life.
Urashima hears his own name called over the sea, sees no other boat, and then notices that the very tortoise he rescued has come beside his boat.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: JAPANESE FAIRY TALES / MY LORD BAG OF RICE / THE TONGUE-CUT SPARROW / THE STORY OF URASHIMA TARO, THE FISHER LAD; lines 856-981
occurrences.motif_label: Animal guide carries human to an undersea otherworld
occurrences.basis: The tortoise serves as guide and mount, taking Urashima down through the sea to the Dragon King’s palace.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The tortoise asks whether Urashima has seen Rin Gin, the Palace of the Dragon King of the Sea, says it lies far away at the bottom of the sea, and offers to be his guide.
The tortoise tells Urashima to ride on its back, suddenly becomes large enough to carry a man, leaps into the sea, and carries Urashima through the water without tiring him or wetting his clothes.
A magnificent gate and the sloping roofs of a palace appear; the tortoise identifies them as the gate and palace of Rin Gin, the Sea King’s Palace.

occurrences.source_title: Jataka tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE WISE AND THE FOOLISH MERCHANT / THE ELEPHANT GIRLY-FACE / THE BANYAN DEER / THE PRINCES AND THE WATER-SPRITE; lines 1228-1339
occurrences.motif_label: exile of rightful heirs to the forest
occurrences.basis: The king sends the older princes away to the forest to preserve their lives and later the eldest returns to take the throne by right.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The king refuses, saying the kingdom must go first to the oldest son, then the second, and only after both are dead to the third.
The king fears the queen may harm the older princes and sends them to live in the forest until his death, telling them to return later to reign in the city that is theirs by right.

The three princes live in the forest until the king dies, then return to the palace; the eldest is made king, has his brothers rule with him, and builds a home for the water-sprite in the palace grounds.

occurrences.source_title: More Jataka Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: XVIII / THE WISE GOAT AND THE WOLF / PRINCE WICKED AND THE GRATEFUL ANIMALS / BEAUTY AND BROWNIE; lines 1582-1626
occurrences.motif_label: seasonal departure and safe return
occurrences.basis: The deer are instructed to leave the forest for the high hills during the crop season and return after the crops are cut.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The father says he, the mother, and older deer will stay in the forest, while Beauty and Brownie must lead their herds to the high hills until the crops are cut.
Beauty travels at night, avoids villages, brings his herd safely to the high hills, and loses no deer.
When crops are cut, the deer return; Beauty brings all his herd back, while Brownie again travels by day past villages and reaches the forest with only a few deer left.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE. / THE SIEGE OF TROY. / RETURN OF THE GREEKS FROM TROY.; lines 10299-10392
occurrences.motif_label: Divine intercession secures the hero's departure
occurrences.basis: Athene intercedes with Zeus, Hermes conveys the order, and Calypso equips Odysseus to depart on a raft toward home.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Athene intercedes with Zeus; Zeus sends Hermes to command Calypso to release Odysseus and provide transport; Calypso obeys, instructs him in raft-building, weaves the sails, and he departs alone.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CERES. / APHRODITE (VENUS). / VENUS. / HELIOS (SOL).; lines 1985-2069
occurrences.motif_label: solar departure and return
occurrences.basis: Helios rises in the east, traverses the sky, descends westward, and in later poetry returns east by a winged vessel.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Helios, son of Hyperion and Theia, rises in the east preceded by Eos, drives a gold fiery chariot with fire-breathing steeds, descends toward the sea, is followed by Selene, and rests on a couch prepared by sea-nymphs.
The passage notes no Homeric or Hesiodic explanation of Helios' return, but later poets invent a winged boat or cup made by Hephaestus to carry him from west to east.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VENUS. / HELIOS (SOL). / EOS (AURORA). / PHOEBUS-APOLLO.; lines 2279-2363
occurrences.motif_label: divine descent to found an oracle
occurrences.basis: Apollo descends from Olympus to earth and travels in search of a place to establish an oracle.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After taking his place among the immortals, Apollo descends to earth to interpret his father's will and travels through many countries seeking an oracle site.
Apollo reaches the southern side of Parnassus near Crissa and finds a secluded ancient oracle where Gaea once revealed the future and later resigned it to Themis.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VENUS. / HELIOS (SOL). / EOS (AURORA). / PHOEBUS-APOLLO.; lines 2441-2527
occurrences.motif_label: god in temporary servitude
occurrences.basis: Apollo is deprived of power and dignity and serves Admetus as a shepherd for nine years; later Apollo and Poseidon serve Laomedon while in exile.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Apollo destroys the Cyclops who forged the fatal thunderbolts; Zeus, after Leto's intercession, mitigates punishment to loss of power and dignity and nine years' servitude as Admetus' shepherd.
Apollo leaves Thessaly for Phrygia, meets Poseidon in similar exile and servitude, and both serve Laomedon of Troy: Apollo tending flocks and Poseidon building the city walls.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: BRAURONIAN ARTEMIS. / SELENE-ARTEMIS. / DIANA. / HEPHAESTUS (VULCAN).; lines 3109-3194
occurrences.motif_label: Cast-down divine child marked by injury
occurrences.basis: Zeus, Hephaestus's father, hurls him from heaven after he supports Hera; the fall ends on Lemnos and leaves him lame.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hephaestus is introduced as son of Zeus and Hera, god of beneficial fire, workmanship, mechanical arts, and hearth; he is deformed and lame after Zeus hurls him from heaven to Lemnos, where the Lemnians receive him and he later teaches metalwork and useful arts.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: GLAUCUS. / THETIS. / LEUCOTHEA. / THE SIRENS.; lines 3548-3566
occurrences.motif_label: flight ending in leap into water
occurrences.basis: Ino and her son are pursued to the sea-shore and enter the deep when escape appears impossible.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Athamas pursues Ino and her son to the sea-shore; seeing no escape, she throws herself with the child into the deep.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VICTORIA. / HERMES (MERCURY). / MERCURY. / DIONYSUS (BACCHUS).; lines 3954-4041
occurrences.motif_label: departure, expedition, and return
occurrences.basis: Dionysus travels through eastern regions and later returns to Greece from his Eastern expedition.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Dionysus leads men, women, fauns, and satyrs bearing Thyrsi and instruments; seated in a panther-drawn chariot, he progresses through Syria, Egypt, Arabia, India, and other regions, conquering, founding cities, and civilizing.

On return to Greece, Dionysus encounters Lycurgus, who drives the nymphs from Nysa; Dionysus leaps into the sea and is received by Thetis; Lycurgus is punished with madness and kills Dryas, mistaking him for a vine.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: FORTUNA. / ANANKE (NECESSITAS). / MOMUS. / EROS (CUPID, AMOR) AND PSYCHE.; lines 4825-4914
occurrences.motif_label: Bride exposed at precipice and conveyed by wind to supernatural spouse
occurrences.basis: Psyche is dressed as for death, taken to a precipice, and transported by Zephyrus to the palace of Eros.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Psyche, youngest of three princesses, is so beautiful that Aphrodite grows jealous; after Delphi’s oracle, her father has her dressed as for the grave and taken to a precipice, from which Zephyrus carries her to a meadow palace.
Eros dwells there and courts Psyche unseen, warning her not to behold him; her sisters visit, envy her, claim her lover is a monster, and give her a dagger.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: ANANKE (NECESSITAS). / MOMUS. / EROS (CUPID, AMOR) AND PSYCHE. / HYMEN.; lines 4964-4987
occurrences.motif_label: journey to festival interrupted by abduction and return
occurrences.basis: The maidens depart from Athens toward Eleusis for a festival, are abducted to an island, and are eventually returned safely to Athens.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hymen disguises himself as a girl and joins maidens, including his beloved, traveling from Athens to Eleusis for a festival of Demeter.
Pirates surprise the travelers, carry them to a desert island, drink deeply, and fall into heavy sleep.
After the parents agree, Hymen returns to the island, brings the maidens safely back to Athens, marries his beloved, and their happy union makes his name synonymous with conjugal felicity.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: SECOND DYNASTY. / CRONUS (SATURN). / SATURN. / RHEA (OPS).; lines 651-698
occurrences.motif_label: Ecstatic mountain search for lost youth
occurrences.basis: Atys flees to the mountains, and the Corybantes annually march into the mountains to seek him with noisy ritual action.

evidence.quote_or_summary: During the wedding feast, the enraged goddess causes panic; Atys becomes temporarily mad, flees to the mountains, and destroys himself.
Cybele institutes yearly mourning for Atys, and her priests, the Corybantes, march into the mountains to seek the lost youth.
After finding Atys, the Corybantes show ecstatic delight through violent gestures, dancing, shouting, and self-wounding.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CEREALIA. / VESTALIA. / PART II.--LEGENDS. / CADMUS.; lines 6563-6631
occurrences.motif_label: abducted beloved or kinswoman prompting a quest
occurrences.basis: Europa is abducted by Zeus, and Agenor sends Cadmus away to recover her, forbidding return without her.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After Zeus abducts Europa, Agenor, king of Phoenicia, sends his son Cadmus to search for her and not return without his sister.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VESTALIA. / PART II.--LEGENDS. / CADMUS. / PERSEUS.; lines 6633-6734
occurrences.motif_label: heroic departure for monster-slaying quest
occurrences.basis: Perseus leaves on an expedition to slay Medusa and must gain special equipment and knowledge before confronting the Gorgons.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Polydectes joins Danae, educates Perseus as a hero, and encourages him toward a deed; the slaying of Medusa is chosen for greatest renown.
Perseus needs winged sandals, a magic wallet, and Aides' helmet from the Nymphs; guided by Hermes and Pallas-Athene, he takes the Graeae's single eye and tooth until they give directions.

With helmet, wallet, Hermes' sickle, and winged sandals, Perseus reaches the sleeping Gorgons; avoiding direct sight and using his shield image, he cuts off Medusa's head, from whose trunk Pegasus and Chrysaor spring.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VESTALIA. / PART II.--LEGENDS. / CADMUS. / PERSEUS.; lines 6834-6902
occurrences.motif_label: winged escape from captivity
occurrences.basis: Daedalus, kept almost a prisoner, makes wings for himself and Icarus and uses them to flee Crete.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Daedalus tires of exile and near imprisonment by Minos, contrives wings for himself and Icarus, and trains his son to use them.
During the flight, Icarus forgets the warning not to approach the sun; the wax melts, he falls into the sea, and drowns.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: PART II.--LEGENDS. / CADMUS. / PERSEUS. / THE ARGONAUTS.; lines 6904-6953
occurrences.motif_label: dispossessed heir departs to reclaim kingdom
occurrences.basis: Jason, son of the displaced king Aeson, leaves Chiron and goes to Iolcus to demand the throne from the usurper Pelias.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Aeson is forced to flee after Pelias usurps Iolcus; Jason is saved, entrusted to Chiron, and trained for ten years in the Centaur’s cave.
Jason desires to regain his paternal inheritance, leaves Chiron, and sets out for Iolcus to demand the kingdom from Pelias.
Pelias entertains Jason, then Jason demands the throne; Pelias consents only if Jason undertakes an expedition for him.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CADMUS. / PERSEUS. / THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE.; lines 6955-7048
occurrences.motif_label: Quest departure by ship with heroic company
occurrences.basis: Jason gathers heroes, commands the Argonauts, performs sacrifice and augury, and sails in the Argo on the expedition connected with the Golden Fleece.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Jason undertook the perilous expedition proposed by his uncle, who hoped to be rid of him through its dangers.

Jason invited young heroes to join him. Argos, guided by Pallas-Athene, built the Argo, a fifty-oared galley with a prophetic board from the speaking oak of Dodona; the ship was strong, light, and ornamented.
Jason was commander-in-chief; Tiphys, Lynceus, Heracles, Peleus, Telamon, Castor, Pollux, Orpheus, Mopsus, and many others are named among the crew or assigned roles.
Before departure Jason sacrificed to Poseidon and other sea-deities, invoked Zeus and the Fates, Mopsus found the auguries favorable, and the Argo sailed from the harbor.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CADMUS. / PERSEUS. / THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE.; lines 7050-7143
occurrences.motif_label: Delayed departure from the quest
occurrences.basis: The Argonauts nearly forget the expedition's object while feasting and are recalled to duty by Heracles.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Jason appears before Hypsipyle; she gives him her father's sceptre, invites him to the throne, and the Argonauts settle into pleasure while Heracles remains on board.
The Argonauts' departure is delayed until Heracles appears and recalls them to their duty.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CADMUS. / PERSEUS. / THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE.; lines 7050-7143
occurrences.motif_label: Hero separated from expedition by divine will
occurrences.basis: The Argo leaves Heracles behind, and Glaucus states that Zeus wills Heracles to remain because he has another mission.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Argo leaves Heracles and Polyphemus behind; Glaucus rises from the waves and says Zeus wills Heracles to remain for another mission; Polyphemus remains in Mysia, founds a city, and becomes king.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: SATURN. / RHEA (OPS). / DIVISION OF THE WORLD. / THEORIES AS TO THE ORIGIN OF MAN.; lines 746-830
occurrences.motif_label: Justice abandons the earth
occurrences.basis: Themis, goddess of Justice, leaves mankind because of evil-doing and returns to heaven.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Themis, goddess of Justice, becomes disheartened at human evil-doing, abandons earth, and flies back to heaven.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CADMUS. / PERSEUS. / THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE.; lines 7524-7533
occurrences.motif_label: aerial escape in a dragon-drawn chariot
occurrences.basis: Medea departs through the air in a golden chariot drawn by dragons.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Medea is seen "gliding through the air in a golden chariot drawn by dragons."

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: PERSEUS. / THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE. / PELOPS.; lines 7535-7585
occurrences.motif_label: exiled hero's departure to a new land
occurrences.basis: Pelops is defeated, forced to leave Phrygia, and emigrates into Greece before the central contest begins.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Pelops is the son of Tantalus; after Tantalus is banished and Pelops is defeated, Pelops goes to Greece, sees Hippodamia, and learns that an oracle foretold Oenomaus's death on the day of her marriage.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE. / PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES).; lines 8170-8264
occurrences.motif_label: accidental killing followed by voluntary exile
occurrences.basis: Heracles accidentally kills a youth at a banquet, is absolved by the father, but chooses to banish himself according to local law.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At Oeneus's banquet Heracles accidentally kills a noble serving youth; although the father absolves him, Heracles chooses legal exile and leaves for Trachin with Deianeira and Hyllus.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES). / BELLEROPHON. / THESEUS.; lines 8404-8503
occurrences.motif_label: hero chooses perilous departure route
occurrences.basis: Theseus leaves for Athens and deliberately chooses the dangerous land route over the safe sea route to prove himself by feats of valour.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Though urged to use the safe sea route, Theseus chooses the dangerous land road to Athens in order to emulate Heracles and distinguish himself by valour.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: HERACLES (HERCULES). / BELLEROPHON. / THESEUS. / OEDIPUS.; lines 8727-8823
occurrences.motif_label: recognition of hidden identity leading to self-punishment and exile
occurrences.basis: Tiresias reveals Oedipus's true relation to Laius and Jocaste; Oedipus blinds himself and leaves Thebes as an outcast.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Tiresias tells Oedipus: "Thou thyself art the murderer of the old king Laius, who was thy father; and thou art wedded to his widow, thine own mother."
The old servant and shepherd confirm the story; Oedipus blinds himself in despair, and Jocaste hangs herself.
Antigone accompanies Oedipus as he leaves Thebes, becomes a homeless beggar, and finally finds refuge in the grove of the Eumenides at Colonus.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THESEUS. / OEDIPUS. / THE SEVEN AGAINST THEBES. / THE EPIGONI.; lines 8979-9016
occurrences.motif_label: abandonment of city to preserve life
occurrences.basis: Tiresias tells the Thebans they can save their lives only by abandoning the city with wives and families, and they evacuate by night.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After losing their leader and many warriors, the Thebans retreat behind the walls and consult the blind old seer Tiresias, who says they can save their lives only by abandoning the city with wives and families.
The Thebans send ambassadors to prolong negotiations, evacuate by night with wives and children, and the next morning the Argives enter and plunder Thebes, placing Thersander on the throne.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE SEVEN AGAINST THEBES. / THE EPIGONI. / ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE.; lines 9109-9206
occurrences.motif_label: Persecuted heroic descendants seeking asylum
occurrences.basis: The children of Heracles flee Eurystheus and seek successive protectors before being received at Athens.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After Heracles' apotheosis, his children are persecuted by Eurystheus, flee with Iolaus to Ceyx at Trachin, then seek refuge at Athens, where Demophoon receives and protects them.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE SEVEN AGAINST THEBES. / THE EPIGONI. / ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE.; lines 9208-9222
occurrences.motif_label: banishment of the offender
occurrences.basis: Hippolytes is designated the offender and is banished from the country for ten years.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The oracle advises that Hippolytes, as offender, be banished for ten years and that troop command be delegated to a man with three eyes.
In obedience to the oracle, Hippolytes is banished, an army and fleet are equipped again, and Oxylus is elected commander-in-chief.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE EPIGONI. / ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE. / THE SIEGE OF TROY.; lines 9224-9321
occurrences.motif_label: Departure by sea on a fated mission
occurrences.basis: Paris is equipped with a fleet for Greece, warned of ruin, and later sails away with Helen toward Troy.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Priam entrusts Paris with a fleet to go to Greece and demand the restoration of Hesione, Priam's sister, who had been carried away by Heracles and given to Telamon.
Before Paris leaves, Cassandra warns him not to bring home a wife from Greece and predicts ruin for Troy and Priam's house if he ignores the warning.
Paris and Helen sail away, are driven by weather to Crania, and after some years proceed to Troy.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE EPIGONI. / ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE. / THE SIEGE OF TROY.; lines 9323-9415
occurrences.motif_label: Departure of an assembled war fleet
occurrences.basis: The army and over a thousand ships gather at Aulis and the fleet sets sail for the Trojan coast.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A hundred thousand warriors and over a thousand ships gather at Aulis; Agamemnon receives command of the host.
The fleet sails but mistakes Mysia for Troy and ravages it; Telephus, king of the Mysians and son of Heracles, drives the Greeks back but is wounded by Achilles' spear.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE EPIGONI. / ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE. / THE SIEGE OF TROY.; lines 9514-9591
occurrences.motif_label: Hero withdraws from battle after dishonor
occurrences.basis: Achilles is angered by Agamemnon's conduct, loses Briseis, and refuses to take further part in the war.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Agamemnon retaliates by taking Briseis from Achilles; Briseis weeps, and Achilles withdraws to his tent and refuses further war service.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE EPIGONI. / ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE. / THE SIEGE OF TROY.; lines 9593-9685
occurrences.motif_label: Hero withdraws from army and is persuaded to return
occurrences.basis: Achilles leaves the Greek army for Lesbos after a dispute and is persuaded by Odysseus to return.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Diomedes claims compensation for Thersites' death, Agamemnon does not intervene, Achilles resents the implied condemnation and sails to Lesbos, and Odysseus persuades him to return.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE EPIGONI. / ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE. / THE SIEGE OF TROY.; lines 9869-9911
occurrences.motif_label: survivor carries father from fallen city and becomes ancestral hero
occurrences.basis: Aeneas, son of Aphrodite, escapes Troy with his son and father, carries Anchises, leaves for Italy, and becomes ancestral hero of the Roman people.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Aeneas, son of Aphrodite, escapes with his son and father Anchises, carries Anchises on his shoulders, goes to Mount Ida and then Italy, and becomes ancestor-hero of the Romans.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas / CONTENTS / LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS; lines 125-193
occurrences.motif_label: Departure and return sequence
occurrences.basis: The titles include “Ingeborg Watches her Lover Depart” and “Frithiof’s Return to Framnäs.”

evidence.quote_or_summary: The listed titles include “Ingeborg,” “Frithiof Cleaves the Shield of Helgé,” “Ingeborg Watches her Lover Depart,” “Frithiof’s Return to Framnäs,” several further Frithiof scenes, “Odin and Fenris,” “The Ride of the Valkyrs,” and “The Storm-Ride.”

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR; lines 2733-2850
occurrences.motif_label: journey to hostile giant realm to counter harmful weather
occurrences.basis: Thor departs with Loki toward Jötun-heim because giants are sending cold blasts that damage buds and flowers.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Giants from Jötun-heim send cold blasts that harm buds and flowers, so Thor decides to make them behave better. He travels with Loki in his chariot to the edge of the giant-world and stays at a peasant's hut.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR; lines 2852-2939
occurrences.motif_label: journey into the giants' realm
occurrences.basis: Thor and companions leave the goats behind, travel on foot, and continue toward Utgard, identified as the giants' realm.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Thor charges a man to care for his goats, bids the young peasants accompany him, travels with Loki, and reaches a bleak, barren, mist-covered country at nightfall.
Skrymir learns they are going to Utgard, proposes to guide them, and offers his wallet of provisions, but Thor and the companions cannot loosen its knots.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR; lines 2942-3047
occurrences.motif_label: giant duel at the boundary of realms
occurrences.basis: Thor challenges Hrungnir to a holmgang at Griottunagard, described as the confines of Hrungnir's realm.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Thor returns, hears Hrungnir's threat concerning Sif, brandishes his hammer, is restrained by the gods because Hrungnir is a guest, and arranges a holmgang at Griottunagard three days later.

Hrungnir awaits the duel with flint heart, skull, shield, and club; Thialfi misleads him about Thor's approach; Thor throws his hammer; the stone club shatters into flints, one fragment wounds Thor, and Hrungnir falls dead with a leg over Thor.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR; lines 3050-3168
occurrences.motif_label: borrowed bird plumage for flight to enemy realm
occurrences.basis: Loki borrows Freya's falcon plumes and flies in bird form across Ifing to Jötun-heim.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Loki borrows Freya's falcon plumes, flies to Jötun-heim, and learns that Thrym has buried the hammer and demands Freya as bride.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR; lines 3171-3290
occurrences.motif_label: hero deprived of usual weapons receives substitute aid
occurrences.basis: Thor leaves his hammer, belt, and gauntlet behind, then receives Grid’s girdle, staff, and glove before facing Geirrod’s dangers.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Geirrod recognizes the bird as a god in disguise, cages Loki without food or drink, and releases him when Loki promises to bring Thor without hammer, belt, or gauntlet; Loki then persuades Thor to visit.
Thor and Loki meet Grid, one of Odin’s wives; seeing Thor unarmed, she warns him and lends him her girdle, staff, and glove.

At Geirrod’s house, Thor sits in a chair that rises; he braces Grid’s staff against the ceiling, forces the chair down, and crushes Geirrod’s daughters Gialp and Greip, who had hidden beneath it to kill him.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: HENRY FESTING JONES. / THE ODYSSEY / BOOK I / BOOK II; lines 1038-1133
occurrences.motif_label: secret departure for a quest
occurrences.basis: Telemachus secretly provisions a ship and leaves at night to seek news of his absent father, with his mother kept unaware.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus asks Euryclea for twelve jars of wine and twenty measures of barley meal in bags, to be kept secret, for his journey to Sparta and Pylos seeking news of his father.
Telemachus tells Euryclea not to fear, says the plan has heaven's sanction, and asks her not to tell his mother for ten or twelve days unless necessary.
At the ship, Telemachus tells the crew to help load the stores, noting that his mother and the maid servants except one do not know; the men bring the supplies as told.
The men loose the hawsers and take benches; Minerva sends a fair west wind; Telemachus orders the sail hoisted, and the ship speeds through deep blue water with foam at the bows.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XXII / BOOK XXIII / BOOK XXIV / FOOTNOTES:; lines 11278-11377
occurrences.motif_label: missionary journey to people ignorant of a god
occurrences.basis: The commentator says Ulysses was to become a missionary and preach Neptune to people who did not know the god's name.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The note says Ulysses was to become a missionary preaching Neptune to people who did not know his name, and discusses a winnowing shovel comparable in length to an oar.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I / BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS.; lines 1136-1230
occurrences.motif_label: young seeker departs to learn absent father's fate
occurrences.basis: Telemachus has taken a voyage and states he seeks news of his absent father Ulysses, whose fate is unknown.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva tells Telemachus not to be shy, because he has taken the voyage to learn where his father is buried and how he came to his end, and tells him to ask Nestor for the truth.
Telemachus tells Nestor they come from Ithaca and that he seeks news of his father Ulysses, who is said to have sacked Troy with Nestor; Ulysses's fate is hidden.
Telemachus says no one can certify where Ulysses perished, whether on land or at sea, and asks Nestor as a suppliant to tell plainly what he saw or heard.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I / BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS.; lines 1424-1514
occurrences.motif_label: Guided departure for a quest journey
occurrences.basis: Minerva directs that Telemachus continue from Nestor's house to Lacedaemon by chariot with one of Nestor's sons and the best horses.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva says Telemachus should sleep at Nestor's house, while she returns to the ship and crew; she instructs Nestor to send Telemachus to Lacedaemon in a chariot with a son and swift horses.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I / BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS.; lines 1516-1558
occurrences.motif_label: departure by chariot for a continuing quest
occurrences.basis: Nestor orders Telemachus's horses yoked, provisions are packed, and Telemachus departs Pylos by chariot with Pisistratus.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Nestor said, “Sons, put Telemachus’s horses to the chariot that he may start at once.”
The housekeeper packs provisions of bread, wine, and sweet meats suitable for sons of princes.
Telemachus enters the chariot; Pisistratus takes the reins beside him, lashes the horses, and they leave Pylos.
They travel all day through open country until sunset and darkness covers the land.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS. / BOOK IV; lines 1762-1847
occurrences.motif_label: Son's journey for news of the absent father
occurrences.basis: Telemachus makes a long sea voyage to Lacedaemon to ask Menelaus for news of Ulysses.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At rosy-fingered Dawn, Menelaus rises, dresses, girds on his sword, sits near Telemachus, and asks why he has taken the long sea voyage to Lacedaemon.
Telemachus says he came to learn about his father, describes suitors wasting his estate while courting his mother, and asks Menelaus as a suppliant to tell plainly what he saw or heard about Ulysses.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS. / BOOK IV; lines 2041-2133
occurrences.motif_label: young hero's secret or opposed departure
occurrences.basis: The suitors learn that Telemachus has departed for Pylos despite their expectations, with a picked crew and a borrowed ship.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Noemon asks Antinous when Telemachus will return from Pylos, explaining that Telemachus has his ship and that he needs it for a journey to Elis.

The suitors are astonished, having believed Telemachus had not gone to Pylos but was somewhere on farms or with herdsmen; Antinous asks when he left, with whom, and whether the ship was lent or taken.

Antinous is angry, says Telemachus has escaped with a picked crew, asks for a ship and twenty men, and proposes lying in wait in the straits between Ithaca and Samos so Telemachus will rue his search for news of his father; the others approve.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS. / BOOK IV; lines 2135-2239
occurrences.motif_label: secret departure on a quest for news of the father
occurrences.basis: Telemachus has sailed to Pylos and Lacedaemon to learn whether his father is dead or alive, and Euryclea says his departure was concealed from Penelope under oath.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “They are going to try and murder Telemachus as he is coming home from Pylos and Lacedaemon” after seeking news of his father.
Euryclea says she knew of Telemachus' departure, supplied bread and wine, and swore not to tell Penelope for ten or twelve days unless asked or unless Penelope heard of it.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS. / BOOK IV / BOOK V; lines 2386-2472
occurrences.motif_label: release and departure of the detained hero
occurrences.basis: Mercury orders Calypso to send Ulysses away, and Calypso offers means for him to voyage home.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Mercury says to send Ulysses away or Jove will be angry and punish Calypso.
Calypso tells Ulysses she will send him away, instructs him to cut beams and build a large raft with an upper deck, and promises bread, wine, water, clothes, and a fair wind if the gods allow.
Ulysses says Penelope is mortal and less beautiful than Calypso, but he wants to get home and will endure further wreck or suffering as part of his troubles.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS. / BOOK IV / BOOK V; lines 2474-2559
occurrences.motif_label: aided departure from an island
occurrences.basis: Calypso provides tools, materials, provisions, clothing, and a fair wind, then sends Ulysses away from the island.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At dawn Ulysses and Calypso dress; Calypso thinks how to speed him on his way, gives him a bronze axe and adze, and leads him to tall dry alder, poplar, and pine at the end of the island.
Ulysses cuts twenty trees, shapes and joins timbers, builds the raft’s deck, gunwale, mast, yard, rudder, wicker protection, and sails; Calypso supplies augers and linen.
After four days of work, on the fifth day Calypso sends Ulysses from the island with clean clothes, wine, water, provisions, meat, and a fair warm wind.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VI / THE MEETING BETWEEN NAUSICAA AND ULYSSES. / BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS.; lines 3176-3259
occurrences.motif_label: departure from divine island captivity or refuge
occurrences.basis: Ulysses recounts a long stay with Calypso on Ogygia and his later departure by raft after she sends him away.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses says Ogygia is a far island where Calypso, daughter of Atlas, dwells alone.
Ulysses stays with Calypso seven years; in the eighth year she tells him to depart, perhaps by Jove's command.
Calypso sends Ulysses on a raft with bread, wine, clothing, and a warm fair wind.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS. / BOOK VIII / BOOK IX; lines 3900-3994
occurrences.motif_label: Exploratory departure to test an unknown people
occurrences.basis: Odysseus leaves most of his company behind and goes with one ship to determine whether the nearby people are savage or hospitable.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odysseus says he will go with his ship to see whether the people are “uncivilised savages, or a hospitable and humane race.”

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS. / BOOK VIII / BOOK IX; lines 4270-4293
occurrences.motif_label: dawn departure over the sea after loss
occurrences.basis: At rosy-fingered Dawn, Ulysses orders the men aboard and they sail away sorrowful but alive.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The men feast through the day, camp on the beach at night, and at Dawn board, row over the grey sea, and sail on sorrowful but glad to have escaped death despite lost comrades.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VIII / BOOK IX / BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE.; lines 4399-4490
occurrences.motif_label: single surviving vessel escapes annihilation
occurrences.basis: Odysseus cuts the cable of his own ship and escapes while no other ships remain.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odysseus cuts his ship's cable, orders hard rowing, reaches open water beyond the rocks, and reports that none of the other ships remain.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VIII / BOOK IX / BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE.; lines 4680-4781
occurrences.motif_label: delay in a divine woman's house before resuming the quest
occurrences.basis: Ulysses stays a year with Circe feasting before his men urge him to resume the homeward journey.

evidence.quote_or_summary: They stay with Circe for a whole twelvemonth, feasting on meat and wine.
When the year has passed, the men tell Ulysses it is time to think about going home if he is to see his house and country.
After feasting, Ulysses gets into bed with Circe and asks her to keep her promise about furthering his homeward voyage.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE. / BOOK XI / THE VISIT TO THE DEAD.88; lines 4783-4874
occurrences.motif_label: divine helper providing means for underworld journey
occurrences.basis: Circe provides the sacrificial animals and sends the steady wind that carries the ship toward the place she had indicated.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The men grieve at the sea shore; Circe brings a ram and ewe, makes them fast by the ship, and passes among the men unseen.
The crew launches the ship, sets mast and sails, puts the sheep aboard, and sails with a fair wind sent by Circe.

At sunset the ship reaches Oceanus and the land and city of the Cimmerians, a place of mist, darkness, and unpierced by sunlight; the crew beaches the ship and follows Oceanus to Circe's indicated place.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XII / THE SIRENS, SCYLLA AND CHARYBDIS, THE CATTLE OF THE SUN. / BOOK XIII / ULYSSES LEAVES SCHERIA AND RETURNS TO ITHACA.; lines 5712-5817
occurrences.motif_label: Departure with escort and gifts
occurrences.basis: Ulysses is sent off with gifts, provisions, an escort, prayers, and drink-offerings.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Alcinous notes the guest's packed gifts of clothing, gold, and valuables and proposes additional tripods and cauldrons from the Phaeacians.
Ulysses bids farewell, asks for drink-offerings, thanks the Phaeacians for escort and gifts, and wishes peace and good fortune to their households and people.
Alcinous orders Pontonous to mix wine for prayer to father Jove; the people make drink-offerings, and Ulysses places the double cup in Arete's hands and bids her farewell.
Ulysses crosses the threshold; Alcinous sends a guide, Arete sends maidservants with clothing, a strong box, corn, and wine, and the crew puts these and other provisions aboard.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: PREFACE TO SECOND EDITION / HENRY FESTING JONES. / THE ODYSSEY / BOOK I; lines 589-680
occurrences.motif_label: absent father hidden without trace
occurrences.basis: Telemachus describes Ulysses as hidden by the gods and carried away by storm-winds, leaving no trace and causing grief and uncertainty.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus says the gods have hidden his father more closely than any mortal, that storm-winds carried him off without trace, and that suitors from Dulichium, Same, Zacynthus, and Ithaca are consuming his house while courting his mother.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: PREFACE TO SECOND EDITION / HENRY FESTING JONES. / THE ODYSSEY / BOOK I; lines 589-680
occurrences.motif_label: divine counsel initiates a quest for news
occurrences.basis: Minerva, later recognized as divine, instructs Telemachus to take a ship and seek information about Ulysses at Pylos and Sparta.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva says heaven will determine Ulysses' return, then advises Telemachus to call an assembly, order the suitors away, send Penelope to her father if she wants remarriage, sail with twenty men to Pylos and Sparta for news, perform rites and build a barrow if Ulysses is dead, and consider killing the suitors; she cites Orestes' fame for killing Aegisthus.
Minerva flies away like a bird into the air, gives Telemachus courage, intensifies his thoughts of his father, and Telemachus recognizes that the stranger had been a god.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XIII / ULYSSES LEAVES SCHERIA AND RETURNS TO ITHACA. / BOOK XIV / ULYSSES IN THE HUT WITH EUMAEUS.; lines 6374-6464
occurrences.motif_label: divine release from bonds and escape by water
occurrences.basis: In the stranger's story, the gods undo his bonds, allowing him to escape the ship by sliding into the sea and swimming ashore.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The stranger says conspirators meant to sell him as a slave, stripped him, dressed him in rags, bound him on the ship, and that the gods freed his bonds so he escaped by sea and hid near a wood before reaching a good man's door.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: ULYSSES LEAVES SCHERIA AND RETURNS TO ITHACA. / BOOK XIV / ULYSSES IN THE HUT WITH EUMAEUS. / BOOK XV; lines 6547-6648
occurrences.motif_label: dangerous departure with ambush avoided by guidance
occurrences.basis: Telemachus prepares to depart while Minerva warns of an ambush and instructs him to sail away from the islands.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva warns that suitors lie in wait in the strait between Ithaca and Samos, instructs Telemachus to sail night and day away from the islands, and tells him to go to the swineherd and send word to Penelope.
Minerva returns to Olympus; Telemachus wakes Pisistratus and calls for the horses and chariot, while Pisistratus says they should wait until morning for Menelaus’s gifts and farewell.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: ULYSSES LEAVES SCHERIA AND RETURNS TO ITHACA. / BOOK XIV / ULYSSES IN THE HUT WITH EUMAEUS. / BOOK XV; lines 6650-6731
occurrences.motif_label: drink-offering before departure
occurrences.basis: Menelaus brings a golden goblet of wine so that a drink-offering may be made before Telemachus and Pisistratus set out.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus and Pisistratus yoke the horses; Menelaus follows with a golden goblet of wine for a drink-offering and asks them to tell Nestor of his treatment of them.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: ULYSSES LEAVES SCHERIA AND RETURNS TO ITHACA. / BOOK XIV / ULYSSES IN THE HUT WITH EUMAEUS. / BOOK XV; lines 6650-6731
occurrences.motif_label: urgent return home by ship
occurrences.basis: Telemachus asks to be brought directly to his ship because he must go home at once, and then orders his men to prepare the ship for departure.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus asks Pisistratus to leave him at his ship rather than take him to Nestor's house, saying he must go home at once.
Pisistratus decides to turn toward the ship, places Menelaus's gifts of gold and raiment in the stern, and urges Telemachus to board before Nestor can come fetch him.
Telemachus calls his men together and orders them to get everything ready on board the ship and set out home.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: ULYSSES LEAVES SCHERIA AND RETURNS TO ITHACA. / BOOK XIV / ULYSSES IN THE HUT WITH EUMAEUS. / BOOK XV; lines 6733-6832
occurrences.motif_label: divine helper sends favorable wind for voyage
occurrences.basis: After the ship is prepared, Minerva sends a strong favorable wind to speed it on its course.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus receives Theoclymenus' spear, lays it on deck, sits in the stern with him beside him, orders the sailing preparations, and Minerva sends a fresh strong wind to speed the ship.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: PREFACE TO SECOND EDITION / HENRY FESTING JONES. / THE ODYSSEY / BOOK I; lines 682-759
occurrences.motif_label: planned departure under divine counsel
occurrences.basis: Telemachus spends the night thinking about an intended voyage and counsel from Minerva.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After singing and dancing until evening, the suitors go home. Telemachus goes to his high tower room, led by Euryclea with blazing torches. Euryclea is described as his nurse and attendant. Telemachus lies under a woollen fleece thinking all night about his intended voyage and Minerva’s counsel.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: ULYSSES LEAVES SCHERIA AND RETURNS TO ITHACA. / BOOK XIV / ULYSSES IN THE HUT WITH EUMAEUS. / BOOK XV; lines 6834-6930
occurrences.motif_label: Forced maritime departure through abduction and sale
occurrences.basis: The Phoenician woman reports being seized by Taphian pirates and sold over the sea, and she later plans to carry off the young Eumaeus in a ship for sale abroad.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The woman says she is from Sidon, daughter of the wealthy Arybas, and that Taphian pirates seized her and sold her over the sea to the owner of the house.

evidence.locator: lines 6834-6930, planned theft and child abduction
evidence.quote_or_summary: The woman says she will bring as much gold as she can and, as nurse to the young son of the house, will carry him off in the ship so the traders can sell him in foreign parts.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: HENRY FESTING JONES. / THE ODYSSEY / BOOK I / BOOK II; lines 938-1036
occurrences.motif_label: departure quest for a missing father
occurrences.basis: Telemachus seeks a ship and crew to travel to Sparta and Pylos for news of his long-missing father, and Minerva prepares the journey.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus asks: “Give me, then, a ship and a crew of twenty men” to go to Sparta and Pylos “in quest of my father.”

Minerva says she will find a ship and come with Telemachus; he is to prepare provisions, including wine in jars and barley meal in leathern bags, while she gathers volunteers and chooses the best ship.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III.; lines 12405-12538
occurrences.motif_label: dangerous mimetic performer honored but expelled
occurrences.basis: The pantomimic poet is reverenced, anointed, crowned, and then sent away to another city because the law does not permit his presence.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The pantomimic poet who can imitate anything is to be worshipped as sweet, holy, and wonderful, anointed with myrrh, crowned with wool, and sent away; the State will use a rougher poet who imitates virtue for souls' health and soldier education.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII.; lines 21268-21405
occurrences.motif_label: exile and return of personified qualities
occurrences.basis: Virtues are expelled, while personified vices are brought back to the house; later some exiled virtues may be re-admitted.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A battle is won; modesty and temperance are cast out, while moderation and orderly expenditure are driven beyond the border by evil appetites.

The soul is emptied and swept clean while being initiated in great mysteries; garlanded vices return and are praised with favorable names; the young man moves into libertinism of unnecessary pleasures.
After time passes, if he is fortunate, he re-admits some exiled virtues and balances pleasures by letting each govern him in turn.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII. / BOOK IX. / BOOK X.; lines 23923-24065
occurrences.motif_label: banished figure conditionally allowed to return
occurrences.basis: Poetry is personified as an exiled figure sent from the State who may return only after making a successful defense.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker defends sending imitative poetry out of the State, says there is an ancient quarrel between philosophy and poetry, cites hostile sayings, and acknowledges poetry's charm, especially in Homer.
The speaker proposes that poetry may return from exile only if she defends herself, and that prose defenders may argue that poetry is useful as well as pleasant.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 3115-3194
occurrences.motif_label: withdrawal of the righteous remnant from a storm of society
occurrences.basis: The few genuine philosophers withdraw from the storm of human life under a wall to preserve innocence and depart in peace.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A small remnant of genuine philosophers may remain; after tasting philosophy and seeing human life as a den of thieves and wild beasts, they stand aside from the storm under a wall and preserve innocence.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 4571-4620
occurrences.motif_label: banishment and return of personified qualities
occurrences.basis: Modesty and temperance are expelled, while vices are brought back, crowned, and renamed; later some exiles may be restored.

evidence.quote_or_summary: False spirits shut the castle gates, win the battle, ally with desires, banish modesty and temperance, and bring back vices crowned with garlands under new names.

The person later alternates between necessary and unnecessary pleasures, sometimes restores some exiles, denies distinctions among pleasures, and shifts among drinking, abstinence, exercise, idleness, philosophy, politics, war, and business.

occurrences.source_title: The Poetic Edda
occurrences.passage_locator: Vafthruthnismol 1-8
occurrences.motif_label: departure_to_liminal_opponent
occurrences.basis: The god leaves home and enters the hall of a powerful giant wisdom-opponent.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In wisdom old with the giant wise / Myself would I seek to match.
Othin goes to test the giant's wisdom, enters the hall, and greets Vafthruthnir.

occurrences.source_title: Persian Literature, Volume 1
occurrences.passage_locator: Zal, the son of Sam; exposure on Alberz, Simurgh fosterage, and return
occurrences.motif_label: mountain_fosterage_and_return
occurrences.basis: Zal is left on Alberz, raised in the mountain refuge, and returned from it with changed status and future promise.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sam leaves the mocked child on Alberz, but the Simurgh pities him on the rock and carries him to its own habitation.
Sam goes to Alberz in person, weeps and prays for forgiveness, and asks for the forsaken child to be restored to him.
The Simurgh tells Zal it has nursed him, named him Dustn, taught him language and understanding, and now must return him to Sam.
The Simurgh gives Zal a feather to burn whenever danger comes, then presents him to Sam as worthy of throne and diadem.

occurrences.source_title: The Mesnevi
occurrences.passage_locator: The Mesnevi, Book I, Proem, The Reed-Flute
occurrences.motif_label: longing for return to source
occurrences.basis: The reed-flute's song begins from separation and turns absence into the desire for return.

evidence.locator: The Mesnevi, Book I, Proem, lines 5400-5429
evidence.quote_or_summary: The reed-flute tells of absence from its reed-bed and voices the grief and joy of the absent lover.
