occurrences.source_title: Heroic Romances of Ireland
occurrences.passage_locator: The Apparition of the Great Queen to Cuchulain; literal translation
occurrences.motif_label: shapechanging_battle_queen
occurrences.basis: The Morrigan appears in disguise, reappears as a black bird, and threatens future combat in eel, wolf, and heifer forms.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The woman answers Cuchulain's challenge with strange names; he leaps into her chariot at spear-point, demands her true name, and the whole company vanishes.

The woman reappears as a black bird, claims that she guards Cuchulain's death, and says that the cow she brought from the fairy-mound of Cruachan to breed by the Black Bull of Cualnge will lead to the Tain bo Cualnge.
The Morrigan says she will attack in eel, wolf, and white red-eared heifer forms during Cuchulain's future equal combat, and he vows to injure each form in reply.

occurrences.source_title: Heroic Romances of Ireland
occurrences.passage_locator: The Courtship of Etain (Leabhar na h-Uidhri version); Etain transformed, wind-borne, swallowed, and born again
occurrences.motif_label: enchanted_transformation_and_rebirth
occurrences.basis: Etain's identity persists through butterfly transformation, magical concealment, swallowing, gestation, and second birth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Fuamnach and Bressal Etarlam transform Etain into a butterfly and a magical wind carries her away for seven years.
Angus Mac O'c recognizes Etain in transformed form and keeps her in a fragrant bower with clear windows and precious herbs.
Etain falls through a roof into a golden cup of milk, is swallowed by Etar's wife, and is carried in her womb until born again as a maiden.
one thousand and twelve years since the time of the first begetting of Etain ... to the time when she was born the second time

occurrences.source_title: The Mabinogion
occurrences.passage_locator: Pwyll Prince of Dyved; encounter with Arawn and year in Annwvyn
occurrences.motif_label: shapeshifted_substitution
occurrences.basis: Pwyll's visible form and semblance are changed so Arawn's household cannot recognize the substitution.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Arawn asks Pwyll to defeat Havgan, sends him to Annwvyn in his stead, and puts his form and semblance on him for a year.
Pwyll enters Arawn's court, is treated as Arawn, sees a splendid household, and feasts there.
Arawn restores Pwyll's form, Pwyll returns to Dyved, friendship is strengthened, and Pwyll is called Chief of Annwvyn.

occurrences.source_title: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer
occurrences.passage_locator: Chuang Tzu, Chapter II, butterfly dream
occurrences.motif_label: dream transformation
occurrences.basis: The speaker moves between human and butterfly identity through dream and questions which identity is primary.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Chuang Tzu dreams he is a butterfly and then questions whether he is a man dreaming a butterfly or a butterfly dreaming a man.

occurrences.source_title: The Book of the Dead
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER IX, A Short Description of the "Doors" or Chapters of the Book of the Dead; summaries of Chapters LXIV, LXXIV-LXXXVIII, CXLIV-CXLVII, and CLV-CLXVII
occurrences.motif_label: ritual_transformation
occurrences.basis: The deceased is enabled by recitation to assume multiple forms at will.

evidence.locator: CHAPTER IX, A Short Description of the "Doors" or Chapters of the Book of the Dead; Chapters LXXVII-LXXXVIII
evidence.quote_or_summary: The Chapters of Transformations let the deceased assume forms including the Golden Hawk, Divine Hawk, Pure Lily, Benu Bird, Swallow, Sata or Earth-serpent, and Crocodile.

occurrences.source_title: The Poetic Edda
occurrences.passage_locator: GRIMNISMOL / THE BALLAD OF GRIMNIR / INTRODUCTORY NOTE / NOTES; lines 4391-4441
occurrences.motif_label: God appears in disguise under many names
occurrences.basis: The notes explicitly state that Othin often appeared in disguise and thus had almost limitless names; multiple by-names are catalogued and glossed.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Notes on the uncertain condition of catalogue stanzas in oral transmission; many names are unattested elsewhere and their significance uncertain; Othin’s frequent disguises are said to necessitate an almost limitless number of names.

Glosses several by-names (e.g., Grim, Gangleri, Herjan, etc.) and describes Snorri’s question-and-answer framing with Har, Jafnhar, and Thrithi; the note says the tripartite form’s meaning is debated and suggests possible early Christian influence.
Additional glosses of Othin’s by-names, including ‘Fjolsvith: Wide of Wisdom,’ and other descriptive epithets (e.g., many-shaped, swift in deceit, long-bearded).

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE TRAVELLER AND HIS DOG / THE SHIPWRECKED MAN AND THE SEA / THE WILD BOAR AND THE FOX / MERCURY AND THE SCULPTOR; lines 2293-2316
occurrences.motif_label: disguised deity seeks human valuation
occurrences.basis: Mercury disguises himself as a man in order to learn the estimation in which mankind holds him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Mercury wants to know how mankind values him, disguises himself as a man, and enters a sculptor's studio containing finished statues for sale.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE EAGLE AND THE COCKS / THE ESCAPED JACKDAW / THE FARMER AND THE FOX / VENUS AND THE CAT; lines 3181-3193
occurrences.motif_label: animal transformed into human
occurrences.basis: A cat is changed by Venus into a woman and later restored to cat form.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A cat falls in love with a handsome young man and begs Venus to change her into a woman.
Venus changes the cat into a beautiful maiden; the young man falls in love with her and marries her.
The young woman immediately pursues the mouse; Venus is disgusted and changes her back into a cat.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE MULE / THE HOUND AND THE FOX / THE FATHER AND HIS DAUGHTERS / THE THIEF AND THE INNKEEPER; lines 3977-4004
occurrences.motif_label: claimed shapeshifting used as a ruse
occurrences.basis: The thief says he will become a ravening wolf after three yawns, but the narrative presents this as a deception rather than an actual transformation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The thief claims that when he has “yawned three times” he becomes “a ravening wolf” and attacks men’s throats.
As the thief begins a third yawn, the innkeeper fears being eaten, slips out of his coat, bolts inside, locks the door, and the thief leaves with the coat.

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE PACK-ASS AND THE WILD ASS / THE ASS AND HIS MASTERS / THE PACK-ASS, THE WILD ASS, AND THE LION / THE ANT; lines 4060-4073
occurrences.motif_label: human beings transformed into animals
occurrences.basis: The former men are changed into ants by Jupiter.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ants were once men and made their living by tilling the soil.
Jupiter became angry at their covetousness and changed them into ants.
"though their forms were changed, their nature remained the same"

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE HAWK, THE KITE, AND THE PIGEONS / THE WOMAN AND THE FARMER / PROMETHEUS AND THE MAKING OF MAN / THE SWALLOW AND THE CROW; lines 5283-5302
occurrences.motif_label: animal-to-human transformation explaining mixed human and beast nature
occurrences.basis: Some beasts are turned into men, explaining people with human forms and beastly souls.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Jupiter tells Prometheus to turn some beasts into men; Prometheus obeys, explaining why some people have "forms of men but the souls of beasts."

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE HAWK, THE KITE, AND THE PIGEONS / THE WOMAN AND THE FARMER / PROMETHEUS AND THE MAKING OF MAN / THE SWALLOW AND THE CROW; lines 5283-5302
occurrences.motif_label: human transformed into bird for protection
occurrences.basis: The Swallow says Juno turned her from an abused princess into a bird to protect her from further injury.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Swallow boasts to the Crow that she was once a princess, daughter of a King of Athens, and that her husband cruelly cut out her tongue.
The Swallow says Juno turned her into a bird to protect her from further injury.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: HONORARY SECRETARIES. / INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA.; lines 1011-1094
occurrences.motif_label: animal assumes human spouse's shape
occurrences.basis: The horse kills and supplants the husband, appears in human shape, and turns back into a horse when beaten.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A beautiful woman's husband goes to the mountains and returns with a deer; at night she cries that he is not her husband, and neighbors come, after which a strong man beats him and he turns into a horse.
The tale states that the husband had been killed and supplanted by the horse; this was the first time the Ainos saw horses, and in ancient days creatures could assume human shape.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA. / II.--MORAL TALES.; lines 1097-1202
occurrences.motif_label: animal or human form change involving divine beings
occurrences.basis: The raven speaks and appears in human-like divine girl form; the liar's body becomes a fox's body and is later restored to human form.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "Though it was a raven, it spoke thus, just like a human being" and invited the man to visit its old father.
The raven flies and the man follows on foot to a large house; inside, the raven appears human in form as a divine girl, with a divine old man and divine old woman present.
A man lies and extorts from people; after hearing a non-human voice and saying the fox-bark 'Pau! pau!', he sees that his own body is a fox's.
Branches break and crash down; he wakes as a man again, worships the tree, returns home, and thereafter does not misbehave.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA. / II.--MORAL TALES.; lines 1204-1297
occurrences.motif_label: Unknown found child as dangerous shapeshifter
occurrences.basis: The found crying boy is later explained as a wicked rat that had taken the shape of a little boy.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A rich childless couple want a child; the wife finds a crying little boy beside a tree in the mountains and brings him to the village.
In a dream a divine-appearing person says the wicked rat took the shape of a little boy, polluted the village, and that the couple shall have a child; the tale says they did get one.
The first tale concludes that a found child or puppy should not be taken into the house without knowing its origin.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA. / II.--MORAL TALES. / IV.--MISCELLANEOUS TALES.; lines 1719-1809
occurrences.motif_label: Shapeshifting divine woman lures human beloved to underworld
occurrences.basis: The pine-tree goddess says a goddess in Hades assumed bear form, lured the hunter into the cavern and underworld, and wished to marry him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In a second dream, the pine-tree goddess says he cannot stay long after eating Hades' fruit; a goddess in Hades wished to marry him and had assumed bear form to lure him underground.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA. / II.--MORAL TALES. / IV.--MISCELLANEOUS TALES.; lines 1811-1905
occurrences.motif_label: Serpent-born child transformed or replaced by human baby
occurrences.basis: The woman bears a little snake, which is thrown away, after which a crying human baby boy is found and raised.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The woman gives birth to a little snake; her mother, weeping, asks what god begot a child in her daughter and throws the snake away because humans cannot keep it.
A baby is then heard crying outside; the old woman brings in a fine baby boy, who is kept, grows into a man, and kills many deer and bears.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA. / II.--MORAL TALES. / IV.--MISCELLANEOUS TALES.; lines 2006-2100
occurrences.motif_label: animal spirit possession obstructing marriage
occurrences.basis: A fox is said to possess the girl, speak from her body, and prevent the approach of an ordinary mortal husband.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In a dream, a girl sees the tree as a house and a lovely goddess says a wicked fox has entered her, speaks from her body, prevents mortal husbands, and has lured her away; the goddess promises help and safe return.

occurrences.motif_label: animal lover revealed and adulterer transformed
occurrences.basis: The black-clad young man who elopes with the stepmother is revealed as a carrion-crow, and she is changed into a crow.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A black-clad young man courts the stepmother while her husband is hunting; she flees with him to a beautiful house, but in the morning the house is leaves and branches, the man is a carrion-crow, and she too has become a crow.

occurrences.motif_label: food causing transformation
occurrences.basis: People who ate the quickly produced grain were transformed into horses.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In the old magical days, rivers flowed conveniently in both directions, people could fly and land on trees, fire-drills were used, crops grew by midday, and eating the quick grain transformed people into horses.

occurrences.motif_label: tree material transforming into divine bears
occurrences.basis: Rotten branches or roots of trees sometimes turn into bears that are divine walking creatures and protected from human killing.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Rotten branches or roots sometimes turn into bears called divine walking creatures, which must not be killed by human hand.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: HONORARY SECRETARIES. / INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA.; lines 485-608
occurrences.motif_label: Spoken wish becomes literal transformation
occurrences.basis: The thunder-god sons state wishes to become a flea and a louse, and their father turns them into those forms.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Two young thunder-gods, sons of the chief thunder-god, love the same Aino woman and say they would become a flea and a louse to be in her bosom.
The chief thunder-god says they shall be taken at their word and turns one son into a flea and the other into a louse.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: HONORARY SECRETARIES. / INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA.; lines 610-713
occurrences.motif_label: Shape-shifting animal trickster outwitted by a human
occurrences.basis: Foxes plan a deception using human and horse shapes, but a man overhears the plan, impersonates one fox, and profits by selling the transformed fox.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In the fox tale, a man gathering bark in the mountains overhears two foxes speaking human language and planning a profit-making scheme in which one becomes a horse and the other a man who sells it.
The man returns, imitates the fox's voice, induces the fox in the hole to become a large chestnut horse, takes it to a rich village, and barters it for food and precious things.
The horse's owner keeps it indoors and feeds it grass; because it is really a fox it wants fish, weakens, escapes through a window, and the two foxes become angry at the man.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: HONORARY SECRETARIES. / INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA.; lines 715-800
occurrences.motif_label: Animal beings assume human form
occurrences.basis: The foxes assume human shape, the mole disguises himself as an old man, and birds are given human shape while retaining bird behavior.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Two brother foxes plan to go among men in human shape and make treasures, leaf garments, food, and cakes from tree gum.

The mole-god sees the foxes, creates a human-like village, disguises himself as a very old man, makes treasures, garments, and food, and gives crows and other birds human shape as village householders.
The foxes arrive in human shape, think the place is a human village, trade their goods, watch the village dance, see bird-villagers fly upward, eat mulberries and grapes, and go home.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: HONORARY SECRETARIES. / INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA.; lines 802-900
occurrences.motif_label: Animals assume human form
occurrences.basis: The first foxes are rebuked for assuming human shape, and in the charm tale the fox-cub and puppy assume the shapes of a boy and a girl.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Foxes make counterfeit treasures from herbs and enter a golden house where the mole appears as a venerable god; he says he is their master, rebukes them for assuming human shape, and tells them to eat fruits dropped by crows instead.
The fox-cub becomes a little boy and the puppy a little girl; they dance and perform antics that amuse the ogre, though he remains suspicious and intends to kill them later.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: HONORARY SECRETARIES. / INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA.; lines 802-900
occurrences.motif_label: Trickster distraction enables recovery of an object
occurrences.basis: The fox-cub and puppy use human forms and dancing antics to amuse and distract the ogre while the rat retrieves the charm.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The fox-cub becomes a little boy and the puppy a little girl; they dance and perform antics that amuse the ogre, though he remains suspicious and intends to kill them later.
The rat nibbles into the box, retrieves the charm, and escapes through the ground passage; the boy and girl disappear, and the ogre chooses not to pursue because he has been taken in by a fox.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: HONORARY SECRETARIES. / INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA.; lines 902-1009
occurrences.motif_label: Humanlike woman transforms into dragon when seized
occurrences.basis: Turesh, first appearing as Okikurumi's food-bearing wife, becomes a wriggling, writhing dragon inside the hut.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In ancient days, the new world is unsettled and burning beneath a thin crust, so people stay in huts; Okikurumi fishes for them and sends Turesh with food, while commanding them not to ask questions or look at her face.

An Aino disobeys by seizing Turesh's hand and pulling her into the hut; she becomes a wriggling dragon, thunder and lightning destroy the hut, and Okikurumi angrily stops feeding the people and departs.

occurrences.passage_locator: END OF THE STORY OF THE THOROUGHBRED. / END OF THE STORY OF THE FORD. / END OF THE STORY ON CONSTANCY. / END OF THE STORY OF THE BULL WHO WON THE BET.; lines 12038-12183
occurrences.motif_label: disguised divine test of righteousness
occurrences.basis: Sakka assumes fish, old-woman, and Titan forms, with the fish and old-woman episodes testing Well-born’s commitment to non-killing and righteousness.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sakka checks whether she can keep good by appearing as a fish; the crane seizes it, sees it is alive, lets it go, and Sakka praises her ability to keep the Commandments.
Well-born is reborn in a potter’s household in Benares; Sakka appears as an old woman with a cart of golden cucumbers, offers them only to the righteous, and leaves them and the cart for Well-born.

Well-born becomes the beautiful daughter of a Titan because of her virtue; her father assembles Titans for a husband choice; Sakka appears as a Titan, she chooses him, and he leads her to the heavenly city.

occurrences.motif_label: Supernatural shapeshifters in human form
occurrences.basis: Snakes, Winged Creatures, and Yakkhas are described as supernatural beings able to assume human appearance.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The superhuman Snakes and Winged Creatures are said to be able, like gods or angels, to assume the appearance of men.

Nāgas, Yakkhas, and Supaṇṇas are named; Yakkhas are characterized by cannibalism, female Yakkhas lure men to destruction like sirens, and Yakkhas are invisible until they assume human shape but are recognized by red eyes.

occurrences.motif_label: Disguised supernatural child-stealer
occurrences.basis: The Yakshiṇī has a craving to eat the child, takes a woman’s form, obtains the child under pretense of nursing, and carries it off.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Yakshiṇī sees the child, wants to eat it, takes a woman’s form, asks whether the child belongs to the mother, asks to nurse it, nurses briefly, carries it off, and claims it as hers when the mother pursues her.

occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 6593-6700
occurrences.motif_label: shape-changing temptation by adversary’s daughters
occurrences.basis: Māra’s daughters assume many female appearances and repeatedly attempt to tempt the Blessed One, who remains unaffected.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Craving, Discontent, and Lust, the three daughters of Māra, find him sorrowful. They offer to subject the Master to their influence and bring him captive, while Māra says he is unwavering and beyond their power.
The daughters approach the Blessed One, but he pays no attention to their words and does not look at them, sitting in the joy of Nirvāna with a mind freed by the extinction of sin.

The daughters decide to tempt him in various forms; each assumes the appearance of a hundred women of different ages and statuses, and six times they profess themselves his handmaidens, but he pays no attention.

The Blessed One says, “Depart ye! Why strive ye thus?” and declares, “I have put away lust, have put away ill-will, have put away folly,” followed by verses asking how the Sinless, Wise One could be allured to a fall.

occurrences.source_title: Buddhist birth stories; or, Jataka tales, Volume 1

occurrences.motif_label: divine helper descends in disguise to aid the holy figure
occurrences.basis: Sakka's throne warns him, and he takes the form of a young Brāhman, descends, and clears a path so the Buddha is not deprived of nourishment.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sakka's throne becomes hot as a warning; he understands that the Buddha may lack nourishment, takes the form of a young Brāhman, descends, makes way, and praises the Buddha, Truth, and Order.
Sakka's verses praise the Blessed One as glorious, freed from sin, one who has crossed the flood, and attended by a retinue; when questioned, the young Brāhman says he is the Buddha's servant.

occurrences.motif_label: shape-shifting water demon lures traveler
occurrences.basis: The demon takes the form of a woodman and tries to entice the Bodisat into the lake with bathing, drinking, lotus food, and flowers.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The demon assumes a woodman's form and invites the Bodisat to enter the lake, bathe, drink, eat lotus stalks, and pick flowers; the Bodisat recognizes him as the captor.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE GRATEFUL BEASTS AND THE UNGRATEFUL PRINCE / THE GOBLIN IN THE POOL / THE FOOLISH FARMER AND THE KING / THE PIOUS WOLF; lines 1489-1529
occurrences.motif_label: Disguised supernatural test of sincerity
occurrences.basis: The fairy changes into a kid specifically to see whether the wolf’s pious fasting is real or sham.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A fairy observes and hears him, decides to test how much is real and sham, changes herself into a pretty little kid, and lands on the rock.
The wolf sees the kid, forgets his prayers, says he can fast tomorrow, smacks his lips, and jumps at the kid.
The kid jumps away repeatedly; the narration explains that it is the fairy and she does not let herself be caught.

occurrences.motif_label: shapeshifting magician in animal form
occurrences.basis: The wingless flying pig is explicitly identified as a great magician who uses the shape of a pig.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A wingless flying wild pig lands and sleeps; a magnificent diamond lies beside it. The man takes the diamond and, after thinking of being in a tree, finds himself in the treetop.
The pig wakes after the man drops a nut on its nose; it is explained that the pig is really a wicked great magician in pig shape, and that all his power lies in the diamond.

occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER I. THE KING OF THE WOOD. / MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE.; lines 3187-3263
occurrences.motif_label: Animal or insect soul-form trapped outside the body
occurrences.basis: The passage gives examples of a soul appearing as a lizard, fly, or butterfly, and emphasizes danger when that form cannot return to the body.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Santal story says a sleeping man's soul, in lizard form, enters a water pitcher, is trapped when the pitcher is covered, and the man dies; when the lizard is released and returns, the body revives.
A Transylvanian witch-trial account describes a motionless woman with open mouth; a captured fly is later released, flies into her mouth, and she wakes, leading the men to regard her as a witch.
The Servian belief described says a sleeping witch's soul often leaves as a butterfly; if the body is turned around, the butterfly soul cannot find the mouth and the witch dies.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 1 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE. / CHAPTER III. KILLING THE GOD.; lines 7109-7181
occurrences.motif_label: deity assumes animal form
occurrences.basis: Dionysus is said to appear or be represented in bull form and to assume goat or kid form in myth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Dionysus is described as often conceived and represented in animal shape, especially as a bull or with bull horns, with many bull-related epithets listed.
At festivals Dionysus was believed to appear in bull form; the women of Elis hailed him as a bull and prayed for him to come to his temple with a bull’s foot.
The passage states that Dionysus assumed goat form, had the name Kid, was changed by Zeus into a kid to escape Hera, and was turned into a goat when the gods fled Typhon.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS; lines 1213-1277
occurrences.motif_label: deity embodied in the animal that injures or is tabooed
occurrences.basis: The passage argues from swine abstention and the boar that killed Attis that the pig may have been an embodiment of Attis, and frames this by comparison with goat Dionysus and pig Demeter.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Frazer turns to Attis and Adonis as vegetation deities with possible animal embodiments, noting Attis worshippers’ abstention from swine, Attis killed by a boar, and a possible meaning of “Hyes Attes” as “Pig Attis.”

occurrences.motif_label: tree spirit with serpent and human appearances
occurrences.basis: The takhien tree spirit is believed to appear sometimes as a woman and sometimes as a serpent.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In Siam, the spirit of the takhien tree is believed to appear sometimes as a woman and sometimes as a serpent.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS; lines 2138-2205
occurrences.motif_label: human transformed into bird
occurrences.basis: The Panes is said to have been a woman who ran to the mountains and was changed into a bird by Chinigchinich.

evidence.quote_or_summary: They said Panes was a woman who ran to the mountains and was changed into a bird by Chinigchinich; they believed the annually sacrificed bird came to life again, returned to the mountains, and became multiplied while remaining one and the same female.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS; lines 2971-3035
occurrences.motif_label: helper giant versus shapeshifting hostile giant
occurrences.basis: The kind giant aids the human protagonist, while the hostile being appears as a whale under the ice, takes human shape, and fights the kind giant.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Fireless and Homeless enters a porcupine burrow, loses his way in darkness, and is released by the kind giant called He who sees before and behind, who cleaves open the earth.
A whale beneath the ice makes noise because it is naked and cold; warned by the man, the kind giant approaches, and the whale takes human shape and attacks as the wicked giant.

During the long struggle the kind giant tells the man to cut the sinew of the leg; the man cuts it, and the wicked giant falls and is slain. This is given as the reason the Indians do not eat the leg sinew.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS; lines 446-522
occurrences.motif_label: escaping crop spirit in human guise
occurrences.basis: The passage says a stranger may be taken for the Corn-goat escaping in human shape from cut or threshed grain.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A stranger passing a harvest-field may be treated as the Corn-goat escaping in human shape, and workers shout He-goat at a passerby, especially at rape-seed threshing in Schleswig if he does not remove his hat.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS; lines 524-594
occurrences.motif_label: human-animal ambiguity of crop spirit
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly notes confusion between anthropomorphic and theriomorphic conceptions of the corn-spirit in last-sheaf customs.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The last sheaf may be shaped as a horned ox and called the Old Man, or made in human form and called the Buffalo-bull; the passage notes confusion between human and animal conceptions of the corn-spirit and compares a wether called a wolf.

In Switzerland and Swabia the last sheaf or bundle may be called the Cow; the last cutter receives cow-related names, flowers or drink, and ridicule, and a corn-and-flower woman figure may represent the Cow.

occurrences.motif_label: Shapeshifting helper
occurrences.basis: The piebald horse turns into a bald-headed man before destroying the Swan-woman's soul-birds.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In another Tartar poem, the Swan-woman's soul is seven little birds inside a golden casket in a black chest at the foot of a copper rock; helper horses retrieve it, the piebald horse changes into a man and beheads the birds, and the Swan-woman dies.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS; lines 7806-7886
occurrences.motif_label: animal-masked initiators and totemic identification
occurrences.basis: Wolf-skin figures, wolf masks, wolf-mimicking men, and cassowary-representing performers appear in rites involving apparent death or initiation, and Frazer explicitly suggests rebirth as a wolf for the Nootka prince.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At Nootka Sound, a chief fires near his son's ear; the son falls as if killed, women lament, armed people enter, and two wolf-skin masked figures moving like beasts carry the prince away.

Frazer notes the prince wore a wolf-head mask, connects the rite to Wolf clan totem practices, and suggests it represented killing the lad so he might be born anew as a wolf, comparing a Basque hunter reborn as a bear.

The Toukaway Indians have a wolf-totem ceremony in which wolf-skin men run on all fours, howl, dig up a living buried tribesman, give him bow and arrows, and tell him to act as wolves do; Frazer compares it to Australian grave-resurrection rites.

In New Britain, boys are initiated into the Duk-duk association by a cane blow from Tubuvan supposed to kill them; Tubuvan and Duk-duk are concealed performers representing cassowaries, female and male respectively, whom women may not see.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS / NOTE. OFFERINGS OF FIRST-FRUITS.; lines 8378-8432
occurrences.motif_label: Ancestor spirits dwelling in material containers or taking animal forms
occurrences.basis: The matmate temporarily inhabit skulls or wood or ivory images and take forms such as birds, pigs, crocodiles, turtles, and sharks; anitos are associated with pots and miniature houses.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In the Tenimber and Timorlaut Islands, first-fruits of paddy with live fowls and pigs are offered to matmate, ancestor spirits worshipped as guardian-spirits or household gods, who enter by the roof, inhabit skulls or images, partake of offerings, help the family, and take animal forms.

The Irayas and Catalangans of Luzon worship ancestor souls called anitos, offer first-fruits to them, and regard them as household deities associated with pots in house corners and miniature houses near dwellings.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS; lines 850-918
occurrences.motif_label: escaping animal as transformed spirit
occurrences.basis: The passage says magical changes of shape make it natural to see the corn-spirit escaping in the form of an animal rushing out of the last corn.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At harvest, wild animals may be driven into the last standing corn and escape as it is cut; reapers may kill them, and the passage says a belief in magical shape-change could identify the escaping animal with the corn-spirit leaving its ruined home.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS; lines 920-982
occurrences.motif_label: Variable stature of a nature spirit
occurrences.basis: The Ljeschi is said to alter his stature according to setting: tree-height in woods, grass-height in meadows, and corn or stubble height around harvest.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Russian Ljeschie are wood-spirits partly human with goat horns, ears, and legs; the Ljeschi can alter stature in woods and meadows, and some change with corn before and after harvest.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS / NOTE. OFFERINGS OF FIRST-FRUITS. / INDEX.; lines 9317-9539
occurrences.motif_label: Deity or spirit in animal form
occurrences.basis: The index lists corn-spirit animal forms, Demeter as a pig, and Dionysus as an animal.

evidence.locator: lines 9317-9539, entries on Corn spirit and animal forms
evidence.quote_or_summary: Entries list the corn-spirit as dog, cock, hare, cat, goat, bull, calf, cow, mare, horse, pig, wolf, and ox, and note parallelism between anthropomorphic and theriomorphic conceptions.

evidence.locator: lines 9317-9539, entries on Demeter and Corn mother
evidence.quote_or_summary: Entries mention Demeter as corn mother, festivals of Demeter, Demeter as a pig, the Phigalian Demeter, Demeter and Proserpine, probable origin of Demeter, prototypes of Demeter, and the corn mother as a prototype of Demeter.
Entries mention Dionysus’s marriage, titles, myth, rites, rites similar to those of Osiris, Dionysus as an animal, and association with Demeter and Proserpine.

occurrences.motif_label: animal assumes human spouse’s form
occurrences.basis: The badger assumes the old woman’s form to greet and deceive the farmer, then returns to his natural form.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The badger assumes the old woman’s form, greets the returning farmer, says the badger soup is ready, serves him, then transforms back and tells him to look for bones in the kitchen.

occurrences.motif_label: shapeshifting dragon ruler
occurrences.basis: The Dragon King appears first as a huge serpent-dragon and then as a man, and he states that he took that shape while waiting on the bridge.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At the bridge of Seta-no-Karashi by Lake Biwa, a huge serpent-dragon lies across the path, filling the bridge and breathing fire and smoke.
After Hidesato passes, a voice calls him; the dragon is gone and a strange man appears, bowing, with red hair, a dragon-head crown, and sea-green shell-patterned clothing.
The Dragon King says the centipede has found his home and carries off his family night after night; he waited in serpent-dragon shape for a brave human, and Hidesato is the first not to flee.

occurrences.motif_label: Animal servants transform into human retainers
occurrences.basis: A train of fish is suddenly transformed into men wearing ceremonial robes and dragon crowns.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A train of fish transforms into men wearing ceremonial robes and dragon crowns; they carry a large bronze bell, a bag of rice, a roll of silk, a cooking pot, and a bell.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE FARMER AND THE BADGER / THE ADVENTURES OF KINTARO, THE GOLDEN BOY / THE STORY OF THE MAN WHO DID NOT WISH TO DIE / THE BAMBOO-CUTTER AND THE MOON-CHILD; lines 2843-2950
occurrences.motif_label: vanishing or shadow transformation to resist coercion
occurrences.basis: Princess Moonlight warns that forced removal to the Palace will make her vanish or become a shadow, and she begins to fade until the Emperor promises freedom.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Princess Moonlight refuses to see the Court lady and says that if forced to obey the Emperor's order to go to the Palace, she will vanish from the earth.
The Emperor falls in love and wants to bring her to court; she says she will turn into a shadow if forced, and her figure fades from sight.
The Emperor promises to leave her free if she resumes her former shape, and she does so.

occurrences.motif_label: goblin or monster in human disguise
occurrences.basis: The passage states that the cannibal goblin takes the form of an old woman.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Adachigahara is said to be haunted by a cannibal goblin who takes the form of an old woman; many travelers have disappeared, with stories saying they were lured to the goblin's cottage and devoured.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE ADVENTURES OF KINTARO, THE GOLDEN BOY / THE STORY OF THE MAN WHO DID NOT WISH TO DIE / THE BAMBOO-CUTTER AND THE MOON-CHILD / THE GOBLIN OF ADACHIGAHARA; lines 3740-3793
occurrences.motif_label: Demonic pursuer in old-woman guise
occurrences.basis: The old woman is suspected and then identified as a cannibal goblin; during pursuit her face changes with rage into a demon.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The man cries out in horror, asks Buddha for help, and wonders whether the kind old woman is really a cannibal goblin who will eat him.
The old hag rushes after him with hair flying, her face changing into a demon, and a large blood-stained knife in her hand.
At dawn the goblin vanishes. The priest recognizes the Goblin of Adachigahara, credits Buddha’s protection, prays with his rosary as the sun rises, and leaves the haunted plain.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE WHITE HARE AND THE CROCODILES / THE STORY OF PRINCE YAMATO TAKE / MOMOTARO, OR THE STORY OF THE SON OF A PEACH / THE OGRE OF RASHOMON; lines 6883-6997
occurrences.motif_label: monster returns in disguise to recover severed body part
occurrences.basis: The ogre appears as an old woman, persuades Watanabe to open the box, seizes the severed arm, and transforms back into the ogre.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At night someone knocks at the porch; the servant finds a respectable-looking old woman who says she was Watanabe's nurse when he was a baby, and Watanabe has her shown in.
The old woman insists that, as his old nurse, she should be allowed to see the arm, and asks whether Watanabe suspects her of being a spy sent by the ogre.
“Oh, joy! I have got my arm back again!” The old woman is then suddenly transformed into the towering figure of the frightful ogre.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE STORY OF PRINCE YAMATO TAKE / MOMOTARO, OR THE STORY OF THE SON OF A PEACH / THE OGRE OF RASHOMON / HOW AN OLD MAN LOST HIS WEN; lines 7245-7362
occurrences.motif_label: old man transforms into white crane and ascends
occurrences.basis: The old man turns into a large beautiful white crane and flies upward into the heavens.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Kokai attacks the old man, who calmly waits, laughs, turns into a large beautiful white crane, and flies upward into the heavens.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: JAPANESE FAIRY TALES / MY LORD BAG OF RICE / THE TONGUE-CUT SPARROW / THE STORY OF URASHIMA TARO, THE FISHER LAD; lines 856-981
occurrences.motif_label: Shapeshifted supernatural woman revealed as rescued animal
occurrences.basis: The princess tells Urashima that she was the tortoise he set free.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The princess says Urashima set free a tortoise, adds, "I was that tortoise," and offers him life forever in the land of eternal youth as her bridegroom.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE WISE AND THE FOOLISH MERCHANT / THE ELEPHANT GIRLY-FACE / THE BANYAN DEER / THE PRINCES AND THE WATER-SPRITE; lines 1228-1339
occurrences.motif_label: disguised supernatural being tests a human
occurrences.basis: The water-sprite appears in the form of a woodsman and engages the eldest prince, who identifies him and answers the test.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The water-sprite comes in the form of a woodsman and invites the prince to bathe in the lake and rest on the bank.
The prince knows the being is a water-sprite and accuses him of carrying off his brothers; the sprite admits it and explains they failed to answer his question.
The eldest brother answers that the Good Fairies are like: "The pure in heart who fear to sin, / The good, kindly in word and deed."

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE. / THE SIEGE OF TROY. / RETURN OF THE GREEKS FROM TROY.; lines 10110-10199
occurrences.motif_label: human-to-animal transformation by an enchantress
occurrences.basis: Circe transforms human beings into wolves and lions and later transforms Odysseus' companions into swine while their human senses remain.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The scouts find Circe's marble palace in a fertile valley; Circe is an enchantress, daughter of the sun-god and Perse; tame wolves and lions guarding the entrance are humans she transformed; she sings and weaves inside and invites the men to enter.
Circe seats the guests amid luxury and serves a banquet; the wine-cup is drugged, and after they drink she touches them with her magic wand and transforms them into swine retaining human senses.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE. / THE SIEGE OF TROY. / RETURN OF THE GREEKS FROM TROY.; lines 10394-10485
occurrences.motif_label: Divine disguise and concealment of the returning hero
occurrences.basis: Athene disguises herself as a shepherd, conceals Odysseus in a cloud, and changes his appearance into an aged beggar and later into royal form.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Athene hides Odysseus in a cloud, appears as a shepherd, tells him he is in Ithaca, reports on his family and the suitors, describes Penelope's weaving stratagem, and Odysseus kisses his native ground.
Athene changes Odysseus into the appearance of an aged mendicant and directs him to the hut of Eumaeus.

Athene urges Odysseus to reveal himself to Telemachus, restores his royal appearance, and father and son embrace; they plan secrecy and a bow contest, then Odysseus resumes beggar form and is recognized by Argo, who dies.

occurrences.passage_locator: RHEA (OPS). / DIVISION OF THE WORLD. / THEORIES AS TO THE ORIGIN OF MAN. / THIRD DYNASTY--OLYMPIAN DIVINITIES.; lines 1081-1171
occurrences.motif_label: Divine unions with mortal women under disguise
occurrences.basis: The passage states that Zeus visited mortal maidens under disguises and gives examples of satyr, swan, and bull forms used with Antiope, Leda, and Europa.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Zeus is described as also allied to mortal maidens, whom he visited under disguises because his true form would destroy mortals; Antiope, Leda, Europa, Callisto, Alcmene, Semele, Io, and Danae are listed.
Zeus appears to Antiope in the form of a satyr; Antiope is identified as daughter of Nicteus, king of Thebes.
Leda is won by Zeus in swan form; her twin sons Castor and Pollux are known for mutual attachment and physical accomplishments.
Europa gathers flowers near the sea-shore; Zeus transforms into a gentle white bull, Europa mounts him, and he carries her across the sea to Crete.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: RHEA (OPS). / DIVISION OF THE WORLD. / THEORIES AS TO THE ORIGIN OF MAN. / THIRD DYNASTY--OLYMPIAN DIVINITIES.; lines 1081-1171
occurrences.motif_label: Maiden carried away by disguised animal-form deity
occurrences.basis: Zeus transforms into a white bull, Europa mounts him, and he carries her across the sea to Crete.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Europa gathers flowers near the sea-shore; Zeus transforms into a gentle white bull, Europa mounts him, and he carries her across the sea to Crete.

occurrences.motif_label: punitive transformation into animal
occurrences.basis: Demeter transforms Ascalaphus into an owl as punishment for revealing a secret.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Demeter transforms Ascalaphus into an owl for revealing a secret.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: RHEA (OPS). / DIVISION OF THE WORLD. / THEORIES AS TO THE ORIGIN OF MAN. / THIRD DYNASTY--OLYMPIAN DIVINITIES.; lines 1173-1257
occurrences.motif_label: god assumes altered form to approach a mortal beloved
occurrences.basis: Zeus approaches Callisto under Artemis' form, Alcmene under Amphitryon's form, and Danae as a shower of gold.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Callisto, Artemis' huntress attendant, is approached by Zeus in Artemis' form; Hera changes her into a bear; Artemis hunts her; Zeus places her among the stars as Arctos after death.
Alcmene is betrothed to Amphitryon; Zeus assumes Amphitryon's form during his absence; Heracles is named as son of Alcmene and Zeus.
"Zeus appeared to Danae under the form of a shower of gold."

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: RHEA (OPS). / DIVISION OF THE WORLD. / THEORIES AS TO THE ORIGIN OF MAN. / THIRD DYNASTY--OLYMPIAN DIVINITIES.; lines 1259-1273
occurrences.motif_label: punitive animal transformation
occurrences.basis: Zeus turns Lycaon into a wolf as punishment.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Zeus is not deceived; he reacts with horror and loathing, overturns the table, turns Lycaon into a wolf, and destroys all fifty sons by lightning except Nyctimus, saved by Gaea's intervention.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: DIVISION OF THE WORLD. / THEORIES AS TO THE ORIGIN OF MAN. / THIRD DYNASTY--OLYMPIAN DIVINITIES. / JUPITER.; lines 1275-1294
occurrences.motif_label: god visits mortals in disguise
occurrences.basis: Zeus is said to visit mankind either as a mortal or under various disguises.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Zeus visits mankind as a mortal or in disguises, whereas Jupiter remains the supreme god of heaven and never appears on earth.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: PALLAS-ATHENE (MINERVA). / MINERVA. / THEMIS. / VESTA.; lines 1776-1867
occurrences.motif_label: Divine punishment by transformation
occurrences.basis: After Stellio ridicules Demeter, she changes him into a spotted lizard.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Stellio ridicules Demeter while she eats porridge during her search; she throws the remaining food in his face and changes him into a spotted lizard.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: PALLAS-ATHENE (MINERVA). / MINERVA. / THEMIS. / VESTA.; lines 1869-1876
occurrences.motif_label: Shapeshifting daughter repeatedly sold in different forms
occurrences.basis: Metra transforms into different animals and is repeatedly sold by her father after each change of form.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Metra, Eresicthon's devoted daughter, has the power to transform herself into various animals.
Metra supports her father by assuming different forms, allowing him to sell her repeatedly and continue his pitiful existence.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CERES. / APHRODITE (VENUS). / VENUS. / HELIOS (SOL).; lines 2071-2157
occurrences.motif_label: mourning transformed into trees, amber, and bird
occurrences.basis: Phaethon's sisters are transformed into poplars, their tears become amber, and Cycnus becomes a swan because of grief.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Phaethon's sisters mourn and are transformed into poplars whose tears become amber; Cycnus grieves and is transformed into a swan near the fatal waters.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VENUS. / HELIOS (SOL). / EOS (AURORA). / PHOEBUS-APOLLO.; lines 2279-2363
occurrences.motif_label: shape-shifting deity recruits ritual specialists
occurrences.basis: Apollo assumes the form of an enormous dolphin to force a Cretan ship to Crissa and appoint its sailors as temple priests.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Apollo sees a ship from Crete, takes the shape of an enormous dolphin, agitates the waters, raises a wind, and drives the ship into Crissa harbor.
Apollo appears as a vigorous youth, reveals himself, and tells the sailors he brought them to Crissa to become his priests and serve in his temple.
At the sacred fane, Apollo teaches the sailors his services and asks to be worshipped as Apollo-Delphinios because he first appeared as a dolphin.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VENUS. / HELIOS (SOL). / EOS (AURORA). / PHOEBUS-APOLLO.; lines 2365-2439
occurrences.motif_label: Transformation of fleeing beloved into sacred plant
occurrences.basis: Daphne flees Apollo, prays for aid, and is transformed into a laurel-bush that Apollo makes sacred and evergreen.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Apollo pursues Daphne; she flees, prays for aid, becomes a laurel-bush as Apollo reaches to embrace her, and Apollo declares the laurel evergreen and sacred to him.

occurrences.passage_locator: CONTENTS. / MYTHS AND LEGENDS OF ANCIENT GREECE AND ROME. / PART I.--MYTHS. / INTRODUCTION.; lines 305-397
occurrences.motif_label: Divine shapeshifting and transformation of humans
occurrences.basis: The passage says gods can assume human or animal forms and can transform humans into trees, stones, animals, or other forms.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The gods are not limited by time or space, can become invisible, assume human or animal form, and transform human beings into trees, stones, animals, and other forms as punishment or protection.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: DIANA. / HEPHAESTUS (VULCAN). / VULCAN. / POSEIDON (NEPTUNE).; lines 3296-3398
occurrences.motif_label: Divine shapeshifting to gain a beloved
occurrences.basis: Poseidon woos Amphitrite as a dolphin and later assumes Enipeus' form to win Tyro's love.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Poseidon marries Amphitrite after wooing her as a dolphin; Amphitrite transforms Scylla with herbs in a well into a twelve-footed, six-headed monster with a dog-like voice, who lives in a high cave and seizes victims from passing ships.
Pelias and Neleus are sons of Poseidon and Tyro; Poseidon assumes the form of the river-god Enipeus to win Tyro; Neleus is father of Nestor.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: DIANA. / HEPHAESTUS (VULCAN). / VULCAN. / POSEIDON (NEPTUNE).; lines 3296-3398
occurrences.motif_label: Jealous transformation of a beloved into a monster
occurrences.basis: Amphitrite's jealousy of Scylla leads her to use herbs in a well to metamorphose Scylla into a monstrous being.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Poseidon marries Amphitrite after wooing her as a dolphin; Amphitrite transforms Scylla with herbs in a well into a twelve-footed, six-headed monster with a dog-like voice, who lives in a high cave and seizes victims from passing ships.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: SEA DIVINITIES. / OCEANUS. / NEREUS. / PROTEUS.; lines 3438-3467
occurrences.motif_label: reluctant shapeshifting seer compelled to reveal knowledge
occurrences.basis: Proteus possesses prophetic power, resists consultation, changes into many forms when seized, and gives information only after being held long enough to resume his true form.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Proteus, known as the Old Man of the Sea, is a son of Poseidon, has prophetic power, and resists being consulted as a seer.
The favorable moment is to seize Proteus; he changes into many forms to avoid demands, but if held long enough he tires, resumes his true form, and gives the desired information.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: OCEANUS. / NEREUS. / PROTEUS. / GLAUCUS.; lines 3469-3487
occurrences.motif_label: human transformed into sea-divinity after tasting a potent natural substance
occurrences.basis: Glaucus tastes grass, is driven into the deep, and becomes a sea-god.

evidence.quote_or_summary: While angling, Glaucus sees caught fish nibble grass on the bank and leap back into the water; curious, he tastes the grass.
After tasting the grass, Glaucus obeys an irresistible impulse, plunges into the deep, and becomes a sea-god.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: NEREUS. / PROTEUS. / GLAUCUS. / THETIS.; lines 3489-3545
occurrences.motif_label: shapeshifting bride resisted and seized
occurrences.basis: Thetis transforms into different shapes to elude Peleus, who holds her until she assumes her true form.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Like Proteus, Thetis can transform herself into many shapes; when Peleus woos her she uses this to elude him, but he holds her until she takes her true form.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: MARS. / NIKE (VICTORIA). / VICTORIA. / HERMES (MERCURY).; lines 3746-3817
occurrences.motif_label: shape-changing test of truthfulness
occurrences.basis: Hermes assumes the form of Admetus to test whether Battus will disclose the theft.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hermes tests Battus by pretending to leave, assuming the form of Admetus, and offering two oxen if Battus reveals the thief; Battus gives the information.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VICTORIA. / HERMES (MERCURY). / MERCURY. / DIONYSUS (BACCHUS).; lines 3954-4041
occurrences.motif_label: god appears in altered youthful form
occurrences.basis: Dionysus appears to Pentheus under the form of a youth in the king's train.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Pentheus forbids Bacchanalian rites; Dionysus appears as a youth and warns him; Pentheus imprisons him and prepares execution, but prison doors open and his chains burst so he escapes.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VICTORIA. / HERMES (MERCURY). / MERCURY. / DIONYSUS (BACCHUS).; lines 4043-4125
occurrences.motif_label: Mortal captors punished after seizing a disguised god
occurrences.basis: The pirates seize Dionysus as a youth; divine signs follow, he assumes lion form, and the crew is punished while the pious pilot is spared.

evidence.locator: lines 4043-4125, paragraph 1, opening of pirate episode
evidence.quote_or_summary: Tyrrhenian pirates see Dionysus as a beautiful youth in radiant garments, seize and bind him, and take him aboard to sell in Asia.

evidence.locator: lines 4043-4125, paragraph 1, fetters and pilot warning
evidence.quote_or_summary: The fetters fall from Dionysus's limbs; the pilot perceives the miracle and warns the crew that he is a god and should be returned to shore.
After the crew refuses, the ship stands still; vines and ivy cover masts and sails, fragrant wine floods the vessel, and heavenly music is heard.
Dionysus assumes lion form; a bear attacks the captain; the sailors leap overboard and become dolphins; only the pious steersman is spared.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: MOIRAE OR FATES (PARCAE). / NEMESIS. / NYX (NOX). / THANATOS (MORS) AND HYPNUS (SOMNUS).; lines 4562-4601
occurrences.motif_label: Shape-changing dream attendant
occurrences.basis: Morpheus is described as chief among the dreams and as able to assume any shape or form he pleases.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In the cave’s centre, Hypnus rests on a black ebony couch with dark bedding, surrounded by innumerable dreams; Morpheus is chief among them and can assume any shape, while Hypnus succumbs to his own sleep-inducing power.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: NYX (NOX). / THANATOS (MORS) AND HYPNUS (SOMNUS). / MORPHEUS. / THE GORGONS.; lines 4616-4661
occurrences.motif_label: Divine punishment by bodily transformation
occurrences.basis: Athene punishes Medusa for her offence by transforming her hair, eyes, and skin into monstrous forms and leaving her under a curse.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Medusa loves Poseidon and is united to him in marriage; Athene punishes her by turning her hair into venomous snakes, changing her eyes, and altering her skin.
Under Athene’s curse, Medusa turns to stone whoever she gazes upon until death at the hands of Perseus comes as deliverance.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: HEBE (JUVENTAS). / JUVENTAS. / GANYMEDES. / THE MUSES.; lines 5052-5157
occurrences.motif_label: Transformation as punishment
occurrences.basis: The Pierides are changed into singing birds after challenging and losing to the Muses.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The daughters of King Pierus challenge the Muses on Mount Helicon; the mortal song darkens the sky, the Muses' song makes nature rejoice, and the defeated Pierides are transformed into singing birds.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: NYMPHS OF THE VALLEYS AND MOUNTAINS. / NAPAEAE AND OREADES. / THE WINDS. / PAN (FAUNUS).; lines 5499-5583
occurrences.motif_label: pursued nymph transformed into plant
occurrences.basis: Syrinx flees Pan, prays for assistance, and is transformed by the gods into a reed just before Pan seizes her.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Pan pursues Syrinx to the river Ladon; she prays for help and is transformed into a reed. Pan hears the reeds, cuts seven of unequal length, joins them, and makes the syrinx in memory of her.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: FLORA. / ROBIGUS. / POMONA. / VERTUMNUS.; lines 5827-5844
occurrences.motif_label: Shapeshifting courtship
occurrences.basis: Vertumnus metamorphoses into a variety of forms to gain Pomona's affection.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A myth is summarized in which Vertumnus changes into several forms to win Pomona: ploughman for Spring, reaper for Summer, vine-gatherer for Autumn, gray-haired old woman for Winter, and finally his true form as a beautiful youth.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: POMONA. / VERTUMNUS. / PALES. / PICUS.; lines 5865-5878
occurrences.motif_label: human transformed into bird after rejected desire
occurrences.basis: Circe changes Picus into a woodpecker after he rejects her advances.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A myth says Picus was a beautiful youth united to the nymph Canens; Circe desired him, he rejected her, and she changed him into a woodpecker, in which form he retained prophecy.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: PALES. / PICUS. / PICUMNUS AND PILUMNUS. / SILVANUS.; lines 5880-5895
occurrences.motif_label: Transformation of a youth into a tree
occurrences.basis: The transformation of Cyparissus into the cypress tree is attributed to Silvanus.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Silvanus is represented as a hale old man carrying a cypress tree; Roman mythology attributes Cyparissus's transformation into that tree to him.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CEREALIA. / VESTALIA. / PART II.--LEGENDS. / CADMUS.; lines 6563-6631
occurrences.motif_label: posthumous transformation into serpents and transfer to blessed realm
occurrences.basis: After death, Cadmus and Harmonia are changed by Zeus into serpents and transferred to Elysium.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Cadmus reigns happily for years, is deprived of his throne by his grandson Pentheus, retires with Harmonia to Illyria, and after death both are changed by Zeus into serpents and transferred to Elysium.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CRONUS (SATURN). / SATURN. / RHEA (OPS). / DIVISION OF THE WORLD.; lines 700-744
occurrences.motif_label: divine flight and animal transformation
occurrences.basis: The gods flee to Egypt and metamorphose into different animals in order to escape Typhon.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Typhon or Typhoeus, youngest son of Tartarus and Gaea, has a hundred heads, terrifying eyes, and frightful voices; he seeks to conquer gods and men, terrifies the gods into fleeing to Egypt and transforming into animals, and is destroyed by Zeus's thunderbolt.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE. / PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES).; lines 7986-8074
occurrences.motif_label: shapeshifting informant compelled to reveal hidden route
occurrences.basis: Nereus alone knows the way and is forced to give information after Heracles restrains him through various metamorphoses.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Heracles kills Cycnus, Ares comes to avenge him, Zeus intervenes with a thunderbolt, and Heracles later receives route guidance from the Nymphs and compels shapeshifting Nereus to reveal the way.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE. / PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES).; lines 8170-8264
occurrences.motif_label: combat for a bride against a shapeshifting river-god
occurrences.basis: Heracles wins Deianeira through single combat with Achelous, who can assume forms and finally becomes a bull.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Heracles woos Deianeira and fights Achelous, a river-god and rival suitor who changes forms; after Achelous becomes a bull, Heracles breaks off a horn and wins.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: RHEA (OPS). / DIVISION OF THE WORLD. / THEORIES AS TO THE ORIGIN OF MAN. / THIRD DYNASTY--OLYMPIAN DIVINITIES.; lines 986-1079
occurrences.motif_label: protective animal transformation
occurrences.basis: A variant says Zeus transformed Leto into a quail so that she could elude Hera and resume her true form at Delos.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In some versions Zeus transforms Leto into a quail to evade Hera, and she resumes her true form at Delos.

occurrences.motif_label: Shapeshifting or human-animal beings
occurrences.basis: The illustration title “The Were-Wolves” explicitly names were-wolves.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The listed titles include “Torghatten,” “The Peaks of the Trolls,” “The Were-Wolves,” “A Hero’s Farewell,” “The Funeral Procession,” “Sigurd and Fafnir,” “Sigurd Finds Brunhild,” “Odin and Brunhild,” “Sigurd and Gunnar,” “The Death of Siegfried,” and “The End of Brunhild.”
