occurrences.passage_locator: LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS / INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN; lines 1298-1437
occurrences.motif_label: Soul departing the body in animal form
occurrences.basis: The soul is said to leave the body in the shape of a mouse and later return.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The soul was believed to escape the body as a mouse from a corpse's mouth or from the mouths of people in trance; life returned when the soul came back.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS / INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN; lines 1298-1437
occurrences.motif_label: Murdered dead return as avenging animals
occurrences.basis: The souls of murdered peasants are said to assume rat forms and kill their murderer.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A vast swarm of rats, identified as the souls of the murdered peasants, pursues Bishop Hatto to a stone tower in the Rhine, gnaws through its walls, and devours him alive.
The rats attack from all directions and “were sent to do judgment on him.”

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA; lines 2123-2236
occurrences.motif_label: transformation into draught animals for supernatural land-making
occurrences.basis: Gefjon changes her four sons into oxen to plough, remove, and relocate land.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Gefjon changes her four sons into oxen, harnesses them to a plough, cuts a wide and deep furrow, wrenches away a large piece of land, drags it into the sea, fastens it, and calls it Seeland.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA; lines 2362-2458
occurrences.motif_label: Wild Hunt with transformed attendants
occurrences.basis: Frau Gode leads the Wild Hunt, and her attendants are described as changed into hounds and wild beasts.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In Mecklenburg the goddess is called Frau Gode or Wode, associated with Wuotan/Odin, prosperity, hunting, the Wild Hunt, a white horse, and attendants changed into hounds and wild beasts.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR; lines 2611-2730
occurrences.motif_label: Trickster shapechanger forced to make restitution
occurrences.basis: Loki is identified as the plotter behind Sif's shorn hair, changes form to evade Thor, and is compelled to promise restoration.

evidence.locator: lines 2611-2730; Sif shorn and Thor pursues Loki
evidence.quote_or_summary: Thor finds Sif shorn, suspects Loki, pursues him despite shapechanging, seizes him, and releases him only after Loki promises new hair.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR; lines 2733-2850
occurrences.motif_label: trickster in animal disguise sabotages sacred craftwork
occurrences.basis: Loki assumes the form of a gadfly and interferes with the dwarfs' forging by stinging Brock, causing the hammer's short handle.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sindri puts more gold on the fire and leaves Brock to blow the bellows; Loki, disguised as a gadfly, stings Brock, but Brock continues until Sindri draws out the ring Draupnir, which produces eight rings every ninth night and is called an emblem of fertility.

A lump of iron is cast in the flames; Loki again appears as a gadfly and stings Brock above the eye until blood blocks his sight. Brock briefly raises his hand, and the resulting hammer is short in the handle.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR; lines 3050-3168
occurrences.motif_label: borrowed bird plumage for flight to enemy realm
occurrences.basis: Loki borrows Freya's falcon plumes and flies in bird form across Ifing to Jötun-heim.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Loki borrows Freya's falcon plumes, flies to Jötun-heim, and learns that Thrym has buried the hammer and demands Freya as bride.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR; lines 3050-3168
occurrences.motif_label: gendered disguise to enter giant realm and recover stolen object
occurrences.basis: Thor dresses as Freya and Loki as a handmaiden to travel to Jötun-heim and recover the hammer.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Heimdall advises disguise; Thor wears Freya's clothes, necklace, and veil, while Loki dresses as a handmaiden, and they depart for Jötun-heim.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR; lines 3171-3290
occurrences.motif_label: shapeshifting flight followed by captivity
occurrences.basis: Loki borrows falcon-garb, travels as a bird, is recognized as a god in disguise, and is caged by Geirrod.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Loki borrows Freya’s falcon-garb, flies to Geirrod’s house, plays at evading capture, and is finally caught.

Geirrod recognizes the bird as a god in disguise, cages Loki without food or drink, and releases him when Loki promises to bring Thor without hammer, belt, or gauntlet; Loki then persuades Thor to visit.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR / CHAPTER V: TYR / CHAPTER VI: BRAGI; lines 3819-3966
occurrences.motif_label: Shapeshifting escape and pursuit
occurrences.basis: Odin changes into a snake to enter the mountain and flies with eagle plumes; Suttung also assumes eagle form in pursuit.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Baugi finishes boring through the mountain; Odin verifies the hole, changes into a snake, and passes through while Baugi thrusts the auger after him to kill him.
Odin uses eagle plumes and flies toward Asgard; Suttung assumes eagle form and pursues him; the Æsir light fuel, singeing Suttung’s wings and causing him to fall into the fire and die.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER IV: THOR / CHAPTER V: TYR / CHAPTER VI: BRAGI / CHAPTER VII: IDUN; lines 3991-4133
occurrences.motif_label: magical bird-form captor
occurrences.basis: The seeming eagle is identified as the storm giant Thiassi, who uses magic and later eagle wings to abduct Idun.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An eagle in a tree prevents the fire from cooking the meat, bargains for food, then takes too much; Loki strikes it with a stake, but the stake adheres to both, and Loki is dragged until he promises ransom.
The seeming eagle is the storm giant Thiassi, who frees Loki only after Loki swears to lure Idun out of Asgard so Thiassi can obtain her and her fruit.

Loki conceals the condition of release, later deceives Idun with a story about similar apples, leads her from Asgard with a crystal dish of fruit, and Thiassi seizes her on eagle wings and carries her to Thrymheim.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER IV: THOR / CHAPTER V: TYR / CHAPTER VI: BRAGI / CHAPTER VII: IDUN; lines 4135-4274
occurrences.motif_label: animal-plumage transformation and aerial pursuit
occurrences.basis: Loki uses falcon plumage, Idun is changed into a nut or swallow, and Thiassi pursues in eagle plumes.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Loki is threatened by the gods, promises to restore Idun, borrows Freya's falcon plumage, flies to Thrym-heim, finds Idun mourning exile from Asgard and Bragi, changes her into a nut or swallow, and carries her back.

The gods wait on Asgard's ramparts with fuel ready; Thiassi returns, sees Idun has been taken by a falcon, dons eagle plumes, pursues Loki, and is brought down by the gods' flames and smoke before being slain.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: HENRY FESTING JONES. / THE ODYSSEY / BOOK I / BOOK II; lines 1038-1133
occurrences.motif_label: shapeshifting divine guide
occurrences.basis: Minerva takes Telemachus's shape and later the form and voice of Mentor while directing preparations for the voyage.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva takes Telemachus's shape, summons crewmen to meet at the ship by sundown, and asks Noemon son of Phronius for a ship, which he gives readily.
Minerva takes Mentor's form and voice, calls Telemachus outside, and tells him the men are aboard and waiting for orders.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XXI / BOOK XXII / BOOK XXIII / BOOK XXIV; lines 10624-10722
occurrences.motif_label: God appearing in another person’s form as helper
occurrences.basis: Medon reports an immortal god taking the form of Mentor, encouraging Ulysses, and attacking the suitors.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Medon and Phemius come from Ulysses’ house; Medon tells the Ithacans that Ulysses acted with heaven’s will and that he saw an immortal god in Mentor’s form aiding him against the suitors.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XXI / BOOK XXII / BOOK XXIII / BOOK XXIV; lines 10724-10815
occurrences.motif_label: goddess in assumed human form
occurrences.basis: Minerva assumes the form and voice of Mentor while acting among humans.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva comes to them, having assumed the form and voice of Mentor.
Minerva, in the form and voice of Mentor, makes a covenant of peace between the contending parties.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I / BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS.; lines 1424-1514
occurrences.motif_label: Divine shapeshifting or epiphany
occurrences.basis: Minerva departs in the form of an eagle, and Nestor interprets the event as the visible manifestation of a goddess.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva flies away as an eagle; Nestor marvels, recognizes Jove's daughter, prays for favor upon himself and household, and vows an unyoked heifer with gilded horns.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS. / BOOK IV; lines 1849-1948
occurrences.motif_label: Shapeshifting sea being resisted by mortal grasp
occurrences.basis: Proteus changes into multiple animal forms, water, and a tree after being seized, while the men maintain their hold.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Idothea instructs the speaker to seize Proteus after he counts the seals and sleeps, hold him through transformations into creatures, fire, and water, and question him when he returns to his original form.
The men rush upon Proteus and seize him; he changes into a lion, dragon, leopard, wild boar, running water, and a tree, then asks the Son of Atreus who helped plot his capture and what he wants.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS. / BOOK IV; lines 2041-2133
occurrences.motif_label: divine likeness or disguised helper as captain
occurrences.basis: Noemon reports seeing Mentor board as captain, or else some god exactly like Mentor.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Noemon says he lent the ship because he could not refuse Telemachus, that the best young men went with him, and that he saw Mentor go aboard as captain, or some god exactly like him.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS. / BOOK IV; lines 2241-2286
occurrences.motif_label: image-likeness as divine messenger
occurrences.basis: Minerva makes a vision in the likeness of Penelope’s sister Iphthime to deliver a message.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva makes a vision in the likeness of Iphthime, sends it to Ulysses’ house, and it enters Penelope’s room through the door thong-hole, hovering over her head.
The vision tells Penelope to take heart because Minerva has gone with Telemachus, has compassion on Penelope, and sent the message.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV / BOOK V / BOOK VI / THE MEETING BETWEEN NAUSICAA AND ULYSSES.; lines 2694-2792
occurrences.motif_label: deity assumes another person's form to instruct a mortal
occurrences.basis: Minerva takes the form of Dymas's daughter and gives Nausicaa instructions at her bedside.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva enters Nausicaa's decorated bedroom, where Nausicaa and two maid servants sleep; she takes the form of Dymas's daughter and speaks by Nausicaa's bedside.
Minerva tells Nausicaa that her clothes are disordered, that she will soon be married, and that she should ask for a wagon and mules to carry clothing to the washing-cisterns at daybreak.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VI / THE MEETING BETWEEN NAUSICAA AND ULYSSES. / BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS.; lines 2992-3088
occurrences.motif_label: divine disguise and guidance of a vulnerable traveler
occurrences.basis: Minerva hides Ulysses and appears as a little girl to guide him to the palace.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses goes toward town; Minerva surrounds him with thick mist and appears as a little girl carrying a pitcher; Ulysses asks for Alcinous' house.
Minerva promises to show the way, tells Ulysses not to speak, look at anyone, or ask questions, and describes the Phaeacians as stranger-wary seafarers with swift ships.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: THE MEETING BETWEEN NAUSICAA AND ULYSSES. / BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS. / BOOK VIII; lines 3398-3494
occurrences.motif_label: Divine disguise validates the hero’s deed
occurrences.basis: Minerva appears in the form of a man, marks Ulysses’ throw, and confirms that no Phaeacian can match it.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses throws a larger and heavier discus beyond all prior marks; the Phaeacians react fearfully to its flight; Minerva in the form of a man marks the spot and says no Phaeacian can approach the throw.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: PREFACE TO SECOND EDITION / HENRY FESTING JONES. / THE ODYSSEY / BOOK I; lines 390-492
occurrences.motif_label: divine disguise among mortals
occurrences.basis: Minerva descends from Olympus and appears at Ulysses' house disguised as the visitor Mentes.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva binds on golden sandals, takes a bronze-shod spear, descends from Olympus to Ithaca, and stands at Ulysses' gateway disguised as Mentes, chief of the Taphians.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VIII / BOOK IX / BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE.; lines 4399-4490
occurrences.motif_label: enchantress with tamed wild beasts
occurrences.basis: Circe is a cunning goddess; wolves and lions around her house are bewitched, tamed by enchantments, and drugged into subjection.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The survivors sail to the Aeaean island where Circe lives; she is a great and cunning goddess, sister of Aeetes, both children of the sun by Perse, daughter of Oceanus.
Wild mountain wolves and lions around the house are bewitched, tamed by Circe's enchantments, drugged into subjection, and fawn on the men rather than attacking them.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VIII / BOOK IX / BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE.; lines 4492-4586
occurrences.motif_label: human companions transformed into animals by an enchantress
occurrences.basis: Circe drugs Odysseus's companions and changes them into pigs while their minds remain human.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Circe invites the companions inside, seats them, gives them a drugged mixture of cheese, honey, meal, and Pramnian wine, strikes them with her wand, turns them into pigs while their minds remain intact, confines them, and feeds them pig food.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VIII / BOOK IX / BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE.; lines 4588-4678
occurrences.motif_label: human-to-animal transformation and restoration
occurrences.basis: Circe's men had been made into pigs; she uses a second drug to remove the animal traits and restore them as men.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Circe goes with her wand, opens the pigsty, and the men come out as hogs; she anoints each with a second drug, their bristles fall away, and they become men again, younger, taller, and better looking.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: PREFACE TO SECOND EDITION / HENRY FESTING JONES. / THE ODYSSEY / BOOK I; lines 494-587
occurrences.motif_label: divine visitor in human identity
occurrences.basis: The narrator calls the visitor Minerva, while the visitor identifies herself to Telemachus as Mentes, king of the Taphians.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus sees Minerva while brooding among the suitors, goes to the gate, takes her hand and spear, welcomes her, and offers food before questions.

Minerva answers as Mentes, son of Anchialus and king of the Taphians, describes a trading voyage and ship at Rheithron under wooded Neritum, claims old family friendship, describes Laertes’ isolation, and says Ulysses is not dead and will find a way home.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE. / BOOK XI / THE VISIT TO THE DEAD.88; lines 4969-5068
occurrences.motif_label: disguised divine lover
occurrences.basis: Neptune approaches Tyro disguised as her river lover Enipeus before revealing his divine identity.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Tyro, daughter of Salmoneus and wife of Cretheus, loves the river Enipeus; Neptune disguises himself as her lover, meets her at the river mouth beneath a great blue wave, reveals himself, foretells twins, and orders secrecy.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XII / THE SIRENS, SCYLLA AND CHARYBDIS, THE CATTLE OF THE SUN. / BOOK XIII / ULYSSES LEAVES SCHERIA AND RETURNS TO ITHACA.; lines 5819-5919
occurrences.motif_label: goddess concealed helper in disguise
occurrences.basis: Minerva makes a fog to conceal Ulysses' arrival and then approaches him disguised as a young shepherd.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses wakes on his own soil but does not know it; Minerva has made a foggy day to conceal his arrival and instruct him before recognition and revenge; the landscape appears changed to him.

Ulysses counts his coppers, cauldrons, gold, and clothes and finds nothing missing; while grieving by the shore, he sees Minerva approaching in the guise of a young shepherd with cloak, sandals, and javelin.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XII / THE SIRENS, SCYLLA AND CHARYBDIS, THE CATTLE OF THE SUN. / BOOK XIII / ULYSSES LEAVES SCHERIA AND RETURNS TO ITHACA.; lines 5921-5999
occurrences.motif_label: Shape-changing divine encounter
occurrences.basis: Minerva takes a different form and Ulysses says her changing appearances make her difficult to recognize.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva smiles, caresses Ulysses, takes the form of a fair, stately, wise woman, and says only an exceptionally shifty liar could surpass him; she says both of them can deceive when needed.
Ulysses says Minerva changes appearance so often that even a knowledgeable man may not recognize her, and recalls her help during Troy and among the Phaeacians.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XII / THE SIRENS, SCYLLA AND CHARYBDIS, THE CATTLE OF THE SUN. / BOOK XIII / ULYSSES LEAVES SCHERIA AND RETURNS TO ITHACA.; lines 6001-6093
occurrences.motif_label: Hero disguises identity before reclaiming household
occurrences.basis: Minerva disguises Ulysses so no human will know him before he goes among the suitors, wife, son, and loyal servant.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva promises to stay attentive, predicts bloodshed among those consuming Ulysses' substance, and says she will disguise him so no human being will know him.
Minerva tells disguised Ulysses to go to the loyal swineherd near Raven rock and the fountain Arethusa while she goes to Sparta to see Telemachus with Menelaus.
Minerva touches Ulysses with her wand, wrinkles and withers his body, removes his yellow hair, blears his eyes, gives him filthy tattered clothing, a deer skin, a staff, and a holed wallet.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: ULYSSES IN THE HUT WITH EUMAEUS. / BOOK XV / BOOK XVI / ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS.; lines 7124-7222
occurrences.motif_label: Divine alteration of human appearance
occurrences.basis: Minerva changes Ulysses from an old ragged-looking figure into a younger, imposing man in clean clothing; Ulysses says the goddess can make him appear poor or rich.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva touches Ulysses with her golden wand, gives him a clean shirt and cloak, makes him younger and more imposing, restores his color, fills his cheeks, and darkens his beard.
Telemachus says he cannot yet believe this is his father and argues that no mortal could make himself old and young so quickly unless a god were with him.
Ulysses says no other Ulysses will come, identifies himself as the one returned in the twentieth year, and explains that Minerva can make him appear as a beggar or as a young man in good clothes.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: ULYSSES IN THE HUT WITH EUMAEUS. / BOOK XV / BOOK XVI / ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS.; lines 7321-7414
occurrences.motif_label: divine disguise of the returning hero
occurrences.basis: Minerva changes Ulysses into an old man with a wand and clothes him in old garments to preserve his concealment after his return.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Eumaeus returns to Ulysses and Telemachus as they prepare supper after sacrificing a young pig; Minerva turns Ulysses into an old man with a stroke of her wand and clothes him in old garments so the swineherd will not recognize him or tell Penelope.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XV / BOOK XVI / ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII; lines 7820-7923
occurrences.motif_label: Gods in disguise testing human conduct
occurrences.basis: The suitors warn that the beggar might be a god, saying gods travel disguised as foreigners to see who acts wrongly and who acts righteously.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The suitors warn that gods may be disguised as foreigners and travel the world to see who acts wrongly or righteously.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XVII / BOOK XVIII / BOOK XIX / BOOK XX; lines 8864-8959
occurrences.motif_label: Disguised divine visitation
occurrences.basis: Minerva comes down from heaven in the likeness of a woman and speaks to Ulysses.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva comes down from heaven in the likeness of a woman, hovers over Ulysses, and tells him that he is in his own house and that his wife and son are safe inside.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: HENRY FESTING JONES. / THE ODYSSEY / BOOK I / BOOK II; lines 938-1036
occurrences.motif_label: divine helper in human likeness
occurrences.basis: Minerva comes to Telemachus in the likeness and voice of Mentor and gives instructions for the voyage.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “Minerva came close up to him in the likeness and with the voice of Mentor.”

Minerva says she will find a ship and come with Telemachus; he is to prepare provisions, including wine in jars and barley meal in leathern bags, while she gathers volunteers and chooses the best ship.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XIX / BOOK XX / BOOK XXI / BOOK XXII; lines 9709-9805
occurrences.motif_label: shape-changing divine helper
occurrences.basis: Minerva assumes Mentor's voice and form, later takes the form of a swallow, and supports Ulysses while not yet granting full victory.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Jove's daughter Minerva comes to them after assuming Mentor's voice and form; Ulysses is glad and feels sure it is Minerva.
Minerva does not give full victory yet, wishing to further prove the prowess of Ulysses and Telemachus; she flies to a rafter in the form of a swallow.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2636-2763
occurrences.motif_label: transformed humans reborn as singing animals
occurrences.basis: Socrates recounts that humans who died from continuous singing now live again as grasshoppers, singing from birth without hunger or thirst.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates tells that grasshoppers were once humans before the Muses; when song appeared they were delighted, sang continually, forgot food and drink, and died.
The former humans live again as grasshoppers, do not hunger or thirst, sing from birth without eating or drinking, and after death go to the Muses in heaven to report who honors them.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 11459-11608
occurrences.motif_label: Rejected divine shapeshifting or deceptive appearance
occurrences.basis: The second principle is introduced through the question of whether God appears in different shapes, changes into many forms, or deceives with semblances of transformation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A second principle is introduced by asking whether God is a magician changing into many forms or deceiving by semblances, or is immutably fixed in his own image.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 11610-11780
occurrences.motif_label: rejected divine shapeshifting
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly discusses stories in which gods disguise themselves or appear in many forms, but presents them as false stories that should not be told about the gods.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker rejects poets saying that “The gods, taking the disguise of strangers from other lands, walk up and down cities in all sorts of forms.”

The speaker warns against mothers scaring children with stories that gods go about by night in the likeness of strangers and in diverse forms, lest children become cowardly and the gods be misrepresented.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1336-1415
occurrences.motif_label: Divine disguise or shapeshifting rejected
occurrences.basis: The passage rejects stories of Here appearing as a priestess and other deities moving at night in strange disguises, because God is said not to change or deceive.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The second principle is that God has no variability or change of form. The passage rejects tales of Here as a priestess and deities in strange disguises at night.
God is described as absolutely true, changing not and deceiving not by day or night, by word or sign; the lying dream of Agamemnon and Thetis’ accusation against Apollo are rejected.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII.; lines 21563-21745
occurrences.motif_label: human consumption leading to wolf transformation
occurrences.basis: The cited Arcadian tale states that tasting human entrails mixed with sacrificial entrails makes the eater destined to become a wolf.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A tale of the Arcadian temple of Lycaean Zeus says that one who tastes a human victim's entrails mixed with other victims' entrails is destined to become a wolf.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VI. / BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII. / BOOK IX.; lines 22824-22996
occurrences.motif_label: composite inner being hidden by human exterior
occurrences.basis: The soul image joins a many-headed metamorphosing monster, a lion, and a man into one being, then covers them with a single outward human form.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The first modeled form is a multitudinous many-headed monster with a ring of tame and wild animal heads, able to generate and metamorphose them at will.
The second form is made as a lion and the third as a man, with the lion smaller than the first and the man smaller than the lion.
The three forms are joined into one and given an outward human shape, so that an observer unable to look inside believes the beast to be a single human creature.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic

occurrences.motif_label: animal-human transformation across lives
occurrences.basis: Human souls choose animal lives, and animals change into one another and into corresponding human natures.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The souls of Orpheus, Thamyras, Ajax, and Agamemnon choose the lives of a swan, nightingale, lion, and eagle respectively, with prior resentments and sufferings affecting their choices.

Atalanta chooses under the attraction of athletic fame; Epeus passes into the nature of a woman skilled in arts; Thersites puts on a monkey’s form; Odysseus, last to choose, seeks and gladly chooses a private man’s life without cares.
Men pass into animals, and tame and wild animals change into one another and into corresponding human natures, with good becoming gentle and evil becoming savage.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The people nurse a protector into greatness; from this root the tree of tyranny springs. The Lycaean fable says tasting human flesh among victims turns one into a wolf, and the protector who tastes human blood becomes a wolf, that is, a tyrant.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The souls of Orpheus, Thamyras, Ajax, and Agamemnon choose or enter forms of swan, nightingale, lion, and eagle.
Atalanta chooses an athlete's honours; Epeus a workwoman's nature; Thersites becomes a monkey; Odysseus chooses the neglected private man's life and rejoices.
Men pass into animals, and wild and tame animals change into one another.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The eagle protests that the attempt is futile because nature has not given the tortoise wings.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A man searching for his lost wife reaches an oak-tree that is also a house; the old man inside identifies himself as the oak-tree god and tells him to ride a golden horse to the sky while singing.

The golden horse flies to a beautiful sky-world city; the man rides and sings there until the inhabitants and chief sky-god object to his lower-world smell and tell him he can find his wife if he leaves.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In 'The Wicked Wizard punished,' a wizard says a man can leap from a mountain peak onto clouds and ride them; the man does so, sees the world, and returns with a map of the worlds of men and gods.
The mountain god appears in a dream and says the wizard received deserved punishment, while the good man was protected and shown the world to become wiser.

The Bodhisatta is born as the universal monarch Vijitāvin, gives offerings to the priesthood, receives the prediction “He will become a Buddha,” hears the Law, gives up his kingdom, becomes a monk, gains faculties, practices meditation, and is reborn in the Brahma heavens.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Because the Sākyas view Siddhattha as younger kin, they plan for youths to bow; the Blessed One perceives this, enters an ecstasy depending on wisdom, rises into the air, and performs a miracle like the double miracle at the Gaṇḍamba-tree.

The man descends, cooks and eats the boar, flies through the air, descends at the eldest hermit’s hut in the Himalayas, serves him for two or three days, and learns of the hatchet’s magical power.

occurrences.motif_label: ascent to heaven to perform repair
occurrences.basis: Jokwa mounts clouds and rides heavenward to reach and mend the broken sky.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Jokwa summons clouds, rides heavenward with the vase of paste, mends the broken sky, repairs the broken pillar with legs of a very large tortoise, descends, and finds the world still dark.

occurrences.motif_label: post-mortem metamorphosis into celestial or natural form
occurrences.basis: Callisto is placed among the stars after death, and Philemon and Baucis are transformed into trees after dying together.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Callisto, Artemis' huntress attendant, is approached by Zeus in Artemis' form; Hera changes her into a bear; Artemis hunts her; Zeus places her among the stars as Arctos after death.
Philemon and Baucis spend the rest of their lives worshipping the gods, die at the same instant, and are transformed by Zeus into trees side by side.

occurrences.motif_label: Sea-born goddess ascending to heaven
occurrences.basis: Aphrodite is born beneath the waves and ascends from the ocean-depths to Olympus; another account has her arise from sea-foam and travel to Cyprus and Olympus.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Dione gives birth to Aphrodite beneath the waves; Aphrodite ascends from the ocean-depths to Olympus.
In the Hesiodic account, Uranus's blood mingles with sea-foam, and Aphrodite arises from the sea, standing in a shell as drops become pearls; she floats to Cythera and Cyprus.
Aphrodite steps onto Cyprus and the sand becomes a meadow; the Seasons dress and ornament her, and nymphs escort her to Olympus, where the gods receive her.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CERES. / APHRODITE (VENUS). / VENUS. / HELIOS (SOL).; lines 1985-2069
occurrences.motif_label: solar departure and return
occurrences.basis: Helios rises in the east, traverses the sky, descends westward, and in later poetry returns east by a winged vessel.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Helios, son of Hyperion and Theia, rises in the east preceded by Eos, drives a gold fiery chariot with fire-breathing steeds, descends toward the sea, is followed by Selene, and rests on a couch prepared by sea-nymphs.
The passage notes no Homeric or Hesiodic explanation of Helios' return, but later poets invent a winged boat or cup made by Hephaestus to carry him from west to east.

occurrences.basis: Apollo ascends to Olympus and is received into the assembly of celestial gods.

evidence.locator: lines 2200-2277; Apollo passage, declaration and Olympus paragraph
evidence.quote_or_summary: Apollo requests a lyre and bow, says he will foretell the future in oracles and announce Zeus’s will, then ascends to Olympus and is welcomed by the gods.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome

occurrences.basis: Otus and Ephialtes try to scale heaven by piling Ossa on Olympus and Pelion on Ossa, but Apollo kills them.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Triton, Rhoda, and Benthesicyme are children of Poseidon and Amphitrite; giant sons Otus and Ephialtes threaten the gods and try to scale heaven by piling mountains, but Apollo destroys them with arrows.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Dionysus descends to the realm of shades to find his mother and brings her to Olympus, where as Thyone she joins the immortal gods.

occurrences.motif_label: apotheosis after successful ordeal
occurrences.basis: After the underworld errand, failure, rescue, and reconciliation, Eros persuades Zeus to admit Psyche among the immortal gods.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Eros awakens Psyche with the point of a golden arrow, reproaches her curiosity and folly, persuades Aphrodite to reconcile with her, and induces Zeus to admit her among the immortal gods.

occurrences.basis: Heracles is said to be received among the immortals after his apotheosis.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hebe later became the bride of Heracles after his apotheosis and reception among the immortals.

occurrences.motif_label: ascent or transport to divine realm
occurrences.basis: Ganymedes is transported from Mount Ida to Olympus by Zeus's eagle.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ganymedes, youngest son of Tros, king of Troy, draws water from a well on Mount Ida; Zeus sees his beauty, sends his eagle to carry him to Olympus, grants him immortality, and makes him cup-bearer to the gods.

occurrences.passage_locator: JUVENTAS. / GANYMEDES. / THE MUSES. / PEGASUS.; lines 5159-5187
occurrences.motif_label: Ascent to a divine mountain
occurrences.basis: Pegasus spreads his wings and immediately flies to the top of Mount Olympus, where the immortals receive him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Pegasus spread his wings, flew to the top of Mount Olympus, and was received with delight by the immortals.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: JUVENTAS. / GANYMEDES. / THE MUSES. / PEGASUS.; lines 5159-5187
occurrences.motif_label: Hero carried aloft by exceptional mount to slay monster
occurrences.basis: At Athene's command, Pegasus carries Bellerophon aloft so that he can slay the Chimaera with arrows.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Pegasus let only gods mount him except Bellerophon, whom he carried aloft at Athene's command so Bellerophon could slay the Chimaera with arrows.

occurrences.passage_locator: LEMURES (LARVAE) AND LARES. / PENATES. / PUBLIC WORSHIP OF THE ANCIENT GREEKS AND ROMANS. / TEMPLES.; lines 6070-6142
occurrences.motif_label: Worship on elevated places to approach sky-dwelling gods
occurrences.basis: The passage states that worshippers selected mountain summits to place themselves in closer communion with gods believed to be above the clouds.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Greeks in remote times had no shrines, worshipped beneath the sky, and selected high mountain summits to be closer to gods believed to be above the clouds.

occurrences.passage_locator: VESTALIA. / PART II.--LEGENDS. / CADMUS. / PERSEUS.; lines 6834-6902
occurrences.motif_label: winged escape from captivity
occurrences.basis: Daedalus, kept almost a prisoner, makes wings for himself and Icarus and uses them to flee Crete.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Daedalus tires of exile and near imprisonment by Minos, contrives wings for himself and Icarus, and trains his son to use them.
During the flight, Icarus forgets the warning not to approach the sun; the wax melts, he falls into the sea, and drowns.

occurrences.motif_label: hero's ascent to divine realm after fiery death
occurrences.basis: After the pyre is lit, flames rise and Athene carries Heracles in a chariot to Olympus, where he is admitted among the immortals.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Flames ascend amid lightning and thunder; Pallas-Athene descends in a cloud and carries Heracles in a chariot to Olympus.
Heracles is admitted among the immortals; Hera reconciles with him by giving him Hebe, goddess of eternal youth.

occurrences.motif_label: prideful ascent to heaven punished by a god
occurrences.basis: Bellerophon attempts to mount to heaven on Pegasus; Zeus punishes him by sending a gadfly, causing his fall and later desolation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Iobates gives Bellerophon rule and his daughter in marriage. Later Bellerophon becomes proud, tries to mount to heaven on Pegasus, and is punished by Zeus, who sends a gadfly; Pegasus throws him, and he wanders in remorse and melancholy.
