occurrences.motif_label: Rainbow bridge between realms
occurrences.basis: Bifröst, identified as the rainbow, arches above Midgard and is used by the gods to travel between earth and the Urdar well near Yggdrasil.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Bifröst, the rainbow bridge of fire, water, and air, arches above Midgard and is used by the gods to travel to earth or to Urdar well near Yggdrasil.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS / INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN; lines 880-1012
occurrences.motif_label: Chosen slain carried to a warrior afterlife
occurrences.basis: Valkyrs select fallen warriors and bear them over Bifröst into Valhalla, where they are welcomed before Odin's throne.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odin's halls and Valhalla are described; Valhalla has 540 doors, a boar's head and eagle above the gate, spear walls, a shield roof, armour-decorated benches, and tables for the Einheriar.

Odin is worshipped as god of battle and victory; he sends Valkyrs to choose half of the dead warriors and carry them over Bifröst into Valhalla, where Hermod and Bragi welcome them before Odin's throne.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE. / BOOK XI / THE VISIT TO THE DEAD.88; lines 4969-5068
occurrences.motif_label: ascent by piled mountains to challenge heaven
occurrences.basis: Otus and Ephialtes try to set Ossa on Olympus and Pelion on Ossa in order to scale heaven and make war on the gods.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Iphimedeia, wife of Aloeus, boasts of Neptune's embrace and bears Otus and Ephialtes; the giant youths threaten Olympus and try to pile Ossa on Olympus and Pelion on Ossa to scale heaven, but Apollo kills them before maturity.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 1190-1207
occurrences.motif_label: ascent of the soul above earthly opinion
occurrences.basis: The passage says the soul's wing is renewed and that she is raised above earthly manikins and their opinions.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "the 'wing of the soul' is renewed and gains strength"
The soul is raised above the manikins of earth and their opinions.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE.; lines 1300-1387
occurrences.motif_label: ascent toward knowledge
occurrences.basis: The passage contrasts a backward-looking age with the unattempted movement to go forward and scale the heights of knowledge.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The age "did not attempt to pierce the mists" or "scale the heights of knowledge," but was lost in doubt and rested on tradition and authority.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 154-206
occurrences.motif_label: Winged soul chariot ascending or falling
occurrences.basis: The soul is figured as a charioteer with winged steeds, including mortal and immortal components, and is described as soaring upward or dropping to earth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: All soul is immortal and source of motion; its form is figured as a charioteer with a pair of winged steeds; divine steeds are immortal, while the human pair includes one mortal and one immortal; the immortal soul soars heavenward and the mortal drops plumes to earth.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 208-288
occurrences.motif_label: Ascent of the soul to a heavenly vision
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly describes wings, chariots, and souls rising to heaven or the empyrean to behold divine realities.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Wings carry the soul upward; Zeus goes forth in a winged chariot, followed by gods, demi-gods, and human souls; the gods ascend to the empyrean, while Hestia remains at home.
Beyond heaven is a formless, colourless, intangible essence perceived by mind; divine minds behold justice, temperance, and knowledge, then return and give horses ambrosia and nectar.
Human souls attempt the same ascent but struggle; the mortal steed can pull them downward, and the charioteer may turn away from the plain of truth.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2188-2244
occurrences.motif_label: ascent of the winged soul
occurrences.basis: The perfect and fully winged soul is described as soaring upward and traversing heaven.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The soul traverses heaven; when perfect and winged it soars upward and orders the world, while when imperfect it loses its wings, droops, settles on the ground, and receives an earthly frame.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2246-2321
occurrences.motif_label: ascent to the divine upper realm
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly describes upward movement by wings and chariots toward the upper region, the vault of heaven, and the realm beyond heaven.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The wing is described as akin to the divine, tending to soar upward; it is nourished by beauty, wisdom, and goodness, but wastes when fed by evil and foulness.
At banquet and festival, the gods ascend to the top of heaven; divine chariots move easily, while others struggle, and the immortals stand outside heaven and behold what is beyond.
Other souls follow God with difficulty, rise and fall, struggle below the surface, tread on one another, and many are lamed or have wings broken by ill-driving.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2323-2387
occurrences.motif_label: ascent through wings and upward longing
occurrences.basis: Philosophical or loving souls acquire wings, look upward, and desire to fly away toward the realm recalled through beauty.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Souls usually require ten thousand years to return and grow wings; philosophical souls or philosophical lovers may acquire wings in the third thousand-year period.
The philosopher recollects the things the soul saw while following God; the philosopher's mind has wings and is initiated into perfect mysteries through these memories.
The fourth kind of madness occurs when seeing earthly beauty recalls true beauty; the person wants to fly away but cannot and is like a bird fluttering and looking upward.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2389-2457
occurrences.motif_label: Ascent from earthly beauty to true beauty
occurrences.basis: The uncorrupted goal is described as rising out of this world to the sight of true beauty in the other world.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The uninitiated or corrupted person does not easily rise to true beauty, while the recently initiated spectator has seen many glories in the other world.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2389-2457
occurrences.motif_label: Winged soul transformed by beauty
occurrences.basis: The soul is described as once wholly winged and as growing wings when it receives beauty through the eyes.

evidence.quote_or_summary: As the lover gazes, beauty comes through the eyes; the wing moistens, warms, melts open, and begins to grow through the soul.
“Mortals call him fluttering love, But the immortals call him winged one” because wing-growth or wing-motion is necessary to him.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2551-2634
occurrences.motif_label: Winged ascent after disciplined love
occurrences.basis: The passage connects self-control, philosophy, lightness, wings, flight, a heavenward pilgrimage, and later receipt of wings.

evidence.quote_or_summary: If self-control, order, and philosophy prevail, the pair live in happiness and harmony, master themselves, enslave vicious elements, emancipate virtuous elements, and become light and winged for flight.

They pass out of the body unwinged yet eager to soar; those who have begun the heavenward pilgrimage do not descend to darkness or the journey beneath the earth, but live in light and later receive wings with the same plumage.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2636-2763
occurrences.motif_label: philosophical honor under heavenly Muses
occurrences.basis: Calliope and Urania are said to be chiefly concerned with heaven and thought, divine as well as human, and the grasshoppers report philosophers to them.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The grasshoppers' reports win the love of Terpsichore for dancers, Erato for lovers, and Calliope and Urania for philosophers; Calliope and Urania are associated with heaven and thought.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 290-374
occurrences.motif_label: Winged ascent after leaving the body
occurrences.basis: The lovers leave the body, proceed on a pilgrim's progress, receive wings, and fly away.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Self-controlled lovers live happily, master themselves, leave the body, proceed on a pilgrim's progress, receive wings, and fly away with the same wings.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 3781-3808
occurrences.motif_label: Divine inspiration leading a human to higher pursuits
occurrences.basis: Socrates says Isocrates has divine inspiration that will lead him to higher things and an element of philosophy in his nature.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says Isocrates has genius above Lysias' orations, will improve with age, will surpass former rhetoricians, will not be satisfied with rhetoric, has divine inspiration leading him higher, and has philosophy in his nature.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 457-547
occurrences.motif_label: ascent from sense-bound love to unseen objects
occurrences.basis: The three degrees of love move from interested love to sense-directed mad love and then to disinterested love directed toward the unseen and dialectic.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Higher rhetoric is based on dialectic; dialectic is inspiration akin to love; true knowledge of heaven and earth rests on enthusiasm or love of ideas present in this world and another. Love is divided into interested love, disinterested or mad love fixed on sense objects, and disinterested love directed toward the unseen.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 549-637
occurrences.motif_label: movement from deficient love to higher view
occurrences.basis: The passage describes passionate and interested forms of love yielding to a higher view of love.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Plato is said to have a higher purpose than showing Socrates as a rival of Athenian rhetoricians; Lysias’ speech contains a germ of truth, Socrates develops it, and successive views of love yield to a higher view.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 639-716
occurrences.motif_label: winged ascent toward rest
occurrences.basis: The passage says figuratively that the two grow wings like doves and are ready to fly away together and be at rest.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "they grew wings like doves" and were ready to fly away together and rest.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 718-802
occurrences.motif_label: ascent or journey by chariot toward truth and light
occurrences.basis: In the comparison to Parmenides, a chariot approaches regions of light and the house of the goddess of truth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The charioteer-and-steeds image is compared with Parmenides, but the passage says Parmenides' horses are not allegorical and that the poet approaches in a chariot to regions of light and the house of the goddess of truth.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 804-884
occurrences.motif_label: Heavenly journey of the soul
occurrences.basis: The passage describes a heavenly journey in which the soul, through the image of charioteer and steeds, encounters absolute forms and invisible essences.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “the charioteers and their steeds stand upon the dome of heaven” and behold intangible invisible essences not objects of sight.
The image of the charioteer and steeds is placed beside absolute forms such as justice and temperance, seen with the eye of the soul in her heavenly journey.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 886-959
occurrences.motif_label: ascent from animal desire to contemplation of forms
occurrences.basis: Higher love is described as rising above animal wants and contemplating forms of justice, temperance, and holiness.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage distinguishes lower and higher love, describes higher love as contemplating forms with religious awe, compares the opposition to flesh and spirit in St. Paul, and mentions the rational soul mastering both steeds in spiritual combat.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 10635-10722
occurrences.motif_label: Difficult path of virtue versus easy path of vice
occurrences.basis: Hesiod is cited for vice as smooth, abundant, and near, while virtue requires toil and an uphill road; Pindar is cited for ascent to a lofty tower by justice or deceit.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Poets are invoked: Hesiod is cited for the easy path of vice and toil before virtue, and Homer for gods being turned by prayers, sacrifices, entreaties, libations, and the odour of fat.
The speaker asks how quickwitted youth, compared to bees on flowers, will respond to such teachings, and quotes Pindar on ascending a lofty tower by justice or crooked deceit.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV.; lines 15157-15248
occurrences.motif_label: ascent to a vantage point for seeing truth
occurrences.basis: Socrates says they are near a place where truth may be seen clearly, invites the interlocutor to come up, and compares the argument’s position to a height or tower of speculation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “we are near the spot at which we may see the truth in the clearest manner with our own eyes”
“Come up hither... and behold the various forms of vice”
The argument is said to have reached a height, like a tower of speculation, from which one may see that virtue is one and vice has innumerable forms, with four special ones worth noting.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 18617-18744
occurrences.motif_label: ascent from hypotheses to a higher principle
occurrences.basis: The higher intellectual subdivision is described as the soul going up beyond hypotheses to a principle above hypotheses.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The lower intellectual subdivision uses figures as images and proceeds hypothetically downward; the higher passes out of hypotheses and goes up to a principle above hypotheses, through ideas themselves.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 18746-18778
occurrences.motif_label: Ascent to a first principle and return through ordered levels
occurrences.basis: Dialectic is described as using hypotheses as steps, soaring beyond them to the first principle of the whole, and descending again through ideas.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Reason, by dialectic, uses hypotheses as steps and points of departure into a world above hypotheses, soars to the first principle of the whole, and descends again through ideas without sensible objects.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 18781-18911
occurrences.motif_label: Ascent from underground darkness to light
occurrences.basis: The released prisoner is dragged up a steep and rugged ascent from the den toward the upper world and the sun.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The prisoner is “reluctantly dragged up a steep and rugged ascent” and forced into the presence of the sun.
The prisoner grows accustomed to the upper world, first seeing shadows, then reflections in water, then objects, then moon, stars, and the night sky.
Last of all, the prisoner can see the sun itself, not merely its reflection in water, and contemplate it in its own place.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 18913-19020
occurrences.motif_label: Ascent of the soul toward intelligible light
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly identifies the upward journey as the ascent of the soul into the intellectual world.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker says the prison-house is the world of sight, the fire’s light is the sun, and the upward journey is the ascent of the soul into the intellectual world.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19022-19142
occurrences.motif_label: ascent from darkness below to light and knowledge
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly describes ascent to the good, being brought from darkness to light, and the soul's ascent from below to the true day of being.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The founders must compel the best minds to ascend until they arrive at the good; after they have ascended and seen enough, they must descend again among the prisoners in the den and share their labours and honours.
"brought from darkness to light,—as some are said to have ascended from the world below to the gods"
The process is not the turning over of an oyster-shell but the turning around of a soul from a day little better than night to the true day of being, called the ascent from below and true philosophy.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19144-19306
occurrences.motif_label: ascent of the soul through knowledge
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly frames the desired study as one that draws the soul from becoming toward being, with arithmetic proposed as a means of turning the soul to reflection.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speakers ask what knowledge would “draw the soul from becoming to being” and add that it should have usefulness in war for young warrior athletes.
Arithmetic is described as a study that leads to reflection and whose true use is “to draw the soul towards being.”

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19308-19466
occurrences.motif_label: intellectual ascent from change to true being
occurrences.basis: The philosopher is said to rise out of the sea of change and lay hold of true being; arithmetic helps the soul pass from becoming to truth and being.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Arithmetic and calculation deal with number and lead the mind toward truth; the man of war needs number to array troops, and the philosopher must rise out of the sea of change and grasp true being; the guardian is both warrior and philosopher.

Legislation should prescribe arithmetic for the principal men of the State, who must study numbers with the mind only, not for trade; arithmetic elevates the soul, reasons about abstract number, preserves indivisible unity, and requires pure intelligence for pure truth.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19468-19613
occurrences.motif_label: turning of the soul toward truth
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly describes mathematical study as turning the soul’s gaze toward the good, eternal being, and truth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Geometry is tested by whether it aids the “vision of the idea of good” and turns the soul’s gaze toward “the full perfection of being.”
Socrates says geometricians speak of practical operations, but knowledge is the object of geometry, and that knowledge concerns the eternal rather than the transient.
Geometry will “draw the soul towards truth,” create philosophy, and “raise up” what has fallen down.
Astronomy is proposed; Socrates says there is an “eye of the soul” that can be “purified and re-illumined” and by which truth is seen.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19468-19613
occurrences.motif_label: upward and downward orientation as epistemic contrast
occurrences.basis: The interlocutor presents astronomy as upward movement from this world to another, while Socrates opposes this with the claim that it may make people look downward.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The interlocutor says astronomy “compels the soul to look upwards” and leads from “this world to another.”
Socrates says those who elevate astronomy into philosophy seem to make people “look downwards and not upwards.”

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19615-19736
occurrences.motif_label: ascent from sensory appearance to intelligible knowledge
occurrences.basis: The passage contrasts looking down toward sensory particulars with the soul looking upward toward being, the unseen, reason, intelligence, true number, and the beautiful and good.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Knowledge of being and the unseen makes the soul look upward; sensory particulars, whether found in the heavens, ground, water, or land, are not science.
The visible starry heaven is beautiful but inferior to true motions, true number, and true figure, which are apprehended by reason and intelligence, not sight.
In astronomy, as in geometry, one should employ problems and leave the visible heavens alone in order to make reason useful.
The inquiry is useful if sought with a view to the beautiful and good, but useless if pursued otherwise.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19738-19854
occurrences.motif_label: Ascent from darkness to light
occurrences.basis: The passage describes release from chains, movement from shadows to light, and ascent from an underground den to the sun.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage describes prisoners released from chains, moved from shadows to images and light, ascending from an underground den to the sun, and first seeing images in water; firelight is contrasted with the sun.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 19738-19854
occurrences.motif_label: Inner faculty lifted from mire to vision
occurrences.basis: The eye of the soul is described as buried in a slough and lifted upward by dialectic.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Mathematical sciences are said to dream about being while hypotheses remain unexamined; dialectic goes to the first principle, removes hypotheses, and lifts the eye of the soul upward from a slough.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1996-2074
occurrences.motif_label: sacred numerical harmony linking sense and ideas
occurrences.basis: The passage says intervals of sound and number are sacred, rise above sense, and connect with the world of ideas.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Plato is said to have a Pythagorean reverence for numbers and numerical proportion.
Intervals of sound and number are called sacred things with their own law; they rise above sense and connect with the world of ideas.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII.; lines 20154-20256
occurrences.motif_label: ascent of vision toward illuminating truth
occurrences.basis: The qualified rulers raise the eye of the soul to the universal light and behold the absolute good as the governing pattern.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At fifty, those who survive and distinguish themselves must 'raise the eye of the soul' to the universal light and behold the absolute good.
The absolute good is the pattern for ordering the State, individual lives, and the rulers’ remaining lives.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VI. / BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII. / BOOK IX.; lines 22657-22822
occurrences.motif_label: ascent toward a true upper realm
occurrences.basis: The passage uses lower, middle, and upper regions and says those without wisdom never pass into the true upper world or taste pure abiding pleasure.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates introduces an analogy of upper, middle, and lower regions; a person moving from lower to middle may mistake the middle for the upper if he has never seen the true upper world, producing wrong ideas about pleasure and pain.

Those who do not know wisdom and virtue are said to move only up and down as far as the mean, never reaching the true upper world; like cattle, they look downward, feed, breed, and fight one another with iron horns and hoofs because of insatiable lust.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII. / BOOK IX. / BOOK X.; lines 24067-24188
occurrences.motif_label: release from oceanic and earthly accretions
occurrences.basis: The soul is imagined as borne by divine impulse out of the ocean and disengaged from stones, shells, earth, and rock while following a superior principle.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker says to look at the soul's love of wisdom, its sought society and converse, and its kinship with the immortal, eternal, and divine; if it followed this superior principle, it would be borne by divine impulse out of the ocean and disengaged from stones, shells, earth, and rock.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII. / BOOK IX. / BOOK X.; lines 24305-24376
occurrences.motif_label: ascent and descent between earth and heaven
occurrences.basis: Souls ascend by a heavenly way, descend by a lower way, ascend out of earth, and descend out of heaven.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The judges send the just upward to the right and the unjust downward to the left; the souls bear symbols or sentences of their deeds.
Er sees souls departing through openings after judgment, and other souls arriving: some ascend from earth dusty and worn, others descend from heaven clean and bright.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII. / BOOK IX. / BOOK X.; lines 24483-24572
occurrences.motif_label: upward ascent to birth
occurrences.basis: After drinking and sleeping, souls are driven upward in all manner of ways to their birth, compared to shooting stars.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After rest, at midnight a thunderstorm and earthquake occur, and the souls are driven upward in many ways to their birth, like shooting stars.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 2519-2584
occurrences.motif_label: Elevated viewpoint over the city
occurrences.basis: The passage invites the reader to come up to a hill over the city to see forms of virtue and vice.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage asks whether justice or injustice is more profitable, invites the reader up to a hill over the city to view one form of virtue and many forms of vice, and says the virtuous state is ruled by reason as monarchy or aristocracy.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 2586-2659
occurrences.motif_label: ascent beyond ordinary human limits
occurrences.basis: The passage says metaphysicians pass beyond the limits of human thought and language and seem to reach a height among 'worlds unrealized.'

evidence.quote_or_summary: Metaphysicians are said to pass beyond human thought and language and to reach a height where they are 'moving about in worlds unrealized.'

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 3196-3254
occurrences.motif_label: philosophical ascent toward eternal order
occurrences.basis: The true philosopher fixes his eye on eternal order and moulds himself and others into the Divine image; education is ordered toward mature return to philosophy.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker says the order of education should be reversed: begin with gymnastics in youth, then increase the gymnastics of the soul as the person strengthens, and finally return to philosophy after active life.

The passage distinguishes true philosophers from false pretenders; the true philosopher despises earthly strife, looks to eternal order, moulds himself and others into the Divine image, and creates private and public virtues.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 3256-3342
occurrences.motif_label: Ascent toward a higher intelligible region
occurrences.basis: The passage speaks of a longer road leading to a higher region and of the good as an inconceivable height above knowledge and truth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The guardian must “take the longer road” and seek a “higher region” above the four virtues.
The good is described as the cause of knowledge, truth, growth, and being, yet greater than these in dignity and power.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 331-413
occurrences.motif_label: ascent to highest speculation
occurrences.basis: The passage uses the image of a summit of speculation for Plato's highest philosophical thought in Books V-VII.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage describes philosophical imagination as moving among ideas, myths, fancies, facts, and figures of speech, and identifies Books V-VII as reaching the summit of speculation.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 3343-3430
occurrences.motif_label: Ascent through knowledge toward the good
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly describes stages or steps in an ascent to the idea of good and connects this ascent with higher forms of knowledge.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Knowledge is described as stages in an ascent to the idea of good and as four divisions with corresponding faculties: pure intelligence, active intelligence, faith, and perception of shadows.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 3508-3587
occurrences.motif_label: ascent through ordered knowledge
occurrences.basis: The passage describes a higher method proceeding by regular steps, with ideas as grades of thought, toward universal knowledge and the end of the intellectual world.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says Plato gives only a glimpse and no clear explanation of his higher method of knowledge.
"regular steps to a system of universal knowledge"; ideas are described as "steps or grades or moments of thought" in a connected whole.
Plato is said to be hastening to the "end of the intellectual world" without making a beginning of the sciences.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 3589-3670
occurrences.motif_label: Ascent to higher truth
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly describes human intelligence ascending by a ladder let down from above toward one self-existent truth and the idea of good.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A truth, one and self-existent, is approached by a ladder from above; unity is like the sun and light, and the mathematical sciences are steps of the ladder toward the idea of good.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 3736-3821
occurrences.motif_label: ascent from darkness to light as acquisition of knowledge
occurrences.basis: The passage presents a movement from the dark den up a steep ascent to the sun, then explicitly identifies the upward way with knowledge and the idea of good.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A captive is dragged up a steep ascent into the sun's presence, gradually perceiving shadows, water reflections, moon, stars, and finally the sun, which is said to give the year and seasons.
The passage interprets the cave as the world of sight, the fire as the sun, the upward way as knowledge, and the idea of good as last seen with difficulty and as author of good and right.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 3822-3899
occurrences.motif_label: Education as ascent from darkness to light
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly frames the formation of rulers as a movement from darkness to light, night to day, and upward elevation of soul and mind.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage asks for the way “from darkness to light” and describes philosophy as “the conversion of a soul from night to day, from becoming to being.”
“All number has also an elevating effect; it raises the mind out of the foam and flux of generation to the contemplation of being.”
The passage says mathematical studies should look upward to eternal existence and that geometry “should elevate the soul” and “raise up what has fallen down.”

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 3901-3981
occurrences.motif_label: Intellectual ascent from sense to good
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly contrasts sense perception with mind and culminates in the soul’s elevation to contemplation of the highest ideal of being.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “The vision of knowledge of which I speak is seen not with the eyes, but with the mind.”
Dialectic is compared with the effort of sight moving from shadows to the images that gave the shadows, and is said to withdraw from sense toward contemplation of the idea of good.
“the royal road out of the cave into the light” and “the elevation of the soul to the contemplation of the highest ideal of being.”

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 3901-3981
occurrences.motif_label: Cave-to-light transformation of sight
occurrences.basis: The passage invokes a royal road out of the cave into light, blinking at the sun, and acquiring a new faculty of sight.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “the royal road out of the cave into the light” and “the elevation of the soul to the contemplation of the highest ideal of being.”

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 3983-4011
occurrences.motif_label: Ascent from ignorance to higher light
occurrences.basis: Dialectic is described as rising above hypotheses and leading the eye of the soul out of ignorance into upper-world light.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Dialectic “rises to the principle which is above hypotheses” and leads the soul's eye from ignorance into “the light of the upper world.”

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 4013-4089
occurrences.motif_label: ascent from sense to the good
occurrences.basis: Selected students withdraw from the world of sense into ideas and later lift their eyes to the idea of good as the pattern for life and rule.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At thirty, a further selection is made of those able to withdraw from the world of sense into the abstraction of ideas.
At fifty the student returns to the end of all things, lifts his eyes to the idea of good, and orders life after that pattern.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 4091-4148
occurrences.motif_label: ascent from darkness to light
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly describes an upward way to true light and a dialectical process represented as movement from darkness to light.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Plato is said to explain the philosopher's relation to the world through allegory; at the start of Book VII he uses the figure of a cave with an opening toward a fire and an upward way to true light, with dialectic represented by the way from darkness to light.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 4241-4307
occurrences.motif_label: ascent from darkness to light and return
occurrences.basis: The passage describes ascent to an upper world, contact with light or eternal ideas, and return or descent to the lower world, with changed perception.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says the allegory has political and philosophical meaning; the den or cave represents the narrow sphere of politics or law, and the light of eternal ideas affects those who return to the lower world.
Those who return are first unable to compete with den inhabitants in measuring shadows and are derided and persecuted, but later see things below in truer proportions than those who never ascended.
The passage symbolizes two kinds of disordered eyesight: the captive transferred from darkness to day and the heavenly messenger who voluntarily descends into the den for the good of fellow-men.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 4241-4307
occurrences.motif_label: distorted sight after crossing between worlds
occurrences.basis: Two forms of disordered eyesight are described, one from transfer from darkness to day and one from descent into the den.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage symbolizes two kinds of disordered eyesight: the captive transferred from darkness to day and the heavenly messenger who voluntarily descends into the den for the good of fellow-men.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 5259-5329
occurrences.motif_label: ascent from lower to upper realm as image of truer knowledge
occurrences.basis: The vertical-region simile depicts movement from lower to middle and the true upper world as a way to distinguish apparent from true pleasure and knowledge.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A simile presents upper, middle, and lower regions; one moving from lower to middle imagines he is going up into the upper world, through ignorance of the true regions.
“Those who feast only on earthly food, are always going at random up to the middle and down again; but they never pass into the true upper world...”

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 5706-5773
occurrences.motif_label: ascent of the just
occurrences.basis: The just are directed to ascend by the heavenly way on the right hand, and ascending pilgrims pass upward with joy when the chasm is silent.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Judges sit between the chasms, directing the just upward on the right with a seal set before them and the unjust downward on the left with a seal behind them.
Ascending pilgrims greatly fear hearing the chasm’s voice, but when there is silence they pass upward with joy; corresponding delights are mentioned.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 6209-6282
occurrences.motif_label: heavenly ascent or elevated viewing of stars
occurrences.basis: The passage describes pilgrims contemplating the heavens, Er and his companions viewing the heavens, and a spectator going out to look at the stars while borne round in the revolution.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The moon, spindle, column of light, and chains are discussed; the passage says the spindle is of adamant, fastened to chains extending to the middle of the column of light, and that the column holds heaven together, though the exact arrangement is not explained.

The Republic's heavenly picture is compared with the Timaeus; fixed stars and planets move around the world's axis. The passage says Er and his companions view the heavens from earth, and a spectator may be imagined looking from above or below, like the heaven of the Phaedrus.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 6989-7077
occurrences.motif_label: self-transcendence or ascent above the lower nature
occurrences.basis: The passage says humans strive to rise above themselves and places higher affection over natural instincts.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage contrasts reformers who isolate the animal part of human nature with the speaker's view of humans as many-sided, moving between good and evil, and striving to rise above themselves.
The passage warns of a condition in which human passions are controlled by no divine or human authority, with no shame, decency, or higher affection sanctifying natural instincts.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 7640-7706
occurrences.motif_label: ascent toward higher truth
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly describes a movement toward perfect truth, with all things ascending to the good and reposing there.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “the good which is the higher sphere of dialectic, is the perfect truth to which all things ascend, and in which they finally repose.”

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 8481-8570
occurrences.motif_label: ascent to philosophical vision
occurrences.basis: The passage says people do not lift their eyes to the hills or awaken at dawn, but in Plato a person reaches a height from which to see the future of the world and philosophy.

evidence.quote_or_summary: People “do not lift up their eyes to the hills” and are “not awake when the dawn appears,” while Plato offers a “height” from which to see the future.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 233-318
occurrences.motif_label: Rebellion against heaven and divine punishment
occurrences.basis: Original humans attempt to scale heaven and attack the gods; Zeus responds by halving them to reduce their strength.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The original beings are described as strong and swift, attempting to scale heaven and attack the gods; the gods deliberate over human pride and the fear of losing sacrifices.
Zeus proposes cutting the beings in two so that their strength is halved and sacrifices are doubled.
Zeus splits them, and Apollo is told to turn their faces, rearrange their bodies, remove wrinkles, and tie the skin at the navel.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 2394-2475
occurrences.motif_label: Ascent from particular beauty to universal beauty
occurrences.basis: The seeker moves from one beautiful form to all forms, minds, laws, sciences, and the final vision of beauty everywhere.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The seeker begins with one beautiful form, advances to all beautiful forms, beauty of mind, laws and institutions, sciences, the vast sea of beauty, and the final vision of the science of beauty everywhere.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 2477-2569
occurrences.motif_label: ascent from earthly beauty to absolute beauty
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly describes mounting upward from earthly beauties as steps toward the essence of beauty.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "begin from the beauties of earth and mount upwards ... using these as steps only" toward the notion and essence of absolute beauty.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 320-409
occurrences.motif_label: ascent from bodily beauty to universal beauty
occurrences.basis: The passage gives a clear ordered progression from one fair form to many forms, minds, laws, sciences, and the final vision of universal beauty.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Diotima announces initiation into the greater mysteries: the lover proceeds from one fair form to many, to beautiful minds, laws, institutions, sciences, and finally universal beauty, beheld by the mind’s eye, producing virtue, wisdom, divine friendship, and immortality.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 411-502
occurrences.motif_label: Ascent from sensual passion to contemplation of truth
occurrences.basis: The passage says love can rise to the loftiest heights, penetrate philosophy's inmost secret, and become mystical contemplation of the beautiful and good.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage describes a mystery of love in man beyond immediate sex; Socrates is passionate but self-controlled; love in Phaedrus and Symposium is mystical contemplation of the beautiful and good and can rise to philosophy's highest secret.
The highest love is described as love of the highest and purest abstraction, figured as a far-off heaven for the eye of the mind, and associated with truth, knowledge, the invisible, and the eternal.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 593-675
occurrences.motif_label: rhetorical ascent of the soul
occurrences.basis: Agathon's rhetoric is said to elevate the soul to sunlit heights.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Agathon's rhetoric is said to elevate the soul to sunlit heights; he distinguishes Love from Love's works, hints that Love is always of beauty, and speaks of Love as creator and artist.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 677-763
occurrences.motif_label: ascent from visible beauty to eternal knowledge
occurrences.basis: The passage describes a progression from earthly or visible beauty through abstract thought to a vision of the eternal and perfect beauty.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Love reaches a higher region of perfect beauty and eternal knowledge, beginning with earthly beauty and culminating in harmony and oneness; the passage uses images of a summit, upward and downward way, and ladder to heaven.

The passage describes arrival at a vision of the eternal, the idea as love or truth, the lover of wisdom as spectator of all time and existence, and a mystery uniting spiritual and fleshly, moral and intellectual faculties.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 765-833
occurrences.motif_label: love of beauty as upward progress
occurrences.basis: The philosopher is said to take the first step in upward progress through beauty, and love is described as enthusiasm for the ideal of beauty.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The philosopher is said to be incited to take the first step in upward progress by the beauty of young men and boys.
Love is described as taking a spurious form of enthusiasm for ideal beauty, like worship of a godlike image of Apollo or Antinous.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 923-996
occurrences.motif_label: philosophical ascent through stages
occurrences.basis: The passage describes movement from this world to another through steps or stages, from sense particulars to universals, and through higher degrees of initiation to the vision of beauty.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Phaedo is compared with the Symposium; unlike Phaedo and Phaedrus, the Symposium has no break between this world and another but rises through steps from sense particulars to universals and a single science.
The passage describes a language of mysteries with higher degrees of initiation leading to a perfect vision of eternal, absolute, divine beauty beyond limits of space and time.

occurrences.source_title: The Mystics of Islam
occurrences.passage_locator: The Mystics of Islam, The Path
occurrences.motif_label: mapped interior pilgrimage
occurrences.basis: Sufi spiritual life is described as a journey, pilgrimage, path, and ascent with stages.

evidence.locator: The Mystics of Islam, The Path, lines 796-837
evidence.quote_or_summary: Nicholson presents Sufi spiritual life as a journey or pilgrimage through stages and states toward gnosis, truth, and union with Reality.

occurrences.basis: The bronze serpent is raised on a pole.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Make a venomous snake, and set it on a pole... when he looked at the serpent of bronze, he lived.

occurrences.source_title: The Poetic Edda
occurrences.passage_locator: VOLUSPO / THE WISE-WOMANS PROPHECY / INTRODUCTORY NOTE / NOTES; lines 1629-1639
occurrences.motif_label: Dragon/serpent associated with cosmic order (Nithhogg at Yggdrasil’s roots)
occurrences.basis: Nithhogg is described as a dragon at the roots of Yggdrasil, linking dragon imagery with the world-tree’s root-region.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The note identifies Nithhogg as the dragon at the roots of Yggdrasil (with cross-reference to earlier stanza and note).

occurrences.source_title: The Poetic Edda
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTORY NOTE / NOTES / PRONOUNCING INDEX OF PROPER NAMES / PRONOUNCING INDEX; lines 23008-23324
occurrences.motif_label: World tree / sacred axis (Yggdrasil as world-ash)

evidence.quote_or_summary: Dīpankara’s city is Rammavatī; his parents, disciples, servitor, female disciples, and Pipphali Bodhi-tree are named; he is eighty cubits high and compared to a deodar pine or sal-tree in bloom.
Koṇḍañña’s city is Rammavatī; his father, mother, chief disciples, servitor, chief female disciples, Sālakalyāṇi Bodhi-tree, eighty-eight-cubit body, and one-hundred-thousand-year life are specified.

occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 4522-4607
occurrences.motif_label: Tree associated with awakened Teacher
occurrences.basis: Each Buddha’s entry includes a named Bodhi-tree or Bo-tree as part of the Buddha’s identifying details.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An unnamed figure is ordained, embraces ascetic life, learns the word of Buddha, attains supernatural faculties and attainments, and is reborn in the Brahma heavens. Mangala Buddha’s details are listed, including a Nāga Bodhi-tree, an eighty-eight-cubit body, a ninety-thousand-year life, and death accompanied by darkness in ten thousand worlds and lamentation.

Sumana appears after Mangala and has three assemblies. The Bodhisatta is the Nāga king Atula, leaves the Nāga world with kinsmen, offers celestial music, gives garments of fine cloth, is established in the Three Refuges, and is foretold to become a Buddha. Sumana’s details include the Golden Mountain assembly and Nāga Bodhi-tree.

Revata appears after Sumana and has three assemblies. The Bodhisatta is born as the brahmin Atideva, hears the Teacher’s preaching, is established in the Three Refuges, raises clasped hands, praises the Teacher, presents a monk’s upper robe, and receives the prediction that he will become a Buddha. Revata’s details include a Nāga-tree as Bo-tree.

Sobhita appears after Revata and has three assemblies. The Bodhisatta is born as the brahman Ajita, hears the Teacher’s preaching, is established in the Three Refuges, gives a great donation to the order with the Buddha at its head, and receives a prophecy of future Buddhahood. Sobhita’s details include a Nāga-tree as Bo-tree.

After an asaŋkheyya, Anomadassin, Paduma, and Nārada are born in one kalpa. Anomadassin has three assemblies. The Bodhisatta is a mighty Yakkha chief, lord of many yakkhas, who comes after hearing that a Buddha has appeared, gives a great donation to the order with the Buddha at its head, and receives the prophecy that he will be a Buddha. Anomadassin’s details include an Arjuna-tree as Bo-tree.

occurrences.motif_label: Buddha-associated sacred tree listings
occurrences.basis: Each Buddha is linked with a named Bo-tree, including Crimson-tree, Sāla-tree, and Champaka-tree.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Paduma has three assemblies and dwells in a forest grove; the Bodisat as a lion venerates him in trance, attends seven days without seeking prey, puts faith in the Order, and receives a prophecy of future Buddhahood. Paduma's city, kin, disciples, Bo-tree, height, and age are listed.

Nārada has three assemblies; the Bodisat as a vowed sage has five kinds of Wisdom and eight sublime Acquisitions, donates to the Order headed by the Buddha, offers red sandal wood, and receives a prophecy of future Buddhahood. Nārada's attributes and Bo-tree are listed.

Padumuttara appears in a distant kalpa and has assemblies, including one on Vebhāra Mountain; the Bodisat as Jaṭila offers robes to the Order headed by the Buddha and receives a prophecy. The passage says all men and angels took refuge in the Buddha, and lists Padumuttara's attributes and Bo-tree.

Sumedha appears after Padumuttara; the Bodisat as the brahman youth Uttara gives eight hundred millions of money to the Order headed by the Buddha, listens to the Law, accepts the Refuges, abandons home, takes vows, and receives a prophecy. Sumedha's attributes and Bo-tree are listed.

occurrences.motif_label: Buddha associated with a named Bo-tree
occurrences.basis: Each listed Buddha is paired with a specific Bo-tree: Bambu, Priyaŋgu, Champaka, Kuravaka, or Kanikāra.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sujāta has three assemblies; the Bodisat as universal monarch hears the Law, gives his kingdom with seven treasures to the Order, takes vows, and receives prophecy. Sujāta's city, family, disciples, Bambu Bo-tree, body height, and lifespan are listed.

Piyadassin appears after eighteen hundred world-cycles; the Bodisat as Kassapa hears the Law, builds a monastery, keeps the Refuges and Precepts, and receives a prophecy after eighteen hundred kalpas. Piyadassin's Priyaŋgu Bo-tree and other attributes are listed.

Atthadassin has three assemblies; the Bodisat as the ascetic Susima brings from heaven a sunshade of Mandārava flowers and offers it to the Teacher, who prophesies to him. Atthadassin's Champaka Bo-tree and bodily glory are listed.

Dhammadassin has three assemblies; the Bodisat as Sakka king of the gods offers sweet-smelling heavenly flowers and heavenly music, and the Teacher prophesies to him. Dhammadassin's red Kuravaka Bo-tree is listed.

Siddhattha appears ninety-four world-cycles ago; the Bodisat as the ascetic Mangala brings a great jambu fruit to the Tathāgata. After eating it, the Teacher prophesies Buddhahood ninety-four kalpas later. Siddhattha's Kanikāra Bo-tree is listed.

occurrences.basis: Each Buddha’s biographical entry names a specific Bo-tree: Asana, Āmalaka, Pāṭali, Puṇḍarīka, or Sal.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Tissa appears ninety-two world-cycles ago. The Bodisat is born as warrior-chief Sujāta, takes vows, gains rishi powers, offers a heaven-grown lotus and Pāricchattaka flowers to Tissa, spreads a flower awning in the sky, and receives a prophecy that he will become a Buddha. Tissa’s city, family, disciples, Asana Bo-tree, height, and lifespan are listed.

Phussa appears in the same Maṇḍakalpa. The Bodisat is born as warrior-chief Vijitavī, lays aside his kingdom, takes vows under the Teacher, learns the three Piṭakas, preaches the Law, fulfills the Perfection of Morality, and receives a prophecy. Phussa’s city, family, disciples, Āmalaka Bo-tree, height, and lifespan are listed.

Vipassin appears ninety world-cycles ago. The Bodisat is born as the mighty snake king Atula and gives Vipassin a golden chair inlaid with seven kinds of gems; Vipassin prophesies that he will become a Buddha. Vipassin’s city, family, disciples, Pāṭali Bo-tree, height, bodily radiance, and lifespan are listed.

Sikhin appears thirty-one world-cycles ago. The Bodisat is born as king Arindama, gives robes and other things to the Order with the Buddha at their head, offers a superb elephant decked with seven gems, and receives a prophecy. Sikhin’s city, family, disciples, Puṇḍarīka Bo-tree, height, bodily radiance, and lifespan are listed.

Vessabhū appears after Sikhin. The Bodisat is born as king Sudassana, gives robes and other things to the Order with the Buddha at their head, takes vows, becomes righteous in conduct, meditates on the Buddha, and receives a prophecy. Vessabhū’s city, family, disciples, Sal Bo-tree, height, and lifespan are listed.

Koṇāgamana has one assembly of thirty thousand monks. The Bodisat as King Pabbata goes with ministers to the Teacher, hears the Law, gives silk and fine gold-woven cloths, takes vows, and receives prophecy; Koṇāgamana’s city, family, disciples, Udumbara Bo-tree, height, and age are listed.

Kassapa has one assembly of twenty thousand monks. The Bodisat as the Brahman youth Jotipāla, friend of Ghaṭīkāra, goes to the Teacher, hears the Law, takes vows, learns the three Piṭakas, serves the religion of the Buddhas, and receives prophecy; Kassapa’s birthplace, family, disciples, Nigrodha Bo-tree, height, and age are listed.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At the Bodisat's birth in Lumbini, the mother of Rāhula, Channa, Kāḷudāyi, Kanthaka, the Bo-tree, and four treasure vases also come into being and are called the Connatal Ones.
People take the Bodisat to Kapilavastu; angels in Tāvatiŋsa heaven rejoice and say that Suddhodana's son will become a Buddha seated under the Bo-tree.
Kāḷa Devala rests in Tāvatiŋsa heaven, asks the angels why they rejoice, and hears that Suddhodana's son will become a Buddha and found a Kingdom of Righteousness.

occurrences.motif_label: miraculous contemplative child under a tree
occurrences.basis: As a child, the Bodisat enters the first Jhāna beneath a Jambu-tree, and the tree's shadow remains fixed and circular.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The king takes his son to the festival site and has the child's couch placed under a dense Jambu-tree shade, with a star-inlaid golden canopy and curtain.
When the nurses leave, the future Buddha looks around, sees no one, sits cross-legged, holds his breath, and enters the first Jhāna.
The shadows of other trees turn, but the Jambu-tree's shadow remains steady and circular; the nurses return, see the Bodisat sitting cross-legged and report the shadow miracle to the king.

occurrences.basis: The Bodisat sits at the foot of the tree, lights the eastern region, and later spends seven times seven days at the foot of the Tree of Wisdom.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sujātā tells Puṇṇā to watch the holy place. The Bodisat, after five dreams, concludes that he will become a Buddha that day and sits at the foot of the tree, lighting it with his glory.

Puṇṇā sees the Bodisat at the tree, the eastern region lit up, and the tree gold-colored by rays from his body; she thinks the god has descended from the tree to receive the offering and reports to Sujātā.

occurrences.basis: The Bodisat proceeds to the Tree of Wisdom and sits at the Bo-tree at the place where all Buddhas sit for attaining Buddhahood.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Bodisat spends the day in a sāla grove and proceeds toward the Tree of Wisdom along a divinely adorned path, while superhuman beings offer flowers and heavenly songs.
The eastern place is identified as where all Buddhas sit cross-legged and as unshaken; the grass forms a fourteen-cubit seat, and the Bodisat vows not to leave until complete insight is attained.

occurrences.motif_label: Sacred tree as site of victory and awakening
occurrences.basis: The Bo-tree's foot is the place where celestial beings celebrate the Buddha's victory and where the Great Being attains knowledge and Enlightenment.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Heavenly hosts announce that the Tempter is overcome and that Siddhattha has prevailed; Nāgas, Winged Ones, Angels, Brahma Gods, and other gods rejoice and honor him at the Bo-tree.
Before sunset the Great Being routs the Evil One's army; while the Bo-tree seems to pay homage, he gains knowledge of past, present, and the causal chain in the three watches of the night.

On realizing the twelvefold chain of causation and attaining complete Enlightenment at dawn, ten thousand world-systems quake and become glorious, with banners, flowers, light, sweet waters, halted rivers, restored faculties, and loosened bonds.

occurrences.basis: The Master remains for weeks near the Bo-tree and later meditates under the Shepherd’s Nigrodha-tree; these tree sites are linked to omniscience, Abhidhamma contemplation, Truth, and Nirvāna.

evidence.quote_or_summary: For the fourth week angels create a house of gems northwest of the Bo-tree; the Master sits there cross-legged and thinks out the Abhidhamma Pitaka. Abhidhammikas give two explanations of the House of Gems.
After four weeks near the Bo-tree, the Master goes in the fifth week to the Shepherd’s Nigrodha-tree, sits meditating on Truth, and enjoys the sweetness of Nirvāna.

occurrences.basis: The Blessed One stays or sits at named trees, including the Mucalinda-tree, Rājāyatana-tree, Shepherd’s Nigrodha-tree, and the neighborhood of the Bo-tree, during post-awakening events.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At the Mucalinda-tree, Mucalinda the snake-king shields the Blessed One during a storm with seven folds of his hood.
The Blessed One goes to a Rājāyatana-tree; seven weeks pass, during which he has no bodily wants and feeds on the joys of Meditation, the Paths, and the Fruit.
The Perfectly Enlightened One returns to the Shepherd’s Nigrodha-tree and, considering the depth of the Truth gained, doubts whether he can explain it to others.

The Master grants the request, considers Aḷāra and Uddaka but perceives them dead, then chooses the five mendicants at the Deer-forest in Benares and resolves to inaugurate the Kingdom of Righteousness there.

occurrences.motif_label: Sacred tree and sacred grove veneration
occurrences.basis: The passage surveys tree-worship, sacred groves, divine trees, sacred oaks, and sacred Roman trees across several European traditions.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Frazer cites Grimm’s argument that the oldest German sanctuaries were natural woods and states that tree-worship is attested for all great European families of the Aryan stock.
The passage names Celtic Druids’ oak-worship, ancient German sacred groves, continuing tree-worship among descendants, and the sacred grove at Upsala where every tree was regarded as divine.
Among ancient Prussians the sacred oaks are central, especially the chief oak at Romove, where priests keep a perpetual fire of oak-wood in a holy grove.

Frazer says tree-worship was prominent among Lithuanians, abundant in ancient Greece and Italy, and preserved in Rome through worship of the fig-tree of Romulus and reverence for a Palatine cornel-tree whose drooping prompted people to rush with water.

occurrences.motif_label: Sacred tree inhabited or animated by spirit
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly describes trees as bodies or dwellings of spirits, gods, or divinities and treats some trees as sacred because of that presence.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Frazer states that spirits may be viewed as incorporated in trees, or, in another view, as dwelling in trees and able to leave them; Pelew Islanders conjure the tree-spirit to leave a tree being felled and settle on another.

Frazer states that sacred trees may be conceived as bodies or dwellings of spirits; old Prussians believed gods inhabited high trees such as oaks, and the great oak at Romove was the god's special dwelling-place.

Battas refused to cut certain trees because mighty spirits dwelled there; Curka Coles believed spirits in treetops would be disturbed and take vengeance; Samogitians believed injury to certain groves or their animals would cause crooked hands or feet.

occurrences.motif_label: Sacred tree or grove as spirit abode and fertility source
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly treats trees and groves as dwellings or embodiments of spirits that provide rain, sunshine, crop growth, and other fertility powers.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Frazer describes a shift from trees as bodies of tree-spirits to trees as dwellings of separable spirits; the spirit can move among trees, becomes a forest god, and may be represented in human shape with a branch or similar woodland symbol.

Frazer states that tree-souls and anthropomorphic tree-gods retain powers connected with rain, sunshine, multiplication of flocks and herds, and easy childbirth, and announces examples of these powers.

Examples are given of Lithuanian women defending sacred groves as a god’s house for rain and sunshine, Mundaris believing sylvan gods withhold rain if grove trees are felled, and Cambodian communities sacrificing to a sacred tree when rains are late.

Tree-spirits are said to make crops grow; examples include Mundari grove deities responsible for crops, sacrifices at tall trees on the Gold Coast, and Swedish peasants placing leafy branches in corn-field furrows.

occurrences.motif_label: Seasonal sacred tree brought into village or household
occurrences.basis: Several rites occur at harvest, wheat-sowing, May-day, or July and involve a tree, branch, or bough brought into a village, household, stable, or central place.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At a Lhoosai harvest festival in South-East India, the chief and people fell a large tree, bring it into the village, set it up, offer sacrifice, pour spirits and rice over it, and end with a feast and dance by unmarried men and girls.

At Gilgit wheat-sowing, wheat from the Raja’s granary is mixed with sprigs of the sacred Chili cedar, held over smoke from a cedar bonfire, and partly baked as a cake for the ploughman; Frazer says this is meant to fertilise the seed by the sacred cedar.

Three chosen unmarried youths purify themselves, take wine, oil, bread, and fruit to a mountain cedar, sprinkle wine and oil on it, eat a sacrificial feast, cut a branch, bring it to the village, place it on a large stone beside running water, and a goat is sacrificed with blood poured over the branch.

After the Gilgit sacrifice, each man takes a cedar spray home; when his wife asks what he has brought, he answers that he has brought children, food, cattle, or whatever is wanted. The wife uses cedar leaves with wine, water, fire, flour, and a ceiling suspension, and addresses the cedar as Shiri Bagerthum.

Frazer states that the Gilgit goat-driving rite is meant to impart the cedar’s fertilising influence, then compares European May-tree customs: German May-trees at stable and byre doors to increase milk, an Irish green bough for summer milk, and a Wendish oak with an iron cock around which cattle are driven to thrive.

occurrences.motif_label: sacred tree as protector of livestock and crops
occurrences.basis: The passage describes Metsik's tree-fastened image and the Circassian pear-tree as protectors of cattle, and Metsik's image as a guard of corn as well.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Some Esthonians believe in Metsik, a mischievous forest spirit with power over cattle welfare; villagers annually make a straw-man image, clothe it, take it to common pasture, and fasten it to a high tree while dancing around it.

Prayer and sacrifice are offered to Metsik for cattle protection; sometimes his image is made from a corn-sheaf and fastened to a tall tree in the wood while people perform antics to induce him to guard corn and cattle.
The Circassians regard the pear-tree as protector of cattle; they cut a young pear-tree from the forest, branch it, bring it home, adore it as a divinity, and almost every house has one.

occurrences.motif_label: ritual bringing of tree or greenery from forest to settlement
occurrences.basis: Frazer states that May-tree and related customs involve cutting trees or branches from the woods and bringing them to villages and houses in spring, early summer, or Midsummer.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Frazer explains May-tree and May-pole customs as widespread because people cut trees or branches from woods in spring, early summer, or Midsummer and bring them to villages or houses to receive blessings in the tree-spirit's power.
Sir Henry Piers reports that on May-eve every family in Westmeath sets a green bush with yellow flowers before the door, or tall slender trees where timber is plentiful.

Northamptonshire had a custom of planting a young tree before each house on May Day; Cornish custom decked doors and porches with sycamore and hawthorn boughs and planted trees or stumps before houses.

In the north of England, young people formerly went into the woods early on May morning with music, broke branches, decorated them with nosegays and flower crowns, and fastened them over doors and windows at sunrise.
At Abingdon in Berkshire, young people formerly went about in groups on May morning singing a carol while bringing a garland to a door.

occurrences.motif_label: tree-mediated fertility and childbirth aid
occurrences.basis: The passage gives examples of women rolling under an apple-tree to obtain offspring, clasping guardian-trees for easy delivery, wearing bark garments for protection in childbirth, and Leto clasping trees before giving birth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Frazer says the May Day green bush before a beloved maiden's house probably came from belief in the fertilising power of the tree-spirit; Kara-Kirgiz barren women roll under a solitary apple-tree to obtain offspring.
In parts of Sweden, a farm had a guardian-tree such as lime, ash, or elm; the tree was sacred, injury to it brought ill-luck or sickness, and pregnant women clasped it for easy delivery.
In some Congo-region tribes, pregnant women make garments from bark of a sacred tree because they believe the tree delivers them from dangers of child-bearing.
Frazer says the story that Leto clasped a palm and olive, or two laurels, before the birth of Apollo and Artemis perhaps points to a similar Greek belief in certain trees facilitating delivery.

occurrences.motif_label: personified vegetation figure
occurrences.basis: The Russian birch is dressed in woman’s clothes or ribbons, treated as an honored guest, visited, and explicitly described by Frazer as conceived as personal.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Russian villagers before Whitsunday go to the woods, sing, weave garlands, cut a young birch-tree, and dress it in woman’s clothes or adorn it with colored shreds and ribbons.

After a feast the dressed birch is carried home with dance and song, set up in a house as an honored guest, visited, then on Whitsunday taken to a stream and thrown into the water with garlands after it.
Frazer says the birch’s woman’s clothing shows the tree is conceived as personal and that throwing it into a stream is most probably a rain-charm.

occurrences.motif_label: raised tree as communal ritual center
occurrences.basis: The decorated May-pole or tree is raised publicly, people flock to it, and communal dances occur around it.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The chief Swedish event is setting up a tall stripped spruce-pine May-pole, decorated with leaves, flowers, cloth, gilt eggshells, hoops or crosspieces, and topped by a vane or flag; village maidens decorate it and people dance around it in a ring.

Frazer turns to May Day May-trees, notes that English May-poles were often permanent but sometimes annually renewed, and cites a Cornish custom of cutting down a tall elm on May Eve, bringing it to town, erecting it publicly, and dressing it with garlands or streamers.

occurrences.motif_label: vegetation spirit represented by tree and human figure
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly pairs a decorated tree with a leaf-, branch-, straw-, or flower-bearing human figure and explicitly calls this a double representation of the spirit of vegetation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In Russian Lithuania on May 1, a green tree is set up, the prettiest girl is crowned and swathed in birch branches, and people dance, sing, and shout beside the May-tree.
In Brie, a decorated May-tree stands in the village; girls dance around it and a leaf-wrapped lad called Father May is led about.
In Bavaria, a tree is erected before a tavern, and a man called the Walber dances around it enveloped in straw, with ears of corn forming a crown.
In Carinthia on St. George’s Day, a decorated felled tree is carried in procession with music; the chief figure is Green George, a young man clad in green birch branches.

Frazer says powers of rain-making and fostering cattle are attributed to a tree-spirit represented by a living man, and compares the Oraon priest’s drenching to Green George’s ducking as a rain-charm that dispenses rain and fruitfulness.

occurrences.motif_label: Tree or vegetation spirit represented by human or object
occurrences.basis: Frazer says the customs show ways the tree-spirit or spirit of vegetation is represented, including May-tree processions, leaf-covered boys, and bride-named girls.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In some Altmark villages at Whitsuntide, boys carry a May-tree or lead a boy covered in leaves and flowers, while girls lead a May Bride dressed as a bride with a nosegay; she sings for gifts and links giving with household abundance.
In Bresse in May, a girl called la Mariée is decorated with ribbons and nosegays, led by a gallant, preceded by a lad with a green May-tree, and accompanied by sung verses.

Frazer says these are ways the tree-spirit or vegetation spirit is represented in European peasant customs and argues from their persistence and similarity that tree-worship was once important among the Aryan race in Europe.

occurrences.basis: Only a runaway slave may break a branch from the tree; success gives him the right to fight the priest for the office.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At Nemi no branch of the certain tree might be broken except by a runaway slave; if he succeeded, he could fight the priest and, by killing him, reign as King of the Wood.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At the Little Daedala, the Boeotians of Plataea go to an ancient oak forest, place boiled meat for birds, follow a raven to an oak, cut it down, make a bride-dressed image from the wood, place it on a bullock-cart with a bridesmaid, and process it to the river Asopus and back with piping and dancing.

occurrences.basis: Frazer explicitly compares the Boeotian festival with Russian, Bohemian, Pyrenean, Angoulême, Cornish, and Dublin customs involving felled trees or bushes used in spring or midsummer rites.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Frazer says the festival resembles European spring and midsummer festivals, including a Russian Whitsuntide custom where villagers fell a birch, dress it in women's clothes, carry it with dance and song, and throw it into water on the third day.

Frazer lists further European parallels: a Bohemian midsummer fir or pine adorned and burned; a Pyrenean May tree kept until midsummer and burned on a hill; an Angoulême poplar burned on St. Peter's Day; a Cornish midsummer bonfire with a summer pole; and a Dublin May-bush cut and burned.

occurrences.basis: Diana’s grove sanctuaries, the Arician grove, and the argument that its cult was essentially that of a tree-spirit or wood deity support a sacred tree/grove motif.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Diana’s attributes are said to be those of a tree-spirit or sylvan deity; her sanctuaries were in groves, she is associated with Silvanus, helped women in travail, and was patroness of wild animals.

Considering his double character as king and priest, relation to the Golden Bough, and the woodland divinity of the grove, the passage provisionally assumes that the King of the Wood was a living incarnation of the tree-spirit, like the May King and Northern European congeners.

The passage says the Golden Bough was a special manifestation of divine life in the grove and that tree-spirits may be represented in double form: by a tree or bough and by a living person.

occurrences.basis: Attis dies under a pine-tree, is changed into a pine-tree, and a cut pine is treated as a divinity with a young man’s effigy attached.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Attis is called a fair youth beloved by Cybele. One account says he was killed by a boar like Adonis; another says he mutilated himself under a pine-tree and died from loss of blood, a local Pessinus story.
The passage says the people of Pessinus abstained from swine and that after death Attis was changed into a pine-tree.

At the spring equinox a pine-tree was cut, brought into Cybele’s sanctuary, treated as divine, adorned with woollen bands and violets, and fitted with a young man’s effigy; violets were said to spring from Attis’s blood as anemones from Adonis’s blood.

occurrences.basis: The erica tree encloses the coffer and becomes a palace pillar, while the Ded pillar is interpreted as Osiris’s backbone and possibly as a tree trunk linked with Osiris as tree-spirit.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Isis mourns and searches, finds the body at Byblus, where an erica tree has grown around the coffer and been made into a palace pillar; she obtains leave to open the trunk and remove the coffer.

The festival ends with the erection of the Tatu/Tat/Ded pillar, a cross-barred column; a Theban tomb shows the king, relations, and a priest raising it. It is later interpreted as Osiris’s backbone and possibly as a stripped tree linked to resurrection.
