occurrences.basis: Osiris's image is buried in a hollowed pine; his body and coffer are represented as enclosed in or sheltered by trees; inscriptions call him present in trees.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Osiris is presented as corn-spirit and tree-spirit; a pine is cut, hollowed, used to make an Osiris image, the image is placed in the tree hollow, kept for a year, and burned like the Attis image attached to a pine-tree.

The tree-cutting ceremony is linked to the mythic body of Osiris enclosed in the erica tree, the Tatu pillar at the annual festival, comparison with May-pole customs, Denderah's conifer enclosing Osiris's coffer, pine-cone offerings, and cedar sprung from Osiris.
Sycamore and tamarisk are called trees of Osiris; inscriptions say he resides in them; Nut is represented in a sycamore; a tamarisk overshadows Osiris's coffer in a sepulchre.

At Philae a tamarisk is depicted with two men pouring water on it near material about Osiris's grave; Osiris appears as a corpse with ears of corn sprouting, is called 'the one in the tree' and 'the solitary one in the acacia,' and appears as a mummy covered with tree or plants.

occurrences.basis: Dionysus is described as a tree god whose image may be a post, tree-stump, or image made from a sacred pine-tree, with boughs or tree materials marking the deity.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Dionysus or Bacchus is described as god of the vine and of trees in general, with Greek sacrifices to 'Dionysus of the tree' and a Boeotian title 'Dionysus in the tree.'
An image of Dionysus is described as an upright post with mantle, bearded mask, and leafy boughs projecting from head or body; a vase shows his effigy appearing from a low tree or bush.
Dionysus is described as patron of cultivated trees; prayers asked him to make trees grow; fruit-growers set up his image as a natural tree-stump in orchards.

The pine-tree is described as sacred to Dionysus; the Delphic oracle told Corinthians to worship a pine-tree equally with the god, and they made two images of Dionysus from it; a pine-cone-tipped wand is carried by the god or worshippers.

occurrences.basis: The passage links mistletoe with the seat of life, the Golden Bough, and the life of the oak, while also listing oak worship, sacred groves, sacred trees, and the sanctuary tree at Nemi.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Mistletoe is indexed as worshipped by the Celts, gathered by the Druids, gathered at Midsummer Eve and at midsummer and Christmas, possessing qualities, viewed as the seat of life, holding the life of the oak, kept from touching the ground, protective against witchcraft, and identified with the Golden Bough.

Oak worship is indexed with the oak as chief sacred tree of the European Aryans, oak-based sacred fires, oak wood burned on Midsummer Day, Balder as the oak, the human representative of the oak slain, the oak's life in mistletoe, oak superstition, and the oak as a store of solar fire.
The index lists the lake of Nemi, the tree within the sanctuary, the priest of Nemi, and Nemi as unchanged.
The index lists sacred groves of the Mundaris, a superstition concerning the felling of sacred groves, a sacred larch-tree at Nauders, and a tree within the sanctuary at Nemi.

occurrences.basis: The Gilyak bear skull is placed on a tree near the house, and the Goldi suspend the skull, jaw-bones, and ears on a tree as an antidote against evil spirits.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Gilyak bear is teased, tied to a peg, shot with arrows, decapitated, decorated with shavings, placed on the feast table, asked pardon and worshiped; its flesh, brain, and entrails are eaten, its skull is placed on a tree, and people sing and dance as bears.

The Goldi sometimes capture and cage a bear, feed it well, call it son and brother, parade it at a festival, kill and eat it, and suspend its skull, jaw-bones, and ears on a tree against evil spirits; eating the flesh is believed to give hunting zest and courage.

occurrences.motif_label: vegetation-spirit represented by human or effigy in leafy framework
occurrences.basis: The passage connects wicker, grass, foliage, and leafy frameworks with human representatives of the tree-spirit or vegetation-spirit.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Gigantic osier or grass-covered images are said to enclose Druidic victims and are compared with leafy frameworks around human representatives of the tree-spirit.
Because land fertility was thought to depend on the sacrifices, Mannhardt is said to view Celtic victims in osiers and grass as representatives of the tree-spirit or vegetation-spirit.

At Luchon on Midsummer Eve, a sixty-foot hollow wicker column interlaced with foliage and surrounded by flowers was filled with combustibles; living serpents were thrown in and the column was set on fire.

occurrences.motif_label: Sacred tree and ritually harvested healing plant
occurrences.basis: Pliny’s quoted account presents oak and mistletoe as sacred, with mistletoe gathered ceremonially from the oak by a priest and treated as a universal healer.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Frazer introduces Pliny’s description of Druidic mistletoe gathering; Pliny says Druids esteem mistletoe and the oak on which it grows, choose oak-woods as sacred groves, and perform no sacred rites without oak-leaves.

Pliny’s quoted account says the Druids gather mistletoe with solemn ceremony in the sixth moon-determined month, prepare sacrifice and feast under the tree, bring two unbound white bulls, and have a white-robed priest cut the mistletoe with a golden sickle into a white cloth before sacrificing the victims and praying for divine prosperity.
Pliny’s quoted account says the Druids believe mistletoe potion makes barren animals bring forth and that the plant remedies all poison.

occurrences.motif_label: Oak as sacred ritual tree
occurrences.basis: The oak is identified as the likely original tree represented at fire-festivals, used in sacred-fire production, fed to a perpetual fire under a sacred oak, and felled and burned at Daedala.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage states that an essential feature of primitive fire-festivals was the burning of a man representing the tree-spirit, and argues that the represented tree was originally the oak.
The passage explains wood-friction fire-making and gives oak-wood examples from Celts, Germans, Slavs, Masuren, ancient Slavic perpetual fire, Germany, and the Scottish Highlands.

The passage says the perpetual fire under the sacred oak at Romove was fed with oak-wood and describes German Midsummer oak logs whose yearly embers are used with seed-corn or gardens for crop growth and protection.
The passage notes that at the Boeotian festival of the Daedala, compared to modern European spring and Midsummer festivals, a great feature was the felling and burning of an oak.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The King of the Wood is said to personify the tree or oak-spirit; his life or death is in the mistletoe on the oak, and, like Balder, he cannot die while it remains intact.

Frazer supposes the King of the Wood was once burned at the midsummer fire festival in the Arician grove; the perpetual fire was probably fed with sacred oak-wood, and later the king escaped fire only to fall by the sword.

occurrences.motif_label: Sacred tree stores and releases hidden fire
occurrences.basis: The oak is described as a reservoir of fire, with fire drawn from its wood to feed or rekindle the sun.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Frazer says midsummer bonfires were probably sun-charms meant to supply the sun with fresh fire, and that this fire was elicited by friction of oak wood.
The oak is described as the storehouse or reservoir of fire; since the oak’s life was conceived to be in the mistletoe, the mistletoe contained the seed or germ of the fire drawn from oak wood.
Frazer generalizes that in societies making fire by friction of wood, trees used in fire-making would be conceived as reservoirs of hidden fire and described as golden, shining, or bright.

occurrences.basis: The passage states that the life of the oak was conceived to be in the mistletoe and that the King of the Wood’s divine life was in the mistletoe or Golden Bough.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The oak is described as the storehouse or reservoir of fire; since the oak’s life was conceived to be in the mistletoe, the mistletoe contained the seed or germ of the fire drawn from oak wood.

Frazer concludes that primitive Aryan worship survived in the sacred grove at Nemi and that the King of the Wood lived and died as an incarnation of the supreme Aryan god whose life was in the mistletoe or Golden Bough.

Balder is described as an oak-spirit who was fair-faced and shining, with light going forth from him, and who was often taken to be the sun.

occurrences.motif_label: tree-mediated transformation from grave to abundance to renewal
occurrences.basis: A tree associated with Shiro’s burial becomes a mortar that yields food; its burned remains become ashes that make trees bloom.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Shiro does not return; the wicked neighbor says he killed Shiro, and Shiro’s master learns the dog was buried under a yenoki tree.
The neighbor gives the tree to Shiro’s master, who cuts it down, carries it home, and makes a mortar from the trunk.
When rice is pounded in the mortar, it increases to about five times its original amount and cakes come out as if made by an invisible hand.
The old man asks for the ashes of the mortar to keep in remembrance of Shiro, and the neighbor gives him a basket of ashes.
In late autumn, ashes scattered on the garden trees make cherry trees, plum trees, and other flowering shrubs burst into bloom like spring.

The olive shoots are so close that wind, sun, and rain cannot get through them.

occurrences.motif_label: divinely endowed inexhaustible garden
occurrences.basis: The garden contains abundant trees, vines, flowers, and streams, with fruit and bloom continuing through all seasons and described as endowed by the gods.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The garden outside the outer court is walled, filled with pears, pomegranates, apples, figs, olives, a vineyard, and flower beds; its fruit and flowers are continuous through the year.
Two streams run through the grounds, one in ducts through the garden and one under the outer court to the house and townspeople; these are called splendours endowed by the gods for Alcinous's house.

occurrences.motif_label: heavenly river linking realms through divine release
occurrences.basis: Gangá moves from heaven to earth and into the underworld only after Śiva receives and releases her, and Brahmá names her Tripathagá, the stream of three paths.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Śiva tells Bhagiratha he is pleased and will fling the mountain-born river's waves upon his head.
Gangá hears the command, descends furiously, and intends to sweep Śiva away, but he catches and confines her in the tangles of his hair.
After Bhagiratha resumes penance, Śiva ends the river's long wandering and sends her down into Vindu's lake.
Seven rivers emerge from Gangá, six flowing east and west while the seventh follows Bhagiratha after first descending on Śiva's head.
Brahmá praises Bhagiratha, says the sons of Sagar have joined the blest, names the river Bhágirathí and Tripathagá, and instructs the king to complete his vow and libations.

occurrences.motif_label: abdication to child sovereign
occurrences.basis: Mikado and Tahitian examples both involve transfer of sovereignty from father to infant or newborn son.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Japanese Mikados are described as transferring supreme power to infant children; a Mikado abdicates to a three-year-old son, a usurper seizes sovereignty, and Yoritomo restores the Mikado's nominal power while retaining actual power and founding the Tycoon line.
Tahitian kings regularly abdicate at a son's birth; the son is proclaimed sovereign and receives the father's homage, perhaps to shift the burdensome restrictions of royalty.

occurrences.passage_locator: MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE. / CHAPTER III. KILLING THE GOD.; lines 5008-5083
occurrences.motif_label: royal son sacrificed for the people in crisis
occurrences.basis: The passage cites rulers giving beloved, only-begotten, eldest, or successor sons to die during national danger, siege, or war.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The king's son is described as the best representative of the king's divine character and therefore the most appropriate person to die for the king and people; this is linked to Semitic Western Asia and the Sacaean festival.
Philo of Byblus is cited: in crisis, a ruler gives his beloved son to die for the whole people as a ransom to avenging demons, and such children are slain with mystic rites.
Cronus, called Israel by the Phoenicians, is said to dress his only-begotten son Jeoud in royal robes and sacrifice him on an altar during wartime danger.
The King of Moab, besieged by Israelites, takes his eldest son and offers him as a burnt offering on the wall.

occurrences.motif_label: divine parent and reborn child
occurrences.basis: Zeus is father of Dionysus and, in some variants, raises him or begets him anew through Semele using Dionysus’s heart.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In the Cretan myth, Dionysus is the bastard son of Jupiter/Zeus, represented as a Cretan king, who transfers the throne and sceptre to Dionysus and entrusts him to guards.

Other versions describe Demeter reassembling Dionysus’s limbs and making him young again, Dionysus rising and ascending, Zeus raising him, Zeus swallowing the heart and begetting him afresh by Semele, or Semele conceiving him through a potion made from the heart.

occurrences.motif_label: Mother-daughter succession of annual corn
occurrences.basis: The passage explains the corn of this year giving rise to next year’s corn, with Proserpine of one year becoming Demeter of the next in an earlier form of the myth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage describes a Breton mother-sheaf, made from the last sheaf with a small corn-doll inside, as representing both the Corn-mother and the unborn Corn-daughter.

The passage explains the Prussian mother as ripe corn and the child as next year’s corn, then interprets Demeter as this year’s ripe corn and Proserpine as seed-corn sown in autumn and returning in spring; Proserpine’s descent is read as sowing and her return as sprouting.

The passage describes an earlier possible annual succession of corn beings and a later myth of two immortal beings: one disappears into and reappears from the ground, while the other mourns and rejoices over this cycle.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS; lines 5381-5418
occurrences.motif_label: conception by sun or divine light
occurrences.basis: The Sicilian princess conceives by the Sun; Danae conceives by Zeus as a shower of gold; the Kirgis maiden conceives when the eye of God falls on her; Frazer states that impregnation by the sun is found in legends.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In a Sicilian story, a seer foretells that a king's daughter will conceive by the Sun; the king encloses her in a windowless tower, but she makes a hole with a bone and a sunbeam enters and impregnates her.

Danae is confined by her father in a subterranean chamber or brazen tower, but Zeus reaches and impregnates her in the shape of a shower of gold; Frazer says this perhaps belongs to the same class of tales.

In the Kirgis ancestry legend, a Khan keeps his daughter in a dark iron house; an old woman shows her the bright world, the eye of God falls upon her and she conceives, and her father sends her floating over the sea in a golden chest.
Frazer states that the shower of gold and eye of God probably stand for sunlight and the sun, and that legends and marriage customs contain traces of women being impregnated by the sun.

The old man orders everyone to keep watch; Princess Moonlight says the measures will be useless when her people come and expresses sorrow at leaving her foster-parents.

The chief messenger says Princess Moonlight must return to the moon, had been sent to earth as punishment for a grave fault, and that the moon beings rewarded the bamboo-cutter by putting gold in the bamboos.

Hera sends a gadfly to torment Io; Io wanders until reaching Egypt, regains her form on the Nile, and gives birth to Epaphus, later king of Egypt and builder of Memphis.

Midas is identified as son of Cybele and Gordius, and Gordius is identified as the king who tied a celebrated intricate knot.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Athene is introduced as goddess of Wisdom and Armed Resistance; she issues from Zeus's head fully armed, and Olympus, earth, sea, and Helios respond to her advent.

Athene enters the assembly of the gods, becomes Zeus's counsellor, is described as his favourite child and counterpart, and receives prerogatives including thunderbolts, life extension, prophecy, and deputy authority.

occurrences.motif_label: Earth-mother goddess lineage and functional succession
occurrences.basis: Demeter is called earth-mother and daughter of Cronus and Rhea; the passage links and differentiates Gaea, Rhea, and Demeter as earth-goddesses with related powers.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Demeter, from Ge-meter, is identified as earth-mother, daughter of Cronus and Rhea, and goddess of vegetation, agriculture, field-fruits, plenty, and productiveness.
The passage says Gaea lost her ruling position with Uranus, yielded honour to Rhea, and is described in an old poem as retiring to a cavern in the earth and sitting in her daughter’s lap.
Gaea represents the whole earth and subterranean forces; Rhea represents productive vegetation; Demeter directs and utilizes Rhea’s powers through agriculture and later assumes Rhea’s functions.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Demeter, wife of Zeus, is mother of Persephone and is deeply attached to her.
Helios and Hecate hear Persephone's cries but cannot help; Demeter grieves and searches for nine days and nights with two torches lit from Mount Etna.

occurrences.basis: Demeter's grief over her daughter drives the famine and the demand for Persephone's restoration.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Celeus builds Demeter's temple; Demeter grieves, the earth becomes barren, Zeus sends Iris and others, and Demeter refuses grain until her daughter is restored.
Zeus sends Hermes to Aides; Hermes finds Persephone sorrowing beside Aides; Aides consents to release her and gives her pomegranate seeds, which she swallows.
Demeter and Persephone reunite; Aides claims anyone who ate in his realm must remain; Ascalaphus witnesses; Zeus arranges six months above and six months below.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THEMIS. / VESTA. / CERES. / APHRODITE (VENUS).; lines 1878-1983
occurrences.motif_label: Protective divine mother aiding wounded heroic child
occurrences.basis: Aphrodite is mother of Aeneas and comes to help him when he is wounded in battle, suffering injury herself.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Aphrodite is mother of Eros and Aeneas; when Aeneas is wounded, she helps him and is wounded while trying to save him.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CERES. / APHRODITE (VENUS). / VENUS. / HELIOS (SOL).; lines 1985-2069
occurrences.motif_label: divine parent-child lineage
occurrences.basis: The passage gives Helios' Titan parents and names his wife and children.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Helios, son of Hyperion and Theia, rises in the east preceded by Eos, drives a gold fiery chariot with fire-breathing steeds, descends toward the sea, is followed by Selene, and rests on a couch prepared by sea-nymphs.
Helios marries Perse, daughter of Oceanus; their children are Aetes, king of Colchis and possessor of the Golden Fleece, and Circe, a renowned sorceress.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CERES. / APHRODITE (VENUS). / VENUS. / HELIOS (SOL).; lines 2071-2157
occurrences.motif_label: challenged divine paternity and quest for proof
occurrences.basis: Phaethon's claim to be Helios' son is challenged, leading him to seek confirmation from Clymene and then Helios.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Phaethon, son of Helios and Clymene, is favored by Aphrodite; Epaphus challenges his claim that Helios is his father.
Clymene points to the shining sun as Phaethon's father and tells him to visit Helios' radiant dwelling if he doubts.
At Helios' dazzling palace, Phaethon approaches the sun-god, who removes his crown of rays and swears by the Styx to grant a favor.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: APHRODITE (VENUS). / VENUS. / HELIOS (SOL). / EOS (AURORA).; lines 2159-2198
occurrences.motif_label: Divine genealogy of star and winds
occurrences.basis: Eos and Astraeus are named as parents of the evening star and the winds.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Eos first marries the Titan Astraeus; their children are Heosphorus or Hesperus, the evening star, and the winds.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VENUS. / HELIOS (SOL). / EOS (AURORA). / PHOEBUS-APOLLO.; lines 2200-2277
occurrences.motif_label: Divine child announces father’s will
occurrences.basis: Apollo is son of Zeus and declares that he will announce Zeus’s will to mankind through oracles.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Apollo is son of Zeus and Leto, born beneath a palm at Mount Cynthus on Delos; earth smiles, Delos flowers, swans gather, and nymphs sing.

evidence.locator: lines 2200-2277; Apollo passage, declaration and Olympus paragraph
evidence.quote_or_summary: Apollo requests a lyre and bow, says he will foretell the future in oracles and announce Zeus’s will, then ascends to Olympus and is welcomed by the gods.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VENUS. / HELIOS (SOL). / EOS (AURORA). / PHOEBUS-APOLLO.; lines 2279-2363
occurrences.motif_label: son fulfilling the will of the father
occurrences.basis: Apollo desires to interpret to mankind the will of his mighty father.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After taking his place among the immortals, Apollo descends to earth to interpret his father's will and travels through many countries seeking an oracle site.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VENUS. / HELIOS (SOL). / EOS (AURORA). / PHOEBUS-APOLLO.; lines 2441-2527
occurrences.motif_label: divine parent avenges slain child and is punished
occurrences.basis: Apollo, angered by the death of his son Asclepius, destroys the Cyclops and is punished by Zeus with loss of status and servitude.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Apollo destroys the Cyclops who forged the fatal thunderbolts; Zeus, after Leto's intercession, mitigates punishment to loss of power and dignity and nine years' servitude as Admetus' shepherd.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VENUS. / HELIOS (SOL). / EOS (AURORA). / PHOEBUS-APOLLO.; lines 2529-2596
occurrences.motif_label: divine children avenge their mother
occurrences.basis: Apollo calls on Artemis to help avenge the insult offered to their mother Leto.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Niobe, daughter of Tantalus and wife of Amphion, boasts of seven sons and seven daughters, ridicules Leto’s worship, and asks Thebans to honor her instead.
Apollo and Artemis avenge the insult to Leto with invisible arrows; Apollo kills the sons and Artemis kills the daughters, including the youngest after Niobe begs for one child to be spared.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: HECATE. / SELENE (LUNA). / ARTEMIS (DIANA). / ARCADIAN ARTEMIS.; lines 2782-2879
occurrences.motif_label: divine parent and child genealogy
occurrences.basis: Artemis is identified as the daughter of Zeus and Leto.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Arcadian Artemis is identified as daughter of Zeus and Leto and twin-sister of Apollo.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CONTENTS. / MYTHS AND LEGENDS OF ANCIENT GREECE AND ROME. / PART I.--MYTHS. / INTRODUCTION.; lines 305-397
occurrences.motif_label: Divine-mortal union producing heroes
occurrences.basis: The passage states that gods and goddesses become attached to mortals, unite with them, and produce heroes or demi-gods.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The gods have higher mental qualities but human passions, punish evil-doers and impious mortals, visit mankind, unite with mortals, produce heroes or demi-gods, and remain immortal though not invulnerable.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: BRAURONIAN ARTEMIS. / SELENE-ARTEMIS. / DIANA. / HEPHAESTUS (VULCAN).; lines 3109-3194
occurrences.motif_label: Cast-down divine child marked by injury
occurrences.basis: Zeus, Hephaestus's father, hurls him from heaven after he supports Hera; the fall ends on Lemnos and leaves him lame.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hephaestus is introduced as son of Zeus and Hera, god of beneficial fire, workmanship, mechanical arts, and hearth; he is deformed and lame after Zeus hurls him from heaven to Lemnos, where the Lemnians receive him and he later teaches metalwork and useful arts.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: POSEIDON (NEPTUNE). / NEPTUNE. / SEA DIVINITIES. / OCEANUS.; lines 3400-3425
occurrences.motif_label: divine genealogy of primordial water being
occurrences.basis: Oceanus is son of Uranus and Gaea and father of the Oceanides by Tethys.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Oceanus was son of Uranus and Gaea.
Oceanus was married to Tethys, one of the Titans, and fathered the Oceanides, said to be three thousand.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: NEPTUNE. / SEA DIVINITIES. / OCEANUS. / NEREUS.; lines 3427-3436
occurrences.motif_label: Divine parent with many daughters in an undersea dwelling
occurrences.basis: Nereus dwells beneath the waves with Doris and their fifty daughters, the Nereides.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Nereus dwells beneath the waves in a beautiful grotto-palace with Doris and their fifty daughters, the Nereides.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: SEA DIVINITIES. / OCEANUS. / NEREUS. / PROTEUS.; lines 3438-3467
occurrences.motif_label: divine parent and sea-divinity offspring
occurrences.basis: Proteus is called a son of Poseidon, and Triton is called the son of Poseidon and Amphitrite.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Proteus, known as the Old Man of the Sea, is a son of Poseidon, has prophetic power, and resists being consulted as a seer.
Triton is described as the only son of Poseidon and Amphitrite and as a minor divinity with little influence.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: NEREUS. / PROTEUS. / GLAUCUS. / THETIS.; lines 3489-3545
occurrences.motif_label: prophecy that a child will surpass the father
occurrences.basis: Zeus and Poseidon abandon courtship of Thetis because it was foretold that her son would gain supremacy over his father.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Thetis is silver-footed and fair-haired, daughter of Nereus or Poseidon; Zeus and Poseidon seek alliance with her but withdraw because her son is foretold to surpass his father; she becomes wife of Peleus.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: NEREUS. / PROTEUS. / GLAUCUS. / THETIS.; lines 3489-3545
occurrences.motif_label: mother-goddess intervention for heroic son
occurrences.basis: Thetis retains influence over the lord of heaven and uses it on behalf of her son Achilles in the Trojan War.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Thetis retains influence over the lord of heaven and uses it in favor of Achilles during the Trojan War.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THETIS. / LEUCOTHEA. / THE SIRENS. / ARES (MARS).; lines 3568-3630
occurrences.motif_label: divine parent and warlike child
occurrences.basis: Ares is explicitly the son of Zeus and Hera, and Zeus’ rebuke frames his violent nature in relation to his parents.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ares is the son of Zeus and Hera and the god of war, delighting in strife, battlefield havoc, slaughter, and extermination.
Zeus says Ares is “of all the gods of Olympus most hateful to me” and delights only in war and strife.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: LEUCOTHEA. / THE SIRENS. / ARES (MARS). / MARS.; lines 3632-3714
occurrences.motif_label: Divine father of city founders
occurrences.basis: Mars is said to be father of Romulus and Remus, founders of Rome, making divine parentage part of civic origin and legitimacy.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Early Italian tribes regarded the deity as spring and agricultural; Romans made him a chief war god, protector, and father of Romulus and Remus.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE SIRENS. / ARES (MARS). / MARS. / NIKE (VICTORIA).; lines 3716-3733
occurrences.motif_label: divine parent-child lineage
occurrences.basis: Nike is described as the daughter of Pallas and Styx.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Nike/Victoria is identified as the goddess of victory and daughter of the Titan Pallas and Styx, nymph of the lower-world river.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VICTORIA. / HERMES (MERCURY). / MERCURY. / DIONYSUS (BACCHUS).; lines 3954-4041
occurrences.motif_label: divine parent and endangered child
occurrences.basis: Dionysus is the son of Zeus and Semele, is rescued by Zeus from Semele's flames, and is moved through caregivers for safety.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Dionysus is son of Zeus and Semele; Zeus snatches him from the flames that kill Semele; Hermes carries him to Ino; Hera's vengeance makes him unsafe; nymphs of Mount Nysa and Silenus care for him.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VICTORIA. / HERMES (MERCURY). / MERCURY. / DIONYSUS (BACCHUS).; lines 4043-4125
occurrences.motif_label: Descent to the shades to recover a parent
occurrences.basis: Dionysus descends to the realm of shades for his mother and conducts her to Olympus, where she is admitted among the immortal gods.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Dionysus descends to the realm of shades to find his mother and brings her to Olympus, where as Thyone she joins the immortal gods.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: PART I.--MYTHS. / INTRODUCTION. / ORIGIN OF THE WORLD.--FIRST DYNASTY. / URANUS AND GAEA. (COELUS AND TERRA.); lines 436-525
occurrences.motif_label: divine parent-child cosmogony
occurrences.basis: Many cosmic beings and groups are presented as children of Uranus, Gaea, Pontus, Nyx, Erebus, or Chaos.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Oceanus is the first-born child of Uranus and Gaea, described as the ever-flowing ocean stream encircling the earth and produced by the combined influence of heaven and earth.
Aether, Aer, and the Nephelae are described as beings occupying the intermediate space between Uranus and Gaea, with the Nephelae existing as clouds between the two atmospheres.
Gaea produces the mountains and Pontus, then unites with Pontus; their offspring are the sea-deities Nereus, Thaumas, Phorcys, Ceto, and Eurybia.
Erebus and Nyx are described as offspring of Chaos; Erebus is Darkness ruling a lower world without daylight, and Nyx represents Night.
Uranus is united with Nyx as god of light, producing Eos and Hemera; Nyx is also married to Erebus.
Uranus and Gaea produce Giants and Titans; the Giants include Briareus, Cottus, and Gyges, each with one hundred hands and fifty heads, able to shake the universe and cause earthquakes.
The Titans are twelve: Oceanus, Ceos, Crios, Hyperion, Iapetus, Cronus, Theia, Rhea, Themis, Mnemosyne, Phoebe, and Tethys.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: BACCHUS OR LIBER. / AIDES (PLUTO). / PLUTO. / PLUTUS.; lines 4365-4377
occurrences.motif_label: divine child of goddess and mortal
occurrences.basis: Plutus is described as the son of Demeter and the mortal Iasion.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Plutus is described as son of Demeter and the mortal Iasion, and as god of wealth.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: NEMESIS. / NYX (NOX). / THANATOS (MORS) AND HYPNUS (SOMNUS). / MORPHEUS.; lines 4603-4614
occurrences.motif_label: Divine parent-child relation
occurrences.basis: Morpheus is explicitly described as the son of Hypnus.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “Morpheus, the son of Hypnus, was the god of Dreams.”

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: EROS (CUPID, AMOR) AND PSYCHE. / HYMEN. / IRIS (THE RAINBOW). / HEBE (JUVENTAS).; lines 5009-5031
occurrences.motif_label: divine parent-child relationship
occurrences.basis: Hebe is explicitly described as daughter of Zeus and Hera.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hebe is daughter of Zeus and Hera and is represented as cup-bearer to the gods despite her distinguished rank.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: HEBE (JUVENTAS). / JUVENTAS. / GANYMEDES. / THE MUSES.; lines 5052-5157
occurrences.motif_label: Divine parent-child origin of specialized deities
occurrences.basis: The Muses are daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne, and Zeus creates them to commemorate Olympian deeds.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Muses are introduced as nine daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne; their functions begin with music, song, and dance and later include arts and sciences such as poetry and astronomy.
Zeus is said to create the Muses after the Titan war in response to a request for divinities who would commemorate the Olympian gods' deeds in song.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE MUSES. / PEGASUS. / THE HESPERIDES. / CHARITES (GRATIAE) GRACES.; lines 5205-5246
occurrences.motif_label: Divine parent-child genealogy
occurrences.basis: The Graces are described as daughters of Zeus and Eurynome, with an alternate later genealogy from Dionysus and Aphrodite.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Graces are described as three lovely sisters named Euphrosyne, Aglaia, and Thalia, daughters of Zeus and Eurynome, or in later accounts of Dionysus and Aphrodite; they personify gentle refining attributes.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: PART I.--MYTHS. / INTRODUCTION. / ORIGIN OF THE WORLD.--FIRST DYNASTY. / URANUS AND GAEA. (COELUS AND TERRA.); lines 527-547
occurrences.motif_label: divine parent-child conflict and succession
occurrences.basis: Uranus imprisons his offspring; Cronus wounds and dethrones his father; Uranus predicts Cronus will suffer a similar fate.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Uranus, described as the chaste light of heaven, abhors his crude and turbulent Giant offspring and fears their power may harm him.
“He therefore hurled them into Tartarus, that portion of the lower world which served as the subterranean dungeon of the gods.”
Cronus wounds his father Uranus.
With help from his brother-Titans, Cronus dethrones Uranus.
Uranus, enraged by defeat, curses Cronus and foretells that he will suffer a similar fate.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: DRYADES, OR TREE NYMPHS. / NYMPHS OF THE VALLEYS AND MOUNTAINS. / NAPAEAE AND OREADES. / THE WINDS.; lines 5469-5497
occurrences.motif_label: children born from union of wind divinity and abducted bride
occurrences.basis: Boreas and Oreithyia are parents of Zetes and Calais, later famous in the Argonaut expedition.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Boreas and Oreithyia are parents of Zetes and Calais, later famous in the Argonaut expedition.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: ORIGIN OF THE WORLD.--FIRST DYNASTY. / URANUS AND GAEA. (COELUS AND TERRA.) / SECOND DYNASTY. / CRONUS (SATURN).; lines 549-631
occurrences.motif_label: threatened divine child hidden from devouring father
occurrences.basis: Cronus swallows his children to avert a prophecy, but Zeus is saved by a substitution and hidden in Crete until he can challenge his father.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Cronus fears his children may rise against his authority and swallows each child as soon as it is born.

evidence.locator: lines 549-631, Rhea's substitution of the stone
evidence.quote_or_summary: Rhea appeals to Uranus and Gaea, wraps a stone in baby-clothes, and Cronus swallows it without noticing the deception.
Zeus is secretly sent to Crete, where Amalthea gives him milk, the Melissae feed him honey, and eagles and doves bring nectar and ambrosia.
Zeus is concealed in a cave in Mount Ida, and the Curetes beat shields at the entrance to hide his cries and repel intruders.
Cronus's army is overthrown, his brothers are sent to the lower world, Cronus is banished, and supreme power passes to Zeus; the war is called the Titanomachia.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: ORIGIN OF THE WORLD.--FIRST DYNASTY. / URANUS AND GAEA. (COELUS AND TERRA.) / SECOND DYNASTY. / CRONUS (SATURN).; lines 549-631
occurrences.motif_label: restoration of swallowed siblings
occurrences.basis: Metis's potion causes Cronus to give back the children he swallowed, restoring them to the light of day.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Cronus fears his children may rise against his authority and swallows each child as soon as it is born.
Zeus grows to manhood and, aided by Metis, causes Cronus to drink a potion that makes him give back the swallowed children; the stone is placed at Delphi as a relic.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: ORIGIN OF THE WORLD.--FIRST DYNASTY. / URANUS AND GAEA. (COELUS AND TERRA.) / SECOND DYNASTY. / CRONUS (SATURN).; lines 549-631
occurrences.motif_label: divine succession war
occurrences.basis: War breaks out between father and son; Zeus defeats Cronus and receives supreme power as successor.

evidence.locator: lines 549-631, armies on Olympus and Othrys
evidence.quote_or_summary: War begins between Cronus and Zeus; Zeus's forces stand on Mount Olympus, while Cronus and his brother-Titans occupy Mount Othrys.
Zeus liberates imprisoned Giants and calls the Cyclops; the Cyclops bring thunderbolts, and the Hecatoncheires hurl them and raise earthquakes.
The battle is marked by towering sea, shaking earth, thunder, lightning, and mist enveloping Cronus and his allies.
Cronus's army is overthrown, his brothers are sent to the lower world, Cronus is banished, and supreme power passes to Zeus; the war is called the Titanomachia.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: NYMPHS OF THE VALLEYS AND MOUNTAINS. / NAPAEAE AND OREADES. / THE WINDS. / PAN (FAUNUS).; lines 5499-5583
occurrences.motif_label: divine parent-child birth with unusual infant form
occurrences.basis: Pan is born as the son of Hermes and a wood nymph, with extraordinary goat-like features that cause his mother to flee.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Pan is called the son of Hermes and a wood nymph and is born with horns and goat-like features; his mother flees at his appearance.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: PAN (FAUNUS). / FAUNUS. / THE SATYRS. / PRIAPUS.; lines 5635-5659
occurrences.motif_label: Divine child exposed and rescued
occurrences.basis: Priapus is the child of Dionysus and Aphrodite; after rejection and exposure on the mountains, he is found and saved by shepherds.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Priapus is named as son of Dionysus and Aphrodite and described as god of fruitfulness and protector of flocks, bees, vines, and garden produce.
Hera punishes Aphrodite by sending her a misshapen son; Aphrodite orders the child exposed on the mountains, where shepherds find him, pity him, and save his life.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: FAUNUS. / THE SATYRS. / PRIAPUS. / ASCLEPIAS (AESCULAPIUS).; lines 5661-5710
occurrences.motif_label: divine parent and gifted child
occurrences.basis: Asclepias is explicitly described as the son of Apollo and Coronis and as possessing exceptional healing abilities.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Asclepias is named as god of healing, son of Apollo and Coronis, and pupil of Chiron, who especially taught him the properties of herbs.
Asclepias discovers cures, perfects healing so that he wards off death and restores the dead to life, and is popularly believed to be aided by Medusa's blood given by Pallas-Athene.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: LIBITINA. / LAVERNA. / COMUS. / THE CAMENAE.; lines 5955-5976
occurrences.motif_label: Divine or nymphic mother of a civilizing founder
occurrences.basis: Carmenta is a prophetic nymph and is celebrated as mother of Evander, who founds a settlement and introduces Greek civilization and worship.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Camenae were prophetic nymphs venerated by ancient Italians; they were four in number, with Carmenta and Egeria the best known.
Carmenta was celebrated as mother of Evander, who led an Arcadian colony into Italy and founded a town on the river Tiber later incorporated with Rome.
Evander is said to have been the first to introduce Greek art, civilization, Greek divinities, and their worship into Italy.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VESTALIA. / PART II.--LEGENDS. / CADMUS. / PERSEUS.; lines 6633-6734
occurrences.motif_label: divine father and threatened child
occurrences.basis: Perseus is born from Zeus and Danae, while Acrisius acts against him because an oracle foretells danger from Danae's son.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Perseus is introduced as son of Zeus and Danae; an oracle warns Acrisius about Danae's son, Acrisius confines her in a brass tower, and Zeus descends as a shower of gold.

Acrisius hears the child, discovers Danae's union with Zeus, orders mother and child placed in a chest and thrown into the sea; Zeus has Poseidon calm the water and the chest reaches Seriphus, where Dictys rescues them.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VESTALIA. / PART II.--LEGENDS. / CADMUS. / PERSEUS.; lines 6736-6832
occurrences.motif_label: Exposed divine child rescued and raised in sanctuary
occurrences.basis: Ion is the child of Creusa and Apollo; he is placed in a wicker basket, hidden in a cave, carried by Hermes to Delphi, and raised by the priestess.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ion is introduced as the son of Creusa, daughter of Erechtheus, and the sun-god Phoebus-Apollo, with the union unknown to Creusa's father.

Creusa fears Erechtheus' anger, places the newborn in a wicker basket with golden charms, invokes divine protection, and hides him in a cave; Apollo sends Hermes to bring him to Delphi, where the priestess adopts and raises him in temple service.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VESTALIA. / PART II.--LEGENDS. / CADMUS. / PERSEUS.; lines 6736-6832
occurrences.motif_label: Oracle assigns unexpected son
occurrences.basis: Xuthus is told by the oracle to accept the first person he meets as his son and finds Ion, who is actually Apollo's child.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ion is introduced as the son of Creusa, daughter of Erechtheus, and the sun-god Phoebus-Apollo, with the union unknown to Creusa's father.

Xuthus marries Creusa, the childless couple consults the Delphic oracle, and Xuthus is told to accept the first person he meets as his son; he meets Ion and welcomes him, while Creusa suspects a secret marriage and grieves.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VESTALIA. / PART II.--LEGENDS. / CADMUS. / PERSEUS.; lines 6834-6902
occurrences.motif_label: divine-origin child reconciled with mortal mother
occurrences.basis: Creusa reveals Ion's divine origin after priestly intervention establishes their mother-son relationship.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Apollo's intervention brings the Delphic priestess, who explains the relationship between Ion and Creusa and produces infant charms and a wicker basket.
Creusa and Ion are reconciled; Creusa reveals his divine origin, and the priestess predicts Ion as father of the Ionians and Dorus as progenitor of the Dorians.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE. / PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES).; lines 7587-7685
occurrences.motif_label: divine parent and heroic child
occurrences.basis: The passage identifies Heracles as the son of Zeus and Alcmene, and later has Tiresias confirm his divine origin.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Heracles is introduced as the renowned hero, son of Zeus and Alcmene, great-grandson of Perseus, and born at Thebes in Amphitryon's palace.
Amphitryon sees the dead reptiles in Heracles' hands, calls the child a gift from Zeus, consults Tiresias, and hears of his divine origin and great future.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Zeus is introduced as presiding deity of the universe, ruler of heaven and earth, and father of gods and men.
As father of the gods, Zeus ensures divine duties, punishes misdeeds, settles disputes, and acts as counsellor and friend.
As father of men, Zeus watches over mortals, rewards virtues, punishes perjury, cruelty, and inhospitality, and advocates for distressed wanderers.

occurrences.basis: Helen is identified as daughter of Zeus and Leda and as the wife whose abduction drives the episode.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Paris arrives in Greece and sees Helen, daughter of Zeus and Leda and wife of Menelaus; her former suitors had sworn to defend the successful husband in future feuds connected with the marriage.
After Menelaus leaves for a hunting expedition, Paris resolves to rob his host of Helen, storms the royal castle with followers, seizes treasures, and carries her off.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Achilles is son of Peleus and Thetis; Thetis dips him in the Styx, leaving only his right heel vulnerable, and later hides him on Scyros after a prophecy about his fate.

occurrences.basis: Achilles calls on his divine mother Thetis, who comforts him and promises to entreat Zeus on his behalf; she later secures new armor for him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Achilles prays at the sea-shore; Thetis emerges from the waves and promises to ask Zeus to avenge him by giving victory to the Trojans.
Achilles returns from apathy, reconciles with Agamemnon, rejoins the Greek army, and receives new armor forged by Hephaestus at Thetis' request.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Memnon, the Aethiopian son of Eos and Tithonus, arrives as a Trojan ally with reinforcements and is described as an equal opponent to Achilles because he too is son of a goddess and has armor made by Hephaestus.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Thetis and Eos hasten to Olympus to intercede for their sons; Zeus refuses to oppose the Moirae, weighs the heroes' fates in golden scales, and Memnon's fate sinks, portending death.
Eos leaves Olympus in despair, sees Memnon's body on the battlefield, and commands her children the Winds to carry it through the air away from enemy desecration.
Ajax and Odysseus recover Achilles' body; Thetis mourns him; a funeral pyre is lit, the Muses chant, and Achilles' bones are put in a golden urn beside Patroclus.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Aeneas, son of Aphrodite, escapes with his son and father Anchises, carries Anchises on his shoulders, goes to Mount Ida and then Italy, and becomes ancestor-hero of the Romans.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odin disguises himself as a Wanderer named Gangrad; he and Vafthrudnir exchange questions about cosmic and divine matters, and Vafthrudnir recognizes Odin when asked what Allfather whispered to Balder on the funeral pyre.
The passage says the myth ends without saying whether Odin slew his rival or what the final answer was; it reports that some mythologists suggested the whispered word was 'resurrection.'

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odin watches King Hrauding's sons Geirrod and Agnar; a storm drives their fishing boat to an island where Odin and Frigga, disguised as an old couple, shelter them through winter. Odin favors Geirrod and teaches arms; Frigga favors Agnar.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odin is treated as heaven and spouse of earth figures: Jörd bears Thor, Frigga bears Balder, Hermod, and perhaps Tyr, and Rinda bears Vali.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Thor's variant parentage is given; he shows great size and strength soon after birth; after dangerous rages he is sent to Vingnir and Hlora, who raise and control him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Thor's wives and children are named; Magni and Modi will survive Thor and the twilight of the gods and rule the new world.

occurrences.basis: Magni, while only three days or three years old in variant accounts, frees Thor unaided and is treated as evidence that divine descendants will surpass their elders.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Magni, Thor's very young son, lifts the giant's foot from Thor; the gods read this as proof that descendants will surpass and survive them.

occurrences.basis: Bragi is named as Odin’s son and Gunlod’s child, receives the harp, sings, and becomes god of poetry and music.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Bragi, child of Odin and Gunlod, is born in the cave; dwarfs give him a magical golden harp and send him out on a vessel; after showing no signs of life, he sits up and sings the song of life while his song reaches heaven and Hel’s realm.
Bragi wins Idun as wife; they go to Asgard, where Odin traces runes on Bragi’s tongue and decrees him heavenly minstrel and composer of songs for gods and heroes.

occurrences.basis: Dag is born to Night and Dellinger and is equipped by the gods to bring light through a chariot and shining steed.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Night has children through Naglfari, Annar, and Dellinger; Dag is born radiant and given a chariot drawn by Skin-faxi, whose mane lights the world.

occurrences.motif_label: Divine mother mourning a heroic son
occurrences.basis: Achilles’ mother comes from the sea with immortal nymphs to view and mourn her son’s body, later supplying burial honours.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Achilles’ mother comes from the sea with immortal nymphs, causing fear among the Achaeans until Nestor explains who has arrived.
After the flames, Achilles’ bones are gathered with ointments and wine; Thetis brings a golden vase, gift of Bacchus and work of Vulcan, in which Achilles’ bones are mingled with Patroclus’.

The Argives build a noble tomb over the Hellespont; Thetis offers divine prizes for contests, and Agamemnon says Achilles’ fame and name endure, while his own return ended in destruction by Aegisthus and his wife.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey

occurrences.motif_label: divine helper enables hero's journey
occurrences.basis: Minerva assists Telemachus by recruiting the crew, obtaining and preparing the ship, inducing sleep in hostile suitors, summoning him, and sending wind.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva takes Telemachus's shape, summons crewmen to meet at the ship by sundown, and asks Noemon son of Phronius for a ship, which he gives readily.
After sunset and darkness, Minerva puts the ship in the water, equips it, places it at the harbour, and encourages the crew when they arrive.
Minerva enters Ulysses's house, throws the suitors into deep slumber, fuddles their drink, makes cups fall from their hands, and sends them to town to sleep.
Minerva takes Mentor's form and voice, calls Telemachus outside, and tells him the men are aboard and waiting for orders.
The men loose the hawsers and take benches; Minerva sends a fair west wind; Telemachus orders the sail hoisted, and the ship speeds through deep blue water with foam at the bows.

occurrences.motif_label: divine parent and child genealogy
occurrences.basis: Polyphemus is explicitly identified as a son of Neptune, and kinship relations are inferred from that divine parentage.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Polyphemus is described as a son of Neptune and therefore half brother to Nausithous, half uncle to King Alcinous, and half great uncle to Nausicaa.

occurrences.motif_label: young seeker departs to learn absent father's fate
occurrences.basis: Telemachus has taken a voyage and states he seeks news of his absent father Ulysses, whose fate is unknown.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva tells Telemachus not to be shy, because he has taken the voyage to learn where his father is buried and how he came to his end, and tells him to ask Nestor for the truth.
Telemachus tells Nestor they come from Ithaca and that he seeks news of his father Ulysses, who is said to have sacked Troy with Nestor; Ulysses's fate is hidden.
Telemachus says no one can certify where Ulysses perished, whether on land or at sea, and asks Nestor as a suppliant to tell plainly what he saw or heard.

occurrences.motif_label: divine ancestry of a ruling house
occurrences.basis: Alcinous and Arete are linked genealogically to Neptune through Nausithous, and Alcinous rules the Phaeacians.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva points out the house, tells Ulysses to seek Arete, recounts the descent of Alcinous and Arete from Neptune, describes Arete's exceptional honor, and says her goodwill may enable Ulysses' return home.

occurrences.passage_locator: PREFACE TO SECOND EDITION / HENRY FESTING JONES. / THE ODYSSEY / BOOK I; lines 390-492
occurrences.motif_label: son prompted to seek father and public standing
occurrences.basis: Minerva plans to embolden Telemachus, Ulysses' son, to address the suitors and travel for news of his father, which will improve his reputation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva proposes sending Mercury to Ogygia to announce the decision to Calypso, while she goes to Ithaca to strengthen Telemachus, confront the suitors, and send him to Sparta and Pylos for news of Ulysses.

occurrences.motif_label: Divine parent invoked by injured child
occurrences.basis: Polyphemus states that Neptune is his father and prays to him after being blinded.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Polyphemus says, “Neptune and I are father and son,” and says Neptune may heal him if he wills.

Polyphemus raises his hands to heaven and prays to Neptune that Ulysses may never reach home alive, or may return late, in distress, after losing all his men, in another man's ship, and find trouble at home.

occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE. / BOOK XI / THE VISIT TO THE DEAD.88; lines 4969-5068
occurrences.motif_label: divine-human union producing notable offspring
occurrences.basis: Tyro and Neptune, Antiope and Jove, Alcmena and Jove, and Iphimedeia and Neptune are each linked to divine embrace and notable children.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Tyro, daughter of Salmoneus and wife of Cretheus, loves the river Enipeus; Neptune disguises himself as her lover, meets her at the river mouth beneath a great blue wave, reveals himself, foretells twins, and orders secrecy.
Neptune dives under the sea; Tyro bears Pelias and Neleus, while her other children by Cretheus are Aeson, Pheres, and Amythaon.
Antiope, daughter of Asopus, is said to have slept with Jove and borne Amphion and Zethus, who founded and walled seven-gated Thebes.
Alcmena, wife of Amphitryon, bears Hercules to Jove; Megara, daughter of Creon, is named as wife of Amphitryon's son.

Iphimedeia, wife of Aloeus, boasts of Neptune's embrace and bears Otus and Ephialtes; the giant youths threaten Olympus and try to pile Ossa on Olympus and Pelion on Ossa to scale heaven, but Apollo kills them before maturity.

occurrences.motif_label: sacred or heroic twins
occurrences.basis: Tyro is told she will bear twins, Pelias and Neleus; Leda bears the paired Castor and Pollux; Iphimedeia bears the paired Otus and Ephialtes.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Tyro, daughter of Salmoneus and wife of Cretheus, loves the river Enipeus; Neptune disguises himself as her lover, meets her at the river mouth beneath a great blue wave, reveals himself, foretells twins, and orders secrecy.
Neptune dives under the sea; Tyro bears Pelias and Neleus, while her other children by Cretheus are Aeson, Pheres, and Amythaon.
Leda, wife of Tyndarus, bears Castor and Pollux; they lie under the earth yet live, dying and coming to life again on alternate days by Jove's dispensation, and they have divine rank.

Iphimedeia, wife of Aloeus, boasts of Neptune's embrace and bears Otus and Ephialtes; the giant youths threaten Olympus and try to pile Ossa on Olympus and Pelion on Ossa to scale heaven, but Apollo kills them before maturity.

occurrences.motif_label: divine favor marks a mortal before the community
occurrences.basis: Minerva gives Telemachus divine-looking comeliness so that the people marvel at him before he speaks in the assembly.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva gives Telemachus divine comeliness; people marvel, and he takes his father’s seat while the oldest councillors make way.

occurrences.motif_label: father and son join in armed restoration of household
occurrences.basis: Telemachus kills an attacker, stands at his father's side, fetches armor, and arms himself and the loyal servants near Ulysses.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Amphinomus attacks Ulysses at the door, and Telemachus strikes him from behind with a spear before returning to his father's side.
Telemachus asks to bring armor, fetches four shields, eight spears, and four brass helmets, and arms himself, the swineherd, and the stockman near Ulysses.

occurrences.motif_label: divine offspring praise formula
occurrences.basis: A quoted verse calls Glaucon and Adeimantus 'Sons of Ariston' and 'divine offspring of an illustrious hero.'

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says, 'Sons of an illustrious father,' and quotes: 'Sons of Ariston... divine offspring of an illustrious hero.'

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 11286-11457
occurrences.motif_label: divine parent-child succession violence
occurrences.basis: The cited Hesiodic material involves Uranus, Cronus's retaliation, and sufferings inflicted on Cronus by his son.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage names Hesiod's stories of Uranus, Cronus, and the suffering Cronus's son inflicted on him, and says such stories should be silenced or restricted to a chosen few in a mystery with an extraordinary victim rather than a common Eleusinian pig.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III.; lines 12131-12273
occurrences.motif_label: Divine-born hero constrained by moral theology
occurrences.basis: The passage discusses heroes identified as children or descendants of gods and argues that poets must not portray them as committing impious and dreadful acts while also calling them divine offspring.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker rejects allegations that Achilles challenged a river-god, offered dedicated hair to dead Patroclus, dragged Hector around Patroclus' tomb, and slaughtered captives at the pyre; Achilles is described as Cheiron's pupil, son of a goddess and Peleus, and descended from Zeus.

The speaker says tales of Theseus son of Poseidon or Peirithous son of Zeus committing rape should not be believed or repeated, and poets must say either the acts were not done or the actors were not sons of gods.
"We will not have them trying to persuade our youth that the gods are the authors of evil, and that heroes are no better than men"

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II. / BOOK III.; lines 13084-13196
occurrences.motif_label: divine healer as child of a god
occurrences.basis: The passage reports that Asclepius is acknowledged as son of Apollo and uses that relation in Socrates’ reasoning about his character.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Tragedians and Pindar are reported as saying Asclepius was son of Apollo, accepted a bribe to heal a rich dying man, and was struck by lightning; Socrates rejects believing both divine sonship and avarice.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1336-1415
occurrences.motif_label: Divine parent-child conflict
occurrences.basis: The passage cites stories of Zeus as an example for beating fathers and of Hephaestus binding his mother and being thrown by Zeus.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Homer and Hesiod are criticized for improper divine stories about Uranus and Saturn, Zeus, Hephaestus, divine strife, and family violence; such stories may have mystical interpretation but youth cannot understand allegory.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1417-1481
occurrences.motif_label: divine parent-child behavior
occurrences.basis: The passage cites the behavior of Zeus toward his father and of Hephaestus toward his mother as examples with serious meaning.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage lists humorous but serious examples: Glaucon's disappointment at the 'city of pigs,' the guardian illustrated by the dog, an almost unprocurable victim for impure mysteries, and the behavior of Zeus to his father and Hephaestus to his mother.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1543-1614
occurrences.motif_label: questioned divine parentage of heroes
occurrences.basis: The passage says the so-called sons of gods were either not sons of gods or were not as poets imagine them.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The amatory exploits of Peirithous and Theseus are called unworthy; the passage says either such sons of gods were not sons of gods or were not as poets imagined, and that gods are not authors of evil.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 18438-18615
occurrences.motif_label: supreme source and child in likeness
occurrences.basis: The good is said to be the parent that begets the sun, its child, in its own likeness.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Glaucon urges Socrates not to turn away from the goal; Socrates says they should not now ask the actual nature of the good, but he may speak of its child, while Glaucon says the account of the parent can remain owed.

Socrates calls the sun the child of the good, begotten in the good's likeness, and says it stands in the visible world to sight and things of sight as the good stands in the intellectual world to mind and things of mind.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 4687-4772
occurrences.motif_label: people as parent overpowered by monstrous son
occurrences.basis: The demus is called the tyrant's father, and the tyrant is a monstrous, unnatural son who beats and disarms that father.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The father is identified as the demus; the parent learns it has nurtured a monster, and the son is said to disarm and beat his father, becoming a parricide and unnatural son.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 6746-6822
occurrences.motif_label: Divine valuation of the vulnerable
occurrences.basis: The passage says the individual has endless value in the sight of God and cites Christ’s parable about angels beholding the Father in heaven while discussing regard for the weakest persons.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says modern readers recoil from the ideal, values regard for the weakest human beings as a noble result of Christianity, affirms the individual’s value in the sight of God, and cites Christ’s parable about angels beholding the Father in heaven.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 1355-1438
occurrences.motif_label: divine parentage distinguishing sacred status
occurrences.basis: The two Aphrodites are differentiated by divine parentage: heavenly Aphrodite as daughter of Uranus without a mother, and common Aphrodite as daughter of Zeus and Dione.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Pausanias says Love is inseparable from Aphrodite; there are two Aphrodites and therefore two Loves: heavenly Aphrodite, daughter of Uranus with no mother, and common Aphrodite, daughter of Zeus and Dione.

occurrences.source_title: Persian Literature, Volume 1

occurrences.motif_label: exposed_child_protected_by_wonder_bird
occurrences.basis: A child marked by an unusual bodily sign is rejected by humans but rescued and nourished by a powerful nonhuman fosterer.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sam leaves the mocked child on Alberz, but the Simurgh pities him on the rock and carries him to its own habitation.
"To thee this mortal I resign, / Protected by the power divine."
The Simurgh's young are also kind to the infant, who is nourished and protected for several years.

occurrences.motif_label: human hero as necessary fairy-tale agent
occurrences.basis: The passage lists fairy-tale examples in which human protagonists encounter dragons, undiscovered islands, enchanted gardens, frozen princesses, and Sleeping Beauty.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Fairy tale is said to revolve on human personality, with examples of a hero fighting dragons, an adventurer on an undiscovered island, a miller's third son finding an enchanted garden with seven frozen princesses, and a prince finding Sleeping Beauty.

occurrences.motif_label: Long heroic trial-path toward Buddhahood
occurrences.basis: The note says the Bodhisattva preferred to endure ages of heroic trials in the exercise of the Pāramitās in order to become a Buddha.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “let me rather qualify myself to become a Buddha, and so save others as well as myself”; this is described as the “great ACT OF RENUNCIATION” by which the Bodhisattva chose ages of trials so he might become a Buddha and redeem mankind.

occurrences.motif_label: Moral struggle toward liberation
occurrences.basis: The Great Struggle is described as overcoming delusion and sin through disciplined effort and attaining Nirvāna.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Great Struggle is moral training: mastery over passions, suppression of sinful thoughts, meditation on seven kinds of Wisdom, and fixed attention, leading to overcoming delusion and sin and attaining Nirvāna.

occurrences.passage_locator: INDIAN TALES FROM TIBETAN SOURCES. / THE RELIGIONS OF INDIA. / BY A. BARTH. / FOOTNOTES:; lines 16667-16811
occurrences.motif_label: Quest through many births for the maker of bondage
occurrences.basis: The speaker runs through many births seeking the architect of the house-like desire, and the main explanation describes a long struggle ending when the jewel of salvation is found.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage explains that pain depends on consciousness and individuality; craving causes consciousness; Nirvāna is the absence of craving; the house of individuality is supported by beams of sin and a ridge-pole of care; the Bodisat is now Buddha and has found the jewel of salvation.

The verses describe many births, seeking the architect of the desire-like house, addressing the house-builder, breaking rafters, destroying the central support, and arriving at the extinction of evil desire.

occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 3130-3233
occurrences.motif_label: quest for deathless release
occurrences.basis: Sumedha deliberately seeks Nirvāṇa, the road to release from existence, through secluded contemplation and doctrinal reasoning.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “I am subject to birth, to decay, to disease, to death” and “There is, there must be a road ... that I may obtain release from existence.”
Sumedha reasons that as pain has pleasure, heat has cold, and evil has good, so existence and birth must have cessation; the fires of lust and passion have an extinction in Nirvāṇa.

occurrences.motif_label: Ascetic quest for supernatural knowledge
occurrences.basis: Sumedha adopts Rishi ascetic life in a hermitage, practices strenuously, and attains the eight Attainments, five Supernatural Faculties, and supernatural knowledge.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After pondering nine similes, Sumedha gives away treasure, renounces pleasures, departs from Amara to Himavanta, builds a hermitage near Dhammaka, embraces Rishi ascetic life, wears bark garments, lives at a tree foot on wild fruits, and practices strenuously.

Within a week Sumedha attains the eight Attainments, five Supernatural Faculties, and supernatural knowledge; verses 38-39 say he gave many thousand millions of wealth to rich and poor, went to Himavanta, and made a hermitage and leafy hut near Dhammaka.

occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 3549-3662
occurrences.motif_label: Renunciation and great exertion before enlightenment
occurrences.basis: The prophecy describes Gotama departing from Kapila, retiring from the world, performing austerities, making the great exertion, and then attaining Buddhahood.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The prophecy describes Gotama’s departure, austerities, rice-milk or rice-pottage meal, Neranjarā riverbank, approach to the Bodhi-tree, salutation of the Bodhi throne, and Buddhahood beneath an Indian fig tree called Assattha.

occurrences.source_title: Buddhist birth stories; or, Jataka tales, Volume 1
occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 3800-3919
occurrences.motif_label: Quest for Buddha-making conditions
occurrences.basis: Sumedha deliberately searches through all directions for the conditions that mature Buddhaship and identifies perfections to undertake.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sumedha resolves, “I shall surely become Buddha,” and searches “above and below, in all the ten directions” for Buddha-making conditions.
He beholds the first Gift-perfection or Almsgiving, described as the high road followed by former sages, and undertakes it for Buddhaship.
Sumedha identifies the second perfection, Morality or Moral Practice, practiced by former sages, and resolves to undertake it for Buddhahood.
Sumedha identifies the third perfection, Abnegation, and is told to look upon all births as prison-houses and set his face toward self-abnegation for release from existence.
Sumedha identifies the fourth perfection, Wisdom, and is instructed to avoid no subject of knowledge and to question wise men constantly.

occurrences.source_title: Buddhist birth stories; or, Jataka tales, Volume 1
occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 3921-4041
occurrences.motif_label: progressive search for Buddha-making conditions
occurrences.basis: Sumedha repeatedly reasons that more conditions remain, seeks or investigates them, and beholds successive perfections leading toward Buddhahood.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sumedha beholds the fifth Perfection of Exertion, said to have been practised by former sages, resolves to attain it, and is instructed to exert himself like a lion, king of beasts, in order to attain Buddhahood.

Sumedha beholds the sixth Perfection of Longsuffering, said to have been practised by former Buddhas, and is instructed to endure praise and reproach as the earth endures pure and impure things thrown upon it.

Sumedha beholds the seventh Perfection of Truth, said to have been practised by former Buddhas, and is instructed not to utter a conscious lie even if a thunderbolt descends, but to keep to truth as Venus keeps its path.

Sumedha beholds the eighth Perfection of Resolution, said to have been practised by former Buddhas, resolves to attain it, and is instructed to remain immovable like a rocky mountain unshaken by winds.
Sumedha beholds the ninth Perfection of Good-will and is instructed to have one mind toward friends and foes, like water that refreshes good men and bad alike.

occurrences.source_title: Buddhist birth stories; or, Jataka tales, Volume 1
occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 4163-4291
occurrences.motif_label: Bodhisatta’s great vow and undertaking of perfections
occurrences.basis: Sumedha takes on the Perfections, makes a firm resolve before Dīpankara, and declares his future attainment of Buddhahood after a vast span.

evidence.quote_or_summary: People of Ramma hear the Buddha’s words, bring offerings to the Bodhisatta, bow to him, and return; the Bodhisatta takes on the Perfections, resolves, bows to Dīpankara, and rises from his seat.
The Bodhisatta resolves that after fulfilling the ten Perfections for four asankheyyas and a hundred thousand cycles he will become a Buddha; he rises into the air and returns to Himavanta.

Verses describe angels and men sprinkling flowers, blessing the Bodhisatta, urging fulfillment of the ten Perfections, and using similes of trees, moon, sun, rivers, and ocean; he takes the ten Conditions and enters the forest.

occurrences.source_title: Buddhist birth stories; or, Jataka tales, Volume 1
occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 4163-4291
occurrences.motif_label: Forest departure after vow
occurrences.basis: The Bodhisatta begins to fulfill the ten Conditions and enters the forest after the vow and blessings.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Verses describe angels and men sprinkling flowers, blessing the Bodhisatta, urging fulfillment of the ten Perfections, and using similes of trees, moon, sun, rivers, and ocean; he takes the ten Conditions and enters the forest.

occurrences.source_title: Buddhist birth stories; or, Jataka tales, Volume 1
occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 4875-4993
occurrences.motif_label: Long quest through many births to Buddhahood
occurrences.basis: The Bodisat comes through vast kalpas and many births, searches for Buddha-making conditions, fulfills Perfections, and proceeds up to Vessantara.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Bodisat is said to have come down through four asaŋkheyyas plus one hundred thousand kalpas, making resolve in the presence of twenty-four Buddhas beginning with Dīpaŋkara; after Kassapa there is no other Buddha besides the present supreme Buddha, and the Bodisat received prophecy from each of the twenty-four Buddhas.

The Bodisat exerts himself according to his resolve at Dīpaŋkara’s feet, searches for Buddha-making conditions, beholds the Perfection of Almsgiving, and comes down through many births fulfilling the Perfections up to Vessantara.

Verses praise rewards of Bodisats destined for Buddhahood: they traverse a long road through vast ages and are not born in hell, between worlds, as hungry ghosts, as small animals, or with certain impairments when born among humans.

occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 4995-5142
occurrences.motif_label: Resolute ocean crossing
occurrences.basis: In the Mahā-Janaka Birth, the Bodisat crosses the Great Ocean with the shore out of sight and others as if dead, exemplifying Resolution.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In the Mahā-Janaka Birth, with the shore out of sight in the midst of the waters and all men as if dead, the Bodisat crosses the Great Ocean and acquires Resolution.

occurrences.motif_label: ritual quest for animal companion through isolation, sacrifice, sleep, and vision
occurrences.basis: The Chontal seeker withdraws to a lonely river or mountain place, prays, sacrifices, sleeps, encounters a visionary animal, offers blood, and receives a nagual companion.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Chontal procedure: a young Indian goes to a lonely place by a river or to a mountain top, prays to the gods, sacrifices a dog or bird, sleeps, sees a jaguar, puma, coyote, crocodile, serpent, or bird, and offers it blood from his body while praying for salt and cacao.
The animal says the first animal met on a later hunt "will be myself, who will always be your companion and nagual."

occurrences.motif_label: human warrior aids supernatural ruler against monster
occurrences.basis: The Dragon King asks a human warrior to kill the centipede that threatens his family, and Hidesato agrees to help.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The man says he is the Dragon King of the Lake, living in the waters under the bridge, and asks Hidesato to kill his mortal enemy, the centipede on the mountain beyond.
The Dragon King says the centipede has found his home and carries off his family night after night; he waited in serpent-dragon shape for a brave human, and Hidesato is the first not to flee.
Hidesato agrees to help and is conducted under the bridge to the Dragon King’s palace; the waters part, his clothes remain dry, and he sees a white marble palace beneath Lake Biwa served by fish.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE STORY OF URASHIMA TARO, THE FISHER LAD / THE FARMER AND THE BADGER / THE ADVENTURES OF KINTARO, THE GOLDEN BOY / THE STORY OF THE MAN WHO DID NOT WISH TO DIE; lines 2251-2371
occurrences.motif_label: Quest for immortality through an elixir
occurrences.basis: Both Shin-no-Shiko and Sentaro seek the Elixir of Life or water of perpetual life in order to escape death.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sentaro lives on inherited wealth, becomes distressed by thoughts of death and sickness, and wishes to live five or six hundred years free from sickness.
Shin-no-Shiko asks his court for the Elixir of Life; Jofuku says hermits in Horaizan possess it, and the king sends him by junk with treasures to obtain it.
Sentaro decides to find hermits and the water of perpetual life, leaves his home, and searches the highest mountain peaks without finding a hermit.
