occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS / NOTE. OFFERINGS OF FIRST-FRUITS. / INDEX.; lines 10629-10848
occurrences.motif_label: Serpent as protected animal
occurrences.basis: The passage says North American Indians spare the rattlesnake.

evidence.locator: lines 10629-10848; entries 'Mongolians', 'Nootka Indians', and 'North American Indians'
evidence.quote_or_summary: The index lists stuffing the skin of a sacrificed animal among the Mongolians, a ceremony at bear killing by the Nootka Indians, and North American Indian practices or beliefs involving sparing the rattlesnake, bear-killing ceremonies, respect for deer and elk, and regard for animal bones.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS / NOTE. OFFERINGS OF FIRST-FRUITS. / INDEX.; lines 11306-11513
occurrences.motif_label: Serpent communion and ritual serpent representation
occurrences.basis: The passage indexes communion with the snake, a Python clan, and a dough snake ceremony.

evidence.locator: within lines 11306-11513; index entries: Senegambia; Snake; Snake tribe
evidence.quote_or_summary: The index lists the Python clan, communion with the snake, and a ceremony performed with a dough snake.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: CONTENTS / NOTE. OFFERINGS OF FIRST-FRUITS. / INDEX. / FOOTNOTES; lines 12820-12959
occurrences.motif_label: Annual serpent killing
occurrences.basis: The passage says the cited writer's statement implies that a serpent is killed annually.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The writer does not expressly state that a serpent is killed annually, but the author says the statement implies it.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: CONTENTS / NOTE. OFFERINGS OF FIRST-FRUITS. / INDEX. / FOOTNOTES; lines 14703-14846
occurrences.motif_label: serpent in or around sacred tree
occurrences.basis: Serpents worshipped by old Prussians are said to live in hollow oaks, and the oaks are described as sacred.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Some serpents worshipped by old Prussians lived in hollow oaks; oaks were sacred among the Prussians; serpents also played an important part in Demeter’s worship, though they should not simply be assumed to embody her.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: CONTENTS / NOTE. OFFERINGS OF FIRST-FRUITS. / INDEX. / FOOTNOTES; lines 14703-14846
occurrences.motif_label: tree spirit with serpent and human appearances
occurrences.basis: The takhien tree spirit is believed to appear sometimes as a woman and sometimes as a serpent.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In Siam, the spirit of the takhien tree is believed to appear sometimes as a woman and sometimes as a serpent.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS; lines 2284-2369
occurrences.motif_label: serpent guardian deity protecting infants
occurrences.basis: The cobra-capella is a guardian deity, and infants are made to touch its skin; Frazer states this places them under the tribal god’s protection.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The people of Issapoo on Fernando Po regard the cobra-capella as their guardian deity, able to bestow good or ill, riches, disease, or death.
After the ceremony, children born in the past year are carried out and made to touch the serpent skin’s tail; Frazer says this places infants under the tribal god’s protection.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS; lines 2284-2369
occurrences.motif_label: birth or infancy marked by clan animal contact
occurrences.basis: The passage groups customs in which infants touch a serpent skin, are visited by a python, or are exposed to snakes in relation to clan identity or protection.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After the ceremony, children born in the past year are carried out and made to touch the serpent skin’s tail; Frazer says this places infants under the tribal god’s protection.
In Senegambia, a python is expected to visit every child of the Python clan within eight days after birth.
The Psylli, called a Snake clan of ancient Africa, exposed infants to snakes, believing snakes would not harm true-born clan children.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS; lines 2576-2642
occurrences.motif_label: Feared serpent ghost inciting kin revenge
occurrences.basis: The rattlesnake is spared because its ghost is feared to incite its kinsfolk to vengeance.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Foulahs are said to respect crocodiles on similar grounds; the Seminoles, Sioux, and Iowa Indians spare the rattlesnake because they fear the ghost of a dead rattlesnake would incite its kin to vengeance.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS; lines 3200-3287
occurrences.motif_label: serpent worship with offerings and promised prosperity
occurrences.basis: The Snake tribe’s annual worship involves a painted dough snake, offerings of food, grain, money, or cloth, and verses promising thriving or a bride if the snake is obeyed or given cloth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Snake tribe in the Punjaub worships the snake annually for nine days; Mirasans make a black-and-red painted dough snake, set it on a winnowing basket, and carry it around the village into houses.
The house-entry and offering formulas invoke well-being and say, in part, “If you obey the snake, / You and yours shall thrive!”

People generally give dough or corn; houses connected with a new bride, departing bride, or newborn son may give money or cloth; sometimes the bearers sing that cloth given to the snake will bring a lively bride.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS; lines 3290-3388
occurrences.motif_label: Effigy animal worship as substitute for living sacred animal
occurrences.basis: The dough snake is buried and worshipped, and the passage explicitly identifies it as a substitute for real snakes worshipped where snakes are found.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After house visits, the dough snake is buried with a small grave; women worship there during nine days of September, offer curds while kneeling and touching the earth, then distribute the rest among children.
The author says the dough snake is a substitute for a real snake, noting that where snakes abound worship occurs in jungles where snakes are known to be.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS; lines 5243-5313
occurrences.motif_label: Serpent wound and ritual expulsion or killing
occurrences.basis: The Chiriguano account says old women hunt the snake that wounded the girl and continue until one declares it killed.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Rio de la Plata girls are sewn into hammocks as if dead, leaving a small breathing hole; Chiriguano girls are hoisted in hammocks and later lowered, after which old women with sticks hunt the snake said to have wounded the girl until one says it is killed.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS; lines 6175-6255
occurrences.motif_label: serpents burned in seasonal fire
occurrences.basis: The Luchon rite places living serpents in a wicker column that is set on fire on Midsummer Eve.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At Luchon on Midsummer Eve, a sixty-foot hollow wicker column interlaced with foliage and surrounded by flowers was filled with combustibles; living serpents were thrown in and the column was set on fire.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS; lines 6771-6845
occurrences.motif_label: serpent or multi-headed creature linked with life-token
occurrences.basis: An old man's strength is in a ten-headed serpent; another tale places the fatal stone within the middle head of a seven-headed hydra.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Greek tale says an old man's strength is in a ten-headed serpent; he feels ill as its heads are cut off and dies when the last head is severed.

In a Roman Aladdin version, a magician's fatal thing is a stone hidden inside a bird, inside a leveret, inside a seven-headed hydra; the prince obtains the stone and the princess places it under the magician's pillow, causing his death.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS; lines 7176-7253
occurrences.motif_label: Serpent as soul-container
occurrences.basis: The witch's soul is specifically a seven-headed speckled snake hidden in her shoe-sole.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In a Tartar poem, an old witch survives disembowelment until her soul, a seven-headed speckled snake in her shoe-sole, is removed and beheaded.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS; lines 7388-7470
occurrences.motif_label: serpent as guardian or embodied counterpart
occurrences.basis: The ihlozi is a guarding serpent, and the naguals of chiefs are said to fight in serpent form.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Zulu belief: every man has an ihlozi, a mysterious serpent that guards and accompanies him underground; a man without one must die, and if the serpent is killed the man dies while the serpent revives.

Legend: in early battles with Spaniards on the plateau of Quetzaltenango, chiefs' naguals fought as serpents; the highest chief's nagual was a great green bird, killed by Pedro de Alvarado, at which moment the chief fell dead.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: COMPILED BY / PREFACE / JAPANESE FAIRY TALES / MY LORD BAG OF RICE; lines 151-260
occurrences.motif_label: shapeshifting dragon ruler
occurrences.basis: The Dragon King appears first as a huge serpent-dragon and then as a man, and he states that he took that shape while waiting on the bridge.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At the bridge of Seta-no-Karashi by Lake Biwa, a huge serpent-dragon lies across the path, filling the bridge and breathing fire and smoke.
After Hidesato passes, a voice calls him; the dragon is gone and a strange man appears, bowing, with red hair, a dragon-head crown, and sea-green shell-patterned clothing.
The Dragon King says the centipede has found his home and carries off his family night after night; he waited in serpent-dragon shape for a brave human, and Hidesato is the first not to flee.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: COMPILED BY / PREFACE / JAPANESE FAIRY TALES / MY LORD BAG OF RICE; lines 262-377
occurrences.motif_label: Hero kills a monstrous serpentine enemy
occurrences.basis: Hidesato, called a brave warrior and preserver, kills a huge centipede whose body is described as serpentine.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hidesato sees an enormous centipede winding around the mountains in starlight, with fire-like eyes and glowing feet moving toward the shore.
The saliva-treated arrow strikes the centipede's brain; its body stops, its fiery lights darken and go out, and a violent darkness, thunder, lightning, and wind shake the palace before clear dawn.
The Dragon King's whole family bows before Hidesato and calls him their preserver and the bravest warrior in Japan.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE JELLY FISH AND THE MONKEY / THE QUARREL OF THE MONKEY AND THE CRAB / THE WHITE HARE AND THE CROCODILES / THE STORY OF PRINCE YAMATO TAKE; lines 6128-6233
occurrences.motif_label: serpent-slaying on a mountain path
occurrences.basis: A serpent appears on Ibuki Mountain, blocks Yamato Take’s path, and is killed by him with his bare hands.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Yamato Take goes to Ibuki Mountain, meets a serpent blocking the path, decides he needs no sword, and strangles it with his bare arms.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE JELLY FISH AND THE MONKEY / THE QUARREL OF THE MONKEY AND THE CRAB / THE WHITE HARE AND THE CROCODILES / THE STORY OF PRINCE YAMATO TAKE; lines 6128-6233
occurrences.motif_label: poisoning by slain serpent followed by healing waters
occurrences.basis: After killing the serpent, Yamato Take suffers burning pains identified as poison and recovers by bathing in hot mineral springs.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After the serpent dies, darkness and rain come over the mountain; Yamato Take later feels ill with burning pains in his feet and knows the serpent poisoned him. He is carried to hot mineral springs heated by volcanic fires.
Yamato Take bathes daily in the hot waters, gradually regains strength, loses the pains, and recovers fully.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: RETURN OF THE GREEKS FROM TROY. / PRONOUNCING INDEX. / A COMPLETE COURSE IN THE STUDY OF ENGLISH. / NOTES; lines 11775-11823
occurrences.motif_label: serpentine hybrid monster
occurrences.basis: Echidna is described as a bloodthirsty monster, half maiden and half serpent.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "Echidna was a bloodthirsty monster, half maiden, half serpent."

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: JUPITER. / HERA (JUNO). / JUNO. / PALLAS-ATHENE (MINERVA).; lines 1430-1518
occurrences.motif_label: serpentine and petrifying protective shield
occurrences.basis: Athene's aegis is bordered with serpents, covered with dragon scales, and bears Medusa's petrifying head.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage distinguishes Athene from Ares, saying her armour signifies virtue and purity and that she takes up arms protectively; it describes the aegis with dragon scales, serpents, and Medusa's petrifying head.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VENUS. / HELIOS (SOL). / EOS (AURORA). / PHOEBUS-APOLLO.; lines 2279-2363
occurrences.motif_label: serpent-slaying at sacred site
occurrences.basis: Apollo kills the serpent Python guarding the oracle and thereby frees the surrounding land and people.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The oracle is guarded by the huge serpent Python, a scourge of the neighborhood and terror of men and cattle.
Apollo attacks and kills Python with arrows, freeing the land and people from their mighty enemy.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VENUS. / HELIOS (SOL). / EOS (AURORA). / PHOEBUS-APOLLO.; lines 2529-2596
occurrences.motif_label: fatal serpent bite
occurrences.basis: A venomous snake concealed in grass bites Eurydice’s foot, causing her death.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Orpheus marries Eurydice, daughter of Nereus; Aristaeus tries to take her, she flees, is bitten by a venomous snake, dies, and Orpheus laments.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: HELIOS (SOL). / EOS (AURORA). / PHOEBUS-APOLLO. / ROMAN APOLLO.; lines 2666-2715
occurrences.motif_label: Divine figure with serpent and tree in statuary
occurrences.basis: The Apollo Belvedere depicts Apollo standing against a tree trunk with a serpent creeping up it.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Apollo Belvedere is described as youthful, mostly unclothed except for a short mantle, standing against a tree trunk with a serpent creeping up it, and extending the left arm as if about to punish.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: EOS (AURORA). / PHOEBUS-APOLLO. / ROMAN APOLLO. / HECATE.; lines 2717-2760
occurrences.motif_label: Serpentine chthonic divine form
occurrences.basis: Hecate’s feet and hair are described as formed of snakes in her fearful apparition.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hecate appears as a gigantic woman with torch and sword; her feet and hair are snakes, and her passage is accompanied by thunderous voices, shrieks, yells, and dogs’ howling.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THETIS. / LEUCOTHEA. / THE SIRENS. / ARES (MARS).; lines 3568-3630
occurrences.motif_label: serpentine and fiery image of contention
occurrences.basis: Eris is depicted with a hissing adder, venomous snakes in her hair, and a burning torch.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Eris is represented as angry and menacing, with dishevelled hair, a poniard, a hissing adder, a burning torch, torn dress, snakes in her hair, and is invoked only for evil purposes.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: NYX (NOX). / THANATOS (MORS) AND HYPNUS (SOMNUS). / MORPHEUS. / THE GORGONS.; lines 4616-4661
occurrences.motif_label: Snake-haired monster with petrifying gaze
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly links the Gorgons, especially Medusa, with snakes for hair and the ability to turn beholders to stone.

evidence.quote_or_summary: They are described as frightful winged monsters with scaled bodies, snakes for hair, brass hands, boar-like tusks, and the power to turn beholders into stone.
Medusa loves Poseidon and is united to him in marriage; Athene punishes her by turning her hair into venomous snakes, changing her eyes, and altering her skin.
Under Athene’s curse, Medusa turns to stone whoever she gazes upon until death at the hands of Perseus comes as deliverance.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: NYX (NOX). / THANATOS (MORS) AND HYPNUS (SOMNUS). / MORPHEUS. / THE GORGONS.; lines 4616-4661
occurrences.motif_label: Origin of venomous reptiles from Medusa’s wandering
occurrences.basis: The passage explains Africa as a hotbed of venomous reptiles because infant snakes fell from Medusa’s hair as she wandered there.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In Africa, infant snakes fall from Medusa’s hair, which the passage gives as an ancient explanation for that land becoming a hotbed of venomous reptiles.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: GANYMEDES. / THE MUSES. / PEGASUS. / THE HESPERIDES.; lines 5189-5203
occurrences.motif_label: serpent or dragon guarding treasure
occurrences.basis: The terrible dragon Ladon becomes the ever-watchful sentinel of the golden-apple treasures.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Because the Hesperides taste the golden fruit entrusted to their care, they are deprived of their office, and the terrible dragon Ladon becomes the ever-watchful sentinel of the treasures.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: FAUNUS. / THE SATYRS. / PRIAPUS. / ASCLEPIAS (AESCULAPIUS).; lines 5661-5710
occurrences.motif_label: serpent as healing and wisdom emblem
occurrences.basis: The serpent is identified as Asclepias' distinguishing symbol and is linked with cures, prudence, and wisdom.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Epidaurus statue shows Asclepias as an old bearded man leaning on a staff around which a serpent climbs; the serpent is his distinguishing symbol, connected with cures, prudence, and wisdom.
The usual attributes of Asclepias are listed as staff, bowl, herbs, pineapple, dog, and serpent.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: ALTARS. / PRIESTS. / SACRIFICES. / ORACLES.; lines 6289-6325
occurrences.motif_label: serpent slain by deity as cultic namesake
occurrences.basis: The Pythia is named after Python, a serpent killed by Apollo.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The priestess was called the Pythia after Python, the serpent killed by Apollo.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CEREALIA. / VESTALIA. / PART II.--LEGENDS. / CADMUS.; lines 6563-6631
occurrences.motif_label: serpent or dragon guardian slain by hero
occurrences.basis: A dragon guards Ares' spring, kills Cadmus' followers, and is then slain by Cadmus.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Cadmus prepares to sacrifice the heifer and sends followers to fetch libation water from a spring sacred to Ares; a fierce dragon guarding the spring kills them.
Cadmus arms himself, finds his followers' remains and the bloody monster, fails to harm it with a rock, then pierces and kills it with his spear.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CEREALIA. / VESTALIA. / PART II.--LEGENDS. / CADMUS.; lines 6563-6631
occurrences.motif_label: posthumous transformation into serpents and transfer to blessed realm
occurrences.basis: After death, Cadmus and Harmonia are changed by Zeus into serpents and transferred to Elysium.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Cadmus reigns happily for years, is deprived of his throne by his grandson Pentheus, retires with Harmonia to Illyria, and after death both are changed by Zeus into serpents and transferred to Elysium.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VESTALIA. / PART II.--LEGENDS. / CADMUS. / PERSEUS.; lines 6633-6734
occurrences.motif_label: serpents generated from monster blood
occurrences.basis: Drops of Medusa's blood fall on Libyan sands and produce many-coloured snakes.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The invisibility helmet and winged sandals help Perseus escape the Gorgons; while he flies over Libya, blood from Medusa's head falls onto the sands and produces many-coloured snakes.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VESTALIA. / PART II.--LEGENDS. / CADMUS. / PERSEUS.; lines 6736-6832
occurrences.motif_label: Hero rescues maiden from dragon-like sea monster and receives her as bride
occurrences.basis: Perseus agrees to slay the dragon for Andromeda's hand and delivers her from the sea monster.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Perseus proposes to Cepheus that he will slay the dragon if Andromeda becomes his bride; Cepheus agrees, and Perseus comforts Andromeda before using the helmet of Aides and rising into the air.
The sea opens, the gigantic beast of the deep advances toward Andromeda, and Perseus shows Medusa's head, causing the monster to become a huge black rock.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CADMUS. / PERSEUS. / THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE.; lines 6955-7048
occurrences.motif_label: Sacred treasure guarded by sleepless dragon
occurrences.basis: The Golden Fleece is installed in the Grove of Ares and guarded by an immense dragon that never sleeps.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Aetes nailed the fleece in the Grove of Ares and dedicated it to the god of War; after an oracle said his life depended on the fleece, he guarded the grove entrance with an immense dragon that never slept.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CRONUS (SATURN). / SATURN. / RHEA (OPS). / DIVISION OF THE WORLD.; lines 700-744
occurrences.motif_label: thunderbolt defeat of many-headed monster
occurrences.basis: Typhon, a terrifying hundred-headed monster, is destroyed by Zeus with a thunderbolt after opposing gods and men.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Typhon or Typhoeus, youngest son of Tartarus and Gaea, has a hundred heads, terrifying eyes, and frightful voices; he seeks to conquer gods and men, terrifies the gods into fleeing to Egypt and transforming into animals, and is destroyed by Zeus's thunderbolt.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CADMUS. / PERSEUS. / THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE.; lines 7145-7238
occurrences.motif_label: Serpentine guardian of treasured object
occurrences.basis: The sons of Phryxus report that the Golden Fleece is guarded by a fearful dragon.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The heroes find four shipwrecked sons of Phryxus, who are Jason's cousins, agree to guide them to Colchis, and report that the Golden Fleece is guarded by a fearful dragon and that Aetes is cruel and superhumanly strong.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CADMUS. / PERSEUS. / THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE.; lines 7240-7332
occurrences.motif_label: Dragon or serpent guardian of treasure
occurrences.basis: A sleepless dragon keeps watch at the foot of the tree where the Golden Fleece hangs.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In the grove, the Golden Fleece hangs from a tall oak-tree; a dreadful sleepless dragon watches at the foot of the tree.
Medea casts potion drops on the dragon, causing deep sleep; Jason climbs the tree, secures the Fleece, and they depart on the Argo.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CADMUS. / PERSEUS. / THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE.; lines 7240-7332
occurrences.motif_label: Sown dragon teeth produce armed adversaries
occurrences.basis: Jason sows dragon's teeth in furrows, and armed men arise from them.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Aetes' task requires Jason to yoke fire-breathing oxen, plough Ares' field, sow poisonous dragon's teeth, and destroy the armed men that arise.
Armed men spring from the furrows; Jason throws a rock among them, they attack one another, and he kills them all.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CADMUS. / PERSEUS. / THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE.; lines 7334-7430
occurrences.motif_label: Serpents born from monster blood in a wasteland
occurrences.basis: The Libyan desert contains venomous snakes said to have sprung from Medusa's blood when Perseus carried her over the plains.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A storm strands the Argonauts on the Syrtes quicksands in Libya, a barren desert inhabited by venomous snakes sprung from Medusa's blood.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CADMUS. / PERSEUS. / THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE.; lines 7524-7533
occurrences.motif_label: aerial escape in a dragon-drawn chariot
occurrences.basis: Medea departs through the air in a golden chariot drawn by dragons.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Medea is seen "gliding through the air in a golden chariot drawn by dragons."

occurrences.motif_label: serpent attack on infant hero
occurrences.basis: Two venomous snakes are sent into the child's chamber, and Heracles strangles both.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After learning whom she nursed, Hera sends two venomous snakes into Alcmene's chamber; the infant Heracles wakes and strangles both, one in each hand.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome

occurrences.motif_label: serpent monster with regenerative heads defeated by hero and helper
occurrences.basis: The Hydra is a monster serpent with nine heads; its heads regenerate until Iolaus uses fire while Heracles cuts them off.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The second task is to slay the Hydra, a monster serpent, offspring of Typhon and Echidna, with nine heads, one immortal, which damages the herds near Lerna.
Heracles and Iolaus go by chariot to the marsh of Lerna; Heracles drives the Hydra from the slimy waters, attacks with his club, and finds that each destroyed head is replaced by two.

A giant crab aids the Hydra by biting Heracles; Heracles kills it, Iolaus sears the Hydra's necks with a burning branch, Heracles buries the immortal head under a stone, and dips his arrows in the poisonous blood.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome

occurrences.motif_label: monstrous guardian of sacred fruit
occurrences.basis: A sleepless hundred-headed dragon guards the sacred tree and warns off intruders with constant hissing.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The eleventh task is to bring the golden apples of the Hesperides from a tree given by Gaea to Hera at Hera's marriage with Zeus; the Hesperides and a sleepless hundred-headed dragon guard it.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE. / PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES).; lines 8076-8168
occurrences.motif_label: serpentine underworld guardian subdued by hero
occurrences.basis: Cerberus has venomous snakes and a dragon tail and is physically subdued by Heracles at Acheron.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Cerberus is described as a monster dog with three heads, poison-dripping jaws, venomous snakes for hair, and a dragon tail.

Aides bars Heracles at his palace; Heracles wounds him and receives permission to take Cerberus if unarmed. Heracles finds Cerberus at Acheron, seizes him, endures the dragon-tail bite, and brings him to the upper world near Troezen.

occurrences.motif_label: water quest interrupted by serpent death
occurrences.basis: The army's search for water leads Hypsipile to leave an infant unattended; during the absence a serpent kills the child.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At Nemea, the Argives seek water, meet Hypsipile nursing Lycurgus' infant son, and she lays the child in the grass before guiding them to a secret spring in the forest.
On returning from the spring, the warriors find the infant killed by a serpent; they slay the reptile and bury the child with funeral honours.

occurrences.basis: A serpent devours birds, is turned to stone by Zeus, and Calchas interprets the event as foretelling nine years of war and victory in the tenth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: During shore sacrifices, a serpent ascends a plane-tree, devours nine young sparrows and their mother, is turned into stone by Zeus, and is interpreted by Calchas as foretelling Troy's fall in the tenth year.

occurrences.motif_label: serpent persecution of pregnant or childbearing goddess
occurrences.basis: Hera sends Python, a dreadful serpent, to terrify and torment Leto, who is loved by Zeus and later gives birth on Delos.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Leto is loved by Zeus, persecuted by jealous Hera, and tormented by the serpent Python sent by Hera.
Zeus brings Leto to Delos, a floating Aegean island made stationary with adamant chains, where she gives birth to Apollo and Artemis.

occurrences.basis: The cat lifted by Thor is revealed as the Midgard snake encircling the world, which Thor nearly pulled out of the sea.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Utgard-Loki explains the hidden identities of the contests: Logi as wild fire, Hugi as thought, the drinking horn as connected to the ocean, the cat as the Midgard snake, and Elli as old age.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Loki and Angur-boda have Fenris, Hel, and Iörmungandr; the monsters grow too large for their cave, and Odin sends Hel to Nifl-heim and Iörmungandr to the sea, where the serpent encircles the earth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Nidhug, a dragon in Hvergelmir, and countless worms gnaw Yggdrasil's roots, aiming to kill the tree; its death would signal the gods' downfall.

occurrences.motif_label: serpent allusion in mythological explanation
occurrences.basis: The passage notes an allusion to the serpent Typho within the discussion of mythology.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage discusses hypothetical discovery of Christian doctrines in Greek legends, says such interpretations are found in sacred literatures and lack a test of truth, notes two story versions, mentions common opinion as sufficient, and notes the serpent Typho and Socrates' remark that he is a poor diviner.

occurrences.motif_label: Monster as image of the undisciplined self
occurrences.basis: Socrates asks whether he is a monster more complicated and swollen with passion than the serpent Typho.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says, 'I must first know myself, as the Delphian inscription says,' and asks whether he is more monstrous than 'the serpent Typho' or a gentler creature.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 63-152
occurrences.motif_label: self-knowledge preferred over monstrous mythic inquiry
occurrences.basis: Socrates says he does not yet know himself and contrasts self-study with concern for unearthly monsters such as the serpent Typho.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Phaedrus asks about the local tradition of Boreas and Oreithyia; Socrates rejects rationalizing mythology, says he does not yet know himself, and compares self-study with inquiry into the serpent Typho.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "Thrasymachus seems to me, like a snake, to have been charmed by your voice"

occurrences.basis: The pine-tree goddess says a goddess in Hades assumed bear form, lured the hunter into the cavern and underworld, and wished to marry him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In a second dream, the pine-tree goddess says he cannot stay long after eating Hades' fruit; a goddess in Hades wished to marry him and had assumed bear form to lure him underground.

occurrences.motif_label: Divine beloved promised marriage after death
occurrences.basis: The god says he loves the woman and that when she dies she will truly become his wife.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The woman learns that sunlight through the roof opening caused conception; in a dream a god says he gave her a child because he loves her, that she will become his wife after death, and that their son will have many children.

occurrences.passage_locator: AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA. / II.--MORAL TALES. / IV.--MISCELLANEOUS TALES.; lines 1907-2004
occurrences.motif_label: Marriage between goddess and mortal man
occurrences.basis: After aiding the good man, the badger-goddess comes to the village and marries him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The senior chief imitates the burial and dies; the badger-goddess comes to the village, marries the good man, and he becomes senior of all the chiefs.

occurrences.passage_locator: AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA. / II.--MORAL TALES. / IV.--MISCELLANEOUS TALES.; lines 2102-2199
occurrences.motif_label: deception leading to false sacred marriage with water deity
occurrences.basis: The rascal claims that a goddess in the river loves him and wants to marry his spirit, using this claim to persuade the chief to be drowned.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The rascal wears the old man's beautiful clothes and tells the chief that a river goddess loved him, caused his misdeeds, and wished to marry his spirit.
Seeing the clothes and believing the rascal, the chief has himself tied in a mat and thrown into the river, where he drowns.

occurrences.motif_label: Union with a divine or animal-associated female
occurrences.basis: The bear-goddess instructs the boy to ask for her and later states that they can live together after the dragon-husband departs.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The woman tells the lad she is the bear-goddess, her husband is the jealous dragon-god, and the boy should ask to buy the woman rather than exchange treasures.

The dragon-god returns with two sets of treasures; the boy asks for the wife, thunder sounds, the house disappears, the dragon-husband leaves in rage, the boy and goddess live together, and the narrator explains the bear's half-human likeness.

occurrences.motif_label: Goddess searching for a lost beloved sits by a well
occurrences.basis: The passage says Isis and Demeter both, in search of the loved and lost one, sit sad and weary on the edge of a well.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The note says the myths of Isis and Demeter agree because both goddesses, searching for the loved and lost one, sat sad and weary on the edge of a well; Eleusinian initiates were therefore forbidden to sit on a well.

occurrences.motif_label: fatal vision of water-fairy
occurrences.basis: The quoted English superstition describes a mortal seeing a fair maiden or water-fairy on a stream and knowing that his life will fade because she is divine and he is mortal.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says an English superstition preserves the belief in faded form: one who sees a water-fairy must pine and die; the cited poem describes seeing a maiden on a stream and expecting life to fade because she is divine.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: JAPANESE FAIRY TALES / MY LORD BAG OF RICE / THE TONGUE-CUT SPARROW / THE STORY OF URASHIMA TARO, THE FISHER LAD; lines 1101-1205
occurrences.motif_label: beloved beyond the sea made unreachable by disobedience
occurrences.basis: Urashima seeks to return to his wife, the Princess beyond the sea, but after opening the box the narrator says he can never return to her or the Sea King’s realm.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Urashima realizes that the few days in the Sea King’s palace were hundreds of years at home; his parents and former acquaintances have died, and he resolves to return to his wife beyond the sea.
On the beach, Urashima cannot find the way back and remembers the tamate-bako, which the Princess told him never to open because it contained a precious thing; he decides to open it for help.
The narrator says Urashima’s disobedience prevents his return to the Sea King’s realm or the Princess, and tells children not to disobey those who are wiser.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE FARMER AND THE BADGER / THE ADVENTURES OF KINTARO, THE GOLDEN BOY / THE STORY OF THE MAN WHO DID NOT WISH TO DIE / THE BAMBOO-CUTTER AND THE MOON-CHILD; lines 2528-2630
occurrences.motif_label: radiant otherworldly maiden
occurrences.basis: Princess Moonlight gives off soft bright light, is compared to a possible daughter of the Moon God, and becomes the object of many suitors’ desire.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After three months the bamboo child has become a full-grown girl; she is dressed in beautiful kimonos, kept behind screens like a princess, and emits light that fills the house.
A celebrated name-giver names her Princess Moonlight because her body gives off soft bright light and she might have been a daughter of the Moon God.
A three-day naming festival is held with song, dance, and music; those who see Princess Moonlight praise her loveliness, and her fame spreads widely.
Many suitors desire to win Princess Moonlight’s hand or see her, and they wait outside the house, making holes in the fence in hopes of glimpsing her.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE FARMER AND THE BADGER / THE ADVENTURES OF KINTARO, THE GOLDEN BOY / THE STORY OF THE MAN WHO DID NOT WISH TO DIE / THE BAMBOO-CUTTER AND THE MOON-CHILD; lines 2632-2740
occurrences.motif_label: heavenly or more-than-mortal beloved
occurrences.basis: The bamboo-cutter says Princess Moonlight seemed like a heavenly being and more than mortal, while suitors seek to marry her.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The suitors return to the bamboo-cutter's house, ask him to speak for them, and describe their long vigil through winter, summer, hunger, sleeplessness, and exposure.
The bamboo-cutter tells Princess Moonlight she has seemed heavenly but was raised by him; she replies that she honors and loves him as her father and cannot remember before she came to earth.
The bamboo-cutter recalls finding her years earlier as a three-inch-high creature hidden in bamboo, with a great white light streaming from it, and says he thought her more than mortal.
The suitors arrive, play flutes, sing love songs, and receive the message that whoever brings Princess Moonlight what she wants may marry her; all accept the trial.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE FARMER AND THE BADGER / THE ADVENTURES OF KINTARO, THE GOLDEN BOY / THE STORY OF THE MAN WHO DID NOT WISH TO DIE / THE BAMBOO-CUTTER AND THE MOON-CHILD; lines 2843-2950
occurrences.motif_label: radiant nonhuman or superhuman beloved sought by ruler
occurrences.basis: The Emperor falls in love with Princess Moonlight after seeing that she is more lovely than a human being and shines with soft radiance.

evidence.quote_or_summary: She is "more lovely than any human being" and "shone in her own soft radiance."
The Emperor falls in love and wants to bring her to court; she says she will turn into a shadow if forced, and her figure fades from sight.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE FARMER AND THE BADGER / THE ADVENTURES OF KINTARO, THE GOLDEN BOY / THE STORY OF THE MAN WHO DID NOT WISH TO DIE / THE BAMBOO-CUTTER AND THE MOON-CHILD; lines 2952-3060
occurrences.motif_label: celestial woman returns to her otherworldly home
occurrences.basis: Princess Moonlight is loved on earth but says she belongs to the moon and is taken back by moon envoys in a flying chariot.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Emperor leaves sadly, regards Princess Moonlight as uniquely beautiful, sends love poems, and receives verses saying she can never marry anyone on earth.
Princess Moonlight says she came from the moon, will be fetched on the fifteenth day of August, has parents there, and has forgotten them and the moon-world during her earthly life.
The cloud obscures the sky and hovers near the ground; in it is a flying chariot with luminous beings, including a kinglike chief who calls to the old man.
The messenger leads Princess Moonlight to the chariot; she comforts the old man and tells him to think of her when looking at the moon.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE JELLY FISH AND THE MONKEY / THE QUARREL OF THE MONKEY AND THE CRAB / THE WHITE HARE AND THE CROCODILES / THE STORY OF PRINCE YAMATO TAKE; lines 6021-6126
occurrences.motif_label: faithful spouse saves unfaithful or neglectful partner
occurrences.basis: Despite Yamato Take’s neglect and promise to marry Miyadzu, Ototachibana acts from love to save his life.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Yamato Take is cold toward Ototachibana, says her place is at the palace rather than the warpath, and she remains despite rebuffs.
Yamato Take visits Miyadzu, forgets his wife and duty, and swears to return to Owari and marry Miyadzu after the war.
Ototachibana rises during the worsening storm and resolves to sacrifice her life to rescue Yamato Take from death if possible.
“I will take the place of His Augustness, Yamato Take... giving my life for his... bring him safely to the shore of Kadzusa.”

occurrences.passage_locator: JAPANESE FAIRY TALES / MY LORD BAG OF RICE / THE TONGUE-CUT SPARROW / THE STORY OF URASHIMA TARO, THE FISHER LAD; lines 856-981
occurrences.motif_label: Otherworldly bride offers eternal youth
occurrences.basis: The princess offers to be Urashima’s bride and to let him live forever in a realm of eternal youth without sorrow.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The princess says Urashima set free a tortoise, adds, "I was that tortoise," and offers him life forever in the land of eternal youth as her bridegroom.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: JAPANESE FAIRY TALES / MY LORD BAG OF RICE / THE TONGUE-CUT SPARROW / THE STORY OF URASHIMA TARO, THE FISHER LAD; lines 983-1099
occurrences.motif_label: Marriage with otherworldly sea princess
occurrences.basis: Urashima is married to Otohime Sama, the Sea King's daughter, in the Sea King's realm with a formal wedding feast and cup.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ceremonial fishes bring food on coral trays; the bridal is celebrated, the young pair pledge themselves with the wedding cup of wine three times three, and fishes dance.
Urashima follows his bride, the Sea King's daughter, through an enchanted land; the palace is built of coral and adorned with pearls, and time and age do not touch youth and joy there.
Urashima tells Otohime Sama he must go back to his old parents; she weeps and asks him to stay another day, but he insists and says he will return.

occurrences.passage_locator: ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE. / THE SIEGE OF TROY. / RETURN OF THE GREEKS FROM TROY.; lines 10299-10392
occurrences.motif_label: Detention by immortal beloved and refusal of immortality
occurrences.basis: Calypso becomes attached to Odysseus, offers immortality and eternal youth if he remains, but he longs for Penelope and his son and is detained unwillingly.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Calypso welcomes Odysseus and ministers to him; attached to him, she offers immortality and eternal youth if he stays, but he longs for Penelope and his son, refuses, and is detained seven years against his will.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: RHEA (OPS). / DIVISION OF THE WORLD. / THEORIES AS TO THE ORIGIN OF MAN. / THIRD DYNASTY--OLYMPIAN DIVINITIES.; lines 1081-1171
occurrences.motif_label: Divine unions with mortal women under disguise
occurrences.basis: The passage states that Zeus visited mortal maidens under disguises and gives examples of satyr, swan, and bull forms used with Antiope, Leda, and Europa.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Zeus is described as also allied to mortal maidens, whom he visited under disguises because his true form would destroy mortals; Antiope, Leda, Europa, Callisto, Alcmene, Semele, Io, and Danae are listed.
Zeus appears to Antiope in the form of a satyr; Antiope is identified as daughter of Nicteus, king of Thebes.
Leda is won by Zeus in swan form; her twin sons Castor and Pollux are known for mutual attachment and physical accomplishments.
Europa gathers flowers near the sea-shore; Zeus transforms into a gentle white bull, Europa mounts him, and he carries her across the sea to Crete.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: RHEA (OPS). / DIVISION OF THE WORLD. / THEORIES AS TO THE ORIGIN OF MAN. / THIRD DYNASTY--OLYMPIAN DIVINITIES.; lines 1173-1257
occurrences.motif_label: god assumes altered form to approach a mortal beloved
occurrences.basis: Zeus approaches Callisto under Artemis' form, Alcmene under Amphitryon's form, and Danae as a shower of gold.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Callisto, Artemis' huntress attendant, is approached by Zeus in Artemis' form; Hera changes her into a bear; Artemis hunts her; Zeus places her among the stars as Arctos after death.
Alcmene is betrothed to Amphitryon; Zeus assumes Amphitryon's form during his absence; Heracles is named as son of Alcmene and Zeus.
"Zeus appeared to Danae under the form of a shower of gold."

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: RHEA (OPS). / DIVISION OF THE WORLD. / THEORIES AS TO THE ORIGIN OF MAN. / THIRD DYNASTY--OLYMPIAN DIVINITIES.; lines 1173-1257
occurrences.motif_label: jealous goddess persecutes mortal beloved of a god
occurrences.basis: Hera changes Callisto, engineers Semele's death, and persecutes Io with custody and a gadfly.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Callisto, Artemis' huntress attendant, is approached by Zeus in Artemis' form; Hera changes her into a bear; Artemis hunts her; Zeus places her among the stars as Arctos after death.
Hera, disguised as Beroe, persuades Semele to ask Zeus to appear in full power; Zeus swears by the Styx, reveals himself with thunder and lightning, and Semele is consumed in flames.
Io, a priestess of Hera, is changed by Zeus into a white cow; Hera obtains her and has Argus-Panoptes, with a hundred eyes, guard her at an olive-tree in Hera's grove.
Hera sends a gadfly to torment Io; Io wanders until reaching Egypt, regains her form on the Nile, and gives birth to Epaphus, later king of Egypt and builder of Memphis.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: RHEA (OPS). / DIVISION OF THE WORLD. / THEORIES AS TO THE ORIGIN OF MAN. / THIRD DYNASTY--OLYMPIAN DIVINITIES.; lines 1173-1257
occurrences.motif_label: fatal revelation of divine majesty
occurrences.basis: Semele asks Zeus to appear in full divine glory and is consumed when he reveals himself with thunder and lightning.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hera, disguised as Beroe, persuades Semele to ask Zeus to appear in full power; Zeus swears by the Styx, reveals himself with thunder and lightning, and Semele is consumed in flames.
