occurrences.passage_locator: CERES. / APHRODITE (VENUS). / VENUS. / HELIOS (SOL).; lines 1985-2069
occurrences.motif_label: divine beloved rivalry and jealousy
occurrences.basis: Helios loves Clytie, turns to Leucothea, and Clytie's jealousy leads her to inform Orchamus.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Helios loves Clytie, then Leucothea; Clytie informs Orchamus, who buries Leucothea alive; Helios tries to restore her and sprinkles nectar on her grave, where frankincense grows.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: APHRODITE (VENUS). / VENUS. / HELIOS (SOL). / EOS (AURORA).; lines 2159-2198
occurrences.motif_label: Divine beloved receives altered mortal fate
occurrences.basis: Eos loves Tithonus for his beauty and obtains immortality for him from Zeus, but the gift lacks eternal youth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Eos later unites with Tithonus, son of Laomedon, asks Zeus to grant him immortality but forgets eternal youth; Tithonus ages, loses beauty, is shut in a chamber, and is reduced nearly to voice alone.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VENUS. / HELIOS (SOL). / EOS (AURORA). / PHOEBUS-APOLLO.; lines 2365-2439
occurrences.motif_label: Unhappy love of a god for mortal or nymph beloveds
occurrences.basis: The passage frames Apollo's love affairs as repeatedly repulsed or fatal, then gives Daphne, Marpessa, Cassandra, and Coronis as examples.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Apollo is said rarely to have been happy in love; his advances are repulsed or his unions end fatally.
Apollo pursues Daphne; she flees, prays for aid, becomes a laurel-bush as Apollo reaches to embrace her, and Apollo declares the laurel evergreen and sacred to him.
Apollo seeks Marpessa; Idas carries her off in a Poseidon-given winged chariot; Apollo pursues and seizes her; Zeus rules she must choose, and she chooses mortal Idas.
Cassandra, daughter of Priam, promises marriage in exchange for Apollo's gift of prophecy, then refuses; Apollo cannot recall the gift and makes her predictions fail to gain belief.

Apollo marries Coronis; a crow reports her affection for a youth of Haemonia; Apollo kills her, cannot restore her to life, and punishes the crow by changing its plumage from white to black and banning it from other birds.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: PHOEBUS-APOLLO. / ROMAN APOLLO. / HECATE. / SELENE (LUNA).; lines 2762-2780
occurrences.motif_label: divine beloved watches over sleeping mortal
occurrences.basis: Selene admires the beautiful shepherd Endymion and descends nightly from heaven to watch over and protect him while he sleeps.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Endymion is a beautiful young shepherd to whom Zeus granted eternal youth and the ability to sleep whenever and as long as he wished.
“Seeing this lovely youth fast asleep on Mount Latmus, Selene was so struck with his beauty, that she came down every night from heaven to watch over and protect him.”

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CONTENTS. / MYTHS AND LEGENDS OF ANCIENT GREECE AND ROME. / PART I.--MYTHS. / INTRODUCTION.; lines 305-397
occurrences.motif_label: Divine-mortal union producing heroes
occurrences.basis: The passage states that gods and goddesses become attached to mortals, unite with them, and produce heroes or demi-gods.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The gods have higher mental qualities but human passions, punish evil-doers and impious mortals, visit mankind, unite with mortals, produce heroes or demi-gods, and remain immortal though not invulnerable.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: DIANA. / HEPHAESTUS (VULCAN). / VULCAN. / POSEIDON (NEPTUNE).; lines 3296-3398
occurrences.motif_label: Divine shapeshifting to gain a beloved
occurrences.basis: Poseidon woos Amphitrite as a dolphin and later assumes Enipeus' form to win Tyro's love.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Poseidon marries Amphitrite after wooing her as a dolphin; Amphitrite transforms Scylla with herbs in a well into a twelve-footed, six-headed monster with a dog-like voice, who lives in a high cave and seizes victims from passing ships.
Pelias and Neleus are sons of Poseidon and Tyro; Poseidon assumes the form of the river-god Enipeus to win Tyro; Neleus is father of Nestor.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: DIANA. / HEPHAESTUS (VULCAN). / VULCAN. / POSEIDON (NEPTUNE).; lines 3296-3398
occurrences.motif_label: Rejected monstrous lover kills successful rival
occurrences.basis: Polyphemus loves Galatea, is rejected in favor of Acis, and kills Acis with a gigantic rock.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Polyphemus, a man-eating Cyclops blinded and outwitted by Odysseus, loves Galatea; when she prefers Acis, Polyphemus kills Acis with a rock, and Acis' blood forms a named stream.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: MARS. / NIKE (VICTORIA). / VICTORIA. / HERMES (MERCURY).; lines 3894-3936
occurrences.motif_label: divine suitor seeks mortal or royal beloved
occurrences.basis: Hermes is struck by Herse's beauty, seeks access to her, removes an obstacle, and persuades her to become his wife.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hermes flies over Athens, sees maidens returning in procession from the temple of Pallas-Athene, and notices Herse, beautiful daughter of king Cecrops.
Hermes goes to the palace and asks Agraulos to favor his suit; she refuses without a large payment, and Hermes returns with a purse.
Athene punishes Agraulos' cupidity by causing the demon of envy to possess her; Agraulos blocks the door and refuses Hermes entry.
Hermes fails to persuade Agraulos, changes her into a mass of black stone, and then persuades Herse to become his wife.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VICTORIA. / HERMES (MERCURY). / MERCURY. / DIONYSUS (BACCHUS).; lines 4043-4125
occurrences.motif_label: Abandoned woman becomes the wife of a god
occurrences.basis: Ariadne, abandoned by Theseus on Naxos, is comforted by Dionysus and consents to become his wife.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Dionysus asks to be landed at Naxos, finds Ariadne asleep on a rock after Theseus abandoned her, consoles her, and she agrees to become his wife.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: FORTUNA. / ANANKE (NECESSITAS). / MOMUS. / EROS (CUPID, AMOR) AND PSYCHE.; lines 4825-4914
occurrences.motif_label: Jealous goddess persecutes mortal beauty
occurrences.basis: Aphrodite becomes jealous of Psyche’s beauty and later imposes extremely difficult tasks on her.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Psyche, youngest of three princesses, is so beautiful that Aphrodite grows jealous; after Delphi’s oracle, her father has her dressed as for the grave and taken to a precipice, from which Zephyrus carries her to a meadow palace.
Psyche wanders over the world searching for Eros, appeals to Aphrodite, receives hard tasks, and is aided by invisible beneficent beings sent by Eros.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: FORTUNA. / ANANKE (NECESSITAS). / MOMUS. / EROS (CUPID, AMOR) AND PSYCHE.; lines 4825-4914
occurrences.motif_label: Bride exposed at precipice and conveyed by wind to supernatural spouse
occurrences.basis: Psyche is dressed as for death, taken to a precipice, and transported by Zephyrus to the palace of Eros.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Psyche, youngest of three princesses, is so beautiful that Aphrodite grows jealous; after Delphi’s oracle, her father has her dressed as for the grave and taken to a precipice, from which Zephyrus carries her to a meadow palace.
Eros dwells there and courts Psyche unseen, warning her not to behold him; her sisters visit, envy her, claim her lover is a monster, and give her a dagger.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: FORTUNA. / ANANKE (NECESSITAS). / MOMUS. / EROS (CUPID, AMOR) AND PSYCHE.; lines 4917-4962
occurrences.motif_label: death-like sleep and awakening by divine beloved
occurrences.basis: The black vapour throws Psyche into death-like sleep, and Eros, her beloved, awakens her with a golden arrow.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After leaving the lower world, Psyche opens the box from curiosity; a dense black vapour comes out and throws her into a death-like sleep.
Eros awakens Psyche with the point of a golden arrow, reproaches her curiosity and folly, persuades Aphrodite to reconcile with her, and induces Zeus to admit her among the immortal gods.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: FORTUNA. / ANANKE (NECESSITAS). / MOMUS. / EROS (CUPID, AMOR) AND PSYCHE.; lines 4917-4962
occurrences.motif_label: ordeal purification before divine reunion
occurrences.basis: Psyche undergoes severe penance and trials before being reunited with Eros and admitted among the immortal gods; the passage explicitly presents the myth as an allegory of the soul purified by suffering before reunion with divine essence.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Psyche undergoes severe penance; Aphrodite orders her to descend into the underworld and obtain from Persephone a box containing charms of beauty.
Eros awakens Psyche with the point of a golden arrow, reproaches her curiosity and folly, persuades Aphrodite to reconcile with her, and induces Zeus to admit her among the immortal gods.
The reunion is celebrated by the Olympian deities; the Graces shed perfume, the Hours sprinkle roses, Apollo plays his lyre, and the Muses sing.
"This myth would appear to be an allegory" of the soul being purified by earthly sorrows and sufferings before reunion with divine essence.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: IRIS (THE RAINBOW). / HEBE (JUVENTAS). / JUVENTAS. / GANYMEDES.; lines 5033-5050
occurrences.motif_label: divine selection of a beautiful beloved youth
occurrences.basis: Zeus sees Ganymedes, is struck by his beauty, and has him brought to Olympus.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ganymedes, youngest son of Tros, king of Troy, draws water from a well on Mount Ida; Zeus sees his beauty, sends his eagle to carry him to Olympus, grants him immortality, and makes him cup-bearer to the gods.
Ganymedes is represented as an exquisitely beautiful youth with short golden locks, delicate features, blue eyes, and pouting lips.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: WATER NYMPHS. / OCEANIDES, NEREIDES, AND NAIADES. / OCEANIDES. / THE NEREIDES.; lines 5342-5365
occurrences.motif_label: divine or nymph beloved and spouse relationships
occurrences.basis: The passage names Thetis as wife of Peleus, Amphitrite as spouse of Poseidon, and Galatea as beloved of Acis.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage names Thetis, Amphitrite, and Galatea as the best-known Nereides and identifies them respectively as wife of Peleus, spouse of Poseidon, and beloved of Acis.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: OCEANIDES, NEREIDES, AND NAIADES. / OCEANIDES. / THE NEREIDES. / THE NAIADES.; lines 5367-5384
occurrences.motif_label: divine-human alliance
occurrences.basis: The passage states that Naiades often form alliances with mortals.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says the Naiades often form alliances with mortals and are wooed by sylvan deities of woods and dales.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: NYMPHS OF THE VALLEYS AND MOUNTAINS. / NAPAEAE AND OREADES. / THE WINDS. / PAN (FAUNUS).; lines 5499-5583
occurrences.motif_label: musical instrument made from transformed beloved
occurrences.basis: After Syrinx is transformed into a reed, Pan cuts seven reeds, joins them, creates the syrinx pipe, and names it in memory of his lost love.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Pan pursues Syrinx to the river Ladon; she prays for help and is transformed into a reed. Pan hears the reeds, cuts seven of unequal length, joins them, and makes the syrinx in memory of her.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: SECOND DYNASTY. / CRONUS (SATURN). / SATURN. / RHEA (OPS).; lines 651-698
occurrences.motif_label: Seasonal vegetation loss figured as lost beloved
occurrences.basis: The passage says the yearly winter fading of flowers and leafless trees was poetically expressed as the goddess’s lost love for Atys.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Cretans interpret winter’s yearly disappearance of vegetation, fading flowers, and leafless trees through the figure of a lost love.
Cybele is attached to the beautiful youth Atys, who proves faithless and is about to marry the nymph Sagaris.
Cybele institutes yearly mourning for Atys, and her priests, the Corybantes, march into the mountains to seek the lost youth.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VESTALIA. / PART II.--LEGENDS. / CADMUS. / PERSEUS.; lines 6633-6734
occurrences.motif_label: divine union in confinement
occurrences.basis: Danae is shut in a brass tower, yet Zeus reaches her in the form of a shower of gold and she becomes his bride, leading to Perseus' birth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Perseus is introduced as son of Zeus and Danae; an oracle warns Acrisius about Danae's son, Acrisius confines her in a brass tower, and Zeus descends as a shower of gold.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES). / BELLEROPHON. / THESEUS.; lines 8505-8590
occurrences.motif_label: Divine claim on mortal beloved
occurrences.basis: Dionysus appears in a dream and states that Ariadne is fated to be his bride, after which she is left on Naxos and wooed by him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At Naxos, Dionysus appears to Theseus in a dream and says the Fates have decreed Ariadne to be his bride, threatening misfortunes if Theseus refuses.
Fearing to disobey Dionysus, Theseus leaves Ariadne on the lonely island, where the wine-god finds and woos her.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: RHEA (OPS). / DIVISION OF THE WORLD. / THEORIES AS TO THE ORIGIN OF MAN. / THIRD DYNASTY--OLYMPIAN DIVINITIES.; lines 986-1079
occurrences.motif_label: serpent persecution of pregnant or childbearing goddess
occurrences.basis: Hera sends Python, a dreadful serpent, to terrify and torment Leto, who is loved by Zeus and later gives birth on Delos.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Leto is loved by Zeus, persecuted by jealous Hera, and tormented by the serpent Python sent by Hera.
Zeus brings Leto to Delos, a floating Aegean island made stationary with adamant chains, where she gives birth to Apollo and Artemis.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA; lines 2238-2359
occurrences.motif_label: Enchantress in cave detains a mortal lover or victim
occurrences.basis: The Hörselberg tradition describes Frau Venus luring mortals into her realm and detaining them; Tannhäuser is named as her most famous victim.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A medieval tradition says Holda dwelt in the Hörselberg as Frau Venus, luring and detaining mortals; Tannhäuser lives under her spell, then escapes to Rome for absolution.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER III: FRIGGA / CHAPTER IV: THOR / CHAPTER V: TYR / CHAPTER VI: BRAGI; lines 3819-3966
occurrences.motif_label: Divine beloved as access to guarded treasure
occurrences.basis: Odin woos Gunlod and obtains permission to drink from the vessels entrusted to her.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Inside the mountain cave, Odin appears before Gunlod, woos her, spends three days with her, receives permission to sip from each vessel, and drains all three vessels of mead.

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER IV: THOR / CHAPTER V: TYR / CHAPTER VI: BRAGI / CHAPTER VII: IDUN; lines 4135-4274
occurrences.motif_label: mourning companion remains in the underworld
occurrences.basis: Bragi refuses to return to Asgard and stays beside Idun in Hel's realm, with his harp silent.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Idun lets the gods wrap her in the wolfskin but refuses to speak or move; Bragi sees her tears, tells the others to return, stays with her in Hel's realm, and his harp remains mute.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK XX / BOOK XXI / BOOK XXII / BOOK XXIII; lines 10298-10348
occurrences.motif_label: detention by immortal female in a cave with offer of marriage and immortality
occurrences.basis: Calypso keeps Ulysses in a cave, feeds him, wants to marry him, and intends to make him immortal and ageless, but cannot persuade him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: On Ogygia, the nymph Calypso keeps Ulysses in a cave, feeds him, wants marriage, and would make him immortal and ageless, but he refuses.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: The Odyssey / PREFACE TO FIRST EDITION; lines 187-272
occurrences.motif_label: divine woman detains and woos mortal man
occurrences.basis: Calypso, a goddess, holds Odysseus and woos him with guileful tales so that he may forget Ithaca.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odysseus alone is away from home, craving wife and return, while Calypso holds him in hollow caves and wants him for her lord.

Athene pities Odysseus, who suffers on a sea-girt wooded island, the navel of the sea, where a goddess, daughter of Atlas, holds him and woos him to forget Ithaca; Odysseus longs for the smoke of his land and desires death.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS. / BOOK IV / BOOK V; lines 2386-2472
occurrences.motif_label: goddess loves or detains a mortal man
occurrences.basis: Calypso describes her love for Ulysses and compares it with Dawn's love for Orion and Ceres' love for Iasion.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Calypso says the gods are jealous and hate seeing a goddess take a fancy to a mortal man and live with him in open matrimony.
Calypso cites Dawn's love for Orion, followed by Diana killing him, and Ceres' union with Iasion, followed by Jove killing Iasion with thunderbolts.
Calypso says she became fond of Ulysses, cherished him, wished to make him immortal and ageless, but cannot oppose Jove's will and will give advice for his safe return.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS. / BOOK IV / BOOK V; lines 2386-2472
occurrences.motif_label: mortal chooses home and wife over immortality with a goddess
occurrences.basis: Calypso offers immortality if Ulysses stays; Ulysses acknowledges her superiority to Penelope in beauty but says he wants only to get home.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Calypso asks whether Ulysses would leave at once and says that if he knew his future suffering he would stay, keep house with her, and let her make him immortal despite his longing for his wife.
Ulysses says Penelope is mortal and less beautiful than Calypso, but he wants to get home and will endure further wreck or suffering as part of his troubles.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS. / BOOK IV / BOOK V; lines 2386-2472
occurrences.motif_label: divine punishment of divine-mortal unions
occurrences.basis: Calypso's examples describe Orion killed after Dawn's love and Iasion killed by Jove's thunderbolts after union with Ceres.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Calypso cites Dawn's love for Orion, followed by Diana killing him, and Ceres' union with Iasion, followed by Jove killing Iasion with thunderbolts.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK IV / BOOK V / BOOK VI / THE MEETING BETWEEN NAUSICAA AND ULYSSES.; lines 2882-2972
occurrences.motif_label: Godlike stranger as potential bridegroom
occurrences.basis: Nausicaa says Ulysses now looks like the gods and imagines a future husband like him, while also reporting possible gossip that a god has come down for her.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Nausicaa admires Ulysses, says the gods have sent him, says he now looks like the gods, and wishes for a husband like him if he stayed.
Nausicaa fears gossip that the stranger is a future husband, foreign sailor, or god come down from heaven, and says she would object to such behavior in another girl.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VI / THE MEETING BETWEEN NAUSICAA AND ULYSSES. / BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS.; lines 3176-3259
occurrences.motif_label: refusal of offered immortality
occurrences.basis: Calypso wishes to make Ulysses immortal and ageless, but he cannot be persuaded to accept.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Calypso takes Ulysses in kindly and wants to make him immortal and ageless, but he refuses.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VII / RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS. / BOOK VIII / BOOK IX; lines 3801-3898
occurrences.motif_label: home-longing resisting foreign divine marriage
occurrences.basis: Ulysses says Calypso and Circe wanted marriage, but he was not persuaded and emphasizes country and parents as dearer than a splendid foreign home.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Calypso kept Ulysses in her cave and wanted marriage; Circe also wanted marriage; Ulysses says home and parents are dearer than a splendid foreign home, and he will tell of adventures on his return from Troy by Jove's will.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK VIII / BOOK IX / BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE.; lines 4680-4781
occurrences.motif_label: delay in a divine woman's house before resuming the quest
occurrences.basis: Ulysses stays a year with Circe feasting before his men urge him to resume the homeward journey.

evidence.quote_or_summary: They stay with Circe for a whole twelvemonth, feasting on meat and wine.
When the year has passed, the men tell Ulysses it is time to think about going home if he is to see his house and country.
After feasting, Ulysses gets into bed with Circe and asks her to keep her promise about furthering his homeward voyage.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE. / BOOK XI / THE VISIT TO THE DEAD.88; lines 4969-5068
occurrences.motif_label: disguised divine lover
occurrences.basis: Neptune approaches Tyro disguised as her river lover Enipeus before revealing his divine identity.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Tyro, daughter of Salmoneus and wife of Cretheus, loves the river Enipeus; Neptune disguises himself as her lover, meets her at the river mouth beneath a great blue wave, reveals himself, foretells twins, and orders secrecy.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK X / AEOLUS, THE LAESTRYGONES, CIRCE. / BOOK XI / THE VISIT TO THE DEAD.88; lines 5171-5269
occurrences.motif_label: eternal bodily punishment for transgression against a divine beloved
occurrences.basis: Tityus is tormented by vultures because he violated Leto, described as Jove’s mistress.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses sees Tityus son of Gaia stretched over nine acres while two vultures tear at his liver; the passage explains that he had violated Leto on her journey through Panopeus toward Pytho.

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: ULYSSES LEAVES SCHERIA AND RETURNS TO ITHACA. / BOOK XIV / ULYSSES IN THE HUT WITH EUMAEUS. / BOOK XV; lines 6733-6832
occurrences.motif_label: beautiful mortal carried off by goddess
occurrences.basis: Aurora carries off Cleitus because of his beauty so that he may dwell among the immortals.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The genealogy continues: Amphiaraus was beloved by Jove and Apollo but died at Thebes; Aurora carried off Cleitus for his beauty; Apollo made Polypheides the greatest seer, and he prophesied in Hyperesia.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 208-288
occurrences.motif_label: Divine-patterned beloved and healing love
occurrences.basis: The beloved appears as a god-like form, cures the lover’s pain, and is chosen according to the god followed in the other world.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The corrupted nature rushes toward sensual pleasure; the true mystic beholds a god-like form with delight, the wing begins to grow again, the beloved is a physician, and love is called dove or winged one by immortals.
Lovers’ characters depend on the god they followed in the other world: followers of Ares are fierce, followers of Zeus seek philosophical and imperial natures, and attendants of Here find royal love.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2188-2244
occurrences.motif_label: divinely inspired love as blessing
occurrences.basis: The passage says love is sent by the gods and calls the madness of love the greatest of heaven's blessings.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker defends inspired madness and says love is sent by the gods for good to lover or beloved; the madness of love is called the greatest of heaven's blessings.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2389-2457
occurrences.motif_label: Beloved as divine image and object of worship
occurrences.basis: The beloved's face is viewed as that of a god, and the lover would sacrifice to him as to the image of a god.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The lover looks on the beloved's face “as of a god” and would sacrifice to him “as to the image of a god.”

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2459-2497
occurrences.motif_label: beloved shaped into divine likeness
occurrences.basis: The beloved is chosen according to the lover’s character, treated as a godlike image, and educated to resemble the god honored by the lover.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Each chooses love according to character and “fashions and adorns as a sort of image which he is to fall down and worship.”

Followers of Here seek royal love; followers of Apollo and every other god seek a beloved made like the god served, imitate the god, persuade the beloved to imitate, and educate him into the god’s manner and nature without envy or jealousy.
The inspired lover’s desire is “fair and blissful” to the beloved and is called “the initiation ... into the mysteries of true love.”

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2499-2549
occurrences.motif_label: beloved as catalyst for recollection of higher beauty
occurrences.basis: The beloved's visible beauty causes the charioteer to remember true beauty, associated with Modesty and holy imagery.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At the beloved's flashing beauty, the charioteer remembers true beauty with Modesty, falls back in adoration, and pulls the reins so both horses retreat.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 2551-2634
occurrences.motif_label: Reciprocal divine or inspired beloved love
occurrences.basis: The beloved is described as like a god, the lover as inspired, and the stream of Desire is linked to Zeus and Ganymede.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The beloved receives the lover into communion and intimacy, recognizes the lover's good-will, and values the inspired friend above other friends or kin.

The passage describes the fountain or stream named Desire by Zeus in relation to Ganymede; it overflows upon the lover, passes through the eyes, returns to the beloved, waters the wing-passages, and fills the beloved's soul with love.

The beloved loves without understanding, is compared to someone catching blindness, sees himself in the lover as in a mirror, experiences Anteros in his breast, and desires to see, touch, kiss, and embrace the lover.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION. / ON THE DECLINE OF GREEK LITERATURE. / PHAEDRUS; lines 3061-3191
occurrences.motif_label: divinely inspired love as beneficial madness
occurrences.basis: Erotic madness is assigned to Aphrodite and Eros, is called the best kind in the review, and the speech is said to praise divine love as author of the greatest benefits.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Divine madness is divided into prophetic, initiatory, poetic, and erotic forms, associated respectively with Apollo, Dionysus, the Muses, and Aphrodite with Eros.
The account of erotic madness is described as the best kind, using a possibly true but partly erring myth and a hymn in honor of Love, called lord and guardian of fair children.

Socrates explains division by natural joints and compares it to a body divided into left and right sides; one discourse found evil left-handed love, while the other found divine love on the right side and praised it as author of the greatest benefits.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 639-716
occurrences.motif_label: divine and eternal kingdom of love
occurrences.basis: The passage contrasts worldly love with another kingdom of love that is divine and eternal.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "another kingdom of love, a kingdom not of this world, divine, eternal"

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 718-802
occurrences.motif_label: love as inspired madness
occurrences.basis: The passage discusses love as madness and connects it with inspiration, imagination, idealism, or communion with God; it also describes repeated vision of the beloved's beauty.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The soul repeatedly beholds the flashing beauty of the beloved, but animal desires must be subjected before that vision can be enjoyed.
The passage asks whether Plato is serious in regarding love as madness and associates such a faculty with genius, inspiration, imagination, idealism, or communion with God.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 804-884
occurrences.motif_label: Divine attachment shaping love and character
occurrences.basis: The passage says the capriciousness of love comes from attachment to some god in a former world and that human characters are referred back to the god served in a former state.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Love’s mystery and associations are explained by reference to a former state of existence; its capriciousness is derived from attachment to some god in a former world; the beloved is said to be more affected than the lover at consummation.
Different human characters are traced to the god served in a former state, perhaps as a mythological figure drawing a veil over matters beyond mortal knowledge.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 1320-1353
occurrences.motif_label: death willingly accepted for the beloved
occurrences.basis: The passage states that Love makes people dare to die for the beloved, with Alcestis and Achilles as examples.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “Love will make men dare to die for their beloved--love alone; and women as well as men.”
Alcestis, daughter of Pelias, is willing to lay down her life on behalf of her husband when no one else will.
Achilles gives his life to avenge his friend Patroclus after Patroclus is dead.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 1493-1543
occurrences.motif_label: dual forms of love from two goddesses
occurrences.basis: The passage contrasts heavenly love associated with a heavenly goddess and other loves as offspring of a common goddess.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Acceptance for the sake of virtue is noble; this love is called heavenly, of the heavenly goddess, and valuable to individuals and cities; other loves are offspring of the common goddess.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 1885-1974
occurrences.motif_label: divine love as cosmic and social harmonizer
occurrences.basis: Love is treated as a god who orders the empire of the gods, gives peace, calms storms, and creates affection among people.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Love is said to have set in order the empire of the gods; in earlier days dreadful deeds were done among gods when they were ruled by Necessity, but since Love's birth every good in heaven and earth has sprung from love of beauty.
"Gives peace on earth and calms the stormy deep, Who stills the winds and bids the sufferer sleep."

Love is said to remove disaffection, fill people with affection, bring them together at banquets, sacrifices, feasts, and dances, and act as saviour, pilot, comrade, helper, and leader for gods and humans.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 233-318
occurrences.motif_label: Lost counterpart and longing for wholeness
occurrences.basis: The divided halves seek one another, embrace, and would accept being melted into one; love is defined as the pursuit of the whole.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The two halves search for one another, embrace to the point of hunger, and Zeus devises a sexual adjustment allowing marriage and ordinary life.
A pair would accept Hephaestus' offer to melt them into one, and the passage says love is the desire and pursuit of the whole.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 2477-2569
occurrences.motif_label: divine beauty as ultimate beloved
occurrences.basis: The passage names true beauty as divine, pure, and the object of looking and converse in the life praised above all others.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The life of contemplating absolute beauty is praised; seeing true divine beauty with the mind enables the beholder to bring forth true virtue and become a friend of God and immortal, if possible.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION. / SYMPOSIUM; lines 2571-2651
occurrences.motif_label: jealous beloved guarding attention
occurrences.basis: Socrates describes Alcibiades' passion as jealous and potentially violent whenever Socrates speaks to or looks at another fair person; the available taxonomy only loosely matches this love-centered rivalry.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates asks Agathon for protection, saying Alcibiades' passion has become serious, that Alcibiades grows envious and jealous when Socrates speaks to or looks at others, and that Socrates fears bodily harm from him.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 411-502
occurrences.motif_label: Love as cosmic creative principle
occurrences.basis: Love is described as running through nature and being and as a mythic personage converted by philosophy into an efficient cause of creation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "The power of love is represented in the Symposium as running through all nature and all being" and extending from animals and plants to the highest vision of truth.
The passage discusses gender, sex in plants, elemental affinities, marriages of earth and heaven, Love as a mythic personage and cause of creation, and male/female among Pythagorean opposites.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 504-591
occurrences.motif_label: divinized love and praise of a love deity
occurrences.basis: The passage refers to exaggerated encomiums of the god Love and says love is the theme of the banquet discourse.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage discusses Alcibiades' narrative, signs of Socrates' absence, Socrates' trance or abstraction, Socrates' drinking powers, his view that the first five speeches are fanciful encomiums of the god Love, satirical appeals to mythology including Zeus reconstructing man, Socratic truth-telling about holy things, and the banquet with love as discourse theme and much wine drunk.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 504-591
occurrences.motif_label: returned love favoured by gods
occurrences.basis: Phaedrus is summarized as saying that gods favour returned love from the beloved more than the original sentiment, because the lover is nobler and more divine.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Phaedrus' discourse is described as half-mythical and half-ethical; it treats honour and dishonour, love's antiquity, the blessing of having a lover, love as an incentive to daring deeds, examples of Alcestis and Achilles, and the claim that gods favour returned love from the beloved because the lover is nobler and more divine.

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 923-996
occurrences.motif_label: vision of eternal divine beauty
occurrences.basis: The passage describes a perfect vision of beauty that is eternal, absolute, divine, unlimited, and the highest knowledge of the human mind.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage describes a language of mysteries with higher degrees of initiation leading to a perfect vision of eternal, absolute, divine beauty beyond limits of space and time.

occurrences.source_title: The Mesnevi
occurrences.passage_locator: The Mesnevi, Book I, Proem, The Reed-Flute
occurrences.motif_label: longing for return to source
occurrences.basis: The reed-flute's song begins from separation and turns absence into the desire for return.

evidence.locator: The Mesnevi, Book I, Proem, lines 5400-5429
evidence.quote_or_summary: The reed-flute tells of absence from its reed-bed and voices the grief and joy of the absent lover.

occurrences.source_title: Mystics and Saints of Islam
occurrences.passage_locator: Mystics and Saints of Islam, Rabia, the Woman Sufi
occurrences.motif_label: divine beloved excludes worldly possession
occurrences.basis: Rabia rejects the whole world because divine love is treated as incompatible with worldly attachment.

evidence.locator: Mystics and Saints of Islam, Rabia, lines 1037-1047
evidence.quote_or_summary: A voice tells Rabia she cannot keep both the world and divine love; Rabia turns from earthly love and prays for absorption in God's love.

occurrences.motif_label: sacred_cauldron_of_renovation
occurrences.basis: The cauldron restores slain bodies to fighting life by the next day.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Bendigeid Vran says the cauldron restores a slain man by the next day, but the revived man cannot speak.
The Irish kindle fire under the cauldron of renovation, fill it with dead bodies, and the bodies rise next day as fighting men unable to speak.

occurrences.basis: The cauldron functions as a vessel into which dead bodies are placed for restoration.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Irish kindle fire under the cauldron of renovation, fill it with dead bodies, and the bodies rise next day as fighting men unable to speak.

occurrences.motif_label: acquittal_and_afterlife_reward
occurrences.basis: After the favourable verdict, Ani is granted offerings, comes before Osiris, and becomes a spirit-body.

evidence.locator: CHAPTER VII, The Judgment of Osiris; Ani before Osiris
evidence.quote_or_summary: Horus tells Osiris that Ani's heart is righteous, has come forth from the Balance, has no sin before any god or goddess, and that Thoth has written the judgment.

evidence.locator: CHAPTER VII, The Judgment of Osiris; close of Chapter VII
evidence.quote_or_summary: Under favour of Osiris Ani then became a sahu, or "spirit-body," and in this form passed into the Kingdom of Osiris.

occurrences.source_title: The Book of the Dead
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER IX, A Short Description of the "Doors" or Chapters of the Book of the Dead; summaries of Chapters LXIV, LXXIV-LXXXVIII, CXLIV-CXLVII, and CLV-CLXVII
occurrences.motif_label: divine_protection_of_the_dead
occurrences.basis: The text describes protective chapters and amulet spells for the deceased.

evidence.locator: CHAPTER IX, A Short Description of the "Doors" or Chapters of the Book of the Dead; Chapter LXIV
evidence.quote_or_summary: Chapter LXIV is an epitome of the whole Book of the Dead, and it formed a "great and divine protection" for the deceased.

evidence.locator: CHAPTER IX, A Short Description of the "Doors" or Chapters of the Book of the Dead; Chapters CLV-CLXVII
evidence.quote_or_summary: Chapters CLV-CLXVII are spells which were engraved on the amulets, giving the deceased the protection of Ra, Osiris, Isis, Horus, and other gods.

occurrences.passage_locator: HELGAKVITHA HJORVARTHSSONAR / THE LAY OF HELGI THE SON OF HJORVARTH / INTRODUCTORY NOTE / OF HJORVARTH AND SIGRLIN; lines 11252-11299
occurrences.motif_label: Hero's death and being 'born again' (rebirth of hero and beloved)
occurrences.basis: The passage reports Helgi's fatal wounding/fall and then explicitly states that Helgi and Svava were born again.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sigar reports Helgi fell in the morning at Frekastein; calls him the noblest king beneath the sun; says Alf has the joy of victory.
Helgi greets Svava, says this is their last meeting in life, and describes his bleeding wounds and a sword near his heart.
The text states that Helgi and Svava were born again.

occurrences.motif_label: reviving the dead companion
occurrences.basis: Okikurumi revives Samayunguru, who is explicitly described as having been dead.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The shark laughs at Okikurumi; Okikurumi cuts the rope, reaches land after a long time, and revives the dead Samayunguru.

occurrences.motif_label: mourning, death, and revival of Adonis
occurrences.basis: The cited note explicitly describes Adonis as mourned as dead, afterward reviving, and connected with killing and resurrection.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Jerome is cited for an Adonis solemnity in which he is mourned as if dead, afterward praised as reviving, and the killing and resurrection of Adonis are followed with mourning and joy.

occurrences.motif_label: death and rebirth of vegetation through seed and crop cycle
occurrences.basis: The passage cites interpretations of Adonis’s killing and resurrection as corresponding to seeds dying in earth and crops growing again.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Cited interpretations identify Adonis with sown grain, describe six months in earth and six with Aphrodite, and interpret Adonis’s death and resurrection through seeds dying in earth and crops being reborn.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 1 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE. / CHAPTER III. KILLING THE GOD. / FOOTNOTES; lines 11851-11982
occurrences.motif_label: buried figure revived or resurrected
occurrences.basis: The Hilaria and cited Firmicus passages describe the recently buried figure as revived, the idol brought out from burial, and rejoicing after mourning.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Hilaria, resurrection, annual mourning, a claim that the buried figure revived, seed-cycle explanation, idol brought from burial, rejoicing, salvation from Hades, and a saved-god formula are cited and compared.

occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE. / CHAPTER III. KILLING THE GOD. / FOOTNOTES; lines 11984-12134
occurrences.motif_label: Dismemberment followed by revivals and regenerations
occurrences.basis: The cited Plutarch note refers to Osiris's dismemberments, revivals, regenerations, and burials.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The cited Plutarch passage is associated with Osiris's dismemberments, revivals, regenerations, and burials.

occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER I. THE KING OF THE WOOD. / MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE.; lines 3499-3538
occurrences.motif_label: death and resurrection through soul transfer
occurrences.basis: The Karen example explicitly states that the dead man comes to life as the sleeper dies, and that a succession of deaths and resurrections may occur.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Karen wizard catches a sleeper’s wandering soul and transfers it to a dead man, causing the dead man to live and the sleeper to die; further thefts can create a succession of deaths and resurrections.

occurrences.passage_locator: PREFACE. / J. G. FRAZER. / CHAPTER I. THE KING OF THE WOOD. / MACAULAY.; lines 355-440
occurrences.motif_label: restored mortal hidden from divine anger
occurrences.basis: Hippolytus is killed, restored to life by Aesculapius, and hidden by Diana from Jupiter at Nemi.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Virbius is identified with Hippolytus, killed by horses, restored by Aesculapius, hidden by Diana at Nemi from Jupiter, and worshipped as a forest king; horses are excluded from the sanctuary because they killed Hippolytus.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 1 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE. / CHAPTER III. KILLING THE GOD.; lines 5305-5354
occurrences.motif_label: ritual death followed by restoration by a healer figure
occurrences.basis: The Wild Man is shot and brought back to life by a doctor; Dr. Iron-Beard is associated with a similar restoration of a dead man.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In the Saxon and Thüringen custom, after the Wild Man is shot he is brought to life again by a doctor.
In the Wurmlingen ceremony Dr. Iron-Beard appears; the passage says he probably once played a similar role and elsewhere pretends to restore a dead man to life.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 1 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE. / CHAPTER III. KILLING THE GOD.; lines 5356-5395
occurrences.motif_label: death followed by revival or resurrection
occurrences.basis: The passage describes the killed tree-spirit representative being brought to life again and Hippolytus or Virbius being restored to life, then links slaying to revival or resurrection in a successor.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In Saxony and Thüringen, the representative of the tree-spirit is killed and then brought to life again by a doctor.
Legend says Hippolytus or Virbius, the first King of the Wood at Nemi, was killed by his horses and restored to life by Aesculapius.
Frazer says the legend fits the theory that slaying the King of the Wood was a step toward revival or resurrection in his successor.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 1 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE. / CHAPTER III. KILLING THE GOD.; lines 5397-5472
occurrences.motif_label: ritual death and revival
occurrences.basis: The Vishnu-related rite explicitly involves pretended sacrifice, feigned death, and restoration to life by blood sprinkling.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Hindu who offends by killing or ill-treating certain animals before Vishnu’s worshippers must expiate by pretended sacrifice and resurrection of a human being, who bleeds, feigns death, and is revived by blood sprinkling.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 1 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE. / CHAPTER III. KILLING THE GOD.; lines 5397-5472
occurrences.motif_label: killing and resurrection of the god
occurrences.basis: Frazer frames the chapter’s argument around a god’s death and resurrection, including the tree-god and later animal or corn forms.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Frazer introduces 'Carrying out Death,' reviews his explanation of the priest of Nemi being slain by his successor, and proposes to examine killing and resurrection of the god as tree-god, animal, corn, or human representative of corn.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 1 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE. / CHAPTER III. KILLING THE GOD.; lines 5474-5552
occurrences.motif_label: Enacted resurrection after ritual death
occurrences.basis: The passage states that sometimes resurrection of the pretended dead person is enacted, then gives examples of a sick man restored to life and buried brandy said to come to life again.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Frazer says resurrection of the pretended dead person is sometimes enacted; in one Swabian example, Dr. Iron-Beard bleeds a sick man who falls as dead, then restores him to life by blowing air through a tube.

In the Harz mountains, after Carnival a man is carried with dirges to a grave, but a glass of brandy is placed in the grave; the next Shrove Tuesday the brandy is dug up and tasted as having come to life again.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 1 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE. / CHAPTER III. KILLING THE GOD.; lines 5746-5781
occurrences.motif_label: Death figure as source of revived life
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly says that life potency may be attributed to the image of Death itself and that, by a kind of resurrection, it becomes an instrument of general revival.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Frazer states that Death is represented by a puppet that is thrown away, while Summer or Life is represented by branches or trees brought back; he adds that sometimes the Death image itself seems to gain life potency and become an instrument of revival.

In parts of Lusatia, women in mourning make a straw Death puppet with a white shirt, broom, and scythe, carry it to the village boundary while boys throw stones, tear it apart, then cut a fine tree, hang the shirt on it, and carry it home singing.

In the second act, one girl is invested with the clothes and ornaments previously worn by the figure of Death and led in procession with hymns; the ceremony ends with a feast, with boys again excluded.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 1 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE. / CHAPTER III. KILLING THE GOD.; lines 6100-6145
occurrences.motif_label: Revival and ascent after mourning
occurrences.basis: At Byblus, the day after mourning, Adonis is believed to come to life again and ascend to heaven before worshippers.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At Byblus, Adonis's death is mourned with weeping, wailing, and breast-beating; the next day he is believed to come to life again and ascend to heaven in the presence of worshippers.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 1 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE. / CHAPTER III. KILLING THE GOD.; lines 6236-6295
occurrences.motif_label: vegetation god revived through water
occurrences.basis: The passage interprets Adonis water rites as effecting the god's resurrection and describes Thammuz as restored by water of life or revived when water is poured over his effigy.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Babylonian legend says Istar descends to Hades to fetch the water of life to restore dead Thammuz; water appears to have been thrown over him during a mourning ceremony around his funeral pyre.

Frazer reports that the legend is probably a mythical explanation of a Babylonian festival resembling the Syrian Adonis festival, where dead Thammuz was likely represented in effigy, water poured over him, and he came to life again.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 1 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE. / CHAPTER III. KILLING THE GOD.; lines 6465-6519
occurrences.motif_label: dying and resurrecting vegetation deity
occurrences.basis: Attis is explicitly described as a vegetation god whose death and resurrection are ritually mourned and rejoiced over at a spring festival.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “Like Adonis, he appears to have been a god of vegetation, and his death and resurrection were annually mourned and rejoiced over at a festival in spring.” The passage adds that their legends and rites were so similar that ancients sometimes identified them.
The fourth day was the Festival of Joy, at which Attis’s resurrection was probably celebrated, following closely after the celebration of his death.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 1 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE. / CHAPTER III. KILLING THE GOD.; lines 6597-6671
occurrences.motif_label: Dying and returning god of Osiris
occurrences.basis: The passage narrates Osiris’s murder, dismemberment, ritual mourning and burial, and ceremonies Frazer connects with resurrection.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Osiris travels spreading civilization; on return Set/Typhon and seventy-two others plot against him, seal him in a decorated coffer with molten lead, cast it into the Nile, and it floats to the sea.

Typhon finds Osiris’s body while hunting by full moon, tears it into fourteen pieces, and scatters them; Isis searches the marshes in a papyrus boat and buries each fragment, with explanations for many graves or effigies of Osiris.

Annual rites include five days of mourning, earth-ploughing, search for the mangled body, rejoicing at discovery, burial, and lamentations attributed to Isis and Nephthys; Brugsch says these lamentations "vividly recall the dirges chanted at the Adonis’ rites over the dead god."

The festival ends with the erection of the Tatu/Tat/Ded pillar, a cross-barred column; a Theban tomb shows the king, relations, and a priest raising it. It is later interpreted as Osiris’s backbone and possibly as a stripped tree linked to resurrection.

Plutarch describes priests carrying a sacred ark to the sea, a golden casket inside receiving drinking-water, a shout that Osiris is found, and mould mixed with water to fashion a crescent-shaped image that is dressed and adorned.

occurrences.passage_locator: MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE. / CHAPTER III. KILLING THE GOD.; lines 7047-7107
occurrences.motif_label: dying and returning vegetation god
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly states that Dionysus dies violently, is restored or resurrected in variant myths, and is associated with spring and vegetation deities.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Dionysus is introduced as a vegetation god believed to have died violently, been brought to life again, and had his sufferings, death, and resurrection enacted in rites.

Other versions describe Demeter reassembling Dionysus’s limbs and making him young again, Dionysus rising and ascending, Zeus raising him, Zeus swallowing the heart and begetting him afresh by Semele, or Semele conceiving him through a potion made from the heart.
Frazer says the Lydians celebrated the advent of Dionysus in spring and supposed that the god brought the season with him.

Frazer states that vegetation deities who spend part of each year underground naturally become regarded as gods of the lower world or of the dead, and adds that Dionysus and Osiris were both so conceived.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 1 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE. / CHAPTER III. KILLING THE GOD.; lines 7047-7107
occurrences.motif_label: life or identity preserved in the heart
occurrences.basis: Dionysus’s heart survives the dismemberment and becomes central to an image, Zeus’s rebirth of Dionysus, or Semele’s conception in different versions.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Minerva keeps Dionysus’s heart and gives it to Jupiter, who learns of the crime, kills the Titans, makes an image containing the heart, and builds a temple in Dionysus’s honour.

Other versions describe Demeter reassembling Dionysus’s limbs and making him young again, Dionysus rising and ascending, Zeus raising him, Zeus swallowing the heart and begetting him afresh by Semele, or Semele conceiving him through a potion made from the heart.

occurrences.motif_label: descent to the dead to retrieve a mother
occurrences.basis: A variant myth has Dionysus descending into Hades to bring Semele up from the dead.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A different form of the myth says Dionysus descended into Hades to bring his mother Semele up from the dead.

occurrences.motif_label: ritual reenactment of divine death and return
occurrences.basis: Frazer states that Cretan rites represented Dionysus’s suffering and death in detail and, where the myth included it, enacted his resurrection; he also links Dionysiac mysteries with immortality teaching.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Cretans celebrated a biennial festival representing Dionysus’s sufferings and death in detail, and where resurrection belonged to the myth it was also enacted in the rites.
Frazer cites Plutarch’s consolation to his wife as evidence that the mysteries of Dionysus taught, or revealed, immortality of the soul.

occurrences.motif_label: return from the underworld through water with offering

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Argive tradition says Dionysus descended through the Alcyonian lake; the Argives annually celebrated his return by summoning him from the water with trumpet blasts and throwing a lamb into the lake for the warder of the dead.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In Beauce, people make a straw-man called the great mondard in late April, process it through the village, place it on the oldest apple-tree, later throw it into water or burn it and cast the ashes into water, and give the title great mondard to the person who plucks the first fruit.
Frazer interprets the straw figure as the tree-spirit, dead in winter and revived with spring apple-blossoms, and the first-fruit plucker as a representative of the tree-spirit.

occurrences.motif_label: resurrection from preserved bones
occurrences.basis: Multiple examples describe animals or people returning to life when bones are preserved, ordered, or kept intact.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A general belief is stated that preserved animal bones may be reclothed with flesh and return to life; Minnetaree bison bones are said to rise again, renewed and fit for slaughter the following June.

Buffalo skulls are described as arranged in circles and piles awaiting resurrection; Dacotas collect, scrape, wash, and bury dog bones after a feast to show respect and because the bones may rise and reproduce another dog.

Lapps preserve bones and selected animal parts, lay them anatomically in a coffin, and bury them, believing the sacrificial god will restore the animal in Jabme-Aimo; Kamtchatkans are said to believe all creatures rise and live underground.

Folk-tales are said to preserve the belief that animals or people revive if bones are kept; in a Magyar tale, a serpent-king orders and washes a dismembered hero's bones, revives him, and replaces a lost shoulder-blade with gold and ivory.

The passage explains Pythagoras's reported golden leg as possibly derived from a resurrection story in which a broken or mislaid leg was replaced with gold.

Pelops is described as restored to life with an ivory shoulder replacing one eaten by Demeter; Osiris is described as having a missing member eaten by fish and replaced by Isis with one of wood, perhaps belonging to the same circle of beliefs.

Frazer cites a common belief in animal resurrection and notes that Lapps bury the male bear skeleton with genital parts in hope of resurrection.

occurrences.motif_label: initiatory death and rebirth
occurrences.basis: Multiple reported rites or beliefs describe novices as killed, buried, swallowed, rendered lifeless, or treated as dead, then revived or returned with adult or initiated status.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Australian examples: Thuremlin kills and restores boys; Bullroarer sound is said to be wizards swallowing and bringing boys up again; the Ualaroi say a ghost kills and revives a boy as a man.
A resurrection ceremony places a disguised old man in a covered grave holding a bush; novices are brought to the grave, a song is sung, the bush moves, and the man rises.
Fijian initiates are shown apparently dead, bloodied men with entrails protruding; at a priest's yell the men rise and run to the river to cleanse themselves of pig blood and entrails.

In Ndembo rites, doctors arrange pretended death and enclosure; after months or years, with fees and feast goods supplied, initiates are brought to life, act ignorant or strange, and receive a special name.

In Ambamba, the fetish priest shakes a calabash; men and lads fall into lifeless torpidity or are carried away by the fetish, later returning without understanding and being re-taught before return to parents.

occurrences.basis: Belli-Paaro candidates are told they must suffer death and the text mentions spiritual resurrection; Huskanaw youths are described as unliving former lives and commencing men after forgetting boyhood.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At the king’s order a forest place is appointed; youths are brought there weeping, told they must suffer death, dispose of property, and are instructed by initiated persons in a dance called killing and songs praising Belli.
The forest life lasts five or six years in a village with hunting and fishing; other boys may arrive later; women and uninitiated persons are barred from approaching the sacred wood.

The Huskanaw account says the youths drink enough Wysoccan, likened to water of Lethe, to forget parents, possessions, and language; doctors gradually restore them, keepers guard them, and they must relearn speech and recognition, thereby commencing men by forgetting they had been boys.

occurrences.motif_label: ritual death and restoration in initiation
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly describes candidates or boys as apparently killed, knocked down, swallowed, buried, or struck dead and then revived, restored, disgorged, uncovered, or reborn as part of admission to societies or rites.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Among the Naudowessies, Carver saw a candidate kneel before a chief, receive a bean-like object, fall motionless as if shot, then revive after blows and expel the object from his mouth.

Other tribes use animal-skin medicine-bags containing charms; a spirit or breath from the bag is believed able to kill and restore life, and thrusting the bag once fells a man while a second thrust revives him.
At Nootka Sound, a chief fires near his son's ear; the son falls as if killed, women lament, armed people enter, and two wolf-skin masked figures moving like beasts carry the prince away.

The Toukaway Indians have a wolf-totem ceremony in which wolf-skin men run on all fours, howl, dig up a living buried tribesman, give him bow and arrows, and tell him to act as wolves do; Frazer compares it to Australian grave-resurrection rites.
On Rook, masked dancers demand boys, make them creep between their legs, announce that Marsaba has eaten the boys and will only disgorge them after receiving pigs, taro, and other provisions.

In New Britain, boys are initiated into the Duk-duk association by a cane blow from Tubuvan supposed to kill them; Tubuvan and Duk-duk are concealed performers representing cassowaries, female and male respectively, whom women may not see.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Mothers and sisters mourn; sponsors return announcing the devil restored the lads to life through priests' intercession, arriving fainting and mud-daubed like nether-world messengers.
Each lad receives a feathered stick from the priest, said to have been given by the devil at restoration and to serve as a token that the lads have been in spirit-land.
The returning lads totter, enter backward or by the back door, hold plates upside down, remain dumb, communicate by signs, and are taught common acts as newborn children.
The boys face food and hair-combing taboos; the high priest later cuts a crown lock in the forest; after the rites they are deemed men and may marry.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage notes numerous untitled or unidentified Jātaka scenes and several Nidānakathā scenes, including worship in heaven of the Buddha’s head-dress, the Palace of Glory, the Descent of the Blessed One illustrating Māyā Devi’s Dream, and the Presentation of Jetavana; it also says some identifications are doubtful.

occurrences.motif_label: pre-birth selection of the Buddha’s conditions
occurrences.basis: The Great Being deliberately selects time, continent, district, caste, father, and mother before birth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Great Being reflects successively on five points: time of advent, continent and country, tribe of birth, mother, and the time when the mother’s life should be complete.

The Great Being reasons that a Buddha’s advent is not suitable when human life exceeds one hundred thousand years or is under one hundred years; the suitable interval is under one hundred thousand and over one hundred years, and he sees that the time has arrived.
Considering the continents, the Great Being decides that Buddhas appear in Jambudvīpa; he then fixes on the Middle Country and Kapilavastu.
The Great Being decides that Buddhas are born in the highest-reputed caste, chooses the predominant Kshatriya caste, and selects Suddhodana the chief as father.

The Great Being chooses Mahā Māyā as mother because she is morally restrained, has fulfilled the Perfections, and has kept the five Precepts; he foresees that her life will last ten months and seven days more.

occurrences.motif_label: Sacred conception and birth announcement
occurrences.basis: The passage narrates the future Buddha's conscious descent to conception, Mahā Māyā's purified dream, the elephant's entry into her womb, and cosmic omens at incarnation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The future Buddha grants the deities' prayer, declares the time has arrived to become a Buddha, enters the Grove of Gladness in the City of Delight, is attended by angels who remind departing beings of merit, leaves that realm, and is conceived in Lady Mahā Māyā's womb.

Four archangels, Guardians of the world, carry Lady Mahā Māyā in her couch to the Himalaya mountains and place her beneath the Great Sāla-tree; their queens take her to Lake Anotatta, bathe her free of human stains, dress her in heavenly garments, anoint her, and adorn her with flowers.

In the dream the future Buddha, as a superb white elephant, wanders on the Golden Hill, ascends the Silver Hill, approaches from the north holding a white lotus, enters the golden mansion, bows three times to his mother's couch, gently strikes her right side, and seems to enter her womb.

At the future Buddha's incarnation, ten thousand world-systems quake and thirty-two good omens appear, including immeasurable light, restored sight and hearing, speech by the dumb, straightening of the crooked, freedom of prisoners, extinction of hellfire, food for hungry ghosts, allaying of sickness, kind speech, gentle animal sounds, and instruments sounding by themselves.

Further omens include clear heavens, a cool breeze, out-of-season rain, water rising from the earth, birds ceasing flight, rivers stopping, the ocean becoming fresh, lotuses and flowers covering earth and water, tree blooms, lotuses emerging through rocks or descending from the sky, and the ten-thousand world-systems clustering like a flower wreath.

occurrences.basis: The passage describes guarded conception, distinctive pregnancy, standing delivery, divine reception, unsoiled birth, heavenly water, immediate standing, seven strides, and speech.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At incarnation, four angels with swords guard the Bodisat and mother; the mother is pure, sees the child clearly, and dies seven days after birth to be reborn in the City of Delight.
Other women vary in term and posture, but the mother of a Bodisat gives birth standing after exactly ten months; this is a distinctive quality of the mother of a Buddha elect.
In Lumbini grove, full of fruits, flowers, bees, birds, and sāla-trees, Mahā Māyā wants to sport; a sāla branch bends down, she takes hold of it, her pains begin, and she gives birth standing.
Four pure-minded Mahā Brahma angels bring a golden net, receive the future Buddha on it, and say to his mother that a mighty son is born.
The Bodisat leaves the womb erect, with hands and feet stretched out, unsoiled, pure, fair, and shining; two showers of water come from heaven to refresh him and his mother.

After searching the ten directions and finding no equal, the newborn takes seven strides. Brahma holds the white umbrella, Suyāma follows with the fan, other deities hold royal symbols, and he shouts a victory cry beginning that he is chief of the world.

occurrences.motif_label: miraculous or marked child recognized as divine successor
occurrences.basis: The Bhotan infant reveals the new incarnation through milk preference; Grand Lama infants may identify themselves and pass tests; the Dalai Lama's spirit is born again in a child.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In Bhotan, the Dhurma Raja is the spiritual head of government and a perpetual incarnation of deity; after his death the new incarnate god appears in an infant who refuses mother's milk and prefers cow's milk.
A rainbow may guide followers to the departed Lama's cradle, or the infant may declare himself the Grand Lama and living Buddha of a particular temple.

Pilgrims, sometimes led by royalty, travel to find the infant god, worship him, question him about his former monastery and death, and ask him to identify previous-life objects such as prayer-books, tea-pots, and cups.

The Dalai Lama of Lhasa is head of all Lamas, regarded as a living god, and at death his divine and immortal spirit is born again in a child; accounts differ between recognition methods and election by lot.

occurrences.basis: The passage gives examples of women rolling under an apple-tree to obtain offspring, clasping guardian-trees for easy delivery, wearing bark garments for protection in childbirth, and Leto clasping trees before giving birth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Frazer says the May Day green bush before a beloved maiden's house probably came from belief in the fertilising power of the tree-spirit; Kara-Kirgiz barren women roll under a solitary apple-tree to obtain offspring.
In parts of Sweden, a farm had a guardian-tree such as lime, ash, or elm; the tree was sacred, injury to it brought ill-luck or sickness, and pregnant women clasped it for easy delivery.
In some Congo-region tribes, pregnant women make garments from bark of a sacred tree because they believe the tree delivers them from dangers of child-bearing.
Frazer says the story that Leto clasped a palm and olive, or two laurels, before the birth of Apollo and Artemis perhaps points to a similar Greek belief in certain trees facilitating delivery.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In West Prussia, the last-sheaf figure is called the Bastard; a boy is wrapped in it, the Corn-mother enacts labor, a grandmother acts as midwife, the child is announced as born, swaddled in a sack, and carried to the barn.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says Iasion begot Plutus, meaning wealth or abundance, by Demeter on a thrice-ploughed field, and compares this with a West Prussian mock birth in which the mother is the Corn-mother and the child is the Corn-baby, a crop charm for the next year.

The passage explains the Prussian mother as ripe corn and the child as next year’s corn, then interprets Demeter as this year’s ripe corn and Proserpine as seed-corn sown in autumn and returning in spring; Proserpine’s descent is read as sowing and her return as sprouting.

occurrences.motif_label: conception by sun or divine light
occurrences.basis: The Sicilian princess conceives by the Sun; Danae conceives by Zeus as a shower of gold; the Kirgis maiden conceives when the eye of God falls on her; Frazer states that impregnation by the sun is found in legends.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In a Sicilian story, a seer foretells that a king's daughter will conceive by the Sun; the king encloses her in a windowless tower, but she makes a hole with a bone and a sunbeam enters and impregnates her.

Danae is confined by her father in a subterranean chamber or brazen tower, but Zeus reaches and impregnates her in the shape of a shower of gold; Frazer says this perhaps belongs to the same class of tales.

In the Kirgis ancestry legend, a Khan keeps his daughter in a dark iron house; an old woman shows her the bright world, the eye of God falls upon her and she conceives, and her father sends her floating over the sea in a golden chest.
Frazer states that the shower of gold and eye of God probably stand for sunlight and the sun, and that legends and marriage customs contain traces of women being impregnated by the sun.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odin with either Vili and Ve or Hoenir and Lodur/Loki walks by the seashore and finds two trees, Ask and Embla, or two human-shaped wood blocks.
Odin gives the logs souls, Hoenir gives motion and senses, and Lodur gives blood and blooming complexions.
The created man and woman receive speech, thought, love, hope, work, life, and death, rule Midgard, have descendants, and are watched over by the gods.

occurrences.motif_label: divine-human union producing notable offspring
occurrences.basis: Tyro and Neptune, Antiope and Jove, Alcmena and Jove, and Iphimedeia and Neptune are each linked to divine embrace and notable children.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Tyro, daughter of Salmoneus and wife of Cretheus, loves the river Enipeus; Neptune disguises himself as her lover, meets her at the river mouth beneath a great blue wave, reveals himself, foretells twins, and orders secrecy.
Neptune dives under the sea; Tyro bears Pelias and Neleus, while her other children by Cretheus are Aeson, Pheres, and Amythaon.
Antiope, daughter of Asopus, is said to have slept with Jove and borne Amphion and Zethus, who founded and walled seven-gated Thebes.
Alcmena, wife of Amphitryon, bears Hercules to Jove; Megara, daughter of Creon, is named as wife of Amphitryon's son.

Iphimedeia, wife of Aloeus, boasts of Neptune's embrace and bears Otus and Ephialtes; the giant youths threaten Olympus and try to pile Ossa on Olympus and Pelion on Ossa to scale heaven, but Apollo kills them before maturity.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Rulers are described as physicians of the State who may use falsehood to arrange desirable unions; good are paired with good, bad with bad, and offspring are either reared or destroyed.
Hymeneal festivals are timed for population; brides and bridegrooms meet; rulers use a contrived system of lots so brave and fair persons pair together and inferiors pair with inferiors.
Children of the brave and fair are carried to an enclosure and nursed; the rest are taken to unknown places; mothers suckle children without recognizing their own; attendants handle night care.

occurrences.motif_label: births governed by a sacred or philosophical number
occurrences.basis: The passage identifies 216 as the Platonic number of births and connects it to mathematical, musical, and Pythagorean structures.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The narrator gives reasons for agreeing that 216 is the Platonic number of births: it fits the description, would be familiar to a Greek mathematician, is the cube of 6 and the sum of 3 cubed, 4 cubed, and 5 cubed, relates to the Pythagorean triangle, is the period of Pythagorean Metempsychosis, corresponds to musical scale positions, derives from the cubes of 2 and 3 in the Platonic Tetractys, and the Pythagorean triangle is called the figure of marriage.

occurrences.motif_label: Autochthonous civic origin
occurrences.basis: The passage identifies the myth of earth-born men as an embodiment of orthodox Hellenic tradition and as a founding fiction of the Republic.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage mentions the myth of earth-born men, the four ages of the world, Hesiod and the poets, the old Greek polis, and Plato's vision of a city in the clouds.

The passage describes Plato's ideal state as impossible in his age yet retained as a pattern; it mentions the philosopher son of a king, the noble lie of earth-born men, and the Republic as a vision only.

occurrences.motif_label: Primordial emergence of Love after Chaos and Earth
occurrences.basis: Phaedrus' cited cosmogonic authorities place Love among the earliest divine beings, with Hesiod naming Chaos first and then Earth and Love.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Phaedrus begins by saying Love is a mighty god, wonderful among gods and men, especially in birth, and eldest of the gods, with no recorded parents.

Hesiod is cited: 'First Chaos came, and then broad-bosomed Earth... And Love.' Parmenides is cited as saying, 'First in the train of gods, he fashioned Love,' and Acusilaus is said to agree with Hesiod.

occurrences.motif_label: birth from contrasting parents explains mixed nature
occurrences.basis: Love’s conception by Poverty and Plenty at a divine feast is used to explain his mixed condition and traits.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Diotima begins the tale of Love’s parentage: at Aphrodite’s birthday feast of the gods, Poros or Plenty, son of Metis or Discretion, is present, and Penia or Poverty comes to the doors to beg after the feast.
Plenty, affected by nectar, sleeps in the garden of Zeus; Poverty, seeking relief from her circumstances, lies beside him and conceives Love, who becomes Aphrodite’s follower and attendant.

Because of his parentage, Love is described as always poor, rough, squalid, shoeless, homeless, exposed on bare earth under the open heaven, resting in streets or at doors, and always in distress like his mother.

Like his father, Love is described as plotting against the fair and good, bold, enterprising, strong, a hunter, weaving intrigues, pursuing wisdom, resourceful, and powerful as enchanter, sorcerer, and sophist.

Diotima says lovers of wisdom are those between the wise and the foolish; Love is one of them because wisdom is beautiful and Love is of the beautiful. His father is wealthy and wise, his mother poor and foolish.
