occurrences.motif_label: sacred grove goddess and blossom festival
occurrences.basis: The Oraon spring festival occurs when sál trees bloom, is associated with the marriage of earth, and involves offerings to Sarna Burhi, a goddess of the grove linked with rain.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Oraons have a spring festival while sál trees are blossoming, because they think the marriage of earth is then celebrated and sál flowers are needed.
The villagers and priest go to the Sarna sacred grove, a remnant of old sál forest where Sarna Burhi, woman or goddess of the grove, is supposed to dwell and influence rain.
At the grove, the priest sacrifices five fowls to Sarna Burhi, gives a morsel to each person present, gathers sál flowers with the villagers, and returns to the village.

occurrences.motif_label: Spring bridal pairing or ritual marriage
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly links May or Whitsuntide customs with bridegrooms, brides, kings, queens, lords, ladies, kissing, dancing, marriage expectations, and married trees.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The vegetation spirit is also represented by king and queen, lord and lady, or bridegroom and bride; Frazer states a parallel with vegetable representations of the tree-spirit, since trees are sometimes married to each other.

Examples from Bohemia, Grenoble, Headington, and Saxon villages include king-and-queen or lord-and-lady processions, garlands, gifts, a linked boy and girl, kissing, hidden bridal pairs sought outside the village, music, and dancing.

Near Briançon on May Day, a deserted young man is wrapped in green leaves, feigns sleep, is awakened by a girl who would marry him, dances with her, and is called the bridegroom of May; his leaf garment is made into a flowered nosegay.

occurrences.motif_label: Vegetation or earth marriage
occurrences.basis: The passage mentions the Oraon marriage of earth and says European customs imply the marriage of the spirit of vegetation by naming a human representative the Bride and dressing her in wedding attire.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Oraons of Bengal celebrate the marriage of earth in springtime when the sál-tree is in blossom, but Frazer says this does not prove equivalent European roles.

In some Altmark villages at Whitsuntide, boys carry a May-tree or lead a boy covered in leaves and flowers, while girls lead a May Bride dressed as a bride with a nosegay; she sings for gifts and links giving with household abundance.
In parts of Westphalia, two girls lead a flower-crowned Whitsuntide Bride from door to door and sing asking for eggs.
In Bresse in May, a girl called la Mariée is decorated with ribbons and nosegays, led by a gallant, preceded by a lad with a green May-tree, and accompanied by sung verses.

occurrences.motif_label: mock marriage used to reconcile divine spouses
occurrences.basis: The explanatory story has Zeus announce a marriage to Plataea and stage a veiled wooden bride to provoke Hera, after which Hera and Zeus are reconciled.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The festival is explained by a story in which Hera leaves Zeus after a quarrel; Zeus pretends he will marry Plataea, has a veiled wooden bride-image conveyed on a bullock-cart, and Hera tears off the veil, discovers the deceit, laughs, and is reconciled to Zeus.

occurrences.passage_locator: PREFACE. / J. G. FRAZER. / CHAPTER I. THE KING OF THE WOOD. / MACAULAY.; lines 2649-2713
occurrences.motif_label: Sacred marriage promoting vegetation
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly treats ritual marriages of vegetation powers, Zeus and Hera, Dionysus and the Athenian Queen, and Dionysus and Ariadne as spring rites connected with fertility or vegetation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Boeotian festival is said to represent the spring or midsummer marriage of vegetation powers; a tree dressed as a woman in Boeotian and Russian ceremonies is compared to the English May-pole and May-queen combined.

The Daedala story of Hera’s quarrel with Zeus and retirement is interpreted as possible crop failure; Demeter’s anger and seclusion after Proserpine’s loss are cited as a parallel, and festival myth is used to infer a rite meant to avert famine through divine marriage drama.

The marriage of Zeus and Hera is said to be dramatically represented at annual festivals in Greece and conjecturally equated with Lord and Lady of the May rites; Homer’s image of the gods on hyacinths and crocuses is mentioned.

The passage discusses the annual spring marriage at Athens of the Queen to Dionysus in Anthesterion; Dionysus is described as a vegetation god, the Queen as a priestly functionary, and her attendants as comparable to bridesmaids of the May-queen.

The story of the forsaken sleeping Ariadne awakened and wedded by Dionysus is compared to a French Alpine May Day drama and possibly to a Cretan spring enactment; Ariadne’s starry wedding-crown is related to a garland of a Greek Queen of May performer.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Zapotec priests, especially the high pontiff, observe continence; on certain feast days the high priest becomes drunk and a consecrated virgin is brought to him; a son from the union is raised as a prince and the eldest succeeds to the pontifical throne.

occurrences.motif_label: sacred marriage of vernal or vegetation figures
occurrences.basis: The Ralî rite marries images of Siva and Pârvatî, and Frazer compares this to European rites of the King and Queen of May, May Bride, and May Bridegroom.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The girls divide into parties for Siva and Pârvatî, marry the images in the usual way without omitting any part of the ceremony, and hold a feast paid for by parental contributions.

Frazer compares the spring marriage of Siva and Pârvatî to European ceremonies representing the marriage of vernal vegetation spirits by the King and Queen of May, May Bride, and Bridegroom of the May.

occurrences.motif_label: fertility rite for obtaining husbands
occurrences.basis: The object of the Ralî fair is said to be securing a good husband, which Frazer links to the fertilising influence of vegetation spirits.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At the next Sankrânt, the girls take the images to the riverside, throw them into a deep pool, and weep as if performing funeral obsequies; boys sometimes dive after the images and wave them about while the girls cry. The fair is said to secure a good husband.

Frazer compares throwing the Indian images into water and mourning them to European customs of throwing the dead vegetation spirit into water and lamenting; he also notes female performance and explains the husband-seeking aim by the fertilising influence of vegetation spirits.

occurrences.motif_label: Sacred marriage followed by death rite
occurrences.basis: The Alexandrian rite celebrates the marriage of Adonis and Aphrodite on one day and carries Adonis's image to the sea as a mourning rite the next day.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At Alexandria, images of Adonis and Aphrodite are displayed on two couches, with ripe fruits, cakes, potted plants, and green bowers twined with anise set beside them.
At Alexandria, the lovers' marriage is celebrated one day; on the next, Adonis's image is borne by mourning women with streaming hair and bared breasts to the seashore and committed to the waves.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Frazer says Alexandrian and Indian ceremonies both celebrate the marriage of two plant-surrounded divinities in effigy, then mourn the effigies and throw them into water; he compares them to European spring and midsummer customs.

occurrences.basis: Frazer interprets midsummer and May pairs, including the Swedish Midsummer Bride and bridegroom, as representatives of the spirit of vegetation in its reproductive capacity.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Sardinian Gossips or Sweethearts of St. John probably correspond to the Lord and Lady or King and Queen of May.
In Blekinge, Sweden, the midsummer festival includes electing a Midsummer Bride who chooses a bridegroom; a collection is made, and the pair are temporarily regarded as husband and wife.
Frazer says midsummer pairs, like May pairs, probably represent the spirit of vegetation in reproductive capacity, in flesh and blood as Siva-Pârvatî and Adonis-Aphrodite images do in effigy.

occurrences.basis: The passage says the productive powers of vegetation are represented as bride and bridegroom, including straw-dressed Oats-bride/Oats-bridegroom figures and the Silesian wedding-like procession for the last-sheaf binder.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The names Bride, Oats-bride, and Wheat-bride are sometimes applied in Germany and Scotland to the last sheaf and to the woman who binds it.
In some German harvest festivals, a straw-dressed man and woman called Oats-wife/Oats-man or Oats-bride/Oats-bridegroom dance, and corn-stalks are then plucked from their bodies.
In Silesia, the woman who binds the last sheaf is called Wheat-bride or Oats-bride and is brought to the farmhouse with harvest crown, bridegroom, bridesmaids, and wedding-like solemnity.

occurrences.motif_label: ritual marriage of crop spirits
occurrences.basis: The Javanese rite names decorated rice ears as Rice-bride and Rice-bridegroom, celebrates their wedding feast, houses them in a bridal chamber, and protects them as a newly wedded pair.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At the rice-harvest in Java, before reaping, a priest or sorcerer selects ears of rice, ties them together, smears them with ointment, adorns them with flowers, calls them the Rice-bride and Rice-bridegroom, celebrates their wedding feast, and then cutting begins.

When the Javanese rice is housed, a bridal chamber is made in the barn with a new mat, lamp, and toilet articles; rice sheaves represent wedding guests; no one may enter the barn for forty days to avoid disturbing the newly wedded pair.

The gods leave ruins behind, return to Asgard, restore Freya’s garments, rejoice over the hammer, and Odin later sees green growth on the conquered land.

Bragi wins Idun as wife; they go to Asgard, where Odin traces runes on Bragi’s tongue and decrees him heavenly minstrel and composer of songs for gods and heroes.

occurrences.basis: After Skadi demands satisfaction for her father’s death, the gods offer compensation that includes choosing a husband from among the gods under specified conditions.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Skadi, Thiassi’s daughter and goddess of winter, comes in armor and winter gear to demand satisfaction for her father’s death; the gods offer a fine, she demands a life, and Loki’s goat antics make her smile.
The gods show Skadi Thiassi’s eyes shining as stars and offer her a husband from among the gods if she chooses by looking only at their naked feet; she selects feet she thinks belong to Balder.

When the bandage is removed, Skadi finds she has chosen Niörd; after time in Asgard she goes to Nôatûn but cannot sleep because of the sounds of sea birds, waves, and seals, and asks to return to Thrym-heim.

occurrences.motif_label: Seasonal alternation of divine spouses
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly interprets Niörd and Skadi as summer and winter, alternating residences according to a three-to-nine pattern and separating because their seasonal domains do not agree.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Niörd consents to take Skadi to Thrym-heim for nine nights out of twelve if she spends three at Nôatûn; he finds the mountain sounds unbearable and rejoices when he can return to Nôatûn. The inserted verse contrasts wolves’ howling with swans’ song.

Under the heading “The Parting of Niörd and Skadi,” the passage says Niörd and Skadi personify summer and winter, alternate between sea and mountain as three summer months and nine winter months, then separate permanently and return home. The quoted stanza says Skade dwells in Thjasse’s former mansion, Thrym-heim.

The passage interprets Skadi’s anger over her father’s death as an emblem of ice-bound earth, softened by Loki as heat lightning and by Niörd as summer; Niörd’s love holds her only three months before she longs for winter storms and mountain activities.

Eurynome and the nurse prepare the bed with torches and coverlets; Eurynome leads Ulysses and Penelope to their room by torchlight; the couple comes joyfully to their old bed while others stop dancing and sleep.
After love, Penelope tells of the suitors’ abuses in the house, and Ulysses tells all of his sufferings and the trouble he caused others while she listens until he finishes.

Agamemnon contrasts Penelope with the daughter of Tyndareus, who killed her lawful husband and whose song will be hateful among men.

occurrences.source_title: Phaedrus
occurrences.passage_locator: Phaedrus / PHAEDRUS / INTRODUCTION.; lines 549-637
occurrences.motif_label: marriage tested against reason, passion, and friendship
occurrences.basis: The passage asks whether marriage is preferable with or without love, criticizes passion-led marriage, and contrasts it with friendship.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A modern Socrates is imagined asking whether marriage is preferable with or without love, parodying Pausanias in the Symposium, opposing sentimental literature, and arguing that passion should not guide a major life contract; marriage is compared to a lottery.

The imagined critic describes marriage as monopolizing affections, excluding friends and relations, causing triviality, lowering one partner, hindering public duties, preventing noble enterprises, and turning fondness into mutual dislike.
Friendship is praised as nobler, less exclusive, less expensive, less likely to take offence, more stable, easier to dissolve, and more improving to the mind than marriage.

occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V.; lines 15706-15845
occurrences.motif_label: sacralized and regulated marriage for civic benefit
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly states that matrimony should be made sacred in the highest degree and identifies the most beneficial arrangement as sacred, within a state-regulated marriage system.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Glaucon names a necessity known to lovers; the speaker says the matter must proceed orderly, licentiousness is unholy and forbidden, and matrimony must be made sacred in the highest degree, with what is most beneficial deemed sacred.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II. / BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V.; lines 15847-15992
occurrences.motif_label: Ritualized state-controlled marriage and procreation
occurrences.basis: The passage presents public hymeneals with sacrifices, prayers, and songs, while rulers regulate which couples unite and how many weddings occur.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Festivals will bring brides and bridegrooms together with sacrifices and hymeneal songs, while rulers determine wedding numbers to preserve population balance amid war and disease.

Those outside the prescribed ages who join public hymeneals act unholily and unrighteously; their child is contrasted with offspring blessed by sacrifices and prayers and called offspring of darkness and strange lust.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 17792-17900
occurrences.motif_label: Abandoned noble bride and unworthy suitors
occurrences.basis: Philosophy is personified as desolate with an incomplete marriage rite; unworthy persons enter and dishonour her, and a simile presents an unsuitable bridegroom marrying a poor desolate daughter.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “philosophy is left desolate, with her marriage rite incomplete”; unworthy persons enter when she has no kinsmen to protect her and dishonour her.
The unworthy entrant is compared to a bald little tinker released from confinement, bathed, newly clothed, and dressed as a bridegroom to marry his master’s poor desolate daughter.
Such marriages are said to have vile and bastard issue; unworthy alliances with philosophy generate sophisms pleasing to the ear but lacking genuine kinship with true wisdom.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 2745-2827
occurrences.motif_label: sacredly regulated marriage
occurrences.basis: The passage institutes holy marriage festivals and regulates unions through rulers, timing, and rules of age and consent.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Licentiousness is forbidden; holy marriage festivals are instituted; Glaucon is asked about careful mating in breeding birds and animals, and human marriage is said to require care.
Hymeneal festivals are timed for population; brides and bridegrooms meet; rulers use a contrived system of lots so brave and fair persons pair together and inferiors pair with inferiors.

Men and women have specified prime reproductive ages; participation outside those ages or outside approved times is impiety; later freedom is allowed with prohibited kinship degrees and possible dispensations.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A clever mechanic or bald blacksmith's apprentice washes and dresses as a bridegroom and marries his master's daughter; the offspring of such marriages are described as vile and bastard.

occurrences.source_title: The Republic

occurrences.motif_label: marriage figured by geometric form
occurrences.basis: The passage says the Pythagorean triangle is called the figure of marriage.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The narrator gives reasons for agreeing that 216 is the Platonic number of births: it fits the description, would be familiar to a Greek mathematician, is the cube of 6 and the sum of 3 cubed, 4 cubed, and 5 cubed, relates to the Pythagorean triangle, is the period of Pythagorean Metempsychosis, corresponds to musical scale positions, derives from the cubes of 2 and 3 in the Platonic Tetractys, and the Pythagorean triangle is called the figure of marriage.

occurrences.motif_label: Consecrated marriage and family order
occurrences.basis: The passage says marriage and family have become more defined and consecrated, and argues for maintaining the sacredness of the marriage tie.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Speculations are unsettling because marriage may appear to be historical growth rather than revelation from heaven; nevertheless marriage and family are said to have become more defined and consecrated, with comparisons among the East, Greeks, Romans, and Christian nations.
"There is more reason for maintaining the sacredness of the marriage tie"; the passage warns that in transition from old to new beliefs people may let go of moral principle.

occurrences.motif_label: Miraculous child becomes great hunter and prosperous ancestor
occurrences.basis: The child of the god becomes a great hunter, rich man, father of children, and ancestor of living descendants.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A baby is then heard crying outside; the old woman brings in a fine baby boy, who is kept, grows into a man, and kills many deer and bears.
The son cannot be caught by bears, is a great hunter and rich man, later takes a wife, has children, becomes rich, and has descendants living to the narrator's day.

occurrences.passage_locator: AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA. / II.--MORAL TALES. / IV.--MISCELLANEOUS TALES.; lines 2102-2199
occurrences.motif_label: culture hero teaches practical arts
occurrences.basis: Okikurumi, with Tureshihi, teaches the Ainos hunting, fishing, and other arts.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Okikurumi, with his younger sister Tureshihi, taught the Ainos arts such as bow-and-arrow hunting, netting fish, and spearing fish.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: LOCAL SECRETARIES. / HONORARY SECRETARIES. / INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE.; lines 435-482
occurrences.motif_label: ancient civilizer figure
occurrences.basis: Okikurumi is described as a mythological name and as the being whom the Ainu regard as their civilizer in very ancient times.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "The only mythological names which appear are Okikurumi, whom the Ainos regard as having been their civilizer in very ancient times, his sister-wife Turesh, or Tureshi[hi] and his henchman Samayunguru."

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: HONORARY SECRETARIES. / INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA.; lines 485-608
occurrences.motif_label: Culture figure reveals origin and disciplines quarrelling beings
occurrences.basis: Okikurumi identifies the hares' origin from sky-children's snowballs and beats the quarrelling hares with a fire-brand.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A large house suddenly appears on a mountain top, containing six beautifully arrayed people who constantly quarrel.
Okikurumi calls the six beings hares and says sky-children's snowballs fell into the world of men and were turned into hares.
Okikurumi beats each hare with a fire-brand; the tale explains the hare's white body as snow and black ears as charred by the fire-brand.

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: HONORARY SECRETARIES. / INTRODUCTION. / AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA.; lines 902-1009
occurrences.motif_label: Divine provider withdraws after human transgression
occurrences.basis: Okikurumi feeds the people in a dangerous world, but after the taboo violation he becomes angry, stops feeding them, and departs.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In ancient days, the new world is unsettled and burning beneath a thin crust, so people stay in huts; Okikurumi fishes for them and sends Turesh with food, while commanding them not to ask questions or look at her face.

An Aino disobeys by seizing Turesh's hand and pulling her into the hut; she becomes a wriggling dragon, thunder and lightning destroy the hut, and Okikurumi angrily stops feeding the people and departs.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 1 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE. / CHAPTER III. KILLING THE GOD.; lines 6597-6671
occurrences.motif_label: Civilizing king introduces agriculture and worship
occurrences.basis: Osiris gives laws, teaches worship of the gods, travels diffusing civilization, and introduces grain cultivation after Isis discovers wheat and barley.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Osiris is introduced as son of the earth-god Qeb/Seb; as king on earth he reclaims Egyptians from savagery, gives laws, and teaches worship of the gods.
Isis, sister and wife of Osiris, discovers wild wheat and barley; Osiris introduces cultivation of these grains, and the people abandon cannibalism for a corn diet.
Osiris travels spreading civilization; on return Set/Typhon and seventy-two others plot against him, seal him in a decorated coffer with molten lead, cast it into the Nile, and it floats to the sea.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 1 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE. / CHAPTER III. KILLING THE GOD.; lines 6725-6799
occurrences.motif_label: grain-giving goddess and personified corn-field
occurrences.basis: Isis is credited with wheat and barley, receives grain processions and harvest laments, and is described with epithets such as green crop, mistress of bread, corn-field, mother of ears of corn, and queen of the wheat-field.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Wheat and barley are attributed to Isis; stalks are carried in procession at her festivals; after first cutting at harvest, Egyptian reapers lay down the stalks, beat their breasts, lament, and call upon Isis.

Isis is called creatress of green crop, green like earth, mistress of bread, personified corn-field, Sochit/Sochet meaning corn-field; Greeks identify her with Demeter; Greek verses call her giver of earth's fruits, mother of ears of corn, and queen of the wheat-field.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: MY LORD BAG OF RICE / THE TONGUE-CUT SPARROW / THE STORY OF URASHIMA TARO, THE FISHER LAD / THE FARMER AND THE BADGER; lines 1413-1523
occurrences.motif_label: culture hero ruler invents guiding technology
occurrences.basis: Kotei invents the shinansha, a south-pointing carriage, to overcome the magician’s fog and guide his army.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage contrasts the north-pointing compass with the shinansha, a chariot bearing a man-shaped figure that always points south.
Kotei returns to his palace, thinks about how to defeat Shiyu, and invents the shinansha so the magician’s fog cannot make his army lose the way.
Kotei places the shinansha before his army; when Shiyu again creates fog, Kotei uses it to guide the troops, pursues Shiyu to a flooded river, and Shiyu crosses by magic to a fortress.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: MY LORD BAG OF RICE / THE TONGUE-CUT SPARROW / THE STORY OF URASHIMA TARO, THE FISHER LAD / THE FARMER AND THE BADGER; lines 1525-1574
occurrences.motif_label: beneficial inventor ruler
occurrences.basis: Kotei invents the first boat, makes other beneficial inventions, restores peace, and is loved by his subjects.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A leaf carrying a spider over the river inspires Kotei to invent the first boat; he then has enough boats made for the whole army.
Kotei takes his army across the river, attacks Shiyu's headquarters, gains complete victory, and ends the war.
Kotei secures peace and prosperity, is loved by his subjects, and makes inventions for their benefit, including the boat and the South Pointing shinansha.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE TONGUE-CUT SPARROW / THE STORY OF URASHIMA TARO, THE FISHER LAD / THE FARMER AND THE BADGER / THE ADVENTURES OF KINTARO, THE GOLDEN BOY; lines 1834-1943
occurrences.motif_label: hero defeats a man-eating monster
occurrences.basis: Kintaro is ordered to rescue frightened people from a cannibal monster, kills it in its den, and is afterward described as the greatest hero of his country.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Raiko’s army includes the elite Four Braves; after Kintaro grows up, Raiko makes him their chief. News then arrives of a cannibal monster, and Raiko orders Kintaro to rescue the people.
Kintaro surprises the monster in its den, cuts off its great head, and carries it back in triumph to his master.
Kintaro becomes the greatest hero of his country, gains power, honor, and wealth, and builds a comfortable home for his mother in the Capital.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: COMPILED BY / PREFACE / JAPANESE FAIRY TALES / MY LORD BAG OF RICE; lines 262-377
occurrences.motif_label: Hero kills a monstrous serpentine enemy
occurrences.basis: Hidesato, called a brave warrior and preserver, kills a huge centipede whose body is described as serpentine.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hidesato sees an enormous centipede winding around the mountains in starlight, with fire-like eyes and glowing feet moving toward the shore.
The saliva-treated arrow strikes the centipede's brain; its body stops, its fiery lights darken and go out, and a violent darkness, thunder, lightning, and wind shake the palace before clear dawn.
The Dragon King's whole family bows before Hidesato and calls him their preserver and the bravest warrior in Japan.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE JELLY FISH AND THE MONKEY / THE QUARREL OF THE MONKEY AND THE CRAB / THE WHITE HARE AND THE CROCODILES / THE STORY OF PRINCE YAMATO TAKE; lines 5813-5924
occurrences.motif_label: royal son pacifies land by defeating rebels
occurrences.basis: The Prince is the King's son, sent as avenger of evil, and his victories bring peace and rest to the land and people before royal reward.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Prince identifies himself as the King's son Yamato, sent by his father as avenger of evil to bring death to rebels and end robbery and murder.
The narrator says Yamato Take prevails against the King's foes through wisdom, bodily strength, and craftiness, bringing peace and rest to the land and people.
When Yamato Take returns to the capital, the King praises him, holds a palace feast, gives rare gifts, and loves him more than ever.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE JELLY FISH AND THE MONKEY / THE QUARREL OF THE MONKEY AND THE CRAB / THE WHITE HARE AND THE CROCODILES / THE STORY OF PRINCE YAMATO TAKE; lines 6128-6233
occurrences.motif_label: warrior hero protects community by confronting a devouring monster
occurrences.basis: The people of Omi fear a monster that devours villagers, and Yamato Take vows to kill it.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In Omi, villagers mourn and fear a mountain monster that raids villages and devours people, keeping men and women from ordinary work.
Yamato Take says it is strange that a wicked monster near the capital terrorizes the king’s subjects, and he declares that he will kill it at once.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE QUARREL OF THE MONKEY AND THE CRAB / THE WHITE HARE AND THE CROCODILES / THE STORY OF PRINCE YAMATO TAKE / MOMOTARO, OR THE STORY OF THE SON OF A PEACH; lines 6236-6369
occurrences.motif_label: heroic youth marked by extraordinary qualities
occurrences.basis: Momotaro grows stronger than other boys and is described as courageous, wise, and hero-like.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At fifteen, Momotaro is taller and stronger than other boys, handsome, courageous, wise, and viewed by the old couple as hero-like.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE QUARREL OF THE MONKEY AND THE CRAB / THE WHITE HARE AND THE CROCODILES / THE STORY OF PRINCE YAMATO TAKE / MOMOTARO, OR THE STORY OF THE SON OF A PEACH; lines 6371-6508
occurrences.motif_label: young champion restoring peace by fighting monstrous raiders
occurrences.basis: Momotaro says he must conquer the devils who raid the land, recover plunder, and bring peace; the old man endorses this purpose.

evidence.locator: lines 6371-6508, Momotaro explains the Island of Devils
evidence.quote_or_summary: Momotaro describes a sea island northeast of Japan as the stronghold of devils who invade, kill, rob, carry off goods, disobey the Emperor, and eat some captives.
The old man says he will not hinder Momotaro and tells him to go to the island, destroy the demons, and bring peace to the land.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE QUARREL OF THE MONKEY AND THE CRAB / THE WHITE HARE AND THE CROCODILES / THE STORY OF PRINCE YAMATO TAKE / MOMOTARO, OR THE STORY OF THE SON OF A PEACH; lines 6510-6645
occurrences.motif_label: Monster-subduing expedition for the country’s welfare
occurrences.basis: Momotaro leads a raid on devils and thinks of killing monsters who have done much harm in his country.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Momotaro says, “The first thing necessary in an army is harmony,” orders the dog, monkey, and pheasant to be friends with one mind, and the pheasant becomes a member of the suite and receives half a cake.

Momotaro obtains a small ship; the four sail in fair weather, the animals become accustomed to the water, they watch for the demons’ island, and Momotaro longs to kill the monsters who harmed his country.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE QUARREL OF THE MONKEY AND THE CRAB / THE WHITE HARE AND THE CROCODILES / THE STORY OF PRINCE YAMATO TAKE / MOMOTARO, OR THE STORY OF THE SON OF A PEACH; lines 6647-6752
occurrences.motif_label: Hero with animal companions conquers demon stronghold
occurrences.basis: Momotaro, aided by the pheasant, dog, and monkey, attacks and defeats the devils who have terrorized the land.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The pheasant flies from the ship to the castle roof, announces Momotaro’s challenge, demands that the devils surrender by breaking off their horns, and threatens them with death by the pheasant, dog, and monkey if they resist.
The pheasant sees Momotaro and his small group rush into the castle from the back while the bird continues fighting.

Momotaro, the dog, monkey, and pheasant overwhelm the devils; some devils fall from the parapet and are dashed on rocks, others fall into the sea and drown, and many are beaten to death by the animals.
The damsels and other enslaved captives are taken safely home, and the country celebrates Momotaro as the hero who freed it from the robber devils.

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE WHITE HARE AND THE CROCODILES / THE STORY OF PRINCE YAMATO TAKE / MOMOTARO, OR THE STORY OF THE SON OF A PEACH / THE OGRE OF RASHOMON; lines 6883-6997
occurrences.motif_label: heroic protection of a city from a night-roaming monster
occurrences.basis: Watanabe's deed is celebrated, and after the ogre escapes it fears Watanabe and no longer troubles Kyoto, allowing people to go out at night safely.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Watanabe is praised as a hero after showing the ogre's arm; he has a strong wooden, iron-banded box made, seals the arm inside, and keeps it in his room under his own charge.
The ogre escapes with the arm; Watanabe waits for another chance, but the ogre fears him, never troubles Kyoto again, and the people can go out at night without fear.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE STORY OF PRINCE YAMATO TAKE / MOMOTARO, OR THE STORY OF THE SON OF A PEACH / THE OGRE OF RASHOMON / HOW AN OLD MAN LOST HIS WEN; lines 7485-7562
occurrences.motif_label: ruler restores cosmic order
occurrences.basis: Jokwa repairs cosmic damage, restores the conditions for sunlight and moonlight, and peace and prosperity follow under her reign.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Jokwa has subjects collect five-colored stones, boils them with porcelain in a caldron, and produces a paste for mending the sky.
Jokwa summons clouds, rides heavenward with the vase of paste, mends the broken sky, repairs the broken pillar with legs of a very large tortoise, descends, and finds the world still dark.
The ambassadors report that Empress Jokwa repaired the roads with stones of five colors and restored the broken pillar with the legs of a great tortoise.
The Sun and Moon test the roads, find the report true, give light to the earth again, and the people rejoice as peace and prosperity follow in China under Jokwa.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: RHEA (OPS). / DIVISION OF THE WORLD. / THEORIES AS TO THE ORIGIN OF MAN. / THIRD DYNASTY--OLYMPIAN DIVINITIES.; lines 1081-1171
occurrences.motif_label: Music or enchanted instrument moves stones
occurrences.basis: Amphion plays a lyre given by Hermes and stones move and fit together to form the walls and towers of Thebes.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Amphion becomes king of Thebes, is linked with music and poetry, and uses a lyre from Hermes to make stones move into walls and towers; Zethus is linked with archery, the chase, and a club in sculpture.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: RETURN OF THE GREEKS FROM TROY. / PRONOUNCING INDEX. / A COMPLETE COURSE IN THE STUDY OF ENGLISH. / NOTES; lines 11638-11773
occurrences.motif_label: musical invention from monstrous lament
occurrences.basis: Athene imitates a dirge-like sound from snake-haired figures on a reed and invents the flute.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After Perseus cuts off Medusa's head with Athene's help, Medusa's two sisters make a dirge-like song from the snakes of their hair; Athene imitates it on a reed and invents the flute.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: RETURN OF THE GREEKS FROM TROY. / PRONOUNCING INDEX. / A COMPLETE COURSE IN THE STUDY OF ENGLISH. / NOTES; lines 11638-11773
occurrences.motif_label: divine teacher of rural arts
occurrences.basis: Aristaeus teaches mankind bee-catching and the use of honey and wax.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Aristaeus is a rural divinity said to have taught mankind how to catch bees and use honey and wax.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: JUPITER. / HERA (JUNO). / JUNO. / PALLAS-ATHENE (MINERVA).; lines 1430-1518
occurrences.motif_label: culture-bringing inventor and teacher
occurrences.basis: Athene teaches or presides over agriculture, numbers, navigation, chariots, the wooden horse, weaving, and the flute.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Athene protects the state, law, and right; supports the Greeks in the Trojan war; institutes the Areopagus; and presides over learning, agriculture, numbers, trumpets, chariots, the Argo, and the wooden horse.

Athene presides over spinning and weaving, makes garments for herself, Hera, and Jason, accepts Arachne's challenge, is defeated, strikes Arachne with a shuttle, and changes her into a spider after Arachne hangs herself.
Athene invents the flute, is laughed at by gods and goddesses for her facial contortions while playing, looks at herself in a fountain, throws the flute away, and never plays it again.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: PALLAS-ATHENE (MINERVA). / MINERVA. / THEMIS. / VESTA.; lines 1634-1698
occurrences.motif_label: Divine introduction of agriculture
occurrences.basis: Demeter is said to have introduced knowledge of agriculture, ending nomadic life and enabling settled habitation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says early humans did not know sowing or tilling and that Demeter’s introduction of agriculture ended the need for nomadic life.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: PALLAS-ATHENE (MINERVA). / MINERVA. / THEMIS. / VESTA.; lines 1776-1867
occurrences.motif_label: Culture-bringer teaches agriculture
occurrences.basis: Demeter sends Triptolemus through the world with corn and a dragon-drawn chariot to teach agriculture and husbandry.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Demeter gives Triptolemus a chariot drawn by winged dragons and grains of corn, sending him to teach agriculture and husbandry throughout the world.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VENUS. / HELIOS (SOL). / EOS (AURORA). / PHOEBUS-APOLLO.; lines 2279-2363
occurrences.motif_label: serpent-slaying at sacred site
occurrences.basis: Apollo kills the serpent Python guarding the oracle and thereby frees the surrounding land and people.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The oracle is guarded by the huge serpent Python, a scourge of the neighborhood and terror of men and cattle.
Apollo attacks and kills Python with arrows, freeing the land and people from their mighty enemy.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VENUS. / HELIOS (SOL). / EOS (AURORA). / PHOEBUS-APOLLO.; lines 2279-2363
occurrences.motif_label: divine foundation of civic and ritual authority
occurrences.basis: The Delphic oracle is linked to temple service, lawgiving, colonization, city foundation, and the approval of enterprises.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Apollo appears as a vigorous youth, reveals himself, and tells the sailors he brought them to Crissa to become his priests and serve in his temple.
At the sacred fane, Apollo teaches the sailors his services and asks to be worshipped as Apollo-Delphinios because he first appeared as a dolphin.

The Delphic oracle is described as widely renowned and consulted by Lydians, Phrygians, Etruscans, Romans, and others; its decrees are linked to Lycurgus' laws, early colonies, city foundations, and enterprises.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VENUS. / HELIOS (SOL). / EOS (AURORA). / PHOEBUS-APOLLO.; lines 2441-2527
occurrences.motif_label: music animates building stones
occurrences.basis: Apollo's lyre music causes huge blocks of stone to move by themselves and fit into Troy's walls during construction.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Apollo helps build Troy's walls with his music; when he plays the lyre, huge stone blocks move by themselves and fit precisely into place.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: BRAURONIAN ARTEMIS. / SELENE-ARTEMIS. / DIANA. / HEPHAESTUS (VULCAN).; lines 3109-3194
occurrences.motif_label: Divine fire-smith as civilizing instructor
occurrences.basis: Hephaestus governs beneficial fire and workmanship, builds forges, teaches metalwork and useful arts to the Lemnians, and produces key divine and mortal crafted works.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hephaestus is introduced as son of Zeus and Hera, god of beneficial fire, workmanship, mechanical arts, and hearth; he is deformed and lame after Zeus hurls him from heaven to Lemnos, where the Lemnians receive him and he later teaches metalwork and useful arts.

Hephaestus is described as indispensable to the Olympian assembly as smith, armourer, and chariot-builder; he makes divine palaces, golden shoes, chariots, brass-shod horses, self-moving tripods, Zeus's aegis, the palace of the sun, and fire-breathing brazen-footed bulls of Aetes.
Hephaestus's renowned works for mortals include the armour of Achilles and Aeneas, Harmonia's necklace, Ariadne's crown, and Pandora as his masterpiece.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: DIANA. / HEPHAESTUS (VULCAN). / VULCAN. / POSEIDON (NEPTUNE).; lines 3296-3398
occurrences.motif_label: Contest of divine gifts deciding city patronage
occurrences.basis: Poseidon and Athene compete by offering gifts to mankind; the gods judge Athene's olive-tree superior to Poseidon's horse and grant her naming rights over Athens.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Poseidon and Athene contest naming Cecropia; Poseidon strikes the ground with his trident and the horse appears, while Athene produces the olive-tree; the gods award victory to Athene and the city is called Athens.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: DIANA. / HEPHAESTUS (VULCAN). / VULCAN. / POSEIDON (NEPTUNE).; lines 3296-3398
occurrences.motif_label: Divine gift of animal domestication and horsemanship
occurrences.basis: Poseidon produces the horse, tames it for mankind, and teaches men to manage horses with the bridle.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Poseidon and Athene contest naming Cecropia; Poseidon strikes the ground with his trident and the horse appears, while Athene produces the olive-tree; the gods award victory to Athene and the city is called Athens.

Poseidon tames the horse, teaches bridle management, is honored in Isthmian horse and chariot races, receives sacrifices, has trident, horse, and dolphin as attributes, and is identified in some places with Nereus.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: MARS. / NIKE (VICTORIA). / VICTORIA. / HERMES (MERCURY).; lines 3746-3817
occurrences.motif_label: culture hero inventor
occurrences.basis: Hermes is credited with inventing the alphabet, teaching interpretation of foreign languages, and inventing the lyre.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hermes is described as messenger and ambassador of the gods, conductor of shades to Hades, patron of youth and athletics, inventor of the alphabet, teacher of interpreting foreign languages, and cunning attendant of Zeus when Zeus travels on earth disguised as a mortal.
Hermes finds and kills a tortoise, stretches seven strings across the empty shell, invents a lyre, plays it skillfully, and places it in his cradle.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VICTORIA. / HERMES (MERCURY). / MERCURY. / DIONYSUS (BACCHUS).; lines 3954-4041
occurrences.motif_label: culture hero brings wine and cultivation
occurrences.basis: Dionysus discovers the vine, learns to make wine, teaches vine cultivation, founds cities, and establishes more civilized and sociable life.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Dionysus roams woods with companions, finds the vine, extracts an exhilarating beverage, and sets out with followers to plant and teach vine cultivation.

Dionysus leads men, women, fauns, and satyrs bearing Thyrsi and instruments; seated in a panther-drawn chariot, he progresses through Syria, Egypt, Arabia, India, and other regions, conquering, founding cities, and civilizing.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: ASCLEPIAS (AESCULAPIUS). / AESCULAPIUS. / ROMAN DIVINITIES. / JANUS.; lines 5712-5790
occurrences.motif_label: wise ruler deified after death
occurrences.basis: Janus is said to have been an ancient king whose wise and moderate rule led his people to deify him after death.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Janus is said to have been an ancient Italian king deified after wise rule; Saturn, identified with Greek Cronus, gave him knowledge of past and future events, explaining his two opposite-facing faces.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: LIBITINA. / LAVERNA. / COMUS. / THE CAMENAE.; lines 5955-5976
occurrences.motif_label: Culture-bringing founder introduces foreign civilization and worship
occurrences.basis: Evander leads a colony, founds a town, and introduces Greek art, civilization, divinities, and worship into Italy.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Carmenta was celebrated as mother of Evander, who led an Arcadian colony into Italy and founded a town on the river Tiber later incorporated with Rome.
Evander is said to have been the first to introduce Greek art, civilization, Greek divinities, and their worship into Italy.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CEREALIA. / VESTALIA. / PART II.--LEGENDS. / CADMUS.; lines 6563-6631
occurrences.motif_label: oracle-directed city foundation
occurrences.basis: The oracle redirects Cadmus to found a city, and Cadmus ultimately builds Thebes.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Cadmus searches unsuccessfully for years, consults Apollo's oracle at Delphi, and is told to abandon the search and found a city where an unyoked heifer lies down.
Pallas-Athene commands Cadmus to sow the dragon's teeth; armed men arise, fight until five remain, and those survivors help Cadmus build Thebes; later noble Theban families claim descent from them.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VESTALIA. / PART II.--LEGENDS. / CADMUS. / PERSEUS.; lines 6736-6832
occurrences.motif_label: Heroic founder and legitimating ancestor
occurrences.basis: Perseus founds Mycenae and Midea, is ancestor of Heracles through Alcmene, and receives heroic honours in multiple places.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Perseus performs funeral rites for Acrisius, exchanges kingdoms with Megapenthes, founds Mycenae and Midea, and gives Medusa's head to Pallas-Athene, who places it on her shield.
Perseus and Andromeda are said to be ancestors of many heroes, especially Heracles through Alcmene; heroic honours are paid to Perseus in Argos, Athens, and Seriphus.

Daedalus tires of exile and near imprisonment by Minos, contrives wings for himself and Icarus, and trains his son to use them.
Daedalus buries Icarus on an island named Icaria and then flies to Sicily, where Cocalus welcomes him and he makes public works.

Erginus gathers an army and comes to Thebes demanding Heracles; Creon considers yielding, but Heracles advances with Amphitryon and brave youths against the Minyans.
Heracles occupies a narrow defile; the Thebans attack the Minyans, kill Erginus, and rout them; Amphitryon dies, and Heracles burns the royal castle and sacks Orchomenus.

Heracles finds the lion, arrows fail, he strikes it with his club and strangles it, makes armor from its skin and head, and frightens Eurystheus, who thereafter sends commands through Copreus.

Athena appears and gives Heracles gigantic brazen clappers made by Hephaestus; from a hill he rattles them, causing the birds to rise in terror, then shoots many and the rest flee permanently.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At Epidaurus Theseus meets Periphetes, son of Hephaestus, who kills travellers with an iron club; Theseus kills him and takes the club as trophy.
At the Isthmus of Corinth Theseus is warned about Sinnis, who kills travellers with a bent pine branch; Theseus kills him with one blow from the club.
In the woody district of Crommyon, Theseus kills a wild dangerous sow that had long ravaged the country.
Near Megara, Scyron forces strangers to wash his feet and kicks them over a rock into the sea; Theseus overcomes him and flings his body over the cliff.
At Eleusis, King Cercyon forces all comers to wrestle with him and kills the defeated; Theseus overcomes and slays him.
Near the Cephissus, Damastes called Procrustes uses long and short iron beds to stretch or cut victims; Theseus kills him by treating him as he treated others.

occurrences.motif_label: divine spirit transmigrating at the death of its human incarnation
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly states that at the death of a human incarnation the divine spirit may transmigrate, then gives Kaffa, Laosian, Bhotan, Grand Lama, and Dalai Lama examples.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage states that at the death of a human incarnation, the divine spirit sometimes transmigrates into another person.
After the Kaffa pope dies, priests declare that Deòce has passed into the king, who then unites spiritual and temporal power and reigns as god and king.
Before work at salt-pans in a Laosian village, workers sacrifice to a local divinity that is incarnate in a woman and transmigrates into another woman at her death.

In Bhotan, the Dhurma Raja is the spiritual head of government and a perpetual incarnation of deity; after his death the new incarnate god appears in an infant who refuses mother's milk and prefers cow's milk.
Buddhist Tartars believe in many living Buddhas serving as Grand Lamas; when one dies, disciples expect him to reappear as an infant and seek his birthplace.

The Dalai Lama of Lhasa is head of all Lamas, regarded as a living god, and at death his divine and immortal spirit is born again in a child; accounts differ between recognition methods and election by lot.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Frazer says resurrection of the pretended dead person is sometimes enacted; in one Swabian example, Dr. Iron-Beard bleeds a sick man who falls as dead, then restores him to life by blowing air through a tube.

In the Harz mountains, after Carnival a man is carried with dirges to a grave, but a glass of brandy is placed in the grave; the next Shrove Tuesday the brandy is dug up and tasted as having come to life again.

occurrences.motif_label: Death and revival of vegetation spirit
occurrences.basis: Frazer explicitly connects the expulsion of Death and bringing in of Summer with the death and resuscitation of the spirit of vegetation in spring.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Frazer infers that the Summer-tree and, in some cases, the effigy called Death embody the tree-spirit or spirit of vegetation; fragments of Death are believed to fertilise vegetable and animal life.
The effigy of Death may be made of birchen twigs, a beech branch, a threshed-out corn-sheaf, or hemp, and may be hung on a small tree and carried by girls collecting money.
The expulsion of Death and bringing in of Summer are described as another form of the death and resuscitation of the spirit of vegetation in spring, like the killing and resurrection of the Wild Man.
The burial and resurrection of Carnival is said probably to express the same idea; burying the Carnival representative under a dung-heap is linked to quickening and fertilising influence.

occurrences.basis: The Kostrubonko rite explicitly enacts death and coming to life, and Frazer states that the figures' death is a preliminary to revival.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At Eastertide in Little Russia, singers circle a girl lying as if dead, sing that Kostrubonko is dead, and then rejoice when she springs up and is said to have come to life.

Frazer states that these Russian customs are of the same nature as Austrian and German Burying the Carnival and Carrying out Death, and interprets Kostroma, Yarilo, and related figures as vegetation spirits whose death precedes revival at a seasonal turning point.

occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly frames Adonis or Thammuz and other deities as representing the decay and revival of vegetation, and describes annual mourning followed by revival rites or belief in renewed life.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Egyptians, Syrians, Babylonians, Phrygians, and Greeks are said to represent decay and revival of vegetation under names including Osiris, Adonis, Thammuz, Attis, and Dionysus, with rites called substantially similar and paralleled in European peasant customs.
His death is annually lamented, chiefly by women; corpse-like images are carried out as to burial and thrown into the sea or springs; in some places his revival is celebrated on the following day.
At Byblus, Adonis's death is mourned with weeping, wailing, and breast-beating; the next day he is believed to come to life again and ascend to heaven in the presence of worshippers.

At Alexandria, the lovers' marriage is celebrated one day; on the next, Adonis's image is borne by mourning women with streaming hair and bared breasts to the seashore and committed to the waves.
At Byblus, Adonis's death is mourned with weeping, wailing, and breast-beating; the next day he is believed to come to life again and ascend to heaven in the presence of worshippers.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says Adonis spends half or a third of the year in the lower world and the rest in the upper world, and Frazer interprets this as vegetation or corn buried in earth and reappearing above ground.
Frazer argues that the death and resurrection of Adonis represent the annual decay and revival of vegetation, a phenomenon he presents as widespread and striking across human societies.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Babylonian legend says Istar descends to Hades to fetch the water of life to restore dead Thammuz; water appears to have been thrown over him during a mourning ceremony around his funeral pyre.

Frazer reports that the legend is probably a mythical explanation of a Babylonian festival resembling the Syrian Adonis festival, where dead Thammuz was likely represented in effigy, water poured over him, and he came to life again.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “Like Adonis, he appears to have been a god of vegetation, and his death and resurrection were annually mourned and rejoiced over at a festival in spring.” The passage adds that their legends and rites were so similar that ancients sometimes identified them.
The fourth day was the Festival of Joy, at which Attis’s resurrection was probably celebrated, following closely after the celebration of his death.

The Osiris section opens by saying there are grounds for viewing Osiris as a vegetation personification whose annual death and resurrection were celebrated, while cautioning that his character and rites combine heterogeneous elements.

occurrences.motif_label: Dying and returning god of Osiris
occurrences.basis: The passage narrates Osiris’s murder, dismemberment, ritual mourning and burial, and ceremonies Frazer connects with resurrection.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Osiris travels spreading civilization; on return Set/Typhon and seventy-two others plot against him, seal him in a decorated coffer with molten lead, cast it into the Nile, and it floats to the sea.

Typhon finds Osiris’s body while hunting by full moon, tears it into fourteen pieces, and scatters them; Isis searches the marshes in a papyrus boat and buries each fragment, with explanations for many graves or effigies of Osiris.

Annual rites include five days of mourning, earth-ploughing, search for the mangled body, rejoicing at discovery, burial, and lamentations attributed to Isis and Nephthys; Brugsch says these lamentations "vividly recall the dirges chanted at the Adonis’ rites over the dead god."

The festival ends with the erection of the Tatu/Tat/Ded pillar, a cross-barred column; a Theban tomb shows the king, relations, and a priest raising it. It is later interpreted as Osiris’s backbone and possibly as a stripped tree linked to resurrection.

Plutarch describes priests carrying a sacred ark to the sea, a golden casket inside receiving drinking-water, a shout that Osiris is found, and mould mixed with water to fashion a crescent-shaped image that is dressed and adorned.

occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly groups Osiris, Adonis, and Attis as gods whose violent deaths are mourned and annually commemorated, and then identifies Osiris with vegetation, corn, crop, and harvest.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “In all three cases we see a god whose untimely and violent death is mourned by a loving goddess and annually celebrated by their worshippers.”
Osiris is described as a vegetation deity because he first taught the use of corn, his annual festival began with ploughing, and he introduced vine cultivation.
In a chamber at Philae, Osiris’s dead body is represented with corn stalks springing from it while a priest waters the stalks from a pitcher.
A name for Osiris was crop or harvest, and ancient writers sometimes explained him as a personification of corn.

At Philae a tamarisk is depicted with two men pouring water on it near material about Osiris's grave; Osiris appears as a corpse with ears of corn sprouting, is called 'the one in the tree' and 'the solitary one in the acacia,' and appears as a mummy covered with tree or plants.

occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly states that Dionysus dies violently, is restored or resurrected in variant myths, and is associated with spring and vegetation deities.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Dionysus is introduced as a vegetation god believed to have died violently, been brought to life again, and had his sufferings, death, and resurrection enacted in rites.

Other versions describe Demeter reassembling Dionysus’s limbs and making him young again, Dionysus rising and ascending, Zeus raising him, Zeus swallowing the heart and begetting him afresh by Semele, or Semele conceiving him through a potion made from the heart.
Frazer says the Lydians celebrated the advent of Dionysus in spring and supposed that the god brought the season with him.

Frazer states that vegetation deities who spend part of each year underground naturally become regarded as gods of the lower world or of the dead, and adds that Dionysus and Osiris were both so conceived.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage reports human sacrifice or tearing in Dionysian rites at Chios and Tenedos, a child sacrifice tradition at Potniae, and an Orchomenus custom in which the priest of Dionysus pursued women with a sword and could slay one.

Frazer says the slain bull, goat, and perhaps human victim represented the slain god, while noting that some human-sacrifice traditions may misinterpret animal rituals; at Tenedos a sacrificed calf was shod in buskins and its mother cow tended like a woman in childbed.

occurrences.basis: The Maize-mother is questioned about her strength; if weak, she is burned and replaced by a fresh figure so the maize will not perish. Frazer explicitly treats this as confirmation of killing the god periodically or occasionally.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Acosta describes fruitful maize placed in a Pirua granary, dressed in rich garments, watched, worshipped as mother of the maize, questioned about its strength, burned if weak, and renewed so the seed of maize may not perish.

Frazer compares the Peruvian Mother of the Maize to the harvest Maiden at Balquhidder and explains that she was normally kept for a year, but if her strength failed she was burned and replaced to prevent the maize from languishing.

The passage describes an earlier possible annual succession of corn beings and a later myth of two immortal beings: one disappears into and reappears from the ground, while the other mourns and rejoices over this cycle.

Frazer warns that the same people may have distinct vegetation deities with representatives slain at different seasons; he compares spring tree-spirit and autumn corn-spirit rites and distinguishes Attis as especially a tree-god from Lityerses as harvest-linked.

Attis and Lityerses are described as parallel vegetation spirits or deities whose personal representatives were annually slain; Attis became a state religion, while Lityerses remained a rustic Phrygian harvest-field rite, possibly involving a human victim for the corn-spirit.

occurrences.motif_label: Animal guide carries human to an undersea otherworld
occurrences.basis: The tortoise serves as guide and mount, taking Urashima down through the sea to the Dragon King’s palace.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The tortoise asks whether Urashima has seen Rin Gin, the Palace of the Dragon King of the Sea, says it lies far away at the bottom of the sea, and offers to be his guide.
The tortoise tells Urashima to ride on its back, suddenly becomes large enough to carry a man, leaps into the sea, and carries Urashima through the water without tiring him or wetting his clothes.
A magnificent gate and the sloping roofs of a palace appear; the tortoise identifies them as the gate and palace of Rin Gin, the Sea King’s Palace.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE. / THE SIEGE OF TROY. / RETURN OF THE GREEKS FROM TROY.; lines 10012-10108
occurrences.motif_label: Descent-like entry into enclosed danger
occurrences.basis: Odysseus enters a cave, becomes enclosed by a rock, faces death for his companions, and escapes through a stratagem.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Near the shore the party enters a vast cave containing piles of cheese and pails of milk; companions urge return, but Odysseus waits for the owner.
Polyphemus, son of Poseidon and owner of the cave, returns with wood and sheep and closes the entrance with a rock too heavy for a hundred men.
Odysseus considers killing the sleeping giant but remembers that the cave is blocked by the rock and begins devising an escape plan.
Polyphemus opens the cave and feels among the sheep; Odysseus has tied companions beneath sheep and escapes himself by clinging to the finest ram.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE. / THE SIEGE OF TROY. / RETURN OF THE GREEKS FROM TROY.; lines 10201-10297
occurrences.motif_label: hero consults the dead for knowledge of the future
occurrences.basis: Odysseus travels to the lower-world entrance, performs sacrifice, and receives prophetic instruction from Tiresias among the dead.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odysseus stays with Circe for a year; at his companions' urging he leaves. Circe, unable to detain him after vowing not to use spells, warns him of dangers, commands him to consult Tiresias in Hades, provisions the ship, and bids farewell.
Odysseus follows Circe's directions to the Cimmerian land at the far end of the world beyond Oceanus, landing where Acheron and Cocytus mingle at the entrance to the lower world.

Odysseus digs a trench, sacrifices a black ram and ewe, and shades rise from a gulf eager to drink the blood, which can temporarily restore their mental vigour; he keeps them back with his sword until Tiresias appears.
Tiresias comes with a golden staff, drinks the sacrifice, reveals Odysseus' future fate, and warns him how to avoid dangers on the voyage and after returning to Ithaca.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VENUS. / HELIOS (SOL). / EOS (AURORA). / PHOEBUS-APOLLO.; lines 2441-2527
occurrences.motif_label: hero descends to tomb and wrests beloved from Death
occurrences.basis: Heracles descends into the tomb, restrains Death, and secures Alcestis' restoration to her family.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Heracles arrives at Admetus' palace, learns of Alcestis' death, descends into the tomb, and holds Death until he promises to restore Alcestis to her family.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VENUS. / HELIOS (SOL). / EOS (AURORA). / PHOEBUS-APOLLO.; lines 2598-2664
occurrences.motif_label: descent to the underworld to recover a beloved
occurrences.basis: Orpheus descends into Hades to plead for the restoration of Eurydice.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Orpheus, longing for Eurydice, descends into Hades with Apollo's golden lyre; his music temporarily halts the torments of Sisyphus, Tantalus, Ixion, and the Furies.

Before Aides and Persephone, Orpheus pleads through song; they consent to release Eurydice if he does not look at her until reaching the upper world, but he looks back near the boundary and loses her forever.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: VICTORIA. / HERMES (MERCURY). / MERCURY. / DIONYSUS (BACCHUS).; lines 4043-4125
occurrences.motif_label: Descent to the shades to recover a parent
occurrences.basis: Dionysus descends to the realm of shades for his mother and conducts her to Olympus, where she is admitted among the immortal gods.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Dionysus descends to the realm of shades to find his mother and brings her to Olympus, where as Thyone she joins the immortal gods.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: MERCURY. / DIONYSUS (BACCHUS). / BACCHUS OR LIBER. / AIDES (PLUTO).; lines 4150-4244
occurrences.motif_label: hero's descent or visit to the underworld
occurrences.basis: Odysseus visits the lower world at Circe's command and communes with heroic shades of the Trojan War.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Odysseus visits the lower world at Circe's command and speaks with Trojan War heroes; Achilles says he would rather be the poorest laborer on earth than rule the shades.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: FORTUNA. / ANANKE (NECESSITAS). / MOMUS. / EROS (CUPID, AMOR) AND PSYCHE.; lines 4917-4962
occurrences.motif_label: descent to the underworld to retrieve a charged object
occurrences.basis: Psyche is commanded to descend into the underworld and obtain from Persephone a box of beauty charms, with specific precautions for the journey and return.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Psyche undergoes severe penance; Aphrodite orders her to descend into the underworld and obtain from Persephone a box containing charms of beauty.

A voice warns Psyche of dangers and instructs her to provide Charon's toll and a cake for Cerberus, avoid the banquets of Aides and Persephone, and bring the box unopened to Aphrodite for a safe return.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE. / PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES).; lines 8076-8168
occurrences.motif_label: hero descent to the underworld
occurrences.basis: Heracles enters the lower world through Taenarum, travels among shades, confronts Aides, and returns to the upper world with Cerberus.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After initiation into the Eleusinian Mysteries and priestly instruction, Heracles goes to the opening at Taenarum; Hermes conducts his descent, shades flee, and Hermes stops him from striking Medusa's shadow.

Aides bars Heracles at his palace; Heracles wounds him and receives permission to take Cerberus if unarmed. Heracles finds Cerberus at Acheron, seizes him, endures the dragon-tail bite, and brings him to the upper world near Troezen.
Eurystheus is aghast at Cerberus and returns the hell-hound to Heracles, who restores him to Aides; this ends Heracles' subjection to Eurystheus.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: PELOPS. / HERACLES (HERCULES). / BELLEROPHON. / THESEUS.; lines 8683-8725
occurrences.motif_label: Descent to the underworld to seize a queen
occurrences.basis: Pirithoeus and Theseus seek the realm of Shades intending to carry off Persephone, queen of Hades.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Pirithoeus asks Theseus to help descend to the lower world and carry off Persephone; Theseus recognizes the peril but accompanies him.
