occurrences.motif_label: ritual response to harvest failure
occurrences.basis: The actions are introduced as a response to a series of bad harvests and culminate in a possible divine marriage involving a fruitful earth-wife.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Wotjaks of Russia, distressed by bad harvests, ascribed the calamity to the wrath of Keremet because he was unmarried.
They processed to the sacred grove in gaily-decked wagons, as when fetching home a bride, and feasted there all night.
The next morning they cut a square piece of turf in the grove and took it home.
“Perhaps, as Bechterew thinks, they meant to marry Keremet to the kindly and fruitful mukyl’c in, the earth-wife.”

occurrences.motif_label: ritual restriction of priestly office
occurrences.basis: The Flamen Dialis and Flaminica are presented through detailed lists of forbidden actions, contacts, and required ritual responses.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Flamen Dialis is subject to numerous restrictions involving horses, armies, rings, knots, sacred fire, food, animals, vines, bed feet, hair and nails, dead bodies, holy-day work, uncovered air, and bonds brought into his house.
The Flaminica observes nearly the same rules as the Flamen and additional rules involving stairs, hair combing, shoe leather, thunder, and expiatory sacrifice.

motifs.label: Ritual retrieval and return of the missing soul

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 1 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER I. THE KING OF THE WOOD. / MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE.; lines 3345-3421
occurrences.motif_label: Ritual retrieval and return of the missing soul
occurrences.basis: Rites include praying for release, calling the sick person's name, catching the soul in cloth, gathering souls in a bag, fishing for a soul in a bowl, and restoring a leaf-wrapped soul to the body.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A sorcerer identifies the devil's abode; the patient's friends bring offerings, pray for the soul's release, release a hen as ransom, return with some items, and announce that the soul is released.
A friend deposits offerings, calls the sick person's name three times, asks the soul to come, catches it with a cloth, returns without turning or speaking, and lays the cloth on the patient's throat.
At an Alfoer house-warming in Celebes, a priest hangs a bag, recites gods through the night, offers egg and rice, and holds the soul-filled bag on each household member's head.
Among the Alfoers, a sick man's soul may be recovered by lowering a bowl by a belt out of a window and fishing for the soul until it is caught and hauled up.
An Alfoer priest bringing back a sick man's soul caught in a cloth is preceded by a girl holding a palm leaf over him and followed by a man brandishing a sword to deter other souls.
The wizards ask women for mats and promise to heal the chief; they open the leaf, let the soul into him again, and he recovers.

occurrences.motif_label: ritual reversal of social hierarchy
occurrences.basis: At the Sacaea, masters and servants exchange places for five days.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Berosus is cited for the Babylonian Sacaea: a five-day festival of master-servant reversal in which a condemned prisoner wore royal robes, sat on the throne, exercised royal freedoms, and was then stripped, scourged, and crucified.

motifs.label: Ritual safekeeping of the soul outside the body during danger

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2)

occurrences.motif_label: Ritual safekeeping of the soul outside the body during danger
occurrences.basis: Frazer describes family souls collected in a bag during a dangerous house entry and a woman’s soul represented by iron during childbirth, both as protective removals of the soul.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Among the Minahassa of Celebes, when a family moves into a new house, a priest collects the family’s souls in a bag and later restores them because entering a new house is believed to involve supernatural danger.

In Southern Celebes, a messenger fetching a doctor or midwife for childbirth carries a piece of iron; the doctor keeps it until confinement is over. The iron represents the woman’s soul and must be guarded because, if lost, her soul is believed to be lost with it.

motifs.label: ritual silence after expulsion

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2)

occurrences.motif_label: ritual silence after expulsion
occurrences.basis: Bali observes a day of silence and inactivity after devils are driven away; Fiji has four days of quiet after the initial clatter.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Balinese priest curses the fiends at the banquet and drives them from the district; then silence and restrictions on movement, work, cooking, market activity, and rice-field labor are observed, with thorn-and-leaf wreaths hung at entrances.

In parts of Fiji, an annual ceremony with the aspect of devil-expulsion is timed by the balolo sea-slug; an influential man climbs a tree and prays to the sky spirit, then loud drumming and shouting are followed by four days of quiet, feasting, and work prohibitions.

motifs.label: ritual specialist inaugurates harvest

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS; lines 1770-1846
occurrences.motif_label: ritual specialist inaugurates harvest
occurrences.basis: Priests, a Curumbar, an astrologer-selected sheaf-cutter, a Libia, and a king each perform acts that open or authorize the first use of the crop.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Among the Alfoers of Celebes, the priest sows the first rice-seed, plucks the first ripe rice, roasts and grinds it, and gives some to each household.
In Bolang Mongondo, an animal offering precedes harvest; the priest plucks rice, later sacrifices an egg, returns the rice, and each family member eats before harvest is free to begin.
Among the Burghers, the first-sheaf grain is made into cakes and offered as a “first-fruit oblation,” then eaten by the Burgher family with the remainder of a sacrificed animal.

Among the Coorgs, an astrologer chooses the first sheaf-cutter; after bathing and field rites, the household prepares and eats a new-rice cake, drinks milk, honey, and sugar, and the cutter may not be touched while cutting.
At Onitsha, the Libia prepares roasted yam, places it on the lips of the eater, who says, “I thank God for being permitted to eat the new yam.”

Among the Kafirs of Natal and Zululand, new fruits are not eaten until a festival at the king’s kraal; boiled produce, sacrificial flesh, and medicine are placed in each man’s mouth by the king, sanctifying him for the year and permitting crop gathering.

motifs.label: Ritual specialist returns soul to body through head, forehead, mouth, or heart

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 1 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER I. THE KING OF THE WOOD. / MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE.; lines 3423-3497
occurrences.motif_label: Ritual specialist returns soul to body through head, forehead, mouth, or heart
occurrences.basis: The passage describes attempts or rites in which a captured soul is placed over the mouth, on the head, into the head, on the forehead, or made to descend into the heart.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Melanesian woman catches a fluttering thing like a moth, declares that she has caught the soul, and opens her hands above the corpse's mouth, but the corpse does not revive.

Through a hole in the roof, the medicine-man brushes in souls shaped like bits of bone and the like, sorts out souls of the dead by firelight, and places each living person's soul on the head until it descends into the heart.

In Amboina a sorcerer uses a branch to recover a soul detained by demons; in the Babar Islands offerings are set at a great tree, a leaf is plucked, and the soul in the leaf is pressed onto the patient.

Among Dyaks of Sarawak a priest conjures a soul into a cup, where it appears as hair or a miniature human being, and thrusts it into the patient's head; in Nias the soul appears as a firefly caught in a cloth and placed on the forehead.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Social distinctions were suspended or reversed; masters waited upon slaves at banquets provided for them, and slaves wore their masters' garments.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In Borneo and Celebes, rice is sprinkled on a person thought infested by dangerous spirits; a fowl picks it up and thereby removes the clinging spirit or ghost, including from funeral attendees.

On the Maclay Coast, a native companion breaks a branch, whispers to it, spits something on each party member’s back, strikes them with the branch, and buries it in the jungle; the rite is believed to protect the party, and Frazer interprets the branch as carrying away malignant influences.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A trial in an ancient law-court presided over by the King determines who murdered the ox; blame shifts among participants until the axe and knife are found guilty, condemned, and cast into the sea.

occurrences.motif_label: ritual tree as crop-quickening power
occurrences.basis: The Karma tree is ceremonially brought in, honored, given barley sprouts, and interpreted by Frazer as fostering rice growth through a tree-spirit or grove deity power.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Frazer says young Oraon and Munda people cut a young Karma tree or branch at rice-planting time and return with it in triumph, dancing, singing, and beating drums.
The Karma tree is planted in the village dancing-ground, receives a sacrifice, is decorated, and the youth dance arm-in-arm in a circle around it.
The head-man’s daughters cultivate pale barley blades in moist sandy soil mixed with turmeric and place some of the plants reverentially before the Karma tree.
Frazer interprets the barley presentation and respectful treatment of the Karma tree as intended to foster rice growth, and calls the throwing of the tree into water a rain-charm.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In the backwoods of Cambodia are reported two mysterious sovereigns, the King of the Fire and the King of the Water, formerly exchanging presents with the King of Cambodia.
The Kings of Fire and Water reside among the Chréais or Jaray in forest-clad mountains and high plateaux; their functions are purely mystic or spiritual, not political, and they live on offerings.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Pausanias pauses; Aristodemus says Aristophanes was next, but hiccoughs forced him to change turns with Eryximachus the physician reclining below him.
Eryximachus agrees to speak in Aristophanes’ turn and advises holding the breath, gargling with water, tickling the nose, and sneezing to cure the hiccough.

Homer is cited as teaching that Ajax, after distinguishing himself in battle, was rewarded with long chines as an appropriate heroic tribute.
The brave are to be honored with “seats of precedence, and meats and full cups” at sacrifices and similar occasions, along with hymns and other distinctions.

occurrences.motif_label: Sacred or dangerous object protected from ground contact
occurrences.basis: The holy ark, sacred clam shell, standing corn, sacred food, and sacred-well water vessel are each described as not touching the ground.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The holy ark of North American Indians is considered sacred and dangerous to touch; when carried against an enemy it is not placed on the ground but rested on stones or logs.
The Omaha Elk clan's sacred clam shell is kept in a sacred bag never allowed to touch the ground; newly born infants in Loango are strongly taboo and not allowed to touch the earth.

In Laos the chief elephant hunter may not touch the earth with his foot and steps on leaves; in parts of Aberdeenshire the last standing corn is not allowed to touch the ground and is placed on the gueedman's lap.
The passage says sacred food may in certain circumstances not touch the ground, and that in Scotland a vessel carrying water from sacred wells to sick people might not touch the ground.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A man from Kāsi, expelled from home, serves sailors, survives a shipwreck with a plank, reaches the island, sees the sleeping boar while looking for fruit, and quietly takes the gem.
The man rises into the air by the gem’s power, sits in the Udumbara-tree, infers that the boar became a sky-walker through the gem, and decides to kill and eat him before leaving.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses addresses Nausicaa as queen, asks whether she is goddess or mortal, compares her to Diana and to a young palm near Apollo’s altar at Delos, and says he has been tossed on the sea for twenty days from the Ogygian island.
Ulysses asks for pity, directions to the town, and something to wrap himself in; he wishes Nausicaa husband, house, and peaceful unity of man and wife.

occurrences.motif_label: skin of slain divine animal as image or bearer of divine life

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage focuses on the skin applied to the god's image, compares preserved buzzard and goat skins, and proposes that a slain divine animal's skin was kept as a memorial containing part of divine life and could become an image if stuffed or stretched on a frame.

The passage proposes a transition from annually renewed skin-images to permanent images annually clad in fresh skins, comparing this with the change from cutting a new May-tree every year to maintaining a permanent May-pole annually decorated with fresh leaves, flowers, and a young tree.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Zeus is introduced as presiding deity of the universe, ruler of heaven and earth, and father of gods and men.
As god of aerial phenomena, Zeus produces storms, darkness, thunder, lightning, clouds, and refreshing rain.
Zeus' statues show noble majesty, beard and hair, eagle companion, thunderbolts, lightning, and sometimes an oak-leaf wreath.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Indian bear-hunters cut out the bear’s little tongue, keep it for hunting luck, or burn it to determine from the crackling whether the slain bear’s soul is angry.
In folk-tales the hero commonly cuts out and preserves the tongue of a slain wild beast as a token; Frazer suggests tongue cutting may prevent slain animals from telling live animals their fate.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Lityerses, a son of Midas, gives strangers food and drink, compels them to reap, wraps them in a sheaf, beheads them with a sickle, and carries away their bodies wrapped in corn stalks.
Hercules slays Lityerses and throws his body into the river; Frazer infers Hercules probably slew him in the same way Lityerses slew others.
Another version says Lityerses challenges people to reaping matches, thrashes defeated opponents, and is finally slain by a stronger reaper.

In a Sicilian story, a seer foretells that a king's daughter will conceive by the Sun; the king encloses her in a windowless tower, but she makes a hole with a bone and a sunbeam enters and impregnates her.

“she puffed and puffed herself out till she was almost as round as a ball” and then “she burst.”

evidence.quote_or_summary: A lion is asleep at the mouth of his den when a mouse runs over his back, tickles him, wakes him, and causes him to look around for the disturbance.
A fox jokes that he has seen a lion afraid of a mouse; the lion testily denies fear and says the mouse's bad manners are what he cannot stand.

The mouse gnaws the ropes with its teeth and succeeds in setting the lion free.
"even a Mouse can help a Lion."

occurrences.motif_label: Small disorder growing into total civic disorder

evidence.quote_or_summary: A spirit of licence begins in amusement, penetrates manners and customs, moves into contracts, laws, and constitutions, and ends in the overthrow of private and public rights.
Youth should be trained from the first in a stricter system, because lawless amusements make lawless youths who cannot become well-conducted and virtuous citizens.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The flea bites the man repeatedly; the man searches for it, catches it, and holds it between his finger and thumb.
The terrified flea begs to be released and not killed, saying it is too little to do much harm.
"whatever is bad has got to be destroyed, no matter how slight the harm it does."

occurrences.motif_label: small or different animals use distinct abilities to protect the vulnerable
occurrences.basis: The Kingfisher uses water, the Turtle uses mud and diving, and the Lion uses roaring intimidation to protect the young hawks.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Kingfisher goes into the lake near the fire and, whenever a hunter climbs toward the nest, beats the water with his wings and sprinkles water on the fire until it goes out.
The Turtle agrees to help, goes to the island, dives into the water, collects mud, puts out the fire with it, and lies still.
The hunters decide to kill the Turtle, make a net from vines and torn clothing, fail to turn him over, and are pulled into deep water when he dives while they hold the net.
The Lion comes roaring; the hunters hear the roar, fear they will all be killed, and run away.

occurrences.motif_label: Social disorder expressed as litigation and disease

evidence.quote_or_summary: When intemperance and diseases multiply in a state, halls of justice and medicine open; reliance on outside physicians and judges is treated as disgraceful for those claiming liberal education.
A further evil is the man who is a life-long litigant, proud of dishonesty, crooked turns, and evading justice for small gains.
Medicine is criticized when needed because indolent habits make bodies like marshes filled with waters and winds, requiring new names for diseases such as flatulence and catarrh.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The dialogue turns to temperance; the speaker says it has the nature of harmony and symphony and involves ordering or controlling pleasures and desires.
The State is called temperate and self-mastering when rulers and subjects agree about who should rule; the dialogue returns to the idea that temperance is a kind of harmony.

motifs.label: social rank transposed by merit

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1996-2074
occurrences.motif_label: social rank transposed by merit
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly describes a system in which caste or rank can be set aside when personal qualities meet a standard.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "One of the most remarkable conceptions of Plato... is the transposition of ranks."
Plato applies tests to guardians; those below a fixed standard are removed from or not admitted to the governing body.
The system of caste should sometimes be set aside for merit, and Plato proposes this novel idea as a 'monstrous fiction.'
Two principles are stated: rank depends on circumstances before the individual, and rank should be broken through by personal qualities.

The passage says the lover may swear and forswear himself, and the gods forgive this because there is said to be no lover's oath; gods and men allow the lover broad liberty.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says a widespread superstition left traces in tales; in a modern Greek tale, the Fates warn that a princess will become a lizard if sunlight reaches her in her fifteenth year.
A Tyrolese story says a lovely maiden is doomed to be transported into a whale's belly if a sunbeam falls on her.
In a modern Greek tale, the Sun gives a daughter to a childless woman and will reclaim her at age twelve; the mother seals the house, but a sunbeam enters by the keyhole and carries the girl off.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Karen funeral practices include tying children during a passing funeral, using split bamboo and sticks at the grave to show souls how to climb out, avoiding burying souls with bamboos, carrying the bamboos away, and using three branch-hooks while calling the spirit to prevent it from remaining with the dead.

Burmese belief says a baby's 'butterfly' or soul may follow its dead mother; a wise woman uses a mirror, cotton down, cloth, and entreaties to recover it. Similar rites may be used for a dead playmate's surviving companion or for a bereaved spouse.

In Bolang Mongondo sickness is ascribed to ancestral spirits carrying off the patient's soul. Priestesses acting as physicians use a cloth doll on a spear, dance and charms, colored cloths, head-wrapping, pursuit around the house, and restoration of the recaptured soul to a sick boy.
"Much in the same way an Australian medicine-man will sometimes bring the lost soul of a sick man into a puppet and restore it to the patient by pressing the puppet to his breast."

In Uea, the dead are credited with stealing souls of the living; a soul-doctor and a troop go to the graveyard, use flutes and whistling to lure the soul home, lead it back with open palms, and command it to enter the patient's body.

In Madagascar, friends of a sick man go to the family tomb, make a hole, ask the patient's father's soul to give a soul for his son, fold the soul into a bonnet, bring it to the patient, and the patient puts the bonnet on his head.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In Amboina a sorcerer uses a branch to recover a soul detained by demons; in the Babar Islands offerings are set at a great tree, a leaf is plucked, and the soul in the leaf is pressed onto the patient.

In other islands, illness after returning speechless from the forest is attributed to evil spirits in great trees keeping the soul; food offerings are left under a tree and the soul is brought home in wax.

Among Dyaks of Sarawak a priest conjures a soul into a cup, where it appears as hair or a miniature human being, and thrusts it into the patient's head; in Nias the soul appears as a firefly caught in a cloth and placed on the forehead.
In Fiji a chief may send for a scarf to catch a criminal's soul; the threat prompts confession, and if carried out the soul is folded in the scarf and nailed to a chief's canoe, causing death.
Danger Island sorcerers set soul-snares of stout cinet near a sick man's house, with different loop sizes for different souls; if the soul as bird or insect is caught, the man dies.
Among the Sereres, a person seeking revenge gives presents to the Fitaure, who conjures an enemy's soul into a red earthenware jar deposited under a consecrated tree, after which the enemy dies.

Some Congo people are described as believing that enchanters enclose human souls in ivory tusks and sell them to white men, who make them work under the sea; the person whose soul is sold dies in due course.

The wizards ask women for mats and promise to heal the chief; they open the leaf, let the soul into him again, and he recovers.

The German Raging Host is called Herlathing in England, Mesnée d'Hellequin in Northern France, and Cain's Hunt or Herod's Hunt in the Middle Ages, with explanations for these names.
In Central France the Wild Huntsman is called the Great Huntsman of Fontainebleau; his shouts are said to have been heard before Henry IV's murder and before the French Revolution.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The old man reaches a bamboo wood, finds his sparrow waiting, hears her speak, sees that a new tongue has grown, and realizes she is a fairy rather than a common bird.
The sparrow leads the old man to a beautiful house in the bamboo grove, furnished with fine mats, silk and crape cushions, vases, lacquer boxes, and tokonoma alcoves.

occurrences.motif_label: supernatural being expelled from household after opposing religious devotion
occurrences.basis: A turret-dwelling fairy repeatedly tries to prevent support for Gotama and his disciples, then is ordered to leave the house and departs with her children.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The fairy thinks there is no peace while Gotama and disciples come to the house, appears to the chief business manager, and urges him to prevent their visits.
At midnight the fairy appears before the now-poor merchant and advises him to stop going to Gotama, stop allowing disciples into the house, and rebuild his family estate through business.
“my faith is firm and established like the great mountain Sineru.” The merchant rejects the fairy's words and tells her to depart from his house.
The fairy dares not stay, takes her children by the hand, leaves, and goes to salute the guardian god of the city.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Indra selects a fifty-league level site and causes a hall made of seven precious stones, with varied jeweled pillars and capitals, to rise from the ground.
Suruci gives gavapāna alms for seven days to a million million priests; angels and men wait upon them, and the monks seat themselves by supernatural power when the space is insufficient.

After an avoided arrow shot, Kokai stretches forth his wand and a great flood arises, sweeping away Jokwa's army and the two generals.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hako and Eiko tell Empress Jokwa that Kokai has supernatural powers; Jokwa decides to ask Shikuyu, the Fire King, to help and lead her army against Kokai.
Shikuyu lives at the South Pole because he burns everything except ice and snow; he is a thirty-foot giant and master of all fire, just as Kokai is master of water.
Shikuyu returns with Eiko, is asked to become Generalissimo, assures Jokwa he will kill Kokai, leads thirty thousand soldiers, and orders them to burn a certain shrub and bag the ashes.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Aeolus gives Ulysses a prime ox-hide sack holding the roaring winds, tied with silver thread; Jove made Aeolus captain over the winds, and only the West wind is left to blow freely for the voyage.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Greeks are said to have exaggerated Orpheus's gifts and attributed supernatural power to his music, including taming beasts, stopping rivers, and moving mountains.

occurrences.motif_label: suppliant stranger under protection
occurrences.basis: Eumaeus says the stranger has taken refuge and is Telemachus’ suppliant; Telemachus discusses how to provide for him while avoiding danger from the suitors.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telemachus asks where the stranger came from; Eumaeus says the stranger claims to be Cretan, a great traveler, fleeing a Thesprotian ship, and that he has taken refuge at the station as Telemachus’ suppliant.

Telemachus says he cannot bring the stranger into his house because he is young, lacks force against attackers, and fears the insolent suitors will mistreat him; he offers clothing, sandals, a sword, food, and direction instead.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Leiodes catches Ulysses' knees, asks for mercy, says he never wronged the women, tried to stop the others, and was the suitors' sacrificing priest.
Phemius the minstrel, holding his lyre, chooses to grasp Ulysses' knees, lays down the lyre, asks mercy, claims divine inspiration, and says the suitors forced him to sing.
Medon hears Telemachus while crouching under a seat beneath a freshly flayed heifer hide, throws off the hide, goes to Telemachus, and grasps his knees.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ulysses debates whether to clasp Nausicaa’s knees as a suppliant or entreat her from a distance, and chooses the distant appeal.

The farmer kills sheep for food, then goats as the storm continues, and finally oxen when the weather does not improve.

The youngest brother retreats, gathers help from the neighbourhood and from Ainos in the land of the Japanese, kills Tun-uwo-ush and his followers, and recovers the deer and woman.

motifs.label: suspension between heaven and earth to contain power

occurrences.motif_label: suspension between heaven and earth to contain power
occurrences.basis: Girls and divine persons are described as safest and least harmful when kept from both earth and sun/heaven, effectively suspended between the two.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Menstrual seclusion is explained as neutralising dangerous influences; first-menstruation precautions include not touching ground or seeing sun, keeping the girl suspended between heaven and earth for her safety and others’.

The same rules are applied to divine kings and priests; Frazer says puberty uncleanness and holiness are manifestations of the same supernatural energy, and the taboos preserve the divine person and dependents.

motifs.label: Sympathetic gesture or object action produces wind effect

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 1 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: PREFACE. / J. G. FRAZER. / CHAPTER I. THE KING OF THE WOOD. / MACAULAY.; lines 854-921
occurrences.motif_label: Sympathetic gesture or object action produces wind effect
occurrences.basis: Blanket flapping, sweeping a raven over water in the desired direction, hanging a skin for the wind to blow down, and opening knots or containers all imply a ritual action corresponding to the desired wind effect.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Omaha Wind clan flap blankets to start a mosquito-driving breeze.

A Haida practitioner seeking fair wind fasts, shoots and singes a raven, sweeps it over the sea four times, places it at a spruce-tree, props open its beak, and requests wind for a set number of days.
Finnish wizards sell wind to mariners, enclosed in three knots; opening successive knots releases moderate wind, half a gale, and a hurricane.
Hottentots hang a fat skin on a pole, believing that if the wind blows it down, the wind will lose its force and fall.

motifs.label: sympathetic magic by mimicking desired natural effects

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 1 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE. / CHAPTER III. KILLING THE GOD.; lines 6236-6295
occurrences.motif_label: sympathetic magic by mimicking desired natural effects
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly says primitive people were thought to produce desired effects by representing or mimicking them, such as sprinkling water for rain or mimicking crop growth for harvest.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Adonis ceremonies are described as charms for growth and revival of vegetation through sympathetic magic, in which mimicking desired effects helps produce them.
Rapid growth of wheat and barley in the gardens was meant to make corn grow, and throwing gardens and images into water was a charm for fertilising rain.

motifs.label: sympathetic magic by resemblance

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 1 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: PREFACE. / J. G. FRAZER. / CHAPTER I. THE KING OF THE WOOD. / MACAULAY.; lines 517-565
occurrences.motif_label: sympathetic magic by resemblance
occurrences.basis: The passage states that actions or qualities are thought to produce consequences resembling themselves, and illustrates this with charms based on animal traits.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Actions are performed or avoided because they are believed to entail good or bad consequences resembling the act; resemblance of qualities may also be involved.
Some Bechuanas wear a ferret as a charm for tenacity of life; others wear a mutilated but living insect for a similar purpose.
Bechuana warriors wear ox hair and frog skin because the hornless ox is hard to catch and the frog is slippery, making the wearer hard to hold.
Sympathetic magic is described as treating one event as necessarily followed by another without spiritual or personal agency; Frazer likens this to a misapplied conception of physical causation.

motifs.label: Sympathetic magic through dramatic representation

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 1 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: PREFACE. / J. G. FRAZER. / CHAPTER I. THE KING OF THE WOOD. / MACAULAY.; lines 2649-2713
occurrences.motif_label: Sympathetic magic through dramatic representation
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly states that ceremonies dramatically represent a desired event and are believed to effect or contribute to producing it.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says these ceremonies were magical charms, not merely spectacles; dramatic representation of spring awakening or May marriage is believed to quicken vegetation or make powers more productive through sympathetic magic.

motifs.label: sympathetic magic to secure game supply

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS; lines 3117-3198
occurrences.motif_label: sympathetic magic to secure game supply
occurrences.basis: The passage describes Australians, and also North American Indians, using sympathetic magic to secure a plentiful supply of game.

evidence.quote_or_summary: North American Indians are said to combine totem reverence with reverence for subsistence animals; Australians are said to use sympathetic magic rather than conciliation to secure game.

motifs.label: sympathetic omen of flourishing or withering

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS; lines 7311-7386
occurrences.motif_label: sympathetic omen of flourishing or withering
occurrences.basis: The flourishing, withering, loss, or destruction of a linked tree or object is used to infer or produce prosperity, misfortune, sickness, or death.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Maoris bury the navel-string in a sacred place and plant a sapling over it; the tree is a sign of life for the child, with flourishing or withering read as good or bad omen.
In Bali, a coconut palm planted at a child’s birth is believed to grow equally with the child and is called the child’s life-plant.
Dyaks of Borneo plant a palm tree on certain occasions and regard its flourishing or withering as an index of good fortune or misfortune.

Families in Russia, Germany, England, France, and Italy are said to plant a tree at a child’s birth; in Aargau an apple-tree is planted for a boy and a pear-tree for a girl, and the child is thought to flourish or dwindle with the tree.

Thomas Chillingworth, passed through such a tree as an infant, preserves it carefully because the patient’s life is believed to depend on the tree’s life and cutting it down would cause rupture to return and mortification to follow.

In the Banks Islands, some people connect themselves with an object, animal such as a lizard or snake, or stone called tamaniu; the person’s life is bound up with it, and if it dies, breaks, or is lost, the person will die.

occurrences.motif_label: syncretic absorption of deities into a solar god
occurrences.basis: The passage states that Ra attracted and absorbed many minor divinities and that numerous named gods were identified with him as the sun.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ra is described as the most important centre of attraction among deities, with Ammon, Horus forms, Chnum, Atum, and even crocodile-shaped Sobk regarded as one god, the sun.

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome

occurrences.motif_label: syncretic adoption of foreign gods
occurrences.basis: Greek settlers are described as adopting Celtic mythology and appropriating divinities with affinity to their own, shaping Roman religious belief.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Greek settlers in Italy encountered Celtic mythology, adopted it, and selected divinities that had affinity with their own gods.
The resulting Roman belief is described as marked by ancient Greek influence, while Roman mythology is characterized as less fanciful and poetic than Greek mythology.

motifs.label: Syncretic identification of a foreign goddess with a Greek goddess

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: SELENE (LUNA). / ARTEMIS (DIANA). / ARCADIAN ARTEMIS. / EPHESIAN ARTEMIS.; lines 2926-2974
occurrences.motif_label: Syncretic identification of a foreign goddess with a Greek goddess
occurrences.basis: The passage states that Greek colonists found Metra's worship already established and identified her with Artemis through a perceived point of resemblance.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ephesian Artemis is described as an ancient Asiatic divinity of Persian origin called Metra, whose worship Greek colonists found in Asia Minor and identified with Greek Artemis.
Metra is described as a twofold divinity representing all-pervading love and the light of heaven; Greek settlers connected her with Artemis as Selene because of celestial light.

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 1 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER I. THE KING OF THE WOOD. / MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE.; lines 4159-4217
occurrences.motif_label: taboo as insulation of spiritual force
occurrences.basis: Frazer states that taboos function like electrical insulators, preventing spiritual danger from reaching the persons or spreading from them to the outer world.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Frazer says seclusion prevents spiritual danger from reaching or spreading from such persons, and compares taboos to electrical insulators preserving spiritual force from harmful contact with the outer world.

motifs.label: taboo on eating a vital animal part

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 2 of 2) / CONTENTS; lines 2971-3035
occurrences.motif_label: taboo on eating a vital animal part
occurrences.basis: Multiple reports describe a rule of removing, discarding, or avoiding a leg sinew from hunted animals, with danger or misfortune attached to eating it.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A half-breed Choctaw report says Indians had a story somewhat resembling Jacob wrestling with an angel and that full-blooded Indians separated the sinew; accounts differ on whether it was eaten as a rarity or avoided like ancient Jews.

James Adair reports that Indians cut a piece from the lower thigh of deer they kill; another informant says northern Indians throw it away and treat eating it as dangerous pollution causing sickness, misfortunes, and spoiled guns.
Petitot confirms the custom among the Loucheux and Hare-skin Indians, who are forbidden by custom to eat animal leg sinew and explain it with a sacred story.

occurrences.motif_label: taboo on eating new fruits before ritual permission
occurrences.basis: The passage states that eating the new fruits before the festival results in death or execution.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Zulu first-fruits feast: a bull is killed; its gall is drunk by king and people; the king breaks a green calabash to open the new year and allow eating seasonal fruits; premature eating brings death or execution.

occurrences.motif_label: taboo protection of the divine ruler or priest

evidence.quote_or_summary: The same rules are applied to divine kings and priests; Frazer says puberty uncleanness and holiness are manifestations of the same supernatural energy, and the taboos preserve the divine person and dependents.

motifs.label: Taboo restrictions around royal or sacred presence

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 1 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE. / CHAPTER III. KILLING THE GOD. / FOOTNOTES; lines 10630-10782
occurrences.motif_label: Taboo restrictions around royal or sacred presence
occurrences.basis: The Korean royal passage imposes restrictions on visibility and posture, and a nearby note cites a discussion of taboo.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Korean king rarely leaves his palace; when he does, prior notice is given, doors must be shut, householders kneel with broom and dust-pan, and windows are sealed so no one looks down on him.
Footnote 575 refers readers to W. Robertson Smith on the nature of taboo.

motifs.label: Tabooed kin threatened by the slain person's ghost

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 1 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER I. THE KING OF THE WOOD. / MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE.; lines 4345-4378
occurrences.motif_label: Tabooed kin threatened by the slain person's ghost
occurrences.basis: In the Pelew example, the slain man's relations are tabooed and observe restrictions to escape the wrath of his ghost.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In the Pelew Islands, after a head is carried off in a raid, the slain man's relations are tabooed and must observe rules to escape his ghost's wrath.
The tabooed relations are confined in the house, touch no raw flesh, and chew betel over which an exorcist has spoken an incantation.
After this rite, the ghost of the slaughtered man goes to the enemy's country in pursuit of his murderer.
Tabooed persons are described as in a perilous state and needing isolation from spirits; this explains a prohibition on touching raw meat.

motifs.label: tabooed knotted remnant of the harvest

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 1 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE. / CHAPTER III. KILLING THE GOD. / FOOTNOTES; lines 12768-12923
occurrences.motif_label: tabooed knotted remnant of the harvest
occurrences.basis: The Russian unreaped and knotted patch is called the beard of Volos and is described as tabooed, with danger to anyone who meddles with it.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In Russia, an unreaped patch of corn is left and the ears are knotted together; this is called the plaiting of the beard of Volos, is treated as tabooed, and is believed to harm anyone who meddles with it.

motifs.label: Tabooed persons or things isolated from earth and heaven

occurrences.motif_label: Tabooed persons or things isolated from earth and heaven
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly frames many examples as instances where tabooed persons or sacred things are kept from sunlight, fire, earth, or ground contact.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage states that tabooed persons and things may need isolation from earth and heaven, and gives Aino mourners wearing caps so sunlight does not shine on their heads as an example.
During a solemn three-day fast, Indians of Costa Rica avoid salt, speak little, light no fires, remain indoors, and cover themselves from sunlight if outside.

motifs.label: transfer of curse, sin, evil, omen, or disease to a substitute

occurrences.motif_label: transfer of curse, sin, evil, omen, or disease to a substitute
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly describes harmful conditions being moved from an afflicted person, crop, horse, king, deceased person, or patient to another person, animal, plant, object, or place.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Batta ceremony for a childless woman: sacrifice of three grasshoppers and release of a swallow with a prayer that the curse fall on the bird and fly away.
Miaotse ceremony when the eldest son reaches seven: the father makes a straw kite and lets it fly in the desert bearing away evil.
In Morocco, wealthy Moors keep a wild boar in stables so that jinn and evil spirits may enter it instead of the horses.
Dyak wise men are believed to neutralize bad omens by eating a farmer’s produce raw and appropriating the omen harmlessly to themselves.
In Travancore, a holy Brahman embraces a dangerously ill Rajah, undertakes to bear his sins and diseases, and is sent away from the country forever.
Among the Badagas, the sins of a deceased person are laid on a buffalo calf after a confession; the calf is set free and not used for common purposes.

Ancient and Roman examples include transferring scorpion pain to an ass, transferring fever to a neighbour through nail parings and wax, and Greek concern over wax figures at doors, tombstones, or crossroads.
Orkney and Bavarian cures transfer sickness or fever through wash water at a gateway, a written paper placed in another person’s pocket, or an elder twig stuck in the ground.
Warts are transferred by knots in a string placed under a stone; gout is transferred to an oak by placing nail parings and leg hair in a bored hole and sealing it.
A Flemish ague cure ties knots in a willow branch; Sunderland and Northamptonshire/Devonshire cough cures use the patient’s hair, a bush, birds, buttered bread, and a dog.
In Carpathus, a priest ties a red thread round a sick person’s neck; friends later tie it to a tree to transfer sickness to the tree.
The passage introduces the European material as similar attempts to shift disease and sin from oneself to another person, animal, or thing.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Frazer states that the custom of killing the god has been found in multiple social stages and that the people's accumulated misfortunes and sins may be laid upon the dying god, who bears them away.
The passage explains the belief that pains and griefs can be transferred like physical burdens to another being, who suffers them in the sufferer's place.

Trouble may be transferred to an animal or thing; examples include epilepsy transferred to leaves, toothache transferred to a heated spear-thrower, and black stones called karriitch thrown toward enemies to give them toothache.
A Moor transfers headache to a lamb or goat by beating it; a Bechuana king sits on an ox while water is poured over him, and the ox is drowned and believed to have died of the king's disease.
Among the Malagasy, a faditra is selected to carry away evils or diseases; possible forms include ashes, cut money, sheep, and pumpkin, each disposed of in a prescribed way.
A Malagasy man warned of bloody death is instructed to carry blood on his head, mount a bullock, spill the blood on its head, and send it into the wilderness where it may never return.

The Vṛihat-kathā is attributed to Guṇādhya, and the Kathā Sarit Sāgara is described as founded on it, including the Vetāla Pañca Viṃṣati and part of the Pañca Tantra, with edition and authorship details.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Pancha Tantra is described as the oldest extant collection, glossed as the Five Books; a similar work was translated into Pahlavi, then Syriac as Kalilag and Damnag and Arabic as Kalilah and Dimnah.
The tales are described as originally Buddhist, favoured among Arabs, and carried toward Europe as Arabs came into contact with Europeans and entered southern Europe.

Jewish translators are credited with early European versions: Symeon Seth's Greek translation, a Hebrew translation, John of Capua's Latin translation from Hebrew, and related Spanish and Latin versions.
A second Latin version is titled 'Aesop the Old'; Baldo is said to have ascribed new stories to the traditional ancient teller of similar stories.

Planudes, a learned monk of Constantinople, is said to have written a work called a collection of Aesop's Fables in the first half of the fourteenth century; later Aesop's Fables derive especially from Planudes.

The passage quotes Benfey’s conclusion that the Pancha Tantra was originally a Buddhist book, supported by the number of its fables and tales traceable in Buddhist writings and by the relation between their forms.

The Fox laps up the soup, while the Stork with her long bill cannot partake; the Fox is amused by her distress.
The Stork later invites the Fox and sets before him a pitcher with a long narrow neck, into which she can easily put her bill.
The Stork enjoys her dinner, while the Fox sits hungry and helpless because he cannot reach the vessel’s contents.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Sumedha beholds the fifth Perfection of Exertion, said to have been practised by former sages, resolves to attain it, and is instructed to exert himself like a lion, king of beasts, in order to attain Buddhahood.

Sumedha beholds the sixth Perfection of Longsuffering, said to have been practised by former Buddhas, and is instructed to endure praise and reproach as the earth endures pure and impure things thrown upon it.

Sumedha beholds the seventh Perfection of Truth, said to have been practised by former Buddhas, and is instructed not to utter a conscious lie even if a thunderbolt descends, but to keep to truth as Venus keeps its path.

Sumedha beholds the eighth Perfection of Resolution, said to have been practised by former Buddhas, resolves to attain it, and is instructed to remain immovable like a rocky mountain unshaken by winds.
Sumedha beholds the ninth Perfection of Good-will and is instructed to have one mind toward friends and foes, like water that refreshes good men and bad alike.

occurrences.passage_locator: PREFACE. / J. G. FRAZER. / CHAPTER I. THE KING OF THE WOOD. / MACAULAY.; lines 567-645
occurrences.motif_label: Water applied to ritual object to procure rain
occurrences.basis: Multiple examples dip, pour, drop, or throw water on stones, crystals, holy images, a cross, or a skeleton as a means of obtaining rain.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Rain-making examples include dipping a Samoan stone representing a rain-making god in a stream; spitting quartz toward the sky and soaking it; dropping water on a creek-bed stone; and throwing water on a slab at the Fountain of Baranton.
Apache people throw spring water on a high point of rock; at Snowdon's Black Lake, wetting the farthest stepping stone called the Red Altar is said likely to bring rain before night.

Frazer connects stone-wetting rites with dipping a cross at Baranton, dipping a holy image in Mingrelia, and taking the image of St. Peter to a river in Navarre, where some pray and others threaten to duck it.
In New Caledonia, rain-makers blacken themselves, bring bones to a cave, hang the skeleton over taro leaves, and pour water over it; they suppose the departed soul makes rain from the water.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE BOLD BEGGAR / THE JACKAL WOULD A-WOOING GO / THE LION AND THE BOAR / THE GOBLIN CITY; lines 2358-2435
occurrences.motif_label: water as boundary against hostile beings
occurrences.basis: The captain reflects that escape by ship would work because goblins hate water, but the ship is gone.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The captain fears they cannot fight goblins; he thinks they could escape by ship because goblins hate water, but the ship is gone.

motifs.label: water as intended death-place and hiding-place

occurrences.passage_locator: THE NORTH WIND AND THE SUN / THE MISTRESS AND HER SERVANTS / THE GOODS AND THE ILLS / THE HARES AND THE FROGS; lines 1323-1339
occurrences.motif_label: water as intended death-place and hiding-place
occurrences.basis: The hares approach the pool intending to drown, while the frogs leap into the same water to hide.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The hares decide to end their lives and run together toward a neighboring pool intending to drown themselves.
Frogs on the bank hear the hares running and leap together into the water, hiding in the depths.

motifs.label: Water as survival in a barren crossing

occurrences.source_title: Buddhist birth stories; or, Jataka tales, Volume 1
occurrences.passage_locator: THE DISTANT EPOCH. / GLORY BE TO THE BLESSED, THE HOLY, THE ALL-WISE ONE. / BOOK I. / END OF THE STORY ON HOLDING TO THE TRUTH.; lines 7876-7994
occurrences.motif_label: Water as survival in a barren crossing
occurrences.basis: The caravan’s water supply is essential for desert travel, is discarded too early, and its absence causes despair; the Bodisat then seeks signs of water.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The desert is twenty leagues across, with very fine and burning hot sand; travellers carry supplies, travel at night, rest under shade by day, and choose a land-pilot who guides by the stars like a voyage over the sea.

After nearly completing the crossing, the merchant orders wood and water thrown away; the pilot lies on the foremost cart looking at the stars, falls asleep, and fails to notice that the oxen have turned back.
At dawn the pilot stops the waggons; the men recognize the previous encampment, say their wood and water are gone and they are lost, then lie despondently under their waggons.
The Bodisat thinks that if he loses heart all will perish, walks while the morning is cool, sees Kusa-grass, and reasons that water must be beneath it.

motifs.label: water barrier halts pursuit while magician escapes

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: MY LORD BAG OF RICE / THE TONGUE-CUT SPARROW / THE STORY OF URASHIMA TARO, THE FISHER LAD / THE FARMER AND THE BADGER; lines 1413-1523
occurrences.motif_label: water barrier halts pursuit while magician escapes
occurrences.basis: A flooded river stops Kotei’s army, while Shiyu crosses by magic and takes refuge in a fortress.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Kotei places the shinansha before his army; when Shiyu again creates fog, Kotei uses it to guide the troops, pursues Shiyu to a flooded river, and Shiyu crosses by magic to a fortress.

motifs.label: water nymph at sacred sanctuary

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 1 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: PREFACE. / J. G. FRAZER. / CHAPTER I. THE KING OF THE WOOD. / MACAULAY.; lines 355-440
occurrences.motif_label: water nymph at sacred sanctuary
occurrences.basis: Egeria is described as a nymph of clear water associated with the sacred site’s cascades and lake.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Egeria is one of two lesser divinities sharing Diana’s forest sanctuary; she is the nymph of clear water cascading into the lake, and one story links Manius Egerius with the first consecration of the grove to Diana.

motifs.label: waters divided

occurrences.source_title: Exodus
occurrences.passage_locator: Exodus 14:13-31
occurrences.motif_label: waters_divided
occurrences.basis: Candidate motif from literal passage evidence.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Lift up your rod, and stretch out your hand over the sea and divide it... the waters were a wall to them on their right hand and on their left.

motifs.label: weak avenger against the strong

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE BAT, THE BRAMBLE, AND THE SEAGULL / THE DOG AND THE WOLF / THE WASP AND THE SNAKE / THE EAGLE AND THE BEETLE; lines 4392-4426
occurrences.motif_label: weak avenger against the strong
occurrences.basis: The beetle, described as small and ignored by the eagle, repeatedly avenges the hare by destroying the eagle's eggs; the stated moral generalizes this pattern.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The beetle warns the eagle not to touch the hare under its protection, but the eagle ignores the small beetle, seizes the hare, and eats her.
The beetle remembers the offense, watches the eagle's nest, and whenever the eagle lays an egg, rolls it out and breaks it.
The beetle makes a ball of dirt the size of an eagle's egg and puts it in Jupiter's lap; when Jupiter shakes out his robe, he accidentally shakes out and breaks the eggs too.
"The weak will sometimes find ways to avenge an insult, even upon the strong."

motifs.label: weak creature able to affect strong creature

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: BY G. K. CHESTERTON / AND ILLUSTRATIONS / BY ARTHUR RACKHAM / INTRODUCTION; lines 175-222
occurrences.motif_label: weak creature able to affect strong creature
occurrences.basis: The mouse is described as unable to fight the lion but able to overcome the cords that hold the lion.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage lists fable examples: a stream cannot befoul its fountain; a mouse cannot fight a lion but can overcome lion-binding cords; a fox may gain from a flat dish and lose from a deep one; a crow denied song receives cheese; a goat's insult from a mountain-top is attributed to the mountain.

motifs.label: weak-seeming animal frightens predator by sound

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE FARMER AND THE VIPER / THE TWO FROGS / THE COBBLER TURNED DOCTOR / THE ASS, THE COCK, AND THE LION; lines 3379-3394
occurrences.motif_label: weak-seeming animal frightens predator by sound
occurrences.basis: The Cock’s crow frightens the starving Lion and prevents the attack on the Ass.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Lion, starving for days, comes along and is about to attack the Ass; the Cock rises, flaps his wings, and gives a loud crow.
The passage states that a Lion is frightened by a Cock’s crowing, and this Lion flees when he hears it.

motifs.label: Weak victim's kin gathers helpers against a stronger cunning enemy

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE HAPPY HUNTER AND THE SKILLFUL FISHER / THE STORY OF THE OLD MAN WHO MADE WITHERED TREES TO FLOWER / THE JELLY FISH AND THE MONKEY / THE QUARREL OF THE MONKEY AND THE CRAB; lines 5295-5401
occurrences.motif_label: Weak victim's kin gathers helpers against a stronger cunning enemy
occurrences.basis: The young crab judges the monkey too strong and cunning to kill alone and recruits the mortar, bee, and chestnut as allies.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The young crab first wants to attack the monkey, then decides this is useless because the monkey is old, cunning, and difficult to overcome alone; he decides to meet cunning with cunning and seek friends' help.
The young crab tells the mortar what happened and asks for help. The mortar agrees, warns him to be careful, and summons the bee and chestnut, who also agree to help avenge the old crab.

motifs.label: wealth contest between rulers

occurrences.source_title: The Ancient Irish Epic Tale Tain Bo Cualnge
occurrences.passage_locator: Pillow-talk, wealth comparison, Brown Bull embassy, and Medb's resolve
occurrences.motif_label: wealth_contest_between_rulers
occurrences.basis: Medb and Ailill test their standing through lineage claims, marriage terms, and a formal comparison of possessions.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Medb rejects Ailill's opening claim, recounts her royal descent, wealth, following, and marriage terms, and insists on her own superiority in largess and power.
Yet so it is... my fortune is greater than thine.
The possessions are found equal until Finnbennach, "deeming it no honour" to stay with a woman, is found among Ailill's cattle and Medb lacks his equal.

motifs.label: wealth displaces virtue in political decline

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK V. / BOOK VI. / BOOK VII. / BOOK VIII.; lines 20629-20813
occurrences.motif_label: wealth displaces virtue in political decline
occurrences.basis: The passage presents the accumulation and honouring of wealth as causing citizens to neglect virtue and transforming the constitution into oligarchy.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says the accumulation of gold in private treasuries ruins timocracy and leads to illegal modes of expenditure.
One person seeing another grow rich seeks to rival him, and the citizens become lovers of money.
“when riches and virtue are placed together in the scales of the balance, the one always rises as the other falls.”
The oligarchs make a law fixing a sum of money as the qualification of citizenship, excluding those below it from government, and may effect the change by arms or intimidation.

motifs.label: wealth displacing virtue and rule passing to the rich

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 4395-4476
occurrences.motif_label: wealth displacing virtue and rule passing to the rich
occurrences.basis: The passage describes the transition to oligarchy as possession of gold and silver grows until riches outweigh virtue and political privileges are confined to the rich.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Oligarchy arises when gold and silver possession grows, illegal spending spreads, riches outweigh virtue, and rule is confined by law to the rich.

motifs.label: wealth gained abroad overshadowed by grief and loss

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK II / BOOK III / TELEMACHUS VISITS NESTOR AT PYLOS. / BOOK IV; lines 1561-1661
occurrences.motif_label: wealth gained abroad overshadowed by grief and loss
occurrences.basis: Menelaus recounts gaining great riches during travel but says his brother's murder, Troy's dead, and Odysseus' unknown fate make the wealth joyless.

evidence.quote_or_summary: While Menelaus was travelling and acquiring riches, his brother was secretly and shockingly murdered through the perfidy of his wicked wife.
Menelaus says he has no pleasure in being lord of wealth and would give much of it for those who died on the plain of Troy to be alive.

evidence.locator: lines 1660-1661 and continuation within supplied passage
evidence.quote_or_summary: Menelaus says he grieves most for Odysseus, whose fate is unknown, and names Odysseus' father, Penelope, and Telemachus as plunged in grief.

motifs.label: wealth gained by extraordinary bodily extension

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales

occurrences.motif_label: wealth gained by extraordinary bodily extension
occurrences.basis: Panaumbe stretches his penis to Matomai, where it is used as a drying pole, then retrieves garments that enrich his house.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Panaumbe stretches his penis to Matomai; the lord of Matomai calls it a pole sent by the gods, clothes and beautiful garments are dried on it, and Panaumbe draws them back to enrich his house.

motifs.label: wealth obtained by damaging a sacred image

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE BEAR AND THE FOX / THE ASS AND THE OLD PEASANT / THE OX AND THE FROG / THE MAN AND THE IMAGE; lines 2498-2508
occurrences.motif_label: wealth obtained by damaging a sacred image
occurrences.basis: The man receives gold only after throwing the wooden image of a god against the wall and splitting it open.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In disgust the man hurls the image against the wall; the blow splits its head and gold coins fall to the floor.
“When I honoured you, you did me no good whatever: but no sooner do I treat you to insults and violence than you make a rich man of me!”

motifs.label: Wealth personified as a morally suspect companion

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE FOX WHO SERVED A LION / THE QUACK DOCTOR / THE LION, THE WOLF, AND THE FOX / HERCULES AND PLUTUS; lines 4924-4936
occurrences.motif_label: Wealth personified as a morally suspect companion
occurrences.basis: Plutus is personified as the god of wealth, and Hercules says he is commonly found with scoundrels.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Plutus is called “the god of wealth”; Hercules looks down, turns away, and pretends not to see him.
Hercules says he dislikes Plutus because Plutus “was to be found in the company of scoundrels.”

motifs.label: weapon returned against its thrower

occurrences.motif_label: weapon returned against its thrower

evidence.quote_or_summary: Geirrod challenges Thor and throws a red-hot wedge; Thor catches it with an iron glove and hurls it back through pillar, giant, wall, and earth.

motifs.label: weapon substitution disables opponent

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE JELLY FISH AND THE MONKEY / THE QUARREL OF THE MONKEY AND THE CRAB / THE WHITE HARE AND THE CROCODILES / THE STORY OF PRINCE YAMATO TAKE; lines 5813-5924
occurrences.motif_label: weapon substitution disables opponent
occurrences.basis: Yamato Take replaces Idzumo Takeru's sword with a jammed wooden sword, leaving the outlaw unable to fight.

evidence.quote_or_summary: On the way back through Idum, Yamato Take meets the outlaw Idzumo Takeru, feigns friendship under an assumed name, and prepares a jammed wooden sword.
Yamato Take invites Idzumo Takeru to swim in the River Hinokawa and secretly changes swords while the outlaw is still swimming.
Idzumo Takeru accepts a sword contest, cannot draw the jammed wooden sword, and Yamato Take kills him with the outlaw's own steel sword.

motifs.label: weather explained as actions of a goddess

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING / CHAPTER II: ODIN / CHAPTER III: FRIGGA; lines 2123-2236
occurrences.motif_label: weather explained as actions of a goddess
occurrences.basis: Snow, rain, and cloud formations are explained as Holda shaking her bed, washing clothes, bleaching linen, or weaving.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In Southern Germany, goddesses such as Holda, Hulda, or Frau Holle are described as having attributes like Frigga’s; Holda gives gifts, presides over weather, is linked with snow, rain, clouds, weaving, spinning, housekeeping, and gives flax to mankind and teaches its use.

motifs.label: wickedness destroys its bearer

occurrences.source_title: Buddhist birth stories; or, Jataka tales, Volume 1
occurrences.passage_locator: INDIAN TALES FROM TIBETAN SOURCES. / THE RELIGIONS OF INDIA. / BY A. BARTH. / FOOTNOTES:; lines 17081-17197
occurrences.motif_label: wickedness destroys its bearer
occurrences.basis: A cited verse says the wicked person makes himself as his enemy might desire, like a creeper dragging down a covered tree.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “He who exceeds in wickedness makes himself such as his enemy might desire, (dragging himself down) as the creeper the tree which it has covered.”

motifs.label: Wild huntress companions and frightened woodland beings

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE NAIADES. / DRYADES, OR TREE NYMPHS. / NYMPHS OF THE VALLEYS AND MOUNTAINS. / NAPAEAE AND OREADES.; lines 5415-5467
occurrences.motif_label: Wild huntress companions and frightened woodland beings
occurrences.basis: Oreades accompany Artemis as huntresses; their hunt causes Napaeae to hide, fawns to seek protection, and Satyrs to flee.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Oreades are mountain nymphs, principal and constant companions of Artemis, tall graceful maidens dressed as huntresses and ardent followers of the chase.
Where the Oreades' wild hunt goes, Napaeae hide behind leaves, fawns kneel beside them for protection, and Satyrs flee.

motifs.label: wild revelry in a god's retinue

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE WINDS. / PAN (FAUNUS). / FAUNUS. / THE SATYRS.; lines 5600-5633
occurrences.motif_label: wild revelry in a god's retinue
occurrences.basis: Satyrs are associated with hunting, wild music, dancing, wine drinking, and the train of Dionysus.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Satyrs live for pleasure, hunting, wild music, dancing, wine drinking, and post-drinking sleep; mortals dread them and woodland nymphs avoid their rough sports.
Satyrs are prominent in Dionysus's train; Silenus is their chief and Dionysus's tutor; older Satyrs are called Silens and are represented as more human in sculpture.

motifs.label: Wind enclosed and released from knots or containers

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 1 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: PREFACE. / J. G. FRAZER. / CHAPTER I. THE KING OF THE WOOD. / MACAULAY.; lines 854-921
occurrences.motif_label: Wind enclosed and released from knots or containers
occurrences.basis: Several examples describe wind contained in knots, bags, leather bags, or bamboo and released or opened to produce winds or storms.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Finnish wizards sell wind to mariners, enclosed in three knots; opening successive knots releases moderate wind, half a gale, and a hurricane.
Similar wind-selling is attributed to wizards and witches in Lappland, Lewis, and the Isle of Man; a Norwegian witch claims to have sunk a ship by opening a bag containing wind.
Ulysses receives winds in a leather bag from Aeolus; Perdoytus keeps winds in a leather bag and pursues, beats, and confines them again when they escape.
The Motumotu think storms are sent by an Oiabu sorcerer who has a bamboo for each wind; Frazer says this point passes from custom into mythology, and notes Shetland women who sell wind.

motifs.label: Wind generated by a giant bird-being

occurrences.source_title: Myths of the Norsemen: From the Eddas and Sagas
occurrences.passage_locator: CONTENTS / LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS / INTRODUCTION / CHAPTER I: THE BEGINNING; lines 594-736
occurrences.motif_label: Wind generated by a giant bird-being
occurrences.basis: Hræ-svelgr, a giant clad in eagle plumes, creates cold winds by raising his arms or wings.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hræ-svelgr, a giant in eagle plumes, sits at the northern edge of heaven; when he raises his arms or wings, cold blasts sweep over earth.

motifs.label: wine as blood of divine enemies

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 1 of 2)

occurrences.motif_label: wine as blood of divine enemies
occurrences.basis: In the Plutarch example, wine is held to be the blood of beings who fought against the gods, and intoxication is explained as being filled with that blood.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Plutarch is cited for Egyptian kings avoiding wine because it was held to be the blood of beings who fought the gods; intoxication was explained as being filled with that blood.

motifs.label: Winged companion sent ahead as advance challenger

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE QUARREL OF THE MONKEY AND THE CRAB / THE WHITE HARE AND THE CROCODILES / THE STORY OF PRINCE YAMATO TAKE / MOMOTARO, OR THE STORY OF THE SON OF A PEACH; lines 6510-6645
occurrences.motif_label: Winged companion sent ahead as advance challenger
occurrences.basis: Momotaro identifies the pheasant’s wings as an advantage and orders it to fly to the castle to engage the demons before the others follow.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The travelers see land with a large castle on a precipitous shore; Momotaro recognizes the devils’ stronghold, thinks about the attack, and orders the pheasant to fly to the castle and engage the demons.

motifs.label: winged maiden as swift supernatural envoy

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: MOMUS. / EROS (CUPID, AMOR) AND PSYCHE. / HYMEN. / IRIS (THE RAINBOW).; lines 4989-5006
occurrences.motif_label: winged maiden as swift supernatural envoy
occurrences.basis: Iris is presented as a beautiful maiden with golden wings and marked swiftness in carrying out divine commands.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Iris is introduced as daughter of Thaumas and Electra, personification of the rainbow, and special attendant and messenger of the queen of heaven.
Iris is represented behind Hera’s chariot, as a slender beautiful maiden in variegated airy robes, bright silver sandals, and golden wings, accompanied by light and spring-flower fragrance.

motifs.label: wish for death reversed by fear of death

occurrences.source_title: Aesop's Fables; a new translation
occurrences.passage_locator: THE FOX AND THE HEDGEHOG / THE CROW AND THE RAVEN / THE WITCH / THE OLD MAN AND DEATH; lines 4996-5007
occurrences.motif_label: wish for death reversed by fear of death
occurrences.basis: The Old Man asks Death to release him from toil but, when Death appears, asks instead for help with his burden.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "he called upon Death to come and release him from his life of toil"
Death stands before the Old Man almost immediately and professes readiness to serve him.
"Good sir, if you'd be so kind, pray help me up with my burden again."

motifs.label: wit overwhelms supernatural force

occurrences.source_title: The Arabian Nights Entertainments
occurrences.passage_locator: The Story of the Fisherman: sealed jar, murderous genius, and return to the vessel
occurrences.motif_label: wit_overwhelms_supernatural_force
occurrences.basis: The fisherman survives by verbal cunning, making the stronger being prove a claim and thereby trapping itself.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The fisherman devises a plot and claims he cannot believe so huge a being ever fit inside the vase.
The genius turns again to smoke and goes back into the vase until a voice calls out from inside.
The fisherman shuts the lead cover on the vase and threatens to cast it into the sea again and warn future fishermen.
Unable to escape because of the enchantment, the genius tries cunning and promises repayment, but the fisherman refuses and introduces another cautionary story.

motifs.label: withdrawal and return of celestial lights

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE STORY OF PRINCE YAMATO TAKE / MOMOTARO, OR THE STORY OF THE SON OF A PEACH / THE OGRE OF RASHOMON / HOW AN OLD MAN LOST HIS WEN; lines 7485-7562
occurrences.motif_label: withdrawal and return of celestial lights
occurrences.basis: The Sun and Moon stop their daily and nightly journeys after the heavenly roads are damaged, then resume giving light after the repairs are confirmed.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Jokwa consults wise men; two say the roads of Heaven were damaged and that the Sun and Moon stayed home because they do not know the roads are repaired.
The ambassadors ask why the Sun and Moon secluded themselves; the Sun and Moon answer that Mount Shu burst forth with fire and damaged the roads of Heaven, preventing their usual journeys.
The Sun and Moon test the roads, find the report true, give light to the earth again, and the people rejoice as peace and prosperity follow in China under Jokwa.

motifs.label: withdrawal to private room creates suspicion

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE FARMER AND THE BADGER / THE ADVENTURES OF KINTARO, THE GOLDEN BOY / THE STORY OF THE MAN WHO DID NOT WISH TO DIE / THE BAMBOO-CUTTER AND THE MOON-CHILD; lines 3389-3500
occurrences.motif_label: withdrawal to private room creates suspicion
occurrences.basis: The girl’s seclusion in her room is used by the stepmother and father as circumstantial support for the accusation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The father knows a popular superstition that one person can cause another’s gradual death by making an image of the hated person and cursing it daily, but he doubts his daughter has such knowledge.

The girl is unhappy because of the stepmother’s mistrust; remembering her dead mother, she goes to her room morning and evening, closes the screens, takes out a mirror, and gazes at it as her mother’s face.
The father enters through the fusama, sees the girl bending over something, and she hides the mirror in her sleeve because she has kept her mother’s last promise secret.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Penelope lies upstairs unable to eat or drink, wonders whether Telemachus will escape, is compared to a trapped lioness surrounded by huntsmen, and falls asleep.

motifs.label: Women-only island confronting arriving male heroes

occurrences.motif_label: Women-only island confronting arriving male heroes
