The Argonauts sent a herald with a staff of peace and friendship; Hypsipyle and her nurse discussed the strangers, and Hypsipyle invited them into the city, where Jason came ashore in a purple mantle from Pallas-Athene.

motifs.label: Women-only land with seasonal husbands

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA. / II.--MORAL TALES. / IV.--MISCELLANEOUS TALES.; lines 1629-1717
occurrences.motif_label: Women-only land with seasonal husbands
occurrences.basis: The chieftainess says the land has no men, keeps the visitors for seasonal husbandhood, and explains practices that maintain a women-only population.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The litter-borne woman says the place is woman-land with no men, where the visitors will be cared for until autumn, become husbands in winter, and be sent home in spring.
At leaf-fall, the chieftainess sends the two sons to two vice-chieftainesses while keeping the chief as her husband.
In spring, the chieftainess explains that women there grow teeth in their vaginas when grass sprouts, conceive by the east wind, kill male children when mature, and must now send the men home.

motifs.label: women-only sacred festival

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: ROMAN FESTIVALS. / SATURNALIA. / CEREALIA. / VESTALIA.; lines 6521-6561
occurrences.motif_label: women-only sacred festival
occurrences.basis: Both Cerealia and Vestalia are described as celebrated exclusively by women.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Cerealia honors Ceres and is solemnized exclusively by women in white garments who carry torches to represent Ceres' search for Proserpine.
Vestalia honors Vesta on June 9 and is celebrated exclusively by women walking barefooted in procession to Vesta's temple.

motifs.label: women's annual festival for a guardian goddess

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THIRD DYNASTY--OLYMPIAN DIVINITIES. / JUPITER. / HERA (JUNO). / JUNO.; lines 1413-1428
occurrences.motif_label: women's annual festival for a guardian goddess
occurrences.basis: The Matronalia is described as an annual festival celebrated by married women of Rome in Juno's honor.

evidence.quote_or_summary: On March 1 the annual Matronalia was celebrated in Juno's honor by all the married women of Rome with solemnity.

motifs.label: wood-god with tree branch attribute

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 1 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE. / CHAPTER III. KILLING THE GOD. / FOOTNOTES; lines 9684-9856
occurrences.motif_label: wood-god with tree branch attribute
occurrences.basis: The passage notes representations of Silvanus, described as the Roman wood-god, bearing a pine branch.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “On the representations of Silvanus, the Roman wood-god ... A good representation of Silvanus bearing a pine branch...”

motifs.label: Woodland deity guarding field boundaries

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: PALES. / PICUS. / PICUMNUS AND PILUMNUS. / SILVANUS.; lines 5880-5895
occurrences.motif_label: Woodland deity guarding field boundaries
occurrences.basis: Silvanus presides over plantations and forests and protects field boundaries.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Silvanus is described as a woodland divinity resembling Faunus and Greek Pan, presiding over plantations and forests, and protecting field boundaries.

motifs.label: woodland king marked by tree materials

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 1 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: MACAULAY. / CHAPTER II. THE PERILS OF THE SOUL. / HEINE. / CHAPTER III. KILLING THE GOD.; lines 5356-5395
occurrences.motif_label: woodland king marked by tree materials
occurrences.basis: The northern kings' bark-and-leaf dress, green bough hut, fir-tree court, and comparison with the King of the Wood support a woodland kingship pattern.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says northern maskers resemble the King of the Wood and are kings marked by bark-and-leaf dress, green bough huts, and fir-trees.

motifs.label: world-edge divine absence

occurrences.source_title: The Odyssey
occurrences.passage_locator: PREFACE TO SECOND EDITION / HENRY FESTING JONES. / THE ODYSSEY / BOOK I; lines 390-492
occurrences.motif_label: world-edge divine absence
occurrences.basis: Neptune is absent from the council because he is at the Ethiopians, described as being at the world's end and divided toward West and East.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Neptune has gone to the Ethiopians at the world's end to accept a hecatomb, while the other gods meet at the house of Olympian Jove.

motifs.label: world egg

occurrences.source_title: Kalevala: The Epic Poem of Finland
occurrences.passage_locator: Rune I, Birth of Wainamoinen
occurrences.motif_label: world_egg
occurrences.basis: Cosmic regions and lights arise from the broken pieces of eggs.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A duck finds Ilmatar's raised knee as a nesting place and lays six golden eggs and a seventh egg of iron.
From one half the egg, the lower, / Grows the nether vault of Terra.

motifs.label: world-encircling cosmic water

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: POSEIDON (NEPTUNE). / NEPTUNE. / SEA DIVINITIES. / OCEANUS.; lines 3400-3425
occurrences.motif_label: world-encircling cosmic water
occurrences.basis: Oceanus is described as the ever-flowing stream that encircles the world and gives rise to rivers and streams.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Oceanus personified the ever-flowing stream encircling the world, from which sprang the rivers and streams watering the earth.

motifs.label: World-illuminating sacred body

occurrences.source_title: Buddhist birth stories; or, Jataka tales, Volume 1
occurrences.passage_locator: TABLE VII. / THE BODISATS. / TABLE VIII. / THE DISTANT EPOCH.; lines 4365-4434
occurrences.motif_label: World-illuminating sacred body
occurrences.basis: Mangala Buddha’s bodily light permanently fills ten thousand worlds and replaces the light of sun, moon, and heavenly bodies.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Mangala Buddha’s bodily light permanently fills ten thousand worlds, gives objects a golden appearance, prevents sun and moon from shining by their own light, and removes ordinary distinction between night and day.
The passage states that other Buddhas possess comparable power at will, but Mangala Buddha’s permanent vast radiance results from a prayer made in a former existence.

motifs.label: world remade from a clean surface

occurrences.source_title: The Republic
occurrences.passage_locator: BOOK III. / BOOK IV. / BOOK V. / BOOK VI.; lines 18132-18283
occurrences.motif_label: world remade from a clean surface
occurrences.basis: The legislators erase the existing picture of the state and manners, leave a clean surface, and then inscribe and paint a new constitution.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The legislators take the state and manners of men as from a tablet, “rub out the picture,” leave a clean surface, and inscribe no laws until such a surface is found or made.
They outline and fill in the constitution by looking to absolute justice, beauty, and temperance and to the human copy, making the ways of men as agreeable as possible to the ways of God.

motifs.label: worldly wealth lost to water contrasted with religious generosity

occurrences.source_title: Buddhist birth stories; or, Jataka tales, Volume 1
occurrences.passage_locator: END OF THE STORY OF THE FORD. / END OF THE STORY ON CONSTANCY. / END OF THE STORY OF THE BULL WHO WON THE BET. / END OF THE STORY OF THE WISE BIRD AND THE FOOLS.; lines 13100-13229
occurrences.motif_label: worldly wealth lost to water contrasted with religious generosity
occurrences.basis: Family property buried in a river bank is washed into the sea, while Anātha Piṇḍika continues supporting the Order.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Traders owe him large sums that he does not ask back. Other family property buried in a river bank is washed away by a storm to the sea, with sealed brazen pots sinking to the ocean bottom.
His house keeps rice ready for five hundred members of the Order; it is compared to a public pool at a four-road meeting place, and the Buddha, Eighty Chief Elders, and many other monks come and go.

motifs.label: Worship of life-giving water powers

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: HORAE (SEASONS). / THE NYMPHS. / WATER NYMPHS. / OCEANIDES, NEREIDES, AND NAIADES.; lines 5307-5329
occurrences.motif_label: Worship of life-giving water powers
occurrences.basis: The passage connects water-deity worship with waters described as necessary for life and with local rivers and springs viewed as beneficent powers.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage states that worship of water-deities is widespread and compares streams, springs, and fountains to blood in a body, calling water a life-awakening element necessary for existence.
Among early Greeks, each tribe is said to regard the rivers and springs of its own state as beneficent powers bringing blessing and prosperity.

motifs.label: Wound healed by the one who inflicted it

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE EPIGONI. / ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE. / THE SIEGE OF TROY.; lines 9417-9512
occurrences.motif_label: Wound healed by the one who inflicted it
occurrences.basis: The oracle says only the one who inflicted Telephus' wound can cure it, and Achilles heals him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Telephus' incurable wound is explained by an oracle as curable only by the wounder; he is healed by Achilles and agrees to guide the Greeks to Troy.

motifs.label: wounded animal healed by humans repays aid

occurrences.source_title: Jataka tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE ELEPHANT GIRLY-FACE / THE BANYAN DEER / THE PRINCES AND THE WATER-SPRITE / THE KING'S WHITE ELEPHANT; lines 1341-1390
occurrences.motif_label: wounded animal healed by humans repays aid
occurrences.basis: The carpenters heal the elephant's injured foot, and the elephant responds by deciding to be useful and by helping with labor.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An elephant limps to the carpenters with a swollen sore foot; the men find a great splinter, pull it out, and wash the sore carefully.
“These carpenters have done so much for me, I must be useful to them.”
The elephant pulls up trees, rolls logs to the river, brings tools, and is fed well morning, noon, and night by the carpenters.

motifs.label: Wounded or bleeding tree

occurrences.source_title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (Vol. 1 of 2)
occurrences.passage_locator: PREFACE. / J. G. FRAZER. / CHAPTER I. THE KING OF THE WOOD. / MACAULAY.; lines 1607-1683
occurrences.motif_label: Wounded or bleeding tree
occurrences.basis: Several examples state that trees cry, groan, bleed, or cause sympathetic injury when cut.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage describes beliefs that trees feel injury, cry, groan, require pardon, bleed when cut, and in the Tyrolean larch example wound the woodman’s body in correspondence with the tree’s wound.

The passage says some trees are believed to contain souls of the dead, including transformed fathers or forefathers; an Annamite story has a bleeding tree embodying an empress and three daughters, and the passage notes a comparison with Polydorus in Virgil.

motifs.label: wrongdoer exposed and faithful helper rewarded

occurrences.source_title: Japanese Fairy Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: THE TONGUE-CUT SPARROW / THE STORY OF URASHIMA TARO, THE FISHER LAD / THE FARMER AND THE BADGER / THE ADVENTURES OF KINTARO, THE GOLDEN BOY; lines 2154-2248
occurrences.motif_label: wrongdoer exposed and faithful helper rewarded
occurrences.basis: Katoda’s disclosure exposes the stepmother’s wrongdoing; she flees in disgrace, and Katoda receives high promotion.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Katoda bows before his master and tells the full account of the wrong, explaining how Hase-Hime came to be in the desolate place with two old servants.
Prince Toyonari is astonished and indignant, gives up the hunt, hurries home with Hase-Hime, and the stepmother flees in disgrace when her wickedness is discovered.
Katoda is rewarded with the highest promotion and lives devoted to Hase-Hime, who remembers that she owes him her life.

motifs.label: Wrongdoer involuntarily reveals hidden crime

occurrences.source_title: Aino Folk-Tales
occurrences.passage_locator: AINO FOLK-LORE. / I.--TALES ACCOUNTING FOR THE ORIGIN OF PHENOMENA. / II.--MORAL TALES. / IV.--MISCELLANEOUS TALES.; lines 1907-2004
occurrences.motif_label: Wrongdoer involuntarily reveals hidden crime
occurrences.basis: The mother tells her husband the true story of what she did while believing she is telling an ancient fairy-tale.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The wife, thinking she is telling an old fairy-tale, recounts the actual events; the husband kills her, and the narrative states that this was how the gods chose to punish her.

motifs.label: wronged spouse as sole healer refuses and dies in remorse

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: THE EPIGONI. / ALCMAEON AND THE NECKLACE. / THE HERACLIDAE. / THE SIEGE OF TROY.; lines 9687-9774
occurrences.motif_label: wronged spouse as sole healer refuses and dies in remorse
occurrences.basis: Oenone alone can heal Paris, but she refuses because of her wrongs; after remorse, she arrives too late and dies on his funeral pile.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Philoctetes wounds Paris with a fatal arrow; Paris seeks Oenone on Mount Ida because she alone can cure him, but she refuses, later repents, and dies in the flames on Paris' body.

motifs.label: Youth drawn beneath spring waters by a nymph

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: CADMUS. / PERSEUS. / THE ARGONAUTS. / STORY OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE.; lines 7050-7143
occurrences.motif_label: Youth drawn beneath spring waters by a nymph
occurrences.basis: Hylas reaches a secluded spring and the fountain nymph draws him down under the waters.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In Mysia, Heracles seeks a fir-tree for an oar; Hylas searches for him, reaches a secluded spring, and is drawn beneath the waters by the fountain nymph; Polyphemus hears his cry and joins Heracles in searching.

motifs.label: youth-renewing divine food

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: EROS (CUPID, AMOR) AND PSYCHE. / HYMEN. / IRIS (THE RAINBOW). / HEBE (JUVENTAS).; lines 5009-5031
occurrences.motif_label: youth-renewing divine food
occurrences.basis: Ambrosia is described as the ever youth-renewing food of the immortals, and Hebe is associated with serving it.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Hebe is described as a modest maiden and is depicted pouring nectar from an upraised vessel or bearing a dish of ambrosia, the youth-renewing food of the immortals.

motifs.label: youthful divine Love as creator and artist

occurrences.source_title: Symposium
occurrences.passage_locator: Symposium / SYMPOSIUM / INTRODUCTION.; lines 593-675
occurrences.motif_label: youthful divine Love as creator and artist
occurrences.basis: Agathon's speech treats Love as present, youthful, and as creator and artist moving in a poetic Olympian setting.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Agathon's speech is described as high, poetic, and tragic, moving among the gods of Olympus; he presents Love as youthful rather than ancient, and Socrates gives half-ironical approval.
Agathon's rhetoric is said to elevate the soul to sunlit heights; he distinguishes Love from Love's works, hints that Love is always of beauty, and speaks of Love as creator and artist.

motifs.label: youthful divinity and state vitality

occurrences.source_title: Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome
occurrences.passage_locator: IRIS (THE RAINBOW). / HEBE (JUVENTAS). / JUVENTAS. / GANYMEDES.; lines 5033-5050
occurrences.motif_label: youthful divinity and state vitality
occurrences.basis: Juventas is associated with imperishable vigor and immortal glory of the Roman state.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Juventas is the Roman divinity identified with Hebe; Romans regarded her attributes as applying especially to the imperishable vigor and immortal glory of the state.
